questions.question:
An agent aggregates six MCP servers holding 140 tools between them. Their definitions fill a large share of the context window before any work begins, and teams add new servers every month. On a typical task the agent uses three or four tools. The team already shortened every tool description once.

What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Cache the 140 tool definitions so the same prefix is reused across every request.

options.label: B
options.text: Shorten the descriptions again, to one line each.

options.label: C
options.text: Split the agent into six agents, one for each MCP server it aggregates.

options.label: D
options.text: Let the agent fetch tool definitions only as a task needs them.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Let the agent fetch tool definitions only as a task needs them.

Two facts decide this: the toolset keeps growing, and a typical task touches three or four tools. Loading all 140 pays for 136 the task will not use, every time. Fetching definitions on demand trades one lookup turn for a context window that stays small as the catalogue grows. The extra turn is worth it only at this size, which is exactly the situation described.

INCORRECT: Cache the 140 tool definitions so the same prefix is reused across every request.

Caching keeps the simple upfront approach and does cut the repeated cost, so it is a real option. New servers arrive every month, and each change invalidates the cached definitions. The window also stays full of 140 tools whether they are cached or not, which is what crowds the context. Caching lowers the price of loading everything, it does not stop loading everything.

INCORRECT: Shorten the descriptions again, to one line each.

Shortening worked in the sense that it reduced the text, so doing more of it feels natural. The team already did this once and the definitions still fill a large share of the window. One hundred and forty short definitions are still 140 definitions. When a fix has been applied and the symptom remains, the size of the fix is not the issue.

INCORRECT: Split the agent into six agents, one for each MCP server it aggregates.

Six focused agents would each carry a smaller tool list, which is a sound instinct. Tasks here span the servers, so the work would need routing between agents and no single agent could finish it. That adds coordination to solve a loading problem. Split a system along how work flows, not along how its tools were sourced.

questions.question:
A support team scores a summarization feature against one written criterion: the summary must be of good quality. Two reviewers grade the same 40 outputs and agree on only 19. Each reviewer defends their own scores. Neither can point to a rule that settles a disagreement. The release has slipped twice.

Which change best fixes the evaluation?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a third reviewer and take the majority verdict on every output they dispute.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the sample to 400 outputs so disagreement averages out.

options.label: C
options.text: Rewrite the criterion to name the specific quality and a scoring scale.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish the 19 agreed outputs as examples of good quality for future grading.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Rewrite the criterion to name the specific quality and a scoring scale.

Good quality gives two reviewers nothing to compare an output against. They agree on 19 of 40 because each one applies a private standard. Naming the quality being measured, such as accurate coverage of the source, and pairing it with a scale, turns a score into a repeatable judgment. The disagreement then has a rule that settles it.

INCORRECT: Add a third reviewer and take the majority verdict on every output they dispute.

More voters looks like a way to break a tie, and majority rules is a familiar fix. The two reviewers already disagree on 21 of 40 outputs, and neither can name the rule behind their own score. A third private standard produces a majority without producing a reason. Voting settles who wins an argument, never what the argument was about.

INCORRECT: Raise the sample to 400 outputs so disagreement averages out.

A bigger sample does reduce noise in a measurement, so this feels like sound practice. The disagreement here is not noise. Two reviewers apply different standards to the same output, so ten times the volume produces ten times the disagreement. Scale multiplies whatever a measurement already does, so fix the definition before the sample size.

INCORRECT: Publish the 19 agreed outputs as examples of good quality for future grading.

Worked examples are a familiar way to calibrate graders, and these 19 outputs are the ones both reviewers accepted. The two reviewers may have agreed on those 19 for different private reasons, so the examples still carry no shared rule. A new grader would keep guessing. Examples illustrate a standard, they do not define one.

questions.question:
An insurance claims assistant is evaluated on one metric, answer correctness, and scores 96 percent. After launch, customers complain that answers cite no source and read as curt. Support escalations rise 30 percent. The team reruns the suite this week against fresh production traffic and still gets 96 percent.

What best explains the gap between the score and the complaints?

options.label: A
options.text: The suite scores one dimension, so citation and tone were never measured.

options.label: B
options.text: The rise in escalations comes from growing ticket volume rather than answer quality.

options.label: C
options.text: Customers apply a stricter bar than the team agreed to.

options.label: D
options.text: Correctness scoring counts a partly right answer as correct.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The suite scores one dimension, so citation and tone were never measured.

Answer correctness is the only thing this suite grades. Both complaints, the missing sources and the curt reading, sit outside that one dimension. A score of 96 percent can stay honest while users suffer. Rerunning on fresh traffic changes nothing, because the suite still asks a single question. Most applications need several success criteria scored side by side.

INCORRECT: The rise in escalations comes from growing ticket volume rather than answer quality.

Escalations do climb when ticket volume climbs, so checking the denominator is good discipline. The complaints name specific defects, missing sources, and curt wording, and volume growth produces none of those. Both defects sit outside the one metric being scored. Read what users report, not only how many of them report it.

INCORRECT: Customers apply a stricter bar than the team agreed to.

Expectation gaps are real, and rising escalations often reflect one. The escalations rose 30 percent on concrete, checkable defects: missing sources and curt wording. Those are quality dimensions the team never chose to measure, not a matter of taste. When users report a specific defect, check whether your evaluation covers it before questioning their standard.

INCORRECT: Correctness scoring counts a partly right answer as correct.

Generous scoring is a real way for a metric to overstate quality, and 96 percent is high enough to invite that suspicion. The complaints are not about partly right answers. Customers say the answers cite no source and read as curt, which correctness never scores in any form. A lenient metric and a missing metric fail differently.

questions.question:
A team grades every case in its 900-case evaluation set by hand, because human grading is the most flexible option. One full run takes three weeks, so the suite runs once a quarter and no longer gates releases. Roughly 600 of the cases check one extracted field against a known value.

Which change best restores the suite as a release gate?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduce the suite to the 200 cases the reviewers can finish inside one week.

options.label: B
options.text: Schedule the suite monthly and hold releases until the run finishes.

options.label: C
options.text: Send every case to a model grader and retire the human review step.

options.label: D
options.text: Grade the 600 exact-match cases in code and keep humans for the rest.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Grade the 600 exact-match cases in code and keep humans for the rest.

Six hundred of the 900 cases compare one extracted field against a known value. That is an exact comparison, so code grades it in seconds and never tires. Human judgment then covers only the cases that genuinely need nuance, and a full run fits inside a release cycle. A mixed framework picks the grading method per case.

INCORRECT: Reduce the suite to the 200 cases the reviewers can finish inside one week.

Cutting scope is the fastest way to make a slow process fit a schedule. The 700 cases dropped include the 600 that code could grade for almost nothing. The team would pay in coverage to save effort it never needed to spend. Drop cases when they stop earning their place, not when the grading method is slow.

INCORRECT: Schedule the suite monthly and hold releases until the run finishes.

A tighter schedule looks like the direct answer to a suite that only runs quarterly, and it keeps every case. One run still takes three weeks, so a monthly cycle spends most of each month grading and blocks every release inside it. The cost is unchanged. Running slow work more often never makes the work itself cheaper.

INCORRECT: Send every case to a model grader and retire the human review step.

Automating everything looks like the clean version of the same idea, and model graders are fast and cheap. The 300 remaining cases sit with humans because they need nuanced judgment. A model grader has to be tested for reliability before it carries that load unsupervised. Validate an automated grader on the hard cases before trusting it with them.

questions.question:
A document intake system scores 100 percent on an evaluation set of 40 cases, hand-graded by two engineers over two days. In production, it fails on scanned faxes, bilingual forms, and pages with no signature block, about 4 percent of daily volume. Every case in the set is a clean, single-language, complete form. The intake code has not changed since the suite last passed.

Why does the suite keep passing?

options.label: A
options.text: A perfect score leaves no room to show the variation these inputs cause.

options.label: B
options.text: The set holds only clean typical forms, so failing inputs go untested.

options.label: C
options.text: Two engineers grading by hand cannot stay consistent enough to catch failures this rare.

options.label: D
options.text: A four percent failure rate is too rare to measure.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The set holds only clean typical forms, so failing inputs go untested.

Every one of the 40 cases is a clean, single-language, complete form. The three failing input types never appear in the set, so the system is never asked to handle them. A score of 100 percent measures the inputs present, not the ones missing. An evaluation set has to mirror the real distribution, edge cases included.

INCORRECT: A perfect score leaves no room to show the variation these inputs cause.

A ceiling effect is a real measurement problem, and a flawless score does look suspicious on its own. The score is not compressed here; it is accurate because the system handles all 40 cases correctly. The failing inputs are absent, not mis-scored. A measurement can be perfectly precise about the wrong sample.

INCORRECT: Two engineers grading by hand cannot stay consistent enough to catch failures this rare.

Grader disagreement is a real weakness of hand grading, and two people make a thin panel. Consistency is not the issue here. The graders never saw a fax, a bilingual form, or a missing signature block, and they graded 40 clean forms correctly. Grading quality cannot rescue a set that omits the input entirely.

INCORRECT: A four percent failure rate is too rare to measure.

Rare events do need volume before they show up, and 4 percent of daily volume sounds small. These failures are not rare inside their own category; they are certain, since every scanned fax fails. A set of 40 cases holding none of that type finds nothing. Coverage decides what volume is able to find.

questions.question:
A team A/B tests a triage assistant. The new variant carries a rewritten prompt and a higher model tier. Both variants ran on the same live traffic across the same two weeks. The new variant scores 8 points higher on resolution rate. Finance will fund the prompt work only if the prompt caused the gain.

Which change best produces that answer?

options.label: A
options.text: Roll the new variant out fully and track resolution rate for a month.

options.label: B
options.text: Extend the current test by another two weeks to firm up the eight point gap.

options.label: C
options.text: Compare the new variant against last quarter's traffic on the old prompt and tier.

options.label: D
options.text: Rerun the test with the prompt as the only difference between variants.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Rerun the test with the prompt as the only difference between variants.

The new variant changed the prompt and the model tier together. The eight-point gain could come from either change, or from both, and the test holds no way to separate them. Running the rewritten prompt on the old tier gives finance the number it asked for. One test measures one change.

INCORRECT: Roll the new variant out fully and track resolution rate for a month.

Shipping the winner is tempting when the number looks good, and production data feels more real than a test result. A full rollout removes the control arm, so the eight-point gain still belongs to the prompt and the tier together. Finance gets no attribution at all. Deploying a result is not the same as explaining it.

INCORRECT: Extend the current test by another two weeks to firm up the eight-point gap.

More data does tighten a noisy measurement, and four weeks reads as more rigorous than two. The size of the gap is not in doubt here; its cause is. Four more weeks of a variant that changed two things at once still returns one blended number. Duration sharpens a measurement; it never splits two changes inside it.

INCORRECT: Compare the new variant against last quarter's traffic on the old prompt and tier.

On paper, this isolates the prompt, since the two records differ by prompt alone. Last quarter's traffic is a different mix of inputs, so it swaps one confound for another. The current test at least ran both arms over the same two weeks. A comparison across two time windows measures the windows as much as the change.

On paper, this isolates the prompt, since the two records differ by prompt alone. Last quarter's traffic is a different mix of inputs, so it swaps one confound for another. questions.question:
A market analysis tool asks Claude to produce a risk rating from three uploaded filings. The pipeline has no retrieval step and no external lookup. An analyst reports a rating that read as confident and was wrong. The rating is a judgment the filings never state outright, so the team has no source text to check it against.

Which check best shows whether the model is fabricating?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the same input several times and compare how far the ratings vary.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower the temperature so the model returns a steadier rating.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a retrieval step so each rating can be traced to a source document.

options.label: D
options.text: Have an analyst review every rating before it reaches a client.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Run the same input several times and compare how far the ratings vary.

The rating is a judgment, not a lookup, so no passage exists to check it against. Repeated runs on the same three filings give a check that needs no source. Wide variation on one fixed input means the model is inventing the rating. Steady output does not prove the rating is correct, but drift does show fabrication.

INCORRECT: Lower the temperature so the model returns a steadier rating.

Erratic output usually points at temperature, and a steadier rating reads as a more reliable one. The analyst already saw a rating that was confident and wrong, so steadiness was never missing. Lowering temperature hides the drift the team needs in order to run any check at all. Never suppress the signal a diagnosis depends on.

Citation trails are a strong defence against fabrication, so reaching for retrieval is a fair instinct. The filings never give the rating outright, so no passage exists for a citation to point at. Retrieval would only return the three documents the tool already holds. Use a citation check when the answer is a lookup, not when it is a judgment.

INCORRECT: Have an analyst review every rating before it reaches a client.

It also puts a person on every output the tool produces. Prefer a check that measures the system over one that inspects each result.

questions.question:
A summarization service scores 91 percent on the team's nightly evaluation harness. Complaint data puts real quality near 70 percent. Three prompt rewrites over two weeks move neither number. The harness runs in a development account, where the team set a cheaper model tier last quarter to control evaluation spend. Production runs the tier named in the design.

What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Complaint counts overstate the real error rate in production.

options.label: B
options.text: The nightly schedule means the harness scores a stale build of the service.

options.label: C
options.text: The harness scores a different model tier than production serves.

options.label: D
options.text: Three prompt rewrites are too few to close a gap this wide.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The harness scores a different model tier than production serves.

The harness runs in a development account on a cheaper tier, set last quarter to control evaluation spend. Production runs the tier from the design. The 91 percent therefore describes a system no user ever meets. Three prompt rewrites moved neither number because the prompt was never the difference between the two.

INCORRECT: Complaint counts overstate the real error rate in production.

Complaint data skews toward unhappy users, so treating it with some suspicion is fair practice. A 21-point gap is far too wide for reporting bias alone, and the question names a concrete configuration difference between the two environments. Discounting the complaints leaves that difference unexplained. Doubt a noisy signal only after ruling out a stated cause.

INCORRECT: The nightly schedule means the harness scores a stale build of the service.

A stale build is a familiar cause of a score that disagrees with production, and nightly jobs do lag. Nothing here points at a build gap, and the rewrites did reach the harness, since the team measured them. The named difference is the model tier. Suspect what the evidence names before what it does not.

INCORRECT: Three prompt rewrites are too few to close a gap this wide.

Prompt work often takes many passes, so more attempts feel like the reasonable next step. These rewrites moved neither the harness score nor the complaint figure. A change that moves nothing on either side is evidence against the prompt, not evidence for more prompting. When a fix produces no movement, question the diagnosis instead.

questions.question:
A drafting tool returns a 900-word contract clause. Generation takes 14 seconds, and the user watches a spinner for all of it. Support tickets call the tool slow. The legal team fixed the quality bar, and both a shorter clause and a smaller model fail it.

Which change best addresses the complaint?

options.label: A
options.text: Replace the spinner with a progress bar showing estimated seconds.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the generation twice in parallel and return whichever finishes first.

options.label: C
options.text: Cut the clause to 400 words so generation finishes in half the time.

options.label: D
options.text: Stream the response so text appears while the model is still writing.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Stream the response so text appears while the model is still writing.

Total generation time is 14 seconds, and the fixed quality bar blocks every way of shortening it. Streaming does not make the model faster. It changes when the user starts reading, from 14 seconds down to under one. The tickets describe waiting with nothing on screen, and streaming removes exactly that.

INCORRECT: Replace the spinner with a progress bar showing estimated seconds.

Progress feedback does reduce frustration, and it aims at perception, which is the right general direction. A progress bar still delivers no clause for 14 seconds. The user wanted the document, not a better description of the wait. Describing progress is not the same as delivering output early.

INCORRECT: Run the generation twice in parallel and return whichever finishes first.

Racing two calls is a real latency trick when response times swing widely. Both calls draft the same 900-word clause on the same model, so both take about 14 seconds. The user still waits in front of an empty screen, and the tool now costs twice as much. Parallel work helps only when the runs actually differ.

INCORRECT: Cut the clause to 400 words so generation finishes in half the time.

Shorter output is the most direct way to cut generation time, and it needs no integration work at all. The question states that the legal team fixed the quality bar and that a shorter clause fails it. This trades a stated requirement for speed nobody authorized. A fix that breaks a fixed constraint is not an option.

questions.question:
Finance asks a platform team two questions. Is Claude spend trending up across the whole organization, and which prompts leave the most cache capacity unused. The team's observability stack traces every agent run in full detail and keeps 30 days. Three weeks of reading traces has answered neither question.

Which two changes best answer both?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Extend trace retention from 30 days to a full year so long-term trends appear.

options.label: B
options.text: Pull organization-wide historical spend from the usage and cost API.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a custom span to each agent run recording its token total.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask each team to send finance a monthly spend summary.

options.label: E
options.text: Report token use and cache hits per prompt from that same account-level data.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Pull organization-wide historical spend from the usage and cost API.

The first question covers the whole organization over time. A trace describes one session, which is why three weeks of reading them produced no trend. A dedicated usage and cost source returns historical spend for the account in a single query. It answers an aggregate question that no individual trace can answer.

CORRECT: Tag each agent run with its prompt id and sum cache tokens by tag.

The second question asks which prompts waste cache capacity. That is a comparison across every run of every prompt, not a detail sitting inside one run. The account-level API groups by workspace, model, API key, and tier. It has no prompt dimension, so it cannot rank prompts. Each trace already stores cache read and cache creation tokens for that run. Add a prompt id tag to every run, then sum those cache fields by tag. That turns per-run cache data into a per-prompt ranking.

INCORRECT: Extend trace retention from 30 days to a full year so long-term trends appear.

Longer history sounds like the missing ingredient for a trend question, and retention is cheap to change. Three weeks of reading traces failed on shape, not on age. A year of per-run records is still per-run records, and somebody must still aggregate them by hand. Storing more of the wrong grain does not change the grain.

INCORRECT: Add a custom span to each agent run recording its token total.

Custom instrumentation is a real fix when a standard view lacks a field, so this reads like sound engineering. Each trace already stores a full token count for that run, including cache read and cache creation tokens. Adding another token total repeats data that already exists. The missing piece is a way to group runs by prompt, not one more number inside a single run.

INCORRECT: Ask each team to send finance a monthly spend summary.

Delegating to the teams closest to the spend feels efficient, and it needs no new tooling. Each team would read the same per-run traces the platform team already cannot aggregate, and a hand-written monthly summary answers neither question reliably. The data sits in one place already. Do not ask people to assemble a number a system reports.

questions.question:
A lending assistant screens every draft reply through a safety classifier before sending. The classifier runs as a separate service, and the client waits 2 seconds for it. During a 40-minute outage last week, the service returned only timeouts, and 1,900 replies went out unscreened, including 3 that promised terms the bank does not offer. The code treats a timeout as a pass.

Which change best fixes this?

options.label: A
options.text: Retry the classifier three times before letting the reply through.

options.label: B
options.text: Hold the reply for human review when the classifier cannot return a verdict.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the client timeout from 2 seconds to 30 seconds.

options.label: D
options.text: Page the on-call engineer whenever the classifier stops returning verdicts during normal business hours.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Hold the reply for human review when the classifier cannot return a verdict.

A timeout is not a verdict. The code read 1,900 unscreened replies as safe, and 3 of them carried terms the bank does not offer. A control that cannot reach a decision has to block or hold, so the protection stays in force at the moment it breaks. Holding sends nothing unscreened while the service is down.

INCORRECT: Retry the classifier three times before letting the reply through.

Retries do rescue a service that fails intermittently, and they cost almost nothing to add. The outage ran 40 minutes, so all three retries fall inside it and all three time out. The reply still goes out unscreened at the end. A retry changes how often a check fails, never what happens when it finally does.

INCORRECT: Raise the client timeout from 2 seconds to 30 seconds.

A short timeout can turn a slow service into a failed one, so more patience looks like the cheap fix. The service returned timeouts for 40 minutes straight, so 30 seconds fails exactly as 2 seconds did. It also adds 28 seconds to every reply. Waiting longer for an answer does not decide what to do without one.

INCORRECT: Page the on-call engineer whenever the classifier stops returning verdicts during normal business hours.

An alert does surface an outage fast, and 40 minutes of silence is exactly what it would break. The engineer learns the classifier is down, and the replies keep going out unscreened while that person responds. Nothing in the request path changed. Telling a human a check is broken does not decide what happens to traffic in flight.

questions.question:
A legal research tool cites case numbers that do not exist. Over six weeks, the team rewrites the system prompt eleven times, adds a warning about accuracy, and lowers the temperature. The invention rate falls from 9 percent to 7 percent and stops moving. The pipeline has no lookup against any case database.

Why has the effort stalled?

options.label: A
options.text: The system prompt never told the model that inventing a citation is unacceptable.

options.label: B
options.text: The model cannot check a citation against ground truth on its own.

options.label: C
options.text: Lowering the temperature removed the variation that made errors visible.

options.label: D
options.text: The 7 percent floor reflects a bug in the citation formatter.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The model cannot check a citation against ground truth on its own.

The pipeline has no lookup against any case database. Nothing in it can compare a generated case number against a real one. That gap sits in how the model works, not in how the prompt is written. Eleven rewrites moved the rate two points and then stopped. The fix has to sit outside the model.

INCORRECT: The system prompt never told the model that inventing a citation is unacceptable.

Explicit prohibitions do help with instruction-following problems, so assuming one is missing is natural. The team rewrote the prompt eleven times and added a warning about accuracy, so the instruction exists in several forms already. The rate still floors at 7 percent. An instruction cannot grant an ability the system does not have.

INCORRECT: Lowering the temperature removed the variation that made errors visible.

Lower temperature does hide variation, and this team did lower it, so the sequence looks suspicious. The invention rate fell rather than went quiet, and the wrong citations are still being counted at 7 percent. The errors remain visible. Check whether a number moved or merely stopped being measured before you read it.

INCORRECT: The 7 percent floor reflects a bug in the citation formatter.

A formatting defect is real and fixable, and 7 percent is a suspiciously stable floor. A formatter changes how a citation looks, not whether the case behind it exists. These citations point at cases that were never filed. Ask whether a defect changes presentation or substance before you hand it the blame.

questions.question:
A content pipeline runs each draft past the same model three times and publishes only when all three runs agree it is safe. The risk register records the odds of an unsafe publication as one in a thousand, computed by cubing the single-run miss rate. In testing, one prompt-injection sample slipped past all three runs on the same input.

What should the architect change first?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the vote from three runs to seven so the margin gets wider.

options.label: B
options.text: Record the three runs as one check and re-rate the risk accordingly.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the bar so one unsafe verdict blocks publication.

options.label: D
options.text: Run the three checks at a higher temperature so their answers diverge more.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Record the three runs as one check and re-rate the risk accordingly.

The three runs share one model, one training history, and one set of blind spots. The injection sample slipped past all three on the same input, which is what a shared blind spot produces. Cubing the single-run miss rate assumes the runs fail independently, and they do not. The register should carry the single-run rate.

INCORRECT: Increase the vote from three runs to seven so the margin gets wider.

More votes do raise confidence when the voters are independent, and seven sounds far safer than three. The sample defeated all three runs on the same input, so four more copies of the same model would have joined them. The blind spot is shared. Adding copies of one judge does not add a second opinion.

INCORRECT: Raise the bar so one unsafe verdict blocks publication.

A stricter bar is the usual lever when a check lets something through, and it costs nothing to tighten. The pipeline already publishes only when all three runs agree it is safe, so a single unsafe verdict blocks it today. The rule would not change. Read what a current rule already does before proposing a stricter one.

INCORRECT: Run the three checks at a higher temperature so their answers diverge more.

Forcing divergence looks like a way to buy back the independence this scheme assumed it had. Higher temperature varies the wording, not the model's underlying judgment about this input. All three runs missed the same injection, and noisier sampling would not have caught it. Randomness is not independence.

questions.question:
A marketing agent drafts and sends campaign emails. A reviewer audits a 10 percent sample of sent campaigns each morning. Last Tuesday the agent misread a segment rule and sent a discount to 84,000 customers at a price the company cannot sustain. The audit found it at 9 the next morning. Legal advised honouring every offer already sent.

Why did the control fail to protect the company?

options.label: A
options.text: The audit sample of 10 percent was too small to catch a send this size.

options.label: B
options.text: The review ran after the emails went out, so it could not stop them.

options.label: C
options.text: The reviewer lacked the authority to recall a sent campaign.

options.label: D

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The review ran after the emails went out, so it could not stop them.

The reviewer looked at sent campaigns the next morning, and the discount reached 84,000 inboxes on Tuesday. A check placed after execution can report, never prevent. Legal advised honouring every offer, so the send cannot be undone at all. That is the class of action needing a gate before it runs.

INCORRECT: The audit sample of 10 percent was too small to catch a send this size.

Sample size is the natural suspect when an audit misses something, and 10 percent leaves most sends unseen. The audit did catch this one, the next morning. Authority is a real weak point in review designs, and a reviewer who cannot act is decoration. No authority would have helped here, because a sent email cannot be pulled back from 84,000 inboxes. This names the proximate cause, and clearer instructions would have prevented this particular Tuesday. The question asks why the control failed to protect the company, not why the agent erred. A control exists precisely because the agent will sometimes be wrong. Design a check for the mistakes you cannot predict, not the one you just saw.

questions.question:
An insurer routes every declined claim to a review queue before the decision goes out. One reviewer works the queue. It receives 2,400 items a day, and the reviewer clears all of them, averaging 7 seconds each and overturning 0.2 percent. Last quarter's audit found 14 declines the reviewer approved that plainly contradicted policy.

Which two changes best restore the check?

Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Add a second approval step after the reviewer signs off each decline.

options.label: B
options.text: Cap the daily queue at what a careful read supports.

options.label: C
options.text: Set a throughput target so the reviewer clears the queue faster each day.

options.label: D
options.text: Staff the review function to the volume the pipeline actually produces.

options.label: E
options.text: Replace the 7 second average with a minimum time per item.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Cap the daily queue at what a careful read supports.

Seven seconds is not a read, and 0.2 percent overturned beside 14 plain policy contradictions show what that produces. The reviewer is clearing the queue rather than checking it. Sizing what arrives to what one person can actually read restores the reading. The items above that line need a destination, not a fast approval.

CORRECT: Staff the review function to the volume the pipeline actually produces.

Capping the queue on its own leaves the remaining declines with no reviewer at all. The pipeline produces 2,400 items a day, and that number comes from the business rather than the review team. Matching people to that volume closes the gap from the other side. Together, the two changes size the loop.

INCORRECT: Add a second approval step after the reviewer signs off each decline.

A second pair of eyes is the standard answer to a missed error, and on paper it adds real coverage. The first reviewer spends 7 seconds per item because 2,400 arrive daily. A second reviewer facing the same queue gets the same 7 seconds. Stacking a check on top of an overloaded check copies the overload.

INCORRECT: Set a throughput target so the reviewer clears the queue faster each day.

Targets do focus effort, and the queue is visibly where the trouble sits. The reviewer already clears every one of the 2,400 items each day. Faster is the direction that produced 14 approvals contradicting policy. When a check is failing because it is rushed, a throughput target pushes it further the wrong way.

INCORRECT: Replace the 7-second average with a minimum time per item.

A minimum dwell time does force slower reading, and it targets the exact number in the incident. It sets no rule for items that no longer fit within a day. The queue simply grows unreviewed behind the reviewer. A pace rule without a volume rule moves a backlog; it does not size one.

questions.question:
A defence contractor runs a document assistant for a workload that requires FedRAMP High and DoD Impact Level 5. The team deployed Claude through a supported cloud platform whose authorization stops at FedRAMP High and IL2. The model is identical to the one in the authorized path, and the team's own security testing passed. The auditor rejected the deployment.

What is the reason?

options.label: A
options.text: The model itself carries no Impact Level 5 assessment.

options.label: B
options.text: Authorization attaches to the deployment path, and this one stops at IL2.

options.label: C
options.text: The team's own security testing cannot stand in for a third-party assessment of the platform.

options.label: D
options.text: FedRAMP High and Impact Level 5 never apply to the same workload.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Authorization attaches to the deployment path, and this one stops at IL2.

The workload requires Impact Level 5, and the platform the team chose is authorized to IL2. An identical model reached through a different platform carries a different ceiling, because the authorization covers the deployment path rather than the weights. The team's own passing tests do not raise that ceiling. The workload has to move.

INCORRECT: The model itself carries no Impact Level 5 assessment.

This has the right shape, since the workload names a level the deployment does not meet. The same model does run under Impact Level 5 authorization through the authorized platform. The model is not the thing that was assessed. Ask what an authorization actually covers before deciding what failed to meet it.

INCORRECT: The team's own security testing cannot stand in for a third-party assessment of the platform.

Self-assessment genuinely does not earn a federal authorization, so this rule is real and worth knowing. The platform this team used already holds a third-party authorization, and that authorization simply stops at IL2. The gap is the level, not a missing assessment. A control that exists at the wrong level still fails.

INCORRECT: FedRAMP High and Impact Level 5 never apply to the same workload.

The two frameworks look like competing labels, so reading one as a replacement for the other is easy. The authorized path carries FedRAMP High together with IL4 and IL5, so one workload can require both at once. Nothing here conflicts. Check whether two requirements exclude each other before treating one as a mistake.

questions.question:
A bank's contract with a client states that prompt and response content must never be stored at rest by any processor. The platform team points to the standard behaviour, where inputs and outputs are held for a bounded period and then deleted automatically. Legal reads the clause again and says that does not satisfy it.

What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn off retention in the organization's settings page.

options.label: B
options.text: Encrypt every prompt and response so stored content stays unreadable.

options.label: C
options.text: Request a zero data retention arrangement through the account team.

options.label: D
options.text: Shorten the retention window to the smallest value the platform allows.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Request a zero data retention arrangement through the account team.

The clause forbids storage at rest, and the standard behaviour stores content and then deletes it. Those are two different guarantees, and only one matches the words legal is reading. A zero data retention arrangement never stores the content once the response returns. It is arranged through the account team, so it belongs in the design timeline.

INCORRECT: Turn off retention in the organization's settings page.

Most data controls do live in a settings page, so looking there first is a reasonable habit. This guarantee is not a toggle, it is an arrangement made with the account team. A design that plans for a switch discovers the lead time late. Check whether a requirement is configured or negotiated before you schedule the work.

INCORRECT: Encrypt every prompt and response so stored content stays unreadable.

Encryption is a strong control, and it satisfies many data clauses, so reaching for it is fair. The clause forbids storing the content at rest, not storing it in readable form. Encrypted content at rest is still content at rest. Read what a clause actually prohibits, not what it would prohibit if it were about confidentiality.

INCORRECT: Shorten the retention window to the smallest value the platform allows.

Less time stored does reduce exposure, and it is the closest thing to compliance available without a new agreement. A shorter window still stores the content first and deletes it afterwards. Legal rejected exactly that pattern. Faster deletion is a smaller version of the thing a no-storage clause rules out.

questions.question:
A hiring screener scores resumes and reports the same accuracy for every group the bank tracks. A candidate says two friends with identical experience received different recommendations, and the only difference on paper was the first name. The team wants a test that settles the question.

Which test best answers it?

options.label: A
options.text: Compare accuracy by group again on a larger evaluation set.

options.label: B
options.text: Resubmit the same resume with only the name changed and compare the recommendations.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove names from every resume before the model sees them.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask a panel of reviewers to re-read both resumes and judge which is stronger.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Resubmit the same resume with only the name changed and compare the recommendations.

The complaint names exactly one difference on paper, the first name. Holding every task-relevant detail fixed and swapping only that detail isolates it. If the recommendation moves, the name alone moved it, and that is the bias equal group accuracy cannot see. The two checks measure different things.

INCORRECT: Compare accuracy by group again on a larger evaluation set.

Subgroup accuracy is the standard fairness check, and more data does sharpen it. The screener already reports equal accuracy for every group the bank tracks, so a larger set repeats a check that already passed. It cannot see one input detail moving one outcome. A group average and a paired comparison answer different questions.

INCORRECT: Remove names from every resume before the model sees them.

Stripping the identifier is a real mitigation, and many teams adopt it after exactly this complaint. It changes the system instead of measuring it, so the team still will not know whether the name mattered. Other details correlate with identity too. Measure an effect before removing the input, or you cannot tell what you fixed.

INCORRECT: Ask a panel of reviewers to re-read both resumes and judge which is stronger.

Human judgment is the natural tiebreaker when two candidates look equivalent, and it sounds fair to the people involved. The question is whether the screener's output changes with the name, which people re-reading resumes cannot answer. It tests the panel instead. Point a test at the component whose behaviour is actually in dispute.

questions.question:
An architect gathers requirements for a claims triage tool from the operations lead, who answers every question within the hour across six weeks. The design is signed off inside the team and built. At the first steering review the compliance director, who was never consulted, rejects it because the design routes documents outside a boundary her office owns.

What should the architect have done differently?

options.label: A
options.text: Asked the operations lead to circulate the design across the other departments involved.

options.label: B
options.text: Established who holds approval authority and engaged that person during discovery.

options.label: C
options.text: Run a second discovery round with the operations lead before building.

options.label: D
options.text: Scheduled the first steering review earlier in the build.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Established who holds approval authority and engaged that person during discovery.

Six weeks of fast answers came from the most available contact, not from the person who could reject the design. The compliance director owns the boundary that stopped it, and nobody asked her. Discovery has to find who can say no, then engage that person first. Responsiveness is not authority.

INCORRECT: Asked the operations lead to circulate the design across the other departments involved.

Delegating outreach to the most engaged contact feels efficient, and that person knows the organization. The compliance director owns a boundary the operations lead does not, so she was never his to invite. Forwarding a design is not the same as consulting an approver. Route a design to whoever can reject it, and do it yourself.

INCORRECT: Run a second discovery round with the operations lead before building.

A second pass does catch requirements the first one missed, and more discovery rarely feels wrong. The same lead would answer the same questions, and he never held authority over the compliance boundary. Repetition does not add a participant. Another round with one source cannot surface what a different source knows.

INCORRECT: Scheduled the first steering review earlier in the build.

An earlier checkpoint does surface objections sooner, and this one arrived after the build. It still puts the approver at the end of a process she should have shaped. The design meets her for the first time already drawn. Bring an approver in when requirements form, not when a review happens to fall.

questions.question:
A discovery report for a document intake system lists 40 statements in one flat list. Two of them, that the vendor feed arrives nightly and that all files are text PDFs, were never confirmed with anyone. The team wrote both from a single conversation. The build assumed both. In week nine, the feed turns out to be weekly, and half the files are scans.

Why did nobody check?

options.label: A
options.text: The report recorded assumptions and confirmed facts in the same flat list.

options.label: B
options.text: The report named no owner for each statement, so nobody felt responsible.

options.label: C
options.text: Reviewers were trusted to remember which statements came from a single conversation.

options.label: D
options.text: The vendor changed the feed schedule after discovery closed.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The report recorded assumptions and confirmed facts in the same flat list.

Two statements came from one conversation and were never confirmed with anyone. In a flat list of 40, they look exactly like the 38 that were checked. Nothing told the build team which entries still needed verifying, so both became load-bearing without a second look. An unmarked assumption reads as settled.

INCORRECT: The report named no owner for each statement, so nobody felt responsible.

Unowned items do drift, and naming an owner per line is a real discipline. An owner cannot act on a line that already reads as a settled fact. Both entries looked exactly like the 38 that were checked, so their owner would see nothing to do. Assign responsibility only after the record shows what is still open.

INCORRECT: Reviewers were trusted to remember which statements came from a single conversation.

Small teams do carry this context in their heads, and whoever wrote the line usually knows its source. The build team was never in that conversation, and by week nine the report is all anyone has. Memory fades exactly where a record is supposed to hold. Never let a control depend on someone recalling what the document does not say.

INCORRECT: The vendor changed the feed schedule after discovery closed.

Suppliers do change schedules, and a late change would explain the weekly feed. It would not explain the scanned files, which no schedule change produces. Both statements were written from one conversation and never confirmed with anyone. When one cause explains half the evidence, look for the one that explains all of it.

questions.question:
An architect presents a caching decision to a finance committee using p99 latency, cache hit ratios, and consistency windows. The committee asks no questions and defers the item twice. A week later, the chief financial officer tells the sponsor the team seems unsure. The same slides drew agreement from the engineering review that morning, and the decision itself is sound.

Why did the committee stall?

options.label: A
options.text: The committee lacks the technical background to evaluate an architecture decision.

options.label: B
options.text: The decision was framed in terms the committee does not use to judge.

options.label: C
options.text: The slides packed far more technical detail into the deck than the decision required.

options.label: D
options.text: The committee was expected to ask when something was unclear.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The decision was framed in terms the committee does not use to judge.

The same slides won agreement from engineers that morning, so the material itself is not wrong. A finance committee decides on cost, speed, and risk, and it received p99 latency and consistency windows. With nothing it could weigh, it deferred twice, and the silence read as doubt. Framing changes with the audience.

INCORRECT: The committee lacks the technical background to evaluate an architecture decision.

Audiences do vary in technical depth, and a finance committee is not an engineering one. This committee weighs cost, speed, and risk every week and defers nothing it can price. It was handed hit ratios and consistency windows instead. A listener who cannot judge your framing is not a listener who cannot judge.

INCORRECT: The slides packed far more technical detail into the deck than the decision required.

Dense decks do lose a room, and cutting slides is the usual first instinct. The engineering review took the same material that morning and reached a decision. Removing half the p99 charts still leaves p99 as the unit of argument. Translate the measure before you shorten the deck, because less of the wrong measure is still the wrong measure.

INCORRECT: The committee was expected to ask when something was unclear.

A room that does not follow you usually says so, and inviting questions feels like enough of a safety net. This committee asked nothing and deferred twice, which is what people do when they cannot tell what to ask. The doubt reached the sponsor a week later instead. Never rest a check on an audience volunteering that it is lost.

html.question:
An architect presents a caching decision to a finance committee using p99 latency, cache hit ratios, and consistency windows. The committee asks no questions and defers the item twice. A week later, the chief financial officer tells the sponsor the team seems unsure. The same slides drew agreement from the engineering review that morning, and the decision itself is sound.

Why did the committee stall?
options: The committee lacks the technical background to evaluate an architecture decision.
The decision was framed in terms the committee does not use to judge.
The slides packed far more technical detail into the deck than the decision required.
The committee was expected to ask when something was unclear.
html.explanation:
CORRECT: The decision was framed in terms the committee does not use to judge.

The same slides won agreement from engineers that morning, so the material itself is not wrong. A finance committee decides on cost, speed, and risk, and it received p99 latency and consistency windows. With nothing it could weigh, it deferred twice, and the silence read as doubt. Framing changes with the audience.


INCORRECT: The committee lacks the technical background to evaluate an architecture decision.

Audiences do vary in technical depth, and a finance committee is not an engineering one. This committee weighs cost, speed, and risk every week and defers nothing it can price. It was handed hit ratios and consistency windows instead. A listener who cannot judge your framing is not a listener who cannot judge.

INCORRECT: The slides packed far more technical detail into the deck than the decision required.

Dense decks do lose a room, and cutting slides is the usual first instinct. The engineering review took the same material that morning and reached a decision. Removing half the p99 charts still leaves p99 as the unit of argument. Translate the measure before you shorten the deck, because less of the wrong measure is still the wrong measure.

INCORRECT: The committee was expected to ask when something was unclear.

A room that does not follow you usually says so, and inviting questions feels like enough of a safety net. This committee asked nothing and deferred twice, which is what people do when they cannot tell what to ask. The doubt reached the sponsor a week later instead. Never rest a check on an audience volunteering that it is lost.

questions.question:
An architect chose a single-region deployment to hit a launch date and told the steering group it was right for now. Nine months on, traffic from a second continent triples, and a director reopens the decision from scratch, asking for a full options paper. The original reasoning still holds, and only the traffic changed.

Which change to how the decision was communicated would have avoided this?

options.label: A
options.text: Name the traffic level at which a second region becomes the right call.

options.label: B
options.text: Present the choice as settled so nobody reopens it casually.

options.label: C
options.text: Send the steering group a monthly report on traffic growth by continent.

options.label: D
options.text: Include the full options paper with the original briefing so nothing was left out.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Name the traffic level at which a second region becomes the right call.

The reasoning behind the original choice still holds, and only the traffic moved. A stated threshold would have turned that move into a trigger the group had already agreed to. The director could then check one number instead of demanding a fresh options paper. A trade-off travels with the condition that would change it.

INCORRECT: Present the choice as settled so nobody reopens it casually.

Firmness does stop a decision from being relitigated on a whim, and constant reopening is a real cost. A choice made for a launch date under one traffic pattern is not settled. Calling it settled makes the eventual change look like a reversal. The traffic tripled. Never buy stability by hiding a decision's real conditions.

INCORRECT: Send the steering group a monthly report on traffic growth by continent.

Visibility does help a group notice a change, and this report would show exactly the change that happened. The director already noticed the traffic. What she lacked was an agreed rule for what that number means. A report supplies data, and data does not tell a group when to act on it.

INCORRECT: Include the full options paper with the original briefing so nothing was left out.

Showing the full analysis up front feels like the thorough version of the same fix, and it does answer the request she eventually made. She asked for that paper because the decision looked permanent, not because the original briefing was thin. Volume is not the gap. Completeness then does not replace a stated trigger.

questions.question:
A team building a claims assistant takes feedback from the operations director, who wants faster turnaround, and the finance director, who wants lower cost per case. Over four sprints, the roadmap flips three times, each time toward whoever raised the issue most recently. Both directors now say the team has no direction.

Which change best stops this?

options.label: A
options.text: Agree now who decides when speed and cost conflict.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask both directors to submit their requests in writing each sprint.

options.label: C
options.text: Split each sprint so both directors get equal capacity.

options.label: D
options.text: Have the team rank the two priorities itself using the business case.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Agree now who decides when speed and cost conflict.

Two directors want opposite things and both are legitimate. With no named tie-breaker the roadmap follows whoever spoke last, which is what three flips in four sprints look like. Naming that person before the next conflict gives the team a rule it can apply in the moment. The authority gets agreed once, not per argument.

INCORRECT: Ask both directors to submit their requests in writing each sprint.

Written requests do reduce hallway steering, and a paper trail helps a team defend its choices. This team already knows what each director wants, in detail, across four sprints. Writing it down produces two clear demands that still conflict. Documenting a conflict does not resolve who wins it.

INCORRECT: Split each sprint so both directors get equal capacity.

Splitting capacity looks fair, and it would stop the flipping immediately. Speed and cost per case pull against each other inside the same feature. Half a sprint each buys partial progress on both and a decision on neither. Neither director gets what they asked for. Fairness is not a priority.

INCORRECT: Have the team rank the two priorities itself using the business case.

Someone has to choose, and the team sits closest to the work, so this reads as practical. Ranking one director's priority below another's is a business call the team cannot make stick. Both directors already say the team has no direction. Push a decision to whoever can be overruled, and it will be.

questions.question:
A retrieval service caps every request at 12 documents. The architecture document records the cap as a current setting and nothing else. A new engineer raises it to 60 to improve recall, and the downstream summarizer starts truncating mid-answer. The cap was set deliberately to keep the summarizer inside its context budget.

Which change to the document best prevents a repeat?

options.label: A
options.text: Record the reason behind the cap alongside the setting itself.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the cap out of the document and into a locked configuration file.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a warning banner telling engineers not to change any documented setting.

options.label: D
options.text: List every current setting in a single table at the front of the document.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Record the reason behind the cap alongside the setting itself.

The document showed 12 as a current value with nothing behind it, so the number read as arbitrary. The engineer had no way to see it was protecting the summarizer's context budget. Written beside the setting, that reason turns an odd-looking value into a deliberate one. A maintainer can only respect a trade-off they can see.

INCORRECT: Move the cap out of the document and into a locked configuration file.

Locking a value does stop an accidental change, and this change was accidental. It moves the problem rather than solving it. The next engineer meets a locked number with no explanation and either unlocks it or works around it. The reasoning is still nowhere. Blocking a change is weaker than explaining it.

INCORRECT: Add a warning banner telling engineers not to change any documented setting.

A blanket warning is quick to add, and it aims at exactly the behaviour that caused this incident. Most documented settings are safe to change, so a rule covering all of them gets ignored within a month. It also never says which ones matter. A warning that applies to everything singles out nothing.

INCORRECT: List every current setting in a single table at the front of the document.

A settings table does make values easy to find, and findability is a real documentation virtue. The engineer already found the cap. What was missing was why it sat at 12. A tidier table repeats the same bare number in a better place. Presentation improves access to a record, not its content.

questions.question:
An architect hands a fraud-scoring service to the platform team. The pack states the model tier, a 400-millisecond budget signed off by the sponsor, a retry policy, a note that legal is still reviewing whether scores may be kept past 30 days, and a comparison of two identity-lookup vendors ending in a recommendation the sponsor has not approved.

Which two items must the pack carry forward as open?

Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: The 400 millisecond budget the sponsor has already signed off.

options.label: B
options.text: The retention period for scores held past 30 days.

options.label: C
options.text: The retry policy, which operations will tune once real traffic arrives.

options.label: D
options.text: Which identity-lookup vendor the service will use.

options.label: E
options.text: The model tier, since the platform team may prefer a different one.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The retention period for scores held past 30 days.

Legal is still reviewing this, so no answer exists yet. A pack that lists it beside the settled items invites the platform team to read it as decided. Recorded as open, it tells them a retention rule is owed before anything gets built on top of it. An unresolved item needs its own line.

CORRECT: Which identity-lookup vendor the service will use.

The pack carries a comparison and a recommendation, and the sponsor has approved neither. A recommendation is a proposal, not a decision. The platform team could easily build against the recommended vendor and find the choice reversed later. Carrying it forward as open names the approval still outstanding.

INCORRECT: The 400 millisecond budget the sponsor has already signed off.

The budget does matter to the receiving team, and every handoff should carry it. It carries a sponsor sign-off, which is what makes an item settled rather than open. The pack should hand it over in the decided section instead. Put a live constraint in the record, but not on the list of things still undecided.

INCORRECT: The retry policy, which operations will tune once real traffic arrives.

Retry settings almost always move after launch, so calling one provisional feels honest. The question asks which items are unresolved, and this one is recorded as the policy in use. Later tuning is ordinary operational work on a decision that was made. An open-items list tracks what nobody has decided, not what somebody will adjust.

INCORRECT: The model tier, since the platform team may prefer a different one.

A receiving team often does have its own view, and leaving room for it sounds generous. Nobody on the platform team has raised the tier, and the pack states it as the tier in production today. An unspoken preference is not a pending decision. Never turn a possibility you have imagined into an item someone now owes you.

questions.question:
A platform team denies the WebFetch tool in managed settings so Claude Code cannot reach external sites from developer machines. Bash stays allowed, because engineers need it for builds. A review of shell history finds curl calls posting file contents to an external host on 14 machines. The deny rule is present and correct on all of them.

Which change best closes the gap?

options.label: A
options.text: Add curl and wget to the denied command list.

options.label: B
options.text: Enable sandboxing with a network domain allowlist at the operating system level.

options.label: C
options.text: Deny Bash outright and let engineers run builds outside the tool.

options.label: D
options.text: Rewrite the tool descriptions so the model avoids making network calls in Bash.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Enable sandboxing with a network domain allowlist at the operating system level.

The deny rule was present and correct, and data still left the machines. Denying a tool by name closes that tool's door, and Bash reached the same network through another one. A sandbox governs the capability itself, so every path to the network meets the same allowlist. The control has to sit below the tool names.

INCORRECT: Add curl and wget to the denied command list.

Naming the offending commands does stop these exact 14 cases, and it is the fastest change available. A shell has many ways to reach a network, and the next engineer uses one the list does not name. A deny list can only see names. Blocking each route by name never closes a capability that has more routes.

INCORRECT: Deny Bash outright and let engineers run builds outside the tool.

Removing the tool that carried the traffic does close this route, and least privilege supports the instinct. The question states engineers need Bash for builds, so this pushes their work outside the environment the team is trying to govern. The traffic moves rather than stopping. A control that drives work out of scope has not reduced risk.

INCORRECT: Rewrite the tool descriptions so the model avoids making network calls in Bash.

Descriptions do steer tool choice, and better wording is cheap to try. A description asks the model to behave, while the requirement here is a guarantee about what is possible at all. On the runs where it does not comply, nothing stops it. Wording shapes a preference, it never enforces a boundary.

questions.question:
A team writes a rule in project memory: run the linter before every commit. Over eight weeks 31 of 214 commits arrive unformatted, and the failures cluster on long sessions rather than on any one engineer. The rule is one clear sentence and every engineer knows it.

Which change best makes the rule hold on every commit?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the rule to the top of the project memory file so it reads first.

options.label: B
options.text: Configure a hook that runs the linter at the commit point.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the rule to a Skill so it loads with more context.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask reviewers to reject any unformatted commit during code review.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Configure a hook that runs the linter at the commit point.

The rule is already one clear sentence, and every engineer knows it, so wording is not the gap. A hook is a shell command the tool runs at a fixed point in its lifecycle. The linter then runs whether or not the model decides to invoke it. The 31 unformatted commits stop being possible. Deterministic control replaces compliance.

INCORRECT: Move the rule to the top of the project memory file so it reads first.

Position does affect what an instruction competes with, and the failures do cluster on long sessions. It still leaves the rule as something the model chooses to act on, and 31 commits already show what that choice looks like under load. A better-placed request is still a request. Ordering changes the odds, never the guarantee.

INCORRECT: Add the rule to a Skill so it loads with more context.

Skills do package guidance well, and moving the rule somewhere more structured feels like progress. A Skill still delivers an instruction the model reads and may or may not follow, which is exactly the surface that failed 31 times. The mechanism is unchanged. Moving an instruction between files does not turn it into an action.

INCORRECT: Ask reviewers to reject any unformatted commit during code review.

Review does catch what automation misses, and a firm rejection rule would eventually train the behaviour. It puts a person in the path of a check a machine performs perfectly, on every commit, for free. The unformatted commits still get written first. Never spend human attention on a check with a deterministic version.

questions.question:
A 60-engineer platform group rolls out an AI coding assistant to every step of its delivery workflow at once. Six months later, cycle time is unchanged. A time study finds coding takes 11 percent of a change's elapsed time, while waiting for a test environment takes 46 percent.

Which change best captures a real gain?

options.label: A
options.text: Extend the assistant to the remaining teams in the organization.

options.label: B
options.text: Point the tooling at the test environment wait, the step consuming 46 percent.

options.label: C
options.text: Measure per-engineer assistant usage and coach the lowest adopters.

options.label: D
options.text: Give the assistant a larger model tier so that its coding suggestions arrive faster.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Point the tooling at the test environment wait, the step consuming 46 percent.

Coding is 11 percent of elapsed time, so making it faster can move cycle time by very little. Waiting for a test environment is 46 percent, more than four times as large. Improvement applied to the step that actually consumes the time is where a measurable gain lives. Find the bottleneck, then apply the tooling.

INCORRECT: Extend the assistant to the remaining teams in the organization.

Wider adoption is the usual next step when a rollout shows no gain, and scale often does reveal one. This rollout already covers every step of the workflow, and cycle time did not move. More teams would repeat the same dilution at greater cost. Spreading a tool further does not find the step that was slow.

INCORRECT: Measure per-engineer assistant usage and coach the lowest adopters.

Uneven adoption does dilute a rollout, and usage data is easy to collect. The time study already explains the flat result, because the assisted step was never the slow one. Perfect adoption across 60 engineers still improves 11 percent of the clock. Check where the time goes before deciding people are the reason it stayed.

INCORRECT: Give the assistant a larger model tier so that its coding suggestions arrive faster.

A stronger tier does improve suggestion quality, and faster suggestions feel like a direct gain. The step it accelerates accounts for 11 percent of elapsed time, so even a large improvement there is nearly invisible in cycle time. The 46 percent is untouched. Improving a small step well cannot beat improving the large one.

Improving a small step well cannot beat improving the large one.

questions.question:
A team adopts an AI coding assistant. Pull requests per week rise from 40 to 115, and the team triples its reviewer pool to match. The checklist reviewers use is the one written for hand-written code. Median time from open to merge still goes from 9 hours to 62. Reviewers say the code looks plausible everywhere, and they cannot tell what to focus on.

What best explains the slowdown?

options.label: A
options.text: The assistant produces lower quality code than the engineers wrote before.

options.label: B
options.text: The review step was never redesigned for what the writing step now produces.

options.label: C
options.text: Three times the reviewers is still too few for 115 pull requests.

options.label: D
options.text: Reviewers need training on the assistant itself before they can review what it writes.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The review step was never redesigned for what the writing step now produces.

The team scaled its reviewers with the volume, so throughput is not the gap. The checklist still targets the mistakes hand-written code makes, and reviewers now face code that reads plausibly everywhere. Nothing tells them what the new failure modes look like. Changing how code is written changes what review has to catch.

INCORRECT: The assistant produces lower quality code than the engineers wrote before.

Quality decline is the first suspicion when review slows down, and it would explain longer scrutiny. Reviewers report that the code looks plausible everywhere, which is not what obviously bad code looks like. Their difficulty is telling good from plausible. A slowdown in review can come from harder judgment, not worse input.

INCORRECT: Three times the reviewers is still too few for 115 pull requests.

Volume did nearly triple, so a capacity explanation fits the shape of the numbers. The reviewer pool tripled with it, and the reviewers describe a focus problem rather than a queue. More people reading with the wrong checklist read the wrong things faster. Match a diagnosis to what the people doing the work report.

INCORRECT: Reviewers need training on the assistant itself before they can review what it writes.

Tooling literacy does help reviewers, and unfamiliarity would explain some hesitation. Knowing how the assistant works does not tell a reviewer which checks now matter, which is the checklist's job. The gap sits in the process rather than in the reviewer's knowledge. Train people once the work has been redefined, not instead.

questions.question:
A document classification service pages on-call four to six times a month, across a rotation of eight engineers. Every page ends the same way: the engineer reads dashboards for 20 minutes, then messages the architect who built the service, who names the check to run, a different one each time, within two minutes. Mean time to resolve is 3 hours, and 2 of those are waiting.

Which change best cuts the wait?

options.label: A
options.text: Add the architect to the on-call rotation so she answers faster.

options.label: B
options.text: Write a runbook mapping each symptom to its first diagnostic step.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a dashboard surfacing the four most common failure signals.

options.label: D
options.text: Automate the checks she names so each one runs before a page fires.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Write a runbook mapping each symptom to its first diagnostic step.

The architect names the right check within two minutes, so the knowledge is small and transferable. Two of the three hours go to reaching her. Written as a symptom and a first step, that knowledge sits with the eight engineers already holding the pager. The wait disappears because nobody has to be found.

INCORRECT: Add the architect to the on-call rotation so she answers faster.

Shortening the path to the person with the answer does cut this wait, and she is clearly the fastest route to it. It makes one person permanently load-bearing for every incident, so her holidays and her departure become outages. The knowledge stays in her head. Never fix a single point of failure by making it more available.

INCORRECT: Build a dashboard surfacing the four most common failure signals.

Better signal does shorten diagnosis, and these engineers already spend 20 minutes reading dashboards. They are not short of data; they cannot tell which reading points to which action. A fifth panel joins the four they already scan. Data answers what is happening; a runbook answers what to do next.

INCORRECT: Automate the checks she names so each one runs before a page fires.

Automating a manual check is usually the better fix, and these checks are well understood. She names a different check each time, so the set is open, and the next incident brings a symptom nobody has automated yet. The engineer is stuck again. Automate a known check, and still write down how to choose one.

questions.question:
An insurer approves a nine-month build of a Claude claims triage system directly from a 40-page requirements document. No working version exists. Two months in, the team finds that 30 percent of claims arrive as scanned faxes the design never accounted for. The programme director asks how to prevent this next time.

What should the architect recommend?

options.label: A
options.text: Extend the requirements document with a new section listing every known claim input format.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a scanned-document specialist to the requirements review before sign off.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a working prototype on real claims data before the full build.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the project timeline so late discoveries have room to be absorbed.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Build a working prototype on real claims data before the full build.

Real claims carried a format the 40-page document never mentioned, and the gap surfaced two months into a nine-month commitment. A prototype run against actual claims meets that same data in days. It tests whether the approach survives real input, not whether the input was described well on paper.

INCORRECT: Extend the requirements document with a new section listing every known claim input format.

More thorough requirements are the standard response to a missed requirement. The document already ran to 40 pages and still missed 30 percent of the inputs. The fax channel was exactly the thing nobody knew to write down, so a longer section would not have caught it. Written specifications cannot reveal what the writers never saw.

INCORRECT: Add a scanned-document specialist to the requirements review before sign off.

Expert review catches what generalists miss, and this gap was a document-format gap. The specialist would have found the fax channel and nothing else. The next project will miss a different input, because the method that hid this one stays in place. Fix the process that produced the blind spot, not the single instance it produced.

INCORRECT: Increase the project timeline so late discoveries have room to be absorbed.

Schedule buffer is a real risk control and costs nothing to propose. It does not move the discovery earlier, and the fax channel still surfaces two months into a committed build. By then the design decisions are made, and reversing them is the expensive part. Buy earlier information rather than budgeting for late surprises.
