questions.question:
A bank's design for a Claude document assistant covers every stage: how files arrive, how they are processed, and how summaries reach branch staff. The demo answers correctly. The requirement document also names 6,000 documents a day at peak, customer identity data under the bank's handling policy, and availability through business hours. Security review rejects the design, and the platform team cannot say what happens at peak.

What is the underlying problem?

options.label: A
options.text: The prototype ran on sample files rather than live records.

options.label: B
options.text: The design meets the functional ask but ignores the stated scale, security and availability needs.

options.label: C
options.text: The summary template was never agreed with the branch staff who read it.

options.label: D
options.text: The design review happened too late for the security and platform teams to shape it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The design meets the functional ask but ignores the stated scale, security and availability needs.

The design already covers arrival, processing, and delivery, and the demo answers correctly, so the functional translation is finished. The requirement also names 6,000 documents at peak, identity data under a handling policy, and business-hours availability. None of those three appear anywhere in the design. That absence is what security rejects and what the platform team cannot answer.

INCORRECT: The prototype ran on sample files rather than live records.

Synthetic data does hide real problems, and reviewers often push back on a demo built from it. Here the rejection lands on the design document, not on the demo, and the demo answered correctly. The handling policy is missing from the design itself, whatever data the prototype used. Test data changes what a demo proves, never what a design promises.

INCORRECT: The summary template was never agreed with the branch staff who read it.

Output formats really do stall approvals, and branch staff is named in the scenario, so the option feels grounded. Nobody raised the template, though. The two objections on record are a security rejection and an unanswered peak-load question. Name a cause that explains the objection actually raised, not the gap you have seen most often.

INCORRECT: The design review happened too late for the security and platform teams to shape it.

Late review is a common delivery failure, and the rejection does arrive at an awkward moment, so timing looks like the culprit. Nothing in the question says when the review happened. The design carries no scale, security or availability content that an earlier meeting could have shaped. Moving a conversation earlier does not add content a document never had.

questions.question:
A hospital network runs a Claude drafter for discharge summaries. Clinicians edit about a third of every draft before signing it. Nine months in, the same three error types still appear, and every edit lives only inside the signed document. The architecture diagram ends at stored signed summary. The architect is asked to make the system improve from its own use.

Which two changes best achieve this?

Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Add a dashboard showing how many summaries the system produces each week.

options.label: B
options.text: Record each clinician edit as a structured entry linked to the draft behind it.

options.label: C
options.text: Give clinicians a thumbs-down button that logs a rating and nothing else.

options.label: D
options.text: Review the recorded edits on a fixed schedule and revise prompts and tests from them.

options.label: E
options.text: Have a senior clinician re-read a monthly sample and email the findings to the team.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Record each clinician edit as a structured entry linked to the draft behind it.

The correction the system needs already exists. Clinicians produce it on a third of every draft, and it is buried inside the signed document where nothing downstream can read it. Storing each edit against the draft that caused it turns a private fix into data. That is the capture half of the feedback stage the diagram is missing.

CORRECT: Review the recorded edits on a fixed schedule and revise prompts and tests from them.

Capture on its own changes nothing. A scheduled review that reads the stored edits and turns them into prompt changes and new test cases is the return path. The same three error types have survived nine months because no step ever reads what clinicians keep correcting. This closes the route from output back into the design.

INCORRECT: Add a dashboard showing how many summaries the system produces each week.

Dashboards are the usual answer when a team says it lacks visibility, and volume is the easiest number to publish. The problem here is three recurring error types, and a weekly count describes none of them. The edits still stay inside the documents. A measure that cannot change a decision is reporting, not a feedback loop.

INCORRECT: Give clinicians a thumbs-down button that logs a rating and nothing else.

It is cheap, it is a genuine capture step, and rating widgets are familiar, so this looks like the low-effort version of the right answer. Clinicians already produce a far richer signal by editing the text. A bare rating never says what was wrong, and nothing reads it. Capture the correction, not just the complaint.

INCORRECT: Have a senior clinician re-read a monthly sample and email the findings to the team.

Expert review does surface real problems, and a monthly cadence sounds disciplined. It adds a second human pass over work the first clinician already corrected, and emailed findings leave nothing the system can read later. Build the loop on the signal the work already produces, rather than on extra effort from another person.

questions.question:
A publisher wants staff to ask questions about its 60-page editorial style guide. Each question stands alone; every answer must quote the section it came from, and traffic runs near 300 questions a day. The guide changes twice a year. There is no multi-stage process to run and no state to keep between questions. The architect must choose the architecture for the first release.

Which design fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Run one model call that retrieves the matching sections and answers from them.

options.label: B
options.text: Chain a classifier call, a retrieval call and a drafting call.

options.label: C
options.text: Let an agent search the guide in a loop until it judges its own answer complete.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish a searchable index of the guide and let staff find the section themselves.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Run one model call that retrieves the matching sections and answers from them.

The stated requirement is one lookup and one answer. Questions stand alone; nothing carries between them, and the quoted section comes straight from retrieval. A single call enhanced with retrieval covers all of that. Orchestration earns its cost when a design needs stages, carried state, or model-directed decisions, and this requirement names none of the three.

INCORRECT: Chain a classifier call, a retrieval call, and a drafting call.

Chaining is the familiar shape for document question answering, and a classifier in front feels tidy and controllable. The question says there is no multi-stage process to run. Retrieval already selects the sections, so the classifier produces output that no later step consumes. Add a stage only when a later stage depends on what it produces.

INCORRECT: Let an agent search the guide in a loop until it judges its own answer complete.

An agent copes with questions nobody anticipated, and searching 60 pages is well within reach, so this reads as the flexible choice. Each question here stands alone and resolves in one lookup. Letting the model decide how many searches to run makes cost and latency differ per question for no gain. Hand step count to the model only when step count genuinely varies.

INCORRECT: Publish a searchable index of the guide and let staff find the section themselves.

Search is cheap to build, and a good index does answer plenty of questions, which makes this look like the frugal option. The stated output is an answer that quotes its section, 300 times a day. A search box returns candidates and leaves the reading to the reader. Check whether an option delivers the stated output or only the raw material for it.

questions.question:
An asset manager screens every investment memo for legal risk, credit risk, and reputational risk. Each check has its own criteria and its own prompt, and none of them needs another's output. The team built a classifier that labels each memo with its single largest risk area and sends it down that one path. Reviewers keep finding issues in the two areas the report never mentions.

What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Improve the classifier prompt so it labels the largest risk area more accurately.

options.label: B
options.text: Run all three risk prompts on every memo and combine their outputs.

options.label: C
options.text: Chain the three risk prompts so each one reads the findings of the previous.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask reviewers to send a memo back for a second screening pass whenever they spot another risk area.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Run all three risk prompts on every memo and combine their outputs.

Three checks with separate criteria, none depending on another, is the shape parallel execution fits: several independent readings of the same input, aggregated afterwards. Routing sorts an input into one category, which is exactly why every report carries one risk area. Running the three together and merging them makes the missing sections appear.

INCORRECT: Improve the classifier prompt so it labels the largest risk area more accurately.

The classifier is the newest component, and a mislabelled memo is a real and common failure, so sharpening it feels like the targeted fix. Reviewers are finding issues in the other two areas. Even a perfect label still discards two checks the memo needed. Accuracy inside a mechanism cannot rescue a mechanism that was the wrong choice.

INCORRECT: Chain the three risk prompts so each one reads the findings of the previous.

A chain does get all three checks to run, and later checks seeing earlier findings sounds richer than three isolated passes. The question states that none of the three needs another's output. Sequencing them adds waiting time and lets one check's framing colour the next. Do not create a dependency between steps that are genuinely independent.

INCORRECT: Ask reviewers to send a memo back for a second screening pass whenever they spot another risk area.

Reviewers are already the ones catching the gaps, so routing their judgment back into the process uses knowledge that exists today. It only fires when a human notices, and the missed areas are precisely the ones nobody screened. The second pass then repeats the same single-path design. A fix that depends on someone noticing cannot cover the misses nobody notices.

questions.question:
A logistics firm drafts shipment-exception emails with one prompt. That prompt reads the tracking record, decides which of six exception policies applies, and writes the email in that policy's required tone. The wrong policy is applied in 18 percent of emails, and the team cannot tell whether the choice or the writing went wrong. Each policy carries a code the firm can verify in its own tables.

What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the prompt to a more capable model tier and keep the single call.

options.label: B
options.text: Add six worked examples, one per policy, to the existing prompt.

options.label: C
options.text: Split it into a policy-selection call, a code check, then a drafting call.

options.label: D
options.text: Have an operations agent approve the chosen policy on every email before the firm sends it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Split it into a policy-selection call, a code check, then a drafting call.

The work is three fixed stages, and the firm can verify a policy code against its own tables between two of them. One call runs all three at once, so nothing is checkable partway and the 18 percent cannot be traced. A chained sequence gates the code before any text is written and shows which stage failed.

INCORRECT: Move the prompt to a more capable model tier and keep the single call.

Policy selection is the hard part of this task, and a stronger tier is the fastest lever available. The team's stated problem is that they cannot tell whether the choice or the writing failed. One call still hides that, whatever model runs it. Capability improves the odds; structure gives you a place to check them.

INCORRECT: Add six worked examples, one per policy, to the existing prompt.

Few-shot examples do lift classification accuracy, and six policies map neatly onto six examples, so the fix looks proportionate. The single call still produces the policy choice and the prose together. The verifiable code never meets the firm's own tables. Prompt content cannot create a checkpoint that the structure does not have.

INCORRECT: Have an operations agent approve the chosen policy on every email before the firm sends it.

An approval gate stops wrong policies reaching customers, and 18 percent is far too high to let through. The firm already holds the policy tables, which makes this check mechanical rather than a matter of judgment. A person on every email scales with volume instead of fixing the design. Never spend human attention on a check that code can make.

questions.question:
A consultancy runs a multi-agent research service. Every request passes through the same four agents: market sizing, competitors, regulation, and a synthesis step. Requests vary widely. One client wanted a patent landscape and supplier concentration, which no agent covers, and received three sections it never asked for. Another needed one of the four in real depth.

What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Add patent and supplier agents to the fixed four-agent pipeline.

options.label: B
options.text: Have a coordinating call read each request and assign the subtasks it actually needs.

options.label: C
options.text: Run all agents on every request and drop the sections that come back empty.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask each client to pick the agents they want before the work begins.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have a coordinating call read each request and assign the subtasks it actually needs.

Two requests broke the fixed pipeline in opposite directions. One needed subtasks no agent covers. The other needed a single agent in real depth. Neither set could have been listed before the request arrived. A coordinator that reads the request and decides its subtasks at run time fits the work to the input. The fixed pipeline fits every input to the same four sections.

INCORRECT: Add patent and supplier agents to the fixed four-agent pipeline.

The named gap was patents and suppliers, so adding exactly those two closes the case sitting in front of the team. The second client needed one agent in depth and still receives sections it never asked for. Six fixed agents reproduce the same mismatch at greater cost. Extending a fixed path never covers the request that has not arrived yet.

INCORRECT: Run all agents on every request and drop the sections that come back empty.

Running everything guarantees nothing in the catalogue gets missed, and filtering empty sections afterwards is trivial to implement. The patent and supplier work has no agent behind it, so a full run still returns nothing there. Every request also pays for every agent. Filtering output afterwards does not change what a system was able to produce.

INCORRECT: Ask each client to pick the agents they want before the work begins.

Clients understand their own questions better than any classifier, and self-service selection removes guesswork from the team. The first client asked for work the catalogue does not contain. A menu of the same four agents hands that client the same gap, with an extra step in front of it. Never ask someone to choose from a list that lacks what they need.

questions.question:
A law firm's coordinator sends a 70-page merger agreement to an analysis agent, which returns a summary. Over the next two hours, a partner asks three follow-up questions about that same summary. The team opens a new agent thread for each follow-up and resends the agreement. Every follow-up costs about as much as the first run, and the third answer contradicts an assumption the first answer stated.

What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: The agreement is too long for one request to carry.

options.label: B
options.text: Each follow-up opens a fresh thread, so nothing from earlier turns carries over.

options.label: C
options.text: The prompt cache expired between follow-ups, so the agreement is processed again each time.

options.label: D
options.text: The agent's instructions never tell it to stay consistent with the answers it already gave.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Each follow-up opens a fresh thread, so nothing from earlier turns carries over.

Two symptoms point the same way. A follow-up costs as much as the original run, which is what resending 70 pages into an empty thread costs. The third answer contradicts an assumption the first one stated, which happens only when the agent cannot see that first answer. A thread kept open holds both the document and the reasoning.

INCORRECT: The agreement is too long for one request to carry.

Large documents really do get truncated, and 70 pages is substantial, so capacity is a reasonable first suspicion. The first run returned a usable summary from that same document. The trouble starts only on the follow-ups. A symptom that appears only on later requests is not explained by the size of the first one.

INCORRECT: The prompt cache expired between follow-ups, so the agreement is processed again each time.

Caching is the usual reason repeated content stops being cheap. Two hours easily outlasts a short reuse window, so the cost pattern seems to fit. The team resends the agreement into a new thread deliberately, so the repeated cost is built in. No cache setting produces a contradicted assumption. A cost symptom sitting beside a correctness symptom rarely has a caching explanation.

INCORRECT: The agent's instructions never tell it to stay consistent with the answers it already gave.

Inconsistent output looks like a prompt gap, and a consistency instruction costs one line to add, which makes this the cheapest-looking fix. The agent never receives the earlier answer at all. No wording can make a model agree with text it was never shown. An instruction cannot govern content the model was never given.

questions.question:
A claims team split adjudication into two steps. Step one extracts the facts from the file and is right 99 percent of the time. Step two decides coverage, applies four exclusions, computes the payable amount, and writes the rationale, and is right 68 percent of the time. The team has rewritten step two's prompt five times with no gain. Neither step needs anything from the other.

What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Move step two to the top model tier and keep the two-step shape.

options.label: B
options.text: Cut the whole process into around twenty short calls, the smallest units possible.

options.label: C
options.text: Split step two until each part is reliably solvable alone.

options.label: D
options.text: Have an adjuster check step two's output on every claim before the payment goes out.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Split step two until each part is reliably solvable alone.

Step one runs at 99 percent, so the boundary between the two steps is sound. Step two still carries four exclusions, a calculation and a piece of writing, and five prompt rewrites left it at 68 percent. That is a piece left too coarse. Cutting it until each decision holds up on its own is the granularity this work needs.

INCORRECT: Move step two to the top model tier and keep the two-step shape.

Sixty-eight percent on a dense reasoning step looks like a capability shortfall, and switching tier is one configuration change away. Step two still bundles four exclusions, an amount, and a rationale into a single judgment. A stronger model carries the same overloaded piece. Capability raises a step's ceiling; it does not reduce how much that step is being asked to do.

INCORRECT: Cut the whole process into around twenty short calls, the smallest units possible.

If step two suffers from being too coarse, cutting everything finer reads as the same medicine at a higher dose. Step one already runs at 99 percent, so splitting it buys nothing and adds hand-offs between twenty pieces. Cut only the pieces that are failing, because every extra boundary costs coordination.

INCORRECT: Have an adjuster check step two's output on every claim before the payment goes out.

A human gate does stop wrong payments, and 68 percent is nowhere near shippable, so review looks like responsible engineering. The adjuster reads the same overloaded output the model struggled with, and a person returns to work the split was meant to make reliable. Review catches a bad result; it does not improve the step that produced it.

questions.question:
A wealth manager's board asks for something the firm cannot do today: same-day personalised market commentary for all 200,000 retail clients. A 12-person research desk currently writes one weekly note for everyone. The team ships a Claude tool that drafts that weekly note 40 percent faster. Analysts like it and adoption is high. The board says the project missed what it asked for.

Why?

options.label: A
options.text: The tool speeds the existing process instead of enabling the capability the board named.

options.label: B
options.text: The research desk is too small to cover 200,000 clients even with a faster tool.

options.label: C
options.text: The board should have named transformation rather than productivity from the start.

options.label: D
options.text: The 40 percent saving was measured on drafts, not on the published note.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The tool speeds the existing process instead of enabling the capability the board named.

The board asked for something the firm cannot do today: same-day personalised commentary for 200,000 clients. That is a new capability. What shipped lets 12 analysts write the same weekly note faster, which is the old process at higher speed. Adoption is high because the tool works. It works on the wrong pillar.

INCORRECT: The research desk is too small to cover 200,000 clients even with a faster tool.

Twelve people cannot personally serve 200,000 clients, so headcount looks like the binding constraint, and the arithmetic supports that reading. The board asked for a capability, not for more desk output. The design left the desk on the path to every client instead of removing it. When the ask is a new capability, headcount is a symptom of the old design.

INCORRECT: The board should have named transformation rather than productivity from the start.

Vague briefs do cause misses, and the words efficiency, productivity and transformation blur together in most requirement documents. This brief was not vague. The board described a service the firm cannot offer today, which is specific enough to design against. When a business says what it cannot do today, that phrasing has already named the pillar.

INCORRECT: The 40 percent saving was measured on drafts, not on the published note.

Measuring the wrong step is a genuine reporting error, and 40 percent is the only number the team put forward, so questioning it feels rigorous. The board's objection is about what the project delivered, not about how the saving was counted. A correctly measured saving is still a saving on the old process. Check what a number claims before questioning how it was taken.

questions.question:
A team pins its production configuration to claude-sonnet-4-6, a current-generation model identifier with no snapshot date. Output stays stable for five months. One Monday, the tone of generated summaries changes, and two regression tests fail. The team deployed no application change over the weekend. The prompt, temperature, API key, and application code are all unchanged.

What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Serving infrastructure changed, such as routing or safety classifiers, under the fixed model ID.

options.label: B
options.text: A nightly job regenerated the regression baselines, so the stored expectations no longer match.

options.label: C
options.text: Monday traffic triggered rate limiting, which routed requests to a smaller tier.

options.label: D
options.text: The prompt cache expired, so the model no longer reuses the stored system prompt and drifts.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Serving infrastructure changed, such as routing or safety classifiers, under the fixed model ID.

Nothing on the team's side changed, yet behavior changed on one date. That pattern points outside the team's control. A pinned model ID keeps the weights fixed for its whole life, Anthropic ships any new snapshot under a new ID rather than moving an old one. The pin covers weights, not the infrastructure around them. Routing, safety classifiers, and sampling logic can shift under a fixed ID, and that can change tone with no deploy in the log.

INCORRECT: A nightly job regenerated the regression baselines, so the stored expectations no longer match.

Broken baselines are a common cause of sudden test failures, so this suspect is fair. The tone of the summaries changed too, and users can see that outside the test suite. A baseline problem would move the tests without moving the product. When output and tests fail together, suspect the thing producing the output.

INCORRECT: Monday traffic triggered rate limiting, which routed requests to a smaller tier.

Monday peaks are real, and quality drops under load are a familiar operational story. Rate limits reject or slow requests, they do not quietly swap in a different model. The change also persisted rather than easing when the peak passed. Ask whether the mechanism you suspect can actually produce the symptom you see.

INCORRECT: The prompt cache expired, so the model no longer reuses the stored system prompt and drifts.

Caching is invisible in normal operation, which makes it an easy place to put unexplained behavior. A cache miss changes cost and latency, not the content of the reply, because the same text is sent either way. The summaries changed in tone, which is a model behavior. Caching affects what a request costs, never what it says.

questions.question:
A team picks a model for a nightly contract-comparison job. Each run sends both contracts and a 60-rule checklist in one request, because the rules compare clauses across the two contracts. The assembled request measures 240,000 tokens. The compact model is cheaper and faster, and its window holds 200,000 tokens. The standard model fits the request. The team ranked the two on cost and latency, and the compact model won.

What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Rule the compact model out, since its window cannot hold the request.

options.label: B
options.text: Split each run into two compact-model requests and merge the answers afterwards.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the compact model and cut the checklist down to its 40 most-used rules, dropping the rest.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the legal team to shorten both contracts before each nightly run.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Rule the compact model out, since its window cannot hold the request.

The request measures 240,000 tokens and the compact model's window holds 200,000. A model that cannot hold the input is not a cheap option, it is not an option. Cost and latency rankings only mean something among candidates that can run the job. Capacity settles who is on the list, and price settles who wins it.

INCORRECT: Split each run into two compact-model requests and merge the answers afterwards.

Splitting a large job across requests is a real technique, and it looks like a way to keep the cheaper model in play. The 60 rules compare clauses across the two contracts, so neither half of a split ever sees both. Merging two partial answers cannot recover a comparison that was never made. Never split an input whose parts have to be read together.

INCORRECT: Keep the compact model and cut the checklist down to its 40 most-used rules, dropping the rest.

Trimming the input to fit is the obvious way to rescue the cheaper choice, and the least-used rules look expendable. The job is defined by all 60 rules, so dropping 20 changes what the system delivers. The saving is then bought with output the business asked for. Do not shrink the requirement to fit the model you preferred.

INCORRECT: Ask the legal team to shorten both contracts before each nightly run.

Shorter inputs would solve the capacity problem, and the legal team does own the documents, so the request sounds reasonable. Those contracts are the material the job exists to compare, and shortening them nightly is manual work with no end. The other candidate already fits. Do not create recurring human work to make an avoidable technical choice viable.

Trimming the input to fit is the obvious way to rescue the cheaper choice, and the least-used rules look expendable. The job is defined by all 60 rules, so dropping 20 changes what the system delivers. The saving is then bought with output the business asked for. Do not shrink the requirement to fit the model you preferred.

INCORRECT: Ask the legal team to shorten both contracts before each nightly run.

Shorter inputs would solve the capacity problem, and the legal team does own the documents, so the request sounds reasonable. Those contracts are the material the job exists to compare, and shortening them nightly is manual work with no end. The other candidate already fits. Do not create recurring human work to make an avoidable technical choice viable.

questions.question:
A procurement agent reads supplier emails and drafts payment approvals. The system prompt states that email text is data and never an instruction, and the application already wraps each email body between the lines BEGIN EMAIL and END EMAIL. Last week one supplier email carried those two marker lines inside its own body, with fresh instructions between them. The agent approved a payment nobody authorised.

What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: JSON-encode each email body so marker text inside it cannot break out of its field.

options.label: B
options.text: Choose a longer marker string that a supplier is unlikely to type by chance.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the untrusted-data rule to the end of the system prompt so the model reads it last.

options.label: D
options.text: Have a buyer read every supplier email before the agent processes it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: JSON-encode each email body so marker text inside it cannot break out of its field.

The boundary here is plain text, the same material as the content it fences. The question shows the email reproducing both marker lines, so the sender can write the fence as easily as the team can. Encoding the body as a JSON string escapes whatever it holds, so marker text arrives as characters inside a field. The format then enforces the boundary.

INCORRECT: Choose a longer marker string that a supplier is unlikely to type by chance.

Guessing a marker is harder when the marker is long, so this looks like it raises the bar. The email did not stumble onto the marker by chance, it reproduced the exact lines the application uses. Rarity defends against accidents, never against an attacker who can read your format. A secret that travels in the same channel as the attack is not a secret.

INCORRECT: Move the untrusted-data rule to the end of the system prompt so the model reads it last.

Recency does affect what a model weighs, and moving an important rule last is a real prompting technique. The rule was already present and already stated clearly, and the question shows it holding for every other email. Position changes emphasis, it does not create a structural boundary. Wording alone cannot enforce a limit that the format leaves open.

INCORRECT: Have a buyer read every supplier email before the agent processes it.

A human reader would spot a forged marker, and the volume may look small enough to review. This puts a person in the path of every email to compensate for a format the application controls, which will not survive growth. It also does nothing the next time the agent runs unattended. Fix a structural weakness in the structure, not in someone's attention.

questions.question:
A tax assistant decides which reliefs apply to a client's situation. Its prompt carries a hand-written nine-step procedure the author wrote from the cases she knew. On those cases the assistant is right almost every time. On cases that need the checks in a different order, or need one the author never wrote, the assistant works through the nine steps anyway and names the wrong relief. Accuracy sits at 71 percent.

What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: The model tier is not strong enough for multi-step tax reasoning.

options.label: B
options.text: Nine steps is more than the model can hold while working a whole case through.

options.label: C
options.text: The scripted procedure forces one order onto cases that need a different one.

options.label: D
options.text: The procedure never tells the assistant it may skip steps that do not apply.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The scripted procedure forces one order onto cases that need a different one.

The split in the results names the cause. Cases matching the author's mental model are almost always right, and cases needing another order or an unwritten check are wrong. The assistant is not failing to reason. It is reasoning down a path someone else fixed in advance. A general instruction to think the case through carefully leaves that path open.

INCORRECT: The model tier is not strong enough for multi-step tax reasoning.

Tax relief decisions are genuinely hard, and 71 percent is the sort of number a capability gap produces, so tier is a fair first guess. The same model is almost always right on the author's cases. Capability that appears on one group of inputs did not vanish on another. A failure that tracks the shape of the input is about the prompt, not the tier.

INCORRECT: Nine steps is more than the model can hold while working a whole case through.

Long procedures do get lost partway, and nine steps is enough to sound like too many, which makes this a reasonable suspicion. The assistant completes all nine steps, including on the cases it gets wrong. Nothing is being dropped. Before blaming length, check whether the steps were followed, because a followed instruction failing is a different problem from a forgotten one.

INCORRECT: The procedure never tells the assistant it may skip steps that do not apply.

Permission to skip sounds like the missing flexibility, and it is a small edit to a prompt that already exists. Skipping steps does not help a case that needs a check the author never wrote, or needs the same checks in another order. The rigid script is the problem, not one missing clause inside it. Patching a fixed plan still leaves a fixed plan.

questions.question:
A compliance assistant answers staff questions about one 200-page policy manual. The manual sits at the top of the prompt, above the instructions and the question, and the whole thing fits in the window with room to spare. There is no retrieval step. Answers read fluently, but about one in six states a rule the manual does not contain or blends two sections into one.

What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Have the model quote the manual passages it relies on before it writes the answer.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the manual below the instructions so the question is read first.

options.label: C
options.text: Split the manual into chunks and add a retrieval step in front of the model.

options.label: D
options.text: Have a compliance officer check every answer against the manual before it reaches staff.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have the model quote the manual passages it relies on before it writes the answer.

Every fact needed is already in the window, and the answers still drift into rules that are not there. Nothing in the current design ties an answer to a place in the text. Pulling the supporting passages out first forces that link before any prose is written. Blended sections also become visible, because two separate quotes cannot merge into one.

INCORRECT: Move the manual below the instructions so the question is read first.

Placement really does change long-context results, so reordering looks like a documented lever worth pulling. The manual already sits at the top, above the instructions and the question, which is the arrangement that helps. Moving it down works against that. Check what a design already does before proposing the change it has made.

INCORRECT: Split the manual into chunks and add a retrieval step in front of the model.

Retrieval is the standard answer to document questions, and chunking feels like the disciplined version of this system. The whole manual already fits with room to spare, so nothing is being left out for retrieval to recover. The change adds an indexing pipeline and a new failure mode. Do not add retrieval to solve a problem that is not about capacity.

INCORRECT: Have a compliance officer check every answer against the manual before it reaches staff.

One wrong rule in six is far too many to publish, and a reviewer holding the manual would catch them. That makes this read as the safe path. The officer would do by hand the exact matching the model was never asked to do. The assistant keeps guessing and a person keeps paying for it. Build the check into the design before you staff it.

questions.question:
A benefits assistant loads eight plan documents into one context, concatenated in the order they were fetched, with nothing between them. Everything fits comfortably. Staff report two problems: answers combine a rule from the salaried plan with one from the contractor plan, and when asked which document a rule came from, the assistant often names the wrong one.

What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Instruct the assistant to name the document behind every rule.

options.label: B
options.text: Wrap each plan in its own tagged block naming its source document.

options.label: C
options.text: Reorder the eight documents by effective date so the newest plan appears first.

options.label: D
options.text: Send one request per document and merge the eight answers together inside the application layer.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Wrap each plan in its own tagged block naming its source document.

Both symptoms come from the same gap. Eight documents run together with nothing between them leave no marker for where one plan stops and the next starts. Nothing labels which is which either. A tagged block per plan supplies both. Rules stop merging across a boundary the model can now see, and attribution reads straight off the label.

INCORRECT: Instruct the assistant to name the document behind every rule.

Asking for citations is the direct response to wrong attribution, and it costs one line, so it looks efficient. The assistant already names documents and names them wrongly. It cannot label what it cannot tell apart, because the eight plans arrive as one undivided block. An instruction to report a boundary is worth nothing when no boundary exists in the input.

INCORRECT: Reorder the eight documents by effective date so the newest plan appears first.

Ordering by date suggests the newest rule wins, which sounds like a fix for contradictory answers drawn from different plans. These plans cover different populations, salaried and contractor, not different vintages of one plan. Sorting them changes which rule appears first and still blends them. Ordering never substitutes for separating.

INCORRECT: Send one request per document and merge the eight answers together inside the application layer.

Eight isolated requests make cross-contamination impossible, which is a real property and an appealing one. Everything already fits in one context, so this pays for eight calls to solve a labelling problem. The merge step then has to decide which plan applies, which is the same judgment moved into code. Prefer structure inside the context over multiplying requests.

questions.question: Twelve teams share one prompt template. It builds each request by writing the instructions, then four worked example pairs as plain text, then the real input. After a wording change to the instructions, some answers began repeating an example's customer name and order number instead of the values in the real request. One team's outputs also started following an example's phrasing as though it were a rule. What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: Four examples is more than the model can generalise from.

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing marks where the examples start and stop, so the model has to infer it.

options.label: C
options.text: The examples sit after the instructions, so the model reads them last and weights them more.

options.label: D
options.text: The twelve teams share one template instead of each writing examples for their own work.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Nothing marks where the examples start and stop, so the model has to infer it.

Instructions, examples and real input arrive as one run of plain text. The model works out which part is which from wording alone, and a wording change moved that judgment. Both symptoms follow: example values get read as data, and example phrasing gets read as instruction. Tags around each example remove the inference entirely.

INCORRECT: Four examples is more than the model can generalise from.

Example count does affect results, and copying from an example is what an overfitted set looks like, so the number is a fair suspect. The set worked until the instructions were reworded, and nothing about the examples changed. A count that was fine yesterday did not become wrong today. When a symptom starts with a change, look at what changed.

INCORRECT: The examples sit after the instructions, so the model reads them last and weights them more.

Recency effects are real, and the examples do sit last before the input, which makes this sound measured. Position would not explain an example's customer name appearing as the answer's data. That is a role confusion, not a weighting one. Separate what the model treats a block as from how strongly it weighs it.

INCORRECT: The twelve teams share one template instead of each writing examples for their own work.

Shared templates do drift away from any single team's needs, and one team is reported as affected, so ownership looks like the issue. Splitting the template into twelve untagged copies reproduces the same ambiguity twelve times. The shared file is not what confused the model. Duplicating a flawed structure spreads the flaw rather than fixing it.

questions.question:
A support assistant builds every request at run time from recent turns, retrieved articles and any files the user attached. The application estimates the size by dividing characters by four. Three percent of requests fail with an overflow error after the user has waited, and the median request uses only 40 percent of the window because the margin is set wide. Which two changes best address this?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window so the overflow errors stop.

options.label: B
options.text: Count the assembled request with the token counting endpoint before sending it.

options.label: C
options.text: Widen the character estimate's safety margin until overflow errors disappear.

options.label: D
options.text: Trim the retrieved articles or refuse the request when that count exceeds the budget.

options.label: E
options.text: Catch the overflow error and ask the user to attach fewer files, then retry.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Count the assembled request with the token counting endpoint before sending it.

The context differs on every call, so its size cannot be known until it is built. Characters divided by four is a guess. The two reported symptoms are the two ways a guess fails: too low and the request overflows, too high and capacity goes unused. Measuring the assembled request replaces the guess with the real number.

CORRECT: Trim the retrieved articles or refuse the request when that count exceeds the budget.

A measurement changes nothing until something acts on it. With the real number in hand before sending, the application can drop the weakest articles or route the call elsewhere. It can also decline with a clear message. That is what removes the three percent of failures the user currently discovers only after waiting.

INCORRECT: Move to a model with a larger context window so the overflow errors stop.

A larger window does absorb today's biggest requests, and it needs no application change, which makes it the quickest relief available. The application still does not know how large a request is. The same estimate now wastes a bigger window and overflows on a bigger attachment. Capacity raises the ceiling; it does not tell you where you sit against it.

INCORRECT: Widen the character estimate's safety margin until overflow errors disappear.

Tuning the margin is the smallest possible change and it does push the failure rate down, so it looks like a pragmatic setting. The median request already wastes 60 percent of the window because the margin is wide. Widening it further trades one reported symptom straight into the other. Do not tune a safety margin when the quantity itself can be measured.

INCORRECT: Catch the overflow error and ask the user to attach fewer files, then retry.

Handling the error is honest engineering, and the attachments are often the part that pushed the request over, so the ask is targeted. The user still waits for the failure before hearing about it, and the retry is a second full round trip. The system learns the size from a failed call. Never discover a limit by crossing it when you can check first.

questions.question: A team marks six short reusable prompt fragments for caching: a tone rule, a formatting rule, a refusal rule and three others. None of the six has changed in months. Traffic is steady at hundreds of requests a minute, so no gap between requests is long enough to matter. Every response reports zero cache reads, and the API returns no error. What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Combine the six fragments into a single cached block.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove the cache markup, since fragments this small change too often to cache.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch the six fragments to the extended cache duration.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the six fragments into a Skill so they load only when a request needs them.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Combine the six fragments into a single cached block.

Steady traffic rules out an expiry problem, and unchanged text rules out invalidation, yet every response reports zero reads and no error appears. That silence is the signal: caching declines to apply to content below a minimum size and says nothing about it. Six small blocks joined into one clears that floor without changing a word of the text.

INCORRECT: Remove the cache markup, since fragments this small change too often to cache.

Zero reads across the board does look like markup that was never going to work, so stripping it keeps the prompt honest. None of the six has changed in months. Churn is not the reason they miss, and removing the markup accepts a cost the design can still avoid. Read the stability of the content before concluding that caching does not suit it.

INCORRECT: Switch the six fragments to the extended cache duration.

A longer lifetime is a real option and the natural fix when entries expire before reuse. It fits the shape of a cache that never reads. Requests arrive hundreds of times a minute, so nothing here survives long enough to expire. A longer window on an entry that was never written changes nothing. Match the setting to the failure, not to the symptom's name.

INCORRECT: Move the six fragments into a Skill so they load only when a request needs them.

On-demand loading is a genuine way to cut repeated prompt cost, and Skills exist for exactly that kind of reuse. All six rules apply to every request, so there is nothing to defer, and the rebuild is large next to joining six blocks. Do not reach for a loading strategy when every request needs the content anyway.

Move the six fragments into a Skill so they load only when a request needs them.

CORRECT: Combine the six fragments into a single cached block.

Steady traffic rules out an expiry problem, and unchanged text rules out invalidation, yet every response reports zero reads and no error appears. That silence is the signal: caching declines to apply to content below a minimum size and says nothing about it. Six small blocks joined into one clears that floor without changing a word of the text.

questions.question: A claims assistant carries a 9,000-token policy block in its system prompt, behind its own cache breakpoint. The block has not changed since launch, and no per-request value sits inside it. Traffic runs steadily through the day. The block cached reliably for two months. The platform team then began shipping tool definition edits several times a day, and the policy block's cache hit rate fell to near zero. What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: Each new tool changes the level above the policy, and that invalidates the policy too.

options.label: B
options.text: The cache lifetime keeps expiring between requests, so every stretch begins from a cold cache.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the tool block loses its cache, and the policy is counted inside it.

options.label: D
options.text: A 9,000-token block is larger than one cache breakpoint holds.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Each new tool changes the level above the policy, and that invalidates the policy too.

The cache is built in a fixed order: tools, then system, then messages. A change at one level clears that level and every level after it. The question rules out the other suspects. The block never changed, no per-request value sits in it, traffic is steady, and it cached for two months. The only thing that started moving is the level above it.

INCORRECT: The cache lifetime keeps expiring between requests, so every stretch begins from a cold cache.

An expired entry is the usual reason a stable prefix stops paying off, and the pattern does look similar. The question says traffic runs steadily through the day, so requests keep arriving well inside any reuse window. A cache that dies of age fails after idle periods, one that dies of a change fails right after the change.

INCORRECT: Only the tool block loses its cache, and the policy is counted inside it.

Expecting a breakpoint to protect what sits behind it is reasonable, and the tool edits are clearly the trigger. The question puts the policy behind its own breakpoint, which still sits below tools in the build order. Its own marker does not lift it out of that order. A breakpoint marks where a prefix ends, not a shield against a change made ahead of it.

INCORRECT: A 9,000-token block is larger than one cache breakpoint holds.

Caching does carry size rules, and a block this large invites the thought that it crossed a ceiling. The same block cached reliably for two months at the same size, so nothing about its size moved. What moved was the release cadence above it. A limit that was never crossed cannot explain a behaviour that changed on a date.

questions.question: A retrieval pipeline splits policy documents into 500-token chunks at fixed boundaries. Retrieved chunks often begin mid-sentence and refer to this exemption without naming it, and answers cite the wrong policy. The index is fresh and the embedding model is current. The team tuned chunk size twice and saw no improvement. What is the underlying cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Fixed-size splitting strips each chunk of the context that made it meaningful.

options.label: B
options.text: The embedding model cannot represent policy language well.

options.label: C
options.text: Chunk overlap is too low, so sentences at each boundary fall between two chunks.

options.label: D
options.text: User questions are too vague, so retrieval matches generic policy wording instead.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Fixed-size splitting strips each chunk of the context that made it meaningful.

The symptoms name the cause. Chunks start mid-sentence and point at an exemption they never identify. A cut made at a fixed offset lands wherever it lands, and the words that gave the passage meaning stay in the neighbouring chunk. Tuning the size moves the cut without restoring what it removed. Prepend short explanatory context to each chunk before indexing.

INCORRECT: The embedding model cannot represent policy language well.

Blaming the embedding model is common when retrieval returns odd results. The embedding model is current, and the same index returns closely related passages for other queries. A chunk that begins mid-sentence is broken text, not hard vocabulary. Look at what you indexed before you doubt the model that indexed it.

INCORRECT: Chunk overlap is too low, so sentences at each boundary fall between two chunks.

Overlap is the standard remedy for a cut that lands mid-sentence, and the symptom names exactly that. Overlap repairs a seam, it does not supply a policy name that sits pages earlier in the document. The team also tuned size twice with no change. Fixing the join does not replace context the split never carried.

INCORRECT: User questions are too vague, so retrieval matches generic policy wording instead.

Vague queries do pull back generic matches, and query quality is a real retrieval lever. The damage here is visible inside the retrieved chunks, which begin mid-sentence and name no policy. A sharper question cannot restore a subject the chunk no longer carries. Read the retrieved text before you blame the text that asked for it.

questions.question: An operations agent holds nine tools, one per capability, with no overlap between them. Each tool returns the vendor API's whole payload: internal record identifiers, audit fields, pagination metadata, roughly 40 fields where the agent reads three. Automatic tool result clearing is already on. A five-step task now fills more than half the window with tool results before the agent reasons about anything. What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Return only the fields the agent reads, with a parameter for the detailed form.

options.label: B
options.text: Merge the nine tools into a smaller set so fewer definitions load.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a summarizing model call between each tool and the agent to trim its payload first.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Return only the fields the agent reads, with a parameter for the detailed form.

Nine tools with no overlap is already a clean tool set, and clearing handles results after they pile up. The waste happens earlier. Every call puts 40 fields into context when three are read. Returning high-signal fields by default cuts that at the source. A response format parameter keeps the full payload available on the turns that need it.

INCORRECT: Merge the nine tools into a smaller set so fewer definitions load.

Consolidation is the standard answer to a bloated tool set, and nine tools sounds like a number worth reducing. The question states there is no overlap between them, so each covers a distinct capability. Fewer definitions also would not shrink a single payload. Count what a tool set returns as well as how many tools it holds.

INCORRECT: Add a summarizing model call between each tool and the agent to trim its payload first.

A summarizer would shrink the payload, and it needs no change to the vendor integration, which makes it look like a clean layer to insert. It buys a second inference pass on every tool call to discard fields the tool could have left out. It can also drop a field the agent needed. Do not spend a model call to undo output you control.

INCORRECT: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window.

More room does absorb oversized results, and it is the change that touches the least code. That makes it read as pragmatic. The stated problem is that tool results crowd out the reasoning, and a bigger window fills the same way from the same 40 fields. Capacity postpones a waste problem rather than removing it.

questions.question: A bank's security review of a Claude agent integration passed with no findings. The review tested identity from end to end: single sign-on, multi-factor, short-lived tokens, no shared logins, replay protection. Three weeks after launch, a junior analyst's session used the agent to post a ledger adjustment that only controllers are permitted to make. Every log line names the analyst correctly. What is the underlying problem?

options.label: A
options.text: The identity provider issued the analyst a token carrying more scopes than her login granted.

options.label: B
options.text: The review confirmed who each caller is and never tested what each caller may do.

options.label: C
options.text: Multi-factor checks do not cover actions an agent takes for a user.

options.label: D
options.text: Controllers and analysts need separate agents so the two roles cannot reach the same tools and records.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The review confirmed who each caller is and never tested what each caller may do.

The logs name the analyst correctly, so identity worked exactly as the review found. The failure sits on the other side: nothing checked that this identity was permitted to post a controller-only adjustment. A review that covers sign-on, tokens and replay has covered one of the two questions. The permissions question needs its own pass.

INCORRECT: The identity provider issued the analyst a token carrying more scopes than her login granted.

A mis-issued token is a real failure and would produce this exact outcome, so the option is credible on its face. The review tested token issuance and lifetime and found nothing, and the analyst was identified correctly throughout. Nothing points at the token. Before blaming the credential, check whether anything downstream was reading it for permissions at all.

INCORRECT: Multi-factor checks do not cover actions an agent takes for a user.

Agents do act after the login, which makes it easy to imagine the second factor falling away somewhere in the chain. The analyst was authenticated and stayed correctly identified for every logged action. A stronger login would not have changed the outcome, because the wrong person was never the issue. Strengthening identity cannot answer a question about entitlement.

INCORRECT: Controllers and analysts need separate agents so the two roles cannot reach the same tools and records.

Splitting by role does create a hard wall, and it is a design many teams reach for after an incident. It builds a new agent for every role instead of checking a role once, and it breaks again the moment a role gains a permission. The gap is a missing check, not a missing boundary. Prefer one enforced rule over a copy per audience.

questions.question:
A document analysis service has raised its extended thinking budget three times. Accuracy moved from 84 percent to 89, then to 89.4, then to 89.5. Over the same three changes, median latency went from 6 seconds to 19 and cost per document roughly tripled. The team is preparing the same configuration for four more document types. Which two changes best address this?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Move the service to a more capable model tier and keep the largest budget.

options.label: B
options.text: Cut the budget back to where the accuracy gain stopped.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the budget once more to confirm the accuracy curve has really flattened.

options.label: D
options.text: Set each new document type's starting budget from its own measured results.

options.label: E
options.text: Ask reviewers to accept the slower responses, since accuracy is higher than it was before.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Cut the budget back to where the accuracy gain stopped.

Accuracy rose five points on the first increase and one half point across the next two. Latency tripled and cost tripled over those same two. The curve flattened after the first change, and everything spent past that point bought latency. Returning to the level where the gain stopped keeps the accuracy the service actually has.

CORRECT: Set each new document type's starting budget from its own measured results.

The plateau sits at a different place for every task, because it depends on how much reasoning the work genuinely needs. Copying this service's largest budget onto four more document types repeats the same overspend four times, on tasks whose curves nobody has looked at. Measuring each one gives a starting point instead of a default.

INCORRECT: Move the service to a more capable model tier and keep the largest budget.

Accuracy stuck below 90 percent does look like a capability ceiling, and a stronger tier is the usual response to one. The numbers show reasoning effort past the plateau adding latency and cost with no accuracy behind it. A stronger tier on the same oversized budget inherits that waste. Fix an unproductive setting before you pay for more capability.

INCORRECT: Raise the budget once more to confirm the accuracy curve has really flattened.

One more data point sounds like good discipline, and two flat readings are a small sample to conclude from. Both increases after the first returned less than a point between them, while cost and latency kept climbing. The pattern is already the documented shape of diminishing returns. Stop buying evidence a trend has already given you.

INCORRECT: Ask reviewers to accept the slower responses, since accuracy is higher than it was before.

Accuracy did improve, and asking users to absorb a trade-off is a normal conversation to have. Almost all of that improvement arrived with the first increase, before latency tripled. Reviewers would be accepting a cost that bought them half a point. Do not negotiate for a trade-off the measurements say you are not getting.

questions.question: A claims assistant runs sessions that used to hit the context window, so the team switched compaction on. Sessions now finish, and the reasoning quality held up. Each session ends by writing a case record that must reproduce the customer's opening complaint word for word. On long sessions those quotes have started drifting from the transcript, sometimes changing a date or a policy number. Short sessions are unaffected. What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: Long sessions still overflow the window, so the earliest turns fall out of context.

options.label: B
options.text: Tool result clearing removed the earliest interactions from the session.

options.label: C
options.text: Once compaction runs, the early turns survive only as a summary.

options.label: D
options.text: The assistant is never told to reproduce the opening complaint exactly.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Once compaction runs, the early turns survive only as a summary.

The split between long and short sessions names the cause. Short sessions never trigger compaction, and their quotes are fine. Long sessions do trigger it, and compaction replaces older content with a concise summary. A summary carries the gist, not the exact date or policy number, so the case record is quoting a paraphrase.

INCORRECT: Long sessions still overflow the window, so the earliest turns fall out of context.

Overflow was the original problem, and long sessions are still the ones failing, so the old cause is a natural suspect. Compaction was switched on precisely to stop the overflow, and the sessions now finish. Nothing is being pushed out. When a fix is in place, check what it does before assuming the old failure survived it.

INCORRECT: Tool result clearing removed the earliest interactions from the session.

Clearing is a real feature, it does remove the oldest interactions first, and that ordering matches a symptom about early content. It operates on tool results, and the missing text is what the customer typed. Nothing here says clearing is even enabled. Match a feature to the kind of content the symptom describes, not just to its position.

INCORRECT: The assistant is never told to reproduce the opening complaint exactly.

A missing instruction is the cheapest possible explanation, and quoting rules are easy to leave out of a prompt. Short sessions reproduce the complaint correctly under the same prompt, so the instruction is doing its job. The difference is what remains in context, not what was asked for. An instruction cannot recover wording the context no longer holds.

questions.question: A clinical intake agent is hard to debug. Traces show durations, model names and tool names, but not what the agent read or wrote. An engineer proposes switching on full content capture: prompt text, tool arguments and raw API bodies. The agent's tools read patient records. The observability backend is a third-party service the platform team approved for operational metrics only. What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch content capture on and tell engineers not to open traces holding patient data.

options.label: B
options.text: Switch it on in staging only, which loads the same patient records.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave content capture off until the backend is approved for patient content.

options.label: D
options.text: Have engineers reproduce each failure by hand rather than reading traces at all, as before.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Leave content capture off until the backend is approved for patient content.

Content capture is off by default, and turning it on exports whatever the agent's tools handle the moment it is enabled. Those tools read patient records, and the backend is cleared for operational metrics only. The debugging need is real, but it is not the question this switch answers. Approval for the data class decides it.

INCORRECT: Switch content capture on and tell engineers not to open traces holding patient data.

Access discipline is a familiar control, and the team asking is small enough that a rule feels enforceable. The export happens when the switch flips, not when someone opens a trace, so the records are already sitting in an unapproved system. Who looks at data is a separate question from where the data is allowed to live.

INCORRECT: Switch it on in staging only, which loads the same patient records.

Limiting a risky setting to a lower environment is sound practice, and staging feels safer by convention. Staging here loads the same patient records and reports to the same unapproved backend, so nothing about the data changes. The label on the environment is not the control. Judge an export by the data crossing it, not by the environment's name.

INCORRECT: Have engineers reproduce each failure by hand rather than reading traces at all, as before.

Manual reproduction avoids the data question entirely, and it is how the team debugged before tracing existed. It converts every investigation into hours of engineering time and still fails on anything that only appears in production. The approval conversation is cheaper than that standing cost. Do not accept permanent manual work in place of one decision.

html.question: A clinical intake agent is hard to debug. Traces show durations, model names and tool names, but not what the agent read or wrote. An engineer proposes switching on full content capture: prompt text, tool arguments and raw API bodies. The agent's tools read patient records. The observability backend is a third-party service the platform team approved for operational metrics only. What should the architect do?
options: Switch content capture on and tell engineers not to open traces holding patient data.
Switch it on in staging only, which loads the same patient records.
Leave content capture off until the backend is approved for patient content.
Have engineers reproduce each failure by hand rather than reading traces at all, as before.
html.explanation:
CORRECT: Leave content capture off until the backend is approved for patient content.

Content capture is off by default, and turning it on exports whatever the agent's tools handle the moment it is enabled. Those tools read patient records, and the backend is cleared for operational metrics only. The debugging need is real, but it is not the question this switch answers. Approval for the data class decides it.

INCORRECT: Switch content capture on and tell engineers not to open traces holding patient data.

Access discipline is a familiar control, and the team asking is small enough that a rule feels enforceable. The export happens when the switch flips, not when someone opens a trace, so the records are already sitting in an unapproved system. Who looks at data is a separate question from where the data is allowed to live.

INCORRECT: Switch it on in staging only, which loads the same patient records.

Limiting a risky setting to a lower environment is sound practice, and staging feels safer by convention. Staging here loads the same patient records and reports to the same unapproved backend, so nothing about the data changes. The label on the environment is not the control. Judge an export by the data crossing it, not by the environment's name.

INCORRECT: Have engineers reproduce each failure by hand rather than reading traces at all, as before.

Manual reproduction avoids the data question entirely, and it is how the team debugged before tracing existed. It converts every investigation into hours of engineering time and still fails on anything that only appears in production. The approval conversation is cheaper than that standing cost. Do not accept permanent manual work in place of one decision.

questions.question: A platform runs agent tasks behind an HTTP API. Telemetry arrives reliably, and every agent span already carries end-user and tenant attributes. Both the API service and the agent runs report to the same tracing backend. When a customer reports a slow request at a given minute, engineers cannot tell which agent run belongs to it: the agent runs appear as their own root traces with no parent above them. What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: The end-user attributes are missing from the spans the agent emits.

options.label: B
options.text: The calling request has no active span for the agent run to nest under.

options.label: C
options.text: Sampling is dropping the intermediate spans that would link the request to the agent run.

options.label: D
options.text: The API service and the agent send their spans to different tracing backends.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The calling request has no active span for the agent run to nest under.

Trace context passes into the agent process from whatever span is active when the agent is called. If the API handler opens no span, there is no parent for the agent's spans to nest under, so each run becomes its own root. That is exactly what engineers see. Instrumenting the calling path is what joins the two.

INCORRECT: The end-user attributes are missing from the spans the agent emits.

Missing identity is a common telemetry gap, and it does make runs hard to attribute, so the option sounds like the right family of problem. The question states every agent span already carries end-user and tenant attributes. Knowing whose run it was still does not say which request started it. Identity answers who; parentage answers what caused this.

INCORRECT: Sampling is dropping the intermediate spans that would link the request to the agent run.

Sampling really does remove spans, and a half-recorded trace looks much like a broken one, so this is a fair thing to check. A dropped span would leave gaps in some traces, not turn every agent run into a root with no parent at all. Consistent structure across every trace points at configuration, not at sampling.

INCORRECT: The API service and the agent send their spans to different tracing backends.

Split backends do break a trace in two, and that is a real deployment mistake worth ruling out first. The question says both report to the same backend, so the spans are already sitting side by side. They still do not connect. Two signals arriving in one place do not become one trace without a shared context.

questions.question: A policy assistant retrieves passages and pastes them into the prompt as one block of text. The prompt tells the model to name the source document for each statement, and it usually does, in prose. The review interface has to highlight the exact passage behind each sentence, so the team pulls those citations out with a regular expression. The phrasing shifts every release and about a fifth of the links break. What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Give the model a stricter wording template so the citation format stops shifting.

options.label: B
options.text: Return each retrieved passage as a search result block carrying its own source and title.

options.label: C
options.text: Have reviewers locate the passage themselves whenever a highlight fails to resolve.

options.label: D
options.text: Store every answer with the passages retrieved for it so links can be rebuilt afterwards.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Return each retrieved passage as a search result block carrying its own source and title.

The attribution exists only inside prose. That is why a regular expression has to recover it, and why a wording change breaks a fifth of the links. Passages delivered as search result blocks each carry their own source and title, and citations come back as structure the interface can read. Nothing then depends on how a sentence happened to be phrased.

INCORRECT: Give the model a stricter wording template so the citation format stops shifting.

Format drift is the visible symptom, and pinning the wording is the direct response to it, at the cost of one prompt edit. The template is still a convention the model follows most of the time, and the parser still reconstructs structure from text. One reworded sentence puts the team back here. A convention is not a contract.

INCORRECT: Have reviewers locate the passage themselves whenever a highlight fails to resolve.

Reviewers know the corpus and would find the passage quickly, so the fallback sounds cheap next to an engineering change. It spends reviewer time on every broken link, and the interface was built to remove exactly that search. The breakage rate also rises with each release. Do not staff a gap that the data format can close.

INCORRECT: Store every answer with the passages retrieved for it so links can be rebuilt afterwards.

Keeping the retrieval set is genuinely useful for audit, and it does mean the evidence is never lost. Knowing which passages were retrieved still does not say which sentence used which one, so the mapping the interface needs is still missing. Archiving inputs is not the same as recording which input a statement came from.

questions.question: A support assistant retrieves 200 candidate chunks for every question and passes all of them to the model. An audit found the correct chunk sits somewhere inside those 200 for 96 percent of questions. The answers still miss it about a quarter of the time, and every request is slow and expensive. Chunking and indexing were rebuilt last quarter. What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Rebuild the index with a stronger embedding model.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the retrieval count to 400 so the correct chunk is present more often.

options.label: C
options.text: Score the 200 candidates with a reranking model and pass only the top few.

options.label: D
options.text: Instruct the model to ignore any retrieved chunk that does not answer the question.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Score the 200 candidates with a reranking model and pass only the top few.

The audit already answers the retrieval question: the right chunk is in the set 96 percent of the time. What fails is everything after that. One useful chunk sits among 199 that mostly do not help, and the model pays to read all of them. A relevance-scoring pass reorders the set so only the strongest few arrive.

INCORRECT: Rebuild the index with a stronger embedding model.

Better embeddings are the usual lever for retrieval quality, and the index is the part most teams reach for first. Recall is already 96 percent, so the index is finding the right chunk. A stronger index would put the same chunk into the same oversized set. Read the recall number before rebuilding the thing that produced it.

INCORRECT: Raise the retrieval count to 400 so the correct chunk is present more often.

More candidates does lift recall a little, and 96 percent leaves a visible four-point gap to chase. Dilution is the actual failure, and doubling the set doubles it while making every request slower and dearer. The stated problems both get worse. When precision is the complaint, widening the net is the wrong direction.

INCORRECT: Instruct the model to ignore any retrieved chunk that does not answer the question.

The model does filter to some degree, and asking it to concentrate costs nothing to try. It still has to read all 200 chunks to decide which to ignore, so latency and cost are untouched. The relevant chunk stays buried among them. Filtering after the content is in context does not recover the cost of putting it there.
