questions.question: A company runs four agents. Each one reaches the same six internal services, so 24 bespoke integrations exist, each with its own auth handling, its own tool descriptions and its own edge cases. A fifth agent is funded and two more services are coming. Each new agent-service pair costs about two weeks to build and is maintained separately. What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Extract a shared client library so all 24 integrations reuse one auth implementation and one retry policy.

options.label: B
options.text: Put the six services behind MCP servers so every agent connects through one protocol.

options.label: C
options.text: Assign one engineer to own all integrations so the cost per pair comes down.

options.label: D
options.text: Merge the four agents into one agent holding every service's tools.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Put the six services behind MCP servers so every agent connects through one protocol.

Four agents times six services is the multiplying integration count a common protocol layer exists to remove. A protocol costs more than a direct call for a single pair, which is why it is wrong at that size. Here each connection would be reused by every agent, and by the fifth agent and two services still coming. The reuse is what pays for it.

INCORRECT: Extract a shared client library so all 24 integrations reuse one auth implementation and one retry policy.

A shared library is the familiar fix for duplicated code, and it would genuinely remove one copy of the auth logic. Each agent-service pair still has its own tool descriptions and its own edge cases, so the count keeps multiplying as agents and services are added. Sharing code inside an integration does not reduce the number of integrations.

INCORRECT: Assign one engineer to own all integrations so the cost per pair comes down.

Concentrated ownership does build fluency, and a specialist would move faster than a rotating team. The pair count grows to 42 with the agent and services already funded, so one owner becomes the queue everything waits in. The cost per pair falls and the number of pairs does not. Never solve a multiplying workload with a single owner.

INCORRECT: Merge the four agents into one agent holding every service's tools.

One agent means one set of integrations, which does collapse the grid, and the arithmetic is appealing. Those four agents exist for four different jobs, and merging them trades an integration problem for one agent carrying every capability in the company. The connection layer is what multiplies here. Fix the layer that multiplies, not the consumers of it.

questions.question: A reporting agent reaches a warehouse through an MCP server. The schema is exposed as a tool the agent can call, and it must be read before any query is written. All tool definitions load upfront. On most turns the agent calls the schema tool first and the query runs. On roughly one turn in eight it writes a query straight from the question and names a column that does not exist. The tool works whenever it is called. What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: The tool's description does not state firmly enough that it must be called before any query.

options.label: B
options.text: The schema is too large for the model to hold while composing the query.

options.label: C
options.text: Progressive tool discovery is leaving the schema tool out of some turns.

options.label: D
options.text: A tool runs only when the model chooses it, so the schema is not guaranteed.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: A tool runs only when the model chooses it, so the schema is not guaranteed.

The tool works every time it is called, and the failures are the turns where it was not called. That is what a tool is: a capability the model chooses to invoke. Reference material every request needs belongs in application-controlled read-only data the server supplies as context. Its arrival then stops depending on a judgment made per turn.

INCORRECT: The tool's description does not state firmly enough that it must be called before any query.

Descriptions do steer tool selection, and firmer wording lifts call rates, so this is the cheapest-looking route to the missing seven turns in eight. Better wording raises a probability and never sets it to one, and the requirement here is that the schema is present every time. Wording improves a tendency; it does not create a guarantee.

INCORRECT: The schema is too large for the model to hold while composing the query.

Losing detail from a long input is a genuine failure mode, and inventing a column name is what that looks like from the outside. On the turns where the tool is called, the query runs correctly against the same schema. The content is retained fine once it arrives. Separate a failure to retain content from a failure to fetch it.

INCORRECT: Progressive tool discovery is leaving the schema tool out of some turns.

On-demand tool loading is a real feature and it does change which definitions a turn can see, which makes it a reasonable suspect. The question says all tool definitions load upfront, so the schema tool is visible on every turn. Being available and being used are different things. Confirm a feature is switched on before treating it as the cause.

questions.question: A finance agent sends the same 18 tool definitions with every request. The set has not changed in eight months. A usage audit shows every one of the 18 is called at least once in most sessions. Traffic runs at 40,000 interactive requests a day, and the repeated cost of that identical block is what the team wants down. What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Cache the tool definition block once and reuse that prefix across requests.

options.label: B
options.text: Consolidate the 18 definitions into fewer, broader tools so the block gets smaller.

options.label: C
options.text: Rewrite each of the 18 descriptions to one line so the block gets smaller.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the agent's traffic through the batch API so the repeated block bills at a lower rate.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Cache the tool definition block once and reuse that prefix across requests.

The question supplies both conditions caching needs. The set has not changed in eight months, so the block is stable, and the audit shows every tool earns its place. What costs money is the same block sent 40,000 times a day, not the size of any one definition. Caching stores that identical prefix once and charges a reduced rate on every request after it.

INCORRECT: Consolidate the 18 definitions into fewer, broader tools so the block gets smaller.

Fewer definitions is a real way to shrink a tool block, and consolidation pays off when several tools overlap. The audit says every one of the 18 is called in most sessions, so there is no idle weight to merge away. Broader tools also leave the model a harder choice. Reshaping content that already earns its place trades accuracy for a saving.

INCORRECT: Rewrite each of the 18 descriptions to one line so the block gets smaller.

Tighter descriptions do cut always-on cost, and this is the cheapest change on the list. A smaller block still travels in full on all 40,000 requests, so the repetition the team named survives the edit. The saving scales with size, while the cost scales with volume. Shrinking a repeated payload lowers its unit price, caching removes the repetition itself.

INCORRECT: Send the agent's traffic through the batch API so the repeated block bills at a lower rate.

Asynchronous batching does cut the rate on high volumes, and 40,000 requests a day looks like the load it was built for. The question calls this traffic interactive, and batch work returns its results later rather than in the moment. A pricing mode that changes when a user gets an answer cannot serve a request that waits on one.

questions.question: A health insurer sets one safety target for its member services assistant. The content filter must flag fewer than 2 percent of replies across 10,000 sampled outputs. A product manager proposed the 2 percent figure in a planning meeting, and nobody can say where it came from. The metric names a specific behaviour and the filter measures it automatically every night. Compliance refuses to sign the launch because the target has no basis. Which change best makes the target defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the sample from 10,000 to 100,000 outputs before each release.

options.label: B
options.text: Reset the threshold from an industry benchmark or the system's own measured prior rate.

options.label: C
options.text: Show the flag rate on a live dashboard and alert the team whenever it moves.

options.label: D
options.text: Have two trained safety reviewers approve every flagged reply before the assistant sends it to a member.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Reset the threshold from an industry benchmark or the system's own measured prior rate.

Compliance objects to the 2 percent figure, not to the metric. The question says the metric names a specific behaviour and the filter scores it nightly, so measurement is already sound. It also says a product manager proposed the number in a meeting and nobody can trace it. A benchmark or the system's own measured prior rate gives that number a source.

INCORRECT: Raise the sample from 10,000 to 100,000 outputs before each release.

A larger sample is attractive because it tightens the measurement, and 10,000 can look small for a safety claim. The question says the filter already measures the rate every night, and compliance never questioned that rate. The objection is the bar itself, not the precision of the number tested against it. Measuring something more precisely never justifies the level you chose to measure against.

INCORRECT: Show the flag rate on a live dashboard and alert the team whenever it moves.

Continuous visibility sounds responsible, and teams often reach for a dashboard when a safety question arrives. A dashboard still reports the rate against the same untraceable 2 percent line, so compliance gains nothing new to sign. The refusal names a missing basis, not missing visibility. Watching a number more closely never tells you which value it should stay under.

INCORRECT: Have two trained safety reviewers approve every flagged reply before the assistant sends it to a member.

Human review feels like the safest option, and a second pair of eyes does catch bad replies. questions.question: A logistics company evaluates a shipping document classifier. Two engineers write every test case by hand and have produced 55 cases in six weeks. The team agrees the set needs several hundred cases to cover the real mix of forms. Twenty of the existing cases fairly represent that mix, and grading already runs in code against known field values. The engineers now spend more time writing cases than reading results. Which change best gets the set to the size the team wants?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask each of the six support agents to contribute ten new hand-written test cases every week.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the 55 cases and review each one more carefully.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the twenty representative cases as a baseline and have Claude generate further cases from them.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace the code grader with an automated model grader so evaluation runs finish faster.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Use the twenty representative cases as a baseline and have Claude generate further cases from them.

The twenty cases already represent the real mix of forms, which is what a generated set needs to copy. Generating from that baseline is the documented route to the volume a thorough evaluation needs. It lifts the ceiling that six weeks of hand writing exposed. Grading already runs in code, so each new case costs nothing extra to score.

INCORRECT: Ask each of the six support agents to contribute ten new hand-written test cases every week.

Spreading the work looks like the obvious way to raise output, and support agents do see real documents. Hand authoring is what caps the set at 55 cases. Moving that work to another team keeps the same manual ceiling and adds coordination. The agents also do not know the field values the grader checks against. Sharing a bottleneck does not remove it.

INCORRECT: Keep the 55 cases and review each one more carefully.

Careful review is a real quality practice, and 55 checked cases beat 55 sloppy ones. The stated goal is several hundred cases covering the real mix of forms. Reviewing the existing set moves that number nowhere and spends more engineering time on the part that already works. Improving what you have is not progress when the problem is how much you have.

INCORRECT: Replace the code grader with an automated model grader so evaluation runs finish faster.

Grading speed is a real bottleneck in many evaluation suites, so the reflex is reasonable. The scenario says grading already runs in code against known field values. The engineers are stuck writing cases, not waiting on results, so this speeds up a stage that is not slow. Name the stage the evidence points at before you optimise a pipeline.

questions.question: A retailer A/B tests two prompts for a returns assistant. The variants differ only in the prompt, and both ran on the same live traffic for two weeks. The team logged four metrics: handle time, containment rate, satisfaction and cost per contact. Handle time improved 9 percent, satisfaction fell 3 points, and the other two are flat. Nobody wrote down which metric decides the test. Two review meetings ended without a call. Which change best produces a decision the team can trust?

options.label: A
options.text: Ship the variant, because three of four metrics did not worsen.

options.label: B
options.text: Send all four metrics to the steering group and let it choose the winner.

options.label: C
options.text: Add six more metrics to the dashboard so the next review has a fuller picture of both variants.

options.label: D
options.text: Name the deciding metric and its passing bar, then rerun the comparison against it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Name the deciding metric and its passing bar, then rerun the comparison against it.

The test design is already sound: one variable changed, the same traffic, the same two weeks. What is missing is the rule that turns four numbers into a verdict. The team is choosing that rule while looking at the results, which is where the trust goes. Fixing the metric and the bar first, then rerunning, gives a verdict reviewers can defend.

INCORRECT: Ship the variant, because three of four metrics did not worsen.

Counting metrics feels like a fair tie-breaker when no rule exists, and three against one reads as a majority. The four metrics were never weighted. This rule appeared after the results did, and it would have crowned a different winner had satisfaction moved instead. A rule chosen once you can see the numbers is a preference, not a criterion.

INCORRECT: Send all four metrics to the steering group and let it choose the winner.

Escalation looks neutral when a team deadlocks, and the steering group does own the product. The group faces the same four numbers with no agreed rule, so it inherits the deadlock instead of resolving it. It also decides after seeing which variant each metric favours. Moving an unmade decision up a level does not supply the rule that was missing.

INCORRECT: Add six more metrics to the dashboard so the next review has a fuller picture of both variants.

More measurement sounds like better evidence, and the four metrics clearly did not settle the question. Ten unranked metrics produce more ways to disagree, not fewer. The team already cannot rank the four it has, so the gap is a decision rule rather than coverage. Extra data never resolves a disagreement about which data decides.

questions.question: A subscription company A/B tests a new billing support prompt. Before starting, the team committed to 14 days and 4,000 conversations, with resolution rate as the deciding metric and a 5 point bar. On day 3, at 380 conversations, the variant led by 7 points. The team shipped it that afternoon. Four weeks later resolution rate sits exactly where it did before the test. Traffic mix, staffing and the model version are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The 5 point bar was set too low to represent a real improvement in the resolution rate.

options.label: B
options.text: The 7 point lead rested on 380 conversations, far short of the sample the team committed to.

options.label: C
options.text: Resolution rate depends on how agents close tickets, so the measure drifts on its own.

options.label: D
options.text: The team measured resolution rate overall rather than separately for each billing issue type.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The 7 point lead rested on 380 conversations, far short of the sample the team committed to.

The team fixed 4,000 conversations and 14 days in advance, then read a verdict at 380 conversations on day 3. Early results swing widely, and a lead that large on a sample that small is the shape noise takes. Traffic, staffing and the model version all held afterwards, and the metric returned to its old level.

INCORRECT: The 5 point bar was set too low to represent a real improvement in the resolution rate.

A bar that is easy to clear does produce false wins, so questioning it is reasonable practice. The variant cleared this bar by 7 points, and the same bar over the full 4,000 conversations would have been a fair test. The failure sits in when the team stopped. Judge a threshold and a sample size as two separate questions.

INCORRECT: Resolution rate depends on how agents close tickets, so the measure drifts on its own.

Metrics that depend on human behaviour really do drift, and resolution rate is often one of them. Drift would show as movement in both directions, not a clean return to the exact pre-test level. The scenario also holds staffing constant. The evidence points at the measurement window, not the measure. Rule out the process before blaming the instrument.

INCORRECT: The team measured resolution rate overall rather than separately for each billing issue type.

Aggregate numbers hide segment level effects, and a per issue view often finds a gain the overall figure buries. Resolution rate was the metric the team named in advance and committed to judge against. It moved, then unmoved. Changing the breakdown would not have made 380 conversations enough. Granularity does not substitute for sample size.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical company runs an assistant that answers regulatory questions from an approved document library. Roughly 8 percent of answers are wrong. Some invent requirements the library never states. Others restate real requirements but apply them to the wrong product class. The team cannot tell the two apart from the answers alone, and three prompt rewrites moved the error rate by less than a point. Which change best separates the two causes?

options.label: A
options.text: Have a trained regulatory specialist check every answer against the approved document library before it reaches a user.

options.label: B
options.text: Have the assistant find a supporting quote for each claim after answering and retract what it cannot support.

options.label: C
options.text: Rebuild the library with smaller chunks and add a second embedding index over it.

options.label: D
options.text: Display a citation beside each answer so a reader can see which document it came from.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have the assistant find a supporting quote for each claim after answering and retract what it cannot support.

The retraction step sorts the errors for the team. A claim with no quote behind it was never in the library, and it disappears from the answer. A claim that keeps a genuine quote and is still wrong shows real grounding applied to the wrong product class. That points at the instructions, so the 8 percent splits into two named causes.

INCORRECT: Have a trained regulatory specialist check every answer against the approved document library before it reaches a user.

Expert review is the standard control in regulated work, and a specialist would catch both kinds of error. It catches them one answer at a time. It also produces no record of which kind each error was, so the team still cannot tell the two causes apart. A control that blocks bad output is not a diagnosis.

INCORRECT: Rebuild the library with smaller chunks and add a second embedding index over it.

Retrieval quality does drive answer quality, and reindexing is a real fix when chunking is the problem. Nothing here points at retrieval. The wrong product class errors restate requirements the library genuinely holds, so the right text was reaching the model. This rebuilds a stage the evidence does not accuse. Match the fix to the stage the symptoms name.

INCORRECT: Display a citation beside each answer so a reader can see which document it came from.

Citations are the documented route to auditable answers, so this sits close to correct and is easy to choose. Showing a source only says which document was consulted. It never checks that the quoted text supports the specific claim, and it never forces a retraction. Visibility without a verification step leaves the reader doing the checking.

questions.question: An internal assistant answers employee questions from a handbook library. On topics the handbooks cover, spot checks find it accurate. On topics they do not cover, such as sabbatical rules, it produces confident policy text that no handbook contains. Retrieval logs show zero matching passages returned for exactly those questions. The system prompt reads: always give the employee one clear, direct answer. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The retrieval step returns the wrong handbook passages for these particular questions.

options.label: B
options.text: The handbook library was chunked too small, so sabbatical rules were split across passages.

options.label: C
options.text: The prompt demands a clear answer every time and offers no permitted way to decline.

options.label: D
options.text: The model tier serving this assistant is too small to recognise when it lacks information.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The prompt demands a clear answer every time and offers no permitted way to decline.

Accuracy holds wherever the handbooks have content, so the model reads its sources correctly. On uncovered topics retrieval returns nothing, and the prompt still requires one clear, direct answer. Invention becomes the only reply that obeys that instruction, so the model complies rather than malfunctions. Explicit permission to say the handbooks do not cover this removes the trap.

INCORRECT: The retrieval step returns the wrong handbook passages for these particular questions.

Wrong context is the usual first suspect when answers go bad, and retrieval sits right before generation. The logs show zero passages returned for these questions, not irrelevant ones. Retrieval reported the gap honestly, and the invention happened after that. Read what the logs actually say before you assume a stage misbehaved.

INCORRECT: The handbook library was chunked too small, so sabbatical rules were split across passages.

Bad chunking is a real failure mode, and it does break topics into fragments retrieval then misses. Splitting a passage would still return something scoring above zero. The logs show nothing returned at all, so coverage and fragmentation left different traces here. A topic the corpus never held cannot be recovered by any chunking strategy.

INCORRECT: The model tier serving this assistant is too small to recognise when it lacks information.

Weaker models do hallucinate more, so tier is a fair thing to suspect. This assistant is accurate on every covered topic, which shows it handles its sources well. No tier will refuse an instruction that forbids refusing. Check what the instructions permit before you conclude the model cannot do better.

questions.question: A media company scores 40,000 archive articles for topic and tone every night. The job fires 40,000 standard requests, finishes in about five hours, and is now the largest line on the Claude bill. Editors read the results the next morning and nobody watches the run. Each request sends a 300 token instruction block plus the article text, which differs every time. Finance wants the cost down without moving to a weaker model. Which change best delivers that?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the nightly scoring job to the cheapest available model tier and accept slightly noisier topic labels.

options.label: B
options.text: Submit the 40,000 articles through the message batches API, which bills asynchronous work at a lower rate.

options.label: C
options.text: Shard the job across three regions so more requests run in parallel each night.

options.label: D
options.text: Cache the 300 token instruction block so its tokens are billed once per night.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Submit the 40,000 articles through the message batches API, which bills asynchronous work at a lower rate.

Every condition for asynchronous processing is present. The volume is large, editors read the results the next morning, and nobody watches the five hour run. Waiting therefore costs the company nothing. Batch submission bills the same model at a lower rate, so the saving arrives without touching capability. The only thing traded away is immediacy this workload never needed.

INCORRECT: Move the nightly scoring job to the cheapest available model tier and accept slightly noisier topic labels.

Tier selection is the first cost lever most teams reach for, and the saving is easy to forecast. Finance asked for the cost down without moving to a weaker model, and this trades away exactly what the question protects. It also degrades the labels editors read. A fix that breaks a stated constraint is not a candidate.

INCORRECT: Shard the job across three regions so more requests run in parallel each night.

Parallel execution is a genuine fix when a job runs too long, and five hours sounds long enough to worry about. Nobody is waiting on this run, and finishing sooner changes no bill. The same 40,000 requests are still charged at the same rate. Name the resource under pressure before you choose a lever.

INCORRECT: Cache the 300 token instruction block so its tokens are billed once per night.

Caching a repeated prefix is a real saving, and the instruction block is genuinely identical across requests. It is 300 tokens against full article text that differs every time. It can only reach a small slice of a bill the articles themselves drive. Size a saving against where the tokens actually sit.

questions.question: A support tool drafts email replies for agents. Last month the platform team lowered the output token ceiling to 300 to control spend. Agents now report drafts that stop in the middle of a sentence, and twice in the middle of a word. The prompt still asks for a full reply covering every point the customer raised. Short customer emails are unaffected. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Long customer threads push the request past the model's context window.

options.label: B
options.text: The streaming client drops the final chunk before it renders the completed draft.

options.label: C
options.text: The output ceiling cuts the reply at 300 tokens rather than making the model write less.

options.label: D
options.text: The prompt asks for every point the customer raised, so replies ramble past what agents need.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The output ceiling cuts the reply at 300 tokens rather than making the model write less.

The ceiling is a hard stop, not an instruction, so it never changes what the model sets out to write. The prompt still asks for a full reply covering every point. The model starts writing one, and generation halts at 300 tokens. That is why breaks land mid sentence and mid word, and why short emails finish untouched.

INCORRECT: Long customer threads push the request past the model's context window.

Context exhaustion is a real limit and long threads are the classic trigger, so the reasoning is sound in general. A request that exceeds the window fails or loses early content. It does not produce a clean draft that stops mid word. Read where the truncation lands to tell an input limit from an output limit.

INCORRECT: The streaming client drops the final chunk before it renders the completed draft.

Client side rendering bugs do swallow trailing text, and this would look identical to an agent reading the screen. The timing points elsewhere. Drafts began breaking after the team lowered the output ceiling, and short emails still complete. A display bug would not track the length of the reply. Let the change that preceded the symptom narrow the candidates.

INCORRECT: The prompt asks for every point the customer raised, so replies ramble past what agents need.

Over broad instructions really do produce bloated drafts, and this prompt is broad. A rambling reply would still finish its final sentence. The reported symptom is a break mid word that started when the ceiling dropped. Asking for brevity shortens what gets written, while a ceiling only cuts off what was already started.

questions.question:
A platform team must show Claude usage and cost inside the observability platform the company already runs. It has scoped six weeks to build a custom collector pipeline. Reviewing the request list, five of the six views are standard spend, token volume and model mix dashboards. The sixth breaks spend down by an internal cost centre code that exists only in the company's own systems. The vendor publishes a ready-made Claude usage and cost integration. Which two changes best deliver this?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Build the full custom collector pipeline as scoped so every view lives in one codebase.

options.label: B
options.text: Adopt the vendor's published Claude usage and cost integration for the five standard views.

options.label: C
options.text: Export usage monthly from the console and have finance rebuild the six views in a spreadsheet.

options.label: D
options.text: Write custom instrumentation only for the cost centre attribute the integration does not carry.

options.label: E
options.text: Replace the company's observability platform with one that ships richer Claude dashboards.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Adopt the vendor's published Claude usage and cost integration for the five standard views.

Spend, token volume and model mix are exactly the dashboards a ready-made integration provides. The company already runs the platform it targets. Adopting it delivers five of the six views with no pipeline to build or maintain. That leaves the team's six weeks free for the one requirement no vendor could have anticipated.

CORRECT: Write custom instrumentation only for the cost centre attribute the integration does not carry.

The cost centre code exists only inside the company, so no published integration could expose it. This is the one view the standard dashboards genuinely cannot serve. Scoping custom work to that single attribute is where engineering effort earns its cost. The build shrinks from six views to one gap nothing else can fill.

INCORRECT: Build the full custom collector pipeline as scoped so every view lives in one codebase.

One codebase is a defensible engineering preference and avoids depending on a vendor's roadmap. Five of the six views already ship in the published integration. This spends six weeks rebuilding work that is available immediately. Consistency is a weak reason to rebuild something that already exists. Check what you can adopt before you price what you would write.

INCORRECT: Export usage monthly from the console and have finance rebuild the six views in a spreadsheet.

Manual export is quick to start and puts numbers in front of finance this week with no engineering time. It moves recurring work onto another team every month. It also leaves the data outside the observability platform the request names, and spreadsheets go stale between exports. A fix that creates a standing manual task is a stopgap.

INCORRECT: Replace the company's observability platform with one that ships richer Claude dashboards.

Choosing the tool with the best native support is reasonable while a platform is still being selected. This platform is already in place across the company. The request is to surface Claude data inside it, not to run a migration, and a new platform would not supply the cost centre view. Solve the stated problem before changing its surroundings.

questions.question: A retail bank runs one safety classifier in front of two features. A branch-hours chatbot answers opening times. A loan explainer describes eligibility terms to applicants. Both call the classifier at the same block threshold, tuned last year. Support logs show the chatbot blocking 14 percent of harmless opening-time questions. The same month, compliance found 6 loan explanations stating terms the bank does not offer, all of which the classifier passed. It returns a verdict on every request. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The classifier's training data no longer matches the language customers use in these two features.

options.label: B
options.text: One threshold serves both features, too tight for one and too loose for the other.

options.label: C
options.text: The chatbot and the explainer send prompts in different formats, confusing the classifier.

options.label: D
options.text: The loan explainer needs a second classifier stage running after the first one already passes it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: One threshold serves both features, too tight for one and too loose for the other.

A blocked opening-time answer costs a customer a few seconds. A loan explanation stating terms the bank does not offer costs the bank a regulatory problem. One setting cannot sit correctly for both, and the evidence shows that exact split. The classifier is healthy and returns a verdict every time, so the shared threshold is what fits neither case.

INCORRECT: The classifier's training data no longer matches the language customers use in these two features.

Drift is a genuine failure mode, and a classifier tuned last year is old enough to suspect. Drift would scatter errors across both features in both directions. Here the errors sort cleanly by feature: over-blocking on one, under-blocking on the other. Evidence that sorts itself by feature points at configuration, not at the model behind the check.

INCORRECT: The chatbot and the explainer send prompts in different formats, confusing the classifier.

Format differences do degrade a shared classifier, and two features built by different teams often send different shapes. Confusion of that kind produces scattered, unpredictable verdicts. The logs instead show consistent over-blocking on one feature and consistent under-blocking on the other. A steady bias in two directions is a calibration signature, not a parsing one.

INCORRECT: The loan explainer needs a second classifier stage running after the first one already passes it.

Layering checks on the riskier feature is a reasonable instinct, and loans are clearly the riskier feature here. It adds a stage to compensate for a threshold that is simply set wrong. It also leaves the chatbot blocking 14 percent of harmless questions. Add machinery only after the setting you already have is correct.

questions.question: An asset manager keeps a risk register for its research assistant, ordered by how often each failure mode occurs. Controls were funded from the top of that list down. Tool timeouts sit first and now have retries and alerts. Confident wrong figures inside generated summaries sit last at 0.4 percent. That mode ran for seven months before a client caught it, because a wrong figure on a page looks exactly like a right one. Why did the register misdirect the spending?

options.label: A
options.text: The 0.4 percent rate for wrong figures was measured too low from the start.

options.label: B
options.text: The register ranked by frequency alone and never weighed how visibly each mode fails.

options.label: C
options.text: The register simply lists too few failure modes to work from.

options.label: D
options.text: Clients should have been asked to report suspect figures long before this one did.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The register ranked by frequency alone and never weighed how visibly each mode fails.

Tool timeouts announce themselves the moment they happen, so they get caught with or without a funded control. A wrong figure looks like a right one and hid for seven months. Ordering only by how often a mode occurs hands the money to the loudest modes. It leaves the silent ones bare, which is the pattern here.

INCORRECT: The 0.4 percent rate for wrong figures was measured too low from the start.

An understated rate does push a mode down a frequency-ordered list, so the reasoning holds together. Even a correct 0.4 percent would still rank last on frequency and still get funded last. The ordering rule is what buried it, not the number fed into that rule. Question the ranking criterion before you question its inputs.

INCORRECT: The register simply lists too few failure modes to work from.

A thin register really does leave gaps, and expanding one is standard governance advice. The mode that caused the loss was already on this register, and it was still funded last. Adding entries below it changes nothing about that. A list that ranks badly does not get better by growing longer.

INCORRECT: Clients should have been asked to report suspect figures long before this one did.

Client feedback is a real detection channel, and it is what eventually surfaced this problem. It puts the burden of catching a silent failure on the people that failure harms. It also arrives seven months late, and the register was meant to fund a control before then. A control that depends on the victim noticing is not a control.

questions.question: A claims processor sends a random 8 percent of decisions to a reviewer before they reach the claimant. The reviewer clears that share comfortably and reads each one with care. The model returns a confidence score with every decision. Last quarter the reviewer overturned 1 decision in 400. Complaints traced 23 wrong outcomes to decisions in the model's lowest confidence band, and the sample had caught none of them. Which change best improves the check?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the sample from 8 percent to a quarter of all decisions.

options.label: B
options.text: Route the model's lowest confidence band to the reviewer in place of the random sample.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask claimants to flag any decision they believe is wrong so it gets a second look.

options.label: D
options.text: Have the model re-check its own low confidence decisions before any of them go out.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Route the model's lowest confidence band to the reviewer in place of the random sample.

The system already scores its own confidence, and every one of the 23 wrong outcomes came from the lowest band. Sending that band instead of a flat slice puts the reviewer on the cases the model is least likely to get right. The reviewer's capacity is unchanged, and the overturn rate of 1 in 400 shows how little the random slice was earning.

INCORRECT: Raise the sample from 8 percent to a quarter of all decisions.

More coverage does catch more errors, and tripling a sample feels like real progress. A random quarter still picks mostly cases the model handles reliably, and it costs the reviewer three times the volume they currently read with care. The 23 wrong outcomes sat in a band the system can already name. Volume is a poor substitute for aim.

INCORRECT: Ask claimants to flag any decision they believe is wrong so it gets a second look.

Claimants are motivated readers and they did surface these 23 outcomes eventually. It moves detection to after the decision has already reached them, which is the moment the existing review was placed to prevent. It also depends on a claimant knowing the rules. A check that fires after delivery cannot do a pre-delivery job.

INCORRECT: Have the model re-check its own low confidence decisions before any of them go out.

Self-checking is cheap, instant, and uses the same confidence signal the better answer uses. The re-check runs on the same model that produced the low score, so it carries the same blind spot into the second pass. Human review exists precisely for what the model cannot judge about itself. A second opinion from the same source is one opinion.

questions.question: A hospital's innovation team wants to run patient summaries through a Claude developer tool. The organization signed a Business Associate Agreement with Anthropic two years ago. To clear privacy review the team switched data retention off, put the tool behind a private network, locked its settings so no engineer can change them, and required multi-factor sign-in. Privacy review still refuses to approve the tool. What should the architect tell the team?

options.label: A
options.text: No setting brings this tool under the agreement, which names its covered products itself.

options.label: B
options.text: The controls are sound but an independent audit has to confirm them first.

options.label: C
options.text: Retention has to be switched off at the organization level as well as on the tool.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the account team to add this developer tool to the agreement's covered product list.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: No setting brings this tool under the agreement, which names its covered products itself.

The team treated coverage as something its own controls could earn. The agreement lists the products it covers, and this developer tool is not one of them. Retention, networking, locked settings and sign-in rules change nothing about that list. Privacy review is reading the agreement, not the control checklist. The controls are good practice and still leave the tool outside the signed scope.

INCORRECT: The controls are sound but an independent audit has to confirm them first.

An audit is a familiar next step when a reviewer will not sign, and these controls would survive one. Privacy review has not disputed that the controls work, so confirming them answers a question nobody asked. The gap is contractual, and no amount of evidence about controls closes it. Proving a control is effective never proves it was the control required.

INCORRECT: Retention has to be switched off at the organization level as well as on the tool.

Retention is the control teams reach for first with patient data, and an organization-level setting does sound stronger than a per-tool one. Turning retention off in more places still leaves this tool outside the products the agreement names. The scope of a control is not the scope of an agreement. Widening a technical setting never widens a legal commitment.

INCORRECT: Ask the account team to add this developer tool to the agreement's covered product list.

Adding the tool to a list sounds like the direct fix, and account teams do handle contract scope. The set of products that can be covered is fixed by what the provider offers, not chosen per customer. A request that assumes an editable list stalls the work while the answer stays no. Check what a provider can offer before asking it to extend a contract.

questions.question: An Australian health insurer must keep member data stored and processed inside Australia under its regulator's rules. The team deployed its assistant on the default global endpoint of a supported cloud platform. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest, and the cloud account and billing are both registered in Sydney. The regulator asks where model processing actually happens, and nobody on the team can answer. Which change best meets the requirement?

options.label: A
options.text: Hold the encryption keys in Australia so stored data stays unreadable elsewhere.

options.label: B
options.text: Deploy the assistant on a regional endpoint for Australia rather than the global endpoint.

options.label: C
options.text: Register the cloud account and its billing in Australia so the whole deployment counts as local.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a contract clause requiring the provider to process member data only inside Australia.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Deploy the assistant on a regional endpoint for Australia rather than the global endpoint.

A regional endpoint guarantees that both storage and model processing stay inside the region you name. The global endpoint makes no such promise, which is exactly why nobody can answer the regulator. Switching the deployment turns an unanswerable question into a stated property of the architecture. The model and the application both stay as they are.

INCORRECT: Hold the encryption keys in Australia so stored data stays unreadable elsewhere.

Key location is a real control, and it does limit who can read data that travels. Encryption governs readability, not geography, and the regulator asked specifically where model processing happens. Encrypted data processed offshore is still processed offshore. Do not answer a location requirement with a confidentiality control.

INCORRECT: Register the cloud account and its billing in Australia so the whole deployment counts as local.

Account geography looks like deployment geography, and many teams treat the two as the same thing. The scenario already has the account and billing in Sydney, and the regulator still has no answer. Where an account is registered says nothing about where a request runs. Read what a setting actually governs before counting it as a control.

INCORRECT: Add a contract clause requiring the provider to process member data only inside Australia.

A written commitment is how many residency obligations get settled between companies, so reaching for one is reasonable. A clause describes an obligation without changing which infrastructure the request reaches. The deployment still points at the global endpoint after the clause is signed. Back a contractual promise with the technical setting that makes it true.

questions.question: A bank evaluates a mortgage document checker on four dimensions: extraction accuracy, completeness, tone and turnaround. Each is reported as one figure across the whole evaluation set, and all four clear their targets. Branches in three rural regions report that the checker misreads their locally issued income statements far more often than head office ever sees. Those statements are 2 percent of the evaluation set. Which change best surfaces what the current report hides?

options.label: A
options.text: Add two further evaluation dimensions so the report covers more of what quality means.

options.label: B
options.text: Report each dimension broken out by the document types and regions the checker serves.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the extraction accuracy target so the current suite stops passing.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the rural branches to report every misread statement so the team can track the rate.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Report each dimension broken out by the document types and regions the checker serves.

The rural statements are 2 percent of the set, so their failures barely move an average built across the whole set. That is why four figures clear their targets while three regions see something else. Splitting each figure by document type and region makes the gap visible in the report the bank already reads.

INCORRECT: Add two further evaluation dimensions so the report covers more of what quality means.

Broader coverage is usually right when an evaluation misses something real. This suite already measures four dimensions, and the failure sits inside one of them, extraction accuracy. It is not a dimension nobody thought to add. Two more whole-set averages would hide the same 2 percent. More dimensions do not help when the problem is who the average covers.

INCORRECT: Raise the extraction accuracy target so the current suite stops passing.

Tightening a target is a standard response to a suite that passes while users complain, and extraction is the right dimension to examine. A higher bar applied to the same whole-set average still lets 98 percent of the data carry the score. The rural cases stay invisible under it. Raising a bar cannot expose what the measurement never separated.

INCORRECT: Ask the rural branches to report every misread statement so the team can track the rate.

The branches already noticed the problem, so they are a working detection channel and the data would be real. It makes routine evaluation depend on affected users doing extra work on every case. The published report would still say what it says now. Measurement a team owns should not be outsourced to the people it fails.

questions.question:
A utility runs an assistant that approves or denies hardship payment plans. When a customer disputes a denial, an engineer opens the logs, finds the prompt and the reply, and writes an explanation from their own understanding of the rules. The logs hold the outcome and a timestamp, but not which account facts drove it. Two explanations have since been withdrawn as wrong. The regulator now requires every denied customer to receive a reason. Which two changes best meet that?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Train support staff to explain a denial over the phone whenever a customer calls to ask.

options.label: B
options.text: Record which account facts drove each decision at the moment that decision is made.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the full request and reply bodies for every decision in long-term storage.

options.label: D
options.text: Send that recorded reason to the customer as part of the denial notice itself.

options.label: E
options.text: Publish the eligibility rules on the website so customers can check their own situation.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Record which account facts drove each decision at the moment that decision is made.

The logs hold an outcome and a timestamp, so the reason must be rebuilt by hand every time. That is how two explanations came to be withdrawn. Capturing the deciding facts as the decision happens replaces reconstruction with a record. Only a design-time change to what gets written can do this, because the information is gone once the request finishes.

CORRECT: Send that recorded reason to the customer as part of the denial notice itself.

The requirement is that a denied customer receives a reason, not that a reason exists somewhere a team could retrieve it. Putting the captured facts into the notice closes the gap between having a rationale and giving one. It reaches every denied customer without waiting for a dispute, which is what separates transparency from a good audit trail.

INCORRECT: Train support staff to explain a denial over the phone whenever a customer calls to ask.

Phone contact is personal, quick to set up, and support staff already field these calls. It reaches only the customers who call, and staff would be rebuilding a reason from the same logs that produced two withdrawn explanations. The regulator asked that every denied customer receive a reason. A channel is not an explanation if nothing reliable flows through it.

INCORRECT: Keep the full request and reply bodies for every decision in long-term storage.

Complete records feel like the safe choice, and raw bodies hold more than the logs hold today. A reader still has to infer which facts mattered from a wall of text. That is the same reconstruction that produced two wrong explanations. It also stores far more customer data than the task needs. Storing everything is not the same as recording what matters.

INCORRECT: Publish the eligibility rules on the website so customers can check their own situation.

Published rules do help people understand a scheme, and policy transparency is worth having on its own. A customer reading general rules still cannot tell which facts in their own account produced their denial. The regulator asked for a reason per decision. Explaining a policy is not the same as explaining an outcome.

questions.question: A grocery chain ran six discovery workshops for a supplier invoice assistant. The requirement document holds 40 statements, all describing what the assistant should do. Build started in week 1. In week 5 the supplier data team says invoice images may not leave the country, a rule that predates the project by years. The document names no limit on data location, retention, cost or response time. Stakeholders confirm nobody ever asked them. Which change best prevents the next one?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a data location section to the requirement document and continue the build.

options.label: B
options.text: Run a discovery pass that asks each stakeholder directly what the system must not violate.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask each stakeholder to reread the requirement document and add anything they can see is missing.

options.label: D
options.text: Freeze the build until legal audits every policy the chain operates.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Run a discovery pass that asks each stakeholder directly what the system must not violate.

Six workshops produced 40 statements about behaviour and nothing about limits. The stakeholders say the country rule was never raised with them, and it has existed for years. It was available to anyone who asked. Asking what must not be violated, as its own deliberate question, turns a constraint nobody volunteers into a requirement the design can meet.

INCORRECT: Add a data location section to the requirement document and continue the build.

Writing the rule down is necessary and the team has to do it anyway. It closes this one gap and leaves retention, cost and response time equally unasked. The workshops produced 40 functional statements and no limits at all. Fix the process that missed a whole class of requirement, not only the instance that surfaced.

INCORRECT: Ask each stakeholder to reread the requirement document and add anything they can see is missing.

Stakeholders own the knowledge and a review pass costs the team almost nothing. People who did not volunteer a rule across six workshops will not spot its absence in a document either. A constraint feels obvious to whoever lives with it, which is why it went unmentioned. Absence is the hardest thing for anyone to review for.

INCORRECT: Freeze the build until legal audits every policy the chain operates.

A full audit would certainly surface the country rule, and a compliance miss in week 5 makes caution feel warranted. It stops delivery to answer a question a targeted discovery session answers in an afternoon. It also looks past the stakeholders who already hold the answer. Match the size of the investigation to the size of the gap.

questions.question: An architect proposed a single shared retrieval index for a publisher's four brands. The steering group approved it in twenty minutes. The team had considered one index per brand and rejected it on cost and duplicated maintenance, and recorded that reasoning internally. The presentation showed only the chosen design. Four months on, one brand's results bleed into another's, and the group calls it an oversight and asks why per-brand indexes were never considered. Which change best prevents this?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a slide listing the known risks of whichever design the architect recommends.

options.label: B
options.text: Present the rejected alternative and the reason it lost beside the recommendation.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a working prototype of both designs before the steering group decides.

options.label: D
options.text: Have the steering group sign a written risk register at the end of every meeting.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Present the rejected alternative and the reason it lost beside the recommendation.

The team did compare the two designs and did have a reason, and that reasoning stayed internal. Showing per-brand indexes and why cost and maintenance ruled them out gives the group the comparison it needs. It also converts cross-brand bleed from a later surprise into a cost the group knowingly accepted in the room.

INCORRECT: Add a slide listing the known risks of whichever design the architect recommends.

Naming risks is real progress on a twenty-minute approval, and it would have put cross-brand bleed on the record. A risk list says what might go wrong without saying what was given up to accept it. The group's complaint was that an alternative went unconsidered. A downside reads as accepted only when the option that avoided it sits beside it.

INCORRECT: Build a working prototype of both designs before the steering group decides.

Evidence beats argument, and a prototype would show the bleed before anyone approved anything. It spends weeks of build time on a decision the team already reasoned through correctly. The chosen design was the right call on cost and maintenance, and the gap sat in what got communicated. Do not spend engineering effort to fix a presentation problem.

INCORRECT: Have the steering group sign a written risk register at the end of every meeting.

A signature creates accountability and makes it harder for a group to disown a decision later. It asks the group to accept risks it still cannot weigh, because the alternative and its trade-offs remain unstated. A signature on an incomplete picture is not informed agreement. Give people what they need to judge a call before asking them to own it.

questions.question: A logistics client asked mid-build for the invoice assistant to also read handwritten delivery notes. The team liked the idea and folded it into current work. The signed agreement commits to a first release in 8 weeks at 95 percent extraction accuracy. Handwriting took 3 of the 6 remaining weeks, and printed-form accuracy fell to 91 percent while the team retuned. The client learned both facts in week 8. Which change best handles the next request?

options.label: A
options.text: Pad every future estimate so that a late request can be absorbed without moving the date.

options.label: B
options.text: Check the request against the committed agreement and put the trade-off to the client first.

options.label: C
options.text: Require the client to submit any scope request in writing on a standard form.

options.label: D
options.text: Decline any scope request that arrives after the build has already started.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Check the request against the committed agreement and put the trade-off to the client first.

The 8 weeks and the 95 percent were both commitments the client relied on. This request cost 3 weeks and 4 accuracy points against them. Raising that before taking the work on lets the client choose between handwriting, the date and the accuracy bar. That choice belongs to the person who set the priorities, not the team that spotted the conflict.

INCORRECT: Pad every future estimate so that a late request can be absorbed without moving the date.

Buffer is honest planning and most teams carry some, so this sounds like ordinary professionalism. It relies on every future request happening to fit the padding. This one consumed half the remaining schedule and moved a quality number as well. Slack absorbs small surprises; it does not replace a conversation about scope.

INCORRECT: Require the client to submit any scope request in writing on a standard form.

A written trail helps everyone remember what was asked and when, and forms do slow casual requests. The team already knew exactly what was asked here. It still absorbed the work without checking it against the agreement. A form changes how a request arrives, not what the team does next. Process paperwork does not substitute for a judgment call.

INCORRECT: Decline any scope request that arrives after the build has already started.

A firm rule protects a schedule and removes the argument each time, which is tempting after a week like this. It also refuses changes the client might happily trade the date for. The handwriting feature may be worth more than the original release date. The goal is an informed choice, not no choice.

questions.question: A team agreed a 3 second response target for a policy assistant at kickoff. Over the next nine months no change request was ever raised and the scope on paper never moved. Usage grew from 40 staff to 900, and the client's document set grew with its business. The team reported uptime every month and never mentioned the 3 second figure again. At acceptance the assistant answers in 6 seconds and the client calls it a breach. Why did this become a dispute?

options.label: A
options.text: No scheduled check-in existed, so the drift never met a moment to reset the number.

options.label: B
options.text: The 3 second target was never realistic for an assistant of this kind.

options.label: C
options.text: The team reported uptime in its monthly updates instead of the response time it committed to.

options.label: D
options.text: The client should have raised a change request as its own usage grew.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: No scheduled check-in existed, so the drift never met a moment to reset the number.

Nothing in this project triggered a conversation about the target. No change request was raised and the written scope never moved, so there was no event to hang a renegotiation on. Meanwhile usage rose from 40 staff to 900 and the document set grew. A commitment revisited only when someone files a change survives every change nobody files.

INCORRECT: The 3 second target was never realistic for an assistant of this kind.

Six seconds against a 3 second promise does suggest the promise was optimistic, and teams do commit to numbers early. The assistant served 40 staff at kickoff and the question reports no complaint then, so the target described that system accurately. A number right once can still go stale. Judge a commitment against the conditions it was made under.

INCORRECT: The team reported uptime in its monthly updates instead of the response time it committed to.

Reporting the wrong metric is a real reporting failure, and monthly updates were the obvious place to surface latency. Showing the number every month would have made the drift visible. Visibility is not agreement, and the client would still have held the kickoff figure. A report tells people what is happening, a review decides what should happen next.

INCORRECT: The client should have raised a change request as its own usage grew.

Clients do own their scope, and growth on their side is what moved the load. The team holds the performance commitment and the knowledge of what load does to it, so the duty to reopen the number sits with them. Push an obligation onto the party without the information and it never gets met. Own the review of any number you committed to.

questions.question: A retailer handed its search assistant to a new platform team with a 62 page design document. The document is accurate and complete. Setup steps sit in section 9. The three settings a team actually tunes sit in section 14. The two failure modes behind most incidents are described inside a discussion of options the original team rejected. The new team asks the original architect four questions a week, and every answer is already in the document. Which change best fixes this?

options.label: A
options.text: Have the original architect hold a weekly office hour for the new platform team.

options.label: B
options.text: Lift the setup steps, key settings and common failure checks into their own section.

options.label: C
options.text: Cut the discussion of rejected options so the document is shorter and easier to read.

options.label: D
options.text: Rebuild the document as a wiki with one page per existing section.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Lift the setup steps, key settings and common failure checks into their own section.

Every answer the new team needs is already written down, so nothing is missing. What defeats them is that operating knowledge sits across sections 9 and 14 and inside a rejected-options discussion. Collecting the actionable material into one place gives a builder a section to open instead of 62 pages to search.

INCORRECT: Have the original architect hold a weekly office hour for the new platform team.

It formalises what already happens and gets answers flowing predictably, which beats four ad hoc interruptions. It makes one person the permanent route to information the document already holds, and that person eventually moves on. The questions keep coming because the answers are hard to find. A standing meeting is not a fix for a findability problem.

INCORRECT: Cut the discussion of rejected options so the document is shorter and easier to read.

Length is clearly part of the problem, and a rejected-options section looks like the obvious thing to lose. That section records why the design has the shape it does, which a team extending the system needs. It also holds two of the failure modes today. Reorganise material before deleting it, or you trade one gap for another.

INCORRECT: Rebuild the document as a wiki with one page per existing section.

Search and linking genuinely help a large document, and 62 pages is large enough to justify the move. Splitting the same structure across pages preserves the arrangement that hid the setup steps and the failure modes. The new team would search 62 pages in a different tool. Changing the container does not change what is buried inside it.

It makes one person the permanent route to information the document already holds, and that person eventually moves on. The questions keep coming because the answers are hard to find. A standing meeting is not a fix for a findability problem.

INCORRECT: Cut the discussion of rejected options so the document is shorter and easier to read.

Length is clearly part of the problem, and a rejected-options section looks like the obvious thing to lose. That section records why the design has the shape it does, which a team extending the system needs. It also holds two of the failure modes today. Reorganise material before deleting it, or you trade one gap for another.

INCORRECT: Rebuild the document as a wiki with one page per existing section.

Search and linking genuinely help a large document, and 62 pages is large enough to justify the move. Splitting the same structure across pages preserves the arrangement that hid the setup steps and the failure modes. The new team would search 62 pages in a different tool. Changing the container does not change what is buried inside it.

questions.question: A bank's architecture document was written at handover 14 months ago and has not changed since. In that time the retrieval store was replaced, a reconciliation agent was added and two endpoints were retired. A new engineer followed the document, pointed a nightly job at a retired endpoint, and the job failed silently for nine days. Six engineers hold edit access to the document. None was ever named as responsible for it. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The engineer should have verified the endpoint was live before pointing a job at it.

options.label: B
options.text: Nobody owned keeping it current, so it drifted into describing a system that no longer exists.

options.label: C
options.text: The document was too detailed to keep in step with a system that changes this often.

options.label: D
options.text: Six engineers holding edit access is too many for one architecture document.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Nobody owned keeping it current, so it drifted into describing a system that no longer exists.

Three architectural changes landed over 14 months and none of them reached the document. That is what happens when six people can edit something and nobody is answerable for it. A stale document does more harm than a missing one, because the engineer had no reason to doubt it. An explicit owner and an update trigger are what keep it trustworthy.

INCORRECT: The engineer should have verified the endpoint was live before pointing a job at it.

Verifying before you build on something is sound practice and would have caught this. It asks a new engineer to distrust the handover document the bank gave them for that exact purpose. A document nobody can trust has no use at all. The failure sits in what the document said. Do not hold a reader responsible for a source's accuracy.

INCORRECT: The document was too detailed to keep in step with a system that changes this often.

Detailed documents really are harder to maintain, and three changes in 14 months is a live system. Detail did not stop the updates, since a shorter document naming the same two endpoints would have gone equally stale. Nobody was assigned to make any edit at any level of detail. Effort explains slow updates, never their complete absence.

INCORRECT: Six engineers holding edit access is too many for one architecture document.

Wide write access does invite inconsistency, so tightening it looks like reasonable governance. Access was never the obstacle here, because all six could have made the edit and none did. Restricting the list would leave fewer people equally unassigned. Permission to act is not the same thing as responsibility to act.

questions.question:
A media group built a headline suggestion assistant three years ago for its print desk. That desk closed 14 months ago. The assistant still runs, still bills every month, and two editors on other desks use it occasionally. The original plan covered discovery, design, launch and monitoring, and ends there. Nobody can name who would decide to switch it off. Which two changes best fix the pattern this exposes?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Switch the assistant off now to stop the monthly charge from continuing.

options.label: B
options.text: Set a scheduled review point at which the system's continued need is decided.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the finance team to flag any service whose monthly cost looks unjustified.

options.label: D
options.text: Write down what retiring it involves, including what depends on it and where users go.

options.label: E
options.text: Rebuild the assistant for the digital desk so the money already spent earns its keep back.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Set a scheduled review point at which the system's continued need is decided.

The plan runs from discovery to monitoring and then stops. That is why an obsolete tool kept running for 14 months with nobody empowered to end it. A dated review gives that decision an owner and a moment. It also turns continued operation into something chosen on purpose rather than something nobody revisited.

CORRECT: Write down what retiring it involves, including what depends on it and where users go.

Nobody can name who would switch it off, and two editors would be stranded if someone did. The decision has no safe path even when it is obvious. Recording the dependencies and where remaining users move makes retirement executable rather than theoretical. A review point with no exit plan behind it produces another deferral.

INCORRECT: Switch the assistant off now to stop the monthly charge from continuing.

The desk it served closed 14 months ago, so the spend is hard to defend. Two editors still use the tool and nothing has been offered to them instead, so this breaks live work. It also leaves the next system with the same missing exit. Do not treat one abrupt shutdown as a substitute for a plan.

INCORRECT: Ask the finance team to flag any service whose monthly cost looks unjustified.

Finance sees the bill and is well placed to notice spend nobody defends, so the signal would be real. It makes retirement a cost conversation started from outside the system, often years late. The question is whether the tool still serves a purpose. Cost is a symptom of a missing lifecycle decision, not the decision itself.

INCORRECT: Rebuild the assistant for the digital desk so the money already spent earns its keep back.

Reusing built software is efficient thinking, and two editors already find it useful enough to keep opening. It commits new investment before anyone has decided the tool should exist at all. That is the decision this group has never made. Sunk cost is a poor argument for further cost.

questions.question: A fintech requires that Claude Code never run its deployment command against production. The platform team wrote that deny rule into each repository's project settings file. An audit across 40 repositories finds the rule present in 34 and absent in 6. Two leads deleted it during a release crunch. Four repositories were forked before the rule existed. Which change best makes the rule hold everywhere?

options.label: A
options.text: Add the rule to the repository template and have each lead confirm it every month.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the deny rule into managed settings, which no project or user file can override.

options.label: C
options.text: State the rule in project memory so Claude Code reads it at the start of every session.

options.label: D
options.text: Run a nightly job that scans all 40 repositories and opens a ticket when the rule is missing.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Move the deny rule into managed settings, which no project or user file can override.

Managed settings sit at the highest scope and cannot be overridden from a project or user file. Neither a deleting lead nor an old fork can drop the rule from there. Permission lists merge across scopes rather than replacing one another, so teams can still add their own denies on top. The rule then holds on all 40 repositories with nobody maintaining it.

INCORRECT: Add the rule to the repository template and have each lead confirm it every month.

Templates do carry a rule into new repositories, and a monthly confirmation creates a paper trail. Neither reaches the two repositories where a lead deleted the rule under deadline pressure. Both leave removal available to the same person. The rule stays only as strong as the discipline of whoever owns the file. A control anyone can delete is not enforcement.

INCORRECT: State the rule in project memory so Claude Code reads it at the start of every session.

Written guidance is quick to add and the model does read project memory, so this feels like it reaches every session. It relies on the model choosing to follow a sentence, where the team needs a deployment command refused outright. It also lives in a file the same leads can edit. Never express a hard restriction as guidance the tool may weigh.

INCORRECT: Run a nightly job that scans all 40 repositories and opens a ticket when the rule is missing.

Continuous detection is real coverage and it would have caught all 6 gaps within a day. It reports a missing rule rather than preventing one, so a repository stays unprotected while the ticket sits open. The audit already found the gaps and the gaps persisted. Detection tells you a control failed; it does not make the control hold.

questions.question: A 45 engineer group shares four skills, two agents and a pre-commit hook that everyone is expected to run. Each engineer copies the files from a wiki page into their own configuration directory. A bug in the hook was fixed six weeks ago, and 19 machines still run the old version. New joiners assemble the set by hand and routinely miss a file. Which change best fixes this?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask every engineer to recopy the files from the wiki whenever the page changes.

options.label: B
options.text: Package the shared set as a plugin and serve it from a private marketplace.

options.label: C
options.text: Commit the configuration directory into each repository alongside the code.

options.label: D
options.text: Build an internal tool that syncs the current version of the files onto every machine nightly.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Package the shared set as a plugin and serve it from a private marketplace.

A plugin gives the set an install step and a version, which per-developer copies lack, and a private marketplace keeps distribution internal. Engineers install rather than assemble, so a new joiner cannot miss a file. The six-week-old hook fix then reaches every machine as a released version, instead of waiting on 45 people to recopy a page.

INCORRECT: Ask every engineer to recopy the files from the wiki whenever the page changes.

It is the cheapest possible change and it names the exact gap, since the 19 stale machines never recopied. It keeps 45 people manually mirroring a page, which is what produced the drift over six weeks. Nothing tells an engineer that the page moved. A process that depends on everyone noticing will always leave a tail behind.

INCORRECT: Commit the configuration directory into each repository alongside the code.

Version control is the natural home for shared files, and checking them in does put them under review. It scopes the set to whichever repository a developer has open. These skills and agents are meant to hold across every project the group touches, and each repository still drifts on its own. Match the distribution boundary to the scope the setup covers.

INCORRECT: Build an internal tool that syncs the current version of the files onto every machine nightly.

Automated distribution is the right instinct and it would close the 19 machine gap reliably. It rebuilds installation, versioning and update delivery that the plugin system already provides. The group then owns and maintains that tool forever. Check what your tooling already ships before writing the same capability yourself.
