questions.question: A payments team rebuilt its release process around an AI assistant. The assistant writes the release notes, drafts the rollback plan and fills the change record. The old manual templates were deleted the week the new process landed. During a two hour provider outage no release shipped and three engineers waited it out. All three have run releases by hand for years and know every step. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The team had no second model provider configured to fail over to.

options.label: B
options.text: The redesign deleted the manual path, so the process had nothing to degrade to.

options.label: C
options.text: The engineers no longer knew the release steps well enough to run them by hand.

options.label: D
options.text: The outage should have been raised as an incident rather than waited out for two hours.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The redesign deleted the manual path, so the process had nothing to degrade to.

The templates went when the new process landed, which left one route through a release and no slower route beside it. All three engineers know the steps, so the knowledge survived and only the path disappeared. A workflow rebuilt around a tool needs a defined way to proceed without it. Otherwise an outage of any length stops the work completely.

INCORRECT: The team had no second model provider configured to fail over to.

Provider redundancy is a real availability control and would have carried this particular outage. It answers only the case where a substitute service exists and is reachable. Any dependency can still fail in ways no failover covers, and the workflow would stall again. Redundancy reduces how often you need a fallback; it does not replace one.

INCORRECT: The engineers no longer knew the release steps well enough to run them by hand.

Skill fade is a genuine cost of automation and it explains plenty of stalled workflows. The scenario says all three have run releases by hand for years. The knowledge was in the room the whole time, and what they lacked was a sanctioned way to use it. Check whether the obstacle is capability or permission before blaming skills.

INCORRECT: The outage should have been raised as an incident rather than waited out for two hours.

Two hours of blocked releases does deserve an incident, and raising one would have drawn attention sooner. An incident coordinates a response to a stall without giving anyone a way to ship, since the manual templates were gone either way. Escalation moves a problem up a chain; it does not create the option that was missing.

questions.question: A retailer generates product descriptions for merchant listings. A merchant reported that the size chart in their descriptions was wrong. Support treated it as one ticket, apologised and regenerated that merchant's 40 listings. Eleven days later a second merchant reported the same fault. A check then showed every description written since a template change 12 days earlier carried the wrong chart, roughly 90,000 listings. Which change best improves the next report?

options.label: A
options.text: Regenerate every listing in the entire catalogue whenever a single merchant reports a bad description.

options.label: B
options.text: Establish whether a report is isolated or systemic before choosing the response.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask merchants to check their own descriptions after every template change goes out.

options.label: D
options.text: Test every template change against a representative sample of live listings before it is deployed.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Establish whether a report is isolated or systemic before choosing the response.

Nothing in the first ticket was hard to diagnose, and support fixed the merchant's 40 listings correctly. What nobody asked was how many other listings shared the cause. A template change 12 days earlier would have answered that immediately. Scope decides the response: one merchant's data needs a regeneration, a bad template needs pulling for everyone.

INCORRECT: Regenerate every listing in the entire catalogue whenever a single merchant reports a bad description.

It guarantees a systemic fault never spreads again, which is exactly what went wrong across these 11 days. It also spends a full catalogue regeneration on the many reports that really are one merchant's data problem. The first ticket here looked ordinary because most of them are. Treating every report as the worst case is as untargeted as treating none that way.

INCORRECT: Ask merchants to check their own descriptions after every template change goes out.

Merchants know their products better than anyone and would spot a wrong size chart quickly. It makes the people harmed by a fault responsible for detecting it, and the second merchant took 11 days to speak up. Reporting was never the bottleneck, because the first report was already in hand. Never build detection on the goodwill of the people you are failing.

INCORRECT: Test every template change against a representative sample of live listings before it is deployed.

Pre-deployment testing is sound practice and would very likely have caught this template. It works on the stage before a fault escapes, and the question is what the team does once a report has arrived. A test that ran two weeks ago cannot triage today's ticket. Fix the stage the question is actually asking about.

questions.question: A logistics team runs an address parsing assistant. Three times in five months a batch of shipments went to the wrong depot, each time because the assistant mishandled the same rare address format. Each time an engineer found the cause within a day, patched the prompt, reprocessed the batch and closed the ticket. The evaluation suite has not changed since launch, and no rule blocks the malformed output. Why does this keep recurring?

options.label: A
options.text: The rare format keeps changing, so each patch addressed a different variant of it.

options.label: B
options.text: Each resolution stopped the symptom without updating the check that let it through.

options.label: C
options.text: The engineers who patched the prompt never wrote up what they changed or why.

options.label: D
options.text: The assistant should be replaced with a deterministic address parsing library.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Each resolution stopped the symptom without updating the check that let it through.

Every incident ended with a working patch, so diagnosis and repair were never the problem. The evaluation suite still holds no case for this format, and no rule blocks the malformed output. Nothing stands between the next occurrence and the wrong depot. A resolution is finished when the check that missed the failure can catch it, not when the symptom stops.

INCORRECT: The rare format keeps changing, so each patch addressed a different variant of it.

Shifting input really does defeat narrow fixes, and address data from the wild is where you expect it. The scenario names the same rare format in all three incidents, so the input held still while the fixes did not. A moving target and an unguarded one look alike in a summary. Read whether the trigger changed before assuming the fix was too narrow.

INCORRECT: The engineers who patched the prompt never wrote up what they changed or why.

Undocumented fixes do cost the next responder time, and three engineers working alone invites exactly that. Each incident was diagnosed within a day regardless, so the missing write-up cost little here. Notes would have helped a human find the cause faster and still let the batch reach the wrong depot. Documentation shortens a response; it does not prevent one.

INCORRECT: The assistant should be replaced with a deterministic address parsing library.

Rule-based parsing is predictable and address formats are a well-solved problem, so this is a defensible opinion. It rebuilds a working component to avoid a failure an evaluation case would have caught. A library also ships its own gaps, with no check watching for them. Do not swap a component out while the process that missed its failures stays unchanged.

The assistant should be replaced with a deterministic address parsing library.

CORRECT: Each resolution stopped the symptom without updating the check that let it through.

Every incident ended with a working patch, so diagnosis and repair were never the problem. The evaluation suite still holds no case for this format, and no rule blocks the malformed output. INCORRECT: The rare format keeps changing, so each patch addressed a different variant of it.

questions.question:
A utility built a Claude assistant that drafts outage notices. It shipped nine months ago. Usage sits at 40 notices a month against a team that writes 900. Control room staff say the drafts read well. The assistant opens from the same console they use all shift, and the usage figure comes from the notice system rather than from the assistant. The build started from a request to put Claude in the control room. No workflow, no metric and no owner were named.
What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The build never named a workflow or a cost, so nothing in the room depends on it.

options.label: B
options.text: The assistant sits outside the tools the control room already uses, so reaching it costs a step.

options.label: C
options.text: Two training sessions were not enough for a team writing this many notices.

options.label: D
options.text: Usage reporting counts only notices sent from the assistant's own screen.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The build never named a workflow or a cost, so nothing in the room depends on it.
Nine months and 40 notices a month is a tool nobody has to use. The brief named no workflow, no metric and no owner, so no part of the control room's day was redesigned around it. Staff who like the drafts still have no reason to change what they do. A design that traces to no stated problem leaves adoption optional.

INCORRECT: The assistant sits outside the tools the control room already uses, so reaching it costs a step.
Friction does hold usage down, and an extra window is a common reason a good tool goes unused. The question says the assistant opens from the same console the staff use all shift, so there is no extra step to pay. Access was never the barrier. Rule out the cheap explanations the question has already closed.

INCORRECT: Two training sessions were not enough for a team writing this many notices.
Thin training does slow adoption, and two sessions for a large team sounds light. Staff report that the drafts read well, which means they have used the tool and can judge its output. They know how it works and still do not reach for it. Ability to use a tool is not the same as a reason to use it.

INCORRECT: Usage reporting counts only notices sent from the assistant's own screen.
Measurement gaps do make real adoption look worse than it is, and that is worth checking early. The question states the figure comes from the notice system rather than from the assistant, so it counts notices however they were written. The 40 is the real number. Check where a figure is measured before you argue the figure is wrong.

questions.question:
A bank offers one explain this charge feature. The mobile team and the web team each call Claude from their own code, each holding its own prompt text, its own model identifier and its own parsing. A customer who asks about the same charge in both apps gets two different explanations, and one of them names a fee the other does not. Both apps read the same charge record from the same service, and in the test both read it in the same second.
What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: One feature is implemented twice, so the two apps run different prompts and different parsing.

options.label: B
options.text: The two apps read the charge record at different moments, so their copies of the data have drifted.

options.label: C
options.text: The model returns different wording on every call that it receives.

options.label: D
options.text: The mobile app is one release behind, so it runs an older version of the feature.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: One feature is implemented twice, so the two apps run different prompts and different parsing.
The customer meets one product and the bank built two. Each app holds its own prompt text, its own model identifier and its own parsing code. Two different prompts over the same record produce two different explanations, and different parsing decides which fee survives into the answer. One feature built twice is two features that happen to share a name.

INCORRECT: The two apps read the charge record at different moments, so their copies of the data have drifted.
Stale data is the usual reason two screens disagree, and it is the first thing most teams check. The question states both apps read the same record from the same service, in the same second during the test. The input was identical and the outputs were not. When the input is held constant, the difference sits in what each path does with it.

INCORRECT: The model returns different wording on every call that it receives.
Wording does vary between calls, so two answers are rarely identical word for word. Varied wording would not make one answer name a fee the other omits, because both calls would be working from the same instructions. A missing fee is a content difference, not a phrasing one. Separate what varies by nature from what varies by design.

INCORRECT: The mobile app is one release behind, so it runs an older version of the feature.
Release skew between two clients is real, and it explains plenty of inconsistencies. There is no shared version of this feature to be behind on, because each team wrote its own prompt and parsing from the start. Both apps are current and still disagree. Version skew needs a shared artifact, and duplicated code has none.

questions.question:
A shared services agent built on Claude handled contract review and tax filing for two years at a tool selection error rate of 6 percent. Last quarter the team added 14 employment policy tools to the same agent. Employment requests tripled the agent's traffic. Since then the error rate per contract review request has risen from 6 percent to 19 percent, and the tax filing rate has risen too. The employment tools themselves work correctly.
What best explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: Three domains now sit in one agent, so tools the request never needed still look plausible.

options.label: B
options.text: Employment requests tripled the traffic, so the agent now handles far more work than it did.

options.label: C
options.text: The new tools were added without rerunning the older regression tests.

options.label: D
options.text: The agent's context window now carries conversation history from three domains in every single session.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Three domains now sit in one agent, so tools the request never needed still look plausible.
Contract review and tax filing ran at 6 percent for two years with two domains in the agent. Adding a third domain is the only change, and both original domains got worse. The agent now chooses from a set that spans work the request never mentioned. Widening what one agent must choose between raises the chance of a wrong pick everywhere.

Source: Multiagent orchestration

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Employment requests tripled the traffic, so the agent now handles far more work than it did.
Load does break systems, and a tripling is a large change to absorb. The figures quoted are error rates per request, not counts, so a bigger denominator cannot move them. Contract review requests fail three times as often each. Read whether a figure is a rate or a total before you explain it with volume.

INCORRECT: The new tools were added without rerunning the older regression tests.
Skipped tests do let regressions through, and a large addition is exactly when teams skip them. Tests would have found this problem sooner and would not have caused it, because the older tools were not changed. The behavior would be the same with a full test run. A missing check explains a late discovery, never a new failure.

INCORRECT: The agent's context window now carries conversation history from three domains in every single session.
Crowded context does degrade reasoning, and three domains sounds like a lot to hold. The question names one change, 14 added tools, and reports no change to what a session carries. What grew is the tool set, not the transcript. Name the thing that actually grew before blaming the context window.

questions.question:
A council has drafted its letters with Claude for two years. Every quarter the team edits the prompt using the complaints received that quarter, keeping the previous wording and adding to it. Each edit fixes the named complaints, and within a month the same three problems return. Officers correct about a quarter of every letter before sending it, and those corrections live only in the sent letter. Nobody holds a record of what officers change.
What is the underlying cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The corrections officers make are never recorded, so each edit starts from complaints alone.

options.label: B
options.text: The prompt grows by addition each quarter, so earlier instructions and newer ones now conflict.

options.label: C
options.text: The complaints come from a small and untypical group of officers.

options.label: D
options.text: Two years is long enough for the letter templates to have changed underneath the prompt.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The corrections officers make are never recorded, so each edit starts from complaints alone.
Officers touch a quarter of every letter, which is the richest signal this system produces, and all of it is discarded. The team works instead from complaints, which arrive late and cover only what somebody bothered to report. The same three problems return because nothing carries them into the next edit. A system improves from its own use only when that use is captured.

INCORRECT: The prompt grows by addition each quarter, so earlier instructions and newer ones now conflict.
Prompts do rot as they grow, and conflicting instructions produce exactly this kind of recurring fault. A prompt written from scratch each quarter would show the same pattern, because the input to every version is the same thin complaint list. The problem arrives before the prompt is written. Look at what a process is fed before you examine how it edits.

INCORRECT: The complaints come from a small and untypical group of officers.
A narrow feedback source does skew what gets fixed, and complaint channels usually are narrow. Even complaints from every officer would still miss the corrections nobody writes down, which is where the daily evidence sits. Widening the channel does not capture the edits. The gap is in what is recorded, not in who speaks up.

INCORRECT: Two years is long enough for the letter templates to have changed underneath the prompt.
Drift between a prompt and the documents around it is real and easy to miss. A template change would produce new problems rather than the same three returning every quarter after each fix. The pattern points at a loop that never closes. Match the shape of the symptom to the shape of the cause you propose.

questions.question:
An architecture board is reviewing a design for an invoice coding service built on Claude. The document specifies the prompt, the model choice and how the reply is parsed, in detail. It does not say how invoices arrive, who checks them on the way in, where coded invoices go, or what happens when a code is rejected. The board must decide what to require before the build starts.
What should the architect recommend?

options.label: A
options.text: Require the design to define how invoices arrive and where coded invoices go.

options.label: B
options.text: Require monitoring and alerting on the model call before the build starts.

options.label: C
options.text: Require a worked example of the prompt and its parsed reply for every invoice type the service will meet.

options.label: D
options.text: Require the team to name an owner for the service before the build starts.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Require the design to define how invoices arrive and where coded invoices go.
Three quarters of this document describes one stage. Arrival, checking, delivery and rejection are all undefined, and each of them is a place work can be lost with nobody responsible for it. Naming those stages now is cheaper than discovering them in production. A design is finished when it covers the whole path, not when its hardest stage is detailed.

INCORRECT: Require monitoring and alerting on the model call before the build starts.
Instrumentation is a fair thing for a board to require, and no design should ship blind. It puts a watch on the one stage the document already describes in detail, and reports nothing about the stages nobody has designed. An invoice lost before the call never reaches the monitor. Watch the part you understand least, not the part you wrote down best.

INCORRECT: Require a worked example of the prompt and its parsed reply for every invoice type the service will meet.
Worked examples do sharpen a specification, and they catch parsing gaps early. They add depth to the stage that is already the most detailed part of the document, while arrival and delivery stay blank. The board would approve a deeper description of the same third. More detail in one place is not coverage.

INCORRECT: Require the team to name an owner for the service before the build starts.
Clear ownership matters, and an unowned service does decay. Naming an owner puts a person against a design that still does not say how invoices reach it or where they go. The owner inherits the same gaps. Assigning responsibility for a decision is not the same as making it.

questions.question:
An insurer is designing a premium validation service. Every submission carries the same nine fields and needs the same four regulatory checks, run in the same order, set by a rule unchanged for three years. Two new submission types arrive next year and use the same four checks. The team is choosing between a fixed sequence of calls to Claude and a Claude agent that plans its own steps.
What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Build a fixed sequence of calls, since the work is identical on every submission.

options.label: B
options.text: Build it as an agent, so the design already absorbs the two new submission types.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a fixed sequence, then have an agent review each result.

options.label: D
options.text: Build an agent and cap the number of steps it may take on any one submission.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Build a fixed sequence of calls, since the work is identical on every submission.
Nine fields, four checks, one order, unchanged for three years. Nothing in that description varies, so there is nothing for a planner to decide. A fixed sequence runs the same path every time, costs the same every time, and can be tested case by case. Give a task the structure its variability earns, and this task earns none.

Source: Building effective agents

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Build it as an agent, so the design already absorbs the two new submission types.
Designing for known change is good practice, and two new types next year is worth planning for. The question states those types use the same four checks, so they need the same fixed path. Flexibility is being bought against a change that is not coming. Read what the future work actually requires before paying for headroom.

INCORRECT: Build a fixed sequence, then have an agent review each result.
A reviewing step sounds like cheap insurance on top of a sound design. It adds a call whose behavior varies to a process the insurer needs to be identical, and gives the review nothing to compare against. Cost and variance both rise. Do not add an unpredictable step to protect a predictable one.

INCORRECT: Build an agent and cap the number of steps it may take on any one submission.
A step cap does bound the worst case, and it is the right control when an agent is genuinely needed. The cap limits how badly the planning can go and still leaves the planning in place for work that never differs. The variance is reduced, not removed. Bounding an unnecessary mechanism is more expensive than not building it.

questions.question:
A firm is designing a pipeline of two Claude agents. A screening agent reads 60 supplier filings and records what it found. A drafting agent then writes a one-page recommendation. The team has written both prompts. The drafting agent's prompt tells it to use the screening results above. Nothing in the design says how those results travel from the first agent to the second.
Which two changes best address this?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Define what the screening agent must return, as a structured record the coordinator can read.

options.label: B
options.text: Have the coordinator place that record in the drafting agent's own input.

options.label: C
options.text: Let the drafting agent call the screening agent whenever it needs a detail.

options.label: D
options.text: Give both agents the same credentials and the same working folder.

options.label: E
options.text: Tell the drafting agent in its prompt to rely only on what it was given.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Define what the screening agent must return, as a structured record the coordinator can read.
A handoff needs something to hand over. Today the screening agent records what it found in whatever shape it likes, and no other component can depend on that. Naming the fields makes the output an artifact rather than a side effect. Once the record has a defined shape, the coordinator can check it arrived and the drafter can rely on it.

CORRECT: Have the coordinator place that record in the drafting agent's own input.
The drafting agent reads its own input and nothing else. A record that exists somewhere the drafter does not read is the same as no record at all. Putting it in the input is the step that turns two prompts into one pipeline. Data reaches an agent because something put it there, never because an earlier agent produced it.

Source: Multiagent orchestration

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Let the drafting agent call the screening agent whenever it needs a detail.

questions.question:
A team is finalizing a research agent that runs on Claude. The design sets a daily spend cap, a target that every run returns inside four minutes, and a rule that unanswerable requests receive a plain no-result reply. The agent searches, reads and searches again until it has enough to answer. Nothing in the design says when to stop. About once a week a request arrives that no source can answer.
What will this design fail to deliver?

options.label: A
options.text: A reply inside four minutes on the weekly request that no source can answer.

options.label: B
options.text: The plain no-result reply, because the run ends at the first empty search.

options.label: C
options.text: The daily spend cap, because a single run will exhaust the whole day's budget before noon.

options.label: D
options.text: Accurate answers on the requests that do have a matching source.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: A reply inside four minutes on the weekly request that no source can answer.
The agent keeps searching until it has enough to answer, and on this request it never will. With no stopping condition the loop has only the spend cap to end it, and that cap is a day long. Four minutes passes with the run still going. A loop that ends only when money runs out cannot hold a time target.

Source: Building effective agents

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The plain no-result reply, because the run ends at the first empty search.
An empty search does look like the natural place for a loop to give up, and many designs stop there. This design says nothing about when to stop, so an empty result leads to another search rather than a reply. The loop treats no result as a reason to keep going. Do not assume a termination rule the design never wrote down.

INCORRECT: The daily spend cap, because a single run will exhaust the whole day's budget before noon.
One run consuming a day of budget is exactly what an unbounded loop does, so the reasoning is close. A cap is not exceeded by being used, and the question asks what the design fails to deliver rather than what it consumes. The cap holds and the day's other work does not run. Distinguish a limit that is breached from a limit that is spent.

INCORRECT: Accurate answers on the requests that do have a matching source.
Runaway behavior on one path often does damage the others, which makes this worth ruling out. A request with a matching source reaches an answer and stops, because the agent has enough to answer. Those runs were never the problem. Check whether a fault has a path to the case you are worried about.

questions.question:
A council's benefits assistant must meet four stated requirements: every answer cites the rule it applied, cost per answered question stays at or below 4 cents, 90 percent of answers return within 3 seconds, and out-of-scope questions are declined. To raise citation accuracy the team adds a second call to Claude that re-reads the rule. On the pilot, cost per answered question is 6.1 cents, p90 latency is 2.4 seconds, every answer cites the rule a caseworker confirmed, and out-of-scope questions are declined.
Which stated requirement does this design fail?

options.label: A
options.text: The cost ceiling, since the second call pushes each answered question to 6.1 cents.

options.label: B
options.text: The citation requirement, since a re-reading call cannot confirm a rule it was handed rather than found.

options.label: C
options.text: The latency target, since a second call adds a round trip.

options.label: D
options.text: The rule on declining out-of-scope questions, since the extra call widens what the assistant reads.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The cost ceiling, since the second call pushes each answered question to 6.1 cents.
The ceiling is 4 cents and the pilot measures 6.1. The other three requirements are met on the same pilot, so this is the only one that misses. The second call bought accuracy the design already required and spent half as much again per question. A stated ceiling is a limit the design must fit inside, not a figure to trade against quality.

INCORRECT: The citation requirement, since a re-reading call cannot confirm a rule it was handed rather than found.
Re-reading what you were given is weak verification, and the objection is fair in general. The pilot reports that every answer cites the rule a caseworker confirmed, so the requirement is met as measured. The doubt is about method, not about the result. Judge a requirement against the measurement the question gives, not against how you would have measured it.

INCORRECT: The latency target, since a second call adds a round trip.
Extra calls do cost time, and 3 seconds is not a generous budget for two model calls. The pilot puts p90 at 2.4 seconds, comfortably inside the target, because the re-read is short. The requirement holds with room left. A change that pushes a figure in the wrong direction has not broken the limit until it passes it.

INCORRECT: The rule on declining out-of-scope questions, since the extra call widens what the assistant reads.
Adding reading does sometimes drag a system into territory it should refuse, so the instinct has some basis. The re-read looks at a rule the first call already cited, which keeps it inside the benefits rules rather than beyond them. The pilot confirms out-of-scope questions are declined. Check the measured result before predicting a side effect.

questions.question:
A pensions team runs a two-step process on Claude. Step one pulls the facts from the member record and is right 99 percent of the time. Step two applies the exclusions, computes the amount and writes the rationale, and is right 71 percent of the time. Regulation adds three new exclusions next quarter. The team will add them to step two and change nothing else about the shape of the process.
What does the team find at review?

options.label: A
options.text: Step two's accuracy falls below 71 percent, since the step now carries more decisions at once.

options.label: B
options.text: Step two runs longer while its accuracy holds near 71 percent.

options.label: C
options.text: Step one's accuracy falls, since it must now extract facts the new exclusions need.

options.label: D
options.text: The two steps behave as before, and the three new exclusions are applied correctly across every claim.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Step two's accuracy falls below 71 percent, since the step now carries more decisions at once.
Step one does one job and is right 99 times in 100. Step two already holds three jobs and is right 71 times in 100, which is what an overloaded step looks like. Three more exclusions add work to the step that is already the weak one. Loading a step that is failing at its current size makes it fail at a larger one.

INCORRECT: Step two runs longer while its accuracy holds near 71 percent.
More rules do take more time, and treating accuracy as a fixed property of a step is a common reading. The 71 percent is the result of asking one call to do several things at once, so it moves whenever that load changes. Time is not the only thing that grows. Accuracy in a combined step is a function of how much the step carries.

INCORRECT: Step one's accuracy falls, since it must now extract facts the new exclusions need.
Upstream changes often follow downstream ones, and new exclusions could well need new fields. Step one pulls the facts from the member record and does one narrow job, which is why it sits at 99 percent. Nothing in the change adds a second job to it. A step that does one thing stays reliable as the work around it grows.

INCORRECT: The two steps behave as before, and the three new exclusions are applied correctly across every claim.
Adding rules to a working process is routine, and most changes do land without incident. The process is not working: step two is wrong on nearly a third of claims before the new exclusions arrive. The change is made to the weakest part of it. Ask how a component is performing today before predicting how it absorbs more.

questions.question:
A logistics firm runs a Claude service that reads delivery exception emails and files a structured claim. The team chose the cheapest tier after testing it on 200 emails pulled from one month of queue traffic. For five months the service was accurate and cheap. Claims filed from damaged-in-transit emails, about one in forty of the total, are now wrong often enough that a clerk rechecks all of them. Nothing in the prompt or the code changed.
What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: The rare type needs capability the cheapest tier does not have, and nobody measured that.

options.label: B
options.text: Damaged-in-transit emails arrive in a format the mail parser strips out before the model reads them.

options.label: C
options.text: Traffic grew over five months, and requests now time out before the model finishes.

options.label: D
options.text: Different owners edited the prompt and left its instructions inconsistent.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The rare type needs capability the cheapest tier does not have, and nobody measured that.
Damaged-in-transit emails are one in forty. The team measured the cheapest tier on 200 emails from one month, so this type had about five examples in the sample. The tier was chosen before anyone knew what accuracy the hardest cases need. It handles the routine emails and falls short on the ones that need judgment.

Source: Choosing the right model

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Damaged-in-transit emails arrive in a format the mail parser strips out before the model reads them.
A parser fault does hit one email type and leaves the rest untouched, so it fits the shape of this failure. Nothing in the code changed, and the clerk finds wrong claims rather than empty ones. Stripped text produces gaps you can see. A wrong answer from complete input points at judgment, not at plumbing.

INCORRECT: Traffic grew over five months, and requests now time out before the model finishes.
Growth over five months is real, and a slow service does degrade as load rises. A timeout ends a request with an error, so the team would see failures rather than filed claims that are wrong. The clerk is rechecking content, not chasing missing output. Match the symptom to the failure mode before you blame load.

INCORRECT: Different owners edited the prompt and left its instructions inconsistent.
Prompt drift across owners is common, and inconsistent instructions do produce uneven quality. The question states that nothing in the prompt changed over the five months. An explanation that contradicts a stated fact is not a candidate, however familiar it looks. Read the stated evidence before you reach for the usual suspect.

questions.question:
Two engineers run the same year-long data migration with the same Claude agent and the same prompt file. Each works in a session of their own, one in the morning and one in the afternoon. The team's handover is a written summary the agent produces at the end of a session, which the same engineer pastes into their next session. Both engineers report that the agent keeps re-deciding naming rules the other one already settled.
Which two factors best explain this?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing outside the sessions holds a settled decision, so each one starts without them.

options.label: B
options.text: The handover summary travels forward only inside the chain that produced it.

options.label: C
options.text: The two engineers run local copies of the prompt file that have drifted apart.

options.label: D
options.text: The agent reasons differently on each run, so it settles naming rules differently.

options.label: E
options.text: A session's context expires overnight, so the morning session starts empty.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Nothing outside the sessions holds a settled decision, so each one starts without them.
Each engineer works in a session of their own. A session holds its decisions only while it is open. When a session closes, the decisions it reached are gone, because nothing outside the session recorded them. A store the agent reads and updates between conversations is the only place a settled rule can wait.

CORRECT: The handover summary travels forward only inside the chain that produced it.
The agent writes the summary at the end of a session, and the same engineer pastes it into their next session. That path runs forward through one engineer's own days. It never crosses to the other engineer. A handover that moves along one chain leaves a parallel chain with nothing to read.

Source: Memory tool

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The two engineers run local copies of the prompt file that have drifted apart.
Drifting copies are a common cause of two runs behaving differently, and the fix is easy to imagine. The question says both engineers run the same agent and the same prompt file. The agent is not applying two different rules. It is settling the same rule twice, because nothing recorded the first decision.

INCORRECT: The agent reasons differently on each run, so it settles naming rules differently.
Model output does vary between runs, and that variation is a real source of inconsistency. The symptom here is not two different rules. It is the same rule being settled again from nothing. Variation explains why two answers differ. It does not explain why the work starts from zero each time.

INCORRECT: A session's context expires overnight, so the morning session starts empty.
An expiry sounds like a plausible reason a session opens with nothing in it. Context does not survive a session and then run down on a clock. It ends when the session ends. Name the boundary a mechanism really has, rather than the one that fits the story you already have.

questions.question:
A grants assistant built on Claude answers staff questions from one 180-page funding handbook. The handbook sits at the top of the prompt, above the instructions and the question, and the whole prompt fits the window with room to spare. Answers read well and staff rate them highly. At a monthly audit, reviewers say they cannot tell which sentences came from the handbook and which the model supplied, and they cannot check an answer without rereading the handbook themselves.
What is the underlying problem?

options.label: A
options.text: The assistant never quotes the passages it used, so no sentence traces back.

options.label: B
options.text: The review tool shows each answer alone, with no handbook text beside it for comparison.

options.label: C
options.text: The handbook carries no section numbers for an answer to cite.

options.label: D
options.text: A 180-page handbook is more text than the model can weigh in one answer.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The assistant never quotes the passages it used, so no sentence traces back.
The handbook is in the prompt and correctly placed, so the content is available. The answer arrives as fresh prose with no passage named. A reviewer then has no link between a sentence and a page. Asking the model to quote what it relies on before it answers makes that link part of the output.

Source: Prompting best practices

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The review tool shows each answer alone, with no handbook text beside it for comparison.
Reviewers do work faster when the source sits next to the answer, so better tooling looks like the fix. The answer names no passage, so a side-by-side view still leaves the reviewer searching 180 pages. The gap sits in the output, not in the screen. A viewer cannot show a link the answer never created.

INCORRECT: The handbook carries no section numbers for an answer to cite.
Section numbers are a convenient anchor, and their absence does make citing harder. A quoted sentence identifies its own source without any numbering. The assistant could quote the text and the reviewer could find it. Missing labels raise the cost of checking. They do not explain an answer that points at nothing.

INCORRECT: A 180-page handbook is more text than the model can weigh in one answer.
Length is a common suspect with a long source, and this handbook is long. The question says the whole prompt fits the window with room to spare and that answers read well. Capacity is not the limit here. When a source is present and correctly placed, look at what the output is asked to show.

options: The assistant never quotes the passages it used, so no sentence traces back.
The review tool shows each answer alone, with no handbook text beside it for comparison.
The handbook carries no section numbers for an answer to cite.
A 180-page handbook is more text than the model can weigh in one answer.
html.explanation:
CORRECT: The assistant never quotes the passages it used, so no sentence traces back.
The handbook is in the prompt and correctly placed, so the content is available. The answer arrives as fresh prose with no passage named. A reviewer then has no link between a sentence and a page. Asking the model to quote what it relies on before it answers makes that link part of the output.

Source: Prompting best practices

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The review tool shows each answer alone, with no handbook text beside it for comparison.

The answer names no passage, so a side-by-side view still leaves the reviewer searching 180 pages. The gap sits in the output, not in the screen. A viewer cannot show a link the answer never created.

INCORRECT: The handbook carries no section numbers for an answer to cite.
Section numbers are a convenient anchor, and their absence does make citing harder. A quoted sentence identifies its own source without any numbering. The assistant could quote the text and the reviewer could find it. Missing labels raise the cost of checking. They do not explain an answer that points at nothing.

INCORRECT: A 180-page handbook is more text than the model can weigh in one answer.

questions.question:
A payments team is writing the model pinning policy for a Claude service that must not change behavior between releases. The configuration names three model identifiers and none of them carries a date. An engineer proposes writing the tier name into one shared configuration value, so every service in the estate resolves the same tier. The policy has to guarantee that a given release produces the same model on every deployment.
Which change best achieves this?

options.label: A
options.text: Check each identifier and pin only the ones documented as a fixed snapshot.

options.label: B
options.text: Write the tier name into one shared configuration value.

options.label: C
options.text: Freeze the configuration file so only a tagged release can change an identifier in it.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a regression test that fails whenever the generated text changes between two consecutive releases.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Check each identifier and pin only the ones documented as a fixed snapshot.
Model identifiers do not all behave the same way. Some dateless identifiers are aliases that resolve to the most recent snapshot for their version. Others are the snapshot itself and never move. The policy needs the same model on every deployment. Each of the three identifiers has to be read in the documentation before it is trusted.

Source: Model IDs and versioning

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Write the tier name into one shared configuration value.
One value in one place is a clean configuration pattern, and it does make the estate consistent. A tier name is not a pin. It still resolves through an identifier, and an identifier that floats puts a new snapshot behind the same tier. Consistency across services is not the same as stability over time.

INCORRECT: Freeze the configuration file so only a tagged release can change an identifier in it.
Change control on configuration is sound practice, and it does stop an accidental edit. The text of an identifier is not what changes here. The model that identifier resolves to changes on the provider's side, with the file untouched. Freezing a pointer does not freeze what it points at.

INCORRECT: Add a regression test that fails whenever the generated text changes between two consecutive releases.
A regression test is the right way to learn that behavior moved, and this team already runs tests. The stated requirement is a guarantee that a release produces the same model, not a signal that it did not. A test reports the shift after it has reached a release. Detection is not a control.

questions.question:
A knowledge team is building one request template before launch. It will write the instructions, then three retrieved policy documents, then two worked examples, then the user's question, all as plain text in one block. A reviewer asks how Claude will tell a worked example apart from a retrieved document or from the user's own question. The team has no answer.
What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Put each worked example inside its own example tag, wrapped in one examples tag.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a line to the instructions naming which block holds the user's question.

options.label: C
options.text: Cut the template down to a single worked example.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace the worked examples with a written description of the output format the team wants.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Put each worked example inside its own example tag, wrapped in one examples tag.
Tags give the model a boundary it does not have to infer. Each example sits inside its own example tag, and the pair sits inside an examples tag. The retrieved documents and the user's question then fall outside that boundary. The model can tell a demonstration from material it must actually use.

Source: Prompting best practices

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Add a line to the instructions naming which block holds the user's question.
An instruction is quick to write and it does tell the model what to look for. The template still delivers four kinds of content as one run of plain text. A sentence describing a structure that is not there leaves the same boundary to inference. Build the structure, rather than describing a structure you did not build.

INCORRECT: Cut the template down to a single worked example.
Fewer examples do reduce the amount of text that could be copied by mistake, so the risk drops. One untagged example sitting beside three documents and a live question has the same boundary problem. The count is not what makes an example distinguishable. Reducing a symptom is not the same as removing its cause.

INCORRECT: Replace the worked examples with a written description of the output format the team wants.
A written format description is clear and it avoids example text entirely. Examples earn their place because they show patterns a description states poorly. Dropping them to solve a labeling problem gives up the technique instead of fixing it. Solve the problem the design has, rather than removing the feature that exposed it.

questions.question:
A platform team is setting up prompt caching and deciding what to put behind cache breakpoints before launch. Each request to Claude carries the tool definitions first, then a 12,000-token system policy that has not changed since drafting, then the message history. A second team edits the tool definitions and ships them several times a day. The policy block is the largest stable content in the request.
What should the architect do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Ship the tool definition edits as one scheduled release each day.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the policy block above the tool definitions so it caches before anything else changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Describe the tools inside the system policy so that the tool level never changes.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave the policy block uncached and cache only the message history.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ship the tool definition edits as one scheduled release each day.
The cache follows a fixed order: tools, then system, then messages. A change to the tool definitions invalidates that level and every level after it, so the policy block loses its cache too. The edits cannot move below the policy, but they can arrive less often. One release a day means one invalidation a day.

Source: Prompt caching

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Move the policy block above the tool definitions so it caches before anything else changes.
Putting stable content ahead of volatile content is the right instinct, and it works inside a level. The order of tools, system and messages is fixed by the platform, so the team cannot rearrange it. The policy sits below the tool definitions and always will. Know which parts of an order you may choose before you plan around it.

INCORRECT: Describe the tools inside the system policy so that the tool level never changes.
Moving volatile content out of the top level does follow the rule the correct answer uses. A tool described in prose is not a tool definition, and the model cannot call it. The definitions still have to be sent, and they still sit at the top. A workaround that removes the capability is not a trade-off.

INCORRECT: Leave the policy block uncached and cache only the message history.
Caching what survives is a reasonable response once a block keeps losing its cache. The policy block is the largest stable content in the request, so it is where most of the saving sits. A tool definition edit invalidates every level after it, so the message history loses its cache too. Do not abandon the largest stable block before you try to protect it.

questions.question:
A claims assistant built on Claude uses a prompt that carries a hand-written seven-step procedure. The insurer adds a new product line whose cases need a solvency check the procedure never mentions. The team adds the new product's rules to the reference material and leaves the seven steps as written. Nothing in the prompt tells the assistant that a case may fall outside the procedure.
What happens next?

options.label: A
options.text: The assistant runs the seven steps and answers without the solvency check.

options.label: B
options.text: The assistant reports that the new cases fall outside its procedure and declines to answer.

options.label: C
options.text: The assistant reorders the seven steps on its own once the new rules contradict them.

options.label: D
options.text: Accuracy on the older product lines falls as the new rules compete for attention.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The assistant runs the seven steps and answers without the solvency check.
The prompt gives a fixed procedure and nothing else. The new rules sit in the reference material, but no step tells the assistant to apply them. A scripted procedure runs the steps it holds, in the order it holds them. The answer arrives complete and confident, and the missing check leaves no mark on it.

Source: Prompting best practices

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The assistant reports that the new cases fall outside its procedure and declines to answer.
A careful system should flag a case it was not built for, and that is what a reviewer would want. Nothing in the prompt tells the assistant that a case may fall outside the seven steps. It has no test for an unfamiliar case, so it cannot raise one. A system reports only the conditions someone wrote down.

INCORRECT: The assistant reorders the seven steps on its own once the new rules contradict them.
Models do adapt to the material in front of them, so some flexibility is plausible. The procedure is written as the task itself, not as a suggestion the assistant may revise. It will follow the steps it was given rather than replace them. An instruction that prescribes an order removes the judgment that would change it.

INCORRECT: Accuracy on the older product lines falls as the new rules compete for attention.
Adding material to a prompt can dilute attention, and that is a real effect. The seven steps still match the older cases exactly, and those cases need no new check. The failure lands on the new product line, where the procedure is incomplete. Extra reference material does not break a procedure that already fits.

questions.question:
A support application assembles each request to Claude at run time from recent turns, retrieved articles and whatever the user attached. Before sending, it divides the assembled text's character count by four and refuses the request when that number passes a budget. The attached file is not part of that text. Text-only traffic has not overflowed in a year. The product team now turns on PDF attachments, and the same check runs unchanged.
What will this design fail to deliver?

options.label: A
options.text: A refusal that arrives before an oversized request is sent.

options.label: B
options.text: A request that still reaches the model once it carries a PDF attachment.

options.label: C
options.text: A character count that matches the text the application assembled.

options.label: D
options.text: A check that runs on every request before the application sends it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: A refusal that arrives before an oversized request is sent.
The check divides the assembled text by four, and the attached file is not part of that text. A PDF adds tokens the count never sees. The number stays under the budget, so nothing is trimmed and nothing is refused. The request goes out larger than the window holds and fails after the user has waited.

Source: Token counting

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: A request that still reaches the model once it carries a PDF attachment.
A wide margin and a strict refusal rule do suggest that new input gets blocked early. The estimate counts assembled text only, so a PDF makes the number smaller than the truth, not larger. These requests pass the check and are sent. An estimate that cannot see an input will never refuse because of it.

INCORRECT: A character count that matches the text the application assembled.
The count is the part of the design that looks suspect, so it draws attention first. Characters in the assembled text are counted correctly. The fault is the step that turns characters into a token budget, and the input that step never receives. Check whether a measure is wrong or simply measuring the wrong thing.

INCORRECT: A check that runs on every request before the application sends it.
The design does fail at run time, so it is tempting to say the check is not running. The check runs on every request, exactly as written. It returns a number that is too small, which is a different fault from an absent control. A control that runs and passes is not the same as no control.

questions.question:
A retailer chose a model tier for a product description service built on Claude. The selection record holds two columns: accuracy on a 500 item sample, and price per thousand descriptions. The cheapest tier clearing the accuracy bar won. Prompts were then hand tuned until that tier matched the house style. Nine months on, two cheaper tiers have shipped and the service has taken neither, because each move costs three weeks of retuning. The architect now writes the selection record for four more services.
What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Score each candidate on the work a later tier change will cost, alongside accuracy and price.

options.label: B
options.text: Re-run the accuracy sample every quarter so the selection record always names the cheapest passing tier.

options.label: C
options.text: Choose the most capable tier so later tier changes become unnecessary.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a human review step that approves each tier change before it ships.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Score each candidate on the work a later tier change will cost, alongside accuracy and price.
The record scored two things, and both were true on the day of the choice. It never scored how hard the choice would be to undo. Nine months later that is the cost the retailer pays, three weeks per move, and it has already blocked two savings. The burden of living with a choice belongs in the choice.

INCORRECT: Re-run the accuracy sample every quarter so the selection record always names the cheapest passing tier.
Refreshing the comparison looks right, because the visible symptom is two cheaper tiers the service did not take. The team already knows those tiers exist, and the question states the block is three weeks of retuning per move. Better information does not shorten that work. A refreshed comparison changes what you know, never what a change costs to make.

INCORRECT: Choose the most capable tier so later tier changes become unnecessary.
Paying for the top tier does end the churn, and it removes the pressure to move at all. The record scores price because the service runs at volume, so this drops a stated dimension to avoid a cost. The hand tuning that couples prompts to one tier also stays. Removing the need to change is not the same as being able to change.

INCORRECT: Add a human review step that approves each tier change before it ships.
A review gate does catch a bad tier change before customers meet it, and approval steps are cheap to add. The delay here is three weeks of retuning work, not an approval wait, so the gate sits in front of a cost it cannot reduce. It adds time instead. A gate decides whether a change ships, it never lowers what the change costs.

questions.question:
A support assistant runs on Claude. The system prompt opens with its boundaries: the topics it may discuss, a ban on disclosing internal pricing rules, and an instruction to ignore any instruction arriving inside a customer message. A red team sends 600 adversarial messages across three rounds. The assistant holds on 573 and discloses a pricing rule on 27. After each round the team rewrote the boundary section to cover every phrasing that had worked. Nothing else inspects a request or a reply.
What best explains the gap?

options.label: A
options.text: The system prompt is the only control, so the boundary depends on the model complying.

options.label: B
options.text: A ban is weaker than a positive instruction, so the pricing rule needs rewording.

options.label: C
options.text: The boundary rules sit too far down a long prompt.

options.label: D
options.text: Twenty-seven failures in 600 messages fall inside normal variation for an adversarial test of this size.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The system prompt is the only control, so the boundary depends on the model complying.
The question states that nothing else inspects a request or a reply. A system prompt asks the model to hold a boundary, and the 27 disclosures show what asking produces under adversarial pressure. Each rewrite closed the phrasings already seen, and the next round supplied new ones. Anthropic's guidance asks for layered strategies, not one control doing all the work.

Source: Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: A ban is weaker than a positive instruction, so the pricing rule needs rewording.
Positive instructions often do outperform prohibitions, so the advice behind this option is sound in general. The team already rewrote the boundary section after every round, and the disclosures continued, so wording is the lever that has been pulled three times. Nothing new is added here. Rewording a single control changes its odds, it never gives you a second control.

INCORRECT: The boundary rules sit too far down a long prompt.
Placement is a common first suspect when a model ignores a rule, and moving a rule is a cheap change. questions.question:
A field service agent books spare parts for technicians. Over three quarters four teams each added a booking tool: one takes a part number, one a catalog code, one a supplier SKU, one a warehouse bin. Every tool works when given the identifier it expects. Call logs show the agent now tries three booking tools on average before one succeeds, and technicians who give a bin number often get the part number tool first. Other capabilities in the same Claude agent are unchanged.
What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Four tools now cover one booking capability, so more than one looks right for any single request.

options.label: B
options.text: Requests from the newly onboarded teams are vaguer than they were.

options.label: C
options.text: Parallel tool calling is off, so the agent tries identifiers one at a time.

options.label: D
options.text: The agent runs on a model tier smaller than the one these booking tools were written and tested against.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Four tools now cover one booking capability, so more than one looks right for any single request.
Every tool works when it gets the identifier it expects, so no tool is broken. The failure sits in the choice. Four separate tools answer one need, and the agent must guess which identifier the technician gave. Three tries before a success is what overlapping tools look like from outside. One capability belongs behind one tool.

Source: Writing effective tools for agents, with agents

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Requests from the newly onboarded teams are vaguer than they were.
Onboarding new teams does bring less precise requests, and that would raise the number of wrong calls. The question says other capabilities in the same agent are unchanged, and the same technicians reach those. Vaguer requests would hurt every capability, not booking alone. When one capability degrades and the rest hold, look at what changed inside that capability.

INCORRECT: Parallel tool calling is off, so the agent tries identifiers one at a time.
Serial calls do make a run slower, and three calls in a row looks like a sequencing problem. Running the four in parallel would still leave the agent unable to tell which tool fits the identifier it was given. The wrong picks would remain. Speed and selection are different problems, so read which one the evidence shows.

INCORRECT: The agent runs on a model tier smaller than the one these booking tools were written and tested against.
Smaller tiers do choose tools less reliably, and a tier change is worth ruling out early. Nothing in the question says the tier moved, while it does say four overlapping tools arrived over three quarters. The change that happened explains the change in behavior. Match a cause to what the timeline shows moved, not to what could move.

questions.question:
A bank is designing a Claude agent that will read and update customer records for 400 branch staff. Roles differ: tellers see their own branch, supervisors see the region, and only three people may reverse a posting. The design so far gives the agent one service credential holding the union of every role's access. Security asks how the record system will enforce per-person limits.
Which two changes best address this?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Pass the requesting person's identity through to the record system on every call.

options.label: B
options.text: Have the record system decide each request against that person's own permissions.

options.label: C
options.text: Cut the service credential down to the smallest set of permissions the agent needs.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the record system's owners to publish a permission matrix the agent team can code against.

options.label: E
options.text: Log the requester's name on every call so the bank can review who asked for what.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Pass the requesting person's identity through to the record system on every call.
The record system can apply a person's limits only if it knows which person is asking. Today it sees one credential holding the union of every role. Sending the requester's identity with each call gives the system the fact it needs. Tellers, supervisors and the three reversal approvers then look different at the point where access is decided.

CORRECT: Have the record system decide each request against that person's own permissions.
Identity alone changes nothing if the decision still rests on the agent's credential. The system holding the records is the last point every path goes through, so the rule belongs there. It can then refuse a teller reaching another branch, whatever the agent asked for. A check at the resource covers callers the design has not thought of yet.

INCORRECT: Cut the service credential down to the smallest set of permissions the agent needs.
Least privilege is sound practice, and a credential holding every role's access is clearly too wide. The agent still needs that union, because it serves tellers, supervisors and approvers from one code path. A narrowed credential is still one permission set for 400 people with three different limits. Trimming a shared identity cannot tell two callers apart.

INCORRECT: Ask the record system's owners to publish a permission matrix the agent team can code against.
A written matrix does help two teams agree on the rules, and somebody has to write the limits down. Enforcement would still sit in the agent, which is the component asking for access rather than granting it. Any caller that bypasses the agent meets no rule at all. A document describes a control, it does not apply one.

INCORRECT: Log the requester's name on every call so the bank can review who asked for what.
Attribution is worth having, and the bank will want it for audit whatever else it builds. A log records a reversal after it has been posted, and the question asks how per-person limits get enforced. Nothing in the path refuses the request. Recording an action and preventing one are different jobs.

questions.question:
A nightly settlement job makes 32 dependent tool calls per run. Each call is its own round trip to Claude. A run takes 76 seconds, and 58 of those are model inference between calls. Operations needs runs under 30 seconds. The team has moved the job to a faster model tier that returns each inference in about half the time. The call sequence is unchanged.
What happens next?

options.label: A
options.text: The run drops to roughly 47 seconds, still short of the 30 second target.

options.label: B
options.text: Cost per run falls while the run time holds, because the round trips set the clock.

options.label: C
options.text: The run now meets the 30 second target with time to spare.

options.label: D
options.text: The 32 round trips collapse into a smaller number of calls, well under the target.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The run drops to roughly 47 seconds, still short of the 30 second target.
Of the 76 seconds, 58 are inference and 18 are everything else. Halving the inference leaves about 29 seconds of inference plus the same 18, near 47 in total. The run is faster and still misses 30. A faster tier shortens each round trip, it never removes one.

Source: Introducing advanced tool use on the Claude Developer Platform

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Cost per run falls while the run time holds, because the round trips set the clock.
The count of round trips is the real limit, so this reads like the right lesson applied. The question states that each inference now returns in about half the time, and 58 of the 76 seconds are inference. Time has to fall. The lesson is that round trips cap the gain, not that they freeze the clock.

INCORRECT: The run now meets the 30 second target with time to spare.
Halving the biggest number in a budget feels like enough, and 58 seconds is most of the run. The 18 seconds outside inference do not move, and half of 58 is still 29 on its own. The two together sit above 30. Check what a change cannot touch before you assume a target is met.

INCORRECT: The 32 round trips collapse into a smaller number of calls, well under the target.
Fewer round trips is the change that would meet this target, so the option names the right goal. A tier change alters how fast a call returns and leaves the call sequence exactly as written. The question says the sequence is unchanged. Speed and structure are separate levers, and only one of them was pulled.

questions.question:
A platform moved its Claude Agent SDK telemetry to a new collector last month. The agents run normally and raise no errors. Nobody can say whether every span now reaches the new endpoint, and the team found the last gap four weeks after it happened. Export failures do not surface in the application. The team wants to learn about the next gap on the day it starts.
What should the architect do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn on exporter diagnostics so failed exports are reported by the agent process, and alert on them.

options.label: B
options.text: Alert on the error rate the new collector reports for the telemetry pipeline.

options.label: C
options.text: Shorten the trace and log export intervals so less telemetry sits in the buffer when a process ends.

options.label: D
options.text: Have an engineer check the telemetry dashboard for missing days every morning.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Turn on exporter diagnostics so failed exports are reported by the agent process, and alert on them.
Export failures do not surface in the application, which is why the last gap went unseen for four weeks. Diagnostics make the failing side speak: the process that could not deliver reports the error itself. An alert on that error fires on the day the export breaks. Watch the sender when the sender is the part that goes quiet.

Source: Observability with OpenTelemetry

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Alert on the error rate the new collector reports for the telemetry pipeline.
Collector metrics are the natural place to look, and most pipelines are watched there. When the agent cannot reach the endpoint, nothing arrives, so the collector has nothing to count and reports a healthy zero. The alert stays quiet through the whole outage. A monitor on the receiving end cannot see data that was never sent.

INCORRECT: Shorten the trace and log export intervals so less telemetry sits in the buffer when a process ends.
Shorter intervals genuinely cut how much data a killed process loses, and the change is a small one. The agents ran normally and raised no errors, so the gap did not come from a killed process. A smaller buffer would have dropped just as quietly. Reducing the size of a loss is not the same as reporting it.

INCORRECT: Have an engineer check the telemetry dashboard for missing days every morning.
A daily look would have caught this gap far sooner than four weeks, so the instinct is sound. It puts a person on watch for a condition a machine can detect, and a missed morning restores the old blind spot. The team asked to learn on the day a gap starts. Do not staff a check that a monitor can hold.

questions.question:
A regulator's 900 rulebooks are being prepared for a retrieval assistant that runs on Claude. Each rulebook names its subject once, in the opening section, and then writes the scheme or this exemption for the rest of the document. The team plans to index passages of about 400 tokens. A pilot on 20 rulebooks returned passages that read correctly but could not be tied to a scheme, and answers named the wrong rulebook.
What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Prepend a short line naming the rulebook and section to each passage before it is indexed.

options.label: B
options.text: Retrieve a wider candidate set and rerank it, so the best passages reach the model.

options.label: C
options.text: Index each rulebook whole, so the subject in the opening section always travels with the text.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the regulator to repeat the scheme name in every section of the rulebooks it publishes from now on.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Prepend a short line naming the rulebook and section to each passage before it is indexed.
The pilot returned passages that read correctly and could not be tied to a scheme. That is the subject going missing at the cut, since each rulebook names it once and then writes the scheme. A line naming the rulebook and section restores the fact the passage lost. Give a passage its context before you index it, not after you retrieve it.

Source: Introducing Contextual Retrieval

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Retrieve a wider candidate set and rerank it, so the best passages reach the model.
Reranking does raise the quality of what reaches the model, and it belongs in a strong pipeline. Every candidate still says the scheme and names no rulebook, so ranking them puts an unattributed passage at the top instead of lower down. The missing subject is still missing. Ranking chooses among what exists, it cannot add what indexing removed.

INCORRECT: Index each rulebook whole, so the subject in the opening section always travels with the text.
Whole documents do carry their own subject, and the problem does come from cutting them. A rulebook is far larger than a question needs, so retrieval returns mostly irrelevant text and the useful passage competes with it. Cost and precision both fall. Solving a chunking problem by not chunking trades one failure for a bigger one.

INCORRECT: Ask the regulator to repeat the scheme name in every section of the rulebooks it publishes from now on.
Better source documents would remove the problem at its origin, which is always worth asking for. The 900 rulebooks already published are the corpus, and none of them will be rewritten. A change to future publications leaves today's index exactly as it is. Do not design around a source you do not control.
