questions.question:
A finance assistant built on Claude answers questions over a warehouse table of 4 million payment rows. Each row is exported as a line of text and embedded. A question asks for total chargebacks in the north region last quarter. Asked on Monday it returns 182,400 dollars. Asked again on Tuesday, worded differently, it returns 149,900. The table did not change between the runs, and both runs read the same quarter and region from the question. Traces show a different set of 50 rows retrieved each time.
What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: The total is computed over the 50 rows retrieved, not over every row that matches.

options.label: B
options.text: Sampling settings let the model's arithmetic vary between runs on the same figures.

options.label: C
options.text: The embedding index was rebuilt overnight, so Tuesday searched a different index.

options.label: D
options.text: The two wordings named different date ranges, so each answer covers a different quarter of the year.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The total is computed over the 50 rows retrieved, not over every row that matches.
A total is right only when every matching row is counted. This pipeline embeds rows and returns the 50 most similar, so the answer is a sum over a sample. The two runs retrieved different 50-row sets, which is why the two totals differ. Similarity decides what is relevant, it cannot decide what is complete.

Source: Text to SQL with Claude

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Sampling settings let the model's arithmetic vary between runs on the same figures.
Model output does vary between runs, so nondeterminism is a fair first suspicion. The traces show a different set of 50 rows going in each time, which means the input differed and not only the output. A stable input would not produce a gap this wide. Look at what entered the model before blaming how it answered.

INCORRECT: The embedding index was rebuilt overnight, so Tuesday searched a different index.
Nightly rebuilds do change results, and a Monday to Tuesday gap fits that story neatly. The question states the table did not change between the two runs, so a rebuild would index the same rows again. The totals would match. Rule out a data change before you explain a difference with one.

INCORRECT: The two wordings named different date ranges, so each answer covers a different quarter of the year.
Wording does steer what a question asks for, and the second run was phrased differently. Both runs read the same quarter and the same region from the question, which the traces confirm. The filter was identical and the row sets were not. A difference has to sit where the evidence shows the two runs diverged.

CORRECT: The total is computed over the 50 rows retrieved, not over every row that matches.
A total is right only when every matching row is counted. This pipeline embeds rows and returns the 50 most similar, so the answer is a sum over a sample. The two runs retrieved different 50-row sets, which is why the two totals differ. Similarity decides what is relevant, it cannot decide what is complete.

Source: Text to SQL with Claude

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Sampling settings let the model's arithmetic vary between runs on the same figures.

The traces show a different set of 50 rows going in each time, which means the input differed and not only the output. A stable input would not produce a gap this wide. Look at what entered the model before blaming how it answered.

INCORRECT: The embedding index was rebuilt overnight, so Tuesday searched a different index.
Nightly rebuilds do change results, and a Monday to Tuesday gap fits that story neatly. The question states the table did not change between the two runs, so a rebuild would index the same rows again. The totals would match. Rule out a data change before you explain a difference with one.

INCORRECT: The two wordings named different date ranges, so each answer covers a different quarter of the year.

The filter was identical and the row sets were not. A difference has to sit where the evidence shows the two runs diverged.

questions.question:
A Claude agent aggregates six MCP servers. Their 140 tool definitions load before every request and already fill about a third of the context window. Typical tasks then read two or three long contracts. A seventh server is being connected, adding 60 more tools and about the same weight again in definitions. Nothing else in the design changes.
What breaks first?

options.label: A
options.text: Tasks that read long contracts run out of room, because definitions now take most of the window.

options.label: B
options.text: The seventh server's tools go unused, because the agent keeps choosing the tools it already knows well.

options.label: C
options.text: Every request returns more slowly, because the seventh server's definitions are fetched when a call is made.

options.label: D
options.text: The original servers start timing out under the extra connections.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Tasks that read long contracts run out of room, because definitions now take most of the window.
Definitions already fill about a third of the window, and the seventh server adds about the same weight again. That leaves roughly a third for two or three long contracts that used to have two thirds. The tasks nearest the limit stop fitting first. Upfront definitions are charged against the same space the work needs.

Source: Tool search tool

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The seventh server's tools go unused, because the agent keeps choosing the tools it already knows well.
Familiar tools do get picked more often, and a new server's tools can sit idle for a while. Every definition is loaded on every request, so the new tools are as visible as the old ones from the first call. Nothing in the design hides them. Selection order is not what the added weight changes here.

INCORRECT: Every request returns more slowly, because the seventh server's definitions are fetched when a call is made.
Fetching on demand does add a step, and that is what a slow first call usually means. This design loads all definitions before every request, which is the condition the question states. Nothing is fetched at call time. Read how a system loads its definitions before predicting where a delay lands.

INCORRECT: The original servers start timing out under the extra connections.
More servers do mean more connections, and connection limits are a real operational failure. Six servers already connect without trouble, and a seventh is a small step on that axis. The pressure the question describes is context, not connections. Name the resource that is actually near its limit.

questions.question:
A bank is writing the security checklist every integration with a Claude agent must pass before launch. The draft has eleven items: single sign-on, token lifetime, replay protection, no shared logins, multi-factor, and seven more of the same kind. A reviewer points out that the last agent to pass this checklist went on to post a ledger entry its user was not permitted to make.
What should the architect change?

options.label: A
options.text: Add items that test what each caller may do, not only who the caller is.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a penetration test against the sign-on flow before any agent integration is allowed to launch.

options.label: C
options.text: Require a second reviewer to sign the checklist for every agent integration.

options.label: D
options.text: Shorten token lifetimes so a caller's access expires sooner after sign-on.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Add items that test what each caller may do, not only who the caller is.
All eleven items test identity: who signs in, how the token behaves, how a login is protected. Not one asks whether a caller is permitted to take the action it requests. That is why an integration passed and then posted a ledger entry its user could not make. A checklist covers the questions it asks, and no others.

INCORRECT: Add a penetration test against the sign-on flow before any agent integration is allowed to launch.
Testing the sign-on flow harder is a real improvement, and penetration testing finds things a checklist misses. The entry was posted by a correctly identified user through a sound login, so the flow under test was never the weak part. A stronger login proves the same fact again. Depth on one axis does not cover a missing axis.

INCORRECT: Require a second reviewer to sign the checklist for every agent integration.
Two reviewers do catch more than one, and sign-off is cheap to add. Both reviewers would work from the same eleven items, and those items ask nothing about permitted actions. A second pair of eyes over the same questions returns the same result. Adding reviewers raises care, it does not add coverage.

INCORRECT: Shorten token lifetimes so a caller's access expires sooner after sign-on.
Short-lived tokens limit the damage a stolen credential can do, which makes this sound prudent. The user's token was valid and their own, and nothing refused the action. A shorter lifetime would not have stopped that user posting the same entry. Narrowing when access works says nothing about what it permits.

questions.question:
A platform runs agents built with the Claude Agent SDK from an HTTP API. Each run nests under the calling request's span, and support uses that link to find the run behind a slow request. The team is moving 40 percent of the work to a nightly scheduler, which will call the same agent code with no incoming request above it. Telemetry settings are unchanged.
What is the most likely outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: Scheduled runs appear as their own root traces and drop out of the request-linked views.

options.label: B
options.text: Durations stop being recorded for the scheduled runs, because no parent span is there to time them.

options.label: C
options.text: The scheduled runs attach to whichever request the platform served last.

options.label: D
options.text: Telemetry stops arriving for the scheduled runs, because the exporter has no request to follow.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Scheduled runs appear as their own root traces and drop out of the request-linked views.
A run nests under a calling request because that request has a span above it. A scheduler calls the same code with nothing above it, so there is no parent to attach to. The run still reports, as its own root trace. Support's view groups by that link, so the scheduled 40 percent is simply absent from it.

Source: Observability with OpenTelemetry

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Durations stop being recorded for the scheduled runs, because no parent span is there to time them.
A missing parent does break the link, so this follows the right observation one step too far. Each span records its own start and end, and a root trace carries durations the same way a nested one does. The numbers arrive, the grouping does not. A parent gives a span its place in a trace, not its clock.

INCORRECT: The scheduled runs attach to whichever request the platform served last.
Traces do sometimes attach in surprising places, and a busy platform always has a recent request. Context is propagated from the caller into the run, and a scheduler passes none, so there is nothing to inherit. An unrelated request is never picked up. Trace context travels along one call, never across two.

INCORRECT: Telemetry stops arriving for the scheduled runs, because the exporter has no request to follow.
Losing telemetry is the outcome teams fear most, so many will predict it first. Export is configured on the process and runs whether or not a parent span exists. The spans arrive and sit at the top level. Ask whether a change affects delivery or only structure before predicting silence.

questions.question:
A payments service moved from static keys to short-lived tokens. Five teams of Claude agents each reach that service directly. In the four weeks after the change, each of the five shipped its own fix, each wrote its own refresh handling, and two of them shipped the same bug. The service published the change eight weeks ahead and held two briefings.
What best explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: Each team holds its own copy of the auth handling, so one change lands five times.

options.label: B
options.text: The service's change notice did not describe the new token flow in enough detail for the teams.

options.label: C
options.text: Nobody was assigned to coordinate the five teams through the change.

options.label: D
options.text: Short-lived tokens are harder to handle than static keys, so bugs were likely.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Each team holds its own copy of the auth handling, so one change lands five times.
Five teams reach the service directly, so five separate integrations exist for one service. Each carries its own authentication code, which is why one provider change produced five pieces of work. Two teams meeting the same bug is what duplicated code looks like. Count the integrations, not the teams, when you want the cost of a change.

Source: Building agents that reach production systems with MCP

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The service's change notice did not describe the new token flow in enough detail for the teams.
Thin documentation does cause exactly this kind of scramble, and it is a common finding. The service published eight weeks ahead and held two briefings, so the teams had the same information well before the date. Perfect notice would still mean five migrations. Information changes how well work is done, not how much of it there is.

INCORRECT: Nobody was assigned to coordinate the five teams through the change.
A coordinator would have caught the repeated bug, and the absence of one is easy to see here. Coordination shares knowledge and leaves the five integrations in place, so each team still writes its own refresh handling. The work stays five-fold. Organizing duplicated effort is not the same as removing it.

INCORRECT: Short-lived tokens are harder to handle than static keys, so bugs were likely.
Refresh logic is real work, and it does invite mistakes that a static key never offered. The same difficulty faced by one team would have produced one fix and at most one bug. What the question shows is the same work done five times. Difficulty explains a bug, repetition explains five of them.

questions.question:
A reporting agent running on Claude will query a warehouse through an MCP server. Every query needs the current table schema, which changes most weeks as teams add columns. The team must decide how the schema reaches the model. They need it present on every turn and current on every turn, with no step that depends on the model deciding to ask for it.
Which change best achieves this?

options.label: A
options.text: Expose the schema as a resource the client reads and attaches to every request.

options.label: B
options.text: Put the current schema in the system prompt and update the prompt when columns change.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the schema tool and insist in its description that it be called first.

options.label: D
options.text: Have the agent call the schema tool, then retry any query that names a column the warehouse does not have.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Expose the schema as a resource the client reads and attaches to every request.
A tool runs only when the model chooses to call it, which is the step the team wants removed. A resource is read by the client, so the schema is attached before the model sees the question. The client reads it fresh each time, so weekly column changes arrive with it. Application-controlled data is present by construction, not by decision.

Source: Understanding MCP servers

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Put the current schema in the system prompt and update the prompt when columns change.
A prompt is always present, which satisfies half of what the team asked for. The schema changes most weeks, and a prompt is updated by whoever remembers. A missed week leaves the model working from columns that no longer exist. Nothing reports the drift. Data that changes on its own should be read, not copied.

INCORRECT: Keep the schema tool and insist in its description that it be called first.
Descriptions do shape tool choice, and a firm one raises the rate of correct calls. The team asked for a design with no step that depends on the model deciding to ask, and a description is exactly that decision. Most turns would comply and some would not. Wording raises a probability, it never sets a guarantee.

INCORRECT: Have the agent call the schema tool, then retry any query that names a column the warehouse does not have.
Retries do recover from a bad query, and this failure is cheap to detect. Every retry costs a round trip, and a wrong column name is only one way a stale schema shows, so quietly wrong results survive it. The schema is still absent on the first attempt. Repairing an outcome leaves the missing input in place.

questions.question:
A trading desk assistant running on Claude sends the same 22 tool definitions with every request, on 50,000 requests a day. To cut the bill the team rewrote every description, taking the block from 3,000 tokens to 2,700. The next week's input token charge for that block fell by about a tenth. Request volume was within 2 percent of the week before. The team expected a much larger drop.
What is the underlying cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The block is charged on every request, so trimming its size leaves the repetition in place.

options.label: B
options.text: The two weeks are not comparable, so the real saving is hidden.

options.label: C
options.text: Tool descriptions are a small part of each request, so the rest of the input dominates.

options.label: D
options.text: Every one of the 22 tools is in use, so none could be dropped from the block.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The block is charged on every request, so trimming its size leaves the repetition in place.
The block went down a tenth and the charge went down a tenth, so the edit worked. A large fall can only come from paying less each time the block repeats. At 50,000 requests a day the repetition is the whole of the cost. Trimming shrinks one copy, and caching cuts what every repeat of it costs.

Source: Manage tool context

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The two weeks are not comparable, so the real saving is hidden.
Comparing two weeks of a live bill is exactly where a measurement error hides, and questioning it is good practice. Request volume was within 2 percent of the week before, so the two weeks are comparable on the figure that drives this charge. The tenth is real. Check whether the question already rules out a measurement error before doubting the figure.

INCORRECT: Tool descriptions are a small part of each request, so the rest of the input dominates.
Tool definitions often are a minor share of a large prompt, and that would flatten any saving. The figure quoted is the input token charge for that block alone, not the whole bill. The rest of the request sits outside the comparison. The tenth is measured on the block itself. Read what a number covers before explaining it away.

INCORRECT: Every one of the 22 tools is in use, so none could be dropped from the block.
Full usage does close off the obvious saving, and an audit that finds every tool used feels like a dead end. The team did not try to drop tools, it rewrote descriptions and removed 300 tokens. Dropping a whole tool would shrink the block a little more and still send it 50,000 times. Both moves shrink a copy, and neither changes what a repeat costs.

questions.question:
A media group runs an internal drafting feature on Claude. It scores the feature each quarter against one written criterion: the draft must be helpful. The same 60 archived drafts are re-scored each time, and no code, prompt or model changed. Last quarter the panel returned 71 percent. This quarter it returns 84 percent. Two of the four reviewers scored for the first time this quarter. Within each run the four reviewers' scores sat within 3 points of each other.
What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: The criterion names no scale, so the panel's idea of helpful moved between the runs.

options.label: B
options.text: Two reviewers were new this quarter, so the panel applied a different standard to the same drafts.

options.label: C
options.text: Sixty archived drafts are too few to hold a quarterly score steady.

options.label: D
options.text: Helpfulness needs several sub-scores, and one combined number hides where the change sits.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The criterion names no scale, so the panel's idea of helpful moved between the runs.
Nothing about the drafts changed, and no code, prompt or model changed either. The only thing that could move is the reading. Helpful names a quality but sets no scale, so each reviewer decides what counts as helpful on the day. A score built that way records who read the drafts and when, not the drafts. Name the quality and pair it with a scale.

Source: Define success criteria and build evaluations

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Two reviewers were new this quarter, so the panel applied a different standard to the same drafts.

INCORRECT: Sixty archived drafts are too few to hold a quarterly score steady.
Small samples do swing, and 60 is not a large evaluation set. The same 60 drafts were scored in both runs, so sampling variation has nothing to vary. Within each run the reviewers agreed to within 3 points, which is a steady measurement of an unsteady rule. A fixed set removes sampling as an explanation for a moving score.

Helpful does cover several qualities, and splitting it would show where a change sits. Sub-scores would still be scored on the same words, with no scale behind any of them. Each one drifts the way the single number drifted. The missing piece is the scale, not the count. Breaking a vague measure into parts gives several vague measures.

questions.question:
A pharmacy chain is building a patient messaging assistant on Claude. The signed requirements name four qualities: the reply must be factually correct, must cite the source leaflet, must read in plain language, and must never give dosing advice. The evaluation suite is still on paper. The team has time to build one automated scorer before the first release and plans to add more later.
What should the architect recommend?

options.label: A
options.text: Score all four named qualities from the first release, even with a simpler check on each.

options.label: B
options.text: Send each reply to one model grader that returns a single pass or fail verdict for it.

options.label: C
options.text: Have pharmacists read a weekly sample of replies and report anything that looks wrong.

options.label: D
options.text: Delay the suite until real traffic exists to score against.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Score all four named qualities from the first release, even with a simpler check on each.
The requirements name four qualities, and the signed document is the bar the release is judged against. A suite that scores one of them can report a pass while three named requirements fail. Simpler checks on all four beat one careful check on one. The set of things you measure decides the set of failures you can see.

Source: Define success criteria and build evaluations

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Send each reply to one model grader that returns a single pass or fail verdict for it.
One grader call is cheap to build, and a model can hold all four rules in a single prompt. A single pass or fail verdict tells the team a reply failed without telling it which of the four requirements broke. Nobody can act on that. A score has to name the dimension it belongs to.

INCORRECT: Have pharmacists read a weekly sample of replies and report anything that looks wrong.
A weekly read by pharmacists brings real expertise, and it would catch dosing advice quickly. A sample read by people does not scale with release volume and produces no number the team can compare between releases. Three of the four qualities stay unmeasured. Use people where judgment is needed, not as the whole measurement.

INCORRECT: Delay the suite until real traffic exists to score against.
Real traffic does produce better cases than anything written before launch, and waiting avoids guesswork. The requirements are signed now, and a release that ships without a suite has no way to show it met them. The first release is where the risk sits. Build the measure before the thing it measures goes live.

questions.question:
An evaluation suite holds 900 cases. 600 compare one extracted field against a known value. 300 need judgment about tone. Hand grading took three weeks, so the team moves every case to a grader built on Claude and runs the suite nightly. In testing, the grader matched human scores on 97 percent of the 300 tone cases. On 50 field cases graded twice, 2 verdicts differed between passes. Nothing in the system under test changes for a month.
What does the team find at review?

options.label: A
options.text: The 600 exact-value cases change verdict between runs, so the pass rate moves.

options.label: B
options.text: The 300 tone cases drift from the old human scores while the 600 field cases hold steady.

options.label: C
options.text: The nightly run costs more to grade than hand grading did.

options.label: D
options.text: Grading the 600 field cases costs less than a code check on the same cases.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The 600 exact-value cases change verdict between runs, so the pass rate moves.
Nothing in the system changed, so any movement in the pass rate comes from the grading. In the trial, 2 of 50 field cases changed verdict on the second pass. A field either equals its known value or it does not, so a code check returns the same verdict every night. The model grader returns a judgment, and across 600 cases some judgments change.

Source: Define success criteria and build evaluations

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The 300 tone cases drift from the old human scores while the 600 field cases hold steady.
Tone is the softer question, so it looks like the place where a model grader would go wrong. The trial says otherwise: the grader agreed with the human scores on 97 percent of the tone cases. The same trial showed field verdicts changing between two passes, so the 600 do not hold steady. Expect instability where a judgment replaced a fixed rule.

INCORRECT: The nightly run costs more to grade than hand grading did.
Grader calls at this volume are a real line on a bill, and the team traded one cost for another. Hand grading 900 cases took three weeks of staff time, and a nightly model run costs far less than that. Cost is not what the review will show. Compare a new cost against the cost it replaced, not against zero.

INCORRECT: Grading the 600 field cases costs less than a code check on the same cases.
Using one grader for everything does simplify the pipeline, and a simpler pipeline feels cheaper. A code check on an exact value is a string comparison, which costs almost nothing and never varies. A model call cannot cost less than that. Use the simplest mechanism that answers the question.

questions.question:
A bank is assembling the evaluation set for a statement-parsing service that runs on Claude before it ships. Production will receive clean PDFs, scanned pages, statements in two languages and pages with a missing account header. The team can hand-write 40 cases or generate 400 with automated checking. Incidents at the bank's other services have all come from the harder input types.
What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Generate the 400 case set with automated checking, and fill it with the harder input types.

options.label: B
options.text: Hand-write one case for each of the four input types, so every type is represented in the set.

options.label: C
options.text: Hand-write the 40 cases, because hand grading reads each one carefully.

options.label: D
options.text: Ship with clean PDF cases and let support report the harder failures.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Generate the 400 case set with automated checking, and fill it with the harder input types.
The bank already knows where its incidents come from, and the four input types are named before a line of the set is written. Volume with automated checking buys enough cases per hard type to show a failure rate rather than a single hit. A larger set with a slightly weaker signal finds more real failures than a small careful one.

Source: Define success criteria and build evaluations

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Hand-write one case for each of the four input types, so every type is represented in the set.
Naming every type and covering each one looks like complete coverage, and it is a tidy plan. One case per type tells you whether a type failed once, never how often it fails or which variants inside it break. Scanned pages differ from each other. Coverage means enough cases per type, not one case per name.

INCORRECT: Hand-write the 40 cases, because hand grading reads each one carefully.
Careful reading does give the cleanest signal per case, and 40 cases are manageable for two people. Forty hand-written cases cannot hold four input types at any useful depth, and the harder types are exactly where the bank's incidents start. Care per case is not coverage. Prefer more questions with automated checking over fewer with hand grading.

INCORRECT: Ship with clean PDF cases and let support report the harder failures.
Production does surface the real distribution, and support tickets are honest evidence. The three harder input types are known now, before the service ships, so this design chooses to learn from incidents it could have prevented. The cost lands on customers. Never use production as the first test of a failure mode you can already name.

questions.question:
A logistics firm releases a rewritten Claude prompt and a new retrieval index in the same release. Weekly answer accuracy across 40,000 requests falls from 88 to 79 percent. Both changes passed the developer test set on their own. The release notes record both changes, their authors and the deploy time. After two weeks of trace reading, nobody can say which change to revert.
What is the underlying cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Every measured request carried both changes, so no number separates their effects.

options.label: B
options.text: The request traces do not record which prompt version served each request.

options.label: C
options.text: The traces show the model's reasoning, which is not reliable enough to attribute a change.

options.label: D
options.text: The prompt and the index were built by two different teams.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Every measured request carried both changes, so no number separates their effects.
The two changes went live together, so all 40,000 requests in the week carry both. Any accuracy number for that week describes the pair. There is no group of requests with the new prompt and the old index to compare against. Reading traces cannot recover a comparison that was never run. A test separates effects only when one thing differs between the two sides.

INCORRECT: The request traces do not record which prompt version served each request.
Version tagging is real instrumentation and its absence does slow many investigations. Every request in this week ran the same prompt version and the same index. A tag on each one would read identically across all 40,000. The tag has nothing to distinguish. Instrumentation records what varied; it cannot create variation that never happened.

INCORRECT: The traces show the model's reasoning, which is not reliable enough to attribute a change.
Stated reasoning is a weak source of truth, and treating it as evidence is a known mistake. The team's problem is not that the traces mislead, it is that every trace was produced under both changes at once. Better traces would say the same thing. The obstacle is the design of the release, not the quality of the record.

INCORRECT: The prompt and the index were built by two different teams.
Split ownership does make a joint failure harder to unpick, and coordination costs are real. Two teams could have shipped these changes a month apart and the attribution would have been clean. One team could have shipped both together and hit exactly this wall. Ownership sets who talks to whom, never what a measurement can show.

questions.question:
A bank runs an A/B test on two prompts for a payments support assistant built on Claude. Both variants run on the same live traffic for three weeks. Containment rate rises 6 points on the new variant. Satisfaction falls 4 points on the new variant. Handle time and cost are flat. The team declares the new variant the winner on containment. The product owner refuses the result. Both sides agree the numbers are correct.
What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Nobody fixed the deciding metric before the test, so each side picks its own.

options.label: B
options.text: The two variants did not receive an equal share of the live traffic during the test.

options.label: C
options.text: Three weeks is too short a window for satisfaction to settle.

options.label: D
options.text: Containment and satisfaction pull against each other, so one had to fall.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Nobody fixed the deciding metric before the test, so each side picks its own.
Both sides agree the numbers are correct, so measurement is not in dispute. Containment rose and satisfaction fell, and nothing written before the test says which of those decides. The team reads containment and the product owner reads satisfaction, and both readings are defensible. A test settles an argument only when the deciding metric and its bar were fixed first.

INCORRECT: The two variants did not receive an equal share of the live traffic during the test.
An uneven split is the first thing a skeptic checks, and it would undermine any comparison. The question states both sides agree the numbers are correct, so nobody is disputing how the traffic was divided. The disagreement is about which number counts. Check what is actually being argued about before questioning how it was measured.

INCORRECT: Three weeks is too short a window for satisfaction to settle.
Satisfaction is slow to move, and short windows do produce unstable readings. A longer run would give a firmer satisfaction number. The team would still hold one metric up and one metric down, with no rule to choose between them. More data does not supply a decision rule.

INCORRECT: Containment and satisfaction pull against each other, so one had to fall.
Deflecting more contacts often does cost satisfaction, so the shape of the result is familiar. Knowing the two trade off explains why the numbers moved as they did, not why the team cannot settle the call. A team that had named its deciding metric would ship or reject on that trade. An explanation of the data is not a decision about it.

questions.question:
A utility company runs a Claude assistant that answers field engineers' questions from a manual library. The library will never cover every meter model the company services. On covered topics the answers are accurate. On uncovered topics the assistant returns confident procedure text that no manual contains, which is a safety risk. The system prompt reads: always give the engineer one clear, direct answer. The team must stop invented procedures reaching engineers.
Which two changes best achieve this?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Permit the assistant to say the manuals do not cover the question.

options.label: B
options.text: Route questions the assistant cannot answer to the on-call desk.

options.label: C
options.text: Add evaluation cases on uncovered meter models, and score a decline as the pass.

options.label: D
options.text: Raise the retrieval match threshold so that weak passages never reach the answering step at all.

options.label: E
options.text: Expand the manual library to cover the meter models engineers ask about most often.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Permit the assistant to say the manuals do not cover the question.
The system prompt demands one clear, direct answer every time and offers no other way to reply. On an uncovered meter model the only reply that obeys that instruction is an invented procedure. Anthropic's guidance is to give the model explicit permission to admit uncertainty, which it says can drastically reduce false information. Remove the instruction that makes fabrication the compliant answer.

CORRECT: Add evaluation cases on uncovered meter models, and score a decline as the pass.
Permission alone is a change nobody has measured. Cases built from meter models the library does not hold turn the decline into a scored behavior. A release that quietly returns to inventing text then fails the suite. The library will always be incomplete, so these cases never go stale. Test the behavior you rely on, not only the behavior you asked for.

Source: Reduce hallucinations

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Route questions the assistant cannot answer to the on-call desk.
A human route is the right destination for a question the library cannot answer, and it protects the engineer in the field. Routing starts after the assistant decides it cannot answer, and the prompt gives it no way to reach that decision. It answers instead, so nothing is ever routed. A handoff needs a trigger before it needs a destination.

INCORRECT: Raise the retrieval match threshold so that weak passages never reach the answering step at all.
Weak passages do produce weak answers, and a stricter threshold is a real retrieval control. No manual covers these meter models, so a stricter threshold only leaves the assistant with fewer passages. The assistant still has to produce one direct answer with no source. Tuning retrieval cannot fix a rule about what counts as a valid reply.

INCORRECT: Expand the manual library to cover the meter models engineers ask about most often.
Filling known gaps is worthwhile work and would reduce how often this happens. The question states the library will never cover every meter model the company services, so uncovered questions keep arriving whatever is added. The behavior on those questions is the safety risk. Design for the gap that will always exist, not only for the gap you can close.

INCORRECT: Route questions the assistant cannot answer to the on-call desk.
A human route is the right destination for a question the library cannot answer, and it protects the engineer in the field. Routing starts after the assistant decides it cannot answer, and the prompt gives it no way to reach that decision. It answers instead, so nothing is ever routed. A handoff needs a trigger before it needs a destination.

Weak passages do produce weak answers, and a stricter threshold is a real retrieval control. Tuning retrieval cannot fix a rule about what counts as a valid reply.

questions.question:
An insurer runs its claims tool on Claude. The tool returns a written decision and shows a spinner until the whole reply arrives. The decision runs 600 words and generation takes 9 seconds. A new regulator rule requires an evidence list with every decision, which roughly doubles the output length. The integration stays synchronous and does not stream. The quality bar blocks any shortening, and adjusters already call the tool slow.
What happens next?

options.label: A
options.text: The spinner runs about twice as long, and complaints about speed grow.

options.label: B
options.text: Token cost per decision rises while the complaints about speed stay where they are now.

options.label: C
options.text: Adjusters see the first half of the decision sooner, because the reply is longer.

options.label: D
options.text: Generation time holds near 9 seconds, because the list is short.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The spinner runs about twice as long, and complaints about speed grow.
Generation time tracks the number of tokens the model has to produce, so roughly twice the output takes roughly twice as long. The integration is synchronous, so the adjuster sees nothing until the last word is written. The 9 second wait becomes close to 18. The complaint that already exists gets worse, because dead time is the thing being measured.

Source: Reducing latency

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Token cost per decision rises while the complaints about speed stay where they are now.
Output tokens are billed, so a longer decision does cost more, and that part is correct. The complaint in this question is about waiting, and the wait is exactly what doubles when a synchronous reply doubles in length. Cost and latency both move here. Answer the effect the question names, not the one that is easiest to state.

INCORRECT: Adjusters see the first half of the decision sooner, because the reply is longer.
Partial output does reach users earlier in many designs, and that instinct is the right one to have. It requires streaming, and the question states the integration stays synchronous and shows a spinner until the whole reply arrives. Nothing is sent early. A benefit that depends on a mechanism the design does not use will not appear.

INCORRECT: Generation time holds near 9 seconds, because the list is short.
Structured output can feel cheaper to produce than prose, so a list reads as a small addition. The question states the change roughly doubles the output length, and the model generates a list token by token like any other text. Length is what costs time. Judge generation time by tokens produced, not by how the text is formatted.

questions.question:
A publisher captions 250,000 archive photos every night. The job fires 250,000 standard requests to Claude and nobody reads the output until editors arrive at 7am. Finance wants the nightly bill cut and the captions unchanged. The team moves the job to the cheapest model tier, keeps every request standard, and does not re-run the caption evaluation set.
What is the most likely outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: Caption quality changes, and the job gives up capability it did not need to.

options.label: B
options.text: The bill falls and the nightly run finishes sooner as well, so both aims land.

options.label: C
options.text: The bill stays flat, because the request count is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Captions read the same as before, because captioning is simple enough for any tier.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Caption quality changes, and the job gives up capability it did not need to.
A cheaper tier is a different model, so the captions it writes differ from the ones Finance asked to keep. The saving was available without that trade. Nobody reads the output until 7am. Anthropic's message batches API charges 50 percent of standard prices for work that can wait, and most batches finish inside an hour. The workload's tolerance for waiting was the lever.

Source: Batch processing

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The bill falls and the nightly run finishes sooner as well, so both aims land.
A cheaper tier does cut the bill, and cheaper models often do respond faster, so this reads as a clean win. Finance asked for a lower bill and unchanged captions, and a different model writes different captions. Run time was never one of the two aims. A design meets its requirements only on the measures that were named.

INCORRECT: The bill stays flat, because the request count is unchanged.
Request volume does drive the bill, and 250,000 requests still go out every night. Pricing follows the tokens and the model, not the number of calls, so moving the same volume to a cheaper tier lowers the total. The count is the wrong variable. Trace a cost to what it is actually charged against.

INCORRECT: Captions read the same as before, because captioning is simple enough for any tier.
Captioning looks like a light task, and simple tasks often survive a tier change well. Finance stated that caption quality must not change, and the team did not re-run the caption evaluation set, so no evidence supports that hope. The assumption is untested. Treat a model swap as a change to the output until a measurement says otherwise.

questions.question:
A pharmacy assistant built on Claude screens every draft reply through a safety service before sending. Last month 1,100 replies went out unscreened, and 4 of them named a medicine the pharmacy does not stock. The service logs show a 200 response and a normal latency for every one of those requests. The response body carried an empty findings list, because a schema change moved the verdict into a new field.
What best explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: The caller treats an absent verdict as clean, so unchecked replies are sent.

options.label: B
options.text: The safety service was never called for any of those 1,100 replies.

options.label: C
options.text: The service's block threshold is too low for these replies.

options.label: D
options.text: The team reviews the service's verdicts once a week instead of on each reply.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The caller treats an absent verdict as clean, so unchecked replies are sent.
The service answered every request with a 200 and a normal latency, so the call itself worked. What came back held no verdict at all. The caller had no branch for that case and sent the reply anyway. A check that cannot return a verdict has not approved anything, and the default has to be a hold rather than a send.

INCORRECT: The safety service was never called for any of those 1,100 replies.
A missing call is the simplest explanation for an unscreened reply, and routing bugs do cause it. The logs carry a 200 response and a normal latency for every one of those requests, which only exists if the call was made. The service answered. Read what the evidence rules out before reaching for the simpler story.

INCORRECT: The service's block threshold is too low for these replies.
A loose threshold does let unsafe content through, and 4 wrong medicine claims fit that shape. A threshold decides what a verdict says, and no verdict was returned at all for these 1,100 replies. There was nothing to compare against a threshold. Separate a check that judged wrongly from a check that did not judge.

INCORRECT: The team reviews the service's verdicts once a week instead of on each reply.
Weekly review of a control is a real gap, and nobody noticed 1,100 unscreened replies for a month. The screen is meant to run before sending, so no review cadence would have stopped these replies going out. It would only have shortened the month. A control that runs after the action cannot replace one that runs before it.

questions.question:
A bank holds a zero data retention arrangement with Anthropic, set up for its original organization. A new team created a second organization under the same account for a claims assistant and reused the same contract language with its client. Both teams test a Claude model that requires 30-day data retention. In the original organization, every request to that model returns a 400 error saying data retention must be enabled. The same requests succeed in the second organization. Neither team changed a retention setting.
What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The arrangement covers one organization, and the second one was never enabled.

options.label: B
options.text: The model reached the second organization first, and the original organization will receive it later.

options.label: C
options.text: The contract language was copied across without a signature.

options.label: D
options.text: The claims assistant runs in a region the arrangement does not reach.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The arrangement covers one organization, and the second one was never enabled.
The error says data retention must be enabled, so the original organization still runs under zero data retention. The second organization accepts the same requests, so it does not. The documentation says zero data retention is enabled per organization and does not automatically extend to other organizations under the same account. The contract language moved to the new team, and the arrangement did not.

Source: API and data retention

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The model reached the second organization first, and the original organization will receive it later.
New software often reaches customers in stages, so a staged release is a fair first guess. The error does not say the model is unavailable. It says data retention must be enabled, which points at a retention arrangement and not at a release schedule. Read the text of an error before you explain it with a cause the text does not mention.

INCORRECT: The contract language was copied across without a signature.
An unsigned contract is a real problem, and copied clauses are a common source of it. The contract binds the bank and its client. The error comes from the platform, and it follows what the account team enabled for each organization. A signature changes an obligation and never changes a platform setting. Keep a commitment and the control that delivers it apart.

INCORRECT: The claims assistant runs in a region the arrangement does not reach.
Regional scoping is a real constraint in regulated work, so it deserves a look. Nothing in the question places the two organizations in different regions, and the error names data retention, not location. The difference follows the organization boundary. Region is an assumption added to the evidence. Build a cause from what the question states, not from what it leaves open.

questions.question:
A regulator asks a utility for the reason behind one hardship decision taken eight months ago. Two engineers are asked separately. Each opens the stored request to Claude and its reply, then writes an explanation. Both quote the same stored text. The two explanations still name different account facts as the reason for the denial. Nothing about the system changed in those eight months.
What is the underlying problem?

options.label: A
options.text: The records never held which facts drove the decision, so each reason is a reconstruction.

options.label: B
options.text: The two engineers opened different log sources, so each saw a different part of the decision.

options.label: C
options.text: Eight months is too long for anyone to reconstruct a decision accurately.

options.label: D
options.text: The two engineers read the eligibility rules differently from each other.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The records never held which facts drove the decision, so each reason is a reconstruction.
Both engineers quoted the same stored text and still named different facts. That only happens when the stored text does not say which facts decided the case. Each engineer read the rules, looked at the account and built a reason that fits. Two honest reconstructions can disagree. A reason has to be recorded when the decision is made, because it cannot be recovered afterwards.

INCORRECT: The two engineers opened different log sources, so each saw a different part of the decision.
Split logging is common and it does produce two different pictures of one event. The question states both engineers quoted the same stored text, so they were reading the same record. The record itself is what falls short. Check whether two people disagree about the evidence or about what the same evidence means.

INCORRECT: Eight months is too long for anyone to reconstruct a decision accurately.
Memory fades and eight months is a long gap, so age feels like the obvious factor. Neither engineer was recalling anything, because both worked from the stored request and reply. The same exercise a day after the decision would have produced the same disagreement. Age exposes a missing record; it does not create one.

INCORRECT: The two engineers read the eligibility rules differently from each other.
Rules do get read differently, and hardship criteria leave room for judgment. The two explanations differ on which account facts mattered, not on what the rules require. Both would still be guessing at the facts even with one agreed reading. Match the diagnosis to what the two answers actually disagree about.

questions.question:
A utility is designing a Claude agent that issues account credits. A credit posts to the customer's account immediately and the utility cannot recall it. The agent will handle about 900 credits a day. The team must be sure that no credit reaches a customer before a person has approved it. Nothing is built yet.
Which two changes best achieve this?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Require a named approver to release each batch before any credit posts.

options.label: B
options.text: Log every credit with the rule that produced it, so a wrong credit can be traced.

options.label: C
options.text: Hold every credit in a pending state that issues nothing until approval arrives.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the customer a message after each credit posts to their account.

options.label: E
options.text: Have the agent restate the eligibility rule in its output before it acts.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Require a named approver to release each batch before any credit posts.
The credit cannot be recalled, so the only moment the utility can act is before it posts. An approval placed after the action can describe what happened and change nothing. Naming the approver also fixes who carries the decision for 900 credits a day. Match the timing of a control to the reversibility of the action it governs.

CORRECT: Hold every credit in a pending state that issues nothing until approval arrives.
An approval step is only a control if the default is to do nothing. Without a defined pending state, a delayed or missed approval leaves the agent free to post the credit and the gate is decoration. The pending state is what makes waiting the safe outcome. Design what happens while a control is undecided, not only what happens when it says yes.

INCORRECT: Log every credit with the rule that produced it, so a wrong credit can be traced.
Recording the rule behind each credit is good practice and it makes any later inquiry far easier. A log is written as the credit posts, and the credit cannot be recalled once it has. Tracing tells the utility what it already cannot change. A record supports a control; it never substitutes for one.

INCORRECT: Send the customer a message after each credit posts to their account.
Telling customers what happened is honest and it may surface some errors quickly. The message arrives after the money has moved, and the customer who received a credit they should not have has no reason to report it. The action is already final. Never place the only check on the party the error favors.

INCORRECT: Have the agent restate the eligibility rule in its output before it acts.
Stating the rule does show the agent's working and makes a review faster to perform. The agent is the thing whose judgment is in doubt, so its own statement is not independent evidence about that judgment. It can state the rule correctly and still apply it wrongly. Self-declared reasoning is not a control on the party declaring it.

questions.question:
A retail bank runs one safety classifier in front of two features at a shared block threshold. A third feature now joins: a Claude assistant drafting letters that explain account closures, where a wrong statement carries regulatory risk. The branch-hours chatbot on that same threshold already blocks harmless questions, and the bank counts those blocks as a cost. The bank wants each feature blocked at the level its own risk needs.
Which change best achieves this?

options.label: A
options.text: Set a block threshold per feature, matched to the risk each one carries.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the shared threshold until the account closure letters are safe at that setting.

options.label: C
options.text: Retrain the classifier on traffic drawn from all three features.

options.label: D
options.text: Route every account closure letter to a human reviewer before it is sent.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Set a block threshold per feature, matched to the risk each one carries.
The three features carry different consequences for a mistake. A wrong sentence about opening hours costs the bank little, and a wrong sentence in a closure letter carries regulatory risk. One number cannot be right for both, which is why the chatbot over-blocks today. Strictness belongs to the feature, so the setting that controls it belongs there too.

INCORRECT: Raise the shared threshold until the account closure letters are safe at that setting.
Choosing the strictest need is the safe instinct, and the closure letters are the riskiest of the three. The chatbot already blocks harmless opening-time questions at the current setting, and the bank counts those blocks as a cost. A stricter shared number makes that worse across every feature. A single setting chosen for the hardest case penalizes the easy ones.

INCORRECT: Retrain the classifier on traffic drawn from all three features.
Training on representative traffic does improve how well a classifier judges, and the new feature brings language it has not seen. Better judgment still returns one score against one shared threshold, so the same setting decides for all three features. Accuracy and strictness are separate dials. questions.question:
Claims that an insurer's Claude assistant declines pass a review queue before the decision goes out. Two reviewers clear about 1,200 items a day between them and each item gets a real read. The insurer's policy requires the queue to be empty at the end of every day. Next quarter a new product doubles declined claim volume. Reviewer headcount stays at two.
What breaks first?

options.label: A
options.text: The read per item shortens until the review passes everything it sees.

options.label: B
options.text: The queue backs up overnight and a backlog alert fires every morning from then on.

options.label: C
options.text: Overturn rates rise, because the new product's claims are unfamiliar.

options.label: D
options.text: Decisions reach customers unreviewed, because the pipeline stops waiting for the queue.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The read per item shortens until the review passes everything it sees.
Two reviewers, twice the items and a policy that the queue must be empty each day leave one variable free. Time per item halves. A read that was real at 1,200 items becomes a glance at 2,400, and a glance approves what it is shown. The queue still reports every item cleared. Capacity sets the quality of a check.

INCORRECT: The queue backs up overnight and a backlog alert fires every morning from then on.
A doubled arrival rate against fixed staffing is the classic shape of a backlog. The insurer's policy requires the queue to be empty at the end of every day, so the reviewers clear it whatever it holds. The pressure lands on the read, not on the depth. Find the variable a rule leaves free before predicting the strain.

INCORRECT: Overturn rates rise, because the new product's claims are unfamiliar.
Unfamiliar work does produce more corrections at first, and a new product brings rules nobody has applied before. Reviewers under a fixed clearance target have less time per item, not more, so unfamiliarity shows up as faster acceptance rather than more overturns. The rate falls instead. Trace what a constraint does to behavior before predicting the number it moves.

INCORRECT: Decisions reach customers unreviewed, because the pipeline stops waiting for the queue.
Bypassing a slow gate under load is a real failure mode and worth ruling out. The queue sits before the decision goes out and the policy keeps it clear, so nothing routes around it. Every item is still reviewed on paper. A check that is always performed can still be worthless, which is the harder failure to see.

questions.question:
A claims processor has capacity to review 500 of the 6,000 decisions Claude makes a day. The team decides to spend that capacity on the 500 highest-value claims, because a wrong outcome there costs most. The model returns a confidence score with every decision, and the design ignores it. Last year's wrong outcomes were spread evenly across claim values.
What will this design fail to deliver?

options.label: A
options.text: A fall in total wrong outcomes, because claim value does not predict error.

options.label: B
options.text: Protection for high-value claims, because 500 careful reads a day cannot be sustained.

options.label: C
options.text: Any saving in reviewer time, because the highest-value claims take longest to read.

options.label: D
options.text: Fewer customer complaints, because complaints follow claim value.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: A fall in total wrong outcomes, because claim value does not predict error.
Last year's wrong outcomes were spread evenly across claim values, so the 500 highest-value claims hold no more errors than any other 500. The review reads a slice chosen by a property that says nothing about correctness. The confidence score does carry that signal, and the design throws it away. Point a fixed review capacity at the cases most likely to be wrong.

INCORRECT: Protection for high-value claims, because 500 careful reads a day cannot be sustained.
Review capacity does erode under pressure, and 500 items is a real daily load. The question states the capacity is 500 decisions a day, so the reads are within what the team can do. High-value claims do get their protection under this design. The gap is which claims were chosen, not whether the chosen ones are read properly.

INCORRECT: Any saving in reviewer time, because the highest-value claims take longest to read.
Larger claims often do carry more documents, so this sounds like a hidden cost of the choice. The team is not trying to save reviewer time; it is trying to stop wrong outcomes reaching claimants with a capacity that is already fixed. Reading time is not the measure in question. Judge a design against the outcome it was built to change.

INCORRECT: Fewer customer complaints, because complaints follow claim value.
Larger losses do prompt louder complaints, so weighting review by value looks like it buys quiet. Wrong outcomes are spread evenly across values, so most of them sit outside the reviewed slice whatever complaint volume they generate. The design misses them either way. Do not let the cost of an error stand in for the chance of one.

questions.question:
A bank runs its mortgage document checker on Claude. The written requirements state two things: extraction accuracy must reach 95 percent, and every document type the checker serves must reach that same bar. The agreed report format gives one extraction accuracy figure across the whole evaluation set. A new region joins whose locally issued income statements are 2 percent of that set.
Which stated requirement does this design fail?

options.label: A
options.text: The per-type bar, because a 2 percent type cannot move the single figure.

options.label: B
options.text: The 95 percent bar, because the new region drags the overall figure below it.

options.label: C
options.text: The per-type bar, because the report is produced only once a quarter.

options.label: D
options.text: The 95 percent bar, because 2 percent of the set is too small to score reliably.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The per-type bar, because a 2 percent type cannot move the single figure.
The requirements name two bars, and the report format answers only one of them. Income statements from the new region are 2 percent of the set. Even total failure on all of them moves the whole-set figure by about two points. The report keeps passing while a named document type fails. Break a measure out by the groups a requirement names.

INCORRECT: The 95 percent bar, because the new region drags the overall figure below it.
A weak input type does pull an average down, and that is how most people expect a new failure to show. A type holding 2 percent of the set cannot carry the figure below the bar on its own. That is precisely why the single number stays green. The size of a group decides how much of it an average can hide.

INCORRECT: The per-type bar, because the report is produced only once a quarter.
Reporting cadence is a real weakness and a quarter is a long time to run blind. A report produced every day in this format would still give one figure for the whole set and still hide the new region. Frequency changes when you look, not what you can see. Fix what a measure reports before changing how often it reports it.

INCORRECT: The 95 percent bar, because 2 percent of the set is too small to score reliably.
Small groups do give noisy figures, and that is a fair reason to want more cases for the new region. The requirement names every document type the checker serves. The answer is to grow that group and report it, not to leave it inside an average. Noise is an argument for more data. It is never an argument for not looking.

questions.question:
A software vendor builds a contract review assistant on Claude. The legal operations lead asks for wider clause coverage. The commercial lead asks for a lower cost per contract. Over two quarters the team delivers every item both leads raised, in the order the items arrived. Coverage is wider and cost per contract is lower. At the quarterly review both leads say the product has no direction.
What is the underlying problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Nobody agreed who ranks the two leads' requests, so arrival order set the priority.

options.label: B
options.text: Two quarters between reviews is too long, so each lead only ever sees their own items ship.

options.label: C
options.text: The team never sized a request against the others before building it.

options.label: D
options.text: Wider coverage and lower cost per contract pull against each other, so neither fully landed.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Nobody agreed who ranks the two leads' requests, so arrival order set the priority.
Both leads got everything they asked for, and both still say the product has no direction. Delivery was never the problem. With no agreed ranker, the team built in the order requests arrived, which is a queue and not a direction. Agreeing who ranks competing demands, before the first conflict, is what turns two request lists into one plan.

INCORRECT: Two quarters between reviews is too long, so each lead only ever sees their own items ship.
Long gaps between reviews hide progress, and a shorter cycle would show each lead what the other received. Both leads sat in the same quarterly review and both had their items delivered, so neither was short of visibility. They objected to the shape of the plan, not its pace. Faster reporting shows a queue sooner; it does not turn the queue into a priority order.

INCORRECT: The team never sized a request against the others before building it.
Sizing work before starting it is real discipline, and it would have shown which requests were cheap and which were not. Effort tells you what a request costs, never what it is worth to the business. The team could have sized all of them and still built in arrival order. A cost estimate is not a ranking until somebody says what matters more.

INCORRECT: Wider coverage and lower cost per contract pull against each other, so neither fully landed.
Coverage and cost often pull apart, since reading more clauses means processing more text. The question states the outcome plainly: coverage is wider and cost per contract is lower. Both goals landed, and the complaint arrived anyway. When a stated result contradicts an option, the option is describing a different situation than the one in front of you.

questions.question:
A research institute starts discovery for a grant reporting assistant that runs on Claude. Interviews with eleven departments will run over three weeks, and three analysts will write up what they hear. Some of what they record will be confirmed with the department that owns it, and some will be a single analyst's reading of one conversation. The build team will work from the write-up alone.
What should the architect recommend?

options.label: A
options.text: Give every finding a verification state and name what would settle the unconfirmed ones.

options.label: B
options.text: Score every finding for confidence, then sort the write-up from the highest score down to the lowest.

options.label: C
options.text: Have each of the three analysts file a separate report.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the eleven departments to review the finished write-up before the build team sees it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Give every finding a verification state and name what would settle the unconfirmed ones.
Three analysts produce one write-up, and the build team never meets the people who spoke. A verification state travels with each line and tells that team which findings are settled and which are one analyst's reading. Naming what would settle the open ones turns each of them into a task somebody can close. An unmarked assumption reads as a fact.

INCORRECT: Score every finding for confidence, then sort the write-up from the highest score down to the lowest.
A confidence score does separate strong findings from weak ones, and sorting puts the shakiest lines where a reader notices them. A score is still one analyst's opinion about a line nobody checked, and it names no action. A low-scored finding stays unverified exactly as long as a high-scored one does. Rating a statement is not the same as testing it.

INCORRECT: Have each of the three analysts file a separate report.
Separate reports do keep each analyst's sourcing visible, and the build team could trace a line back to its author. Three documents hand that team three flat lists instead of one, each holding the same mix of checked and unchecked lines. Splitting a record does not label it. Change what a record says about itself before changing how many records exist.

INCORRECT: Ask the eleven departments to review the finished write-up before the build team sees it.
Departments own the knowledge, and a review pass would catch a misheard requirement. A department cannot tell which lines it is being asked to confirm when confirmed and unconfirmed findings look identical on the page. It reads its own section and agrees with all of it. Give a reviewer a marked record, or the review confirms nothing in particular.

questions.question:
An architect must take one decision, moving a claims assistant built on Claude from a single region to two, to the engineering board and to the finance committee in the same week. The engineering board judges designs on latency, consistency and operational complexity. The finance committee judges them on cost, delivery date and risk. The decision itself is settled and the architect has one prepared deck.
What should the architect do?

options.label: A
options.text: Recast the decision twice, once in cost, date and risk, once in latency and complexity.

options.label: B
options.text: Build one deck carrying both the finance measures and the technical measures in full, for both meetings.

options.label: C
options.text: Present to the engineering board first and let it brief the finance committee.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the finance committee's session to the following month instead.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Recast the decision twice, once in cost, date and risk, once in latency and complexity.
The question names what each group judges on, and the two lists share nothing. A board that weighs latency and complexity cannot act on a delivery date, and a committee that weighs cost and risk cannot act on consistency. One settled decision can be stated in either set of measures without changing. Frame the same call in the measures the listener already uses.

INCORRECT: Build one deck carrying both the finance measures and the technical measures in full, for both meetings.
One complete deck looks safe, and neither group can complain that something was withheld. Each group then has to find its own measures inside the other group's material, which is the work the architect was meant to do. Nothing in the deck is framed for either audience. Covering every measure is not the same as framing a decision for one room.

INCORRECT: Present to the engineering board first and let it brief the finance committee.
An approval from engineers carries weight, and passing it on saves the architect a meeting. The board judges on latency, consistency and complexity, so it would hand the committee the framing that the committee cannot act on. The translation problem moves rather than gets solved. Never hand your framing problem to an audience that does not share the second audience's measures.

INCORRECT: Move the finance committee's session to the following month instead.
A later date does buy preparation time, and rushed sessions do go badly. Time was never the constraint here, because the decision is settled and the deck already exists. In a month the same deck still speaks in latency and consistency windows. Delay changes when a mismatch is met, never whether it is there.

questions.question:
A logistics operator receives a handoff pack for a route planning assistant built on Claude. The pack has one section, headed Decisions. It lists the model tier, the monthly service budget, the escalation path and a chosen address validation supplier. Procurement is still comparing that supplier against one other and has signed neither. The operator's change control will not approve an interface to an unsigned supplier. The platform team wires the chosen supplier's response format through three services and books an approval slot.
What breaks first?

options.label: A
options.text: The approval slot is refused, because the interface points at an unsigned supplier.

options.label: B
options.text: Procurement signs the chosen supplier before the slot, so the approval proceeds exactly as booked.

options.label: C
options.text: The three services fail integration testing on the response format.

options.label: D
options.text: The escalation path is rewritten before anyone notices the supplier is unsigned.

questions.explanation:

questions.question:
A regional insurer runs its claim summary assistant on Claude. The assistant passes every acceptance test. It meets all forty statements in the requirement document, which came from four discovery workshops on what the assistant should do. At the go-live gate, finance names a standing ceiling of four cents per claim that predates the project by years. The assistant sends the full policy wording with every claim and costs eleven cents.
What happens next?

options.label: A
options.text: Go-live slips while the design is reworked and the acceptance tests run again.

options.label: B
options.text: Finance raises the ceiling to eleven cents, because the assistant meets every stated requirement and passed every test.

options.label: C
options.text: The overspend is charged against what remains of the build budget.

options.label: D
options.text: The insurer runs the assistant on a sample of claims to stay under the ceiling.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Go-live slips while the design is reworked and the acceptance tests run again.
The assistant costs eleven cents against a four cent ceiling, and the cost follows the policy wording it sends with every claim. Cutting what it sends changes retrieval and prompt assembly, which the acceptance tests cover. So the tests have to run again. Forty statements about behavior never asked what the assistant must not exceed, and the gate is where that shows.

Source: Pricing

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: Finance raises the ceiling to eleven cents, because the assistant meets every stated requirement and passed every test.
A finished system that passes every test is an uncomfortable thing to stop, and the argument feels strong in the room. The ceiling predates the project by years, so it was never set to fit this build. Meeting forty functional statements is no evidence about a cost limit. A standing limit is not softened by how well the thing that breaks it works.

INCORRECT: The overspend is charged against what remains of the build budget.
Build budgets do absorb surprises, and treating the gap as a funding question buys a launch. The eleven cents is a running cost per claim, charged for as long as the assistant operates. A one-off build budget cannot cover a recurring charge that grows with volume. Match the kind of money to the kind of cost before calling a gap funded.

INCORRECT: The insurer runs the assistant on a sample of claims to stay under the ceiling.
Partial rollout is a real way to hold a cost line, and it would keep the total under the ceiling. The ceiling is stated per claim, so processing fewer claims leaves every processed claim still at eleven cents. The insurer also gets a fraction of what it specified. Check whether a limit is a total or a rate before you throttle volume against it.
