questions.question:
Eighteen months ago a hospital group's architects compared one shared document index for their Claude assistant against one index per department. They chose the shared index, because per-department indexes cost more to run and duplicated maintenance. That reasoning sits in an internal ticket. The design document names only the shared index. The sponsor who approved it has left. The new sponsor reads the design document and directs the team to move to per-department indexes. Budget and maintenance staffing are unchanged.
Which two outcomes follow?
Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: The team repeats a comparison it already completed and recorded.

options.label: B
options.text: The higher running cost and duplicated maintenance that ruled the option out return unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: The comparison is redone from scratch, and per-department indexes win on the numbers this time.

options.label: D
options.text: The departing sponsor is asked back to explain the original decision.

options.label: E
options.text: The move completes inside the quarter, because per-department indexes need no extra staffing.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The team repeats a comparison it already completed and recorded.
The architects compared both designs and recorded why the per-department option lost. None of that reached the design document, so the new sponsor has never seen it. Work the team has already done has to be done again to answer a question it already answered. Reasoning that stays internal buys nothing the next time somebody asks.

CORRECT: The higher running cost and duplicated maintenance that ruled the option out return unchanged.
The two reasons the option lost were running cost and duplicated maintenance. The question states that budget and maintenance staffing are unchanged, so nothing has moved to make the option cheaper. Building it now produces the costs the architects priced eighteen months ago. A decision reversed without its reasoning reproduces whatever the reasoning avoided.

INCORRECT: The comparison is redone from scratch, and per-department indexes win on the numbers this time.
Eighteen months is long enough for prices and tooling to move, so a different result is easy to imagine. The question holds budget and maintenance staffing fixed, which removes the two variables the original call turned on. Nothing in the evidence points to a changed answer. Do not assume a reversal is justified because time has passed since the decision.

INCORRECT: The departing sponsor is asked back to explain the original decision.
Asking the person who approved it looks like the shortest route to the reasoning. That sponsor has left, and the reasoning was written down rather than held in one head. Chasing a former colleague is slower than reading the ticket nobody linked. When a record exists but is unreachable, fix where the record lives, not who remembers it.

INCORRECT: The move completes inside the quarter, because per-department indexes need no extra staffing.
A per-department split sounds like a smaller unit of work, so a fast delivery reads as plausible. The architects rejected the option partly because it duplicates maintenance, and staffing is stated as unchanged. The same people would carry more indexes. Read the rejected option's stated costs before predicting that rebuilding it is cheap.

questions.question:
A government agency runs a two year resettlement program with an end date written into its funding agreement. A contractor builds a case summary assistant on Claude for the program's caseworkers. The delivery plan covers discovery, design, launch and monitoring, and stops at monitoring. The assistant runs on the agency's shared platform account and bills to a central cost center each month. No role in the plan owns the decision to stop it.
What is the most likely outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: The assistant keeps running and billing with nobody holding the decision to stop it.

options.label: B
options.text: The funding agreement is extended, and the assistant continues to run under the same delivery plan.

options.label: C
options.text: The monitoring reports stop being read within a few months.

options.label: D
options.text: The central cost center refuses the monthly charge in the month after the program closes.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The assistant keeps running and billing with nobody holding the decision to stop it.
The program has a fixed end date and the plan ends at monitoring. Nothing in it names who decides to stop the assistant, and the charge goes to a central account rather than the program's own. So the end date arrives and nothing acts on it. A system with no owned exit becomes permanent by default rather than by choice.

INCORRECT: The funding agreement is extended, and the assistant continues to run under the same delivery plan.
Programs are extended often enough that planning for it feels reasonable. The end date is written into the funding agreement, and the question gives no sign anyone is renegotiating it. Even an extension would leave the plan with no exit at the new date. A possible reprieve is not a lifecycle plan.

INCORRECT: The monitoring reports stop being read within a few months.
Reports do lose readers as attention moves elsewhere, and this plan ends at monitoring. Unread reports would change nothing here, because no step after monitoring exists to trigger. The assistant keeps billing whether anyone reads the reports or not. A missing decision point is a different failure from a decision nobody acts on.

INCORRECT: The central cost center refuses the monthly charge in the month after the program closes.
Central accounts do get reviewed, and an obsolete charge is the kind of thing a review catches. Pooled charges are what hide a single service, and nothing in the question says this account is reviewed against program end dates. Cost review is not a retirement decision. Do not expect a finance process to supply a lifecycle owner nobody named.

questions.question:
A software company runs two delivery teams of similar size on the same product. Both adopt Claude Code in the same week. Change size is comparable. A time study finds coding takes 34 percent of elapsed time in the checkout team and 9 percent in the billing team, where a regression suite takes three days of machine time whoever starts it. After four months the checkout team's median cycle time has fallen by a third. The billing team's has not moved.
What best explains the gap?

options.label: A
options.text: Coding is 9 percent of the billing team's elapsed time, so the assistant misses its slow step.

options.label: B
options.text: The billing team maintains an older service, so the assistant's suggestions there need heavier correction before every merge.

options.label: C
options.text: One tester runs the billing team's regression suite, so testing staff is the limit.

options.label: D
options.text: The checkout team's engineers write fuller prompts than the billing team's engineers do.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Coding is 9 percent of the billing team's elapsed time, so the assistant misses its slow step.
Both teams got the same tool in the same week, so the tool is not the variable. The difference sits in the time study. Coding is 34 percent of the checkout team's clock and 9 percent of the billing team's. The billing team's time sits in a regression suite the assistant does not touch. A gain is capped by the share the assisted step holds.

INCORRECT: The billing team maintains an older service, so the assistant's suggestions there need heavier correction before every merge.
An older service does make suggestions need more correction, and that difference between teams is easy to believe. Even suggestions that needed no correction at all would only speed the 9 percent of the billing team's clock that coding holds. The three days in the regression suite stay. A cause has to be big enough to produce the effect you are explaining.

INCORRECT: One tester runs the billing team's regression suite, so testing staff is the limit.
One tester on a suite does look like a staffing limit, and adding a second tester is a common first move. The question states the suite takes three days of machine time whoever starts it, so the wait is the run, not the queue. Staff cannot shorten it. Read what a number measures before you treat it as a headcount problem.

INCORRECT: The checkout team's engineers write fuller prompts than the billing team's engineers do.
Prompt quality does change how much rework a suggestion needs, and teams do differ in how they write them. Whatever the prompts look like, the assistant still works inside the 9 percent of elapsed time that coding holds in the billing team. The percentages, not the prompts, set the ceiling. Check the size of the step before blaming how it is used.

questions.question:
A payments group will give Claude Code to 40 engineers next quarter. A four-week trial on one team raised merged changes per week from 9 to 26, and defects found after release stayed flat. The review checklist the group uses was written eight years ago for hand-written code. Reviewers in the trial said every change read plausibly and they could not tell where to look hardest. The rollout plan covers licenses, training and usage rules only.
What should the architect recommend?

options.label: A
options.text: Rewrite the review checklist around the failure modes assistant-written code produces, before the rollout.

options.label: B
options.text: Require the assistant to write a plain-language summary of every change for the reviewer who takes it.

options.label: C
options.text: Roll the assistant out to one new team each month.

options.label: D
options.text: Cap merged changes per engineer at fifteen in any week.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Rewrite the review checklist around the failure modes assistant-written code produces, before the rollout.
The trial already showed what changes: 9 merged changes a week became 26, and reviewers could not tell where to look hardest. That is a focus problem, not a queue. The checklist still names the mistakes people make by hand, and the code arriving is no longer written by hand. Change the check before the output that defeats it arrives at scale.

INCORRECT: Require the assistant to write a plain-language summary of every change for the reviewer who takes it.
A summary does help a reviewer orient, and the trial's complaint was that nothing told them where to look. The summary comes from the same system that wrote the change, so a reviewer cannot use it to check the change. It describes, it does not direct. An artifact written by the thing under review is not a review aid.

INCORRECT: Roll the assistant out to one new team each month.
A staged rollout is careful practice, and it would keep the volume rise slow enough to watch. The trial team already met the problem at 26 changes a week, so a slower ramp only delays the same review failure. The checklist is wrong at every speed. Pacing a rollout buys time, it does not fix what the rollout exposes.

INCORRECT: Cap merged changes per engineer at fifteen in any week.
Capping output does hold review load steady, and it is the fastest lever the group controls. The stated goal is to give 40 engineers an assistant that raises their output, and a cap removes the gain the group is paying for. It also leaves the checklist untouched. A limit that undoes the benefit is not a design.

questions.question:
A document classification service running on Claude moves from its build team to a central platform rotation. The rotation grows from 8 engineers to 30, and the service keeps paging four to six times a month. The architect who built it still names the right check within two minutes, a different one each page, and nobody in the rotation can name it without her. The handover pack lists dashboards, alert thresholds and escalation contacts.
What is the most likely outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: Mean time to resolve rises, because each engineer meets a given symptom far less often.

options.label: B
options.text: Mean time to resolve falls as the larger rotation covers more symptoms.

options.label: C
options.text: Resolution time holds steady, because the dashboards in the handover pack carry the diagnosis the rotation needs.

options.label: D
options.text: Pages fall below four a month once the platform team tunes the alert thresholds.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Mean time to resolve rises, because each engineer meets a given symptom far less often.
The paging rate does not change, but the number of people sharing it almost quadruples. Eight engineers split four to six pages a month and built some pattern memory. Thirty engineers split the same pages, so most meet a given symptom for the first time. The handover pack names where to look, never which check to run next.

INCORRECT: Mean time to resolve falls as the larger rotation covers more symptoms.
More engineers does mean more people touch the service, and shared exposure usually does spread knowledge. Exposure per engineer is what matters here, and it drops as the same four to six pages spread across thirty people. Nobody gets the repetition. Knowledge spreads through what is written down, not through how many people are on the list.

INCORRECT: Resolution time holds steady, because the dashboards in the handover pack carry the diagnosis the rotation needs.
The handover pack is the obvious place for diagnosis to live, and dashboards, thresholds and contacts do look complete. Each of those items reports state. None of them says which check to run for the symptom in front of you, which is the step that only the architect can supply. A view of a system is not a procedure for it.

INCORRECT: Pages fall below four a month once the platform team tunes the alert thresholds.
Threshold tuning is real work a platform team often does at handover, and fewer pages would help. The question states the service keeps paging four to six times a month after the move, so the page rate is given rather than open. Nothing in the pack changes it. Answer with what the question fixes, not with what a team might also do.

Thirty engineers split the same pages, so most meet a given symptom for the first time. The handover pack names where to look, never which check to run next.

INCORRECT: Mean time to resolve falls as the larger rotation covers more symptoms.
More engineers does mean more people touch the service, and shared exposure usually does spread knowledge. Exposure per engineer is what matters here, and it drops as the same four to six pages spread across thirty people. Nobody gets the repetition. Knowledge spreads through what is written down, not through how many people are on the list.

INCORRECT: Resolution time holds steady, because the dashboards in the handover pack carry the diagnosis the rotation needs.
The handover pack is the obvious place for diagnosis to live, and dashboards, thresholds and contacts do look complete. Each of those items reports state. None of them says which check to run for the symptom in front of you, which is the step that only the architect can supply. A view of a system is not a procedure for it.

INCORRECT: Pages fall below four a month once the platform team tunes the alert thresholds.
Threshold tuning is real work a platform team often does at handover, and fewer pages would help. The question states the service keeps paging four to six times a month after the move, so the page rate is given rather than open. Nothing in the pack changes it. Answer with what the question fixes, not with what a team might also do.

questions.question:
A platform team rolls out Claude Code to 240 Windows laptops and 80 Macs. Four requirements are stated: every machine gets the same permission deny list; a developer cannot remove that deny list from their own machine; a managed value beats a conflicting project settings value; and a policy change reaches every machine within one working day. Windows machines receive the settings at HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode from a sign-in script that runs daily. Macs receive the com.anthropic.claudecode plist through MDM.
Which stated requirement does this design fail?

options.label: A
options.text: The removal rule, since a developer can edit HKCU without administrator rights.

options.label: B
options.text: The precedence rule, since HKCU is the lowest priority of the four managed sources.

options.label: C
options.text: The uniformity rule, since Macs and Windows use different channels.

options.label: D
options.text: The delivery rule, since a sign-in script applies a change only at the next sign-in.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The removal rule, since a developer can edit HKCU without administrator rights.
HKCU is the signed-in user's own registry branch, and writing to it needs no elevation. A developer who deletes the ClaudeCode policy key there drops the deny list from that machine until the next sign-in. The documentation calls HKCU a convenience default rather than an enforcement channel, and names the plist and HKLM locations as the ones that resist tampering.

Source: Set up Claude Code for your organization

Tip: use Ctrl+click, or Cmd+click on a Mac, to open the source in a new tab.

INCORRECT: The precedence rule, since HKCU is the lowest priority of the four managed sources.
HKCU really is the lowest of the four managed delivery mechanisms, so the ranking in this option is read correctly. That ranking settles conflicts between managed sources only. Managed values still take precedence over user and project settings, whichever mechanism delivered them. A ranking inside one tier says nothing about how that tier compares with another.

INCORRECT: The uniformity rule, since Macs and Windows use different channels.
Two delivery paths do often drift apart, and the channels named here are genuinely different products. Both paths carry the same permission deny list to every machine, and the requirement is about the content each machine receives. Nothing in the design sends one list to Macs and another to Windows. Different delivery of identical policy is not a gap in coverage.

INCORRECT: The delivery rule, since a sign-in script applies a change only at the next sign-in.
A script that waits for an event does delay a change, and delivery windows are a real risk in any rollout. The question states the sign-in script runs daily, which puts every change inside the one working day the requirement allows. The deadline is met. Measure a timing requirement against the stated cadence, not against the worst case you can imagine.

questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro validates cargo manifests with a system that queries the customs registry before it answers. The contract with the shipping lines commits to validation in under 90 seconds from the moment the manifest is submitted, with a penalty for every breach. Ignacio's team measures and reports the model call time, which rarely exceeds 20 seconds. The shipping lines record waits of more than two minutes, and the monthly committee has stopped trusting the report. What should Ignacio do with the indicator?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep measuring the team's own component and add a note to the report stating that the network and the customs registry fall outside the team's scope.
options.feedback: Stating the scope is honest, but the contract starts the clock at submission: an indicator that covers only your component does not describe the service level the shipping line receives.

options.label: B
options.text: Redefine the indicator so that it measures the full path the contract describes, from manifest submission to validation returned.
options.feedback: Correct: the indicator is measured at the same boundary that defines the commitment, so the measurement, the internal target and the penalty all refer to one number.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the committed threshold to 150 seconds so that the measurement reported today falls comfortably inside the contract.
options.feedback: Moving the threshold changes the promise without fixing the measurement: the report would still describe part of the path, and the gap with the shipping line would remain.

options.label: D
options.text: Add one indicator for every internal pipeline step and present all twelve at the monthly operations committee meeting.
options.feedback: Per-step indicators help with diagnosis, but multiplying them scatters the committee's attention and none of them answers the question the contract asks.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an SLI is a quantitative measure of some aspect of the service level being delivered, and it is only useful when it is measured where the customer experiences it. When the commitment starts the clock at manifest submission and the instrumentation starts it at the model call, the two numbers describe different things and the argument with the customer cannot be settled. Redefining the indicator over the full path aligns measurement, internal target and penalty on one boundary. The distinction against adding a scope note is that the contract fixes the boundary of the indicator, not the edge of the team that measures it.

RULE: Start the clock where the contract starts it: an indicator that covers only your component does not describe the service the customer receives.

TRAP: Confusing the time of the component you control with the service level the customer experiences end-to-end.

TRY IT: Take a service level agreement in force at your organization, mark in the text where the clock starts and where it stops, and compare that with the exact point where your instrumentation records the start.

SOURCE: https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/

questions.question: Pampero Agro has budget for a single AI pilot this year, and the board will want evidence before it funds the next stage. Valentina, the solutions architect, has four candidates and a four-month window that closes when the season starts. The business already measures how many hours it takes to produce an agronomic report, and it keeps six years of reports written by advisers. Which candidate should Valentina choose?

options.label: A
options.text: The agronomic report, because it has abundant data and a metric the business already measures, so the return is proven before the season.
options.feedback: Correct: a pilot is chosen for having meaningful, measurable success metrics, a clear return and abundant data, and here the business already counts the hours the project aims to cut.

options.label: B
options.text: The conversational assistant for advisers with no coverage, because it is the most ambitious case and shows the board what the platform can do.
options.feedback: Technical ambition is not a pilot selection criterion: with no metric the business already tracks, the board gets a demonstration rather than evidence of return.

options.label: C
options.text: The redesign of seeding planning, because it involves more departments and adoption therefore spreads across the whole company.
options.feedback: Touching many departments sounds like scale, but a good pilot disrupts existing processes as little as possible, and coordinating several of them eats the four-month window.

options.label: D
options.text: Pest detection in images, because it is the only process with no prior data, which makes the contribution of the tool more visible.
options.feedback: Absence of data is the opposite of the criterion: with no abundant data there is nothing to build the pilot on and nothing to evaluate it against inside the deadline.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the first use case is chosen for the evidence it can produce, not for how impressive it looks. The published criteria for selecting a pilot are fit with model capabilities, meaningful and measurable success metrics, a clear return, abundant data and minimal disruption to existing processes. The agronomic report satisfies the three that decide it here: the metric is already measured, the data already exists, and the result fits inside the window. The distinction against the most ambitious case is that a striking demonstration with no prior metric never becomes a defensible business case.

RULE: Choose the first use case for the evidence it can produce: a metric already measured, data that already exists, and a deadline it already fits.

TRAP: Assuming the most technically ambitious case is the one that convinces a board asking for measurable return.

TRY IT: List your organization's candidate use cases and mark for each whether the business already measures the metric you expect to move; drop the ones that have none.

SOURCE: https://assets.anthropic.com/m/66daaa23018ab0fd/original/Anthropic-enterprise-ebook-digital.pdf https://claude.com/blog/driving-ai-transformation-with-claude

questions.question: The Colibrí Pay support agent handles questions about balances, disputes, cards and fraud alerts with six tools and a single context. Tomás proposes replacing it with a coordinator and four specialized subagents, one per area, splitting the same six tools among them. A ticket review shows that 94% touch a single area and that the areas almost never consult each other. The monthly token budget is fixed, and first response is committed at 20 seconds. What effect will the change have?

options.label: A
options.text: Mean latency per ticket will drop because the four subagents work in parallel and each ticket finishes in the time of the slowest subagent.
options.feedback: Parallelism helps when there is independent work to spread out; with 94% of tickets touching one area, three of the four subagents would have nothing to do.

options.label: B
options.text: Token consumption will multiply several times with no gain in resolution, because each ticket stays sequential and confined to one area.
options.feedback: Correct: a multi-agent system burns on the order of three to ten times the tokens of a single agent, and here there is neither parallelism nor isolated context to pay for that multiplier.

options.label: C
options.text: Total cost will stay about the same because each subagent reasons over a smaller context than the current agent does.
options.feedback: Each subagent does reason over less context, but the contexts add up: the coordinator repeats the framing on every delegation and the total rises instead of holding.

options.label: D
options.text: Tool selection will improve noticeably because each subagent sees only the tools that belong to its own area.
options.feedback: Splitting tools helps when an agent juggles fifteen or twenty and picks the wrong one; six does not reach that threshold, and the first documented remedy for tool overload is not another agent.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a multi-agent architecture is justified by genuine parallelization, by information that exceeds one agent's context window, or by interaction with numerous complex tools, and only when the value of the task pays for the increase in cost. None of the three conditions holds here: tickets travel a single branch, the context fits, and there are six tools. What does show up is the multiplier, since multi-agent systems consume on the order of three to ten times the tokens of a single agent and every handoff loses context. The distinction against the expectation of lower latency is that parallelism pays when the subtasks are independent; on sequential work it only adds coordination.

RULE: Multi-agent is paid for in tokens: reserve that architecture for real parallelism, context that does not fit, or many tools, never for sequential work.

TRAP: Confusing multi-agent with parallelism and expecting speed from a split where every case travels a single branch.

TRY IT: Take one hundred real runs of your agent and count how many contain at least two subtasks that could run at the same time without waiting; if there are few, the token multiplier never pays back.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

questions.question: AndesWare runs a code-review agent over 1,200 pull requests a week and tracks spend per squad. The system prompt was written two model generations ago and still carries this line: system: "Before you answer, reason step by step inside and do not show that block; then write the review." The team has just migrated to the current model in the family, which ships with adaptive thinking on by default. If you leave that line as it is, what do you expect for the cost and the quality of the reviews?

options.label: A
options.text: The scratchpad replaces adaptive thinking, so the model stops generating internal reasoning and the cost per review drops.
options.feedback: Adaptive thinking is the model's own decision, driven by the configured effort; an instruction written in prose does not switch it off, so the scratchpad adds to the reasoning instead of replacing it.

options.label: B
options.text: The model reasons twice, once in the scratchpad and once in its thinking blocks, and reviews improve for a slightly higher cost.
options.feedback: Reasoning twice sounds like extra care, but the documented prompt audit treats a hand-written scratchpad as a defect that costs accuracy points, not as a reinforcement.

options.label: C
options.text: The scratchpad duplicates reasoning the model already does, adds billed output tokens and can cost accuracy.
options.feedback: Correct: asking for reasoning in prose was the fallback technique for when thinking is off; today reasoning is requested with a request parameter and the hand-written block is billed as output.

options.label: D
options.text: Nothing changes: on models with adaptive thinking, reasoning instructions written in prose are ignored entirely.
options.feedback: The instruction is followed: the model writes the block and bills it as output tokens. What is true is that it no longer adds anything, which is why it has to come out of the prompt.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that hand-written chain-of-thought is the fallback technique for when thinking is off: on current models the reasoning is requested with a request parameter and read in the thinking blocks, not in prose. A legacy prompt that orders a scratchpad does not switch adaptive thinking off, it adds to it. You pay output tokens on every review, and the documented prompt audit lists this kind of leftover text as one that no longer fits the new model and costs accuracy. The distinction against the idea that reasoning twice helps is that the second pass is neither independent nor better: it is a poorer copy of the one the model already does.

RULE: When you migrate models, audit the prompt: what was a fallback technique in the last generation is usually a defect you pay for in tokens in this one.

TRAP: Treating a reasoning instruction written in prose as if it controlled the model's thinking, when today a request parameter decides that.

TRY IT: Run the same review with the legacy prompt and with the scratchpad removed over ten real pull requests, and compare output_tokens and the quality of the findings in each version.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence

questions.question: Agencia Nacional de Ingresos published a service commitment for its taxpayer assistant: the user must see text on screen in under 1 second, although the full answer may take up to 8. Every call goes out with this configuration: {"stream": false, "max_tokens": 1200, "service_tier": "auto"}. Measurements show 5.2 seconds to full response at the 95th percentile, inside the commitment, but taxpayers report that the screen stays blank for almost all of that time. Which configuration change addresses what they are reporting?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn on streaming for the call, so the assistant shows text as soon as the first token appears.
options.feedback: Correct: streaming is the lever for perceived latency, which is exactly what the commitment promises, and it leaves total generation time untouched.

options.label: B
options.text: Turn on fast mode with the speed field, which multiplies the model's output tokens per second.
options.feedback: Fast mode raises generation speed, but it does not bring the first token forward: the screen would stay blank for the same initial stretch.

options.label: C
options.text: Send the queries through the Message Batches API and take advantage of the 50% discount on price.
options.feedback: The batch discount is real, but batch is asynchronous with a window of up to 24 hours, which is no use with a taxpayer waiting.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower max_tokens to 400 so the answer finishes sooner and the taxpayer's overall wait gets shorter.
options.feedback: Cutting the output shortens total time, which is already met, and the user still sees nothing until the whole answer arrives.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to pick the lever that matches the metric you committed to. Perceived latency and time to first token are addressed with streaming, generation speed with fast mode, peak saturation with priority capacity, and cost with batch processing. Here the commitment says nothing about total time, which is already met with room to spare. It is about when the person sees something, and streaming delivers the text as it is produced. The distinction against fast mode is that fast mode improves output tokens per second but does not bring the first token forward, so it never moves the committed number.

RULE: Before you pull a lever, read which metric the agreement promises: first token, generation speed, or cost. Each one has its own.

TRAP: Confusing perceived latency with total generation time, and buying speed where what is needed is an earlier start.

TRY IT: Run the same query with streaming on and with streaming off, and time in each case how many milliseconds pass before the first character appears on screen.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros is about to put automated claims triage into production: 6,000 reports a day that the system classifies and routes. The risk committee will not approve the launch until the team presents success criteria that can be measured before and after every change. Renata, the solution architect, has 2,000 reports already labeled by adjusters and four weeks. Which two success criteria should she propose? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Classification accuracy of at least 0.85 F1 on the held-out set of 2,000 reports labeled by adjusters.
options.feedback: Correct: it names the metric, the threshold and the set it is measured on, which is what lets you compare the system before and after every change.

options.label: B
options.text: Adjuster satisfaction with the triage, collected in a quarterly survey and reviewed by the risk committee.
options.feedback: Qualitative signal is worth having alongside the numbers, not instead of them: a quarterly survey cannot say whether last week's change improved the triage or hurt it.

options.label: C
options.text: Routing decisions must be explainable and consistent with the underwriting policy, as judged by the compliance team.
options.feedback: Explainable and consistent describes what the regulator wants, but with no metric and no threshold nobody can decide whether the system already complies.

options.label: D
options.text: Under 1% of replies carrying the policyholder's personal data, verified with a binary classifier over 500 cases.
options.feedback: Correct: it turns a sensitive dimension into a number with a measurement method and a sample size, and it measures something other than accuracy rather than a variant of it.

options.label: E
options.text: 100% accuracy across the six claim categories, including those that appear fewer than ten times a year.
options.feedback: A target has to be achievable: demanding 100% in categories with very few cases a year guarantees the criterion is never met and stops working as a launch gate.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a success criterion works when it is specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and that most use cases need multidimensional evaluation: several dimensions, each with its own number. An F1 threshold on a held-out labeled set covers task fidelity, and a threshold on personal-data leakage verified with a binary classifier covers privacy. The two are independent measures and both can be re-run after every change. The distinction against the qualitative criteria is that numbers give clarity and scale, and qualitative signal only helps when it is applied consistently alongside them. A target today's technology cannot reach stops being a criterion and becomes a blocker.

RULE: A success criterion with no number, no measurement method and no dataset is not a criterion: it is an intention.

TRAP: Confusing an ambitious target with an achievable one, and setting 100% exactly where there are not enough cases to measure it.

TRY IT: Take the success criterion your system has today and rewrite it with a metric, a threshold, a set size and a measurement method; if you cannot fill all four fields, it is not measurable yet.

questions.question: Colibrí Pay's support agent connects to four remote MCP servers: two internal and two from outside vendors. The contract with its largest corporate client commits to a first response in under 5 seconds. Since the fourth server was added, the 95th percentile of that first response has gone from 2.1 to 9.4 seconds, and one session in ten opens with a connection error against the antifraud scoring server. The answers, when they arrive, are correct. Mateo started by reviewing the prompt and the model. Where should he look first?

options.label: A
options.text: At the size of the catalog: four servers together hold enough definitions to degrade selection of the right tool.
options.feedback: The degradation threshold from tool count is real, but it shows up as wrong choices, not as delays or failures when the session starts.

options.label: B
options.text: At the startup dependency: the session waits for each remote server to connect and list its tools, and the slowest one sets the floor.
options.feedback: Correct: every remote server is a first-turn dependency with its own connection timeout, so a slow one delays startup and a dead one breaks it.

options.label: C
options.text: At prompt caching: changing the tool definitions invalidates the whole prefix and forces a cache rewrite on every session.
options.feedback: It is true that modifying the tools invalidates every level of the prefix, but that raises the cost of the call. It does not produce a connection error against one specific server.

options.label: D
options.text: At the model: a faster one in the family would bring the first response down without touching the integration at all.
options.feedback: Changing the model moves generation time, and here the delay happens before the model receives the first request.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to attribute the symptom to the layer where it occurs. A connection error and a delay that both appear before the model produces any text belong to the integration, not to the prompt or the model. Every remote MCP server connects and lists its tools when the session opens, with a default timeout of 30 seconds, so the slowest external server sets the floor for the first response and an unavailable one makes it fail. An in-process MCP server, running inside the application itself, never delays the first turn, which is why the choice of integration mechanism matters when a first response is committed. The distinction against having too many tools is that an oversized catalog is paid in selection accuracy and in tokens.

RULE: Every remote server you add is a first-turn dependency: the slowest one defines your startup and a failing one takes the session down.

TRAP: Searching the prompt or the model for a symptom that occurs before the model receives the first request.

TRY IT: Time your agent's startup with every MCP server connected, then repeat the measurement with the slowest one disconnected: that difference is what your first response is paying.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/mcp https://claude.com/blog/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk

questions.question: Bastión Legal labels every precedent in its internal repository with its subject matter and its outcome, and wants that output to keep the same structure every time. According to the prompting documentation, how should examples be used inside the prompt?

options.label: A
options.text: A single very detailed and extensive example, so the model does not copy accidental patterns from several different cases.
options.feedback: One example fixes the format but does not cover the edge cases; diversity is exactly what keeps the model from generalizing the wrong pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: At least twenty examples in every request, which is the documented minimum for classification tasks.
options.feedback: Twenty or more examples do perform well when that block is cached, but they are not a minimum: the documented recommendation for starting out is three to five.

options.label: C
options.text: No examples: describing each category with explicit, exhaustive rules in the system prompt is enough.
options.feedback: Clear instructions are the foundation and the model follows them well, but for fixing format and structure, examples work better than an abstract description.

options.label: D
options.text: Three to five relevant and diverse examples, wrapped in tags that separate them from the instructions.
options.feedback: Correct: three to five relevant and diverse examples, wrapped in tags, is the documented recommendation for improving accuracy and format consistency.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that examples are the most reliable way to steer format, tone and structure, and that their value rests on three properties: they have to be relevant to the real case, diverse enough to cover the edges, and wrapped in tags so the model does not mistake them for instructions. The documented number to start with is three to five. More examples are not forbidden, and twenty or more do perform well once that block is cached, but that is a later optimization and not a minimum. The distinction against the zero-example option is that explicit rules work for content, while structure travels better when you show it.

RULE: Three to five relevant, diverse, tagged examples; raise the count only once that example block is cached.

TRAP: Reading the cached variant with twenty or more examples as if it were a mandatory minimum for any classification task.

TRY IT: Label twenty precedents with no examples, with one, and with four diverse examples, and count how many come back with exactly the output structure you asked for.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom's platform team added a hook that must block edits to the scripts that compute the contractually committed first response time. Since Malena saved this block in the repository's ".claude/settings.json", the hook never fires, and the "permissions.deny" rules in that same file have stopped applying across every team session. The block is: {"hooks": {"PreToolUse": [{"matcher": ["Edit", "Write"], "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/hooks/proteger.sh"}]}]}}. A deployment ships tonight. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The "proteger.sh" script is not executable, and a hook that exits with code 127 never gets to block the call.
options.feedback: A missing or non-executable script does exit with 127 and leaves the gate silently open, but that would not explain why the permission rules in the same file stopped applying too.

options.label: B
options.text: The matcher is written as a JSON array instead of a string, and that schema error causes the whole settings file to be rejected.
options.feedback: Correct: that is why the hook and the permission rules that shared the file fail at the same time. The matcher takes the string "Edit|Write" or a comma-separated list inside a string.

options.label: C
options.text: Hooks are read only from the "~/.claude.json" file, which is where Claude Code keeps the effective configuration of each project.
options.feedback: That file does exist, but it holds application state and preferences: the "permissions", "hooks" and "env" keys placed there are ignored. The file Malena chose is the right one.

options.label: D
options.text: Changes to the settings file are read only when the session opens, so sessions already running keep the previous configuration.
options.feedback: Edits to the settings file apply to the running session after a short file-stability wait; no restart is needed, and that would not explain the permission rules failing either.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when you diagnose configuration is to look first at how far the symptom reaches: if other keys in the same file stopped applying alongside the hook, the problem is the file and not the hook. The matcher has to be a string, and writing it as an array is a schema error that makes Claude Code reject the entire user, project or local settings file, so the permission rules that lived there disappear for the session. That is exactly the distinction against the non-executable script hypothesis: a missing or non-executable script leaves the gate silently open, but it does not touch the rest of the file.

RULE: When more breaks than what you touched, suspect the schema: one mistyped field invalidates the whole settings file, not just the key you edited.

TRAP: Confusing a hook that fails to run with a settings file that never loaded at all.

TRY IT: Write the matcher as an array in a test project's settings, open "/hooks" to see that the hook is missing, and run "claude doctor" to read which file was rejected; then switch it to the string "Edit|Write" and repeat.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/debug-your-config https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud wants a triage system for patient queries across its forty clinics before the winter peak. Camila has two engineers and six weeks, and the clinical department has already written the criteria that make a query correctly routed. The team is arguing whether to start from an orchestrator with subagents per specialty or from something simpler. What order of work should you propose?

options.label: A
options.text: Optimize a single call with retrieval and examples, measured against the clinical criteria → add tools if they are needed → add routing only if the categories get confused.
options.feedback: Correct: the recommendation is to find the simplest possible solution and increase complexity only when it is needed, because for many applications optimizing a single call with retrieval and examples is enough.

options.label: B
options.text: Stand up the orchestrator with one subagent per clinical specialty → measure the quality of each branch separately → drop the subagents that add nothing later on.
options.feedback: An orchestrator is legitimate when you cannot foresee the subtasks, but starting there with two engineers and six weeks pays for coordination before anyone knows it was needed.

options.label: C
options.text: Define the full set of clinical tools → build the autonomous agent on top of them → write the evaluation from the cases that fail in production.
options.feedback: Tools are necessary, but defining them all before measuring inverts the order: the evaluation guides the build, it does not document after the fact what has already failed.

options.label: D
options.text: Pick the most capable model and the largest thinking budget → write the prompt on that basis → define the success criterion when the pilot closes.
options.feedback: The model and the thinking budget are real levers, but the success criterion is set before the model is chosen, because it is what tells you whether that model is enough.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to start from simple prompts optimized against a complete evaluation, and to add multi-step agentic systems only when the simple version falls short. The customer support guide describes the same ladder: optimize the prompt, then add tools, and only when the system handles very varied tasks add a classifier that routes the initial query. With two engineers, six weeks and clinical criteria already written, that ladder is also the only one that leaves time to measure before the peak. The distinction against starting at the orchestrator is that complexity is added when the measurement demands it, not as a starting point.

RULE: Climb one step at a time: one well-measured call, then tools, and routing only when the categories demand it.

TRAP: Assuming a more elaborate architecture shortens the path, when what it does is pay the coordination cost before any measurement exists.

TRY IT: Write down on one sheet what a single call with retrieval and three examples would produce for the case you are about to build; if you cannot say why that would fall short, you do not need an agent yet.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/customer-support-chat

questions.question: A platform team needs to answer two questions about one specific API call: whether prompt caching is working, and exactly which call failed. Which TWO official signals answer them? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The organization's daily Cost API report, grouped by workspace and by description.
options.feedback: The Cost API reconciles organization spend in daily buckets. It does not identify a single call, and it carries no cache detail.

options.label: B
options.text: The anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-remaining and anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-reset headers on the response.
options.feedback: Those headers tell you how much quota is left before throttling, which is capacity. They do not say whether the prefix was read from cache, or which call it was.

options.label: C
options.text: The cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens fields in the response usage object.
options.feedback: Correct: if both come back at zero the prefix was not cached, and that failure is silent because no error is returned.

options.label: D
options.text: The usage.service_tier field, which reports whether the request was served with priority capacity.
options.feedback: It is useful data for analyzing latency and capacity, but it answers neither of the two questions asked.

options.label: E
options.text: The response request-id header, together with the request_id field the error body carries.
options.feedback: Correct: that identifier locates the exact call among millions, and it is what you attach when you report a specific problem.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that each operational question has its own official surface, and it pays not to mix them. The usage object on every response is the only source that says whether the prefix was read from cache, and that matters because when the prefix falls below the minimum cacheable size no error is returned at all: both counters sit at zero and the saving simply does not happen. The request identifier, in turn, is what lets you point at one concrete call. The rate limit headers and the cost report answer different questions, about quota and about aggregate spend, and they arrive at a different granularity.

RULE: One question, one surface: usage for what happened in the call, request-id for which call it was, and the Cost API only for aggregate spend.

TRAP: Asking the cost report, which arrives aggregated and delayed, for answers about one individual call.

TRY IT: Take any response from your service, note its request-id and its two cache fields, and check whether your dashboard stores both or only the token total.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

questions.question: Catalog enrichment at Mistral Retail classifies 40,000 new products every night into a tree of 600 categories, inside a six-hour window and with no users waiting. A wrong category breaks search on the site, so the cost of an error is commercial and immediate. Joaquín's failure analysis shows that nearly all errors happen between sibling categories in the same family, inside footwear for example, and almost never across families. Which design is the right one?

options.label: A
options.text: Send all 600 categories in a single prompt and move up to the most capable model in the family until accuracy reaches the commercial target.
options.feedback: A flat prompt with 600 labels is exactly the case the guide solves with a taxonomy; changing models does not change the fact that sibling categories share almost all of their context.

options.label: B
options.text: Retrieve the most similar already-classified products from a vector store and use them as dynamic few-shot examples in the flat classifier.
options.feedback: Examples retrieved by similarity are a documented alternative and raise accuracy considerably with variable inputs, but they do not give different instructions for each branch of the tree.

options.label: C
options.text: Run every product three times through the same classifier and keep the most voted category, taking advantage of the nightly window.
options.feedback: Repeating the classification and voting raises confidence when the errors are random; here they are systematic between siblings, so all three runs go wrong the same way.

options.label: D
options.text: Classify in a cascade down the levels of the tree, with its own prompt per family, accepting the extra latency of chained classifiers.
options.feedback: Correct: organizing the categories into a tree and chaining classifiers by level allows a different prompt per branch, and the nightly window absorbs the extra latency.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for a large classification space is to organize the categories into a tree structure and create classifiers at each level, routing in a cascade. The documented benefit is more nuance and accuracy, because you can write a different prompt for each parent path; the documented cost is latency, because several classifiers run in series. That cost does not bite here, since the work runs at night in batch and nobody is waiting, and the errors sit precisely between siblings, which is what a prompt per family separates. The distinction against examples retrieved by similarity is that they improve a flat classifier but never give it different criteria per branch.

RULE: When the errors live between sibling categories, break the taxonomy into levels and pay the latency if the window allows it.

TRAP: Assuming a bigger model fixes a decomposition problem, when what is missing is a different criterion for each branch of the tree.

TRY IT: Take 50 misclassifications from your system and group them by family; if most fall between siblings, write a prompt for that family and measure only that subset again.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/ticket-routing

TRY IT: Take 50 misclassifications from your system and group them by family; if most fall between siblings, write a prompt for that family and measure only that subset again.

questions.question: Minera Nevado uses an assistant that classifies operational safety reports and proposes which ones get investigated first; about 2,400 reports arrive each month. Camila, the compliance lead, has noticed that reports filed by women workers and by foreign contractor staff end up with lower priority. The safety committee wants quantitative evidence before next month's audit, and right now neither a bias in the system nor a genuine difference in severity between the reports can be ruled out. What should you do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Run a fixed set of reports again while varying only the demographic data, and measure the priority difference in both directions.
options.feedback: Correct: holding the technical content constant while varying a single attribute isolates the effect of the system, and looking both ways reveals negative as well as positive discrimination.

options.label: B
options.text: Add an instruction to the system prompt telling the model to disregard gender and nationality when it assigns priority.
options.feedback: Prompt engineering is the documented mitigation and it does reduce measured discrimination, but applying it before measuring leaves the committee without the baseline it asked for.

options.label: C
options.text: Rebalance the set of historical reports that feeds the search so that every group ends up equally represented.
options.feedback: Rebalancing attacks the computational and statistical bias of a dataset, which is one of the three categories and not the one that has been shown here.

options.label: D
options.text: Move up to the most capable model in the family, which reasons better about nuance in the text and narrows the gap between groups.
options.feedback: Changing models is a lever on capability and cost; it produces neither the evidence the committee asked for nor proof that the difference has gone away.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a suspicion of bias becomes evidence only when you isolate the variable. The documented method is to run a fixed set of decision scenarios again while varying the demographic information in the prompt systematically, then compare the results, because that is what surfaces both negative and positive discrimination, which an aggregate average hides. With that baseline in hand, correcting the prompt is the documented mitigation and you can also show how much it narrowed the gap. The distinction against correcting first is that without a prior measurement nobody can tell whether the difference came from the system, or whether the correction worked.

RULE: Measure by varying one attribute before you touch the prompt: with no baseline you know neither that bias existed nor that your fix reduced it.

TRAP: Treating an observed difference between groups as proof of system bias without isolating the attribute that produces it.

TRY IT: Take ten real cases from your system, duplicate each one changing only a single demographic attribute on the form, and compare the decisions that come back; note the differences in both directions, not only the unfavorable ones.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/news/evaluating-and-mitigating-discrimination-in-language-model-decisions https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/

questions.question: The broker-reply assistant at Zafiro Seguros returns a JSON object with three fields that the CRM loads with no human review. 4% of replies arrive with a field missing or with the policy number as text, the CRM rejects them, and the automatic retry the team added already eats 9% of monthly spend. The prompt describes the format in detail and shows two examples. Mateo has to eliminate the rejections, not reduce them. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add three more examples of the expected JSON and repeat the format at the end of the prompt to reinforce the structure.
options.feedback: More examples improve consistency and are good practice, but they remain a statistical guide: they cannot guarantee the schema holds on case number 5,000.

options.label: B
options.text: Use structured outputs with the JSON schema declared, which guarantees conformance instead of asking for it by prompt.
options.feedback: Correct: the documentation says to use structured outputs rather than prompting techniques when the output must always match a schema, because it constrains sampling to valid outputs.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the model's effort so it spends more reasoning building the reply and stops omitting fields.
options.feedback: More reasoning can improve the content of the reply, but the problem is neither judgment nor capability: nothing is enforcing the shape of the output.

options.label: D
options.text: Repair the output with your own parser that fills the missing fields and converts the types before handing it to the CRM.
options.feedback: Repairing afterward hides the symptom and adds one more piece to maintain; a parser that guesses the type of a policy number can also introduce silent errors.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that when the output must always satisfy a schema, the documented answer is structured outputs and not more prompting: the constraint is applied during sampling, so valid JSON stops being a likely result and becomes a guarantee. Prompting, examples and a described format raise the hit rate, which is exactly what the team already has, but they leave a tail of failures that here is paid for in retries. The distinction against raising the effort is that the model is not failing for lack of reasoning: it gets the content right and the shape wrong, and the shape is the only thing structured outputs secures.

RULE: If the schema has to hold every time, enforce it in the request with structured outputs: the prompt describes the shape, it does not guarantee it.

TRAP: Treating a format failure as a capability failure and spending effort or a bigger model where a schema constraint was needed.

TRY IT: Send one hundred requests with your current prompt and count how many replies break the schema; repeat with that same schema declared in output_config.format and compare the two counts.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

questions.question: Minera Nevado is connecting its environmental permits assistant to an MCP server run by an outside provider. Security has not audited that server and has not put it on the trusted server list. The server exposes tools to query case files and to file amendments with the regulator. A filed amendment is irreversible, and the regulatory deadline leaves no room to withdraw it. Tomás is deciding how human control over those calls should work. Which of these statements about that design is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The MCP specification says there should always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny a tool invocation.
options.feedback: That is a true and normative statement from the specification, so it cannot be the answer to a question that asks for the false one.

options.label: B
options.text: The client should show the user the tool inputs before sending them to the server, because that is where accidental or malicious exfiltration is caught.
options.feedback: Also true: the specification assigns this to the client, along with validating the results before they are passed to the model.

options.label: C
options.text: If the provider's server marks its tools with annotations such as "readOnlyHint", the client can rely on them to decide which ones need human confirmation.
options.feedback: Correct as the false statement: annotations are declarations made by the server, and the client must treat them as untrusted unless they come from trusted servers, which this provider is not.

options.label: D
options.text: Logging every tool invocation for audit is the responsibility of the client, while limiting how often tools may be invoked belongs to the server.
options.feedback: True: the specification splits the obligations that way, with logging on the client side and rate limiting on the server side.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that human control over an irreversible action is decided by the client, not by the server that offers the tool. The MCP specification asks that a human able to deny an invocation always be present, that the client show the inputs before sending them, and that it log invocations for audit. Annotations such as "readOnlyHint" or "destructiveHint" are metadata declared by the server itself, and the specification requires treating them as untrusted unless they come from trusted servers, so they are no basis for skipping a confirmation. The key distinction is between a description of intent and a control enforced in code.

RULE: A server annotation describes an intent; the human gate is your client's decision and it is written in your code.

TRAP: Treating a hint declared by a third party as if it were a verified security control.

TRY IT: List the tools of an MCP server you already use, mark the ones that take irreversible actions, and check whether your client asks for confirmation because of a server annotation or because of a rule you wrote yourself.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación grades 40,000 written assignments a week. Every request carries a grading guide of about 6,000 tokens that is identical across subjects, the specific criteria for the eight subjects (another 9,000 tokens, of which each assignment uses one), and the student's text. The per-student budget is cents, and the ask is to cut spend without touching quality. Requests arrive in bursts, seconds apart, and the agent already has the code execution tool enabled. Which two reuse measures do you apply? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Put the shared guide first and set the cache breakpoint at the end of that block, so gradings share the prefix.
options.feedback: Correct: the cache requires the prefix to repeat byte for byte, so what is identical across subjects goes before the breakpoint and what varies goes after.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the cache TTL to one hour, so the prefix stays alive even though the gradings arrive seconds apart.
options.feedback: The one-hour duration costs double on the write and is meant for gaps of five minutes to an hour; with bursts seconds apart, the short cache refreshes for free on every use.

options.label: C
options.text: Move each subject's criteria into its own Skill, so only the one the grading activates is loaded.
options.feedback: Correct: until it activates, a Skill occupies only its name and its description, so you stop paying on every grading for the criteria of the seven subjects that do not apply.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to the most capable model in the family so each grading needs fewer retries and costs less per assignment.
options.feedback: A more capable model can cut retries, but that is a cost-for-intelligence trade and quality here is already good enough: the levers that leave it alone come first.

options.label: E
options.text: Trim the shared guide below the model's cacheable minimum to reduce the input billed on every request.
options.feedback: Below the cacheable minimum, caching silently stops applying with no error, so trimming the guide can make the flow more expensive rather than cheaper.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that free levers come before trades: prompt caching and token hygiene cut spend without touching quality, while switching models moves quality and cost at the same time. There are two distinct and compatible reuses here. The block that is identical across subjects is written to cache once and read on all 40,000 gradings, and the criteria that apply to a single subject leave the prompt and become Skills, which until they activate occupy little more than their metadata. The distinction against raising the TTL is that the long duration exists to cover gaps between requests, and here there are no gaps to cover.

RULE: Cache what is the same for everyone and load on demand what applies to only some: paying context for what goes unused is the commonest leak.

TRAP: Assuming a longer cache duration always saves, when the write costs double and the saving only appears if there are gaps to cover.

TRY IT: Measure cache_read_input_tokens on two consecutive gradings from different subjects; then take the subject criteria out of the prefix and check how much input_tokens drops per request.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview

questions.question: At Bastión Legal, the contract review agent currently receives the counterparty's clauses and the review checklist in the same block of user text. The professional liability insurer requires that checklist to be applied to every contract. Joaquín proposes that the "fetch_contract" tool return both together inside a tool_result, arguing that the model will then treat all of it as data rather than as instructions. What effect will the change have?

options.label: A
options.text: The clauses end up better placed, and the checklist will be applied more strictly, because what arrives in a tool_result weighs more than a user turn.
options.feedback: The first half is right, but the second inverts the rule: the content of a tool_result is read with skepticism, not with added authority.

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing changes on either side, because the type of block affects how the conversation is displayed but not how the tokens are processed.
options.feedback: The type of block does change the treatment: the model is trained to distrust instructions that appear inside a tool_result.

options.label: C
options.text: The clauses end up where they belong, but the checklist may be ignored or flagged as an injection attempt, because a tool_result is treated as untrusted content.
options.feedback: Correct: that is why your own instructions have to travel in a later user turn, not inside the same tool_result as someone else's document.

options.label: D
options.text: Prompt injection risk disappears for that agent, because the model is trained not to follow instructions that arrive inside a tool_result.
options.feedback: The placement lowers the chance that an injected instruction succeeds, but no defense at the model layer is completely effective.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that someone else's content goes in a tool_result and your own instructions do not. The model is trained to treat instructions that appear inside a tool_result with skepticism: that is exactly what you want for the counterparty's clauses and exactly what ruins the checklist. The documentation says it plainly, that your own instructions placed in a tool_result may be ignored or flagged as a possible injection attempt, and that they should be sent in a following user turn. Because the policy requires the checklist on every contract, that side effect is no detail: it turns a security improvement into a compliance failure.

RULE: Someone else's content goes in the tool_result; your instructions go in the user turn that follows. Never mix them in one block.

TRAP: Assuming that the safest block for someone else's text is also the most obeyed block for your own.

TRY IT: Send the same request twice, once with your checklist inside the tool_result and once with the checklist in a later user turn, and count how many checklist points are actually applied in each response.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks

questions.question: The Agencia Nacional de Ingresos hands its filing classification system to an internal team and to an external contractor that will maintain it for three years. The tender requires that the data residency rule and the list of approved models cannot be changed from a developer workstation, and the audit will verify this every six months. Malena, the project architect, is assembling the documentation and implementation package. How should she split that content?

options.label: A
options.text: Write a long architecture document describing the residency rule and hand it over signed, together with the source code of the system.
options.feedback: A document describes the rule but does not enforce it; the tender asks that it cannot be changed from a developer workstation, and only a control that executes delivers that.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave in CLAUDE.md the conventions that guide daily work and move what cannot be broken into managed policy with permissions and hooks.
options.feedback: Correct: CLAUDE.md is for how we work here, and permissions and hooks are for the limits that must hold whatever the model decides, which is what the tender requires.

options.label: C
options.text: Put the residency rule in capitals at the top of the repository CLAUDE.md and require by contract that the contractor never edit that file.
options.feedback: Writing the rule in capitals makes it visible, not binding: CLAUDE.md is guidance for the model, and it is a file anyone with repository access can edit.

options.label: D
options.text: Log every use of a model outside the approved list with a hook and review that log in the semiannual audit the tender requires.
options.feedback: The log leaves a trail for the audit but does not prevent the call; observing a forbidden action is not the same as blocking it, and the breach would already have happened.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that documentation and control solve different problems: CLAUDE.md tells the model how your project works so that it makes good decisions, while permissions and hooks impose limits regardless of what the model decides. Use CLAUDE.md for the conventions that say how things are done here, and permissions or hooks for security boundaries and for anything that must never happen, that is, when you need a guarantee rather than guidance. A tender requiring that a rule cannot be changed from a developer workstation is asking for exactly a guarantee. The distinction against highlighting it inside CLAUDE.md is that the file is editable advice.

RULE: Write guidance in CLAUDE.md and enforcement in permissions or hooks: advice and guarantee do not live in the same file.

TRAP: Treating an instruction written in the project documentation as if it were a control enforced by the system.

TRY IT: Open your project configuration and mark each rule as advice or as guarantee; for the ones you marked guarantee, check whether a permission or a hook enforces it when the model decides otherwise.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/debug-your-config https://code.claude.com/docs/en/admin-setup

questions.question: The clinical-record summarizer at Red Vicuña Salud prepends a stable block of about 11,000 tokens to every request, holding the clinical protocol and the output format, marked with a cache breakpoint; today almost every request reads it from cache. To trace each summary in the internal audit, Camila proposes adding a line at the start of that block with the clinic code, the physician's license number and the exact time of the request. The per-clinic budget is fixed and 12,000 summaries are generated daily. What effect will the change have?

options.label: A
options.text: The prefix will still be read from cache, because a line that short cannot alter the protocol block behind it.
options.feedback: A cache hit requires the prefix to match a recent request exactly; the size of the change does not enter that comparison.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the block holding that line will be invalidated and the protocol will still be read from cache, so the extra cost is marginal.
options.feedback: Invalidation is not scoped per block: a change drags its level and every level after it, so the entire protocol is rewritten.

options.label: C
options.text: Input spend will drop, because with a different prefix on every call the system stops writing cache and charges only base input.
options.feedback: The block is still marked, so every request creates a new cache entry, and writing one costs more than base input, not less.

options.label: D
options.text: No request will read from cache again and each one will rewrite the whole protocol, so input spend will rise.
options.feedback: Correct: text that changes on every call, placed at the front of the prefix, invalidates all of it and turns a cheap read into an expensive write.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the cache compares the request prefix in order, tools first, then system, then messages, and there is a hit only when that prefix matches a recent request exactly up to the breakpoint. A line that changes on every call, placed ahead of the protocol, breaks the match for everything behind it: nothing is read from cache and the whole block is written again, which is the expensive operation. That pushes input spend up, and it can land above what the same work would cost with no cache at all. The key distinction is where the variable data lives: what changes on every request goes in the newest user turn, behind the stable prefix, and from there it invalidates nothing.

RULE: Data that changes on every request goes in the newest user turn: one variable line in front of the prefix invalidates all of it.

TRAP: Assuming the cache tolerates small differences, when it compares the whole prefix and whatever sits at the front drags everything behind it.

html.question: The clinical-record summarizer at Red Vicuña Salud prepends a stable block of about 11,000 tokens to every request, holding the clinical protocol and the output format, marked with a cache breakpoint; today almost every request reads it from cache. To trace each summary in the internal audit, Camila proposes adding a line at the start of that block with the clinic code, the physician's license number and the exact time of the request. The per-clinic budget is fixed and 12,000 summaries are generated daily. What effect will the change have?
options: The prefix will still be read from cache, because a line that short cannot alter the protocol block behind it.
Only the block holding that line will be invalidated and the protocol will still be read from cache, so the extra cost is marginal.
Input spend will drop, because with a different prefix on every call the system stops writing cache and charges only base input.
No request will read from cache again and each one will rewrite the whole protocol, so input spend will rise.
html.explanation:
The general rule is that the cache compares the request prefix in order, tools first, then system, then messages, and there is a hit only when that prefix matches a recent request exactly up to the breakpoint. A line that changes on every call, placed ahead of the protocol, breaks the match for everything behind it: nothing is read from cache and the whole block is written again, which is the expensive operation. That pushes input spend up, and it can land above what the same work would cost with no cache at all. TRAP: Assuming the cache tolerates small differences, when it compares the whole prefix and whatever sits at the front drags everything behind it.
