questions.question: Mistral Retail has to enrich the listings of 400,000 products before the promotional campaign, 12 days from now. Every request carries the same taxonomy and the same style instructions, about 5,000 tokens, plus the listing data. The result is loaded into the catalog overnight, so nobody waits on the response, and the project spend cap is already fixed and approved. Which two measures do you take? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Send the work through the Message Batches API, which bills at 50% and suits a process with no immediate response.
options.feedback: Correct: the batch charges half on every token type and its only cost is asynchrony, which does not hurt here because the catalog load happens overnight.

options.label: B
options.text: Turn on streaming so the team sees the listings as they are generated and the cost per enriched product falls.
options.feedback: Streaming improves the feel of speed when someone is watching the screen; it reduces neither tokens nor price, and it is not available inside a batch.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise max_tokens so no description is cut off and those products do not have to be processed again.

options.label: D
options.text: Turn on fast mode so the batch closes several days before the date of the promotional campaign.

options.label: E
options.text: Cache the taxonomy and instructions block, identical across all 400,000 listings, whose discount stacks with the batch discount.

With an overnight process that needs no immediate response, the Message Batches API charges half on every token type; and the taxonomy and instructions block, identical across all 400,000 listings, is written to cache once and read afterward at a fraction of the input price. The two discounts stack, so they do not compete. The other three options move something else: streaming changes perceived latency, max_tokens is a ceiling the model cannot see, and fast mode buys output speed at a premium rate on top of being incompatible with the batch.

RULE: If nobody is waiting on the response, send the work as a batch; and cache the block that repeats, because the two discounts add up.

TRAP: Looking for the saving in latency levers such as streaming or fast mode, which move perceived speed or output speed and not the price of the token.

TRY IT: Estimate the spend of the whole batch with and without caching on the 5,000 shared tokens; then send 100 listings through the Batches API with identical cache_control blocks and look at the cache hit rate.

questions.question: Pehuén Energía opens its work-order system to contractor firms through its own MCP server over HTTP, configured like this: {"mcpServers": {"ot": {"type": "http", "url": "${OT_MCP_URL}"}}}. The server accepts the access token each client sends and forwards it unchanged to the work-order API; it treats any request whose MCP-Session-Id appears in its session table as authenticated; it publishes its tools without annotations; it answers 403 with insufficient_scope when a permission is missing; and it requires the Authorization header on every HTTP request. The regulator demands being able to reconstruct which contractor executed each order. Which TWO security gaps do you have to close? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: That the tools declare no annotations such as readOnlyHint or destructiveHint to mark the ones that write.
options.feedback: Annotations help show which tool writes or destroys, but they are hints the client must treat as untrusted: they document, they do not authorize.

options.label: B
options.text: That the server forwards to the API the token it received from the client, one never issued for the server.
options.feedback: Correct: this is token passthrough, the anti-pattern the specification forbids, and it breaks the audit trail because the downstream API logs an identity that is not the contractor's.

options.label: C
options.text: That the server answers 403 with insufficient_scope instead of 401 when the request is missing a permission.
options.feedback: That is the correct behavior: 401 signals that authorization is missing or the token is invalid, and 403 with insufficient_scope enables the step-up flow for permissions.

options.label: D
options.text: That the token travels in the Authorization header on every HTTP request and not once when the session opens.
options.feedback: This is also what the specification requires: the token accompanies every request, even inside one logical session, and it never travels in the query string.

options.label: E
options.text: That a request counts as authenticated because its MCP-Session-Id is still live in the session table.
options.feedback: Correct: the specification forbids using sessions for authentication. A session identifier proves continuity, not identity, and whoever obtains it acts as the contractor.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an MCP server over HTTP may only accept tokens issued for itself, and it has to verify every incoming request on its own. Forwarding the client's token downstream is token passthrough and is explicitly forbidden: it bypasses the controls that depend on the audience, and it leaves the upstream API logging an identity that is not the contractor's, which is precisely what the regulator wants to be able to reconstruct. If the server needs to call that API, it must obtain its own token from the appropriate issuer. The second gap is treating the session as a credential: a session identifier is conversation continuity, not proof of identity. The other three behaviors described are what the specification asks for, or metadata with no control value.

RULE: Accept only tokens issued for your server, get your own to call downstream, and verify every request: a session is not a credential.

TRAP: Treating the client's token as if it were a valid delegation and the session identifier as if it were proof of identity.

TRY IT: Send your MCP server a token issued for another service: if it answers anything other than 401, your audience validation does not exist.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/security_best_practices https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization

questions.question: The root CLAUDE.md of the AndesWare monorepo reached 900 lines after a year of additions. It loads in every session for all 400 developers, half of its content applies to three of the sixty subdirectories, and nobody owns the file. The platform team is three people and cannot review every change. What should you propose to them?

options.label: A
options.text: Split it into one CLAUDE.md per monorepo subdirectory and let each team maintain its own, leaving untouched the root file that loads every time.
options.feedback: One file per subdirectory is the documented practice for a monorepo, but on its own it does not touch the 900 lines in the root, which are what loads in every session.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask each team to review the file every quarter and delete whatever no longer applies to its part of the monorepo.
options.feedback: Reviewing documentation like any other change is the recommendation, though a quarterly cleanup does not scale to 400 developers and does not reduce what loads every time.

options.label: C
options.text: Move all the content to an MCP server over the code search index, so that it can be queried when it is needed.
options.feedback: An MCP server over an existing index is one of the documented remedies, but moving the conventions that must always apply leaves them to whether the model decides to go looking.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep in the root what applies everywhere, move the procedures to on-demand skills, and package the rest as a plugin.
options.feedback: Correct: the always-on conventions stay in the file that loads, multi-step procedures become skills that load when they are used, and what platform maintains travels as a versioned plugin.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that each kind of content has its own artifact: conventions that always apply go in CLAUDE.md, which is best kept under two hundred lines; multi-step procedures go in a skill; anything that affects only one part of the code goes in a path-scoped rule; and anything that must always happen goes in a hook. When per-directory documentation stops scaling, conventions drift, files go stale and nobody owns the root; the documented remedy is to move content out of the file that always loads and into on-demand skills or plugins, which are versioned packages of skills, hooks and commands with an owning team. The distinction against splitting by subdirectory is that it spreads ownership without reducing what loads in every session.

RULE: What always applies goes in the file that always loads; the rest drops down to on-demand skills and to plugins with an owner and a version.

TRAP: Assuming that spreading the documentation across directories reduces context, when the root file still loads whole in every session.

TRY IT: Open the root CLAUDE.md of your repository and mark each block as an always-on convention, a procedure or a detail of one area; if the first group is under half, the file is doing another artifact's job.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

questions.question: Banco Altamar's digital banking assistant replies with streaming. Support reports that some conversations cut off mid-response and that, from that point on, the assistant refuses everything the customer types. The operations dashboard shows zero HTTP errors in that window, and the service level committed to the business is measured on exactly that error rate. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add retries with exponential backoff to the responses that cut off, treating them as transient provider failures.
options.feedback: Retry with backoff is the right answer to an overload or a rate limit; here there is no error to retry, because the response arrived with a 200 code.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower the temperature and rewrite the system prompt so the assistant is less prone to refusing customer queries.
options.feedback: Tuning the prompt can reduce needless refusals, but it explains neither why the conversation gets stuck nor how the event becomes visible on the dashboard.

options.label: C
options.text: Count responses whose stop_reason equals refusal separately, and reset the conversation context when they appear.
options.feedback: Correct: the refusal arrives as HTTP 200, so error monitoring never sees it, and the documentation requires resetting the context before continuing.

options.label: D
options.text: Continue the same conversation with a clarifying turn that tells the model the customer's query is legitimate.
options.feedback: Continuing without resetting the context is precisely what the documentation warns against: the result is chained refusals, which is the second symptom reported.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that not every failure arrives in the shape of an error. When the streaming classifiers step in, the response comes back with HTTP code 200 and with stop_reason equal to refusal, so a dashboard built on the error rate shows nothing and the service level looks intact while customers are left without an answer. That is why the refusal has to be counted as a signal of its own. The documentation adds an operational duty: on receiving a refusal you must reset the conversation context, because pressing on with the same context produces chained refusals, which is exactly the second symptom support reports.

RULE: What is not an error will never appear in the error rate: count refusals separately and reset the context when they happen.

TRAP: Confusing a model refusal with a service failure because both leave the customer without an answer.

TRY IT: Look at your dashboard and see whether any counter exists for responses with stop_reason equal to refusal; if there is none, work out how many of the last thousand responses fell outside your error rate.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/handle-streaming-refusals

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom has had its first-line support assistant in production for four months, and the supervisors say it has been answering worse lately, without being able to point to a specific case. There is no automated evaluation: until now the team tested by hand before every deployment. Paula, the tech lead, has to leave the first suite running in two weeks. Where should you start?

options.label: A
options.text: Generate 500 synthetic cases with the same model that serves the assistant, to cover every query category quickly.
options.feedback: Synthetic cases help fill out coverage, but they do not reflect the real distribution or the edges that generate the complaints, and generating them with the model under evaluation makes the set complacent.

options.label: B
options.text: Wait until enough cases from all the query categories have been collected before writing the first evaluation task.
options.feedback: Waiting for full coverage leaves the problem unmeasured just as it starts to show; 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures are a sufficient start.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the supervisors to grade a weekly sample by hand and use that average as the single measure of quality.
options.feedback: Human review is useful for calibrating and for looking at edge cases, but it is slow and expensive as the only measure, and a weekly average does not say what broke.

options.label: D
options.text: Take 30 real failures from the ticket queue and turn them into tasks with inputs and a success criterion, several runs each.
options.feedback: Correct: the first tasks come out of the support queue and the manual checks you already did, and several runs per task keep noise from being read as a regression.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the first suite is built from the failures you already have: the manual checks you run before deploying and, in a production system, the support queue and the incident tracker. Twenty to fifty simple tasks drawn from real failures are enough to start, and each task needs defined inputs and a success criterion so it can be repeated. Because model output varies between runs, a single execution per task says little: you run several and look at the set. The distinction against waiting for full coverage is that the suite is built iteratively, and the moment users say the system got worse is precisely when informal testing stopped being enough.

RULE: The first evaluation is written from your real failures, not from invented cases: twenty to fifty tasks and several runs per task.

TRAP: Assuming an evaluation set needs full coverage before it is useful, when what makes it useful is coming from failures you have already seen.

TRY IT: Open the last 30 tickets the assistant escalated and turn five into tasks with an input, a success criterion and three runs; measure how many pass today.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Three weeks ago AndesWare's platform team fixed a bug in the review plugin that was letting unapproved dependencies through, and published the fix to the internal marketplace. The entry still reads: {"name": "andes-tools", "owner": {"name": "Plataforma"}, "plugins": [{"name": "revisor-monorepo", "source": {"source": "github", "repo": "andesware/plugins"}, "version": "1.0.0"}]}. All 400 developers still see the earlier behavior, and Monday's release train requires everyone to run the fixed version. What fixes the cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the version number in the marketplace entry and in the plugin manifest, because otherwise the cached copy is kept.
options.feedback: Correct: with a pinned version, users receive the update only when that number changes; on git sources, leaving it out makes the resolved commit apply, so it updates every time.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask every developer to run the marketplace validation on their copy before Monday and report the result.
options.feedback: The validation checks the structure of the marketplace and its entries, but it distributes nothing: a valid marketplace whose version has not changed still serves the old copy.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the marketplace to "extraKnownMarketplaces" in the monorepo settings, so that the whole set installs automatically.
options.feedback: That key registers the source and, together with "enabledPlugins", installs the team's set; it does not force an update of a plugin that is already installed.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the plugin from "enabledPlugins", ask each team to reinstall it by hand, and enable it again after Monday's release train.
options.feedback: Reinstalling can unblock a single team, but across 400 developers it is not feasible before Monday and it leaves the cause intact for the next publication.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that plugin distribution is decided by the declared version number, not by the commit at the source. If the marketplace entry or the plugin manifest pins a version, users receive the update only when that number changes, and until then they keep the cached copy no matter how published the fix is. For git sources, leaving the version out makes the resolved commit apply, so the plugin updates on every commit; in archives the digest plays that role. The distinction against reinstalling by hand is that reinstalling unblocks whoever does it and leaves the same problem waiting at the next publication.

RULE: Raise the version on every publication: while that number stays the same, your users keep running the copy they already have.

TRAP: Assuming that publishing the fix at the source is enough, when what triggers the update is the declared version number.

TRY IT: Publish a visible change to a test plugin without touching the version, install it on another machine and confirm the earlier behavior still arrives; then raise the number and install again.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces

questions.question: The agent that classifies filings at Agencia Nacional de Ingresos aggregates four internal MCP servers and exposes 180 tools. This week's measurement: it picks the wrong tool in one file out of five, and it opens with about 55,000 tokens of definitions before doing anything. The annual token budget was closed in the public procurement and cannot be extended until next year. The team proposes splitting the work across four specialized agents. What is the correct diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: The catalog passed the threshold where selection degrades and definitions fill the context: defer their loading.
options.feedback: Correct: selection accuracy falls above 30 to 50 tools and definitions are paid in context; deferring their loading takes them out of the window without removing capabilities.

options.label: B
options.text: The model cannot reason over a catalog of that size: step up to the most capable model in the family available.
options.feedback: A more capable model does not fix an ambiguous catalog: if an experienced person cannot say which tool fits each case, neither can the agent.

options.label: C
options.text: The results the tools return saturate the context: run those tools from code so the results never enter the window.
options.feedback: That lever addresses saturation from results, which is a different kind of excess. Here the problem is the definitions, which are paid before the first call.

options.label: D
options.text: The conversation grows too much on each file: enable compaction to summarize the case history as it accumulates.
options.feedback: Compaction summarizes a context that already grew. It is a recovery mechanism, not a discovery one, and it does not touch the definition tokens loaded at the start.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to identify what is growing before choosing the remedy: here the tool definitions are growing, not the results and not the history. Above 30 to 50 tools the choice of the right tool degrades, and a catalog that aggregates several servers consumes tens of thousands of tokens before the agent starts working. Deferring the loading of those definitions takes those tokens out of context and improves selection while keeping every capability. The distinction against splitting the work across agents is economic and documented: a multi-agent implementation consumes on the order of three to ten times more tokens than a single-agent one, and the budget is already closed.

RULE: When you have too many tools, defer their definitions first: splitting the work across agents is paid in tokens before it is paid in clarity.

TRAP: Confusing an excess of definitions with an excess of results, or solving with more agents what is solved by taking out of context what goes unused.

TRY IT: List the tools your agent exposes and mark which ones 90% of a week of traffic actually uses: the difference is how many definitions you pay for on every request without using them.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them

The general rule is to identify what is growing before choosing the remedy: here the tool definitions are growing, not the results and not the history. Above 30 to 50 tools the choice of the right tool degrades, and a catalog that aggregates several servers consumes tens of thousands of tokens before the agent starts working. Deferring the loading of those definitions takes those tokens out of context and improves selection while keeping every capability. The distinction against splitting the work across agents is economic and documented: a multi-agent implementation consumes on the order of three to ten times more tokens than a single-agent one, and the budget is already closed.

RULE: When you have too many tools, defer their definitions first: splitting the work across agents is paid in tokens before it is paid in clarity.

TRAP: Confusing an excess of definitions with an excess of results, or solving with more agents what is solved by taking out of context what goes unused.

questions.question: The fraud detection team at Zafiro Seguros changed the classifier prompt and the evaluation suite score rose from 0.81 to 0.88. In the same week, the platform updated the model the suite runs on. The risk committee demands a written justification of where each improvement came from before it goes to production, and the deployment window closes on Friday. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ship the change: the score rose seven points on the same suite, and that is what the committee asks you to justify.
options.feedback: A higher score does not say where the improvement came from: with two variables moved at once, the justification collapses the moment one of them has to be rolled back.

options.label: B
options.text: Re-run both prompt versions with the model pinned to the same version, to separate what each change contributed.
options.feedback: Correct: pinning the model version keeps a platform update from being mistaken for the effect of the prompt, which is the change the committee has to approve.

options.label: C
options.text: Extend the suite with more cases and measure again, to confirm the rise holds on a larger set.
options.feedback: More cases reduce the noise of the measurement, but they do not separate the two causes: the larger set would still be measuring the prompt and the model together.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask a judge model to compare the outputs of the two prompt versions and draft the justification for the committee.
options.feedback: A judge can describe how the outputs differ, but it cannot attribute the credit to one of the two variables or replace a controlled comparison.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of an A/B comparison is to move one variable at a time and pin the rest of the environment. When the model is updated in the same week as the prompt, the score difference mixes two effects and neither can be attributed: the documented practice is to pin the model version in the suite run so a platform deployment is not mistaken for an improvement or a regression of the prompt. With the model pinned, the difference between the two prompt versions is what the prompt contributed, which is exactly what the committee asks you to justify. The distinction against extending the suite is that more cases improve the precision of the measurement, not its attribution.

RULE: Pin the model when you compare prompts and pin the prompt when you compare models: one variable per run, or the result cannot be attributed.

TRAP: Reading a score increase as evidence that your change worked, when something else in the environment moved in the same window.

TRY IT: Run your suite with the old prompt and the new one pinned to the same model version, then with the prompt fixed and the model changed; compare the two differences to see what each change contributed.

questions.question: Siete Lagos Viajes processes changes and cancellations of corporate itineraries. The contract with the wholesalers requires the same sequence every time: check the penalty rules, confirm availability, issue the change and notify the traveler. Any audit has to be able to reproduce step by step a change made six months ago. In high season the volume multiplies tenfold. Which architectural pattern should you choose?

options.label: A
options.text: A workflow with the steps defined in code and programmatic checks between them, leaving each concrete step to Claude.
options.feedback: Correct: a workflow orchestrates the model and the tools through predefined code paths, which is what a fixed sequence that must be auditable step by step demands.

options.label: B
options.text: An autonomous agent with the four tools available and an iteration limit, deciding the order from what each request asks for.
options.feedback: Agents are reserved for open-ended problems where you cannot predict how many steps will be needed; here the sequence is fixed by contract and has to repeat identically every time.

options.label: C
options.text: An orchestrator that splits each change request among subagents specialized by wholesaler and synthesizes the result.
options.feedback: An orchestrator is useful when you cannot anticipate which subtasks will be needed; here all four are known in advance and their order does not depend on the case that arrives.

options.label: D
options.text: A single call with the penalty rules and the full wholesaler catalogs loaded into the context.
options.feedback: Loading the full catalogs avoids integrations, but high-season volume and the freshness of availability call for tools, and the sequence stops being reproducible.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the difference between a workflow and an agent is who controls the flow: in a workflow the model and the tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, while in an agent the model directs its own processes and its own tool use dynamically. When the contract fixes the sequence and an audit has to reproduce a case from six months ago, control of the flow belongs to the code and not to the model. The programmatic checks between steps are also what makes each transition verifiable. The distinction against the autonomous agent is that this pattern is reserved for open-ended problems where you can neither predict the number of steps nor fix a path.

RULE: If the sequence is fixed by contract and has to be reproducible, control of the flow lives in the code: that is a workflow, not an agent.

TRAP: Choosing an agent for the flexibility it promises in a process where flexibility is exactly what the contract forbids.

TRY IT: Take a process you have already automated and ask who decides the next step: if the answer is your code, you do not need an agent however much you use the model at each step.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

questions.question: AndesWare analyzes the monorepo's test execution history every night to spot flaky tests. The script builds the prompt by pasting in a CSV of 1,800 rows, about 90,000 tokens, and asks 25 questions about that same block. The answers are right less than half the time and the process already eats 40% of the platform's monthly budget. Ximena has to cut spend and raise accuracy. Which change do you make?

options.label: A
options.text: Split the CSV into blocks of 300 rows and ask the 25 questions on each block, joining the partial answers afterward.
options.feedback: Splitting the file lowers the context per request, but it multiplies the calls and breaks the questions that need to look at every row at once.

options.label: B
options.text: Cache the whole CSV as a stable prefix, so that night's 25 questions read it from cache instead of billing it in full again.
options.feedback: Caching would cut the cost of resending the same block and is worth having, but the model would still answer by reading over 90,000 tokens: accuracy does not move.

options.label: C
options.text: Upload the CSV as a file and let the model query it with the code execution tool instead of pasting it into the prompt.
options.feedback: Correct: with the file loaded, the model writes and runs code to query it, so only the result enters the context and accuracy stops depending on reading.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the analysis to a model with a larger context window, so the 1,800 rows fit with room to spare and do not compete.
options.feedback: More window lets the file in comfortably, but accuracy and recall fall as the context grows, and the cost per question does not drop.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that tabular data does not belong in the prompt: pasting it turns every question into a reading exercise over tens of thousands of tokens, which is expensive and inaccurate as well. Loading it as a file and letting the model query it by running code changes the nature of the task: the code does the computation, only the result reaches the context, and the documented measurement of that change improves accuracy and cost at the same time. The distinction against caching the CSV is that caching attacks only the price of resending the same text: the 25 answers would still be derived from a reading over 90,000 tokens, which is where the errors come from.

RULE: Data goes in files and instructions in the prompt: if the answer is a computation over rows, let code do it and not the model's reading.

TRAP: Treating an accuracy problem over tabular data as if it were only a context price problem, and caching what should have been taken out of the prompt.

TRY IT: Take five of your questions and answer them first with the CSV pasted into the prompt and then with the file loaded and code execution; compare the hits and input_tokens on each path.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence

questions.question: Yaguareté Logística packaged its tariff-classification guide as a Skill so that customs brokers stop pasting it by hand into every conversation. The SKILL.md frontmatter came out like this: name: documents, description: Helps with foreign trade documents. With 12,000 customs filings a day and another 30 Skills installed in the workspace, the Skill almost never activates and the brokers end up pasting the guide anyway. What should you fix?

options.label: A
options.text: Paste the full guide into the body of the SKILL.md, so the model has all the detail when deciding whether to use it.
options.feedback: The body of the SKILL.md is loaded only once the Skill activates, so adding detail there changes nothing about the decision that is failing today.

options.label: B
options.text: Uninstall from the workspace the Skills the customs team does not use, so there are fewer candidates to choose between.
options.feedback: Each unactivated Skill occupies only its name and its description, so having thirty installed is not the problem: uninstalling removes useful options without touching the cause.

options.label: C
options.text: Give the Skill a specific name and rewrite the description in the third person, saying what it does and when to use it.
options.feedback: Correct: the name and the description are all the model sees when it decides, and that description has to say what the Skill does and when it should be used, written in the third person.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the brokers to invoke the Skill by name at the start of every conversation instead of relying on routing.
options.feedback: Invoking it by hand works as a patch, but it hands the brokers back the work the Skill was meant to remove and does not scale to 12,000 customs filings a day.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a Skill is discovered through its metadata: until it activates, only its name and its description occupy context, and that description is the routing key the model uses to choose among many available Skills. That is why it is written in the third person and has to say two things, what the Skill does and when it should be used; generic names such as documents or utils are a documented antipattern. When a Skill exists but is never chosen from the users' natural phrasing, the cause lies in that description, not in the content and not in how many Skills are installed. The distinction against expanding the body of the SKILL.md is that the body is read only after the decision that is failing here.

RULE: A Skill description is not documentation: it is the routing key, and it says what the Skill does and when to use it, always in the third person.

TRAP: Assuming a Skill that never activates needs more content, when all the model read of it was its name and its description.

TRY IT: Write five sentences the way a customs broker would say them and check how many activate your Skill; then rewrite the description naming those situations and repeat the test.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices

questions.question: Banco Altamar has finished building its complaint classifier and is handing it to an operations team that took no part in the project. Internal audit requires being able to check at any time that the system still behaves as specified. The classifier handles complaints from eight million customers and receives configuration changes every month. Andrés, the project architect, is assembling the handover package. Which TWO elements cannot be missing? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: An exhaustive architecture document with every component and every decision taken during the project.
options.feedback: A long document tends to be saved for later and forgotten; it also describes the system without letting anyone check that it still behaves as specified.

options.label: B
options.text: A set of evaluations built from real failures, with an acceptance criterion, that operations can rerun.
options.feedback: Correct: evaluations are built from real failures, twenty to fifty simple tasks are already a good start, and they are what operations can rerun after every change.

options.label: C
options.text: A service level commitment to the business with the same number the system reached in testing.
options.feedback: Setting the target at observed performance is the classic antipattern: it leaves no room for any degradation and turns every variation into a visible breach.

options.label: D
options.text: Monitoring of real production traffic, because it reveals user behavior the evaluations do not cover.
options.feedback: Correct: evaluations and production monitoring are complementary, because real traffic shows at scale what synthetic tests never capture.

options.label: E
options.text: Operations access to the vendor cost dashboard to watch the classifier's monthly spend.
options.feedback: Seeing the spend is useful for operating, but it says nothing about whether the classifications are still correct, which is exactly what the audit wants to be able to check.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of a handover is that the receiving team has to be able to answer two different questions: whether the system still meets the specification after each change, and what it is actually doing with real traffic. The first is answered by evaluations, which are best built from real failures and from the manual checks the team already ran before each release. The second is answered by production monitoring, which reveals user behavior at scale and catches problems synthetic tests do not see. The two are complementary and neither replaces the other. The distinction against the exhaustive document is that the document describes how the system ended up, not how to check that it stays that way.

RULE: Hand over two capabilities, not a document: evaluations that can be rerun and monitoring of real traffic.

TRAP: Assuming that complete documentation replaces the ability to check that the system still behaves as specified.

TRY IT: Ask the team that would receive your system to check today, without your help, that it still meets its acceptance criterion; whatever they cannot do alone is what is missing from the handover.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/

questions.question: A product team is going to use Claude to draft coverage recommendations that are shown directly to policyholders. Under Anthropic's Usage Policy, what is required before each recommendation goes out?

options.label: A
options.text: That the decision be recorded in an audit log that the compliance team can query at any time.
options.feedback: A record helps reconstruct what happened, but the policy requires an intervention before dissemination, not a trail that is reviewed afterward.

options.label: B
options.text: That the policyholder be able to request a human review after receiving the recommendation they were sent.
options.feedback: Review on request arrives too late: the requirement is that it happen before the content is disseminated or finalized.

options.label: C
options.text: That a qualified professional in the field review the content or the decision before it is disseminated or finalized.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the high-risk requirement of the policy for advice, recommendations and subjective decisions that affect people.

options.label: D
options.text: That a moderation classifier evaluate the output and automatically block any recommendation that it flags as high risk.
options.feedback: A classifier is a useful application control and it complements the human, but the policy asks for review by a qualified professional, not an automatic filter.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that in the high-risk cases the Usage Policy lists, human review is a contractual condition and it happens first. When the product is used to give advice, recommendations or subjective decisions that directly affect people or consumers, a qualified professional in that field must review the content or the decision before it is disseminated or finalized, and insurance is one of those domains. There is also a separate disclosure duty: if the output is presented directly to the person, you have to tell them AI is in use, at least at the start of each session. The distinction against offering review on request is the moment at which the person steps in.

RULE: In high-risk work with consumer-facing output, the qualified person reviews before dissemination; after dissemination it is not review, it is a complaint.

TRAP: Escalating to a human after the recommendation has already gone out, and calling that human-in-the-loop.

TRY IT: Take a flow of yours that falls into one of the high-risk domains and mark the exact point where a qualified person steps in; if that is after sending, the flow does not meet the requirement.

questions.question: An architect installs twenty Skills on her agent so that not all the reference material has to be loaded on every request. Which part of each Skill stays in the context from the start of the session, even if that Skill is never used?

options.label: A
options.text: The full body of SKILL.md, which is what the model reads to decide whether the Skill applies to the request.
options.feedback: The body of SKILL.md loads only when the description matches the request, and it takes under five thousand tokens.

options.label: B
options.text: The metadata, and also every reference file that SKILL.md mentions inside its instructions.
options.feedback: Bundled files consume no context until they are read, which is why a Skill can ship extensive documentation with no penalty.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the Skill's metadata, its name and its description, on the order of a hundred tokens per Skill.
options.feedback: Correct: that level is always loaded, which is why the description has to say what the Skill does and when to use it.

options.label: D
options.text: Nothing: everything loads only when the person invokes the Skill by name inside the conversation.
options.feedback: For a Skill to activate, its description already has to be in context. If nothing were loaded, the model would have nothing to decide with.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of progressive disclosure is to keep a cheap identifier loaded at all times and defer the expensive content until it is needed. In Skills that is three levels: the metadata, with the name and the description, is loaded from startup for every installed Skill; the body of SKILL.md loads when the description matches the request; and bundled files cost nothing until they are read, so there is no penalty for what goes unused. From that follows the part that usually surprises people: progressive disclosure moves the cost, it does not remove it, and twenty installed Skills are already a permanent floor of context.

RULE: With progressive disclosure you always pay for the index: every Skill's metadata is loaded from the start and the rest arrives when needed.

TRAP: Assuming that what goes unused costs nothing, when the metadata level is loaded for every installed Skill.

TRY IT: Count the Skills installed on your agent and multiply by roughly a hundred tokens: that is what you pay on every request before any of them activates.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

In Skills that is three levels: the metadata, with the name and the description, is loaded from startup for every installed Skill; the body of SKILL.md loads when the description matches the request; and bundled files cost nothing until they are read, so there is no penalty for what goes unused. From that follows the part that usually surprises people: progressive disclosure moves the cost, it does not remove it, and twenty installed Skills are already a permanent floor of context.

RULE: With progressive disclosure you always pay for the index: every Skill's metadata is loaded from the start and the rest arrives when needed.

TRAP: Assuming that what goes unused costs nothing, when the metadata level is loaded for every installed Skill.

TRY IT: Count the Skills installed on your agent and multiply by roughly a hundred tokens: that is what you pay on every request before any of them activates.

questions.question: The Banco Altamar architecture committee reviews proposals for turning business problems into solutions with Claude, starting with credit documentation extraction. To structure the discussion, the committee wrote four principles it will apply to every new proposal it receives. Which of those principles is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: For many applications, optimizing a single model call with retrieval and in-context examples is enough, with no agentic system at all.
options.feedback: This principle is correct: the explicit recommendation is that optimizing individual calls with retrieval and in-context examples is often enough for many applications.

options.label: B
options.text: If the problem has no automatable success signal, it is better solved with an autonomous agent, because the agent judges when it is done.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the wrong principle. Domains that qualify for an agent do so because success is measured objectively, and without that signal the only one deciding the task is done is the agent itself.

options.label: C
options.text: Agentic systems usually trade latency and cost for better task performance, and it is worth evaluating when that trade-off makes sense.
options.feedback: This principle is correct: the documentation names that trade-off in those terms and asks you to consider the situations where accepting it makes sense.

options.label: D
options.text: A fuzzy criterion such as safe outputs can be made measurable, for example a maximum percentage of outputs flagged by the filter over a fixed number of tests.
options.feedback: This principle is correct: the canonical example turns safe outputs into under 0.1% of outputs flagged by the content filter over ten thousand tests.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when translating a business problem is that the case qualifies when success can be measured objectively and, where possible, automatically: support qualifies because resolution is defined by the user, and coding qualifies because solutions are verified by automated tests. A verification loop exists precisely so that the session knows the work is done and not merely plausible; without one, the only thing deciding the agent has finished is the agent. The absence of an automatable signal is therefore a reason not to choose an autonomous agent, never a reason to choose one. The other three principles reproduce the guidance: start simple, weigh the latency and cost trade-off, and turn a fuzzy criterion into a measurable one.

RULE: With no objective success signal there is no agent worth building: the verification loop is what separates done from plausible.

TRAP: Assuming that the autonomy of the agent substitutes for verification, when it is precisely what makes verification indispensable.

TRY IT: Write down for your use case the check that would say whether an output is correct without a person looking at it; if you cannot write it, you do not yet have a case for an agent.

questions.question: Mistral Retail generates review summaries every night for its 220 stores and for the e-commerce catalog, and nobody reads them until the following morning. Management asked for the monthly bill of that process to come down without touching the prompt and without degrading summary quality. Facundo is reviewing the options before the budget meeting. What should he propose?

options.label: A
options.text: Send the whole job through the Message Batches API, which is asynchronous and billed at 50% of the standard price.
options.feedback: Correct: all usage submitted through batches is charged at 50% of the standard price, and the work is already asynchronous, so the processing window bothers nobody.

options.label: B
options.text: Turn on streaming for every call so that generation finishes sooner and less server processing time gets billed each night.
options.feedback: Streaming improves perceived responsiveness, not price: the same input and output tokens are billed whether you show them as they arrive or not.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on prompt caching over the block of reviews for each product, which is the longest part of the prompt.
options.feedback: Caching pays when the prefix repeats across requests; the reviews change with every product, so each call would write a new entry and cost more, not less.

options.label: D
options.text: Drop to the cheapest model in the family for the whole catalog and accept the loss in summary quality.
options.feedback: Dropping model is a real cost lever, but management expressly asked not to degrade summary quality, which is exactly what this option trades away.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to pick the cost lever that matches the shape of the work. Batch processing charges all usage at 50% of the standard price and is meant for cases where no immediate response is needed, in exchange for a window of up to twenty-four hours and no streaming. A nightly process whose output is read the next morning fits that profile without friction. The other levers are real but do not apply here: caching only pays if the prefix repeats across requests, streaming does not change what is billed, and dropping model collides with the quality constraint management set.

RULE: When nobody is waiting for the answer, the work goes in a batch: batch charges half the price in exchange for a window of hours.

TRAP: Confusing streaming with a cost lever, when it only changes when the user sees the text and not how many tokens are billed.

TRY IT: Take a process of yours that runs at night, work out its current monthly cost and that same cost halved; if the difference matters, the only question left is whether you tolerate a window of hours.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

questions.question: Assisted grading at Grupo Aurora Educación has been in production for a semester. The evaluation set that cleared the launch now passes at 99%, while teachers keep reporting wrong corrections in their courses. The per-student budget does not allow adding human review, and the next iteration has to be defined in two weeks. What should you do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Move up to the most capable model in the family, since the current evaluation shows no visible room left to improve.
options.feedback: A more capable model may help, but with an evaluation that no longer distinguishes there is no way to know whether it helped: the problem here is the measurement, not the capability.

options.label: B
options.text: Refresh the evaluation set with the failures the teachers report, because the current one has stopped discriminating.
options.feedback: Correct: saturation is the documented signal that the acceptance criterion has stopped distinguishing, and the new tasks come from real failures, not from imagined cases.

options.label: C
options.text: Triple the size of the current set with synthetically generated cases over the same distribution as always.
options.feedback: More automated volume is usually worth more than a few hand-crafted cases, but tripling the same distribution adds cases the system already solves and does not recover the signal.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace the evaluation with production monitoring, which shows the real behavior of the users.
options.feedback: Production monitoring reveals real behavior at scale, but it complements evaluations rather than replacing them: without them there is no fast iteration.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an evaluation is an instrument with a service life: when it saturates, that is, when almost every task passes, it stops distinguishing one version from another and no longer works as an acceptance criterion. The signal is right here, because the set passes at 99% while the teachers keep reporting errors. The documented source of new tasks is real failures and the manual checks the team already runs, not invented cases: twenty to fifty tasks taken from real failures are a good start. The distinction against replacing it with monitoring is that the two are complementary, because monitoring shows what happens at scale but cannot compare two versions before release.

RULE: When the eval always passes and the users keep complaining, the eval is what is failing: refresh it with real failures.

TRAP: Confusing a saturated instrument with a correct system, and looking for the improvement in the model rather than in the measurement.

TRY IT: Run your evaluation set against two different versions of your system; if both score almost the same, the set no longer discriminates and needs new cases.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: The Ceibo Telecom retention agent has an internal target of answering in under 6 seconds in 98% of cases, while the contract with the corporate customer commits to 8 seconds with a penalty. The product team wants to add a retrieval step that improves the offer but adds latency, and every release reopens the argument between product and platform. Paula is looking for a rule that closes that argument. What should she agree?

options.label: A
options.text: Set an error budget against the internal target and stop the releases that affect latency once it is spent for the month.
options.feedback: Correct: the error budget is the rate at which the target may be missed, it is tracked daily or weekly, and it replaces the negotiation with a rule agreed in advance.

options.label: B
options.text: Require every change to pass a latency test before it ships and decide case by case whether the result is acceptable.
options.feedback: A latency test per change is a sound technical control, but deciding case by case reopens the negotiation at every release and nobody sees the risk accumulated over the month.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the internal target to the 8 seconds in the contract, to leave enough headroom for the new features.
options.feedback: Matching the internal target to the external commitment removes the safety margin: the internal target is kept at least as strict as the contract, never looser.

options.label: D
options.text: Reserve the last week of every month for performance fixes, regardless of how the indicator has behaved.
options.feedback: Reserving fixed time for performance helps, but it treats a quiet month like a bad one, because it does not tie the decision to what the indicator actually measured.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the error budget is the rate at which objectives may be missed, and it is tracked daily or weekly; its job is to turn a recurring argument into a rule agreed in advance about how much risk is left in the period. Keeping the internal target stricter than the external commitment is what makes that budget run out before the customer sees anything, because the margin absorbs chronic problems. The distinction against reviewing change by change is that individual review does not accumulate: every release looks acceptable on its own and the month degrades anyway.

RULE: Turn the per-release argument into an error budget: once it is spent, latency stops being negotiable until it is earned back.

TRAP: Assuming that approving change by change controls the risk, when none of those decisions sees what the earlier ones already consumed.

TRY IT: Work out how many monthly breaches your current target tolerates and how many you have accumulated this month; that remainder is your error budget and you can already use it as a release rule.

SOURCE: https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/

questions.question: Pehuén Energía put a control-room assistant into production. It follows a fixed sequence of steps defined in code, rather than the autonomous agent the vendor had proposed. Joaquín, the architect, chose that shape because the maintenance window carries a regulatory SLA of 45 minutes and an agent's variability was not tolerable. Twelve months later the regulator audits the system and asks for the justification behind each technical decision. Joaquín no longer works at the company. What artifact should the team have left behind to answer that question?

options.label: A
options.text: A design document describing the assistant's whole architecture, with the decisions taken and the ones still open gathered in one file.
options.feedback: A design document describes the system as it stands today and helps whoever operates it, but mixing every decision together dilutes the reason behind each one and hides which alternative was discarded.

options.label: B
options.text: A message in the team channel with the conclusion and a link to the diagram, available to anyone who asks during the audit.
options.feedback: The channel is the place to spread a technique someone can reuse tomorrow, but it is not a durable record: twelve months later nobody finds the thread or knows whether that conclusion still holds.

options.label: C
options.text: A record that captures that single decision, the requirement behind it, the alternatives discarded and the consequences accepted.
options.feedback: Correct: an architecture decision record documents one justified decision and the reasoning behind it, which is exactly what an audit asks for and what survives turnover on the team.

options.label: D
options.text: A new section of the operations manual explaining how the assistant behaves in each type of maintenance task.
options.feedback: The manual answers how the system works, which is a different question. An auditor who wants to know why the autonomous agent was ruled out still finds neither the criterion nor the requirement behind it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an architecture decision is documented one per record, together with the requirement that makes it architecturally significant, the options considered and the consequences accepted. That format answers the question an audit actually asks, which is not how the system works but why this design was chosen and what was given up. The set of those records forms the decision log, and it stays readable once the person who decided has gone. The distinction against the design document is scope: the document describes the whole system in its present state, while the record preserves the reasoning behind a single choice.

RULE: One decision per record, with its requirement, its discarded alternatives and its consequences: if it does not name what was rejected, it does not document a decision.

TRAP: Confusing documenting how the system works with documenting why it was built that way; the first answers nothing for an auditor who asks about the criterion.

TRY IT: Take an architecture decision you made this quarter and write it in ten lines: the requirement behind it, the option chosen, two alternatives discarded and the consequences accepted. If you cannot name the alternatives, that decision was not made, it was assumed.

questions.question: Minera Nevado indexes 400,000 technical documents and environmental permits. Operational safety files about 600 queries a day on which conditions the current permit requires for a given blast: each query is worth little on its own and repeats constantly. By law the blast authorization is signed by a responsible engineer, and the environmental authority audits that signature. Renata works with a closed monthly budget and intermittent connectivity at the site. Which design translates this business problem best?

options.label: A
options.text: A multi-agent system with one agent per permit type exploring in parallel and a coordinator that synthesizes the final recommendation.
options.feedback: Multi-agent pays off when the task is broad exploration and its value covers the overhead; here each query is worth little, repeats constantly, and multiplying tokens per query breaks the closed budget.

options.label: B
options.text: An autonomous agent with a tool that marks the operation as authorized in the site system and escalates to a human only when it is unsure.
options.feedback: Escalating on low confidence is a valid pattern, but here the irreversible action runs before the review, and the signature the authority audits belongs to a person, not to the agent.

options.label: C
options.text: A workflow that classifies the operation, retrieves the permit and has three instances of the model vote on whether the blast should be authorized.
options.feedback: Voting exists to gain confidence through several attempts at the same task, but it triples the cost of a cheap query and still automates a decision a person has to sign.

options.label: D
options.text: A single call with retrieval that returns the applicable clauses with their citation and leaves the authorization to the signing engineer.
options.feedback: Correct: optimizing a single call with retrieval is enough for most applications, fits the budget at this volume, and respects that the signed decision stays human.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to look for the simplest solution that works and add complexity only when it is needed: for many applications, optimizing single calls with retrieval and in-context examples is enough. Multi-agent requires tasks whose value is high enough to pay for the extra performance, and a document query repeated 600 times a day under a closed budget is the opposite of that. The distinction against the multi-agent system is economic before it is technical: what justifies several agents is not the size of the corpus but the value per task and real parallelization. On top of that, the legal responsibility to authorize sits with a person, so the system has to deliver cited evidence rather than an authorization.

RULE: Translate the problem into the simplest system that solves it, and leave to a person the decision that a person signs.

TRAP: Assuming that a large corpus calls for a large architecture: what justifies multi-agent is the value per task, not the volume of documents.

TRY IT: Estimate the daily cost of your case at one call per query and multiply it by the factor a multi-agent system adds; then ask what each query would gain from that architecture and whether the gain covers the difference.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

questions.question: Mistral Retail's security policy requires all model traffic from its 90 developers to leave through the corporate gateway, so every workstation exports ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and takes its credential from an apiKeyHelper. Valentina, who leads the after-sales agent platform, publishes the organization policy with server-managed settings from the admin console, and also ships a managed-settings.json by MDM that includes forceLoginOrgUUID so nobody works from a personal account. The promotional campaign change freeze is two weeks away. Which two effects will that rollout have? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing published in the console reaches the workstations: that delivery needs a direct connection to api.anthropic.com and is skipped with a non-standard ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL.
options.feedback: Correct: the fetch that brings that part of the policy goes to api.anthropic.com, and a non-standard base URL cancels the delivery, so only what arrived by MDM applies.

options.label: B
options.text: Developers will not get a session started: forceLoginOrgUUID blocks ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and the apiKeyHelper that supplies the gateway credential.
options.feedback: Correct: either forced-login key, with any value at all, rules out the gateway credential, and the session ends by saying that managed settings require a first-party login.

options.label: C
options.text: OpenTelemetry metrics will stop reaching your collector, because the gateway does not forward the OTLP traffic that every developer session generates.
options.feedback: The OpenTelemetry export leaves the machine for your own collector and does not depend on where the model calls are routed; it is the one path that works in any rollout.

options.label: D
options.text: Every session will get a 403, because prompts that carry code and XML-style tags trigger the rules of the WAF that protects the gateway.
options.feedback: This is a documented false positive when a WAF sits in front of the gateway, but nothing in this change introduces it: the symptom would appear just the same before the policy was published.

options.label: E
options.text: Organization spend limits will start applying to the routed sessions, because the gateway reports each session's consumption to the admin console.
options.feedback: Organization spend limits govern per-seat consumption on Teams and Enterprise; what your own gateway spends is controlled at the gateway or in the provider's billing.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a central policy only helps if it reaches the machine and does not stop the machine from starting. Delivery from the console travels over a direct connection to api.anthropic.com, so a session routed through your own gateway never receives that payload and only what was shipped by MDM applies. Inside that file, the forced-login key blocks any gateway credential at startup, so the developer never even opens a session. The other three effects do not depend on this change: telemetry goes straight to your collector, the WAF 403 would exist before anything was published, and organization spend limits do not reach a gateway you run yourself. With the gateway as a non-negotiable requirement, the whole policy goes through the file-based channel and without forcing the login.

RULE: If you route through a gateway, deliver the policy by file or by operating system policy, and keep forced login out of the managed settings.

TRAP: Assuming that a policy published in the console reaches every machine, when it travels over exactly the connection the gateway has just diverted.

TRY IT: Export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointing at any host and run claude doctor: the Managed settings (remote) line will tell you the delivery was skipped and why.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-rollout https://code.claude.com/docs/en/server-managed-settings

html.question: Mistral Retail's security policy requires all model traffic from its 90 developers to leave through the corporate gateway, so every workstation exports ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and takes its credential from an apiKeyHelper. Valentina, who leads the after-sales agent platform, publishes the organization policy with server-managed settings from the admin console, and also ships a managed-settings.json by MDM that includes forceLoginOrgUUID so nobody works from a personal account. The promotional campaign change freeze is two weeks away. Which two effects will that rollout have? (Select TWO)
options: Nothing published in the console reaches the workstations: that delivery needs a direct connection to api.anthropic.com and is skipped with a non-standard ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL.
Developers will not get a session started: forceLoginOrgUUID blocks ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and the apiKeyHelper that supplies the gateway credential.
OpenTelemetry metrics will stop reaching your collector, because the gateway does not forward the OTLP traffic that every developer session generates.
Every session will get a 403, because prompts that carry code and XML-style tags trigger the rules of the WAF that protects the gateway.
Organization spend limits will start applying to the routed sessions, because the gateway reports each session's consumption to the admin console.
html.explanation:
The general rule is that a central policy only helps if it reaches the machine and does not stop the machine from starting. Delivery from the console travels over a direct connection to api.anthropic.com, so a session routed through your own gateway never receives that payload and only what was shipped by MDM applies. Inside that file, the forced-login key blocks any gateway credential at startup, so the developer never even opens a session. The other three effects do not depend on this change: telemetry goes straight to your collector, the WAF 403 would exist before anything was published, and organization spend limits do not reach a gateway you run yourself. With the gateway as a non-negotiable requirement, the whole policy goes through the file-based channel and without forcing the login.

RULE: If you route through a gateway, deliver the policy by file or by operating system policy, and keep forced login out of the managed settings.

TRAP: Assuming that a policy published in the console reaches every machine, when it travels over exactly the connection the gateway has just diverted.

TRY IT: Export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointing at any host and run claude doctor: the Managed settings (remote) line will tell you the delivery was skipped and why.

questions.question: Banco Altamar runs the digital banking assistant for 8 million customers, and internal audit requires that any response can be reconstructed up to 90 days later. Ximena, the platform SRE, is building the dashboard from three sources: the usage field on every response, OpenTelemetry telemetry from the agent, and the organization's Usage & Cost API. Four claims are circulating in the review of that design. One of them is NOT correct. Which one?

options.label: A
options.text: The Usage & Cost API reconciles spend by workspace, by API key and by model, but its data lands a few minutes late and the cost report has daily granularity only.
options.feedback: True: it is a reconciliation surface, with data arriving minutes later and daily buckets in the cost report, not a live trace.

options.label: B
options.text: The request-id header returned on every response identifies the exact call, and it is the field to store so that a single case can be traced later.
options.feedback: True: every response carries its request-id and every error body its request_id, and that is the identifier support asks for to review one call.

options.label: C
options.text: A 429 from a spend cap differs from a throughput 429 because it carries error_code enforced_spend_limit_reached and arrives with no retry-after header.
options.feedback: True: with no retry-after, retrying does nothing until the limit or the billing cycle changes, so this case deserves an alert of its own.

options.label: D
options.text: The input_tokens field on the response totals every input token in the request, so accumulating it is enough to know input consumption.
options.feedback: Correct as the false claim: input_tokens counts only what follows the last cache breakpoint, and the total is cache_read plus cache_creation plus input_tokens.

questions.explanation:
No single observability source answers every question. The usage field describes what one call cost, telemetry describes what the agent did step by step, and the Usage & Cost API describes what the organization spent, a few minutes behind. Three of the four claims hold up against the documentation exactly as written. The one that fails is the input_tokens claim: that field counts only the tokens after the last cache breakpoint, so total input is cache_read_input_tokens plus cache_creation_input_tokens plus input_tokens. The distinction matters because a dashboard built on that assumption underreports consumption precisely when caching is working well, which is when most tokens are read from cache.

RULE: Total input is cache_read plus cache_creation plus input_tokens; input_tokens alone counts only what was left after the last breakpoint.

TRAP: Treating input_tokens as the whole input, when it is only the remainder left after the last cache breakpoint.

TRY IT: Send a request with a cached prefix, add cache_read_input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens and input_tokens, and compare that total against input_tokens alone: the gap is what your dashboard would be missing.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/usage-cost-api

questions.question: AndesWare has standardized Claude Code across its 400 developers and distributes the plugin that carries the secret-review skill through an internal marketplace. A client contract requires the corrected version of that skill to be active in every session before the sprint closes, but two days after it was published the machines still load the previous one. The version field in the marketplace entry and in plugin.json has not been touched for three releases. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the version number in the marketplace entry and in plugin.json on every release, so that machines stop serving the cached copy.
options.feedback: Correct: when the entry declares a version, the user only receives the update if that value changes; leave it alone and every machine keeps what it already had cached.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the 400 developers to uninstall the plugin and install it again every time the platform team publishes a correction.
options.feedback: Reinstalling solves the immediate case, but it leaves contract compliance resting on 400 people performing a manual step inside the deadline.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the marketplace to strictKnownMarketplaces in the managed settings, so that plugins can only be installed from the company-approved repository.
options.feedback: This is the right key for controlling where plugins may come from, but it governs provenance and not freshness: an approved origin serves a stale copy just as well.

options.label: D
options.text: Declare the plugin in enabledPlugins inside each repository's .claude/settings.json, so that it installs on its own when the project is opened in the monorepo.
options.feedback: The extraKnownMarketplaces and enabledPlugins pair automates the first install for anyone working in that repository, but it does not fetch content again while the declared version stays the same.

questions.explanation:
The general rule in a marketplace rollout is that the declared version is the update trigger: if the entry has a version, the user only receives new content when that value changes, and until then keeps the cached copy. That is why the corrected skill was published but reached no session. Raising the version on every release is the practice the documentation asks for precisely to avoid this case, and it demands nothing from the 400 developers. The distinction against locking the marketplace down is that that key decides where plugins may come from, not when they update.

RULE: Bump the version on every release: with no version change, what you published stays in your repository and never reaches the team's machines.

TRAP: Confusing control over a plugin's origin with control over its freshness: the approved marketplace serves the old version just as faithfully as the new one.

TRY IT: Publish a trivial change to a plugin of your own without touching version, open a session and confirm the content did not change; then raise the version, reopen and compare.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces

questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro is about to classify customs manifests to decide which operational queue each container enters. The sponsor asked for a system that classifies well, with no further precision, and wants to be in production in six weeks. Each vessel has a twelve-minute operating window, so a classification that arrives late gets in the way as much as a wrong one. Ximena, the architect, has last quarter's manifests and the manual corrections the customs team made. What should she do before construction starts?

options.label: A
options.text: Agree with the sponsor on a demonstration over ten hand-picked manifests and take that approval as the project's acceptance criterion.
options.feedback: A demonstration convinces a room, but volume with automated grading beats a few carefully chosen cases: ten selected manifests do not represent the real distribution of traffic.

options.label: B
options.text: Adopt the accuracy figure the industry publishes for document classification as the target and measure the system against that reference at closing.
options.feedback: External benchmarks help you know what is achievable, but the criterion has to be relevant to these manifests and measured on them, not on somebody else's task.

options.label: C
options.text: Set a threshold for each dimension that matters, accuracy and response time, measured over real manifests and their corrections from the quarter.
options.feedback: Correct: the criterion is specific and measurable, it covers the two dimensions that decide the operational outcome, and it is built from failures already observed.

options.label: D
options.text: Define a single global accuracy metric so the team does not lose focus, and leave latency for a second phase once the system is stable.
options.feedback: One metric makes for a simpler dashboard, but most cases need multidimensional evaluation: with a twelve-minute window, latency is an acceptance criterion, not a later adjustment.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a good success criterion is specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and that most cases need several dimensions at once. Here the operating window turns response time into an acceptance requirement at the same level as accuracy, so a single target leaves out half the problem. The documented starting point for assembling the test set is the failures that already happened, which at this terminal live in the quarter's manual corrections. The distinction against a demonstration on hand-picked cases is that volume with automated grading beats a few carefully chosen cases, because only volume reflects the distribution of real traffic.

RULE: A requirement you cannot measure is not a requirement: put a number and a threshold on every deciding dimension, over real cases that already failed.

TRAP: Treating a demonstration on hand-picked cases as an acceptance criterion, and discovering in production the distribution that sample left out.

TRY IT: Take the vaguest requirement in your backlog and rewrite it as one sentence with a metric, a sample and a threshold; then pull twenty already-failed cases from last month's tickets and check whether your threshold separates them.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/define-success https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
