questions.question: The Ceibo Telecom retention agent answers questions about plans and promotions with the commercial catalog loaded into every request. An internal audit found that in 6 percent of conversations the agent invents lock-in terms that are not in the catalog, and the regulator has already flagged two of them. The contract with the corporate client fixes the first response at under 3 seconds at the 95th percentile, and the service margin allows no more than one model call per turn. Mateo has to bring that rate down without adding calls. Which two measures attack the cause within that constraint? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Run every query three times with the same prompt and return the answer that matches across two of the three runs.
options.feedback: Comparing several runs is a documented way to detect hallucination through inconsistency, not to correct it, and it triples calls and latency exactly where the contract has no room.

options.label: B
options.text: Instruct the model to answer only from the catalog it is given and never to fill gaps from its own general knowledge.
options.feedback: Correct: restricting the model to the documents it is handed is a documented countermeasure against hallucination, and it adds no model call.

options.label: C
options.text: Move every retention query to the most capable model in the family and leave the rest of the flow exactly as it is today.
options.feedback: A more capable model hallucinates less on average, but the problem here is grounding: nothing forces the answer to rest on the catalog, and cost per conversation goes up.

options.label: D
options.text: Add the 120 frequently asked questions from the catalog to the system prompt so the model always has everything at hand.
options.feedback: More context is not automatically better: retrieval degrades as the token count grows, and cost per turn rises without touching the missing grounding.

options.label: E
options.text: Require every term the agent cites to carry the verbatim catalog clause, and drop the term when no clause backs it.
options.feedback: Correct: checking every claim against a citation and dropping what has no backing is the documented countermeasure, and it happens inside the same response.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a hallucination is fought by grounding the answer in a source and making it auditable, not by buying more model capability. Restricting the model to the documents provided closes the path by which it fills gaps from memory. Requiring the verbatim citation, and removing whatever has no backing, turns every claim into something a reader can check. Neither measure adds a call. The distinction against running the query several times is that comparing runs detects inconsistency rather than correcting it, and it multiplies the cost and the latency the contract caps. None of these techniques removes hallucination entirely, so human review of the critical cases is still needed.

RULE: Ground the answer in the source and make it auditable: restrict outside knowledge and require the citation that backs every claim.

TRAP: Confusing a detection technique, such as comparing several runs against each other, with a countermeasure that corrects the problem.

TRY IT: Take twenty real answers from your agent and mark how many claims you can trace to a verbatim citation from your source; count again after adding the outside-knowledge restriction.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations

questions.question: Siete Lagos Viajes automated the drafting of corporate itineraries. In three months the average drafting time fell from 18 to 6 minutes, the 40 advisors use the tool on 90% of itineraries, and the cost per itinerary also fell. Even so, the finance office sees no change: the number of itineraries closed per month is the same and the margin has not moved either. Availability confirmation with the wholesalers still takes two days per itinerary. What is the most likely cause of the benefit not showing up?

options.label: A
options.text: The model degrades at high-season peaks, so the saving measured in the pilot does not hold up at the real volume.
options.feedback: Degradation under volume is a real risk, but it contradicts what was measured: drafting time fell steadily over three months and cost per itinerary followed.

options.label: B
options.text: Token spend grew along with the volume and ended up absorbing the time saving that the team had reported to the business.
options.feedback: That would be a valid explanation if cost had risen, but the case says cost per itinerary fell; it would also explain the margin rather than the number of itineraries closed.

options.label: C
options.text: The improvement landed on a stage that does not limit the outcome: the confirmation with the wholesalers still sets the total.
options.feedback: Correct: automating a step that is not the bottleneck improves a task metric without moving any business metric, which is exactly what the finance office sees.

options.label: D
options.text: Real adoption is low, and the reported average reflects only the few advisors who have really built the tool into their daily work.
options.feedback: Low adoption is a frequent cause of benefits that never appear, but it is ruled out here: the tool is used on 90% of the itineraries of all 40 advisors.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that value is demonstrated with concrete business metrics, not with the metric of the task that was automated. Saving twelve minutes per itinerary does not change how many itineraries close if the total is dominated by a two-day wait nobody touched. That is why pilot selection requires a problem with clear return and meaningful metrics, not merely one that can be automated. The distinction against the other causes is that adoption, cost and stability are all measured and all good; the one thing never measured is where the real limit of the process was.

RULE: Measure the business outcome, not the step you automated: a saving outside the bottleneck never shows up in any income statement.

TRAP: Confusing the metric of the automated task with the business metric, and presenting the first as return on the investment.

TRY IT: Draw the full path of one of your operations with the time of each stage and mark which stage dominates the total; if the step you automated is not that one, work out how much it would have to improve to move the total by 10%.

questions.question: The document check that precedes a truck entering the gate at Terminal Puerto Claro was rebuilt as an agent that decides on its own what to consult. Every truck requires the same six documents, always in the same order, against the same three systems. Since the change, the 95th percentile went from 12 to 40 seconds, and two runs in every hundred walk the documents in a different order, which confuses the operators. The gate window is four minutes per truck and the queue is growing. Where should you look first?

options.label: A
options.text: The tool descriptions are not clear, the agent chooses badly and repeats calls until it hits the right one.
options.feedback: A poor description does send an agent down wrong paths, but even with perfect selection the control flow would still be decided on every run and the variability would not go away.

options.label: B
options.text: There is no stopping condition to bound the iterations, which is why some runs stretch out without control.
options.feedback: Stopping conditions are a mandatory part of an agentic design, but they bound the worst case: they explain neither why the median got worse nor why the order of the steps changes between runs.

options.label: C
options.text: The chosen model is too slow for the window, and with the fast model of the family the 95th percentile would fit again.
options.feedback: Switching models is a real latency lever, but the design deserves a look first: here the extra time comes from deciding on every run a path that is known in advance.

options.label: D
options.text: The control flow was left to the model even though the sequence of steps is always the same for every truck.
options.feedback: Correct: when the steps are known in advance, the order belongs in code; leaving it to the model buys flexibility nobody needs and pays for it in latency and variability.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the difference between a workflow and an agent is who holds the control flow: a workflow orchestrates models and tools along paths defined in code, while an agent directs its own process at run time. Agentic systems trade latency and cost for better performance on tasks whose path cannot be predicted, and this check has six fixed documents in a fixed order. So the first thing to review is the choice of pattern, not the tuning of the agent. The distinction against bounding the iterations or switching models is that both relieve the symptom without giving back the determinism the gate needs.

RULE: If you know the steps in advance, the control flow belongs in code; keep the agent for when you cannot predict how many steps are needed.

TRAP: Treating agentic as a synonym for better: autonomy is paid for in latency and variability, and it only pays off when the path cannot be fixed.

TRY IT: Take six real runs of the same kind of case in your agent and write down the tool sequence of each; if all six match, you have a workflow disguised as an agent and you can fix that order in code.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

RULE: If you know the steps in advance, the control flow belongs in code; keep the agent for when you cannot predict how many steps are needed.

TRAP: Treating agentic as a synonym for better: autonomy is paid for in latency and variability, and it only pays off when the path cannot be fixed.

TRY IT: Take six real runs of the same kind of case in your agent and write down the tool sequence of each; if all six match, you have a workflow disguised as an agent and you can fix that order in code.

questions.question: Minera Nevado searches 400,000 technical documents and environmental permits against an internal target of 2.5 seconds at the 95th percentile. After shipping a retrieval improvement, Joaquín measures 3.9 seconds at that percentile and a cost per query 40% higher, with accuracy almost unchanged. The deployment log reads: hybrid 0.8 semantic and 0.2 BM25 unchanged, top_k 5 to 20, reranking off to on over 150 candidates, streaming off to on. Which two causes explain the jump in latency and cost? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Reranking adds a cross-encoder pass per query over the 150 over-retrieved candidates, which costs 100 to 200 ms on every question.
options.feedback: Correct: that is the documented cost of reranking, and it is the lever that buys accuracy by paying latency on every single query.

options.label: B
options.text: Turning streaming on lengthens total generation time, because the model emits deltas one by one instead of returning the whole response.
options.feedback: Streaming is real and changes what the user perceives, but it improves perceived latency and time to first token; it adds no generation time and no cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Going from 5 to 20 chunks multiplies the input tokens of every request, and that longer prompt is processed in full before the first token.
options.feedback: Correct: retrieved chunks are billed and processed as input on every turn, so raising top_k moves latency and cost at the same time.

options.label: D
options.text: The index fell out of date against the source documents, so each query walks more candidates before it reaches the right chunk.
options.feedback: A stale index produces confident but wrong answers, not slower queries: search walks the index exactly as it stands.

options.label: E
options.text: Hybrid fusion runs BM25 after the semantic search, and that second trip to the index adds to the time of every query.
options.feedback: The lexical leg does add work, but the log says hybrid fusion was left unchanged: what moved was reranking and top_k.

questions.explanation:
Every retrieval lever has a bill of its own: reranking charges milliseconds per query, and the size of the retrieved context charges input tokens on every turn. Both moved at once here, which is why latency and cost rose while accuracy did not follow. The reranking pass adds 100 to 200 ms per question, and quadrupling top_k puts four times more text into a prompt that is processed in full before the first token appears. The documentation also warns that adding chunks is not monotonically better, because excess material distracts the model, and that explains the flat accuracy. The distinction against blaming streaming is that streaming changes when the first token appears, not how long the full generation takes or what it costs.

RULE: Reranking is paid in milliseconds per query and top_k in input tokens per turn: never raise both at once without measuring which one buys accuracy.

TRAP: Charging streaming with a generation cost it does not have: it changes when you see the first token, not how long the whole response takes or what it costs.

TRY IT: Run the same twenty queries with reranking on and off and note the p95 difference; then drop top_k from 20 back to 5 and compare input_tokens and accuracy.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/capabilities-contextual-embeddings-guide https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval

questions.question: Agencia Nacional de Ingresos connected a fourth MCP server to its taxpayer-assistance assistant, and the inventory now reads: {"agente": "asistente_contribuyente", "servidores_mcp": 4, "tools": 62, "definiciones": "48,000 tokens"}. Among the 62 sit consultar_presentacion, buscar_presentacion, listar_presentaciones, obtener_presentacion_por_id and traer_presentaciones_del_periodo. Since the change, the assistant picks the wrong tool on one query in five, and the room left for taxpayer filings, which are long, is no longer enough. Public procurement has frozen any new service for two quarters. Which two changes attack the cause? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Split the 62 tools across four specialized subagents, one per MCP server, coordinated by a lead agent that synthesizes.
options.feedback: Specializing by tool set is a real pattern, but delegating costs 3 to 10 times more tokens, and the documentation asks you to try tool search before splitting.

options.label: B
options.text: Turn on tool search with defer_loading and keep loaded only the three to five tools that serve most of the traffic.
options.feedback: Correct: 62 tools and 48,000 tokens of definitions clear the documented thresholds by a wide margin, and deferring returns context to the real work.

options.label: C
options.text: Consolidate the five tools that query filings into one tool with explicit parameters, and retire the ones that overlap.
options.feedback: Correct: if a member of the team cannot tell which of the five applies in each case, the model cannot either, and that ambiguity is fixed in the design.

options.label: D
options.text: Turn on programmatic tool calling so that the results the tools return never enter the model's context window.
options.feedback: This is the right lever for a different problem: it shrinks the volume of the results, not the definitions and not the ambiguity between look-alike tools.

options.label: E
options.text: Describe in the system prompt when each of the 62 tools applies, with examples of the five that are confused today.
options.feedback: Documenting helps, but the model chooses from each tool's name and description, and the 62 definitions still occupy the same context.

questions.explanation:
Capability bloat is attacked along two independent lines: cut how much context the definitions occupy, and remove the ambiguity about which tool applies. Tool search covers the first, and the documentation sets the thresholds precisely: ten tools or 10,000 tokens of definitions are enough to turn it on, adding MCP servers is the explicit case, and only the three to five most used tools should stay undeferred. Consolidating the five tools that query filings covers the second: when an engineer cannot decide which one to use, an agent cannot either. The tempting alternative is to split the catalog across subagents, but delegation costs 3 to 10 times more tokens and exists to isolate contexts or parallelize work, not to tidy a tool inventory.

RULE: Facing a bloated catalog, defer the definitions first and remove the overlaps second; splitting the work across agents is the most expensive answer.

TRAP: Assuming that spreading tools across subagents cleans up the context, when it multiplies tokens and leaves the ambiguity between look-alike tools untouched.

TRY IT: List the tools your agent exposes, mark which ones 90% of the traffic really uses, and add up the definition tokens of everything that fell outside that list.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

questions.question: The platform team at Terminal Puerto Claro is handing the customs integration over to the operations team. The conventions file loaded into every session has grown to 600 lines: about 80 are coding conventions and the rest is the twelve-step procedure for regenerating the customs code mapping, which runs once a month. The receiving team will pay for that context in every one of its sessions. What should the platform team do with that content before the handover?

options.label: A
options.text: Split the file into several files by subdirectory, all of them always loaded, so that none goes over two hundred lines.
options.feedback: Splitting by subdirectory works for conventions specific to each area of the code, but a monthly procedure still loads in every session, only now spread across several files.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the file as it is and trust compaction to drop the unused content from the context when that becomes necessary.
options.feedback: Compaction summarizes the conversation as it nears the limit; it does not stop instructions that are always injected from loading. What has to persist belongs where it loads by decision, not by inertia.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the multi-step procedure into a skill that loads when it is invoked and leave only the conventions in the file.
options.feedback: Correct: conventions that always apply belong in the file that always loads, and a multi-step procedure used once in a while belongs in a skill that loads on demand.

options.label: D
options.text: Turn the procedure into a hook so that it runs by itself and nobody has to read it before regenerating the code mapping.
options.feedback: Hooks are for what must happen always, without exception and without human judgment; regenerating the mapping is a monthly task somebody decides to start, not an automatic step of every session.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for splitting documentation is by frequency and by shape: conventions that apply to everything go in the always-loaded file and that file should stay short, multi-step procedures go in a skill that loads when invoked, and what has to happen always without exception goes in a hook. Here the procedure takes up 85% of a file the receiving team will pay for in every session even though they use it once a month. The distinction against splitting the file across subdirectories is that the split changes where the text lives but not when it loads. A clean handover leaves the permanent context small and the occasional knowledge available on demand.

RULE: What always applies goes in the file that always loads; a multi-step procedure used once in a while goes in a skill.

TRAP: Assuming that documenting more is documenting better: everything that always loads is paid for in every session, whether anyone uses it or not.

TRY IT: Open your project's conventions file, count its lines and mark which ones really apply to every session; move to a skill every block that is a procedure with numbered steps.

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud generates summaries of clinical notes for its 40 clinics. Mateo replaced the single-agent solution with four chained subagents: one extracts, one structures, one writes the summary and one reviews it, and each receives only the output of the previous one. Since the change, token spend has tripled, latency has risen, and the reviewing physicians report that data which used to appear is now missing. The department's annual budget cannot absorb that consumption. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The work was split by phases of a single task, so every handoff pays coordination and leaves part of the context behind.
options.feedback: Correct: decomposition has to follow context that can genuinely be isolated, and successive phases of the same work are exactly the cut that produces context loss at each handoff.

options.label: B
options.text: The subagents do not get enough tools to solve their part and go back to the coordinator to ask for what they are missing.
options.feedback: A badly equipped subagent does return half-finished work, but that would explain retries, not data disappearing after the first link had already discarded it.

options.label: C
options.text: A verifier subagent is missing to check the final summary against the criteria before it goes back to the coordinating agent.
options.feedback: Verification in a separate subagent is one of the highest-yield uses, because it needs very little context, but adding a fifth link does not recover the data lost at the first one.

options.label: D
options.text: The concurrent subagent limit makes the tasks queue up, and part of the information is lost while they wait.
options.feedback: When the concurrency limit is reached, an attempt to launch a subagent returns a notice and the task waits, but queuing does not erase information: that is a throughput problem, not a content problem.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to take a context-centric view rather than a problem-centric one: work is split only when the context can genuinely be isolated. Splitting by successive phases of one task, of the plan, execute and review kind, is documented as the wrong cut, because each link spends more on coordination than on work and loses context at every handoff. The symptom confirms it here: tokens and latency go up, and data that an earlier link decided not to pass along disappears. The distinction against adding a verifier is that a fifth agent can only review what reaches it, and what was lost never reached anything.

RULE: Split by isolatable context, not by phases of the same work: every handoff between phases pays coordination and drops what the previous link did not know was needed.

TRAP: Treating the process diagram as if it were the architecture: extract, structure and review are phases of one task, not independent contexts.

TRY IT: Look at a trace of your multi-agent system and add up the tokens spent passing context between agents against the tokens spent on the work itself; if coordination approaches the work, you split by phases.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

questions.question: A platform team is about to process personal data of European customers with the API, for an internal document-search assistant. Which two statements about the split of roles and the contractual instruments are correct? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Pseudonymizing the prompts before they are sent puts that processing outside the scope of GDPR.
options.feedback: Pseudonymization is a safeguard that reduces the link to the person without cutting it: the data is still personal data. Only true anonymization takes information out of scope.

options.label: B
options.text: For the API and Claude for Work, the customer is the controller and Anthropic acts as processor on that customer's behalf.
options.feedback: Correct: the customer determines purposes and means, and Anthropic processes on its instructions. Consumer products split it differently, and there Anthropic is the controller.

options.label: C
options.text: Consent from the data subject is the only lawful basis available when the processing runs through a language model.
options.feedback: Consent is one of the six bases in Article 6(1), neither the default one nor the only one; legitimate interests, for example, carries its own three-part test.

options.label: D
options.text: The DPA with Standard Contractual Clauses is incorporated when you accept the Commercial Terms, with no separate signature.
options.feedback: Correct: Anthropic documents that the DPA with SCCs is incorporated automatically into the Commercial Terms, so accepting the terms is accepting the DPA.

options.label: E
options.text: A DPIA is mandatory for any automated processing, whatever risk that processing actually involves.
options.feedback: Article 35 requires a DPIA when the processing is likely to result in a high risk to rights and freedoms: the trigger is the risk, not the automation.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to separate who decides on the processing from who carries it out, and not to mistake a technical safeguard for a contractual instrument. For the API and Claude for Work the customer determines purposes and means, so the customer is the controller and Anthropic processes on its behalf as processor. The DPA with SCCs is not signed separately, because it already comes incorporated into the Commercial Terms. The most tempting option is pseudonymization, since it does lower the risk, but pseudonymized data is still personal data and changes neither the lawful basis nor the contract you need.

RULE: Whoever decides purposes and means is the controller; whoever executes on instruction is the processor, and the DPA travels already incorporated inside the Commercial Terms.

TRAP: Treating pseudonymization as if it were anonymization, and assuming a technical measure can stand in for the lawful basis or the processing contract.

TRY IT: Find the sentence in the Commercial Terms that incorporates the DPA by reference, then write in one line who is controller and who is processor in your own deployment.

questions.question: The Agencia Nacional de Ingresos enabled the taxpayer support assistant in three regional offices. Paula, the internal champion for the tax inspection division, staffs the channel where the team asks questions during the first weeks. An inspector asks in that channel where the filing data is stored and whether it leaves the country, something the data residency rule governs and internal audit reviews every six months. Paula knows the tool well, but she took no part in configuring the deployment. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Answer with what the product's public documentation says about data handling and leave the link pinned in the channel.
options.feedback: Public documentation describes the general behavior of the product, but what governs here is the concrete configuration of the agency's deployment, which may well be more restrictive.

options.label: B
options.text: Answer with the configuration she has on her own machine, as a concrete example of what happens to the data in practice.
options.feedback: A concrete example is good teaching when you are showing a technique, but an individual configuration is not the agency's policy and may differ from the one applied to the other offices.

options.label: C
options.text: Route the question to the administrator, because the deployment and data policy is already defined and improvising that answer is not her call.
options.feedback: Correct: the security and data handling question is the one a champion must not answer alone, because the policy is already configured by whoever administers the deployment.

options.label: D
options.text: Take the question to the weekly sharing session so the rest of the division can contribute what each of them understood about it.
options.feedback: The weekly session is for sharing findings and reusable techniques, but a regulatory question is not settled by consensus among people who did not configure the deployment either.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for support during the enablement phase is that the champion multiplies usage but does not set policy. The question about security and data handling is flagged as the explicit exception: it goes to the administrator, because the organization's deployment and data handling policy is already configured and must not be improvised. In an agency with regulated data residency and a semiannual audit, an approximate answer in an internal channel later turns into a finding. The distinction against quoting the public documentation is that the page describes the product in general, while what has to be answered is what this organization configured.

RULE: The champion multiplies usage, it does not define policy: the question about data and security always goes to whoever administers the deployment.

TRAP: Assuming that whoever uses the tool best also knows what was configured for the organization, and answering a regulatory question from memory.

TRY IT: Ask your administrator for your organization's official answer on where the data goes and with what retention, and pin it in the channel with a link to the internal policy before somebody improvises one.

questions.question: Colibrí Pay is rebuilding the index behind the assistant its anti-money-laundering analysts use to search internal typology notes and closed case files, a corpus that tripled with last year's growth. Analysts ask in their own words, describing a behavior instead of quoting an identifier, so the semantic leg does almost all the work. The console promises an answer in 900 ms at the 95th percentile and generation already uses the rest, which leaves retrieval 120 ms; the provider in use spends 70 of them at the peak of 40 queries per second. A specialized provider scores six points higher on the team's retrieval eval, and its lookup measures 180 ms at that same peak. What should Valentina do?

options.label: A
options.text: Adopt the specialized provider for its higher in-domain score and take the extra time out of the generation step.
options.feedback: The 900 ms is an end-to-end promise and the generation step has no slack to hand over; moving the overrun somewhere else does not take it out of the percentile.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep a provider whose lookup fits inside the 120 ms: at this volume speed weighs as much as domain fit.
options.feedback: Correct: domain fit is one documented criterion for an embedding model, and lookup speed with end-to-end latency is another, named as particularly important in large-scale production deployments.

options.label: C
options.text: Adopt the specialized provider and lower top_k from 20 to 5 to win back the milliseconds it adds per query.
options.feedback: Lowering top_k trims input tokens and distraction, but those 180 ms are what the embedding lookup costs before anything is ranked, and fewer chunks do not make that call faster.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask for Anthropic's own embeddings model so that the index and the generation stay with one vendor.
options.feedback: Anthropic does not offer an embedding model: the documentation points to third-party providers and asks you to assess several against your own use case.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an embedding model is chosen against several documented criteria, not one. The first is the size of the training corpus and how close it is to the domain you want to embed, which is what the specialized candidate wins on. The second is embedding lookup speed and end-to-end latency, described as a particularly important consideration for large-scale production deployments, and it is the criterion the numbers settle here: 180 ms does not fit in a slot of 120 ms at 40 queries per second, and what was promised is the whole answer, not the retrieval step. The third criterion, continued training on private data, says nothing about a decision that has to be taken on today's corpus. The distinction against taking the better score is that an in-domain gain nobody sees, because the answer arrives late, is not a gain.

RULE: Domain fit is only one criterion for choosing embeddings: at production scale lookup speed weighs as much, and the retrieval budget decides between the two.

TRAP: Treating in-domain accuracy as the only criterion for an embeddings provider and finding out what its lookup costs only at the peak.

TRY IT: Time the embedding lookup of your current provider at your peak query rate and subtract it from your retrieval budget: what is left is all a candidate provider can spend.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/embeddings

questions.question: After a security advisory, the security group at Mistral Retail approved a closed range of versions and requires that no Claude Code session start outside that range during the year-end change freeze. Developers on the catalog team update on their own, and several are two versions behind. Bruno is preparing the managed settings for the rollout. Which key meets the requirement as written?

options.label: A
options.text: requiredMinimumVersion and requiredMaximumVersion, which make the CLI refuse to start when the installed version falls outside the range.
options.feedback: Correct: it is the only option that prevents a session from starting outside the approved range, which is literally what the change freeze demands.

options.label: B
options.text: minimumVersion, which stops the auto-update from installing a version below the floor the organization has set.
options.feedback: This is a real and useful key, but it only blocks auto-update downgrades: anyone already below the floor keeps working, and the upper end goes uncontrolled.

options.label: C
options.text: DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER in the env block of the managed settings, to freeze the installed version on every machine on the team.
options.feedback: Freezing the updater prevents new movement, but it leaves untouched the machines that are already outside the range, which are exactly the ones that worry you today.

options.label: D
options.text: A SessionStart hook that compares the installed version against the approved one and writes a warning when they do not match.
options.feedback: The warning works as a signal, but SessionStart is not a blocking event: the message is shown to the developer and the session carries on regardless.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to pick the key by what it prevents, not by what it sounds like. minimumVersion only stops the auto-update from dropping below a floor, while requiredMinimumVersion and requiredMaximumVersion make the CLI refuse to start when the version falls outside the approved range, which is the guarantee a change freeze asks for. The distinction against the warning hook is that SessionStart does not block: it informs and the session continues, so the requirement would go unmet on precisely the machines that are behind.

RULE: minimumVersion stops downgrades; requiredMinimumVersion and requiredMaximumVersion stop the startup. If the requirement says it must not start, use the pair that refuses to launch.

TRAP: Confusing a key that governs future updates with one that decides whether the session is allowed to begin at all.

TRY IT: Set requiredMinimumVersion above your current version in a test managed-settings.json and start Claude Code: you will see it refuse to launch instead of warning.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/admin-setup

questions.question: The credit-documentation extraction team at Banco Altamar added this configuration entry: {"mcpServers": {"core-creditos": {"type": "http", "url": "${CORE_MCP_URL}"}}}. The server exposes a single tool, consultar_estado_deudor, which wraps one endpoint of the mainframe core, and its only consumer is the nightly process that classifies files inside a 40-minute window. Two engineers keep the platform running, and every new service adds to the on-call rotation. What should be done with this integration?

options.label: A
options.text: Migrate the server to stdio transport so the process starts it as a subprocess and it takes its credentials from the environment.
options.feedback: stdio is the right transport when a single local client uses the server, but it keeps a protocol layer whose only consumer is a process the bank wrote itself.

options.label: B
options.text: Replace it with a direct call to the core API, and save MCP for integrations that several clients will reuse.
options.feedback: Correct: one capability, one consumer and both ends owned in house do not justify a protocol whose value is standardized, reusable integration.

options.label: C
options.text: Expose the capability as a resource instead of a tool, so the application decides when to put the debtor status into context.
options.feedback: The resource-versus-tool distinction is real and decides who controls invocation, but it does not answer whether a single consumer needs an MCP server at all.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish it behind the Messages API MCP connector so the model can reach it without the bank running its own infrastructure.
options.feedback: The connector avoids operating an MCP client, but the server still exists and it adds a remote dependency inside a 40-minute nightly window.

questions.explanation:
MCP is chosen when an integration will be reused by several clients, or when the authentication and transport plumbing is itself the work, because the protocol supplies the standardized integration that solves that part. Neither condition holds here: one capability, one consumer, and both ends belong to the same team, so the server only adds a startup dependency to a process with a fixed window and one more service to the on-call rotation of two engineers. A direct call to the endpoint covers the whole case and leaves MCP available for the day several applications need the same thing. The distinction against moving to stdio is that transport decides where the server runs and where its credentials come from, not whether the protocol is needed.

RULE: Choose MCP when several clients are going to reuse the integration; with one consumer and both ends in house, the direct call is enough.

TRAP: Assuming that wrapping an endpoint of your own in an MCP server improves it, when it only adds a layer nobody else will reuse.

TRY IT: Count how many distinct clients consume each MCP server you operate today; for any server with a single consumer that you wrote yourself, write down what the protocol gives you that a direct call does not.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros tested a new prompt for broker replies. Valentina ran the suite in two arms, one with the new prompt and one with the current one, and the report summarizes: cases 40, runs per case 3, new variant score 0.92, current variant score 0.91, delta 0.01, threshold 0.90. The committee wants to approve the change because 0.92 clears the agreed threshold and the rollout is set for the quarter-close week. What does this result actually show?

options.label: A
options.text: That the suite already passed without the new prompt: the delta is the change's contribution, and here it is near zero.
options.feedback: Correct: a high score in both arms with a delta near zero proves the change is not what makes the cases pass.

options.label: B
options.text: That the change works and the margin is small because the suite is calibrated to sit very close to the agreed threshold.
options.feedback: The threshold only decides whether a case passes; it says nothing about what the change contributes, which is exactly what the delta measures.

options.label: C
options.text: That more runs per case are needed, because with three the difference stays inside the noise of the judge.
options.feedback: More runs reduce noise and three is a reasonable minimum, but the problem here is not measurement precision: both arms perform the same.

options.label: D
options.text: That the judge is too weak and is penalizing formatting differences between the two prompt variants.
options.feedback: A weak judge can mark correct answers wrong, but that would sink the score of one arm rather than leave the two arms tied.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an absolute score does not prove your change helped; the difference between the arm with the change and the arm without it does. If a case scores the same with and without the variant, the variant is not what makes it pass, however high the number. Here both arms sit above the threshold and the delta is one hundredth, so the suite was already solving those 40 cases with the current prompt. What is missing is a set of cases the new prompt actually changes. The distinction against asking for more runs is that noise affects the precision of the delta, not its magnitude: a delta of zero measured with more runs is still zero.

RULE: Measure the delta against the arm without the change: a high score in both arms means your change is not what made the cases pass.

TRAP: Treating the absolute score of the variant as evidence of improvement, when the evidence lives in the comparison with the control arm.

TRY IT: Run your suite once with the change and once without it over the same cases, then sort the cases by delta: the ones that come back at zero tell you which part of the suite measures nothing.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals

questions.question: Pampero Agro wants to produce agronomic reports from field notes and sensor series. The business asked outright for an agent that decides on its own which sources to consult and assembles the whole report. The team is two engineers, the season starts in five weeks and concentrates 4,000 reports a week over three months, while the rest of the year the volume is marginal. There is still no measured case and no written quality criterion. What is the first design you should take to production?

options.label: A
options.text: Implement the autonomous agent exactly as the business asked and tune the guardrails afterward, so the start of the season is not delayed.
options.feedback: Honoring the request speeds up agreement, but an agent brings higher cost and compounding errors, and nothing measured here shows that the complexity is needed.

options.label: B
options.text: Launch one subagent per data source running in parallel, so that the architecture absorbs the volume peak of the high season.
options.feedback: Parallelism between subagents is for exploring more broadly, not for absorbing volume: a seasonal peak is a problem of capacity and submission shape, not of agent count.

options.label: C
options.text: Chain five prompts with checks between the steps from the start, so the design does not have to be redone when the scope grows.
options.feedback: Chaining is useful when you need to inspect intermediate results or force a structure, but adopting it before you have evidence adds steps nobody has yet shown to improve the outcome.

options.label: D
options.text: Start with one call augmented with retrieval and examples, measure it against defined criteria and add steps only if it falls short.
options.feedback: Correct: the recommendation is to start from the simplest solution, optimize it with evaluation and add agentic layers only when the simple version proves insufficient.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to start with simple prompts, optimize them with thorough evaluation and add multi-step agentic systems only when the simple solutions fall short. For many applications a well-optimized single call with retrieval and in-context examples is already enough, and complexity is added only when it demonstrably improves the outcome. With two engineers, five weeks and no measured case, any extra layer is paid for in build time and in how hard the result is to debug. The distinction against chaining steps from the start is that chaining is justified when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or impose a structure, and that is not established yet.

RULE: Start with the simplest solution that solves the problem and add complexity only when evaluation shows the simple version falls short.

TRAP: Assuming that a seasonal volume peak is solved with more agents, when it is a question of capacity and of how the work is submitted.

TRY IT: Run twenty real reports with a single call using retrieval and examples, count how many pass your criteria, and only with that number decide which extra layer to add and what you expect it to improve.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

questions.question: AndesWare wants an agent that writes, on every pull request in the monorepo, the impact note for the squads whose contracts the change touches. Nobody writes that note today: the impact shows up after the merge, as an incident. The platform committee funds one quarter and wants evidence at the end of it that the agent does the job, so the criterion cannot be agreed once the quarter is over. Nicolás has two weeks with four squads before anyone writes code. In what order should he proceed?

options.label: A
options.text: Build a first version with the squads' conventions → let them use it for a month → gather complaints in the channel → derive the criteria from them
options.feedback: Informal checking works while you are prototyping and stops working once something is in production; it also closes the quarter with complaints instead of evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: Mine the incident history for changes that broke a contract → turn each one into a case → agree a threshold with the squads → build against it
options.feedback: Real failures are the documented entry point when the work is already done by hand; here the note has never been written, so the history says which change broke something but not what a good note said about it.

options.label: C
options.text: Write the tasks that define the note, each with its expected result and its grader → build until they pass → widen the set with the pilot failures
options.feedback: Correct: when the capability does not exist yet you define it by building the evals first and then iterating until the agent performs well, and that same set is the evidence the committee asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: Choose the model and the tools → measure what that setup produces on a sample → take the threshold from those results → hand it to the squads
options.feedback: A threshold copied from whatever the first setup happens to produce fixes the criterion to today's performance, and it cannot tell the committee whether the agent does the job.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that discovery has to leave behind a criterion someone else can check, and the documented way to get one for a capability that does not exist yet is eval-driven development: build the evals that define the planned capability before the agent can fulfill it, then iterate until it performs well. The order also answers the committee, because the evidence at the end of the quarter is that same set of tasks run again. Sourcing cases from real failures is the documented starting point when people already do the work by hand and their mistakes are on record, which is the right move in that situation and not in this one. The distinction against prototyping first is that informal checking breaks down exactly when a system reaches production, and that is where this quarter ends.

RULE: When nobody performs the task yet, write the evals that define it before you build: the criterion comes first and the evidence is that same set run again.

TRAP: Assuming that acceptance criteria can be derived afterward from complaints, when nothing in the channel says what a correct output looks like.

TRY IT: Take a capability your team is about to build and write three tasks with their expected result and how each one is graded; if you cannot write the grader, the requirement is not defined yet.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud launches a triage chat in two weeks, which patients at its 40 clinics enter from the app. The commercial agreement requires compliance with the Usage Policy, and the ethics committee wants evidence of that compliance before the feature is enabled. Camila, who owns compliance, is reviewing how the patient is told that an AI is behind the answers. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the notice in the terms and conditions the patient accepts when registering in the app, because that leaves a signed record.
options.feedback: Acceptance at registration does leave a record, but the obligation is set per session: someone coming back months later has no notice in front of them.

options.label: B
options.text: Show a notice at the start of every chat session, before the first answer, saying that an AI is answering.
options.feedback: Correct: the disclosure has to be delivered at minimum at the start of each chat session, which is the moment the patient begins interpreting what is on screen.

options.label: C
options.text: Instruct in the system prompt that Claude clarify it is an AI whenever the patient asks about it explicitly.
options.feedback: Answering honestly when asked is desirable, but it leaves disclosure in the hands of the patient and the model instead of having the application guarantee it.

options.label: D
options.text: Show the notice only when triage refers the patient to an in-person visit or to a hospital emergency room.
options.feedback: Reserving the notice for serious cases inverts the criterion: disclosure governs how the whole conversation is read, not only how it ends.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that transparency toward the person is an obligation of the application and has a defined moment: when outputs are presented to consumers you have to tell them AI is in use, and in a public-facing chat that disclosure is delivered at minimum at the start of each session. A notice buried in the terms and conditions misses that moment, and letting the model clarify only when asked turns an obligation into a coincidence. In health there is also a separate requirement, review by a qualified professional before the recommendation reaches the patient, and it does not replace the disclosure.

RULE: The notice that an AI is answering goes at the start of every session, and the application delivers it, not the model when someone asks.

TRAP: Treating a consent signed once at registration as if it covered the duty to disclose in every conversation.

TRY IT: Enter your chat as a new user and as a returning user, and note in each case when the AI notice appears and whether it arrives before the first answer.

Show a notice at the start of every chat session, before the first answer, saying that an AI is answering.
Instruct in the system prompt that Claude clarify it is an AI whenever the patient asks about it explicitly.
Show the notice only when triage refers the patient to an in-person visit or to a hospital emergency room.
html.explanation:
The general rule is that transparency toward the person is an obligation of the application and has a defined moment: when outputs are presented to consumers you have to tell them AI is in use, and in a public-facing chat that disclosure is delivered at minimum at the start of each session. A notice buried in the terms and conditions misses that moment, and letting the model clarify only when asked turns an obligation into a coincidence. In health there is also a separate requirement, review by a qualified professional before the recommendation reaches the patient, and it does not replace the disclosure.

RULE: The notice that an AI is answering goes at the start of every session, and the application delivers it, not the model when someone asks.

TRAP: Treating a consent signed once at registration as if it covered the duty to disclose in every conversation.

TRY IT: Enter your chat as a new user and as a returning user, and note in each case when the AI notice appears and whether it arrives before the first answer.

questions.question: Colibrí Pay runs a support agent that checks balances, issues refunds and blocks cards, with 3x year-over-year growth. The regulator requires that every refund above a given amount be authorized by a person and that every automatic action be reconstructable afterward. Malena is designing the full path of a request, from intake to the verification loop that closes the cycle. Which two elements must that design include to meet the requirement? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Record every proposed refund as a pending operation with its own identifier and apply it only after an approval outside the conversation.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented pattern is to propose the write, leave it pending with an identifier and apply it only when a person approves it outside the chat.

options.label: B
options.text: Close the loop with deterministic checks of the policy rules over every output, reporting which rule failed and why it failed.
options.feedback: Correct: the best form of verification is a defined set of rules that explain which one failed, and it doubles as reconstructable evidence of why an operation was stopped.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the agent confirm the operation with the user inside the chat and record that confirmation in the case ticket.
options.feedback: A confirmation typed into the conversation approves nothing: it is granted by the same loop that wants to run the action, so it is not an authorization control.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a second model that scores each agent response and automatically blocks the ones that fall below the defined threshold.
options.feedback: Model-graded judgment helps where no criterion can be programmed, but it is not a robust method and it adds latency; for an amount limit, the deterministic check is superior.

options.label: E
options.text: Store the full transcript of every conversation so that what happened in each reviewed case can be reconstructed later.
options.feedback: Storing transcripts helps explain a run after the fact, but that is observability: it records the improper operation, it does not stop it from being applied without authorization.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for an end-to-end design with sensitive actions is that the write is proposed, verified and applied in separate steps. The reference architecture leaves each change pending with a server-generated identifier and applies it only after an approval outside the conversation, because an approval typed into the chat approves nothing. The verification loop closes with deterministic rules, which are the best form of feedback because they say which rule failed and why, ahead of visual review and ahead of another model's judgment. The distinction against storing transcripts is one of timing: the record explains what happened, the control prevents it from happening.

RULE: Propose the write, verify it with rules and apply it outside the conversation: an approval typed into the chat approves nothing.

TRAP: Confusing the agent asking for permission with the existence of a control, when that permission is granted by the same loop that wants to run the action.

TRY IT: Take the most dangerous action your agent can run today and mark at which step it is recorded as pending, which rule validates it and who applies it; if all three are the same step, you have no control.

questions.question: The Red Vicuña Salud message triage routes 22 percent of messages to the emergency room when the clinical protocol would expect around 8 percent, and every unnecessary referral takes a bay the network does not have. Two physicians built the eval suite from 30 real cases in which referral was warranted, three runs per case, and it has scored above 0.95 for four months. Joaquín has two days of clinical time a month to extend it. What most likely explains why the suite never anticipated the over-referral?

options.label: A
options.text: The suite only contains cases in which the referral has to happen, so it cannot show when the agent refers too often.
options.feedback: Correct: you have to test both the cases where the behavior should occur and the cases where it should not; a single polarity optimizes toward one side only.

options.label: B
options.text: The suite is saturated: it has sat near its ceiling for months and gives no signal for further improvement.
options.feedback: A saturated suite stops signaling improvement and deserves harder cases, but harder cases of the same kind still would not measure a wrong referral.

options.label: C
options.text: There are far too few cases: with 30 examples, run-to-run variance explains a deviation of that size.
options.feedback: Volume beats a handful of heavily curated cases, but the over-referral is systematic rather than a fluctuation: no case in this suite could reveal it.

options.label: D
options.text: The model is not good enough for the clinical task, and a more capable family is worth evaluating before spending clinical time.
options.feedback: A model change is decided with an eval that measures the problem; with this suite you could not tell whether the new option refers better or worse.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an eval can only show what its cases put to the test, which is why it has to include both situations where the behavior should occur and situations where it should not. A suite made only of correct referrals rewards referring and never penalizes referring too often. It optimizes toward one side, so it can score very high while the system fails in production. The missing cases come from what already fails: the real messages that ended in an empty bay. The distinction against saturation is that a saturated suite measures the right thing and has run out of headroom, while this one measures only half the problem.

RULE: Test both polarities: for every case where the action should happen, include one where the correct behavior is to hold back.

TRAP: Assuming a high score covers the whole system, when the suite contains only examples of the behavior you want to happen.

TRY IT: Count how many cases in your suite expect the action and how many expect restraint; if the second number is zero, add five false-positive cases from your support queue and run it again.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Banco Altamar turns on Zero Data Retention in the organization that runs claim classification. Internal audit requires a written statement before go-live about what the provider retains, and any claim that cannot be supported with official documentation is recorded as a finding. Mateo is drafting that text. What will he be able to state accurately once ZDR is on?

options.label: A
options.text: That no data from the bank is retained under any circumstance, because ZDR removes every form of retention on the provider side.
options.feedback: This is the absolute reading of the term and the one that generates findings: even with ZDR there can be retention when the law requires it or when automated systems flag a session.

options.label: B
options.text: That turning it on covers the other organizations in the account on its own, including the credit documentation pilot.
options.feedback: ZDR is enabled per organization and each new organization needs it enabled separately; extending it in the statement without checking is exactly the kind of claim audit flags.

options.label: C
options.text: That prompts and responses are not stored at rest after the response is returned, although what trust and safety systems flag may be retained.
options.feedback: Correct: it states what stops being kept at rest and acknowledges the exception the documentation itself points out for material flagged by the automated systems.

options.label: D
options.text: That the DPA is no longer needed for that organization, because with no storage afterward there is no personal data left to frame.
options.feedback: The processing happens all the same even when no storage remains, and the contractual instruments still apply: ZDR is a retention setting, not a change of legal framework.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for a compliance statement is to assert exactly what the provider documents and not a word more. ZDR means prompts and responses are not stored at rest after the response is returned; it is enabled per organization and does not extend on its own to the other organizations in the account. The documentation also makes clear that material may be retained when the law requires it or when automated trust and safety systems flag a session, so the absolute claim will not survive an auditor. The distinction against declaring the DPA dead is that retention and the contractual framework are different things: the processing still happens.

RULE: ZDR describes what is not kept at rest and is enabled per organization; it is not a promise that nothing, ever, is retained.

TRAP: Extrapolating from not stored at rest to nothing can ever be retained, and from one enabled organization to the whole account.

TRY IT: Write in three lines what your organization can claim about retention and check each line against the official data retention page: mark the one you cannot find supported word for word.

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación is testing the automatic tutor with twelve teachers before enabling it for 180,000 students. The budget per student is very tight, so a broad rollout that later has to be reversed is expensive. Valentina has three weeks to decide whether the tutor is extended, and she wants that decision to rest on what the pilot teachers actually experience, not on a general impression. How should she organize the pilot group's feedback?

options.label: A
options.text: Send out a satisfaction survey at the end of the term, when accumulated usage has made the averages stable.
options.feedback: A late survey measures satisfaction with statistical precision, but it arrives after the date the decision has to be made, so it feeds no decision at all.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask each teacher to use it this week on a real task and post what worked, what annoyed them and what surprised them in the shared channel.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the documented ask for a pilot cohort, because it ties the feedback to real use, keeps it short and public, and arrives in time to decide the rollout.

options.label: C
options.text: Collect the feedback in one-on-one meetings with each teacher and consolidate it afterward into a report for management.
options.feedback: One-on-one meetings give depth, but they hide each answer from the rest of the group, who then cannot learn from what somebody else already solved, and they delay consolidation.

options.label: D
options.text: Measure only the actual usage on the platform, because usage data is more reliable than the opinions of the people taking part.
options.feedback: Adoption metrics show drops that suggest friction, but they do not explain the cause: seeing that somebody stopped using the tutor does not say what made them quit.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for a feedback loop in a pilot is to ask for little, ask about real work and ask where everyone can see it. The documented ask has three parts: use it on at least one real task that week, leave a short note with what worked, what annoyed and what surprised, and know in advance that this feedback decides how the tool extends to the rest. The three questions work because they are concrete and quick to answer, and the shared channel makes each answer useful to the others as well. The distinction against measuring usage alone is that adoption metrics point at where the friction is, but the cause comes from the person who felt it.

RULE: Ask for a real task, a short note in a shared channel, and say in advance which decision depends on it.

TRAP: Leaving the feedback until the decision is already made: a survey afterward measures satisfaction, it does not decide a rollout.

TRY IT: Write in two lines the ask you would make of your pilot group this week, with the real task, the three questions and the concrete decision that feedback will settle; if you cannot name the decision, the pilot has no exit.

questions.question: Yaguareté Logística processes 12,000 customs dispatches a day with its tariff-classification agent. The system prompt now carries 62,000 tokens: the full classification manual plus the customs procedures of the four countries, even though each dispatch touches a single country and most consult no procedure at all. The shipping documents the agent has to read are long and compete for the same space. Malena wants to free up context without losing material. Which design should she choose?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn on prompt caching over the whole manual block so that prefix is read at a fraction of the price on every dispatch.
options.feedback: Caching does make a stable prefix cheaper and is worth using anyway, but it does not change that 62,000 irrelevant tokens still compete with the documents for attention.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the manual and the procedures into a vector index and retrieve the five chunks closest to each dispatch.
options.feedback: An index serves large, changing corpora; this material is bounded, stable and procedural, and chunking it splits instructions that are meant to be read whole.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on compaction so the context is summarized only once the conversation approaches the limit of the window.
options.feedback: Compaction is a recovery mechanism: it shrinks a context that already grew, instead of keeping it from growing with material nobody asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: Package each procedure as a Skill: the metadata stays loaded and the body is read only when the query calls for it.
options.feedback: Correct: progressive disclosure leaves about 100 tokens of metadata per Skill and pulls in the body, and only then the bundled files, when the dispatch needs it.

questions.explanation:
Progressive disclosure loads up front only what the agent cannot discover on its own and leaves the rest behind a reference that resolves at runtime. Skills implement that in three levels with published costs: the metadata, on the order of 100 tokens per Skill, is always loaded; the body enters only when the description matches the query; and the bundled files cost nothing until they are read. With one country per dispatch, that returns the window to the shipping documents, which are the real work. The distinction against caching is that caching makes the prefix cheaper without curing it: the documentation warns that retrieval degrades as the token count grows, so curating what enters is still necessary.

RULE: Load up front only what the agent cannot discover on its own; the rest is declared with a good description and read when the query asks for it.

TRAP: Confusing making context cheaper with curating it: caching lowers the price of the prefix, not the attention that prefix consumes.

TRY IT: Measure what percentage of your dispatches consult each procedure and compare it with the percentage of the system prompt that procedure occupies: that gap is what you load without using.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Pampero Agro builds its agronomic reports by pasting the plot sensor table in as text, some 12,000 distinct rows per report, and asking for averages, deviations and comparisons against the previous season. The usage field of a typical response returns input_tokens 96,400, cache_read_input_tokens 0, output_tokens 640. During harvest the company issues 9,000 reports a day against a closed monthly budget, and the agronomists have already found miscalculated averages. Malena wants one change that attacks the cost and the arithmetic errors at once. Which one do you choose?

options.label: A
options.text: Summarize the table with the cheapest model in the family and pass only that summary into the final report.
options.feedback: A cheap pre-pass does cut tokens, but the summary loses the rows the averages rest on, and the arithmetic errors stay or get worse.

options.label: B
options.text: Mark the table with cache_control so that those rows are read from the cache instead of billed as new input.
options.feedback: Caching only pays when the prefix repeats across requests; here every report carries the table of a different plot, so there would be nothing to read back.

options.label: C
options.text: Pass the table as a file and have the model compute over it with code execution, leaving the instructions in the prompt.
options.feedback: Correct: tabular data belongs in a file rather than in the prompt; the computation becomes exact and the report stops paying for the rows on every request.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the flow to the model with the largest context window so that the 12,000 rows fit with room to spare.
options.feedback: The table already fits: the problem is not capacity but that accuracy falls as the token count grows, and you pay for those rows in every report.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that tabular data is handed to the model as a file and processed with code, not pasted inside the prompt. Pasted in, the rows become input tokens on every request and force the model to do arithmetic over thousands of lines, which is exactly where the miscalculated averages come from. Handed over as a file and computed with code execution, the results are exact and those rows leave the bill. The distinction against caching is that the cache only saves when the same prefix repeats across requests, and here each report carries a different plot's table, which the usage field already confirms with a cache read of zero. A larger window does not help either: accuracy degrades as the context grows and the cost per report is unchanged.

RULE: Data goes in a file and the math goes in code: the prompt carries the instruction, not the table.

TRAP: Assuming every token problem is fixed by caching, even when the large block changes completely on every request.

TRY IT: Take a thousand-row table of your own, ask the same numeric question with it pasted into the prompt and with it uploaded as a file for code execution, and compare the answer and the input_tokens of each run.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows

questions.question: The Grupo Aurora Educación academic help desk works with teachers in long sessions. Each conversation opens with a stable prefix of some 18,000 tokens holding the assessment regulations and the promotion criteria, then runs twenty-five to thirty turns in which every question builds on the one before it. The team marks a single breakpoint at the end of that prefix today, so everything the conversation accumulates after it is sent uncached on every turn. The per-student budget for the cycle is closed. Which caching configuration fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Spread the four available breakpoints across the sections of the regulations, so that each section is cached on its own.
options.feedback: Four breakpoints help when the prefix has parts that change at different rates, but the regulations already read from cache: what is paid in full is the conversation growing behind them.

options.label: B
options.text: Close the session and open a new one every five questions, so the conversation never grows and the prefix stays short.
options.feedback: Cutting the session keeps the context from growing, but it pays for a new cache write every time and takes away the thread of what the teacher already asked.

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat a summary of the regulations in every user turn, so the model does not lose sight of it as the conversation grows.
options.feedback: Repeating the summary adds new tokens on every turn and caches nothing; the regulations are already in the prefix, which does read from cache.

options.label: D
options.text: Use automatic caching with a single "cache_control" field at the top level, so the breakpoint moves forward on its own.

With explicit breakpoints you decide by hand which blocks are cached, which suits a prefix whose parts change at different rates. With automatic caching a single "cache_control" field at the top level is enough, and the system applies the breakpoint to the last cacheable block and keeps moving it forward, which is the documented mode for multi-turn conversations. Here the regulations already read from cache and what grows bill after bill is the accumulated turns, so the lever is to let the breakpoint advance with them. questions.question: Pehuén Energía is preparing the control-room assistant, where operators need an answer in seconds during an alarm. The definition reads: {"agente": "asistente_sala_control", "tools": ["leer_alarma", "consultar_tendencia", "abrir_orden_trabajo", "consultar_manual", "registrar_novedad", "notificar_guardia"], "definiciones": "1,800 tokens"}, and pilot telemetry shows that almost every interaction uses five of the six. Nicolás proposes turning on tool search and deferring the load of all six definitions. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the six definitions loaded: with fewer than ten tools, deferring them adds a search round trip before every answer.
options.feedback: Correct: below ten tools, with definitions that fit comfortably, loading everything up front is usually faster, and time is exactly what is protected here.

options.label: B
options.text: Turn on tool search and leave only the three most used undeferred, to trim the definition tokens out of every request.
options.feedback: That is the recommended pattern when there are dozens of tools; with six, keeping three loaded and searching for the rest adds a step and frees negligible context.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on defer_loading for all six, so the definitions stop traveling in the payload of each request and input cost drops.
options.feedback: A frequent confusion: deferring removes the definitions from the model's context, but they are still sent in full in the tools array of every request.

options.label: D
options.text: Consolidate the six into two generic tools with an operation parameter, so the model has fewer options to choose from.
options.feedback: Consolidation helps when several tools overlap; these six have distinct purposes, and a generic tool with a parameter makes the choice more ambiguous, not less.

questions.explanation:
Progressive disclosure pays off when the catalog is large: the documentation recommends turning tool search on from ten tools, from 10,000 tokens of definitions, when selection accuracy drops, or when several MCP servers are added, and keeping standard loading when there are fewer than ten tools or the agent uses them all on every request. This agent falls on the standard-loading side twice over: six tools, 1,800 tokens of definitions, and five of them used in almost every interaction. Deferring returns no appreciable context and does introduce a discovery round trip before the work starts, which is exactly what a control room cannot pay for during an alarm. The key distinction is that deferral moves the cost; it does not remove it.

RULE: Progressive disclosure pays off with large catalogs; below ten tools that are used almost every time, loading everything up front is faster.

TRAP: Assuming that defer_loading takes the definitions out of the request, when it only takes them out of the model's context: they are still sent on every call.

TRY IT: Add up your agent's definition tokens with the count endpoint and divide them by the size of your window: if they do not reach 10%, deferring costs you a round trip and returns little.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/tool-search https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool
