questions.question: Mistral Retail has to regenerate the listings for 900,000 catalog products before the promotional campaign, which starts in eight days. The platform's quarterly budget is already 80% spent and there will be no extension. Listings are not published until merchandising approves them by sampling, so nobody needs them instantly, but a drop in quality would force the batch to be redone and that does break the deadline. Tomás is looking for the cost lever that saves the most without touching the result. What should he do?

options.label: A
options.text: Send the work through the Message Batches API, split into batches below the request limit, and take the 50% discount.
options.feedback: Correct: the work needs no immediate response, the batch discount is 50% off standard pricing, and eight days leave ample margin against the expiration of each batch.

options.label: B
options.text: Turn on streaming in the calls to watch progress live and cut off earlier the listings that are coming out badly.
options.feedback: Streaming improves perceived latency, not cost: the billed tokens are the same, and it is not available in batch processing anyway.

options.label: C
options.text: Spread the catalog across several subagents working in parallel, to cover it in less time with the same team.
options.feedback: Multi-agent systems consume on the order of three to ten times the tokens of a single agent: they speed up broad exploration, but here they would worsen the very constraint that is tight.

options.label: D
options.text: Move all the work to the cheapest model of the family and accept a drop in quality on the listings that get generated.
options.feedback: Routing to the cheapest model is a legitimate cost lever, but here it is paid for in merchandising rejections and a redo that the eight-day deadline cannot absorb.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to reach for the cost lever that does not touch quality before the ones that do. Batch processing bills at 50% of standard pricing and is meant for exactly this kind of load, one that does not require an immediate response, which is the case for a catalog reviewed afterward by sampling. Its per-batch limits mean 900,000 listings have to be split across several submissions, and the 24-hour expiration of each batch fits comfortably inside an eight-day window. The distinction against dropping to a cheaper model is what you pay with: the batch saves without changing the output, while the cheaper model shifts the cost onto merchandising rejections and the redo.

RULE: When the work does not need an answer right now, the first saving is in how you submit it, not in dropping the model or adding agents.

TRAP: Looking for the saving in the way the answer is displayed or in more agents in parallel, when the lever is in the way the work is submitted.

TRY IT: Take this month's bulk load, count how many requests it is and work out the spend at half price; then check whether you can tolerate results in hours instead of seconds and how many batches you would have to split it into.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them

questions.question: Minera Nevado's operational-safety assistant builds a weekly report per mine site: it gathers the shift logs, analyzes the risks against the standing procedures, drafts the report and reviews it before publishing. Each step uses the result of the one before it. Bruno proposes splitting the flow across four subagents, one per phase. The monthly token budget is already at 85% with nine days to go, and the report has a committed publication date. Which architecture should the team choose?

options.label: A
options.text: Split the flow into four subagents, one per phase, coordinated by a lead agent that assembles the final report.
options.feedback: This is the phase decomposition the documentation names as an antipattern: every boundary is a handoff that loses fidelity and adds coordination tokens.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep a single agent and raise effort to the maximum so it reasons better in each of the four phases of the report.
options.feedback: Raising effort increases how much the model reasons and how much it spends; the question on the table is how to divide the work, not how deeply to reason.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the chain in one agent and delegate only the final review to an agent that validates the report without its history.
options.feedback: Correct: verification is the delegation that pays off consistently, because the verifier does not need to know how the result was built in order to judge it.

options.label: D
options.text: Split the phases across agents but share one conversation thread, so none of them loses the context the previous one left.
options.feedback: Agents share the sandbox and the credentials, but each one runs in its own thread with an isolated history: there is no way to split phases without handoffs.

questions.explanation:
Start with a single agent and delegate only when the work demands isolated contexts, real parallelism or distinct tool sets, because multi-agent systems consume 3 to 10 times more tokens than an equivalent single agent. The four phases here are strictly sequential and each one consumes the result of the last, so splitting them is the by-problem decomposition the documentation describes as a game of telephone: every handoff degrades fidelity and adds coordination that produces no report. The documented exception is the verifier: an agent dedicated to validating the main agent's work performs well precisely because it does not need the history of how the result was built. With the budget at 85% and a committed date, it is also the only delegation this month can absorb.

RULE: Divide by context, not by phase: the delegation that almost always pays is a verifier that does not need to know how the result was built.

TRAP: Confusing multi-agent with parallelism: splitting sequential steps across agents multiplies tokens and adds a handoff at every boundary.

TRY IT: Mark which steps of your flow could run at the same time without waiting on each other; if the number is zero, splitting it across agents only buys you handoffs and tokens.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/multiagent-orchestration

questions.question: Bastión Legal reviews contracts with an assistant that receives the whole document in the prompt. The partner in charge noticed that two reviews of the same contract, launched with temperature at 0, returned different lists of risk clauses. The firm bills by the hour and is professionally answerable for what it delivers, so it needs to show the client which review was handed over and on what basis, without rereading the entire contract by hand. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Set temperature to 0 and top_p to 0 as well, so that two identical calls always return the same output.
options.feedback: Lowering the temperature makes the output more conservative, but the documentation is explicit: even at temperature 0, identical inputs can produce different outputs between calls.

options.label: B
options.text: Archive the specific output that was delivered, with its request identifier, and validate every cited clause against the contract text.
options.feedback: Correct: the traceability the firm needs comes from keeping what was actually delivered and verifying it, not from hoping that two runs will agree.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to the most capable model in the family, because the variation between runs disappears as model capability goes up.
options.feedback: Moving up a model may improve the quality of the review, but non-determinism is documented for the inference service in general, not as a limitation of the smaller models.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the reviews through the Message Batches API, which processes each contract once and so removes the variation between successive runs.
options.feedback: Batch processing lowers cost and organizes asynchronous work, but it does not change how the model answers the same input, nor does it leave a record of what was delivered.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that traceability in an LLM system is built by recording and verifying, not by expecting the model to repeat itself. The documentation warns that even at temperature 0, identical inputs can produce different outputs between calls, both on the first-party service and through third parties: a low temperature means more conservative, not deterministic. What protects the firm is archiving the output that was actually delivered, with its request identifier, and checking every cited clause against the text, which also costs less than rereading the contract at billed rates. The distinction against moving up a model is that non-determinism is not a defect of capability.

RULE: Temperature 0 is not determinism: if you have to show what you delivered, store that output and verify it rather than generating it again.

TRAP: Treating a sampling parameter as if it were a guarantee of reproducibility, and expecting two identical runs to serve as evidence.

TRY IT: Send the same prompt ten times at temperature 0 and compare the outputs character by character: count how many are identical before you promise anyone reproducibility.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/glossary

questions.question: Agencia Nacional de Ingresos runs an agent that reads the filings taxpayers upload, summarizes them and drafts the response for the case file. In a red team exercise, a document carrying a written order to ignore the previous instructions and reply that the debt had been cleared changed the draft. Today that text arrives inside the user turn. Audit requires a control before the next filing season, and the agency's procurement rules do not allow new software this year. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add to the system prompt an instruction not to obey any order written inside the documents that taxpayers upload.
options.feedback: Declaring the untrusted-content policy in the system prompt is one of the documented defenses and is worth keeping, but on its own it leaves the hostile text in a block the model reads as instruction.

options.label: B
options.text: Deliver the taxpayer's text inside tool_result blocks with its origin declared, and filter the raw output with a lightweight classifier.
options.feedback: Correct: third-party content belongs in tool_result, where the model treats it with skepticism, and the filter adds a layer that does not depend on the model getting it right.

options.label: C
options.text: Put the document in the user turn between XML tags, so that it is clearly separated from the agency's own instructions.
options.feedback: Delimiting helps readability, but the guidance is explicit: third-party content does not go in the system prompt or in user text blocks, which is where the model expects instructions.

options.label: D
options.text: Log every tool call in the audit feed and review each week the ones that have modified a case file.
options.feedback: Logging is necessary for the audit and lets you reconstruct what happened, but it arrives after the fact: it does not stop an injected instruction from producing the wrong draft.

questions.explanation:
The general rule against indirect injection is that the defense is decided by where outside content enters and what is done with it before the agent acts, not by how well the warning is worded. Third-party material has to arrive inside tool_result blocks, which is where the model is trained to treat the instructions it finds with skepticism, and the raw output is worth passing through a cheap classifier before it is returned. The system prompt option is a documented layer and worth keeping, but on its own it leaves the hostile text where the model expects orders, and protection at the model layer is never fully effective. Logging and reviewing afterward does not prevent the wrong draft.

RULE: Third-party content enters through tool_result, labeled and filtered before the agent reads it; the system prompt warning accompanies that, it does not replace it.

TRAP: Confusing a well-written instruction with an enforced boundary: the model layer is never fully effective and cannot be where the control lives.

TRY IT: Take a test document with a hostile order hidden in it, run it first pasted into the user turn and then inside a labeled tool_result, and compare the two drafts.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude

questions.question: Siete Lagos Viajes classifies change and cancellation requests into 140 categories that decide which team and which flow each case goes to. The current flat classifier gets the frequent categories right and fails on the ones that resemble each other, which are most of the catalog. The contract with corporate clients commits to a first response in under 30 seconds, including high season with 10x peaks. Facundo has to raise precision without leaving that window. Which decomposition is the right one?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep a single classifier and put the 140 categories with their examples in the prompt, which in the end is still one call.
options.feedback: One call looks like the cheap option on latency, but context is a resource with diminishing returns: the more categories stacked in, the worse the model discriminates between similar ones.

options.label: B
options.text: Launch one subagent per branch of the tree and have them vote on the final category, so the result gains confidence on doubtful cases.
options.feedback: Voting exists to gain confidence by repeating the same task, but it multiplies cost and latency, and the problem here is not confidence but the lack of nuance between neighboring categories.

options.label: C
options.text: Split the work into phases: one model extracts the request data, another decides the category and a third writes the response.
options.feedback: Separating extraction, decision and drafting is a reasonable pipeline for other things, but it does not touch the problem: the failing step still chooses among 140 options in one shot.

options.label: D
options.text: Organize the categories into a tree and chain one classifier per level, running each level with the fastest model of the family.
options.feedback: Correct: a taxonomic structure with cascading routing gives more nuance because each level has its own prompt, and the fastest model is the documented mitigation for the extra latency.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for a large classification space is to organize it into a taxonomic tree and chain classifiers by level, with cascading routing. The advantage is nuance: each branch has its own prompt holding only the categories that compete with each other, which is exactly where the flat classifier fails. The documented cost is latency, because several chained classifiers take longer than one, and the recommended mitigation is to run the cascade with the fastest model of the family. The distinction against stacking the 140 categories into a single prompt is that more context does not improve discrimination: context has diminishing returns and attention is spread across options that look alike.

RULE: When the categories are many and alike, split them into a tree and classify by level; the extra latency is covered by the fastest model.

TRAP: Assuming that stacking every category into one prompt is free because it is a single call, and ignoring that attention degrades as the context grows.

TRY IT: Group your categories into five branches, write the first-level classifier and measure the time of the two chained calls against your current flat classifier, and the precision of both on the cases that get confused today.

html.question: Siete Lagos Viajes classifies change and cancellation requests into 140 categories that decide which team and which flow each case goes to. The current flat classifier gets the frequent categories right and fails on the ones that resemble each other, which are most of the catalog. The contract with corporate clients commits to a first response in under 30 seconds, including high season with 10x peaks. Facundo has to raise precision without leaving that window. Which decomposition is the right one?
options: Keep a single classifier and put the 140 categories with their examples in the prompt, which in the end is still one call.
Launch one subagent per branch of the tree and have them vote on the final category, so the result gains confidence on doubtful cases.
Split the work into phases: one model extracts the request data, another decides the category and a third writes the response.
Organize the categories into a tree and chain one classifier per level, running each level with the fastest model of the family.
html.explanation:
The general rule for a large classification space is to organize it into a taxonomic tree and chain classifiers by level, with cascading routing. The advantage is nuance: each branch has its own prompt holding only the categories that compete with each other, which is exactly where the flat classifier fails. The documented cost is latency, because several chained classifiers take longer than one, and the recommended mitigation is to run the cascade with the fastest model of the family. The distinction against stacking the 140 categories into a single prompt is that more context does not improve discrimination: context has diminishing returns and attention is spread across options that look alike.

RULE: When the categories are many and alike, split them into a tree and classify by level; the extra latency is covered by the fastest model.

TRAP: Assuming that stacking every category into one prompt is free because it is a single call, and ignoring that attention degrades as the context grows.

TRY IT: Group your categories into five branches, write the first-level classifier and measure the time of the two chained calls against your current flat classifier, and the precision of both on the cases that get confused today.

questions.question: Before writing the first eval for the first-level technical support assistant, Lucía sits down with the operations team at Ceibo Telecom to agree on the success criteria. That team has committed to a first response time by contract, and it audits how customers are treated every month. Which of the following statements about evaluation criteria and metrics is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Latency and price are success criteria in their own right and are agreed alongside accuracy, not discovered after measuring them.
options.feedback: True: both appear among the documented success criteria and belong to the set you define before building the eval.

options.label: B
options.text: A criterion about safety becomes measurable when you state it as the fraction of outputs the filter flags over a fixed number of tests.
options.feedback: True: it is the documented example of how to quantify a fuzzy attribute instead of settling for asking for safe outputs.

options.label: C
options.text: When the attribute is subjective, such as tone, the qualitative scale replaces the quantitative measure and expert judgment suffices.
options.feedback: Correct as the false statement: the qualitative adds value applied alongside the quantitative, and tone is scored just as well on a one-to-five scale.

options.label: D
options.text: Most use cases need a multidimensional evaluation: several criteria measured over one and the same held-out test set.
options.feedback: True: the documentation combines accuracy, toxicity and response time into a single criterion over one held-out set.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a success criterion has to be specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and that the measurable part rules: numbers give clarity and they scale, while the qualitative adds value only when it is applied consistently alongside them. That is why fuzzy attributes are not left out of the eval, they are quantified. Tone is scored on a one-to-five scale, and safety as the fraction of outputs flagged over a fixed number of tests. Latency and price are documented success criteria too, not constraints you discover later. The false statement is the one that treats the qualitative scale as a replacement for measurement instead of a complement.

RULE: Every criterion that matters is expressed as a number: the qualitative accompanies the quantitative, it never substitutes for it.

TRAP: Assuming a subjective attribute cannot be measured and leaving it out of the eval, in the hands of whoever reviews that day.

TRY IT: Take the three criteria you describe in words today and rewrite each one with a metric, a threshold and the size of the set you will measure it on.

questions.question: The case-law search at Bastión Legal prepends a stable prefix of some 60,000 tokens, holding internal precedents and citation criteria, to every query. The lawyers work in bursts: Ignacio measured the gaps inside a single session and found that one pause in four falls between five minutes and one hour, while pauses longer than an hour are rare. The final answer is emitted with structured outputs to feed the brief. The firm bills by the hour, and the prefix is rewritten and paid for at every pause. What should you configure?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the five-minute TTL and resend the previous request with max_tokens set to zero every four minutes to keep the prefix warm.
options.feedback: Warming the cache is a real procedure, but that request is rejected when the flow uses structured outputs, which is exactly this case.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the five-minute TTL and accept the rewrite, since the cache refreshes at no cost every time it is used.
options.feedback: The free refresh only happens inside the live window; with one pause in four above five minutes you would pay the write again and again.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the precedent prefix to the end of the prompt, after the query, so the variable block does not invalidate the cache.
options.feedback: That inverts the rule: the cache hashes the prefix in order and the stable part goes first; with the large block last there is no shared prefix to cache.

options.label: D
options.text: Buy the one-hour cache duration for the prefix breakpoint, even knowing that this write costs more than the five-minute one.
options.feedback: Correct: with more than one pause in twenty falling between five minutes and one hour, and longer pauses infrequent, the one-hour duration is the indicated option.

questions.explanation:
Choosing the cache duration is an exercise in counting. If more than one pause in twenty falls between five minutes and one hour, and pauses longer than an hour are rare, the one-hour duration is worth buying; if turns arrive seconds apart, or long gaps are the norm, the five-minute one stays. Here one pause in four lands in that band, so the more expensive write is paid once and saves rewriting 60,000 tokens on every burst. The distinction against periodic warming is that the maintenance request is rejected in flows with structured outputs, with manual thinking or with a forced tool, and for those cases the documentation itself points to buying the hour.

RULE: Count your pauses: more than one in twenty between five minutes and one hour, and few longer, justifies the one-hour cache.

TRAP: Treating periodic cache warming as a universal alternative to a long TTL, without looking at which requests reject it.

TRY IT: Log the intervals between requests inside a single session for a day and compute what fraction falls between five minutes and one hour; compare that fraction with one in twenty before paying for the more expensive write.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

questions.question: At Banco Altamar, the agent that extracts data from credit documentation reads between 30 and 60 documents per folder, and toward the end of each folder the quality of the extraction degrades. Camila moves the reading into subagents, one per document type, each with its own window and a defined output format. Internal audit requires that every extracted field can be traced back to the document that supports it. What effect should you expect from this change?

options.label: A
options.text: Total token cost will go down, because each subagent works within a window much smaller than the main agent's.
options.feedback: A smaller window per subagent does not mean fewer tokens overall: each subagent makes its own requests, and the set of them usually consumes considerably more than one conversation.

options.label: B
options.text: The main agent will still see the text that each subagent read, only now sorted by the type of document it came from.
options.feedback: That is not how it works: the main agent receives only each subagent's final message as the tool result, not the content that subagent read to produce it.

options.label: C
options.text: The main context will grow with summaries and not with text, at the price of more tokens and of losing what you do not ask for.
options.feedback: Correct: context isolation compresses what comes back to the main agent, but total spend rises and any field the output format does not require stays behind in the subagent.

options.label: D
options.text: Total latency will drop in proportion to the number of subagents, because all of the documents are now read in parallel at once.
options.feedback: Parallelism shortens the reading phase, but the main benefit is thoroughness rather than speed: total time usually does not drop proportionally and sometimes goes up.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of context isolation is that a subagent can explore as much as it likes inside its own window, but only its final message comes back to the main agent: a brief synthesis, not the whole reading. That fixes the degradation at the end of the folder, because the main context stops filling up with document text. The price is more total tokens, since each subagent makes its own requests, and the loss of every detail the output format does not explicitly ask for. With an audit that requires traceability, the practical consequence is that the reference to the source document has to be in each subagent's output format, or it is lost.

RULE: A subagent returns its summary, not its reading: what you do not ask for in the output format never reaches the main agent.

TRAP: Assuming that isolating context saves tokens, when what it saves is attention in the main window and what it spends is the repeated work of each subagent.

TRY IT: Have one of your subagents read three documents and compare what the main agent receives with what the subagent read; then add the traceability field that was missing to the output format and run the test again.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

questions.question: The claims triage suite at Zafiro Seguros runs 120 cases against a test environment that includes the case-file database and a simulated mailbox. Renata sees the same eight cases fail together on every execution, sees the failing set change with the order in which the cases run, and finds that a case run on its own always passes. The team has two weeks to certify the agent with the regulator. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The runs share state in the test environment, and what one case does changes the starting point of the next.
options.feedback: Correct: every run has to start from a clean environment; state shared between executions produces exactly this kind of correlated failure.

options.label: B
options.text: The eval judge is non-deterministic and its verdict varies more the longer the text it has to read.
options.feedback: Judge variance does grow with the length of the text, but it produces scattered failures, not a block that falls together and depends on order.

options.label: C
options.text: There are too few runs per case, and with a single execution the model's variability explains the pattern.
options.feedback: Repeating runs is good practice against noise, but a case that always passes when run alone rules out model variability as the cause.

options.label: D
options.text: The eight cases are badly defined and describe an outcome the agent cannot reach with the tools it has been given.
options.feedback: A broken task is recognized because it never passes, under any condition; these cases pass when they run in isolation.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that every trial has to start from a clean environment, because state that survives from one run to the next produces correlated failures that say nothing about the agent. The three signals point the same way: the failures arrive in a block, the block changes with execution order, and the isolated case passes. If the environment is not reset between runs, what the suite measures is interference between cases rather than the capability of the system, and certifying on that measurement in front of the regulator would not hold. The distinction against a broken task is that an impossible task fails always, even in isolation; and against judge noise, that noise scatters failures instead of grouping them.

RULE: Isolate every run in a clean environment: if execution order changes who fails, what you are measuring is your shared state.

TRAP: Attributing to model variability a failure pattern that repeats as a block and shifts with execution order.

TRY IT: Run your suite twice with the cases in a different order and compare what fails in each execution; if the list changes, reset the environment between runs and compare again.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: A team exposes a tool that cancels orders to its agent through an MCP server. According to the MCP specification, what keeps a human in the loop over that invocation?

options.label: A
options.text: Marking the tool with destructiveHint in its annotations, so that the client asks for confirmation automatically.
options.feedback: Annotations are hints declared by the server, and the client has to consider them untrusted unless that server is trusted: they describe an intent, they do not enforce a control.

options.label: B
options.text: Having the client display the tool inputs and ask for an explicit confirmation before it calls the server.
options.feedback: Correct: the specification asks that there always be a human able to deny the invocation, and it puts displaying the inputs and asking for confirmation on the client.

options.label: C
options.text: Having the server validate the tool inputs, sanitize its outputs and apply rate limiting on the invocations.
options.feedback: These are genuine server obligations and they limit abuse, but none of them puts a person in front of the decision before the cancellation actually runs.

options.label: D
options.text: Having the server require an authenticated session, because the session identifier records which user approved the action.
options.feedback: The specification is blunt: MCP servers must not use sessions for authentication, and a session identifier records no human approval at all.

questions.explanation:
The general rule in MCP is that the human decision lives in the client. The specification says there should always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny a tool invocation, and it asks the client to display the inputs before calling the server, to request confirmation on sensitive operations and to log the use for auditing. Annotations such as destructiveHint only declare an intent on the server side, and the client has to treat them as untrusted unless the server is trusted, so they do not work as a control. Server-side validation and rate limiting are separate obligations: they limit abuse, but they put nobody in front of the decision beforehand.

RULE: The client presents the human confirmation before the call; server annotations are untrusted hints, not an authorization mechanism.

TRAP: Treating a hint declared by the server as if it were a rule the client will enforce on the user's behalf.

TRY IT: Review your MCP client and note, for the three most destructive tools you expose, whether the user sees the inputs before approving; if not, the approval is blind.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools

questions.question: Pehuén Energía's predictive-maintenance agent reads technical manuals going back 30 years. It runs for the whole maintenance window, six hours, in a single session. Valentina sees that from the fifth or sixth step onward the agent repeats queries it already made and loses earlier findings. Her measurements: 12 tools loaded, 4,100 tokens of definitions, and every call to consultar_manual returns the full section, around 18,000 tokens. Where is the cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The tools return entire sections, so what saturates the window is the volume of results, not the definitions.
options.feedback: Correct: 4,100 tokens of definitions are paid once per request, but 18,000 tokens of results pile up turn after turn until they push out what came before.

options.label: B
options.text: Too many tools are loaded: selection accuracy degrades once 30 or 50 tools are available to choose from.
options.feedback: The 30-to-50-tool threshold is real and worth keeping at hand, but with 12 tools loaded this agent sits far below it, and the measurement confirms it.

options.label: C
options.text: The manual index fell out of date and the agent queries again because it receives chunks that no longer match the source.
options.feedback: A stale index returns content that no longer exists in the source, and that produces confident but wrong answers, not the loss of earlier findings.

options.label: D
options.text: The thinking budget is low for a session this long and the model cannot hold the thread between one step and the next.
options.feedback: More thinking budget deepens the reasoning of one turn; it creates no room in a window that is filling up with the text the tools return.

questions.explanation:
Two different kinds of bloat have to be told apart: definition bloat, which is paid once per request and is attacked with tool search, and result bloat, which accumulates on every turn and is attacked by returning only high-signal information, with filters, pagination or truncation. The measurements separate the two cases without ambiguity: 12 tools and 4,100 tokens of definitions sit far below the threshold where selection degrades, while 18,000 tokens per call fill the window in a handful of steps and push earlier findings out of it. Anthropic recommends precisely that a tool return relevant context rather than a full dump, which is why Claude Code caps the size of tool responses by default. The distinction against blaming the number of tools is which quantity grows with the turns.

RULE: Before blaming the number of tools, look at the size of what they return: definitions are paid per request and results accumulate per turn.

TRAP: Diagnosing capability bloat from the number of tools when the window is being filled by the volume of their results.

TRY IT: Count the tokens of your tool definitions and compare them with the average result of the most used tool; if the result wins by an order of magnitude, the problem is in the return.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool

questions.question: AndesWare is about to route the sessions of all its development squads through its own gateway. Bruno is writing the implementation guide the tech leads will follow on Monday; the cost office needs to attribute consumption to each person and nobody should be blocked on the day of the change. Bruno wants any configuration failure to show up before the mass distribution, not in the teams. What order of steps should the guide set out?

options.label: A
options.text: Hand the base URL and the credentials to the teams → confirm the gateway routes the model names → test it from the gateway host → collect the error reports
options.feedback: Distributing first turns the teams into the test bench: a model name with no route returns an error to anyone who selects it, and the failure shows up multiplied across the organization.

options.label: B
options.text: Confirm the gateway routes every model name → issue one credential per developer → test it with the configuration you are going to distribute → verify from a development machine
options.feedback: Correct: routing is checked, one credential is issued per person, the test uses the same configuration that will be handed out, and verification happens from a development machine, which is the real path.

options.label: C
options.text: Test the gateway from the host it runs on → distribute the configuration to every squad → confirm which model names fail → rotate the team's shared credential
options.feedback: Testing from the host does not cover the network path developers use, and leaving the model names for later means discovering them through the errors the teams receive.

options.label: D
options.text: Issue one shared credential for everyone → distribute the base URL to the teams → test a sample model name → verify the result from the gateway host
options.feedback: A shared credential makes it impossible to attribute consumption per person and to revoke somebody without affecting the rest, which is exactly what the cost office needs.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of a phased rollout is to test with the configuration you are going to hand out and to verify from the target population, not from the team that administers it. questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación generates study material in batch for 180,000 students and runs all of it today on the most capable model in the family. The per-student budget for the next cycle drops 20 percent, and Tomás has three weeks to decide whether he can hold quality with a cheaper configuration. Quality is judged with a rubric the team already applies over 200 real pieces. Which two actions support that decision? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Compare the options over that set of pieces, measuring the cost per finished piece and not the price per token.
options.feedback: Correct: models are compared by cost per completed task, because a more capable one reaches the result with fewer passes and fewer rewrites.

options.label: B
options.text: Rank the options by their published price per million tokens and keep the cheapest one that the rubric still accepts.
options.feedback: Price per token ranks them badly: it does not count how many attempts are needed, nor that the same text can consume a different number of tokens.

options.label: C
options.text: Project the saving from the cost of the median piece multiplied by the monthly volume expected for the cycle.
options.feedback: The median hides the tail: a few hard pieces concentrate much of the spend, and it is that tail that decides the bill.

options.label: D
options.text: Sweep the effort parameter on the current model and measure the rubric at each level before changing models.
options.feedback: Correct: tuning effort is usually a better lever than changing models, and the sweep gives the quality-against-spend curve the decision needs.

options.label: E
options.text: Change the model and rewrite the prompt in the same measurement window to get the decision in on time.
options.feedback: Moving two variables at once makes the quality change impossible to attribute, and a prompt tuned for another model is not a neutral control either.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the model choice is decided with an eval over real tasks and on cost per completed task, not on price per token. A more capable model finishes the task with fewer passes, and newer models consume more tokens for the same text, so a per-token comparison penalizes them by construction. Before switching families it is worth sweeping effort on the current model, because that parameter trades intelligence against cost and latency inside one model and is usually the better lever. The two actions are independent: one fixes the metric for comparison, the other exhausts the cheapest lever before moving the expensive one.

RULE: Sweep effort before you change models, and compare on cost per finished task, never on price per token.

TRAP: Extrapolating spend from the median task, when a few hard tasks concentrate most of the bill.

TRY IT: Take twenty real tasks, run your current model at three effort levels and record quality and cost per finished task at each one; then compare that curve with the model you are evaluating.

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom enabled a diagnostic assistant for its 60 first-line support agents. Sofía, a platform engineer, is supporting the adoption, but the contact center has an occupancy target that does not allow pulling agents off the floor for long training sessions, and she can give this work only about forty minutes a week. She wants the channel to sustain itself without her within a month. Which four-week sequence should she follow?

options.label: A
options.text: Seed the channel with your own examples and prompts → open the weekly exchange and answer in public → offer short pairing and pin a FAQ → hand the channel to a second person
options.feedback: Correct: this is the documented four-week sequence, and each stage has its own signal of progress, until the questions are answered by somebody other than the person who started.

options.label: B
options.text: Run a general two-hour training session for the whole team → open the questions channel → collect the questions by private message → write a complete manual
options.feedback: Mass training collides with the contact center's occupancy target, and answering privately stops each answer from serving the rest of the team.

options.label: C
options.text: Publish the assistant's complete manual → wait for the questions to appear → answer them by private message → assemble an adoption report for management
options.feedback: A long document tends to get saved for later and forgotten; what gets copied and tried is a short example with context, and the report arrives when it changes nothing.

options.label: D
options.text: Name champions per area from the first day → hand out the supporting material → measure the adoption every week → write the FAQ once usage stabilizes
options.feedback: Naming champions before anyone has used the tool is guesswork: the person best suited for that role is whoever asked you the most questions during the first weeks.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for support in the enablement phase is to seed, set a rhythm, consolidate and hand over, in that order and with a signal of progress at each stage. You start by publishing your own examples with the prompts included, because what gets copied is a concrete technique and not an announcement; then you keep a weekly exchange going and always answer in public, so that every answer serves the whole group; then the repeated questions are consolidated into a pinned FAQ and short paired sessions are offered; and at the end the channel is handed over. The distinction against naming champions from the start is that the second champion is identified by evidence, not by title: it is whoever asked the most.

RULE: Your own examples first, then a public rhythm, then consolidation and only at the end the handover: the second champion comes from whoever asked you the most.

TRAP: Starting with the manual and the mass training, when what moves adoption is a reusable example and a question answered where everyone can see it.

TRY IT: Publish one real example of your own this week with the prompt included and a screenshot, and count how many replies it gets in two days; if nobody answers, review the example before blaming the tool.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/champion-kit

questions.question: The tariff classification system prompt at Yaguareté Logística still carries two blocks written for the previous generation of models: one asks the model to reason inside scratchpad tags before answering, the other orders it to verify every tariff code twice before emitting it. Last month the team migrated to the most capable model in the family, with adaptive thinking on, and left the prompt untouched; cost per shipment rose and accuracy did not improve. With 12,000 shipments a day, Ximena proposes removing both blocks. What is most likely to happen?

options.label: A
options.text: Cost per shipment falls, but accuracy drops, because the model stops reasoning before it answers and loses the verification step.
options.feedback: The reasoning does not disappear when the block goes: in current models it is a request parameter, not an instruction written in prose.

options.label: B
options.text: Cost per shipment falls appreciably and accuracy holds or improves, because the model already does that work on its own.
options.feedback: Correct: the prompt audit documents that removing redundant verification makes the task cheaper, and that a hand-written scratchpad competes with the real reasoning.

options.label: C
options.text: Nothing measurable changes, because the two blocks add few input tokens next to the size of each shipment file.
options.feedback: The cost is not in the tokens of the block but in the behavior it provokes: the model follows the instruction literally and generates extra work on every shipment.

options.label: D
options.text: Cost rises, because without the scratchpad the model needs more turns to reach the same tariff code for the shipment.
options.feedback: That inverts the effect: a hand-written scratchpad duplicates reasoning that already happens, and removing it shortens the output rather than adding turns.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a prompt written for an earlier generation is not a neutral control when you change models: it has to be audited. Two patterns repeat. Instructions the new model follows literally cost money, and asking it to verify twice is the documented example, where removing the instruction made the task cheaper with no loss of accuracy. Text that no longer fits the model costs accuracy, as a hand-written scratchpad does when reasoning is a request parameter. So the expected outcome is to spend less and measure the same or better. The distinction against fearing a quality drop is that the reasoning does not live in the prompt, it lives in the thinking configuration.

RULE: After a migration, audit the prompt: what the new model already does on its own, written out in prose as well, is paid for twice.

TRAP: Treating the inherited prompt as a harmless constant, when it is the variable that makes the new model expensive without making it accurate.

TRY IT: Run fifty of your own cases with the inherited prompt and with a version stripped of the redundant verification instructions, and compare accuracy and output tokens per case.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

questions.question: The agent on Ceibo Telecom's self-service channel exposes 23 tools covering billing, network diagnostics, commercial offers and complaint handling. Last quarter tool selection got worse and the 95th percentile of latency ended up at the edge of the contractual first-response commitment. The platform team is three people and proposes splitting the agent into four specialized agents. Which two measures come first, given the latency constraint and the size of the team? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Create one agent for each internal team that owns a tool today, so that each owner maintains their own.
options.feedback: Splitting by internal owner copies the org chart, not the context: what is left are coupled agents passing work to each other, and every handoff loses information.

options.label: B
options.text: Launch the four agents in parallel on every query and keep the first response that comes back complete.
options.feedback: Running several attempts in parallel helps gain confidence on one task, but here it multiplies the spend per query and does nothing to improve tool selection.

options.label: C
options.text: Defer the tool schemas, so that only the names load at the start and the full schema arrives when it is needed.
options.feedback: Correct: with a high number of tools, the first documented measure is to defer the schemas, which greatly reduces the context loaded up front and improves the selection.

options.label: D
options.text: Move up to the most capable model of the family so it chooses better among the 23 tools, accepting the extra latency.
options.feedback: A more capable model does choose somewhat better, but it pays with latency exactly where the contractual commitment is already at the limit, and it leaves the context causing the confusion intact.

options.label: E
options.text: Split the block of network diagnostic tools into an agent of its own, since it shares no context with the rest.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented signal for specializing is that the tools span unrelated domains, and the cut is made only where the context can genuinely be isolated.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to start with a single agent and add agents only when the context can genuinely be isolated, because each extra agent is another failure point and another set of prompts to maintain, which weighs heavily on a team of three. When one agent handles on the order of twenty tools and starts choosing badly, the first documented remedy is not another agent but deferring the schemas so that only the names load at the start. The second legitimate signal for specialization is that the tools span unrelated domains, and there the cut justifies itself. The distinction against splitting into four is that three of those blocks share commercial context and would be passing work back and forth continuously.

RULE: With too many tools, defer the schemas first; add an agent only where the context can genuinely be isolated.

TRAP: Reading the number of tools as if agents were missing, when it first indicates there is too much context loaded up front on every request.

TRY IT: List your agent's tools, mark which ones 90% of the traffic uses and note which domain each belongs to; if a whole block goes unmarked and belongs to another domain, there is the only boundary that justifies itself.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use

questions.question: Since the November campaign, the Mistral Retail after-sales agent has delegated catalog searches to subagents. The FinOps dashboard adds up the tokens the team records at each agent step and lands on a third of what is finally billed that month. Bruno has to close cost attribution per order before the accounting close, with traffic peaks of 10x on promotional dates. What are the two most likely causes of that gap? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The dashboard counts parallel tool calls twice, because all of them carry the same message identifier.
options.feedback: That effect is real and forces you to deduplicate by identifier, but it inflates the dashboard total; here the dashboard falls short of the invoice.

options.label: B
options.text: The dashboard queries the usage and cost API too infrequently and shows data from hours before the close.
options.feedback: The data appears a few minutes later and is queried at most once a minute; a delay shifts the period, it does not leave two thirds of the spend out.

options.label: C
options.text: The telemetry does not record tool content, so the dashboard never sees what the catalog searches consume.
options.feedback: Content is off by design and is enabled separately, but what is missing from the dashboard is counted tokens, not the text of the calls.

options.label: D
options.text: The usage field of the result message counts only the main agent loop and leaves the subagents out.
options.feedback: Correct: accounting for the whole tree comes from the per-model breakdown, not from the usage field, which undercounts as soon as nesting appears.

options.label: E
options.text: The SDK cost figures are client-side estimates and not the authoritative source for reconciling against the invoice.
options.feedback: Correct: for billing you reconcile against the administration usage and cost API, not against estimated values computed on the client.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that accounting for a multi-level agent does not come from the usage field of each step. That field counts only the main agent loop and undercounts as soon as a subagent appears, which is exactly what changed when the searches were delegated. The per-model breakdown does include the whole tree, and that is what has to be summed. The second cause is about source: the cost figures the SDK returns are client-side estimates, useful during development and unfit for reconciling with the invoice, while the authoritative source is the usage and cost API. The two causes are independent: one explains which tokens are missing, the other which figure closes the month.

RULE: Account for the whole tree with the per-model breakdown and close the month against the usage and cost API, never against client-side estimates.

TRAP: Assuming that summing the usage of each step equals total spend, when that field ignores everything the subagents consume.

TRY IT: Take one execution with subagents, compare the usage of the result message with the per-model breakdown for that same execution, then check the day's total against the usage and cost API.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/cost-tracking https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/usage-cost-api

questions.question: AndesWare standardized a shared prompt that drafts the migration note for every pull request across its 400 developers. The note has to follow the house format: fixed sections, an impersonal tone and a closing block of rollback steps. Today 38 percent come back rejected by the reviewer because a section is missing or the tone drifts, and the prompt already carries twenty-two rules written in prose. Since that prompt travels in every pipeline run, Paula does not want it to grow any further. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a more explicit rule for each drift observed and expressly forbid the tone mistakes that the team makes most often.
options.feedback: More prohibitions lengthen the prompt and work less well than showing the wanted result; say what to do instead of what not to do.

options.label: B
options.text: Define a JSON schema with structured outputs so that the output meets the house format in a guaranteed way.
options.feedback: Structured outputs guarantee conformance to a JSON schema, but the migration note is prose with sections and a tone, not an object the reviewer consumes.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the model to reason step by step inside tags before drafting and only then produce the final note.
options.feedback: Hand-written step-by-step reasoning is a resource for when thinking is off, and the problem here is not reasoning but form.

options.label: D
options.text: Include three to five diverse examples of a well-formed note, wrapped in tags, and drop the rules they already show.
options.feedback: Correct: examples are the most reliable way to pin format and tone, and swapping rules for examples keeps the prompt from growing.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that format and tone are fixed by showing examples, not by piling up abstract instructions. Three to five relevant and diverse examples, wrapped in tags so the model tells them apart from the instructions, are the documented way to make the output look like what you expect. Saying what to do also works better than forbidding, so every negative rule replaced by an example improves the result and shortens the prompt that travels on every run. The distinction against structured outputs is the object itself: they guarantee a JSON schema, and what the reviewer receives is prose with fixed sections and an agreed tone.

RULE: Show instead of prescribe: three to five diverse examples in tags pin format and tone better than twenty rules in prose.

TRAP: Answering every drift with a new rule, until the prompt weighs more than the result it is trying to describe.

TRY IT: Take your last three rejected notes, turn them into well-formed examples inside tags, remove five prose rules, and measure over twenty pull requests how many come back rejected.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency

Three to five relevant and diverse examples, wrapped in tags so the model tells them apart from the instructions, are the documented way to make the output look like what you expect. Saying what to do also works better than forbidding, so every negative rule replaced by an example improves the result and shortens the prompt that travels on every run. The distinction against structured outputs is the object itself: they guarantee a JSON schema, and what the reviewer receives is prose with fixed sections and an agreed tone.

RULE: Show instead of prescribe: three to five diverse examples in tags pin format and tone better than twenty rules in prose.

TRAP: Answering every drift with a new rule, until the prompt weighs more than the result it is trying to describe.

TRY IT: Take your last three rejected notes, turn them into well-formed examples inside tags, remove five prose rules, and measure over twenty pull requests how many come back rejected.

questions.question: At Agencia Nacional de Ingresos, the inconsistency-detection system retrieves rulings and regulations with fixed-size chunks of 2,000 tokens, no overlap and no added context. Mateo proposes cutting them in half to gain precision. A full reindex fits only in one weekend window per quarter, and the team measures its retrieval failures over the top 20. Which effect should the team anticipate?

options.label: A
options.text: Precision will rise proportionally, because each chunk will hold a single idea and cosine similarity will come out cleaner.
options.feedback: Smaller chunks do focus a topic better, but the documentation promises no such relationship: size, boundary and overlap all affect performance and have to be measured.

options.label: B
options.text: Indexing cost will drop by nearly half, because fewer tokens have to be embedded for each document of the indexed corpus.
options.feedback: The embedded text is the same; what changes is how many vectors it is spread across. The same token count is indexed, in more entries and with more metadata.

options.label: C
options.text: Latency per query will rise noticeably, because the index will hold twice as many vectors to traverse on every search.
options.feedback: The index does grow in number of vectors, but Anthropic documents no such latency relationship, and the dominant effect of this change lands on retrieval quality.

options.label: D
options.text: The share of chunks retrieved well but arriving with no reference will rise, because the neighboring text that identified them is left out.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the problem contextual retrieval solves, by prepending 50 to 100 tokens of document context to each chunk before embedding and indexing it.

questions.explanation:
Shrinking the chunk improves focus and degrades reference: the smaller it is, the more it depends on a context that no longer travels with it. That is exactly the failure Anthropic describes when introducing contextual retrieval: traditional RAG strips context at encoding time, leaving chunks that are correct but that, outside their document, say nothing about which regulation, which period or which taxpayer they refer to. With zero overlap the effect gets worse, because sentences and section headings end up separated from their content. The documented move that does reduce the failures measured over the top 20 is to prepend 50 to 100 tokens of context generated from the whole document to each chunk, before embedding it and also before indexing it for BM25.

RULE: The smaller the chunk, the more context you have to prepend before embedding it: size gives focus, context gives identity.

TRAP: Assuming that a smaller chunk is always more precise, when what is lost is exactly the context that made it identifiable.

TRY IT: Pull ten random chunks out of your index, read them in isolation and ask yourself which document and which period they describe; the ones you cannot place are what contextual retrieval fixes.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval https://academy.claude.com/courses/building-with-the-claude-api/text-chunking-strategies

questions.question: A data team rebalances the set it uses to evaluate its system because one region was underrepresented in the sample. Under the bias categories of the NIST AI RMF, which kind of bias does that measure address?

options.label: A
options.text: Systemic bias, because it corrects the way the organization and its processes framed the problem to be solved.
options.feedback: Systemic bias also shows up in the data, but its origin is in the norms and practices of the organization and of society: rebalancing a sample changes neither who framed the problem nor on what criteria.

options.label: B
options.text: Human-cognitive bias, because it changes the way people interpret what the system returns to them.
options.feedback: Human-cognitive bias describes how people perceive the information a system gives them and what they assume about its purpose; you work on it with design and disclosure, not with the sample.

options.label: C
options.text: Computational and statistical bias, because it arises from unrepresentative samples in the data and in the algorithmic process.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the category the AI RMF ties to data and to algorithmic processes, and an underrepresented region is its textbook case.

options.label: D
options.text: All three equally, because the AI RMF treats bias as a single category managed inside the MANAGE function.
options.feedback: The AI RMF distinguishes three categories with different origins, and GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE describe the risk management cycle, not a taxonomy of bias.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that each bias category has its own origin and therefore its own lever. The NIST AI RMF distinguishes systemic bias, which sits in the data, in the organization's norms and in society; computational and statistical bias, which appears in data and in algorithmic processes and often comes from unrepresentative samples; and human-cognitive bias, which is how people perceive the information a system gives them. Rebalancing a sample attacks the second. The distinction worth keeping is that no data correction reaches the other two: if the problem was framed wrong, the balanced set will go on measuring the wrong thing.

RULE: Rebalancing data corrects computational and statistical bias; systemic and human-cognitive bias are corrected outside the dataset.

TRAP: Assuming that balancing the evaluation set covers all bias, when it touches only one of the three categories in the framework.

TRY IT: Take a bias you have found in your own system and classify it into one of the three AI RMF categories; if it is not the computational one, note what measure outside the dataset would correct it.

SOURCE: https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/

questions.question: Pampero Agro rewrote the prompt of its assistant for field advisors and the suite backs the change: cases 60, runs per case 3, overallScore 0.94, casesPassed 57/60, threshold 0.90, mean delta 0.07. Harvest starts in two weeks, when traffic multiplies by six and many advisors work without stable coverage. Facundo has to put the change into production knowing that an urgent fix might not reach them in time. How should he deploy it?

options.label: A
options.text: Promote the new prompt to all traffic now, since the suite cleared the agreed threshold and two weeks of margin remain.
options.feedback: An eval that passes is one layer of defense, not all of them: no suite on its own covers what shows up in production with real traffic.

options.label: B
options.text: Wait until harvest is over and deploy in the next maintenance window, with the year's campaign already closed.
options.feedback: Postponing avoids the risk of the peak, but it also postpones the measured improvement in exactly the period that carries the year's work.

options.label: C
options.text: Deploy to all traffic and roll back with an emergency deployment if the advisors report a drop in quality.
options.feedback: Depending on a deployment to roll back stretches the exposure; the goal is that going back requires deploying nothing.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish the new version, send it a fraction of traffic as a canary and compare it with the pinned version before promoting.
options.feedback: Correct: each version stays immutable and the caller picks which one to use, so the canary measures in production and rolling back is not a deployment.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an eval result authorizes a trial in production, not a wholesale replacement. No evaluation layer catches everything, which is why the suite, production monitoring, comparison against the previous version and human review are combined. Deploying by immutable versions is what makes that comparison possible: the new version is published, the caller chooses which one to use, and a fraction of traffic serves as a canary. If something degrades, going back means asking for the previous version rather than running a deployment. The distinction against promoting to all traffic is exposure: with the peak ahead and advisors working without stable coverage, the cost of being wrong is measured across the whole campaign.

RULE: Publish immutable versions and promote with a canary: rolling back should be switching versions, not deploying in a hurry.

TRAP: Treating an eval above the threshold as proof that the change will behave the same way against real traffic.

TRY IT: Write in one sentence how you would roll back your last prompt change today; if the answer includes a deployment, pin the version in the caller and write it again.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/managed-agents-cma-prompt-versioning-and-rollback https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Pehuén Energía exposes its work-order system with an MCP server over HTTP that three different agents consume. The security review summarizes the implementation this way: the server accepts the Authorization: Bearer that each client sends and forwards it unchanged to the work-order API, where a single service token with scope "read:all, write:all" covers the three agents. The regulator requires that every work order be attributable to the person who authorized it. Which two corrections apply? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Reject any token whose audience is not this server, and request upstream a token of its own, issued for the work-order API.
options.feedback: Correct: the specification requires validating that the token was issued for this server and forbids relaying any other; upstream, the server acts as an OAuth client.

options.label: B
options.text: Bind the session to the caller's identity and use that session identifier as the credential on the calls that follow.
options.feedback: Sessions are not credentials: the specification forbids using them to authenticate and requires the Authorization header on every request, even within one logical session.

options.label: C
options.text: Migrate the server to stdio transport so that each agent starts it locally and takes the credentials from its own environment.
options.feedback: stdio is the right choice when a local client starts the server as a subprocess, but three remote agents consume this one, and the gap is authorization.

options.label: D
options.text: Record every call in the audit log together with the user who originated it, so the team can reconstruct later who asked for each order.
options.feedback: The audit trail is necessary and the regulator demands it, but it records the problem without preventing it: with token forwarding, the destination system still sees one identity.

options.label: E
options.text: Replace the full-scope service token with per-operation permissions, validated by the server before it executes each call.
options.feedback: Correct: a token with full scope bundles privileges nobody needs together, and declared scopes never replace the authorization logic of the server itself.

questions.explanation:
Authenticating the caller is not the same as authorizing the call, and an MCP server is not a credential tunnel. The security specification covers both fronts explicitly. First, an MCP server must not accept any token that was not issued for it, and if it needs to call an upstream API it must obtain its own token from that API's issuer instead of forwarding the client's: forwarding breaks traceability, bypasses the controls that depend on the audience, and turns the server into an exfiltration proxy if a token leaks. Second, scope: one full-permission service token shared by three agents is the textbook case of excessive scopes, and the specification itself warns against treating declared scopes as sufficient without authorization logic in the server. Auditing or changing transport touches neither gap.

RULE: An MCP server accepts only tokens issued for it and requests its own upstream; permission is decided per operation, not per agent.

TRAP: Treating the client's token as if it were a valid delegation and forwarding it downstream, when it only proves that somebody authenticated somewhere else.

TRY IT: Send your MCP server a token issued for another resource and see whether it answers 401; then check upstream whether the token it calls with is the same one it received.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/security_best_practices https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization

questions.question: Banco Altamar told internal audit it had a control that stops any Claude Code session from running commands against the production core database. Joaquín, from the internal platform team, shipped it in the managed settings like this: {"hooks": {"PreToolUse": [{"matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "/opt/altamar/guard.sh"}]}]}}. The script detects the forbidden pattern, writes the reason to stderr and ends with exit 1. In the audit test, the command ran all the same. What explains that result?

options.label: A
options.text: Only exit code 2 blocks the call; with any other code, Claude Code treats it as a non-blocking error and carries on.
options.feedback: Correct: the hook ran and gave its opinion, but exit 1 is recorded as a non-blocking error and the call continues. To block, exit with 2 and leave the reason on stderr.

options.label: B
options.text: The hook never ran, because PreToolUse hooks are skipped when the session runs with edits accepted automatically.
options.feedback: It is the other way around: PreToolUse hooks fire before any mode check, in every mode, including bypassPermissions, where their denial is honored just the same.

options.label: C
options.text: The matcher would have to be an anchored regular expression; written as Bash it matches no tool in the session.
options.feedback: A matcher made only of letters is read as an exact match on the tool name, so Bash does match; anchoring matters when the matcher carries regular expression characters.

options.label: D
options.text: The script wrote the reason to stderr, and a hook that prints no JSON on stdout leaves the command waiting for manual approval.
options.feedback: stderr is exactly where the reason for a block with exit 2 is written, and a hook never leaves a call waiting: it either blocks it or lets it through.

questions.explanation:
The general rule with hooks is that the exit code decides the block, not the intent of the script. A PreToolUse hook that ends with exit 2 blocks the call and sends Claude whatever it wrote to stderr; any other non-zero code, 1 included, is recorded as a non-blocking error and execution continues, which is exactly what the audit saw. The documented alternative is to return JSON on stdout with permissionDecision set to deny. The distinction against the matcher hypothesis is that a matcher made only of letters matches the tool name exactly, so the hook was firing on every command.

RULE: In a hook, exit 2 blocks and the reason travels on stderr; any other non-zero code is an opinion nobody obeys.

TRAP: Assuming that a script which detects the violation and fails is already a control, without looking at which exit code it ends with.

TRY IT: In a test repository add a PreToolUse hook that writes a reason and ends with exit 1, launch the command that should be blocked, then repeat with exit 2 to see the difference.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide

questions.question: The support agent at Colibrí Pay checks balances, issues refunds and blocks cards. The team proposes asking for human confirmation on every tool call, with no distinction between them. What documented problem does that decision have?

options.label: A
options.text: None: the more confirmations there are, the more control is exercised over what the agent actually gets to do.
options.feedback: It looks like the safest choice, but what has been observed in real deployments points the other way: when approving is the default gesture, the review stops being a review.

options.label: B
options.text: The confirmations are not recorded, so the regulator will not be able to reconstruct afterward who approved each operation.
options.feedback: Logging tool use for auditing is a client responsibility and can be implemented regardless; the problem with confirming everything is a different one.

options.label: C
options.text: The model learns from the approvals and ends up no longer asking permission for actions that have already been repeated.
options.feedback: Permission is decided by the harness that executes the tools rather than by the model, and it does not relax just because an action has been approved many times.

options.label: D
options.text: It produces approval fatigue: approving becomes automatic and leaves behind a false sense of security.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the documented failure of indiscriminate human in the loop. Confirmation is reserved for what is irreversible and the rest is bounded by removing scope.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for human in the loop is that a person's attention is a finite resource: a gate that fires on every call ends up being approved without being read. The published work on containing agents describes exactly this approval fatigue, where a very high approval rate produces a false sense of security, which is why confirmation is reserved for the irreversible, such as refunding money or blocking a card, while balance lookups are bounded by removing scope instead of by asking. The distinction against the logging option is that logs serve to reconstruct what happened rather than to prevent it, and you can have them anyway.

RULE: Reserve human confirmation for the irreversible and remove scope from the rest: a gate on every call turns into an automatic click.

TRAP: Assuming that more confirmations means more control, when an approval rate close to total means nobody is reading anymore.

TRY IT: Look at a week of your agent's approvals and work out what percentage were approved: if it is close to all of them, your gate measures reflexes and not judgment.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros is taking the claims triage design to the risk committee. The regulator requires explainability of automated decisions and that every claim above a given amount be reviewed by a person. Valentina has a single session to get approval, and she knows that afterward the record of that decision will be the only written trace left of the debate. Which two things should she include in what she presents and puts on record? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Attach the full architecture diagram and the agent's tool list, so that the committee can see the whole scope.
options.feedback: The diagram helps orient the committee, but it describes the system in its current state and records no decision and no alternative that was ruled out when it was taken.

options.label: B
options.text: Commit to the committee the same number the team measures in production today, so that two different figures do not coexist.
options.feedback: Matching the external commitment to the internal measurement removes the margin: the internal target has to be at least as strict as what is promised outside, never equally loose.

options.label: C
options.text: Put on record what stays as written guidance in the prompt and what limit is enforced in code, outside the model's judgment.
options.feedback: Correct: the written instruction steers the model's decision, while the permission enforced in code guarantees it; a committee that asks for guarantees needs to see that separation.

options.label: D
options.text: Present the chosen evaluation method along with what it gives up: code grading is fast and reproducible but loses nuance.
options.feedback: Correct: each grading method has a documented trade-off, and stating it next to the choice lets the committee accept the risk with its eyes open.

options.label: E
options.text: Put on record the vendor's certifications, so that the system built on top of them is covered by their scope.
options.feedback: The vendor's certifications say what controls the platform has, not that the application built on top complies: the scope of the triage remains the insurer's responsibility.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when communicating an architecture decision is to separate what is guidance from what is a guarantee, and to pair every choice with what it gives up. An instruction written into the prompt tells the model how work is done here; a limit enforced through permissions or code happens no matter what, and it is the only thing that answers a committee asking for a guarantee about the amount that requires human review.
