questions.question: Yaguareté Logística classifies 12,000 customs declarations a day by tariff code and has to be able to show, during an inspection in any of the four countries, the exact nomenclature rule that supports each classification. The operating window allows up to 40 seconds per declaration, an ample margin against the manual process it replaces. Ignacio is designing the context retrieval stage of the new system and is torn between two paths. Where should he start?

options.label: A
options.text: Build the semantic index over the whole nomenclature first, because with 12,000 declarations a day latency is what rules.
options.feedback: Semantic search is usually faster, but it is also less exact, harder to maintain and less transparent, and here there are 40 seconds of margin that do not force you to pay that price.

options.label: B
options.text: Start with agentic search over the nomenclature exposed as files and add a semantic index only if the window gets tight.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented recommendation is to start from agentic search and add semantic search only when you need faster results.

options.label: C
options.text: Load the complete nomenclature into the prompt of every request, so the model always has the whole context available at once.
options.feedback: Putting everything in the prompt leads to high costs, slower responses and context limits; on top of that, context has diminishing returns and accuracy does not improve by stacking text.

options.label: D
options.text: Put one agent per country querying its own customs system and a coordinator that synthesizes the final tariff classification.
options.feedback: Several agents make sense when there are independent paths to explore in parallel; here each declaration gets a single classification and the coordination only adds cost and failure points.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for the retrieval stage is to start with agentic search and add semantic search only if you need faster results, because semantic search is usually quicker but less exact, harder to maintain and less transparent. In a tariff classification that an inspection can challenge, transparency is not a luxury: you have to be able to show the exact paragraph that supports the decision, and an explicit walk through the nomenclature leaves that trail. The distinction against building the index first is in the constraint: the 40-second window is ample, so latency is not what decides, and there is no reason to pay up front in accuracy and traceability.

RULE: Start with agentic search and add the semantic index only when latency demands it: you gain accuracy and traceability, and you pay in time.

TRAP: Choosing the fastest path when the constraint that rules is being able to show where the answer came from, and finding that out only during an inspection.

TRY IT: Take ten real classifications from your system and ask for the exact rule that supports each one; count in how many you can go from the result to the source paragraph without looking it up by hand.

questions.question: The compliance committee at Zafiro Seguros wants a success criterion for fraud detection that can be reported to the regulator every month. The fraud team reviews at most 300 alerts a day, and today, with the manual process, one alert in three turns out to be legitimate. There are 20,000 historical claims labeled by adjusters. Andrés has to write the criterion before Friday's committee. Which one should he commit to?

options.label: A
options.text: Fewer than one legitimate alert in five, measured over the 20,000 labeled claims, without exceeding 300 alerts a day.
options.feedback: Correct: it names the metric, the threshold, the set it is measured on and the second dimension the team's capacity imposes, and it improves on the current process.

options.label: B
options.text: No alert at all on a legitimate claim, because an unfounded accusation harms the insured and exposes the company to the regulator.
options.feedback: The goal is relevant but not achievable: criteria are set against a prior or expert performance, not against an ideal no process reaches.

options.label: C
options.text: An F1 of 0.95 over the full historical set, which is the highest figure published for comparable detection tasks.
options.feedback: It is specific and measurable, but leaning on somebody else's figure does not make it achievable, and it says nothing about the volume of alerts the team can review.

options.label: D
options.text: That the alerts look reasonable and well founded to the adjusters who review them each morning.
options.feedback: Expert judgment is valuable for calibration, but without a metric and a threshold there is nothing to report to the regulator month after month.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a success criterion has to be specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and that most real cases need more than one dimension. Achievable means anchored in a prior performance, in expert judgment or in what a model can do today, not in an ideal: committing to zero false positives sounds responsible and guarantees failure. The correct option fixes the metric, the threshold, the set it is measured on and a second dimension, the volume the team can review, which is the real constraint of the service. The distinction against copying a published figure is that somebody else's number is not your own baseline: you do not know whether your set, your labels and your task admit that value.

RULE: A criterion is committed with a metric, a threshold, a measurement set and a baseline of your own; without those it is an aspiration.

TRAP: Confusing an ambitious goal with an achievable one, and committing to a zero that neither the manual process nor the system sustains.

TRY IT: Rewrite the criterion you use today by adding the set it is measured on and the improvement over your current process; if you cannot name that baseline, it is not yet achievable.

questions.question: The contract review agent at Bastión Legal processes drafts sent in by counterparties. In two cases the draft carried a hidden line instructing the agent to leave the penalty clause out of the summary, and the agent left it out. The firm bills by the hour and the internal commitment is to return the summary in under twenty seconds, so a second model call per document does not fit that latency budget. Sofía is reviewing the architecture of the flow. What should you change?

options.label: A
options.text: Deliver the contract text only in tool_result blocks and declare in the system prompt that this content is data, not instruction.
options.feedback: Correct: the model is trained to treat instructions arriving in a tool_result with skepticism, and the declared policy reinforces the separation without adding latency.

options.label: B
options.text: Put a lightweight model in front to classify every draft as suspicious or clean before the agent starts reviewing it.
options.feedback: A pre-screen is a documented defense, but it adds a call per document exactly where the latency commitment has no room for one.

options.label: C
options.text: Include the contract in the system prompt and add the warning there not to obey instructions coming from the document.
options.feedback: The system prompt is read as the operator's instruction, so placing third-party text there hands it the very authority you are trying to deny.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a line inside the tool_result reminding the agent to summarize every clause, including the penalty ones.
options.feedback: Your own instructions inside a tool_result are treated as untrusted data and may be ignored; they belong in the user turn that follows.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that where you put a text decides how much authority it carries. The system prompt is read as the operator's instruction, so third-party content never goes there. Inside a tool_result, by contrast, the model is trained to treat any instruction that appears with skepticism, and a policy declared in the system prompt completes the defense. That change is architectural and adds no call, which is what decides it against a pre-screen with a lightweight model: that defense is real and documented, but it costs a call per document and the latency commitment does not allow one. Your own instructions do not belong inside the tool_result either, because there they are treated as untrusted data.

RULE: Outside content travels in tool_result and your instructions in the user turn: the block you write in decides the authority of the text.

TRAP: Believing a warning in the system prompt neutralizes the third-party text you placed in that same system prompt.

TRY IT: Build a test document with a hidden instruction, put it through your flow first in the system prompt and then inside a tool_result, and compare what the agent does in each case.

questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro runs a pilot that answers questions about manifests and customs paperwork with this pipeline: chunk_size 2000, overlap 0, top_k 3, no reranking, index rebuilt every 30 days. Operator queries are almost always identifier lookups, of the kind that ask what the container on a given booking holds; manifests are corrected several times an hour, and the window to release a truck is minutes. Paula reviews the pilot before extending it to the whole terminal. Which change applies?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower chunk_size and add overlap so that no container identifier is cut in half between two neighboring chunks.
options.feedback: Size and overlap are real levers against cuts in mid-sentence, but they do not change that the index can be up to 30 days behind the manifest.

options.label: B
options.text: Rebuild the index every night and raise top_k from 3 to 10 to compensate for what the index has not taken in yet.
options.feedback: Reindexing more often shortens the lag without removing it: with hourly corrections and windows of minutes, any schedule falls short, and top_k does not touch that cause.

options.label: C
options.text: Add reranking over 150 over-retrieved candidates so that the right manifest climbs to the top of the list of candidates.
options.feedback: Reranking is the highest-impact improvement over a candidate list, but here it would reorder stale documents and add 100 to 200 ms to every query.

options.label: D
options.text: Query the operational system by identifier with a tool, and leave the index for the regulatory corpus, which is stable.
options.feedback: Correct: the data lives in a system that can be queried by key and changes while you answer, so read it live and keep the index for what does not move.

questions.explanation:
The retrieval strategy is chosen by the shape of the data and by the query pattern. An index suits a corpus that is large, stable, or reachable only through a search API; the live query suits a system that can be traversed by key and data that changes while you are answering. Anthropic flags freshness as a first-class risk of index-based pipelines, which return stale state when the source moves faster than reindexing, and describes the index-free approach as the one that delivers current state without maintaining a copy to protect and synchronize. Here the queries are identifier lookups against manifests corrected several times an hour, with windows of minutes: tuning the chunking, reindexing more often or reordering candidates are real improvements applied to the wrong architecture.

RULE: Index what is large and stable; query live what changes while you are still answering.

TRAP: Treating operational data that changes by the hour as if it were a document, and trusting an index rebuilt long after the change.

TRY IT: Take your ten most frequent queries and note how much staleness the data tolerates in each one; if the answer is measured in minutes, no reindexing schedule is enough.

questions.question: Assisted grading at Grupo Aurora Educación handles the thirty-five submissions of a course in a single conversation, one after another, with the criteria guide at the start. Teachers say the first pieces of feedback are good and that toward the end the assistant mixes up criteria and skips whole sections of the guide. The usage field of the last request in one of those conversations shows: "input_tokens": 186400, "cache_read_input_tokens": 11800, "output_tokens": 640. Nicolás proposes moving the flow to the model with the largest context window. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the flow to the model with the largest context window available, so that the thirty-five submissions fit with room to spare.
options.feedback: The submissions already fit: the problem is not missing room but that accuracy and recall fall as the token count grows.

options.label: B
options.text: Grade each submission in a clean conversation, with the criteria guide as the only prefix and no graded work carried over.
options.feedback: Correct: each submission is an independent task, so giving it a clean context removes the carryover that degrades the last pieces of feedback.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the effort level for the last submissions of each conversation, which are the ones that come out worst.
options.feedback: More reasoning does not recover what the model is already reading badly: the decay comes from the size of the context, not from the depth of the analysis.

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat the criteria guide at the end of every turn, so it stays close to the text being graded.
options.feedback: Repeating the guide brings it closer to the end of the context, but it also fattens every turn and accelerates the very growth causing the decay.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a bigger window is no substitute for curating the context: as the token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, so what goes into the context matters as much as how much room is left. The shape of the symptom confirms it. The first pieces of feedback come out well and the last ones do not, which is the signature of a context loaded with work unrelated to the task at hand. Since each submission is independent of the others, the right move is to give each one a clean context with the guide as its only prefix. The distinction against changing model or raising effort is that neither touches the cause: the assistant would still be reading thirty-four pieces of feedback it does not need.

RULE: An independent task deserves a clean context: if quality falls toward the end of the session, you have too much accumulated, not too little window.

TRAP: Treating long-context degradation as a lack of room and buying a bigger window to keep accumulating the same thing.

TRY IT: Grade ten already-assessed submissions twice, once in a conversation shared with thirty others and once in a clean conversation, and compare how many criteria from the guide are actually applied in each case.

questions.question: The clinical note summaries at Red Vicuña Salud are generated during the consultation, and the doctor needs one before closing it. The complaints say the summary arrives late. A week of measurement shows the first word appearing at 0.8 seconds and the full summary, around 900 tokens, finishing at 14 seconds; the prefix with the clinical protocol already reads from cache and there are no overload errors. The per-clinic budget is closed for the year. Where is the problem, and what corrects it?

options.label: A
options.text: In the perceived wait: turn on streaming so the doctor sees the summary while it is being generated.
options.feedback: Streaming improves the perceived response and pulls the first word forward, which here already arrives at 0.8 seconds, and it does not shorten total generation time.

options.label: B
options.text: In the contracted capacity: move the traffic to a priority service tier so that the consultations stop competing.
options.feedback: The priority tier reduces overload errors at the peaks, and the measurement says there are none; it does not speed up writing the answer either.

options.label: C
options.text: In the output volume: ask for the summary with a sentence limit per section and lower the effort level.
options.feedback: Correct: with a fast first word and a slow finish, what rules is how many tokens have to be generated; less output and less reasoning shorten the total.

options.label: D
options.text: In the prefix: add a second cache breakpoint so that the entire clinical protocol reads from cache.
options.feedback: Caching lowers cost and pulls the first word forward, but the prefix already reads from cache and the time is going into generating the output.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to separate two measurements: time to the first word and total generation time. If the first word arrives fast and the ending arrives late, the bottleneck is how many tokens have to be generated, not the queue and not the prefix. So the lever is to shorten the output and lower the effort level, and the limit is better asked for in sentences or paragraphs than in number of words, because the model counts tokens and not words. The distinction against streaming is that streaming improves the perceived response and pulls the first word forward, which here is already good, without reducing the total work; and a priority tier addresses overload, which the measurement rules out.

RULE: Separate time to first word from total time: if the first is good and the second is not, the problem is how much you write.

TRAP: Treating streaming as a real latency reduction, when all it changes is when the user starts seeing the answer.

TRY IT: Measure time to the first word and to the last across twenty requests, then repeat the measurement asking for a limit of two sentences per section: the difference tells you how much of the latency is output.

The distinction against streaming is that streaming improves the perceived response and pulls the first word forward, which here is already good, without reducing the total work; and a priority tier addresses overload, which the measurement rules out.

RULE: Separate time to first word from total time: if the first is good and the second is not, the problem is how much you write.

TRAP: Treating streaming as a real latency reduction, when all it changes is when the user starts seeing the answer.

TRY IT: Measure time to the first word and to the last across twenty requests, then repeat the measurement asking for a limit of two sentences per section: the difference tells you how much of the latency is output.

questions.question: The internal AndesWare agent that modernizes legacy modules ends 18 percent of its runs with stop_reason max_tokens and leaves the work half done; the configuration pins max_tokens 16384 and leaves effort at its default value. The platform team proposes moving the agent to a more capable model to solve it, with cost per squad under monthly control. What should you do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the agent to the most capable model in the family, which finishes long tasks with fewer attempts and fewer rewrites.
options.feedback: A more capable model does solve more tasks, but the cutoff you are seeing comes from a ceiling in your own request, which would stay just as low.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise max_tokens to a value with room for agentic work and measure again before touching the model.
options.feedback: Correct: a cutoff at max_tokens is fixed by raising that ceiling, and giving it room does not make the solved task more expensive, because only what is needed is consumed.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower the effort so that the agent writes less and finishes inside the current request limit.
options.feedback: Less effort is cheaper and faster, but here it would trim the reasoning to fit an arbitrary ceiling instead of correcting it.

options.label: D
options.text: Split each module into smaller tasks so that no run reaches the limit of the request.
options.feedback: Decomposition helps when the work exceeds the context window, not when what is missing is permission for a longer answer.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that max_tokens is a hard ceiling on a single response and the model does not see it, so lowering it does not make the model economize, and leaving it short only truncates work you already paid for. When runs end with that stop_reason, the documented move is to raise the ceiling to a value with room for agentic work and measure again. Cost per solved task does not rise from giving it room, because only what the task needs is consumed. The distinction against changing models is that the symptom points to a configuration limit rather than a capability gap, and moving the model before measuring mixes two variables into one decision.

RULE: A cutoff at max_tokens is your own ceiling, not a limit of the model: raise it and measure again before changing family.

TRAP: Reading a truncated response as a sign that the model is not good enough for the task you gave it.

TRY IT: Count what percentage of your runs end with stop_reason max_tokens, raise the ceiling and repeat the measurement over the same tasks, comparing cost per solved task.

questions.question: Mistral Retail is about to rebuild its after-sales agent, which handles questions on order status, exchanges, returns and warranties for 220 stores and the digital channel. The team has two weeks before the campaign and no evaluated case yet. Camila wants to add layers only when each one proves that it is needed, and she wants the evaluation to be what decides when to take the next step. In what order should she build?

options.label: A
options.text: Add an intent classifier that routes each query → optimize the prompt of each branch → add the tools of each branch → measure with real cases at the end
options.feedback: Routing first locks in a category split nobody has validated yet, and it leaves the measurement for a point where several layers exist and you cannot tell which one contributed what.

options.label: B
options.text: Optimize the prompt and evaluate it with real cases → give the assistant the tools to look up the order → add an intent classifier → consider an agent
options.feedback: Correct: this is the documented ladder, which starts by optimizing the prompt with evaluation, then adds tools, and separates the routing only when the tasks are highly varied.

options.label: C
options.text: Give the assistant tools → launch subagents per query category → optimize the prompts of each subagent → evaluate with real cases at the close
options.feedback: The subagents show up far too early: a single well-equipped agent solves considerably more than people tend to expect, and each extra agent adds coordination and cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Build the autonomous agent with every tool → measure it in production → trim the tools according to real usage → write the final prompts
options.feedback: Measuring in production with the most complex design is the most expensive way to learn: the errors compound and no simple baseline is left to compare against.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to start with simple prompts, optimize them with thorough evaluation and add multi-step agentic systems only when the simple version falls short. The documented ladder for a support assistant is exactly that: first the prompt with its evaluation, then the tools that give it access to order status, and only if the assistant covers highly varied tasks does it pay to separate an intent classifier that routes the initial query. The agent comes last, for when the path cannot be fixed. The distinction against starting from the routing is that every layer added before measuring makes it impossible to attribute the improvement, and with a two-week deadline that is paid for in blind decisions.

RULE: Prompt and evaluation first, tools next, routing when the categories diverge, and an agent only if the path cannot be fixed.

TRAP: Starting from the routing or from the subagents and leaving the evaluation for the end, when it can no longer tell which layer produced the improvement.

TRY IT: Run your twenty most frequent after-sales queries with prompt only and count how many it resolves well; with that number decide whether the next layer is tools or routing, and measure again after adding it.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/customer-support-chat

questions.question: Banco Altamar enabled the digital banking assistant for its 8 million customers, and the product team considers the project finished. Internal audit will not let it close until the plan for keeping the system running over the coming years is written down. The assistant depends on an external identity verification service and on the core banking system, and an outage in either one leaves customer queries unanswered in the middle of business hours. Ignacio, the platform architect, has one week to complete the operations plan. Which TWO elements does that plan need? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: A recurring review of the assistant's behavior, at a stated frequency and with one named person responsible for running it.
options.feedback: Correct: the operations stage requires the review to be planned, with a defined cadence and clear ownership; with no owner and no frequency, the review never happens.

options.label: B
options.text: A documented contingency procedure for a failure of the external verification service, naming the degraded mode that takes over.
options.feedback: Correct: when the system depends on a critical third party, the plan has to cover the procedure for its failure, and that procedure is written before anyone needs it.

options.label: C
options.text: A monthly maintenance window to retrain the model on the previous month's conversations and recover accuracy.
options.feedback: Retraining sounds like maintenance, but there is no in-house model to retrain here: what gets tuned is the prompt, the retrieval and the tools, and none of that needs a fixed monthly window.

options.label: D
options.text: An expanded evaluation set, extended until it scores 100% before any later change to the system is authorized.
options.feedback: Expanding the evaluation is healthy, but demanding 100% turns it into paperwork: when a set stops discriminating you refresh it with real failures rather than chase the score.

options.label: E
options.text: A criterion for declaring an incident that waits for the business area to confirm before the technical team is called in.
options.feedback: Waiting for business confirmation delays the response: a problem visible to the customer, or unresolved after an hour of analysis, already justifies declaring the incident.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the operations stage is designed with the same seriousness as development: it has to be written down who reviews the system, how often, and what happens when something outside your control fails. A recurring review with a defined frequency and a named owner is what turns monitoring into practice. The contingency procedure covers the risk a third-party dependency introduces into a critical system. The two measures are independent: one watches your own behavior and the other prepares for someone else's failure. The distinction against expanding the evaluation set is that the set measures today's version, while what is missing here is the plan that sustains the system once the project closes.

RULE: A system enters operation with two things written down: who reviews it and how often, and what happens when something you do not control fails.

TRAP: Confusing closing the project with delivering the system, so with no review cadence and no contingency plan the operation falls to whoever complains first.

TRY IT: Take one of your own systems in production and write two lines: who reviews its behavior and how often, and what happens if its most critical external dependency goes down; the line you cannot fill is what you are missing.

SOURCE: https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/govern/ https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/

questions.question: The assistant used by Pehuén Energía's distribution crews aggregates three internal MCP servers and exposes 68 tools. A month ago Camila turned on tool search with defer_loading, and startup context dropped from 46,000 to 6,000 tokens. Since then the regulator has found a gap: the lockout and tagout check, mandatory on 100% of operations, shows up in one session out of five. In the traces, the tool that performs it is called consultar_estado, its description reads "Checks the status of an element", search never returns it among its results, and its definition never reaches the context. The other tools on that same server are used normally. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Tool search matches only against tool names and descriptions, and this one's are generic, so it never gets surfaced.
options.feedback: Correct: with deferral the tool exists, but it enters the context only if search finds it, and that search runs over the name and the description. A vague name covers far fewer ways of asking for the check than a specific one.

options.label: B
options.text: The catalog passed the 30 to 50 tool threshold where selection degrades, so the tools should be split across agents by trade.
options.feedback: That threshold is real, but it describes the model choosing badly among tools it can already see. Here the definition never loads, and with deferral only what search returns reaches the context.

options.label: C
options.text: The MCP server exposing that tool goes past the default 30 second connection limit, so its catalog misses most sessions.
options.feedback: The connection timeout exists and does leave slow servers out, but then every tool on that server would drop. The rest are still being used without trouble.

options.label: D
options.text: Results from the other tools fill the window, and context cleanup deletes the deferred definitions before the agent uses them.
options.feedback: Context cleanup acts on tool results, not on definitions, and it targets result bloat. The symptom here happens earlier, when search does not even propose the tool.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that progressive disclosure moves the cost of context, but it works only if what you defer can be found: search matches the request against tool names and descriptions, not against code or usage history. A name like consultar_estado and a five-word description cover very few ways of asking for the check, so the tool sits installed, deferred and invisible. The fix is to rename and redescribe it in the words the crews use, not to trim the catalog or split the agent. The distinction against the 30 to 50 tool threshold is that the threshold describes a wrong choice among visible tools, while here the definition never enters the context.

RULE: What you defer exists only if it can be found: name and describe every tool with the words people will use to ask for it.

TRAP: Assuming that turning deferral on is enough, when what decides whether a deferred tool loads is the quality of its name and its description.

TRY IT: Take the five least used tools in your agent, write down how a real person would ask for each one, and check whether those words appear in the name or the description. Rewrite the ones that do not, then measure again how often they load.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/tool-search https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool

questions.question: Yaguareté Logística classifies goods for 12,000 shipments a day. The prompt sends the instructions and three labeled examples first, then the query, and the shipment documentation last. That documentation runs about 30,000 tokens and is different for every shipment. Ximena, the solutions architect, proposes reordering the prompt so the documentation sits at the very top and the query goes last, with nothing else changed. The quarterly token budget is already committed and allows no additional spend. What effect does that reordering have?

options.label: A
options.text: The prompt starts hitting the cache, because the largest block now sits at the start of the prefix and stops being reprocessed on every shipment.
options.feedback: Caching requires the prefix to repeat byte for byte across requests. The documentation changes with every shipment, so placing it first creates nothing reusable.

options.label: B
options.text: Latency per shipment drops noticeably, because the model processes less context before it reaches the query it has to answer.
options.feedback: Reordering removes no tokens: exactly the same content is sent and processed, only in a different order.

options.label: C
options.text: The classifications stop citing tariff codes that are absent from the shipment, because the model reads the source text before the instruction.
options.feedback: Placement helps attention, but the documented answer to unsupported claims is to extract the verbatim quotes first and check every claim against them.

options.label: D
options.text: Classification quality improves with no change in spend, because with long inputs the documentation goes on top and the query goes last.
options.feedback: Correct: the guidance for long inputs is to place the long material above the query, the examples and the instructions, and the number of tokens sent does not change.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for inputs over twenty thousand tokens is to put the long material first and the query last, because that placement measurably improves the response across current models. The change is one of order, not of volume: the same tokens are sent, so there is no saving and no extra cost, and the committed budget still covers the quarter. The distinction against the most tempting alternative is that caching rewards repetition, not position. It only hits if that block is identical across requests, and the shipment documentation changes with every dispatch.

RULE: With long inputs, the document goes on top and the question goes last: order moves quality, not the bill.

TRAP: Confusing moving a large block to the front with making it cacheable, when the cache rewards repetition rather than position.

TRY IT: Take ten real shipments, run the same prompt with the documentation last and with the documentation on top, compare the hits, and confirm in usage that total input did not change between the two versions.

questions.question: Pampero Agro wants an assistant for the technical advisers who work in areas without stable coverage and who write each field-visit report by hand today. Management set two conditions: the assistant has to be in production before the sowing campaign, ten weeks away, and the cost per report cannot exceed what the adviser's time costs today. Malena, the solutions architect, has the business problem stated and nothing else. In what order should she proceed?

options.label: A
options.text: Define the ideal interaction and the tasks the assistant covers → write measurable success criteria with their evaluation → choose the model and build the prompt → add tools and deploy.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented order starts from the scope and the ideal interaction, breaks out the tasks, fixes success criteria with their evaluation, and only then picks the model, because the model is chosen against a criterion.

options.label: B
options.text: Choose the model that fits the cost per report → build the prompt on that model → measure the results with the advisers → define the success criteria from what was measured.
options.feedback: Choosing the model first looks prudent under a cost ceiling, but with no measurable criterion you cannot tell whether the cheap model is enough or the capable one is overkill.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a prototype with the tools at hand → show it to the advisers of two regions → collect their comments → derive the success criteria and the scope from those.
options.feedback: An early prototype helps uncover the scope, but criteria written after the build end up measuring exactly what the prototype already does.

options.label: D
options.text: Integrate the sensor feeds and the field reports first → deploy retrieval over them → add the model on top → define at the end how the result is measured.
options.feedback: Data integration is real work and often the biggest blocker, but leaving how the result is measured until last leaves the project with no way to show that it works.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the build order runs from the business problem to the system and not the other way around: define the scope and the ideal interaction, break out the tasks the system has to cover, fix measurable success criteria with their evaluation, and only then choose the model, build the prompt, add tools and deploy. What separates the options is that the success criteria come before the model choice, because the model is selected on the balance of cost, accuracy and response time those criteria demand. The distinction against starting from the model or from a prototype is that both fix the system before anyone knows what will be asked of it, and ten weeks leaves no room to redo it.

RULE: First what it has to achieve and how that is measured; the model is chosen against that criterion, never before it is written down.

TRAP: Assuming a cost ceiling forces the model choice to come first, when without a measurable criterion there is no way to know whether that model is enough.

TRY IT: Take a project of yours in flight and write its success criteria with a number and a threshold before you look at which model it uses; if you cannot write them, you do not yet know which model you need.

questions.question: A shipping line wants to add a penalty for document validation errors to its contract with Terminal Puerto Claro. Renata's team measures 96% accuracy today on a set of 300 cases prepared during development, and the commercial area proposes committing to that 96% with a monthly penalty. options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Commit to 90% to leave some headroom and keep measuring with the same case set prepared during the development.

options.label: C
options.text: Postpone any number until a full year of traffic accumulates and describe the expected quality qualitatively meanwhile.
options.feedback: Waiting is prudent and avoids overpromising, but a contract with no measurable indicator protects neither of the two parties.

options.label: D
options.text: Define the indicator over real traffic, measure it for a few weeks and set the internal target before discussing the commitment.
options.feedback: Correct: a contractual commitment rests on an indicator defined over the service the customer receives and measured continuously, and the internal target is set on it before any penalty appears.

So the order is to define the indicator over production, measure it, set the internal target, and only then discuss which part of that becomes a commitment with consequences. The distinction against committing to the 96% is that the number describes a fixed set of 300 cases, not a service.

TRAP: Treating the result of an evaluation set as if it were a measurement of the service, and carrying it straight into a clause with a penalty.

TRY IT: Take the quality metric you report externally today and answer two questions: what traffic is it computed over, and how often is it refreshed; if the answer is a fixed set of cases, you do not have a service level indicator yet.

questions.question: At Banco Altamar, credit document extraction runs through an orchestrator that splits each file among four subagents: income, collateral, outstanding debt and corporate records. Each one returns its summary to the orchestrator, which assembles the report. Since volume rose to 1,200 files a day, audit has found a pattern: when the collateral subagent finds a related company that changes how the debt should be read, the report mentions it in one section and ignores it in the other, and the analyst has to redo the file. Latency and cost are within forecast. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The subagents share one system prompt and compete for the same sources, which duplicates reads and produces different versions of the same fact.
options.feedback: Duplication from vague briefs is a real failure of multi-agent systems, but each subagent here has its own assigned domain, and the symptom is not repeated work: it is information that never crosses.

options.label: B
options.text: A finding that changes another subagent's work can only get there through the orchestrator, and the subagents do not talk to each other.
options.feedback: Correct: in an orchestrator and subagents design all the information passes through the center, the subagents do not speak to one another, and whatever the orchestrator does not relay never reaches the rest.

options.label: C
options.text: The daily volume exceeds the limit on subagents running at the same time, and some runs return partial results with no warning.
options.feedback: A concurrency limit does exist, but it shows up as runs that never start and say so in their result; here all four subagents deliver their part and the problem appears when those parts are combined.

options.label: D
options.text: Each subagent starts with an empty context, so none of them knows the credit policies and each one ends up applying its own judgment.
options.feedback: It is true that a subagent starts without the orchestrator's conversation, but the policies travel in its brief; that would explain inconsistent judgment, not a fact present in one section and absent from the other.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that in the orchestrator and subagents pattern the orchestrator is the only channel: it plans, delegates bounded subtasks and synthesizes, which is what makes it an information bottleneck. Subagents report to the orchestrator and cannot talk to each other, so a finding from the collateral subagent that changes how the debt reads only reaches the debt subagent if the orchestrator relays it, and by then the work has already been handed out. The symptom fits: each part is correct on its own and the report contradicts itself once they are combined. The distinction against the empty-context explanation is that inconsistent judgment would show from the start, whereas here the fact exists and does not travel.

RULE: With an orchestrator at the center, what one subagent finds reaches another only if the orchestrator carries it: design that handoff or accept the bottleneck.

TRAP: Assuming that several specialized subagents share what they find, when each one only returns its own summary to the orchestrator.

TRY IT: Take one multi-agent run of your own and mark a finding from one subagent that should have changed another's work; check whether the orchestrator forwarded it or whether it died inside that summary.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/multi-agent-coordination-patterns https://claude.com/blog/subagents-in-claude-code

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros compares two versions of the claims triage prompt before promoting one. The run report says: cases 14, runs per case 1, threshold 0.80, variant A score 0.83, variant B score 0.88, a single llm grader over the full report of each claim with the rubric "Is the report useful? Yes/No". Renata wants to promote variant B this week, and the committee that audits changes meets only once a month. Which two design flaws prevent the conclusion that B is better than A? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The threshold of 0.80 is low for a system the regulator audits, and it lets variants below the required quality through.
options.feedback: Raising the bar is reasonable as a promotion policy, but a higher threshold does not make two unstable measurements comparable.

options.label: B
options.text: Each case ran only once, and one run of a non-deterministic system does not separate a real improvement from run-to-run noise.
options.feedback: Correct: a single run says little about a non-deterministic agent, and the documented practice is to run each case several times before trusting a difference.

options.label: C
options.text: The llm grader should be the same model that writes the report, so that it judges by the criteria the report was written with.
options.feedback: It is the other way around: the official examples recommend grading with a model different from the one that produced the output under evaluation.

options.label: D
options.text: The only grader is an llm that reads the whole report, and its verdict varies more the longer the text it has to read.
options.feedback: Correct: long artifacts are graded with deterministic graders over their content, and llm graders are reserved for short outputs.

options.label: E
options.text: The set has no edge cases: fourteen claims do not cover ambiguous inputs or incomplete documentation from the policyholder.
options.feedback: Edge case coverage decides whether the result generalizes, but it is not what invalidates the comparison: with one run and an unstable judge, not even the fourteen current cases can be compared.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a comparison between variants only holds if the measurement is stable. The system under evaluation and the grader that scores it are both non-deterministic, so the gap between 0.83 and 0.88 may be entirely noise. Running each case several times reduces the variance of the system under evaluation. Grading the long report with a deterministic grader over its content removes the variance of the judge, which grows precisely with the length of the text. These are two different sources of noise and both have to be attacked. The distinction against raising the threshold is that a threshold filters results but does not improve the quality of the measurement that produces them.

RULE: Before you trust a difference, make it repeatable: several runs per case, and deterministic graders over the long texts.

TRAP: Treating the gap between two single-run scores as an improvement, when the noise of the system and of the judge is larger than that gap.

TRY IT: Run your most representative case three times with the same prompt and nothing changed, and note the three scores: if the spread between runs exceeds the difference you want to attribute to your change, you have not measured anything yet.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: AndesWare keeps the shared skills of its payments platform in a separate repository that each squad clones next to the monorepo, and the client audit requires a single versioned copy of those skills. Bruno, on the platform team, delivered them to the 120 developers of the payments squad with this line in the project's ".claude/settings.json": {"permissions": {"additionalDirectories": ["../plataforma-comun"]}}. Since then Claude reads and edits the files in that directory without trouble. But "/skills" lists none of the ones that live in "../plataforma-comun/.claude/skills/revision-pagos/SKILL.md", and "/context" does not show them either. What explains the symptom, and what fixes the delivery?

options.label: A
options.text: The relative path resolves against the directory the session was opened from, so it has to be written as an absolute path under that same key.
options.feedback: Relative paths are a frequent cause of load failures, especially with MCP servers, but here Claude already reads and edits that directory: the path resolves fine.

options.label: B
options.text: Skills from another repository only reach a team packaged as a plugin in the internal marketplace, so they have to be published there first.
options.feedback: A plugin is the documented way to hand skills to a whole organization, but it does not explain the symptom and it forces you to repackage something already at hand.

options.label: C
options.text: The SKILL.md file is missing inside each skill folder, so the loose files left at the root have to be reorganized into folders.
options.feedback: A skill stored as a loose file instead of a folder with its SKILL.md never shows up, but the path in the question already ends in SKILL.md.

options.label: D
options.text: The "additionalDirectories" key only grants access to files, so the session has to be opened with "--add-dir", which does load the skills.
options.feedback: Correct: the settings key grants access and nothing else, while "--add-dir" and "/add-dir" also load the skills, commands and agents of the added directory.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that granting access to a directory and loading the configuration that lives in it are two different things. The "permissions.additionalDirectories" key grants access to files and nothing more: it never loads the CLAUDE.md, the rules or the skills of the added directory. The "--add-dir" flag and the "/add-dir" command do load ".claude/skills", ".claude/commands" and ".claude/agents" from that directory, and the CLAUDE.md only through the environment variable meant for it. So the symptom is exactly what you should expect: the files are read, and the skills do not exist for the session. The distinction against packaging a plugin is that a plugin solves distribution across the whole organization, which is not what is broken here.

RULE: Granting access to a directory is not loading its configuration: "additionalDirectories" opens the files, and "--add-dir" also brings skills, commands and agents.

TRAP: Assuming the two ways of adding a directory are equivalent, when one grants access and the other also loads what sits in its ".claude".

TRY IT: Add a directory that holds a skill through "permissions.additionalDirectories", open the session and run "/skills" and "/context"; then open another with "--add-dir" on the same directory and compare the two lists.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases

questions.question: Siete Lagos Viajes builds corporate itineraries with an assistant that queries four wholesale suppliers. Last quarter, 6 of every 10 itineraries rejected by clients were rejected because the assistant offered fares or availability the wholesaler had already changed; the rest split between wording errors and traveler preferences. The investment committee has budget for a single front this quarter and wants rejections cut in half before the high season. Where should that money go?

options.label: A
options.text: Into the most capable model of the family for the whole flow, so that the assistant reasons better about the options it assembles.
options.feedback: Moving up a model improves the reasoning, but no model can infer a fare that changed in the wholesaler's system after the last synchronization.

options.label: B
options.text: Into the integration with the wholesalers, so that fares and availability are queried at the moment the itinerary is assembled.
options.feedback: Correct: the measured failure is in the data and not in the reasoning, and the most frequent brakes on these deployments are integration with existing systems and access to current data.

options.label: C
options.text: Into a second agent that reviews each finished itinerary and flags the inconsistencies before it goes out to the client.
options.feedback: A reviewer catches internal inconsistencies, but it has nothing to compare against: querying the same stale copy, it will confirm the error rather than find it.

options.label: D
options.text: Into extending the prompt with the commercial rules of the four wholesalers and with examples of well-built itineraries.
options.feedback: More context helps with the wording and with the commercial rules, which explain the minority of the rejections; availability changes by the hour and does not fit in a prompt.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that investment goes to the measured cause and not to the most visible piece of the architecture. Six of every ten rejections here come from data that had already changed in the wholesaler's system, so the front that moves the needle is the integration: query fares and availability at the moment the itinerary is assembled. The obstacles that slow these deployments most inside organizations are exactly integration with existing systems and the quality of data access, ahead of model capability. The distinction against moving up a model or adding a reviewer is that both operate on the same stale data and cannot correct what the source no longer says.

RULE: Invest where the cause was measured: when the error comes from the data, no change of model repairs it.

TRAP: Treating a problem of integration and data freshness as if it were a problem of model capability.

TRY IT: Classify the last fifty errors of your system by cause: stale data, retrieval, prompt or criteria; the largest category tells you where the quarter's budget goes.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/how-enterprises-are-building-ai-agents-in-2026 https://claude.com/blog/driving-ai-transformation-with-claude

questions.question: Agencia Nacional de Ingresos runs inconsistency detection overnight across 40,000 filings and needs the results by seven in the morning; nobody is waiting at a screen. Each filing goes out with this configuration: {"thinking": {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 48000}, "max_tokens": 64000, "stream": false}. Extended reasoning is what holds up the quality of the finding, because every inconsistency is later justified to the taxpayer. Since the budget was raised, one request in five ends in a timeout or a closed connection, and monthly spend has landed 30% above the approved budget. What should be done with this workload?

options.label: A
options.text: Send it through the Message Batches API, the indicated path for thinking budgets above 32,000 tokens, billed at 50%.
options.feedback: Correct: the documentation sends any thinking above 32,000 tokens to batch, precisely because those long requests collide with timeouts and open connection limits, and the overnight window makes the asynchrony free.

options.label: B
options.text: Turn on streaming for every request, which is what avoids HTTP timeouts when max_tokens is large, and keep running synchronously.
options.feedback: Streaming does avoid the connection drop when max_tokens is large, but it leaves 40,000 long synchronous requests running all night and moves the cost not one point.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower budget_tokens to the 1,024 token minimum so each request finishes fast and monthly spend comes back within budget.
options.feedback: Cutting the budget fixes time and cost, but it sacrifices the reasoning that supports the justification of each finding, which is a requirement of the process.

options.label: D
options.text: Split each filing across several subagents in parallel so none of them piles up such long reasoning or exhausts its connection.
options.feedback: Parallel delegation shortens wall clock time when there are independent parts, but it multiplies tokens by 3 to 10 times, and the analysis of one filing does not split into branches.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to pick the lever that matches the stated constraint: if the results are not needed until the next morning, asynchrony costs nothing and the 50% batch discount is real money. There is also an explicit instruction for this case: above 32,000 tokens of thinking budget, process in batches, because the requests get long and collide with timeouts and open connection limits, which is exactly the symptom measured. Batch supports extended thinking and prompt caching, so no depth of analysis is lost. The distinction against streaming is that streaming avoids the connection drop but keeps the workload synchronous and never touches the cost.

RULE: If nobody is waiting for the answer, process in batches: the asynchrony is free, the discount is not, and very long thinking belongs in batch.

TRAP: Treating a dropped connection as a transport problem and answering with streaming, when the whole workload never needed to be synchronous.

TRY IT: Take a hundred filings from your overnight run, send them through the Message Batches API with the same thinking budget, and compare two numbers against today's synchronous run: total run time and billed cost.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing

options.label: A
options.text: The two variants are equivalent in quality, so the right move is to keep the cheaper of the two and close the decision this month.
options.feedback: Tying at the top of the scale is not tying in quality: it means the test no longer discriminates, not that the variants are the same.

options.label: B
options.text: The suite is saturated: at 1.00 it only warns about regressions on what it already covers and leaves no room to show an improvement.
options.feedback: Correct: an evaluation at its ceiling works as a regression alarm but gives no signal of improvement, and the documented answer is to build new and harder cases.

options.label: C
options.text: The number of runs per case is insufficient, and the differences between the two variants get lost when the results are averaged together.
options.feedback: Repeating runs reduces noise, but with the 120 cases at the maximum there is nothing to average: no run can raise the score.

options.label: D
options.text: The automated grader is too strict and rejects correct summaries that are simply written in a different format.
options.feedback: A strict grader pushes scores down and produces false negatives; here the opposite happens, everything passes.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an evaluation sitting at the top of its scale is saturated: it still works as a regression alarm, but it stops giving any signal for improvement, because no variant can beat the ceiling. The practical consequence is that two very different prompts tie and the suite cannot arbitrate. What the documentation prescribes at that point is to build new and harder tasks drawn from the failures actually reported, and to keep the old suite only as a tripwire. The distinction against reading the tie as equivalence is that the tie is produced by the instrument, not by the system under evaluation: the omitted history the committee sees is exactly the material for the cases that are missing.

RULE: A suite at its ceiling is a regression detector, not a compass: to choose between two improvements you need cases that can still fail.

TRAP: Reading a tie at the top of the scale as a tie in quality, when what has been exhausted is the power of the test to discriminate.

TRY IT: Take the last three real complaints your suite would not have caught, turn them into new cases, and run the two variants again: if they separate now, what you had was saturated.

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación runs the automated tutor of twelve faculties on a single service, with one credential toward the API. The contract with each faculty requires reporting its consumption separately, but the trace panel shows only the service name. On top of that, short single-question queries leave no trace at all, while long study sessions show up complete. Nicolás, the platform SRE, has to explain both things before the month closes. What are the two causes? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The identity attributes describe the credential of the calling service, not the tenant on whose behalf the agent acted in that run.
options.feedback: Correct: the default identity is the one of the service, and attributing by faculty requires injecting the tenant or end-user identifier into every call.

options.label: B
options.text: The per-user analytics API returns the detail in real time, and the panel is not querying it to complete the breakdown by faculty.
options.feedback: That API delivers metrics aggregated by day with up to an hour of delay, and it describes development activity, not the consumption of a tutor per faculty.

options.label: C
options.text: Content logging is off, and without the text of the prompts there is no way to attribute consumption to any of the faculties.
options.feedback: Attribution comes from resource attributes, not from content; logging prompts would add data risk without solving anything, which is why it ships disabled by default.

options.label: D
options.text: The usage and cost API cannot separate spend by credential or by workspace, so consumption per faculty is not observable.
options.feedback: It does group by API key, workspace and model, and it is the authoritative billing source; what it does not do is distinguish students inside one shared service.

options.label: E
options.text: Short runs finish before the export interval, and the final flush is bounded by a timeout, so their spans are lost.
options.feedback: Correct: with short runs you have to lower the export interval, and the exporter diagnostic shows whether telemetry is being dropped silently.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that default telemetry describes structure and not people: it records durations, model and tool names, and the identity of the credential making the call. That is why a service shared by twelve faculties always appears under the same name, and attribution per tenant is achieved by injecting that identifier into every run. The second symptom is about delivery, not content: exporters buffer and send in batches, and the flush on exit is bounded, so a run shorter than the interval is lost whole. The distinction against reconciling with the usage and cost API is that this source is authoritative for the bill and groups by key and workspace, but it does not identify the end user inside a shared service and does not recover traces that were never sent.

RULE: Telemetry identifies the caller, not the requester: if you need attribution per tenant, inject that identity into every run.

TRAP: Assuming that whoever appears in the trace is the end user, when what gets recorded by default is the credential of the service.

TRY IT: Run a single-turn query and a long session with the exporter diagnostic on and compare what reaches the collector; then add a tenant attribute to one call and check that it shows up in the span.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/observability https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/usage-cost-api

questions.question: Bastión Legal runs two products on the same engine. One answers case-law questions for the lawyers in its corporate clients' legal departments. The other is a portal opening in six weeks where people describe their employment situation and receive guidance written by the model. The commercial contract requires compliance with Anthropic's Usage Policy, and the risk committee will not clear a launch with any requirement missing. Ximena, who leads compliance, has to settle what applies to each product. What should she establish?

options.label: A
options.text: Both requirements on both products, because the engine is the same and the policy applies to the system rather than to whoever finally receives the output.
options.feedback: Applying everything to everything looks prudent, but the policy scoped these high-risk requirements to consumer-facing output and left business-to-business interactions outside them.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither one, because the party under contract is always a company and logging every query handled is enough for the firm's own audit.
options.feedback: It is true that a company signs the contract, but what sets the scope is who receives the output, and in the portal a person receives it.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the AI disclosure on both products, because professional review is already covered by the signature of the lawyer who answers to the client for the result.
options.feedback: The disclosure is mandatory in the portal, but it does not replace the review: the policy asks a qualified professional to review the content before it goes out, not afterward.

options.label: D
options.text: On the consumer portal, review by a qualified professional before release and an AI disclosure at the start of each session; the B2B tool triggers neither.
options.feedback: Correct: legal guidance sits among the high-risk cases, where the policy requires prior professional review and an AI disclosure, while business-to-business use falls outside that scope.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the scope of the Usage Policy's high-risk requirements is decided by who receives the output, not by the technology that produces it. When the system delivers advice, recommendations or subjective decisions that directly affect people, the policy requires a qualified professional to review the content before release and requires the use of AI to be disclosed at least at the start of each session. Legal interpretation and guidance is on that list, so the portal triggers it. The distinction against applying everything to both products is that those requirements were scoped to consumer-facing output and do not reach business-to-business interactions, where another professional receives the output.

RULE: High-risk requirements are triggered by who reads the output: if a person reads it, there is prior professional review and an AI disclosure at the start of the session.

TRAP: Treating the policy as if it applied to the engine, when what decides is whether the output goes to a consumer or to another business.

TRY IT: Take two flows from your product, write in one line who reads the output of each, and mark which one needs review by a qualified professional and a disclosure at the start of the session.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup https://www.anthropic.com/news/usage-policy-update

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom is putting its first-line technical support assistant into production for the customers on its 9 million lines. The contract with the corporate segment commits to a first response in under 5 seconds, and Sofía's team has to close the feedback loop before switching it on: today the architecture answers the query and stops, with no signal coming back. Which TWO elements close that loop with an objective signal? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: A judge based on another model that scores every answer inline before delivery and blocks the ones below the threshold.
options.feedback: A judge based on another model helps when no rule can decide, but it is the least robust verification method and it adds latency to a flow that promises to answer in under 5 seconds.

options.label: B
options.text: A quarterly satisfaction survey sent to the technical leads of the largest corporate accounts in the segment.
options.feedback: A quarterly survey adds context about the commercial relationship, but it arrives late and with far too few cases to decide what to fix in the assistant.

options.label: C
options.text: A dashboard with query volume per hour and response time, reviewed by the operations team every morning.
options.feedback: Volume and response time tell you the system is alive and whether you are meeting the contractual commitment, but not whether the query was resolved.

options.label: D
options.text: A record of whether the customer considered the query resolved, as a success signal measured on every interaction.
options.feedback: Correct: support is a good automation candidate precisely because success is measured by the resolution the user declares, and that signal arrives on every interaction.

options.label: E
options.text: The cases the assistant escalates to a person, added as new cases to the set used to evaluate the next version.
options.feedback: Correct: real failures are the best source of evaluation cases, and every escalation is a case where the assistant fell short; the set then grows with what actually fails.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an end-to-end architecture does not stop at the answer: it needs an objective return signal that feeds the next version. Recording whether the customer considered the query resolved supplies the per-interaction success signal, which is precisely what makes support a good case to automate; adding the escalations to the evaluation set supplies the hard cases the next version is measured on. The two measures are independent: one measures the outcome in production and the other improves the evaluation that precedes deployment. The distinction against the inline judge is that it adds latency to a flow committed to 5 seconds and is the least robust of the available verification methods.

RULE: Close the loop with two signals: the outcome declared by whoever uses the system, and real failures turned into evaluation cases.

TRAP: Confusing a volume and latency dashboard with a feedback loop: it tells you the system answers, not whether it resolved anything.

TRY IT: Look at your system in production and answer which success signal you record per interaction and where the last ten cases you added to your evaluation set came from.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents https://claude.com/blog/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk

questions.question: A platform team doubles the context it sends on every call of its agent, convinced that more context always improves the answer. What does Anthropic document about model behavior as the number of tokens in the window grows?

options.label: A
options.text: Accuracy holds steady up to the window limit and falls only when the input is truncated, so the extra context carries a financial cost and nothing else.
options.feedback: The cost does rise, but the documentation also describes a loss of accuracy in retrieving information well before any truncation.

options.label: B
options.text: The model prioritizes the relevant passages on its own, so the surplus context sits inert and changes neither the quality nor the cost of the answer.
options.feedback: The model attends to what is relevant better than a naive search does, but its attention budget is limited and the surplus material competes for it.

options.label: C
options.text: The degradation appears only when documents from different domains are mixed, and it is corrected by giving each source its own block in the prompt.
options.feedback: Ordering the sources helps readability, but the degradation described does not depend on mixing domains; it tracks the total number of tokens in the window.

options.label: D
options.text: As tokens in the window grow, the accuracy with which the model retrieves that information drops: context is finite and has diminishing returns.
options.feedback: Correct: the documentation calls this context rot and explains it by a limited attention budget and by pairwise relationships that grow with the square of the token count.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that context is managed as a scarce resource and not as a warehouse. The documentation describes context rot: the more tokens sit in the window, the lower the model's ability to retrieve accurately what is in there. The mechanism it cites is a limited attention budget, pairwise relationships between tokens that grow with the square of their number, and less model experience with dependencies that span the whole context. The calibrated phrasing to use with a stakeholder is that the model remains capable over long contexts but shows reduced accuracy at retrieving information and at reasoning over long distances.

RULE: Treat context as a finite resource with diminishing returns: every token you add competes for the same attention budget.

TRAP: Assuming that filling the window only costs money, when the volume itself degrades retrieval of what was already inside.

TRY IT: Take a question whose answer sits in one specific paragraph, run it with that paragraph alone and then with twenty documents around it, and compare whether the model still cites it correctly.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Minera Nevado is a subsidiary of a group headquartered in the European Union. Its operational safety assistant processes about 3,000 incident reports a month that name its own workers and contractor staff, and the classification it produces feeds the prioritization of investigations and the precautionary suspensions the site manager decides. The group committee will not clear the pilot if any GDPR requirement on that processing is missing. Andrés, who leads compliance, is assembling the file. What should it include?

options.label: A
options.text: A data protection impact assessment, because the processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights of the people involved.
options.feedback: Correct: Article 35 requires one when the processing is likely to result in a high risk to rights and freedoms, which is the case here given the volume, the profiling and the effect on employment.

options.label: B
options.text: A signed consent form from every worker before the pilot, because consent is the lawful basis GDPR requires by default in order to process personal data.
options.feedback: Consent is one of the six bases in Article 6, not the default basis, and in an employment relationship it is rarely considered freely given.

options.label: C
options.text: The processing contract with the vendor, because once a processor acts on the controller's behalf that instrument covers the assessment required.
options.feedback: That contract is needed whenever someone processes data on the controller's behalf, but the engagement triggers it and the risk does not, so it does not replace the assessment.

options.label: D
options.text: A short retention period agreed with the vendor, because limiting how long data is kept satisfies the regulation's data minimization principle.
options.feedback: Capping the period answers storage limitation, not minimization, and neither principle replaces a prior assessment when the risk is high.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that in GDPR each obligation has its own trigger. The Article 28(3) contract arises from the fact that someone processes data on the controller's behalf. The Article 35 impact assessment arises from the level of risk, and it is mandatory when the processing is likely to result in a high risk to people's rights and freedoms. Here there is sustained volume, profiling of identified individuals and a concrete effect on their employment, so the Article 35 trigger is active. The distinction against leaning on the vendor contract is that the contract is needed in any case, but it neither assesses nor documents the risk of the processing.

RULE: Every GDPR obligation has its own trigger: the processor contract comes from the engagement, the impact assessment comes from high risk.

TRAP: Treating the vendor contract as if it covered the risk assessment, when the two answer different triggers in the regulation.

TRY IT: Write on one page, for a processing activity of your own, who is controller, who is processor, which of the six Article 6 bases supports it, and whether the risk triggers the Article 35 assessment.

SOURCE: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32016R0679
