questions.question: The platform team at Banco Altamar published two plugins in its internal marketplace for the 260 developers of digital channels: one applies the bank's secure coding checklist and the other generates the change log internal audit asks for. Six weeks later, fewer than 15% of sessions load them, and audit demands evidence that the control ran in every affected repository. Nicolás wants adoption to stop depending on each person installing them by hand. Which two measures are documented to achieve that? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Publish a how-to on the bank's wiki and ask each tech lead to remind the team about the install in the daily standup.
options.feedback: Communication helps, but it leaves adoption resting on each person acting, and it produces no evidence at all that the plugin was active.

options.label: B
options.text: State in the root CLAUDE.md of each repository that the checklist is mandatory, so that the plugin is loaded when the session starts.
options.feedback: CLAUDE.md is instruction text for Claude, not an installation mechanism: it describes the convention, but it activates no extension.

options.label: C
options.text: Use "strictKnownMarketplaces" to block every marketplace except the internal one, so that no alternative to the bank's plugins remains.
options.feedback: The marketplace allowlist does keep unapproved sources out, but restricting the catalog installs nothing and activates nothing in any session.

options.label: D
options.text: Commit a ".claude/settings.json" in each repository with "extraKnownMarketplaces" and "enabledPlugins", so that whoever works there gets them enabled.
options.feedback: Correct: the repository settings file registers the marketplace and enables the team's plugin set for anyone who opens a session there.

options.label: E
options.text: Declare a "relevance" block in the marketplace entry and enable that marketplace in "pluginSuggestionMarketplaces" in the managed settings.
options.feedback: Correct: with relevance declared and the marketplace enabled in that list, Claude Code suggests the plugin when the context matches, and the person confirms the install.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that adoption ships by configuration and not by communication. A ".claude/settings.json" committed in the repository, with the marketplace in "extraKnownMarketplaces" and the plugins in "enabledPlugins", leaves the set active for anyone who works there, with no manual steps. The second lever is different and complementary: declare the relevance block with its topic and its signals in the marketplace entry, and enable that marketplace in "pluginSuggestionMarketplaces" in the managed settings, so that the suggestion appears in the right context. Declaring relevance on its own produces no suggestion until an administrator enables the marketplace, and Claude Code never installs on its own: the person always confirms. The distinction against blocking marketplaces is that restricting sources keeps out what is not approved, but it hands out nothing.

RULE: Ship the tool through repository configuration and add the contextual suggestion on top; a how-to on the wiki installs nothing.

TRAP: Confusing restricting the catalog with handing out the tool: blocking marketplaces leaves not one more plugin active.

TRY IT: Add a ".claude/settings.json" with "extraKnownMarketplaces" and "enabledPlugins" to a test repository, open the session from there, and confirm with "/plugin" that the set is active without installing anything by hand.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-relevance

html.question: The platform team at Banco Altamar published two plugins in its internal marketplace for the 260 developers of digital channels: one applies the bank's secure coding checklist and the other generates the change log internal audit asks for. Six weeks later, fewer than 15% of sessions load them, and audit demands evidence that the control ran in every affected repository. Nicolás wants adoption to stop depending on each person installing them by hand. Which two measures are documented to achieve that? (Select TWO)
options: Publish a how-to on the bank's wiki and ask each tech lead to remind the team about the install in the daily standup.
State in the root CLAUDE.md of each repository that the checklist is mandatory, so that the plugin is loaded when the session starts.
Use "strictKnownMarketplaces" to block every marketplace except the internal one, so that no alternative to the bank's plugins remains.
Commit a ".claude/settings.json" in each repository with "extraKnownMarketplaces" and "enabledPlugins", so that whoever works there gets them enabled.
Declare a "relevance" block in the marketplace entry and enable that marketplace in "pluginSuggestionMarketplaces" in the managed settings.
html.explanation:
The general rule is that adoption ships by configuration and not by communication. A ".claude/settings.json" committed in the repository, with the marketplace in "extraKnownMarketplaces" and the plugins in "enabledPlugins", leaves the set active for anyone who works there, with no manual steps. The second lever is different and complementary: declare the relevance block with its topic and its signals in the marketplace entry, and enable that marketplace in "pluginSuggestionMarketplaces" in the managed settings, so that the suggestion appears in the right context. Declaring relevance on its own produces no suggestion until an administrator enables the marketplace, and Claude Code never installs on its own: the person always confirms. The distinction against blocking marketplaces is that restricting sources keeps out what is not approved, but it hands out nothing.

RULE: Ship the tool through repository configuration and add the contextual suggestion on top; a how-to on the wiki installs nothing.

TRAP: Confusing restricting the catalog with handing out the tool: blocking marketplaces leaves not one more plugin active.

TRY IT: Add a ".claude/settings.json" with "extraKnownMarketplaces" and "enabledPlugins" to a test repository, open the session from there, and confirm with "/plugin" that the set is active without installing anything by hand.

questions.question: Mistral Retail freezes changes during the November campaign: the on-call team of the e-commerce channel is only allowed to run the smoke tests, which launch with "npm run smoke:checkout". Paula, on the platform team, shipped this policy in the managed settings of the 90 workstations: {"permissions": {"deny": ["Bash"], "allow": ["Bash(npm run smoke:*)", "Read(./src/**)"]}}. What will the on-call team find in the first session?

options.label: A
options.text: The most specific rule wins, so the smoke tests run without asking for confirmation and every other command stays blocked.
options.feedback: Rules are evaluated in the order deny, ask and allow, and specificity does not change that order: the first match, which here sits in deny, decides.

options.label: B
options.text: Claude will ask for confirmation before every Bash command, because a broad deny with a narrower allow resolves as an ask rule.
options.feedback: An ask category does exist, but it has to be written explicitly: combining a deny with an allow never produces an intermediate confirmation.

options.label: C
options.text: The lists in the managed settings merge, so it is enough for the team to add its own allow rule in the repository's ".claude/settings.json" file.
options.feedback: Permission lists do merge entries from every source, but that extends what is managed rather than subtracting from it: what one level denies, no other level allows.

options.label: D
options.text: Claude will not see the Bash tool at all: deny is evaluated first and, written as a bare name, it removes the tool from the session context.
options.feedback: Correct: besides losing the commands, a deny written with the bare tool name withdraws the tool from context, so the model does not even propose it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that permissions are evaluated in a fixed order: deny, then ask, then allow; the first match decides and specificity does not alter that order. The allow for the smoke test is never reached because the deny already matched, and what one level denies no other level can permit. There is also an effect that surprises people in the first session: a deny written as a bare tool name withdraws the tool from the model's context, while one scoped in parentheses leaves the tool available and blocks only what matches the pattern. For the smoke test to be permitted, the allow cannot have a deny sitting in front of it.

RULE: Deny, then ask, then allow: the first match decides, specificity does not change the order, and a deny with the bare tool name erases the tool from context.

TRAP: Assuming the most specific rule wins, as in a firewall, when the order is set by the type of rule and not by its precision.

TRY IT: Put a deny "Bash" next to an allow "Bash(npm run smoke:*)" in your settings, open the session, run "/permissions" to see the resolved rules, and then ask for a smoke test.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/admin-setup

questions.question: Bastión Legal bills by the hour, and its lawyers wait in front of the screen for each contract review opinion. The measurement for the week says: TTFT p95 0.8 s, total time p95 46 s, output_tokens average 3,400, cache_read_input_tokens 92% of input. Joaquín proposes turning on the fast service mode, which the model in use supports, without changing the prompt or the model. What should you expect from that change?

options.label: A
options.text: TTFT drops clearly and total time barely moves, because the lever acts on how the response starts.
options.feedback: It is the other way around: the documented benefit is in output tokens per second, not in the time to first token.

options.label: B
options.text: Total time drops and the cost per opinion holds, because the same model runs at the same rate as always.
options.feedback: The model and its behavior are the same, but fast mode is billed with a multiplier over the standard rates.

options.label: C
options.text: Total time drops because the output tokens per second rate rises, TTFT barely moves, and the price per opinion goes up.
options.feedback: Correct: fast mode is the same model with a faster inference configuration, with no change in intelligence, and its benefit concentrates in output tokens per second.

options.label: D
options.text: Total time drops and the cache keeps hitting as it does today, because neither the prefix nor the model changes when the mode is turned on.
options.feedback: Requests at different speeds do not share a cached prefix, so that 92% of reads is lost until the cache is rebuilt.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that each latency lever moves a different metric. Fast mode is the same model served with a faster inference configuration, and its benefit is in output tokens per second, while streaming improves perception and the time to first token. With a TTFT that is already healthy and responses of thousands of tokens, what hurts here is the generation rate, which is exactly what fast mode accelerates, in exchange for a price multiplier. The distinction that usually costs points is that changing speed splits the cache: requests at different speeds do not share a prefix, so a system that today reads 92% of its input from cache pays full writes while it warms the prefix again.

RULE: Fast mode buys output tokens per second, not a faster start: if the initial wait is what hurts, you are paying for the wrong lever.

TRAP: Treating fast mode as another model or as priority capacity, when it is the same model running faster, at a higher rate and with the cache split by speed.

TRY IT: Run the same opinion in standard mode and in fast mode, compare TTFT and total time, and look at the cache fields of the first request of each series to see what it costs to warm the prefix again.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency

questions.question: The assisted grading module at Grupo Aurora Educación has started answering questions about enrollment dates and tuition fees inside the feedback on an essay. Every request is built like this: {"system": "You are a helpful assistant.", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": ""}]}. The scope and tone rules live in an internal document that nobody injects into the request. With a very tight budget per student there is no room for an extra filtering call. What is wrong, and what should be changed?

options.label: A
options.text: The system prompt sets no role, no scope and no expected conduct for the situations that already recur; write them there with the answer.
options.feedback: Correct: the role belongs in the system prompt, where even one sentence changes behavior, and the documented technique is to anticipate the frequent situations with the expected answer for each one.

options.label: B
options.text: The essay arrives as user text; it should be delivered in a tool result block so that the model treats it with skepticism.
options.feedback: That move changes how instructions hidden in third-party text are handled, but it does not define what the assistant is allowed to answer and does not fix the scope.

options.label: C
options.text: The chosen model falls short of holding the scope; move up to the most capable model of the family and measure the off-topic response rate again.
options.feedback: Moving up a model is a real lever for capability problems, but here there is no defined scope for the model to respect, and the budget per student does not allow it.

options.label: D
options.text: The scope rules should be repeated at the end of every user turn, which is where the model reads them closest to its own answer.
options.feedback: Reminders in the user turn help reinforce something already defined, but resending them on every request costs tokens and still gives the assistant no identity.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the identity and the limits of the task live in the system prompt: that is where the model reads who it is and what it is supposed to do, and the documentation insists that even a single sentence of role changes behavior and tone. The second half of the technique is to prepare the model for predictable situations, giving it the list of frequent cases with the answer expected in each one, which is exactly what is missing when a grading module starts answering about tuition fees. The distinction against moving the essay into a tool result block is that this change protects against instructions hidden in third-party content, while the problem here is not the authority of the text but an undeclared scope.

RULE: The role and its limits go in the system prompt, and the situations you already know will happen go written down with the answer you expect.

TRAP: Assuming that an assistant with no declared role will infer the scope of the product from the content the user sends it.

TRY IT: Write in five lines the role, the two scope limits and the three frequent situations with their expected answer, put them in the system prompt, and run twenty real essays again counting how many pieces of feedback go off topic.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

questions.question: The Ceibo Telecom retention assistant is maintained by a team of two. Its implementation guide, which loads into every working session and is used to onboard new people, has accumulated 40 instructions written over a year ago to work around limitations of the previous model version. Since the last upgrade, half of those instructions produce longer and worse answers, and nobody knows which ones are still needed. With the budget frozen and a retention campaign six weeks away, what should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Freeze the guide exactly as it stands and review it in full once a quarter, when the pressure of the campaigns lets up.
options.feedback: A quarterly review beats no review, but it leaves the guide out of step exactly when it changes most: right after a model upgrade.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the 40 instructions into a procedure that loads only when someone invokes it, without reviewing their content.
options.feedback: Moving the content into an on-demand procedure unloads the context of every session, but it does not address the fact that half of those instructions are already surplus.

options.label: C
options.text: Review the inherited instructions whenever the model version changes and treat edits to the guide as code changes.
options.feedback: Correct: what was written to work around a previous version's limitation becomes overhead once the model handles the case, and the way to keep it from aging is to review it at every version change and inside the same flow used to review code.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the model to rewrite the whole guide every month and accept the result whenever the automated tests still pass.
options.feedback: Delegating the rewrite saves work, but it accepts changes to the document that governs the system without anyone deciding which instruction is still necessary.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that documentation guiding an implementation ages along with the system and with the model, so its maintenance has to be hooked to the events that make it obsolete. Two documented mechanisms apply here. The first is to review edits to the guide inside the same flow used to review code, so the conventions follow the system. The second is to review it again after a major model change, because instructions written to work around an earlier limitation turn into overhead once the model resolves the case on its own. The distinction against moving everything into an on-demand procedure is that this changes where the text lives, not whether the text is still true.

RULE: Review the guide where you review the code, and again when the model changes: what was written for an old limitation becomes dead weight.

TRAP: Assuming an instruction that once improved the answers still helps after the model has changed underneath it.

TRY IT: Open your project's guide or conventions file, mark the instructions written to work around a specific limitation, and run a real task with and without them.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases

questions.question: Minera Nevado publishes the environmental permits for its sites through an MCP server of its own that acts as a proxy in front of the environmental authority's API. After a phishing campaign, Ignacio reconstructs the incident: several people who had authorized the proxy months earlier received a link, none of them saw a consent screen, and the authorization code ended up on the attacker's server. The security review noted five deviations in the proxy. Which two explain that an authorization code was issued without anyone approving anything? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: That it forwards to the environmental authority's API the same token it receives from the MCP client, instead of getting one issued for itself.
options.feedback: Token passthrough is a documented anti-pattern and it breaks downstream traceability, but it is a different attack: it does not explain a code issued with no consent screen.

options.label: B
options.text: That it uses a single static client_id with the environmental authority while it lets each MCP client register its own redirect_uri.
options.feedback: Correct: with a shared client_id, the consent a person gave once stays attached to that client, and any redirect_uri registered afterward inherits that earlier authorization.

options.label: C
options.text: That it treats a request as authenticated because its session identifier is still live in the server's table of open sessions.
options.feedback: Using sessions as authentication is forbidden by the specification and is a valid finding, but this incident happens inside the authorization flow, before any session exists.

options.label: D
options.text: That it accepts the access token in the query string of the URL instead of requiring it in the Authorization header of every request.
options.feedback: The specification expressly forbids the token in the query string, so fix it anyway, but a token exposed in the URL is not what skipped the consent screen.

options.label: E
options.text: That it starts the flow toward the environmental authority without checking it against its own registry of the clients each user has approved.
options.feedback: Correct: the proxy has to keep its own registry of client_id values approved per user and ask for explicit consent before forwarding the flow. Without that step, the third party's consent cookie keeps the screen from appearing again.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a proxy sitting between an MCP client and a third-party API inherits responsibility for consent. The confused deputy needs four conditions at once: the proxy always presents the same client_id, it lets clients register dynamically, the third-party authority already left a consent cookie from the first use, and the proxy asks for no consent of its own per client. With those four, the screen is skipped and the code lands at the attacker's redirect_uri. Of them, the proxy controls two: how it registers with the third party, and whether it verifies consent per client before forwarding the flow. The distinction against token passthrough is that there the problem is forwarding downstream a token that was not issued for you, not getting a code without approval.

RULE: If you proxy in front of a third party, require your own per-client consent before you forward the flow: a shared client_id tells nobody apart.

TRAP: Confusing the confused deputy with token passthrough: one obtains a code without consent, the other forwards a token that was never issued to it.

TRY IT: Review your MCP proxy server and answer two questions: whether a table of client_id values approved per user is consulted before the flow starts, and whether redirect_uri values are compared by exact match. Each no is a condition of the attack.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/security_best_practices

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud's triage chat takes about 18,000 patient queries a day across its 40 clinics. The clinical committee requires that no risky message go untreated, whether by automatic block or by nurse review, and that the queue reaching human review stay under the 400 conversations a day that team can handle, a capacity that cannot be expanded. With the current classifier, which only answers whether there is a violation or not, the system either blocks too much or floods the review queue. Sofía is redesigning the control. Which documented approach satisfies both constraints?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the most capable model in the family as the classifier and keep the binary output, so that the violation flag becomes more reliable.
options.feedback: Model choice in moderation is mostly a cost lever; a binary output still cannot tell what has to be blocked from what has to be reviewed.

options.label: B
options.text: Write the escalation rules into the triage assistant's system prompt and trust it to refuse and recommend going to the clinic when it detects risk.
options.feedback: An instruction in the prompt steers what the model tries to do, but it is not a control enforced in code and it feeds no review queue.

options.label: C
options.text: Flag for review every conversation classified as a violation and add nursing staff until the flagged volume is covered.
options.feedback: Reviewing everything flagged is defensible at low volume; with 18,000 queries a day and 400 reviews possible, the queue overflows on day one.

options.label: D
options.text: Classify risk on a scale of 0 to 3, block the high-risk queries automatically and send to human review those who accumulate medium-risk queries.
options.feedback: Correct: grading the risk lets you block the high end automatically and reserve human capacity for the medium-risk pattern, which is where judgment adds value.

questions.explanation:
The general rule in moderation is that grading the risk pays off more than a binary decision, because it lets you attach different actions to different levels. The documentation describes that scale, from 0 for no risk to 3 for high risk, with automatic blocking of high-risk queries and escalation to human review for users who accumulate medium-risk queries. Nursing capacity then goes where there is genuine doubt instead of confirming the obvious. The distinction against reviewing everything flagged is arithmetic: the daily volume far exceeds the review capacity that was committed, so any criterion that does not prioritize breaks the agreement with the clinical committee.

RULE: Grade the risk instead of deciding yes or no: block the high end automatically and reserve human review for the medium-risk pattern.

TRAP: Confusing a binary classifier with an escalation control: without levels, everything doubtful lands in the same queue.

TRY IT: Take 50 real conversations, ask the classifier for a level from 0 to 3 instead of a yes or a no, and count how many would reach human review under each criterion.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/content-moderation

Classify risk on a scale of 0 to 3, block the high-risk queries automatically and send to human review those who accumulate medium-risk queries.
html.explanation:
The general rule in moderation is that grading the risk pays off more than a binary decision, because it lets you attach different actions to different levels. The documentation describes that scale, from 0 for no risk to 3 for high risk, with automatic blocking of high-risk queries and escalation to human review for users who accumulate medium-risk queries. Nursing capacity then goes where there is genuine doubt instead of confirming the obvious. The distinction against reviewing everything flagged is arithmetic: the daily volume far exceeds the review capacity that was committed, so any criterion that does not prioritize breaks the agreement with the clinical committee.

RULE: Grade the risk instead of deciding yes or no: block the high end automatically and reserve human review for the medium-risk pattern.

TRAP: Confusing a binary classifier with an escalation control: without levels, everything doubtful lands in the same queue.

TRY IT: Take 50 real conversations, ask the classifier for a level from 0 to 3 instead of a yes or a no, and count how many would reach human review under each criterion.

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros automated claims triage: the system proposes approving, requesting more documentation or rejecting, and today it closes the lowest-value claims on its own. The regulator requires that any automated decision affecting a policyholder can be explained, and the insurer has ten business days to answer each complaint. Renata, who leads the project, is preparing the plan before extending the scope to high-value claims. Which two measures apply? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Replace the model with the most capable one in the family, because a better model produces decisions that are easier to explain to the regulator.
options.feedback: Moving up a model can improve the quality of the decision, but explainability is a property of the system and of what it records, not of model size.

options.label: B
options.text: Hand the classifier's full system prompt to the regulator, because publishing the instructions is the most direct form of transparency.
options.feedback: Transparency means making information available to whoever interacts with the system; exposing the prompt adds leakage risk and does not tell how each decision was reached.

options.label: C
options.text: Have a qualified professional review the decision before it is communicated to the policyholder, because this is a high-risk case with consumer-facing output.
options.feedback: Correct: claims triage sits among the high-risk cases where the policy requires a professional in the field to review the content before it is released or treated as final.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the model to justify every rejection and file that justification as the official explanation handed to the regulator.
options.feedback: A justification written by the model itself is a plausible after-the-fact reason, not a representation of the mechanism that produced the decision, which is what explainability means.

options.label: E
options.text: Record in each case file the planning steps, the inputs consulted and the system output, so that any decision can be reconstructed.
options.feedback: Correct: showing the planning steps and keeping inputs and outputs is the documented transparency practice for agents, and it is what lets you reconstruct a case months later.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that transparency is built from what the system records and shows, not from the size of the model or the exposure of its instructions. In subjective decisions that directly affect a consumer, such as claims triage, the Usage Policy requires a qualified professional to review the content before it is released or finalized, and that review also gives the policyholder a person to take the matter up with. The second measure is independent: keeping the trail of the decision, with the inputs consulted and the planning steps in plain view, is what lets you reconstruct a specific case when the regulator asks, inside the ten business days. The distinction against asking the model to justify itself is that such a justification describes a plausible reason and not the mechanism that operated.

RULE: Explaining an automated decision means showing its trail and having a qualified person review it before it goes out, not asking the model to justify itself.

TRAP: Treating the justification the model writes itself as if it were the explanation of the mechanism that produced the decision.

TRY IT: Take a case your system has already decided and try to reconstruct it from what you store today: if you cannot say which inputs were consulted or who reviewed it, that is the gap.

questions.question: The AndesWare architecture committee decided to standardize one assisted development environment for its 400 developers and published the decision along with the alternatives it rejected. Two technical leads, who between them hold half the repositories, reply that they are faster without the tool and do not intend to adopt it. The rollout starts in two weeks and the purchase is already signed. Nicolás, the architect who took the decision to the committee, has to talk to them. How should he order that conversation?

options.label: A
options.text: Restate that the decision is made and signed → ask them to comply within their teams → offer general training → measure adoption by team the following month.
options.feedback: Leaning on the authority of the decision closes the conversation without answering the objection, and adoption by two teams that hold half the code does not come from an instruction.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask them to try the tool for a full month → collect their objections at the end of the period → take those to the committee → revisit the decision if they persist.
options.feedback: An unfocused month of trial turns the objection into a long formality, and the tool is judged better on one concrete task than over an open-ended period.

options.label: C
options.text: Escalate the resistance to technical leadership → attach the adoption figures from the rest → wait for the instruction → pass it on to the two teams.
options.feedback: Escalating may unblock the calendar, but it leaves the technical reason for the objection untouched and turns a question of judgment into a hierarchical conflict.

options.label: D
options.text: Acknowledge the objection → reframe it against what the decision was for → propose a demonstration on their own code → time the same task both ways.
options.feedback: Correct: the pattern that works is to acknowledge the concern, offer a brief reframe and propose a concrete demonstration on that person's own code, because most objections dissolve in one successful experience.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that communicating an architecture decision to someone who resists it is not about repeating the argument, but about creating the experience that makes the argument unnecessary. The documented pattern has three moves: acknowledge the concern, offer a brief reframe, and propose a concrete demonstration on that person's own work, closing with a measurable comparison, for example timing the same tedious task both ways. The distinction against leaning on the decision already being signed is that authority buys formal compliance and not adoption, and here the two teams that object hold half the repositories.

RULE: Faced with an objection, acknowledge, reframe and demonstrate on the objector's own code: a good experience convinces more than the right argument.

TRAP: Confusing a decision being made with it being communicated, and answering a technical objection with the committee's signature.

TRY IT: Pick the objection you hear most in your team, write its reframe in one sentence, and prepare a ten-minute demonstration on a real file belonging to whoever raises it.

questions.question: The Colibrí Pay team is reviewing the end-to-end design of the support agent, which checks balances, issues refunds and blocks cards for customers in Peru and Bolivia. The regulator requires that no refund is ever left in an indeterminate state, so Valentina wants it written down how the flow behaves when a step fails: a custom tool, a server tool, or the API call itself. Four statements about error handling are left on the whiteboard. Which one is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Declaring the refund tool with the destructive tool annotation adds the confirmation control: the loop stops until a person authorizes it.
options.feedback: Correct as the answer, because it is the false statement: tool annotations are metadata, not execution control. Apart from readOnlyHint, which decides whether a tool can be called in parallel with other read tools, the rest are informational, and confirmation before an irreversible action is applied by the code that exposes the tool.

options.label: B
options.text: Returning the failure inside the tool_result with is_error and a message explaining what happened lets the agent retry, use another tool or explain it.
options.feedback: True: the documentation says to return the error message in the content together with is_error, and with that the model takes the failure in and can retry, try another tool or explain it instead of cutting the run short.

options.label: C
options.text: With server tools the errors are handled by Claude transparently, so on the client side there is no need to deal with their is_error results.
options.feedback: True: for server tools the documentation says Claude handles those errors transparently and that, unlike client tools, is_error results do not need to be handled.

options.label: D
options.text: The official SDKs retry transient failures on their own with exponential backoff, twice by default, and respect the retry-after header when it comes.
options.feedback: True: the SDKs retry transient failures such as connection errors, rate limits and 5xx with exponential backoff and two retries by default, respecting the retry-after header when it is present.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when reviewing an end-to-end design is to separate what is metadata from what is a control applied by code. Tool annotations describe the intent of whoever wrote the tool and serve as a hint to the client, but they stop no call: that is why the statement about the destructive annotation is the incorrect one, and confirmation before a refund has to live in the code that exposes the tool. The other three describe documented error handling: a custom tool failure comes back inside the tool_result with is_error so the agent can adapt, server tool errors are resolved by the API without your having to handle them, and the SDKs already retry transient failures on their own with exponential backoff. The distinction that decides is who enforces the control: metadata informs, code prevents.

RULE: An annotation describes the tool; it does not stop it. What cannot run without confirmation is blocked in the code that exposes the tool, not in its metadata.

TRAP: Treating declarative metadata as if it were an execution control, and assuming confirmation of an irreversible action is covered because the tool was marked destructive.

TRY IT: Make the refund tool fail on purpose in a test environment, return the error with is_error and a message saying what happened, and watch what the agent does on the next step; then mark it destructive in the annotations and confirm the call still runs.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/custom-tools https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors

questions.question: Pehuén Energía is about to instrument the control-room assistant with OpenTelemetry: 40 units, some 9,000 sessions a day, and a metrics backend with a contracted quota of 200,000 active series, half of it in use today. Renata proposes enabling telemetry with the default configuration and exporting metrics and events to the area's collector. Facundo, who operates that backend, asks for an impact estimate before the maintenance window, because raising the quota takes a purchase that runs for months. What will happen with the default configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: Operator prompts and assistant responses will be exported to the collector, so operational content will leave the system.
options.feedback: Content logging is a real privacy concern, but it ships turned off and is enabled variable by variable, so it does not happen with the default configuration.

options.label: B
options.text: Metrics will go out labeled with the session identifier, which opens a new series per session and eats the backend quota in days.
options.feedback: Correct: the session identifier is included in metrics by default, and it is the high-cardinality label that blows up a time series backend. It is switched off with a variable of its own.

options.label: C
options.text: The telemetry variables will propagate to the processes the agent launches, so MCP servers and commands will end up instrumented on their own.
options.feedback: The opposite happens: those variables are not passed to subprocesses, so whatever the agent invokes stays dark unless you instrument it separately.

options.label: D
options.text: Tool use events will be exported once a minute, so you will lose the detail of each individual call inside that time window.
options.feedback: The one-minute interval belongs to metrics. Events go out every few seconds and each call is emitted as an event of its own, so the detail is not lost.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that agent telemetry scales badly on cardinality before it scales badly on volume: every label with near-unique values multiplies the series the backend has to keep alive. The session identifier is included in metrics by default, so with 9,000 sessions a day the quota of 200,000 series runs out in a few days, and the documented control is to turn that label off, not to sample or to cut back the instrumentation. Per-session detail is still available where it belongs, which is events and traces, not aggregated metrics. The distinction against the fear about content is that prompt and response logging is off by default and is only turned on explicitly.

RULE: Before you turn on telemetry at scale, look at which labels your metrics carry: cardinality is paid in active series, not in bytes.

TRAP: Assuming the default configuration is conservative about everything: it turns content off, but it leaves the session label on in metrics.

TRY IT: Export one hour of your agent's metrics to a test collector and count how many distinct series appear with the session label on and how many with it off, then extrapolate that number to your daily sessions.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage

questions.question: Pampero Agro builds agronomic reports with an agent that queries sensors, field notes and lab analyses. At harvest the volume multiplies by six, and the monthly token budget is fixed. Each report runs about twenty tool calls, the sensor results stay whole in the conversation until the end, and the 80 tool definitions of the six internal systems travel complete in every request. Valentina has to cut input spend without giving up report quality. Which two measures attack the cause? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window, so that the results accumulated in the conversation stop competing for the available space.
options.feedback: A larger window changes how much fits, not how much you pay, and dragging more context degrades retrieval instead of improving it.

options.label: B
options.text: Prune the sensor results already used at each subtask boundary and leave a one-line extract of what is kept in their place.
options.feedback: Correct: pruning at the boundaries cuts the context resent on every turn and, because it edits the tail of the conversation, it leaves the cached prefix intact.

options.label: C
options.text: Declare the tools with deferred loading and let the agent search for the one it needs, instead of sending the whole catalog every time.
options.feedback: Correct: with large catalogs the definitions are paid on every request without adding precision, and tool search avoids sending them all.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower max_tokens so that each report comes out shorter and less of the agent's own text enters the turns that follow.
options.feedback: That cap is invisible to the model, so it does not make it economize: it cuts a response that has already been billed, sometimes mid-sentence.

options.label: E
options.text: Turn on server-side context editing so that the system trims on its own whatever is left over in the middle of the task.
options.feedback: It is a real lever, but in the published measurements it did not pay off on short runs, and on long ones it did not beat pruning at boundaries, which also leaves the context far smaller.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the input spend of an agent has two sources, and both are paid on every turn: what the conversation drags along, and what is declared before it starts. Pruning at subtask boundaries attacks the first, because it replaces bulky results already consumed with an extract and edits the tail of the conversation, so the cached prefix survives. Deferred tool loading attacks the second, because a large catalog costs money on every request without improving tool choice. The two levers are independent and they add up. The distinction against context editing is that it rewrites content in the middle of the task and in what has been measured it did not beat pruning, and against the larger window, that the window is not a cost lever at all.

RULE: Input spend lives in what you drag and in what you declare: prune the results already used and offer the tools on demand.

TRAP: Believing that a larger context window is a cost lever, when it only changes how much fits and makes retrieval worse.

TRY IT: Take one real report, measure the input of each request and split how much comes from tool definitions and how much from earlier results; then prune the results at the first subtask boundary and measure again.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

questions.question: The Minera Nevado operational safety assistant serves the site supervisors. Queries fall into three clearly different groups: frequent questions about standard procedures, which are the vast majority; checks on what a current environmental permit requires; and incident analyses, few and hard. The monthly platform cost is capped and today every query goes through the same flow on the most capable model. Valentina has to bring the spend down without losing quality on the incidents. Which pattern should she apply?

options.label: A
options.text: Run each query three times with different prompts and keep the answer that agrees across the majority of the runs.
options.feedback: Running the same task several times and deciding by majority helps when you need more confidence in a hard judgment, but it triples the cost exactly where the volume is.

options.label: B
options.text: Put an orchestrator in place that builds each query's subtasks on the fly and hands them out to specialized subagents.
options.feedback: An orchestrator that builds the subtasks on the fly is the answer when you cannot predict which subtasks will be needed; here the three categories are known in advance.

options.label: C
options.text: Classify the query on arrival and send it to the flow and model that fit it, with the most capable reserved for incidents.
options.feedback: Correct: there are distinct categories better handled separately, and sending the frequent ones to a fast, cheap model while reserving the most capable one for the hard cases is the documented way to cut cost without losing quality where it matters.

options.label: D
options.text: Chain three fixed calls per query: one that summarizes it, one that looks up the procedure and one that writes the answer.
options.feedback: A fixed three-step chain adds calls to every query, including the frequent and simple ones, which is exactly where you need to spend less.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that routing applies when there are distinct categories better handled separately and the classification is reliable; it is also the cost optimization pattern par excellence, because it lets easy, frequent questions go to a fast, cheap model and reserves the most capable one for the hard ones. Here the three categories are clearly delimited, most of the volume is repetitive, and quality is critical only on the incidents. The distinction against the orchestrator with subagents is that this pattern exists for when the subtasks cannot be predicted, and the distinction against voting is that the technique buys confidence by paying for several runs per query.

RULE: When the categories are distinct and known, classify and route: the expensive model is reserved for the hard minority.

TRAP: Treating a mix of traffic as if it were a capacity problem, and paying for the most expensive model on the trivial queries too.

TRY IT: Classify a sample of one hundred queries from your system by category and difficulty, and work out what share of today's spend goes to the ones a faster model could answer.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

TRAP: Treating a mix of traffic as if it were a capacity problem, and paying for the most expensive model on the trivial queries too.

TRY IT: Classify a sample of one hundred queries from your system by category and difficulty, and work out what share of today's spend goes to the ones a faster model could answer.

questions.question: The Mistral Retail after-sales agent serves the 220 stores and the digital channel, with peaks of 10x on promotional dates. Compliance requires that 100% of conversations be reviewed against the return and warranty policies, because last quarter the agent approved returns outside policy. The internal agreement fixes a response in under 4 seconds at the 95th percentile and a maximum cost per conversation. Which design meets all three conditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the same policy classification three times with different prompts and settle it by majority before the answer reaches the customer.
options.feedback: Voting across several runs of the same task raises confidence on borderline cases, but it multiplies the cost per conversation and the time, and both are capped here.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the policy review in a parallel instance that runs alongside the answer and blocks delivery if there is a violation.
options.feedback: Correct: a review as a parallel instance that examines the conversation while another one answers it is the documented way to apply guardrails without adding a serial step to the critical path.

options.label: C
options.text: Chain the review after the answer is generated, so that every conversation goes through both steps in sequence.
options.feedback: Reviewing after generating gives the right result, but it adds the time of a second call to every conversation, and at the peak that breaks the committed 95th percentile.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the whole conversation to the most capable model and describe in the system prompt the policies it cannot break.
options.feedback: A more capable model with the policies in the system prompt is still an instruction and not a control: nothing stops an answer outside policy from going out, and the cost rises across all the traffic.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that sectioning splits work into independent subtasks that run at the same time, and the canonical example is precisely a guardrail: one model instance processes the user query while another one screens it. Because the two calls run in parallel, the cost goes up but the critical path does not absorb the latency of the second, which is what keeps the 95th percentile within reach at the peak. The distinction against chaining the review at the end is that there the two times add up; and against voting, that the technique repeats the same task to gain confidence, not to cover 100% of the traffic with an independent review.

RULE: A guardrail that has to see all the traffic runs in parallel, not in line: a serial step is paid for at the 95th percentile.

TRAP: Confusing voting with review: repeating the same classification does not examine the answer, it only buys confidence at three times the cost.

TRY IT: Measure the 95th percentile of your flow with the review in series and measure it again firing both calls at once: the difference is what the queue costs you.

questions.question: Pehuén Energía has to report to the regulator on the assistant that control-room operators use during maintenance windows, which last 20 minutes and cannot be extended. The operations committee proposed fourteen indicators for the monthly report and wants a target set on all of them. Two people per shift are the ones who respond to alerts. Joaquín has to define what gets a target and what stays as diagnostics. What should he propose?

options.label: A
options.text: Set a target on all fourteen of the indicators, because any one of them can explain a failure inside the maintenance window.
options.feedback: Every indicator can explain something, but with targets on fourteen of them nobody knows which to look at first; with two people per shift, attention is the scarce resource.

options.label: B
options.text: Combine the fourteen into a single assistant health index and set a monthly target on that composite number.
options.feedback: A composite index looks tidy in the report, but mixing different signals stops it saying what broke, and it is useless for acting inside the window.

options.label: C
options.text: Set targets on the few indicators describing the operator's experience in the window and leave the rest as diagnostics.
options.feedback: Correct: choosing a few indicators that describe the service as the person using it receives it keeps attention where it matters, and the rest keeps being measured without becoming a target.

options.label: D
options.text: Set a target only on the indicator the regulator requires and drop the others to avoid extra measurement work.
options.feedback: Measuring only what the regulator asks for satisfies the formality, but it leaves unwatched the behavior that affects the operator and that the regulator does not name.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a target is set on an indicator, and that choosing too many indicators makes it hard to pay proper attention to the ones that matter, while choosing too few leaves significant behavior unexamined. The criterion that separates them is whether the indicator describes the service as the person using it receives it: inside a 20-minute window that cannot be extended, that means the availability of the answer and its usefulness to the operator. The rest keeps being measured, but as diagnostics. The distinction against the composite index is that a blended number tells a two-person shift neither what broke nor what to do, which is the only thing that helps inside the window.

RULE: A few indicators carry targets and many stay on the dashboard: the target goes on what describes the experience of whoever uses the service.

TRAP: Assuming that measuring more means watching better: fourteen targets split the attention until none of them triggers an action.

TRY IT: List your service's indicators and mark which ones describe what the person using it receives; keep targets only on those and count how many alerts turn out to be surplus the following week.

questions.question: Colibrí Pay packaged as a Skill the chargeback procedure of the agent that handles merchant claims, which carries three times last year's volume. The file ended up like this: name: contracargos-procedimiento, description: "Internal Colibrí Pay procedure.", body of SKILL.md: 9,000 tokens with the full manual of deadlines, forms and resolved cases. Paula measures two problems: when an analyst asks about a chargeback the agent answers with generic criteria and the Skill does not activate, and in the few sessions where it does activate the context fills up before the case is closed. Which two changes fix the design? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Rewrite the description so it says what the Skill solves and in which situations to use it, in the terms of the business.
options.feedback: Correct: the description is the text the request is matched against, so it has to say what the Skill does and when to use it. A generic line leaves the Skill installed but invisible.

options.label: B
options.text: Paste the body of the Skill into the agent's system prompt so the procedure is guaranteed to be there on every query.
options.feedback: It guarantees availability, but it pays the 9,000 tokens on every request, including the ones that have nothing to do with chargebacks: that is a return to the monolithic context the Skill was meant to avoid.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on compaction so the context gets summarized when the Skill loads the manual and the session can run until the case is closed.
options.feedback: Compaction rescues a conversation that has already grown, but it does not keep it from growing. Here the material comes in whole without being needed, and summarizing it afterward loses procedural detail.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave a short body in SKILL.md with the procedure and move the full manual to reference files that get read when needed.
options.feedback: Correct: bundled files consume no context until they are opened, so the body stays light and the manual comes in only for the case that truly asks for it.

options.label: E
options.text: Turn the Skill into a tool with defer_loading so that tool search finds it whenever a chargeback case comes up.
options.feedback: Tool deferral attacks definition bloat, not instruction bloat, and it drags the same underlying problem along: with a generic description, search will not find it either.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of progressive disclosure is that material is declared with a precise description and read when it is needed: the metadata is always loaded, the body arrives when the request matches, and bundled files cost nothing until they are opened. The two symptoms point to two different levels. That the Skill does not activate is a problem of the description, which is exactly what the model matches against the request. That the context fills up when it does activate is a problem of the body, which should hold only the essentials and point to the manual as a reference file. The distinction against compaction is that summarizing repairs a context that has already grown, while what you want here is for it not to grow.

RULE: Describe a Skill by what it solves and when to use it, keep the body minimal, and send long material to files opened only when needed.

TRAP: Assuming that packaging something as a Skill already defers its cost, when the body enters whole on activation and a vague description keeps it from activating.

TRY IT: Write two versions of the description for one of your Skills, one generic and one that names the situations of use, then check across ten real queries how many times each one activates.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview

questions.question: The Agencia Nacional de Ingresos will enable the taxpayer support assistant for 900 employees across twelve regional offices. Ximena drafted the internal implementation guide from the vendor reference material, with its generic examples and its bracketed placeholders. Institutional communications authorizes a single mass mailing this month, and after that the channel stays closed until the following quarter. In what order should she prepare and distribute that guide?

options.label: A
options.text: Publish the vendor reference material exactly as it stands → collect the corrections that come back through the channel → publish an erratum → consolidate the final version.
options.feedback: Publishing and correcting later works when the channel stays open; here there is a single mailing, and an erratum nobody reads leaves the wrong version in circulation.

options.label: B
options.text: Rewrite the material in the agency's own voice with real cases → replace every placeholder → verify what depends on the version → distribute.
options.feedback: Correct: the reference material is draft copy and not a deliverable; it gets rewritten in the organization's voice with its own examples, the placeholders get replaced, and whatever depends on the version gets verified before it goes out.

options.label: C
options.text: Distribute the guide to the leads of the twelve offices → ask each one to adapt it to their own reality → gather the twelve versions → publish the one most used.
options.feedback: Delegating the adaptation produces twelve versions with no owner and contradicts the goal of one common guide; it also burns the single mailing available.

options.label: D
options.text: Verify the technical details with the vendor first → wait for written confirmation → publish the reference material unchanged → adapt it the following quarter.
options.feedback: Confirming details is reasonable, but distributing the generic material without adapting it wastes the only mailing and tells nobody what to do in their own work.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a vendor's reference material is draft copy: it has to be rewritten in the organization's voice, the generic examples swapped for real tasks from the work at hand, and the placeholders replaced before it is sent, because the communications that win adoption are the ones that look as if they were written in-house. On top of that comes a final check of everything that depends on the product version, which changes often and should not be distributed without being compared against the documentation. With a single authorized mailing, that order is also the only way not to waste the opportunity. The distinction against publishing and correcting later is that here there is no second pass.

RULE: Vendor material is a draft: rewrite it with your own cases, replace the placeholders and verify what depends on the version before you send it.

TRAP: Confusing reference material with a deliverable, and spending the only authorized mailing on examples that are not your own.

TRY IT: Take the last internal guide you distributed and count how many of its examples come from your own operation; if most of them come from the vendor material, you already know why it went unread.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/communications-kit

questions.question: Mistral Retail migrated catalog enrichment to the newest model of the same family without touching a comma of the prompt, and the cost per listing rose by more than 80%. The usage field for the same listing, before and after, says: before cache_read_input_tokens 7,800, input_tokens 1,300, output_tokens 260; after cache_read_input_tokens 10,200, input_tokens 1,700, output_tokens 690 with thinking_tokens 430. The team has a target cost per listing for the promotional season. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: A
options.text: The tokenizer of the new model produces more tokens for the same text, and thinking is on by default and billed as output.
options.feedback: Correct: the same text yields more tokens in the more recent generation, and reasoning tokens are charged as output even when they are not shown.

options.label: B
options.text: The cache stopped hitting when the model changed, and now every request pays to write the prefix instead of reading it as before.
options.feedback: Changing model does invalidate the prefix the first time, but usage shows cache reads in the same proportion as before the migration.

options.label: C
options.text: The new model is more verbose in the visible listing, and lowering max_tokens is enough to get back to the target cost of the season.
options.feedback: The visible response does tend to be longer, but that cap is an invisible cut for the model that discards work already billed instead of avoiding it.

options.label: D
options.text: The catalog grew between the two measurements, and input rose in proportion to the size of the listing being sent.
options.feedback: The comparison is over the same listing and with the prompt unchanged, so growth of the catalog does not explain the observed difference.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when changing model is to count again before drawing conclusions, because two things move without the prompt changing: the same text produces more tokens with the tokenizer of the recent generations, and the reasoning of the model is on by default and billed as output tokens even when it is not returned. Both fingerprints are visible in usage: input grows evenly in the cached part and in the uncached part, and output almost triples with thinking tokens inside it. The distinction against blaming the cache is that cache reads rose in the same proportion as the rest of the input, a sign that the prefix is still hitting; and against lowering max_tokens, that this cap cuts work already paid for without correcting the cause.

RULE: After a migration, count again: the same text can cost more tokens, and the reasoning you do not see is billed as output.

TRAP: Reading a cost rise after a model change as a prompt or cache problem, without recounting the tokens against the new model.

TRY IT: Count the same listing with the counting endpoint against the old model and against the new one and compare the two input_tokens values; then look at thinking_tokens in a real response to separate how much of the rise is reasoning.

questions.question: The agent that answers broker queries at Zafiro Seguros scores 85% on the internal evaluation, and the team reports it to the regulator as 85% accuracy. Brokers resend the query when the answer does not convince them. Audit repeated 200 queries three times each, on the same file and with no changes in the source systems, and in close to four out of ten there was at least one answer different from the other two. The regulator requires that the same query receive the same treatment. What is the most likely cause of the gap?

options.label: A
options.text: The evaluation set is small, and the 85% carries a margin of error larger than the difference audit is observing.
options.feedback: A small set widens the interval around the number, but it does not explain why the same query gets different answers across attempts.

options.label: B
options.text: The automated grader is more permissive than audit and approves answers that a human reviewer from the area would reject without hesitation.
options.feedback: A miscalibrated judge inflates the number, and calibrating it against experts is worth doing, but that would move the measured level, not the variability across attempts.

options.label: C
options.text: The suite reports accuracy per attempt and the commitment is consistency: at 85% per attempt, three in a row falls to 61%.
options.feedback: Correct: when the requirement is that every attempt succeed, the right metric is the one that multiplies the attempts, not the one that settles for one.

options.label: D
options.text: The agent queries data that changes between resends, so the different answers reflect the state of the file and not an error.
options.feedback: That would be a valid explanation with live data, but audit repeated on the same file and with no changes in the source systems.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the metric is chosen by the commitment being made: pass@k measures that at least one of k attempts succeeds and fits when a human reviews and one good result is enough, while pass^k measures that all of them succeed and is the metric of systems that must be consistent to the user. At 85% per attempt, the probability of succeeding three times in a row is 0.85 cubed, around 61%, and the complement matches the discrepancies audit found. The reported number is not miscalculated: it describes something other than what the regulator requires. The distinction against blaming the grader is that a permissive judge would move the level of the score, not the variability across attempts of the same query.

RULE: Choose the metric by the promise: if you promise consistency, measure that every attempt succeeds, not that some attempt does.

TRAP: Reporting per-attempt accuracy as if it were the accuracy of the experience, when the user retries and keeps the worst of the answers.

TRY IT: Take twenty real queries, run each of them three times and count in how many all three succeed; compare that percentage with the per-attempt accuracy you report today.

questions.question: The regulations and circulars search that holds up claim classification at Banco Altamar runs this pipeline: split by section, chunk_size 800 tokens, overlap 10%, embeddings plus BM25, weighted fusion 0.8 and 0.2, top_k 20, no per-chunk context and no reranking. The 95th percentile of the retrieval step is 210 ms against a budget of 300 ms. Mateo proposes prepending 50 to 100 tokens of context to each chunk, generated from the full document, before embedding it and before indexing it in BM25. What effect will the change have?

options.label: A
options.text: Retrieval failures will drop, but every query will add 100 to 200 ms because the chunk context is built at query time.
options.feedback: That range of 100 to 200 ms per query is what a reranking pass adds, and reranking does run on every query. Chunk context is computed at indexing time and never touches the query path.

options.label: B
options.text: Retrieval failures will drop with no added latency per query, because the context is generated and indexed once per document.
options.feedback: Correct: contextualizing is an indexing cost, not a query cost. The work happens while the index is built, with caching of the document, and the query still reads an index that is already assembled.

options.label: C
options.text: Retrieval failures will not change, because the text of the chunk stays the same and the only thing that grows is the size of the index.
options.feedback: The index does grow, that much is true, but what gets embedded and indexed is no longer the isolated fragment: it is the fragment placed in its document, and that changes which queries it matches.

options.label: D
options.text: Failures will drop only on the semantic leg, because BM25 indexes the literal text and gains nothing from any added context.
options.feedback: The technique has two halves for exactly that reason: the context is prepended before indexing in BM25 as well, and it is that contextual version of the lexical index that adds on top of the embeddings.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to place each cost in its own stage: some levers are paid once at indexing time and some are paid on every query, and a latency constraint only discriminates among the second kind. Prepending chunk-specific context before embedding it and before indexing it in BM25 reduces retrieval failures by a measured margin, and its cost is an indexing cost, on the order of one dollar per million document tokens thanks to caching, without touching the query path. With 90 ms of headroom against the budget, this is exactly the improvement that fits today. The distinction against reranking is that reranking reorders candidates on every query and therefore adds 100 to 200 ms, which is where the budget would have to be negotiated.

RULE: Separate the improvements you pay for at indexing time from the ones you pay for at query time: only the second kind competes with your latency budget.

TRAP: Confusing the cost of contextualizing, which is per document and paid once, with the cost of reranking, which is charged in milliseconds on every query.

TRY IT: Contextualize a hundred chunks of your corpus with the fastest model in the family, reindex that sample, and compare it against the current index on how many queries put the right chunk in the top twenty and on how long the retrieval step takes.

questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro wants to automate the coordination of each port call among the shipping line, customs and the trucking companies: there are between 30 and 40 events per call and the operating windows are minutes long. The port authority requires being able to reconstruct, within the same shift, which decision was taken, on what information and in what order. An event lost without warning costs the berth. The team is comparing four architectures for coordination between agents. Which one fits those constraints?

options.label: A
options.text: A message bus where each agent publishes and subscribes to the events that concern it, with a router that distributes them.
options.feedback: A bus scales well and fits a flow of events, but if the router misclassifies or drops an event the system fails silently, and debugging that is harder than following an orchestrator's sequence.

options.label: B
options.text: Autonomous agents that read and write over shared state, with no orchestrator, each one reacting to whatever it finds.
options.feedback: Shared state avoids a single point of failure, but with no orchestrator you get duplicated work and contradictory decisions, and termination conditions have to be defined.

options.label: C
options.text: An orchestrator that plans, delegates bounded subtasks and synthesizes the results, accepting that all the information passes through it.
options.feedback: Correct: with bounded subtasks and a requirement to reconstruct the sequence of decisions, the central orchestrator pays for its bottleneck with an ordered trace and no silent failures.

options.label: D
options.text: A team of agents that pull tasks from a shared queue and report when done, working autonomously and in parallel.
options.feedback: A team with a shared queue suits long parallel work, but detecting that everything has finished is harder and conflicts over shared resources appear inside the window.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the coordination pattern is chosen by the shape of the work and by what the business has to be able to explain. The subtasks here are bounded and known, and the authority requires reconstructing what was decided and in what order within the shift: that favors an orchestrator that plans, delegates and synthesizes, because its sequence of decisions is exactly what can be audited. The known price is that the orchestrator becomes an information bottleneck. The distinction against the message bus lies in the failure mode: a misclassified or dropped event disappears without warning, and with windows of minutes and a berth at stake, a silent failure is worse than a visible bottleneck.

RULE: Choose the coordination pattern by the failure mode you can tolerate: the bus fails silently, the orchestrator congests in plain sight.

TRAP: Choosing the message bus for its elegance with events, without asking what happens when the router loses one.

TRY IT: Draw your coordination flow and mark where a lost event would be detected; if there is no point where anyone notices, you have a silent failure waiting.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/multi-agent-coordination-patterns

questions.question: At AndesWare, a team is about to build a service that touches four repositories of the monorepo and several contracts between squads. The product manager described what he wants in a half-hour meeting and asked them to start tomorrow; nobody has written down yet what the service has to do. Bruno, the technical lead, knows that redoing the work after the first week costs the team the whole sprint. How should he start?

options.label: A
options.text: Write the code for the first part → show it to the product manager → adjust it to his corrections → write the specification at the end with whatever is left.
options.feedback: Building first and documenting later is fast in the first week and expensive in the second: if the problem was misunderstood, the code already written is what gets thrown away.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the product manager to write the specification himself → review it when it arrives → start building → validate against the document at the end.
options.feedback: Having the stakeholder write the specification sounds orderly, but it delegates the part that decides the design to someone who does not know the technical constraints.

options.label: C
options.text: Split the four repositories among four people → have each one define their own part → integrate at the end of the week → document what was integrated.
options.feedback: Splitting by repository before knowing what has to be built fixes the architecture to the shape of the team and leaves the contracts between squads for last.

options.label: D
options.text: Let the assistant interview you about the requirements → write the specification from that → run it in a fresh session → review the change against it.
options.feedback: Correct: the guided interview surfaces what the meeting left implicit, the written specification pins the agreement down, and running it in a fresh session keeps understanding the problem separate from solving it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to separate research and agreement about the problem from implementation, so as not to solve the wrong problem precisely. The documented path is to let the assistant run the requirements interview, asking for whatever is missing, pour the result into a written specification, and execute it afterward in a fresh session whose context is dedicated entirely to building. The specification is also the artifact the product manager can review before a single line of code exists. The distinction against starting from the code is that work discarded after a week equals the whole sprint, which is exactly the cost this team cannot pay.

RULE: Interview and written specification first, implementation in a clean session second: understanding the problem and solving it do not share a context.

TRAP: Confusing speed with progress: starting to build before writing down what gets built gains the first week and repeats the second.

TRY IT: On your next multi-file task, have the assistant interview you until a one-page specification is full, and only then open a fresh session to implement it.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
