questions.question: Yaguareté Logística processes 12,000 customs filings a day. Of those, 85% are repeat shipments from 200 regular clients, with the same goods and a tariff classification that customs already confirmed on earlier filings; the remaining 15% is new or doubtful merchandise. Every filing goes through the same flow today, with tools and model review. Management wants the cost per filing down 30% without increasing release time. What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Move down a model across the whole flow and offset the loss of accuracy with more examples in the classification prompt.
options.feedback: Moving down a model cuts the unit cost, but it applies that cut where accuracy decides a fine too, and examples do not make up for a genuinely new case.

options.label: B
options.text: Send all 12,000 filings overnight in batches to take the batch discount and free up capacity during the day.
options.feedback: Batch submission costs half and works when nobody is waiting for the answer, but holding a filing until night worsens the release time management wants to protect.

options.label: C
options.text: Split the flow across several subagents specialized by the type of merchandise, to shorten the total time of each filing.
options.feedback: Specialized subagents help when the work is parallelizable, but they multiply the tokens of the process and miss the cause: 85% of the volume needs no model at all.

options.label: D
options.text: Resolve the repeat shipments with the confirmed classification and reserve the model flow for the doubtful merchandise.
options.feedback: Correct: where a confirmed answer already exists, a lookup against history resolves it with no model, and the flow with tools is left for the 15% that genuinely requires judgment.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when translating a business problem is to identify which part of the work has a deterministic answer and take it off the model's path, and only then optimize what is left. Here 85% of the volume is repeat shipments with a classification customs already confirmed: that is a lookup against history, not a language problem, and it removes the cost of those filings without touching release time. The distinction against moving down a model or sending batches is that both levers still treat the whole volume as if it were the same work: the first also cheapens the 15% where an error costs a fine, and the second buys a discount in exchange for the time management asked not to worsen.

RULE: Before optimizing the model, take out of the flow whatever already has a deterministic answer: the repeated part of the work needs no model.

TRAP: Assuming a cost target is solved by choosing a model, when most of the volume already has a confirmed answer on file.

TRY IT: Measure what percentage of your system's requests repeat an input already resolved before, and work out how much of the monthly bill corresponds to that percentage.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing

questions.question: At Grupo Aurora Educación, the automatic tutor can verify every answer with a second call before showing it. With 180,000 students that raises the cost per student by 20% and leaves the program at the edge of the annual budget; without that verification, close to 3% of the answers contain an error the student does not catch. Neither option is obviously better and the school year starts in three weeks. Andrés, the platform architect, is preparing the meeting with the academic committee. What should he bring?

options.label: A
options.text: The option he considers technically soundest, already decided, with the detail of the architecture that supports it.
options.feedback: Bringing the decision already made saves a meeting, but what separates the options is how much error is accepted per student and what avoiding it costs, and that is weighed by whoever answers for the budget and for academic quality.

options.label: B
options.text: Both options described in architectural terms, so that the committee chooses with the full technical picture.
options.feedback: Describing the architecture of both is necessary but not sufficient: an academic committee cannot choose between two diagrams if nobody has translated what each one means in cost per student and in errors reaching the student.

options.label: C
options.text: Both options with the requirement that separates them and its measurable consequence, so the budget owner decides.
options.feedback: Correct: the decision is presented tied to the requirement that makes it significant and with the measurable consequence of each alternative, and the choice is left with whoever answers for the business commitment.

options.label: D
options.text: A proposal to postpone the decision until two months of real usage data exist with both schemes running in parallel.
options.feedback: Running both schemes in parallel would produce data, but it consumes the budget of both options at once and arrives after the school year has started.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an architecture decision is communicated together with the requirement that makes it significant and with the consequences of each alternative, and that when the deciding variable is a business one, the choice belongs to whoever answers for it. What separates the options here is not technical: it is how much error is tolerated reaching the student and how much the organization will pay to avoid it. The architect's job is to make that comparison explicit and measurable, and then record the decision along with the rejected alternative. The distinction against bringing the option already chosen is that it turns a business decision into a technical preference and leaves the committee without the part that is genuinely theirs to weigh.

RULE: Present the requirement that separates the options and the measurable consequence of each one; when the deciding variable is a business one, the choice is not yours.

TRAP: Confusing having the technical criterion with having the decision: choosing on the committee's behalf removes the one input only it can weigh.

TRY IT: Take a pending decision in your team and write it in three lines: the requirement that decides it, the measurable consequence of each option, and who answers for that variable.

SOURCE: https://adr.github.io/ https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/

questions.question: Mistral Retail's after-sales agent is developed against an MCP server that queries the CRM. Ignacio, who opens the session at the repository root, has it working; the four developers who open Claude Code inside "apps/posventa" see it as failed in "/mcp", and they have already accepted the project-scope approval prompt. The ".mcp.json" versioned at the root says: {"mcpServers": {"crm": {"type": "stdio", "command": "./scripts/crm-mcp.sh", "args": ["--perfil", "dev"]}}}. With the promotional peak four days away, what fixes the problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Reconnect the server from "/mcp" and, if it still lists zero tools, read the server's stderr with "claude --debug=mcp" in the session log.
options.feedback: Reconnecting and reading stderr is the documented path when the server connects but publishes no tools; here it does not even start, so it would treat a different symptom.

options.label: B
options.text: Write a "command" path that does not depend on the launch directory, because a relative one resolves against wherever the session was opened.
options.feedback: Correct: relative paths in "command" and in "args" resolve against the directory Claude Code was launched from, not against the location of the ".mcp.json".

options.label: C
options.text: Move the entry to ".claude/settings.json" under an "mcpServers" key, so that the configuration travels with the rest of the repository settings.
options.feedback: The settings file does not read an "mcpServers" key: the entry would be ignored and the server would disappear for the person who has it working today.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask each developer to approve the server from "/mcp", because a project-scope server stays disabled until that approval is given.
options.feedback: That approval is a real requirement and its absence does leave the server disabled, but the team already gave it and the state they see is failed, not waiting.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when diagnosing an MCP server is to separate three states that look alike and are not: pending approval, failed to start, and connected with zero tools, because each has its own cause and its own remedy. Here the server shows as failed, and only for the people who open the session in a subdirectory, which points at a path that resolves differently depending on where you launch from. Relative paths in "command" and "args" resolve against the launch directory and not against the location of the ".mcp.json", a frequent cause in large repositories. The distinction against reconnecting and reading stderr is that this path is the one for a server that does connect but publishes no tool at all.

RULE: A relative path in a ".mcp.json" resolves against the directory you open the session from, not against the file: change the folder and you change the result.

TRAP: Reading a startup failure as if it were an approval problem or an empty tool list, and applying the remedy that belongs to another state.

TRY IT: Open the session from the repository root and then from a subdirectory, run "claude mcp list" in each case, and compare the status of the same server.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/debug-your-config https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

questions.question: Siete Lagos Viajes answers questions about the change and cancellation terms of 40 wholesalers against an index of its own. Valentina measured across 200 labeled queries: precision 0.44, recall 0.71, MRR 0.52 and end-to-end accuracy of 68%. The right fragment is almost always among the retrieved candidates, but it arrives in low positions. The budget for the retrieval step is 400 ms at the 95th percentile and 180 are used today. High season multiplies traffic by ten, and cost per query already eats half the channel's margin. Which two changes are worth making? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Raise top_k from 20 to 50 so the right fragment gets more chances of making it into the model's prompt.
options.feedback: More fragments do raise the chance of including what is relevant, but recall is already high: you would be adding tokens on every query and distracting material, exactly what the peak cannot absorb.

options.label: B
options.text: Rebuild the index more often so the terms of the wholesalers are always up to date in the search engine.
options.feedback: Freshness matters when the source changed and the index went stale, but the symptom is not outdated content: the right fragment is there and arrives badly positioned.

options.label: C
options.text: Over-retrieve around 150 candidates and add a reranking pass that keeps the first twenty of them.
options.feedback: Correct: reranking attacks ordering, which is the measured problem, and its 100 to 200 ms per query fit inside the 220 ms free in the budget.

options.label: D
options.text: Cut to eight the fragments that reach the prompt once reranking has ordered the candidate list.
options.feedback: Correct: with the list well ordered the useful material concentrates at the top, so lowering top_k cuts tokens per query and removes distraction without losing what the model needs.

options.label: E
options.text: Send the query to the most capable model in the family so it tells apart similar terms from two wholesalers.
options.feedback: Moving up a model does not change which fragments reach the prompt: if the right one lands in position forty nobody will read it, and cost per query rises in the middle of high season.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to look at which metric moved before touching the pipeline: with high recall and low MRR, the right fragment is being retrieved and ordered badly, so the problem is ranking and not coverage. Reranking is the pass that reorders an over-retrieved set, and it is the retrieval improvement with the largest measured return. Its price is 100 to 200 ms per query, which fits in the available margin. With the list already ordered, lowering the number of fragments that reach the prompt cuts tokens and distraction, because more information is not monotonically better. The distinction against raising top_k is that this lever moves recall, which is no longer the bottleneck, and it gets more expensive in the window of highest traffic.

RULE: Recall says whether the fragment is there; MRR says whether it arrives at the top. With high recall and low MRR, reorder and trim instead of retrieving more.

TRAP: Treating an ordering problem as if it were a coverage problem and raising top_k, which adds tokens and distraction without moving the position of the right fragment.

TRY IT: Take fifty labeled queries from your system and compute MRR as well as recall, then run the same queries with a reranking pass over 150 candidates and compare both numbers along with the 95th percentile of the retrieval step.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/capabilities-contextual-embeddings-guide https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/capabilities-retrieval-augmented-generation-guide

html.question: Siete Lagos Viajes answers questions about the change and cancellation terms of 40 wholesalers against an index of its own. Valentina measured across 200 labeled queries: precision 0.44, recall 0.71, MRR 0.52 and end-to-end accuracy of 68%. The right fragment is almost always among the retrieved candidates, but it arrives in low positions. The budget for the retrieval step is 400 ms at the 95th percentile and 180 are used today. High season multiplies traffic by ten, and cost per query already eats half the channel's margin. Which two changes are worth making? (Select TWO)
options: Raise top_k from 20 to 50 so the right fragment gets more chances of making it into the model's prompt.
Rebuild the index more often so the terms of the wholesalers are always up to date in the search engine.
Over-retrieve around 150 candidates and add a reranking pass that keeps the first twenty of them.
Cut to eight the fragments that reach the prompt once reranking has ordered the candidate list.
Send the query to the most capable model in the family so it tells apart similar terms from two wholesalers.
html.explanation:
The general rule is to look at which metric moved before touching the pipeline: with high recall and low MRR, the right fragment is being retrieved and ordered badly, so the problem is ranking and not coverage. Reranking is the pass that reorders an over-retrieved set, and it is the retrieval improvement with the largest measured return. Its price is 100 to 200 ms per query, which fits in the available margin. With the list already ordered, lowering the number of fragments that reach the prompt cuts tokens and distraction, because more information is not monotonically better. The distinction against raising top_k is that this lever moves recall, which is no longer the bottleneck, and it gets more expensive in the window of highest traffic.

RULE: Recall says whether the fragment is there; MRR says whether it arrives at the top. With high recall and low MRR, reorder and trim instead of retrieving more.

TRAP: Treating an ordering problem as if it were a coverage problem and raising top_k, which adds tokens and distraction without moving the position of the right fragment.

TRY IT: Take fifty labeled queries from your system and compute MRR as well as recall, then run the same queries with a reranking pass over 150 candidates and compare both numbers along with the 95th percentile of the retrieval step.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/capabilities-contextual-embeddings-guide https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/capabilities-retrieval-augmented-generation-guide

questions.question: At AndesWare an agent writes the description of every pull request and writes it straight into the ticket system field through a tool, with no intermediate step where the text could be cleaned. That field shows plain text, and the 400 developers open about 600 requests a week. The system prompt has accumulated a list of formatting prohibitions, and headers, bullets and the usual opening sentence keep arriving anyway. Tomás has to fix this in the current iteration. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a new prohibition for every formatting element that shows up, to cover the cases the current list does not yet name.
options.feedback: It is the usual reflex and it half works: the documented guidance is to say what output you want instead of listing what you do not want.

options.label: B
options.text: Describe the desired output and its purpose, and write the prompt itself in that same style, with no formatting, instead of banning elements.
options.feedback: Correct: describing the form you want and explaining what it is for lets the model generalize, and removing formatting from the prompt reduces formatting in the response.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the agent up to the most capable model of the family, which follows formatting instructions more precisely than the current one.
options.feedback: Moving up a model is a capability lever, expensive in an organization that controls spend per team, and here the instruction itself is the problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a step that strips the markdown from the response before it is saved into the ticket system field.
options.feedback: Cleaning afterward is a valid answer when that intermediate step exists; here the agent writes straight through the tool and the cause remains untouched.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the model responds better to a description of the output you want than to a list of prohibitions, and better still when it is told what that form is for, because from the explanation it generalizes to the cases the list does not name. The documentation illustrates it with this very case: instead of banning markdown, ask for a response made of prose paragraphs. To that it adds a less obvious technique: the style of the prompt carries over to the style of the response, so removing headers and bullets from the prompt itself lowers the amount of formatting in the output. The distinction against cleaning afterward is that post-processing only exists if there is somewhere to do it, and here the tool writes straight into the ticket.

RULE: Describe the output you want and say what you want it for: one positive instruction with a reason beats three loose prohibitions.

TRAP: Answering each unwanted format with a new prohibition, when what fixes the form is describing the expected output and writing the prompt in that same style.

TRY IT: Turn every prohibition in your prompt into a sentence that describes the desired output with its reason, remove the formatting from the prompt itself, and count in twenty descriptions before and after how many carry headers or bullets.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency

questions.question: A team puts its human review control in the "canUseTool" callback of the Agent SDK and, to move faster, adds allow rules for the read tools and works in acceptEdits mode. What is wrong with that design?

options.label: A
options.text: The callback runs but cannot deny the call: it only records the decision the permission rules had already made before it.
options.feedback: The callback can deny a call; the problem is not what it is able to do, but that there are calls that never reach it.

options.label: B
options.text: Calls approved at an earlier step never reach the callback and skip that check silently; whatever must always run belongs in a hook.
options.feedback: Correct: a tool approved by an allow rule, by acceptEdits or by bypassPermissions skips the callback, and the documentation says to put whatever must run on every call in a PreToolUse hook.

options.label: C
options.text: Deny rules are evaluated after the callback, so a decision to permit taken there cancels out what the organization had already denied.
options.feedback: The documented order is the reverse: hooks, deny, ask, permission mode, allow, and only then the callback, so nothing decided there overwrites a deny rule.

options.label: D
options.text: The callback is consulted only for tools from MCP servers, so the built-in tools fall outside human review entirely.
options.feedback: The callback does not discriminate by where the tool comes from; what sidelines it is a prior approval, whether it comes from a rule, a mode or a hook.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a human review control is worth exactly as much as the point in the flow where it is hooked in. In the Agent SDK the evaluation order is hooks, deny rules, ask rules, permission mode, allow rules and finally the "canUseTool" callback, so any call approved earlier never reaches it: the check does not fail, it simply does not run, and that is worse because it leaves no trace. Generous allow rules, or a mode that approves on its own such as acceptEdits, are exactly what switch the control off without warning. The documentation gives the alternative: whatever has to run on every call, with no exception, goes in a PreToolUse hook, which executes ahead of all the other steps.

RULE: Whatever must run on every call goes in a PreToolUse hook: the "canUseTool" callback sees nothing that was approved before it.

TRAP: Assuming a permission callback is a universal gate, when any earlier approval keeps it from running at all.

TRY IT: Run your agent with an allow rule for one tool and a log line inside the callback: that call prints nothing; then move the check to a PreToolUse hook and repeat the test.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud transcribes and structures the consultation notes of its 40 clinics: some 9,000 a day, with a cost per note that finance has already fixed and an obligation for the clinician to review the structured note in the same shift. Mateo is going to break that work into units delegated to subagents and wants to avoid the mistakes he already saw in another project. Which TWO decomposition criteria should he apply? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Write for each delegated unit its objective, the expected output format, the sources it may use and the limits of the task.
options.feedback: Correct: with no objective, no output format, no guidance on sources and no clear limits, subagents duplicate work, leave gaps or fail to find what was needed.

options.label: B
options.text: Split the work into successive phases of the same process and assign one of them to each subagent, with its own prompt.
options.feedback: Splitting by phases of the same work is the most expensive cut: every handoff re-explains what came before, and the coordination cost eats the benefit.

options.label: C
options.text: Scale the effort to the case: a single call for the short notes and wide decomposition only for the complex consultations.
options.feedback: Correct: effort scales with the complexity of the case, and spending a wide decomposition on a short note is overinvestment that shows up immediately when the cost per note is fixed.

options.label: D
options.text: Launch one subagent per note, so that each note gets its own clean context, isolated from all the rest.
options.feedback: One subagent per note looks tidy, but on short tasks the cost of delegating exceeds the benefit, and the daily volume multiplies that cost.

options.label: E
options.text: Let the model decide how many subagents to launch on each note, with no cap, so that it adapts to the case.
options.feedback: Leaving the decision open and with no cap produces exactly the known failure of launching many subagents for simple work.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a decomposition works when each unit can be worked with isolated context and when the brief that goes with it is complete. That is why the two correct measures are independent of each other: one defines what each delegated unit carries, with an objective, an output format, sources and task limits, and the other decides how much decomposition each case deserves, reserving the wide deployment for the complex work and resolving the short work in a single call. The distinction against splitting by phases is that the cut follows the process and not the context: every handoff between phases pays coordination and loses whatever the previous link failed to anticipate.

RULE: Every delegated unit carries an objective, a format, its sources and its limits; and the size of the decomposition matches the difficulty of the case.

TRAP: Assuming that decomposition always improves things: on short tasks the cost of delegating exceeds what it saves.

TRY IT: Take the brief you hand a subagent today and check whether it has all four parts: objective, output format, permitted sources and limits; add the one that is missing and compare the results.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them

questions.question: Yaguareté Logística runs an MCP server over stdio on the machine of each of its 60 customs brokers; that server queries the customs systems of four countries and takes its credentials from the environment variables of each machine. The customs audit demands being able to say which broker originated each tariff classification, and sustaining four integrations across 60 machines already costs a week of work per release. Joaquín proposes publishing a single remote server over Streamable HTTP. What changes with that migration, beyond centralizing maintenance?

options.label: A
options.text: The tool definitions will have to be rewritten, because the HTTP transport uses a definition schema different from the one stdio uses.
options.feedback: The transport changes how messages travel, not how tools are declared: the definition is the same in both cases, so that work does not exist.

options.label: B
options.text: Latency per call will drop, because the server moves to data center infrastructure instead of running on each person's machine.
options.feedback: Centralizing does not shorten the path: it adds a network hop and one more dependency on the first turn, so if latency moves at all, it moves up.

options.label: C
options.text: Each broker will keep authenticating with the environment variables on their own machine, which is what the specification indicates for remote servers.
options.feedback: That is precisely what the specification indicates for stdio, and it inverts it for HTTP: a remote server exposes authorization of its own instead of trusting the client's environment.

options.label: D
options.text: The server will have to implement its own authorization over OAuth, with protected resource metadata and tokens validated for its audience.
options.feedback: Correct: authorization follows the transport, so a server over HTTP has to conform to the authorization specification, and that is also what makes it possible to attribute each classification to a broker.

questions.explanation:
The general rule in MCP is that authorization follows the transport: implementations over stdio do not follow the authorization specification and take their credentials from the environment, while implementations over HTTP have to conform to it. Migrating from one local server per machine to a shared remote one does not change the tool definitions and does not shorten latency, but it turns authentication into the server's job: protected resource metadata, tokens issued for that server, and audience validation on every request. That is exactly what the audit asks for, because identity stops being the machine's and becomes the caller's. The distinction against keeping the environment variables is that the practice belongs to the transport being abandoned.

RULE: Authorization travels with the transport: stdio takes credentials from the environment, HTTP forces you to stand up OAuth and validate the audience of every token.

TRAP: Assuming that changing transport is an infrastructure move, when what changes owner is authentication.

TRY IT: Review the configuration of your MCP servers and classify them by transport; for each one over HTTP, check whether it publishes its protected resource metadata and whether it rejects tokens whose audience is not itself.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture

questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro is going to automate the arrival notice that three people assemble by hand for each vessel today. The sponsor says the system has to work well; the head of operations says it must never get the berthing window wrong. Five weeks remain until the first trial and both of them sign off on acceptance. Camila, the solutions architect, needs to turn that into something that can be verified. How should she obtain the criteria?

options.label: A
options.text: Take the notices that went out wrong or late in recent months, turn them into the acceptance set and agree it with both.
options.feedback: Correct: the cases that already failed in the operation are the best source of criteria, because they describe the real distribution of the work and get both signatories agreeing on concrete examples instead of adjectives.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask each of them for their list of requirements in writing and consolidate the two lists into a single acceptance document.
options.feedback: Consolidating lists produces a document with two wishes and no measure: working well and never getting it wrong cannot be verified as they are written.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a prototype in two weeks and use whatever fails in the demonstration as the definition of the system's acceptance criteria.
options.feedback: A prototype reveals requirements, but it ties the definition of success to what that prototype did on that day, and it consumes two of the five weeks available.

options.label: D
options.text: Wait until the operations team has labeled a thousand notices before fixing any acceptance criterion at all.
options.feedback: A thousand labeled cases give a solid base, but a set of twenty to fifty real cases is enough to start and arrives inside the deadline.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that acceptance criteria come from real failures and not from statements of intent: twenty to fifty cases taken from what already went wrong are enough to start and describe the true distribution of the work. That set turns working well and never getting it wrong into something verifiable, and it doubles as a common language between the sponsor and the head of operations, who stop arguing about adjectives and start arguing about cases. The distinction against consolidating the lists of requirements is that those lists cannot be measured, and with five weeks ahead the team needs a definition of success that exists from Monday.

RULE: Take the criteria from real failures: twenty to fifty cases that already went wrong are worth more than two lists of wishes.

TRAP: Confusing gathering requirements with gathering opinions: with no cases, each signatory understands something different by working well.

TRY IT: Ask for the last twenty cases your team had to correct by hand and write for each one what the system should have done: that is already your first acceptance set.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/define-success

questions.question: The case-law search assistant at Bastión Legal holds sessions of up to 25 turns with each lawyer. Even when the question is whether a precedent applies or not, the answer always comes back as a five-section memo with all the reasoning. Each practice group has a monthly token cap that ran out before month end two months in a row, and the firm bills by the hour, so the wait costs too. Malena has to cut consumption without losing precision in the answers. What is the right move?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower max_tokens until the memo fits inside the cap, and accept that some answers get cut off before the conclusion.
options.feedback: That cap is invisible to the model, so it does not lead it to economize: it cuts text already billed, sometimes mid-sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask for the answer with a limit in sentences or paragraphs, and keep the long memo for when the lawyer asks for it.
options.feedback: Correct: limits in sentences or paragraphs work better than limits in words, and shortening the output also lowers the input of every turn that follows.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask in the system prompt that no answer go past 150 words, which is the length the firm considers acceptable.
options.feedback: A cap in words is the least effective version of the same idea, because the model counts tokens and not words as it writes.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower the effort of the model so that it reasons less and naturally returns answers that are shorter than the ones it gives today.
options.feedback: Lowering effort reduces the volume of reasoning, but it does not reliably shorten the visible response, which is what consumes the budget here.

questions.explanation:
The general rule in a long conversation is that output is also input: every token the model writes comes back as part of the context in all the turns that follow, so an unnecessary memo is paid many times over in a session of 25 turns. That is why the right lever acts on what is asked for, not on what is cut off. The documentation is specific about how to ask for it: since the model counts tokens and not words, a limit in sentences or paragraphs guides better than a number of words. The distinction against lowering the effort is that effort moves the volume of reasoning and does not reliably shorten the visible response, and against max_tokens, that this cut discards work that has already been billed.

RULE: In a conversation, what the model writes you pay again as input on every turn: ask for length in sentences or paragraphs, not in words.

TRAP: Asking for a maximum number of words or lowering max_tokens believing it amounts to asking for a short answer: the model does not count words and does not see the cap.

TRY IT: Take a real session of twenty turns, add up the output_tokens and see what part of the input of the last turn is your own earlier answers; repeat asking for a paragraph of three sentences and compare the two totals.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence

questions.question: The Siete Lagos Viajes changes and cancellations assistant finished its pilot with 200 requests and reached the agreed accuracy threshold. The high season starts in five weeks and multiplies the volume tenfold; the sponsor wants it enabled for the 40 advisers next week. The platform team has no out-of-hours on-call, nobody has measured the cost per request at high volume, and the rollback procedure is not written down. What is the right thing to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable it now, because the agreed accuracy threshold is the condition the pilot had to meet in order to move on to production.
options.feedback: The accuracy threshold is one of the conditions and not the only one: moving to production also means closing out the operational readiness and the risk controls.

options.label: B
options.text: Extend the pilot with another 200 requests to confirm the accuracy before exposing it to the volume of the high season.
options.feedback: More cases of the same kind reinforce a dimension already satisfied and say nothing about the cost, the stability or the rollback at ten times the volume.

options.label: C
options.text: First close out the missing operating conditions: cost and stability at high volume, on-call cover and a rollback procedure.
options.feedback: Correct: a pilot moves to production when it meets the performance thresholds and the operation is also ready, with support available, stability proven at the expected volume and risk controls in place.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep it as an internal reference tool through the whole high season and decide on enabling it once the peak is over.
options.feedback: Postponing until after the peak removes the risk and the benefit too: the value of the assistant lies precisely in the season where the volume grows.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that moving from pilot to production does not depend on performance alone: there are three families of conditions, the performance thresholds (accuracy, response time and cost efficiency), the operational readiness (system stability, support available and a trained team) and the risk management infrastructure, with its controls and its way back. Only the first is closed here, and the peak of the high season is precisely where the other two fail. The distinction against enabling it now is that the accuracy threshold was measured on 200 requests and under conditions the peak does not reproduce.

RULE: A pilot graduates to production on three conditions: measured performance, a prepared operation and risk control, not the first one alone.

TRAP: Taking the accuracy threshold as the single gate to production and discovering at the peak that there was no on-call and no way back.

TRY IT: Write down the three production conditions for a system of yours: the measured performance threshold, who answers out of hours and how it is rolled back; the one you cannot complete is the one you are missing.

SOURCE: https://assets.anthropic.com/m/66daaa23018ab0fd/original/Anthropic-enterprise-ebook-digital.pdf

questions.question: The system prompt of Banco Altamar's digital banking assistant carries the internal thresholds that trigger fraud verification and the fee waiver limits the assistant is allowed to offer. A red team exercise got the assistant to reproduce part of those rules for a customer. The risk policy forbids those thresholds from leaving the bank, the committee wants a measure in production by the next close, and the weekly quality evaluation cannot get worse. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add an explicit instruction to the system prompt never to reveal its instructions, and consider the risk closed with that single measure.
options.feedback: Such an instruction lowers the risk somewhat, but no prompting technique is foolproof and the sensitive data still sits inside the prompt, within reach of the next attempt.

options.label: B
options.text: Rewrite the entire system prompt with leak-resistant techniques before touching anything else, because that is where the sensitive content sits.
options.feedback: This is a documented technique, but the documentation leaves it for after monitoring and output filtering, and warns that the complexity it adds can degrade performance on the rest of the task.

options.label: C
options.text: Trust the model to refuse, because the platform classifiers already filter the vast majority of jailbreak and prompt leak attempts.
options.feedback: Those classifiers do cut jailbreaks sharply, but the documentation warns that they do not stop all of them, and a prompt leak does not need an openly malicious attempt.

options.label: D
options.text: Filter the output in post-processing, monitor the responses, and take the thresholds the assistant does not need out of the prompt.
options.feedback: Correct: the documentation puts monitoring and output filtering ahead of any attempt to harden the prompt, and recommends leaving out unnecessary proprietary details.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for reducing prompt leak is to attack first what costs no quality: monitor the responses, filter the output in post-processing, and keep out of the prompt the proprietary details the system does not need. The documentation is explicit about that order, because hardening the prompt adds complexity that can degrade performance on the rest of the task, and here the weekly quality evaluation is a firm constraint. None of these measures is foolproof, as the documentation itself says, which is one more reason to remove from the prompt what should not be there. The distinction against rewriting the system prompt is one of sequence and cost: it is the most expensive measure in quality terms and the slowest to reach production.

RULE: Against prompt leak, monitor and filter the output first and take out what is not needed; hardening the prompt comes later, because it costs quality.

TRAP: Treating a confidentiality instruction written inside the prompt as if it were a control, when the sensitive data is still sitting there.

TRY IT: Ask your assistant in five different ways to repeat its instructions; then add an output filter that looks for your internal terms and run the same five tests again.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-prompt-leak

questions.question: Filing classification at Agencia Nacional de Ingresos resolves each case with five tool calls in strict order: validate the taxpayer, fetch the filing, compare it against the previous return, classify it and record the result. Each call depends on what the model concludes from the one before, and the agent exposes only those five tools. There are 9,000 cases a day and the platform team wants to cut input tokens without losing accuracy. Nicolás proposes turning on programmatic tool calling. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn it on for the whole flow: the measured savings of 20 to 40% of input tokens apply to any agent that has several tools in play.
options.feedback: Those savings are measured in agents that spread work across many calls and take back bulky results; this chain has neither of those two things.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the calls direct: in strictly sequential chains, where each step depends on the prior reasoning, the technique saves nothing.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the documented weak case for programmatic calling, where accuracy does not move and cost rises by around 8%. The saving is on another lever.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on tool search with defer_loading so the definitions of the five tools do not take up context on every case handled.
options.feedback: Deferring definitions pays off with large catalogs; with five tools that are always used, search adds an extra round trip and there are no spare definitions to remove.

options.label: D
options.text: Split the five steps across five specialized subagents so that each one works with a far smaller context of its own.
options.feedback: Splitting by phase creates handoffs that lose context and multiplies tokens by 3 to 10 times: it is the decomposition by problem that is worth avoiding.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that each kind of bloat has its own lever and none of them works outside its shape: programmatic calling takes tool results out of the context, and it pays off when the agent spreads work across many calls or takes back bulky responses. Here the flow is a chain of five steps where the model needs to read each result to decide the next one, and that is the documented weak case: accuracy does not change and cost rises by around 8%. With five tools used on every case, there are no definitions to defer either. If input savings are what you want, they are in the stable prefix of the prompt and in the size of what the tools return, not in changing the invocation mechanism.

RULE: Match the lever to the shape of the work: programmatic calling pays off in fans of calls, not in chains where each step waits for the one before.

TRAP: Extrapolating a saving measured in agents with many tools and large results to a short, strictly sequential chain.

TRY IT: Take a week of your agent's log and count how many tool calls happen in parallel and how large the average result is; if almost all of them are sequential and short, this is not your lever.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/programmatic-tool-calling

questions.question: The after-sales agent at Mistral Retail carries a stable prefix of about 20,000 tokens with return policies, typified reasons and examples. Every response is forced against a fixed schema with structured outputs, because it feeds the ticket system. In the promotional season the customer takes between eight and twenty-five minutes to find the order number, and the panel shows cache writes on almost every turn. The agent answers live and there is a target cost per conversation. What is the right move?

options.label: A
options.text: Hold the prefix with a maintenance request every four minutes, with max_tokens at 0, while the customer looks for the order.
options.feedback: Warming is a real technique, but the request with max_tokens at 0 is rejected precisely when the workload uses structured outputs, thinking enabled or a forced tool.

options.label: B
options.text: Stay with the short duration and accept the writes, because writing the short cache costs less than writing the long one.
options.feedback: The multiplier of the short write is lower, but with pauses of eight to twenty-five minutes you pay that write on almost every turn instead of reading.

options.label: C
options.text: Buy the one-hour duration for the stable prefix, which is indicated when the pauses fall between five minutes and an hour.
options.feedback: Correct: with that distribution of pauses the long duration is the documented option, and it is also the intended way out when the workload prevents warming the cache.

options.label: D
options.text: Group the conversations of the day and send them all through the Message Batches API to keep the 50% discount on the tokens.
options.feedback: The batch discount is real, but processing is asynchronous and the customer is waiting on the other side of the conversation.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for choosing the cache duration is to count the pauses: when an appreciable share of the gaps falls between five minutes and an hour, and almost none exceeds it, the long duration pays off despite its higher write multiplier. Here there is also a constraint that closes the discussion: the cheap alternative, holding the prefix alive with maintenance requests, is rejected in workloads that force an output schema, enable thinking or force a tool, and the documentation itself points to buying the one-hour duration in those cases. The distinction against staying with the short duration is that its lower multiplier only helps if there are reads: with pauses of eight to twenty-five minutes you pay a write almost every time.

RULE: When you cannot warm the cache, buy it: the maintenance request does not work with structured outputs, thinking enabled or a forced tool.

TRAP: Assuming that the trick of holding the prefix alive works for any workload, when it is rejected precisely in the ones that force an output schema.

TRY IT: Send a request with max_tokens at 0 against your real prompt with the forced schema and watch it be rejected; then count across twenty conversations how many cache writes you pay with the short duration and with the long one.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

questions.question: The control room assistant at Pehuén Energía answers questions about technical manuals thirty years old, and the fragment retrieved for each query exceeds twenty thousand tokens. Audit found recommendations that cite steps which do not exist in the manual. During the regulatory maintenance window the operator needs the answer in under ten seconds, and every recommendation is recorded for the regulator. Andrés, the technical lead, has to close the problem before the next window. What should he implement?

options.label: A
options.text: Run every query three times in parallel and return the answer that matches in two of the three runs.
options.feedback: Comparing several runs is a hallucination detector, not a correction, and it triples the spend and the wait inside a window of ten seconds.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the assistant up to the most capable model of the family so that the procedure comes out right on the first answer.
options.feedback: More capability helps with reasoning problems, but the invented step is not in the model: it is in the missing grounding to the manual it is handed.

options.label: C
options.text: Extract the verbatim quotes from the manual first and require every step to be backed by one, retracting whatever lacks it.
options.feedback: Correct: with long documents, extracting the quotes first anchors the answer, and verification with retraction leaves out whatever has no support.

options.label: D
options.text: Let the assistant fill in with its general knowledge the steps the manual does not cover, as long as it says so.
options.feedback: Declaring the origin is better than hiding it, but in an audited procedure the documented instruction runs the other way: stick to the documents provided and admit that information is missing.

questions.explanation:
The general rule against unsupported claims is to ground the answer in the source text: with documents over twenty thousand tokens, the documented technique is to ask for the verbatim quotes first and only then the answer, and to make it auditable by requiring every claim to carry its quote, retracting the one that cannot get it. That also fits the record the regulator asks for, because it leaves a trail of which part of the manual each step rests on. The distinction against running the query several times is one of function: comparing runs detects inconsistency, it does not correct it, and it multiplies cost and wait inside a window of ten seconds. None of these techniques removes the problem entirely, so the review by the operator remains part of the design.

RULE: Quote first and claim second: whatever cannot be supported by a quote from the document gets retracted, not rounded off.

TRAP: Treating the comparison of several runs as a cure for hallucinations, when it is only a detector and on top of that multiplies cost and wait.

TRY IT: Take ten queries from the last maintenance window, ask for the manual quotes first and the recommendation afterward, and count how many steps are left with no quote to back them: those are the ones that go out unsupported today.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations

questions.question: The internal help desk at Agencia Nacional de Ingresos migrated all its material to progressive disclosure, and the agent now starts like this: {"contexto_inicial": "empty", "skills": 31, "tools": 40, "defer_loading": true}. Among the Skills there is one called mapa-sistemas, with the list of internal systems and what each one is for. Cost per session dropped by half, but on 40% of queries the agent asks the person which system to search in, or queries the wrong one and takes three turns to correct itself, against a target of resolution in two turns. Which change fixes the design?

options.label: A
options.text: Load the 31 procedures back into the system prompt, so the agent has all the material in view from the first turn.
options.feedback: It restores orientation, but it puts back at startup everything the migration had taken out: the problem is knowing where to look, not having the full procedure in front of you.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise to twenty the number of results that tool search returns, so the agent sees more options before it chooses.
options.feedback: Seeing more candidates helps when the agent searches well and chooses badly. Here it does not even know which system holds the answer, and twenty more definitions only take up context.

options.label: C
options.text: Load the systems map up front and leave the procedures and the tool definitions deferred, to be discovered by searching.
options.feedback: Correct: autonomous exploration works when the agent has enough initial context to know where to look, and that orientation is the one thing it cannot discover by searching.

options.label: D
options.text: Turn on compaction so the context does not grow while the agent explores systems and can sustain the three turns without degrading.
options.feedback: Compaction summarizes a context that has already grown. Here the context is emptier than it should be, and what is missing is orientation, not free space.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the choice between monolithic context and progressive disclosure is made by type of content, not by whole system. Autonomous search fails in a very specific way: not because of poor embeddings, but because the agent does not know where to look, and that is corrected with input context, not with more search capacity. That is why well-built agents keep their orientation document loaded up front and defer the procedures, the reference files and the tool definitions. The distinction against putting everything back in the system prompt is that only the map turns out to be impossible to discover by searching; the rest is discoverable, and that is where the saving is preserved.

RULE: Load up front what the agent cannot discover on its own, starting with the map of where each thing is; leave the rest for when it is needed.

TRAP: Applying progressive disclosure to orientation as well, which is precisely the context the agent needs in order to know what to search for.

TRY IT: Open a session with your agent's current startup context and ask it to list which systems it can query and when it uses each one; if it cannot answer without searching, that orientation is what you are missing up front.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents https://claude.com/blog/how-claude-code-works-in-large-codebases-best-practices-and-where-to-start

questions.question: An AndesWare agent runs long refactoring sessions over the monorepo, with a cached prefix of around 60,000 tokens. Halfway through a migration, Sofía needs to add a rule that did not exist before: from here on, do not touch the generated files of one directory. Today the team rebuilds the system field and resends the conversation, and each team has a monthly spend cap that this practice burns through fast. The model in use supports mid-conversation system messages. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Edit the system field with the new rule and resend the whole conversation, as the team has been doing until now.
options.feedback: A change in system invalidates that level and everything that comes after it, so the session pays again to write the 60,000 tokens.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the rule to the description of the editing tool, so that it travels with every call the agent makes on files.
options.feedback: Changing a tool definition invalidates the entire cache, and the description describes the tool, not the rules of this session.

options.label: C
options.text: Restart the session with a system prompt that already includes the rule and load the context of the refactor in progress again.
options.feedback: Starting over complies with the rule, but it loses the state of the migration and pays the full write of the prefix anyway.

options.label: D
options.text: Append a system message inside messages at the point where the rule starts to apply, without touching the system field.
options.feedback: Correct: the instruction enters with operator authority at the point where it is needed, and the cached prefix stays intact.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the cache is computed over the prefix in the order tools, system, messages, and a change at one level invalidates that level and all the levels after it. Editing the system field halfway through a session is therefore the most expensive way to add an instruction: it forces the whole prefix to be written again. The mechanism designed for instructions that appear late is to append a system message inside messages, at the point of the conversation where the instruction starts to make sense: the text keeps operator authority and the cached prefix is untouched. questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro runs three services against the API: the manifest validator, the agent that coordinates with shipping lines, and an overnight reconciliation process. All three use the same organization API key, created two years ago and kept in the vault; rotation is manual and nobody remembers the last one. The port audit requires that no static credential live longer than twelve hours and that every call be attributable to the service that originated it. The three services already run on a platform with an identity of its own. What should you propose?

options.label: A
options.text: Federate the identity of each service so it exchanges its platform token for short-lived credentials tied to its service account.
options.feedback: Correct: federation issues short-lived tokens from the identity the platform already signs, removes the static key, and leaves every call attributed to its service account.

options.label: B
options.text: Rotate the key every twelve hours with an automatic script and distribute the new one to the three services through the port's vault.
options.feedback: Rotating often shrinks the exposure window, but the credential is still static and shared: it neither meets the lifetime limit nor lets you tell who called.

options.label: C
options.text: Issue one key per service, each one limited to its own workspace, and review its expiry date at every quarterly audit of the port.
options.feedback: Separating keys per service and scoping them to a workspace improves blast radius and attribution, but they are still long-lived static credentials, which is what the audit forbids.

options.label: D
options.text: Generate a long-lived token for the automated processes and store it encrypted, with access limited to the platform team.
options.feedback: That token exists and serves processes with nobody in front of them, but it is long-lived by design: it changes the format of the credential without shortening its life.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a long-lived static credential is not fixed by rotating it more often: it is replaced by an identity that is verifiable on every call. Workload identity federation does exactly that: the service presents the token its platform signs, a rule matches it to a service account, and it gets back a short-lived token with the minimum scope. The shared secret disappears and every call is attributed to a specific service, which are the two requirements of the audit. When migrating it is also worth cleaning the environment, because an API key forgotten in a variable takes precedence over federation and cancels it silently. The distinction against one key per service is that this option improves attribution but leaves static credentials alive.

RULE: Against static credentials, federate identities: let every workload exchange its platform token for a short-lived one with a scope of its own.

TRAP: Confusing rotating a key with eliminating the static credential: rotation shortens the window, but the shared secret is still there and still identifies nobody.

TRY IT: List your organization's active API keys with their creation date and their scope, and mark the ones shared by two or more services: each of those is a credential that federation can replace.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/workload-identity-federation https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/administration-api

questions.question: Colibrí Pay's antifraud check runs inside payment authorization: the issuer cuts off at 700 ms at the 95th percentile and the step with Claude consumes 480 today. Nicolás proposes enabling extended thinking with a budget of 16,000 tokens to bring down false positives, which cost the business more than the fraud they catch. Volume is 1.2 million authorizations a day and it triples every year. Which configuration is the right one?

options.label: A
options.text: Leave the inline check without thinking and send the doubtful transactions to a second asynchronous review with a generous budget.
options.feedback: Correct: the latency budget rules the inline path, and depth of reasoning is paid where nobody is waiting, over the subset that truly needs it.

options.label: B
options.text: Enable thinking with the minimum budget of 1,024 tokens on the inline check, which is the smallest reasoning spend possible.
options.feedback: The minimum is real, but the budget is a target and not a strict cap: you add tokens and latency on every authorization, with 220 ms of headroom and no guarantee of staying inside it.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on streaming on the inline check so the decision starts arriving sooner and the issuer does not get to cut the authorization off.
options.feedback: Streaming improves perceived latency when somebody is reading the response. An issuer waiting for a complete decision perceives nothing until the last token.

options.label: D
options.text: Raise effort to its highest level on the inline check so the model reasons better without declaring a thinking budget.
options.feedback: Effort governs how many tokens the model spends on text, on tools and on thinking, so raising it pushes in the opposite direction from the 700 ms budget.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a latency constraint applies to the path where somebody is waiting, not to the whole system: inside authorization there are 220 ms of headroom, and extended reasoning spends time exactly there, with a budget that is in addition a target and not a strict cap. Splitting the flow into two stages preserves the fast decision and takes the deep analysis to the doubtful subset, where it can be paid in seconds or in minutes. That attacks the real business cost, which is the false positives, without risking the issuer's cutoff. The distinction against enabling thinking with the minimum budget is that this option spends latency on every authorization to gain depth only on the fraction that needs it.

RULE: Put the depth where nobody is waiting: a short decision inline and long reasoning in the asynchronous review of the doubtful cases.

TRAP: Treating the thinking budget as a guaranteed cap, when it is a target, and spending it on every request to improve only a fraction of the cases.

TRY IT: Measure the 95th percentile of your inline step with and without thinking over the same hundred transactions, and compute what percentage of decisions would change with extended reasoning: that fraction is the one that justifies a second stage.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency

questions.question: The monthly bill of the fraud detection agent at Zafiro Seguros tripled, while request volume grew barely 20%. Nobody changed the prompt or the model, the quality of the flags is what it always was, and response times did not move. The agent runs between fifteen and thirty turns per case and answers online, because an analyst waits for the flag before releasing the payment. Ignacio has a week to explain the deviation. Where should you look first?

options.label: A
options.text: At the model: resolve the first filter with a cheaper one and escalate to the current model only the cases that stay doubtful.
options.feedback: It is a valid architecture, but it changes quality and budget at once, and it does not explain why the spend tripled with nothing changed.

options.label: B
options.text: At the sending mode: moving the work to the Message Batches API leaves 50% of the cost on every class of token.
options.feedback: The discount is real and significant, but the process is asynchronous, and here an analyst waits for the flag before releasing the payment.

options.label: C
options.text: At the split of the input: compute what part of each request is read from cache and find what changed in the shared prefix.
options.feedback: Correct: in an agent the cache read should dominate the input, and when it does not, something is breaking the prefix on every turn.

options.label: D
options.text: At the output: lowering max_tokens bounds the response, which is the most expensive class of token per unit in any model.
options.feedback: Output costs several times more per token, but in an agent of thirty turns the bulk of the spend is input, and that cap discards work already billed.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the cost of a request decomposes into five token counters, and in an agent loop the cache read is usually the largest of them, because every turn resends the whole conversation. When that term does not dominate, what you have is a prefix that stopped matching: one block that changes on every request, placed before the breakpoint, is enough to pay writes where there used to be reads, and the cost of an agent grows steeply with the number of turns. That is why the first measurement is the split of the input, not the choice of model. The distinction against batching is that the discount exists but demands asynchrony, and here the flag blocks the release of a payment.

RULE: Before changing model or architecture, look at the input split: in an agent the cache read should dominate, and if it does not, something is breaking the prefix.

TRAP: Looking for the saving in a cheaper model or in the batch discount before checking that the cache you already pay for is hitting.

TRY IT: Take a hundred requests from one day and compute what fraction of total input comes from cache_read_input_tokens; if it falls well short of the bulk, compare two consecutive requests and find the first point where the prefix stops matching.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación packaged the material generation guides of eleven degree programs as Agent Skills and is considering leaving them all available in the same workspace, with a very tight budget per student. Before deciding, Paula reviews with the team what having many Skills installed implies. Which of the following statements about Agent Skills is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The instruction body of every installed Skill is loaded when the session starts, so having eleven makes every request more expensive.
options.feedback: Correct as the answer to the question, because it is the false statement: before being activated, each Skill takes up only its name and its description, around one hundred tokens.

options.label: B
options.text: The description is written in the third person and says what the Skill does and when to use it, because it is what picks among many.
options.feedback: This one is true: the description is injected into the system prompt and works as the routing key among dozens of available Skills.

options.label: C
options.text: A script included in a Skill does not enter the context: only the output it produces when it runs consumes tokens.
options.feedback: This one is true: the code of the script is not loaded into the context window, which is why packaged material that goes unused costs nothing.

options.label: D
options.text: Custom Skills do not sync across surfaces: uploading one on a surface does not leave it available on the others.
options.feedback: This one is true: portability is limited and each surface keeps its own publication and sharing scope.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is progressive disclosure in three levels: the name and the description of each Skill are always loaded at the start and cost around one hundred tokens per Skill, the instruction body is loaded only when the Skill is activated, and packaged resources cost nothing until someone reads them. That is precisely the property that allows many Skills to be installed with no context penalty, which is what Aurora needs with a tight budget per student. The other three statements describe documented behavior: the description as a routing key in the third person, scripts that contribute only their output, and the lack of synchronization across surfaces.

RULE: A Skill costs its index card until it is used: name and description always, instructions on activation, resources only if they are read.

TRAP: Counting the total size of a Skill as if it were loaded whole at the start, when what takes up context before use is its routing card.

TRY IT: Install two Skills of very different sizes, run a query that activates neither of them, and compare the input_tokens with those of the same query with no Skill available.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices

questions.question: A team invokes Anthropic's evaluation guide, which recommends avoiding human grading wherever possible, in order to drop the review of the recommendations its product delivers to consumers. Why does that argument not hold?

options.label: A
options.text: Because that guide applies only to code evals and not to those that grade free text, which still demand a trained human grader.
options.feedback: The guide does not split by type of content: it ranks grading methods and recommends prioritizing a volume of cases with automated grading.

options.label: B
options.text: Because human grading always beats automated grading in quality, and both reviews are worth sustaining in parallel while there is budget for them.
options.feedback: Human grading is the most flexible and highest-quality method, but the guide itself calls it slow and expensive and asks you to avoid it where automation is possible.

options.label: C
options.text: Because these are two different questions: the guide is about how to grade an eval, and the Usage Policy requires professional review before release.
options.feedback: Correct: how you grade a test set is one thing, and what is required before handing a recommendation to a person is another; the evaluation guide does not decide that.

options.label: D
options.text: Because reviewing the eval and reviewing the product are the same thing, and the one requiring it is the infrastructure provider where the system runs.
options.feedback: They are not the same: one measures the system against test cases and the other reviews what a real person will receive, and what requires it is the usage policy you accepted.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is not to mix the question of how you measure your system with the question of what you are obliged to do before delivering an output. The evaluation guide ranks grading methods, puts code-based grading first, recommends avoiding human grading where possible, and prefers many automated cases to a few hand-reviewed ones: all of that is about the test set. The Usage Policy, by contrast, requires a qualified professional to review the content before release when there is advice, a recommendation or a subjective decision that directly affects people. They are different sources with different triggers, and the second one is not satisfied by an eval, however good it is.

RULE: Avoiding human grading applies to your evals, not to what you deliver: in high-risk cases the prior review remains mandatory.

TRAP: Extrapolating a recommendation about how to grade a test set into an obligation about what gets handed to a person.

TRY IT: Write two lines for a flow of your own: how you grade the eval, and who reviews the output before a user sees it; if the second line is empty, that is the gap.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom committed by contract to a first response time in first-level support and misses it at the night peak. Telemetry shows that, in the requests that complete, the time to first token and the total time are still within target. A fraction of the peak requests returns error 529, and the client retries after a fixed wait of thirty seconds. Nobody changed the prompt or the model. What is the most likely cause of the breach?

options.label: A
options.text: It is capacity contention: the 529 signals overload, and what breaks the commitment is the time each fixed retry adds.
options.feedback: Correct: the percentile degrades because of the retries on top of an overload error, not because of the speed of the model, which is still on target.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the generation rate: turning on fast mode raises the output tokens per second during the peak hours.
options.feedback: Fast mode raises the output rate, but the total time of the requests that complete is already inside the committed target.

options.label: C
options.text: It is perception: with streaming the user sees the text sooner and the first response indicator stops being missed at the peak.
options.feedback: Streaming improves the perceived response and the first token, but it does not change when the answer is delivered and does not avoid an overload error.

options.label: D
options.text: It is the effort of the model: lowering the effort shortens generation and brings the committed percentile back within target.
options.feedback: Lowering effort is a legitimate latency lever, but it acts on a generation time that already meets the target.

questions.explanation:
The general rule in a latency diagnosis is to separate work time from wait time: the levers of model, effort, fast mode and streaming act on the first, and here the first already meets the target. Error 529 signals capacity contention at the moment of the peak, and the percentile that is missed is built by the retry policy sitting on top: a fixed wait of thirty seconds adds those full seconds to every affected request. The answers live in how overload is handled, not in the prompt: retries with backoff, priority capacity where a commitment exists, and running off-peak the work that does not need an immediate answer. The distinction against streaming is that it improves what is perceived and not the instant when the answer is actually delivered.

RULE: Separate the error from the slowness: a 529 is missing capacity, and what breaks the commitment is the retry policy that goes on top.

TRAP: Looking for the cause in the speed of the model when what gets added to the percentile is the wait your own retry imposes.

TRY IT: Split in your panel the 95th percentile of the requests answered on the first try from the one of the requests that went through a retry, and see how much of the breach lives only in the second group.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/service-tiers https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency

TRAP: Looking for the cause in the speed of the model when what gets added to the percentile is the wait your own retry imposes.

TRY IT: Split in your panel the 95th percentile of the requests answered on the first try from the one of the requests that went through a retry, and see how much of the breach lives only in the second group.

questions.question: A team applies every documented technique for reducing hallucinations: letting the model say it does not know, asking it for verbatim quotes from the document, and having it withdraw the claim if it cannot find the quote. What remains true according to the documentation?

options.label: A
options.text: With citation grounding the fabrication rate drops to zero, as long as the document sits whole inside the model's context window.
options.feedback: Verbatim quotes anchor the answer to the document and cut fabrication sharply, but the documentation promises a zero rate in no configuration at all.

options.label: B
options.text: The techniques cut hallucinations sharply but do not eliminate them, and validating what is critical falls to whoever builds the system.
options.feedback: Correct: the documentation closes with that warning and asks you to always validate critical information, and the commercial terms put that evaluation on the customer's side.

options.label: C
options.text: Responsibility for evaluating whether the output is fit for the use case passes to the model provider once the commercial terms are signed.
options.feedback: The commercial terms say the opposite: the customer is the one who evaluates whether the output is appropriate for its case, including where human review belongs.

options.label: D
options.text: Verification with several generations of the same question guarantees that any fabricated claim is caught before the end user ever sees it.
options.feedback: Comparing several generations helps spot inconsistencies that suggest fabrication, but agreement across runs does not prove the claim is true either.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that hallucination mitigations are statistical and not guarantees. The documentation lists techniques that work, among them letting the model say it does not know, extracting verbatim quotes before answering about long documents, and requiring it to withdraw the claim if it cannot find the quote, and it closes with an explicit warning: they reduce hallucinations a great deal, but they do not eliminate them, and critical information must always be validated in high-impact decisions. The commercial terms place that evaluation on the customer's side: the customer judges whether the output is appropriate for its case, including where human review is needed, and does not rely on factual statements without checking them. The distinction against believing that grounding closes the problem is that it lowers the probability without taking it to zero.

RULE: Hallucination mitigations lower the probability, they do not take it to zero: what is critical gets validated, and that validation is on you.

TRAP: Confusing a documented reduction of error with a guarantee, and treating as transferred to the provider an evaluation the contract leaves with the customer.

TRY IT: Take ten answers from your system that carry quotes, look each quote up in the source document, and count how many do not appear verbatim or do not support the claim they accompany.
