questions.question: The suite of the fault diagnosis agent at Ceibo Telecom has 400 cases written like this: {"caso": "no data service", "esperado": "call verificar_estado_linea, then consultar_incidencias, then answer exactly: We have detected an incident in your area"}. It fails 38% of the cases, and when someone from the area reviews those failures the conclusion is that the agent resolved the complaint well by another route. The team ships one release a week and cannot sustain manual review on every run. What should you change first?

options.label: A
options.text: Score the produced result with partial credit and leave a single path check, that the state of the line was queried.
options.feedback: Correct: what the agent achieved is what gets graded, and one path check is enough to secure the indispensable step without punishing valid routes.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the exact text and extend the expected sequence with the tools the agent uses today in the cases that are failing.
options.feedback: Copying the observed route makes today's cases pass and fails again with the next valid route the agent finds.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the graders with an llm judge that reads the full transcript of each case and decides whether the complaint was resolved.
options.feedback: A judge adds nuance, but its verdict varies more the longer the text it reads, and 400 transcripts per run are paid at every release.

options.label: D
options.text: Have someone from the area review the 400 cases on every run and settle by hand the differences the grader marks wrong.
options.feedback: Human grading is the highest-quality method, and the documentation asks you to avoid it where possible: it does not sustain a weekly release of 400 cases.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to grade what the agent produced and not the route it took, because agents find valid paths that whoever wrote the test did not anticipate; a suite that pins the sequence of tools and the literal text measures obedience to a script, not resolution of the complaint. The correction is twofold: define what has to be true at the end, with partial credit for multi-step tasks, and keep a single trajectory check for the step that really is indispensable. A 38% failure rate that human review contradicts is a sign of a broken test, not of an incapable agent. The distinction against extending the expected sequence is that this path chases routes forever, and against the llm judge, that it adds variance and cost at every weekly release.

RULE: Grade what the agent achieved, not the road it took: the correct route is the one that resolves the case, not the one imagined by whoever wrote the test.

TRAP: Reading a high failure rate as incapacity of the agent, when what fails is a test that pinned the sequence of tools and the literal text.

TRY IT: Take ten cases that fail and that a person considers resolved, write for each one what has to be true at the end, the diagnosis and the next step, and run them again scoring that result.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud runs an agent that transcribes the consultation note, structures it and loads it into the medical record: five tool steps per visit. When a physician reports that a note came out incomplete, reconstructing what happened takes days. The current telemetry emits one line per model call, shaped like this: span llm_request, duration_ms 2140, model, input_tokens 6100, output_tokens 320. No field links that call to the other four from the same visit. The clinical committee requires that any incident be explained in under 24 hours. Which two instrumentation changes should you make? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Raise telemetry sampling to 100% of visits so that no model call is left out of the log.
options.feedback: Logging everything avoids gaps, but the problem is not missing lines: the lines you already have cannot be grouped by visit.

options.label: B
options.text: Emit a correlation identifier that ties the model call, each tool execution and the final result into one trace.
options.feedback: Correct: an identifier that groups every event of a single request is what lets you reconstruct the execution end-to-end.

options.label: C
options.text: Record for each tool its duration, its call count and its errors, plus whether the run ended up waiting on a person.
options.feedback: Correct: per-tool telemetry is what attributes the lost time and the failure to a specific step, and it is what Anthropic recommends collecting.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep only the final state of the medical record after each run, which is what the committee reviews when a complaint arrives.
options.feedback: Grading the final output is good evaluation practice, but a result with no trace does not say at which agent step the data was lost.

options.label: E
options.text: Query the usage and cost API every minute to follow the spend of each agent step through the day.
options.feedback: That API is the authoritative source for consumption and cost, but it returns totals aggregated by period and does not reconstruct one visit.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that monitoring tells you something is wrong and observability lets you explain what happened in one specific run. For a non-deterministic multi-step agent that takes two different things: a correlation identifier that ties every event of one request into a single trace, and per-tool telemetry with duration, count and errors to locate the step that failed. The difference against raising the sampling rate is that more loose lines do not add up to a story: with no shared identifier they stay events that nobody can group. Keeping only the final state is useful for grading the output, not for locating the failure.

RULE: Instrument to answer what happened in this request: one identifier that ties every event together, and per-tool telemetry with duration, count and errors.

TRAP: Confusing having more logs with having traceability: with no shared identifier, each line describes a step and none describes the request.

TRY IT: Take one real run of your agent and try to reconstruct it from your logs alone: if you cannot link the first model call to the last tool without opening the database, you are missing the correlation identifier.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

questions.question: The Agencia Nacional de Ingresos is standardizing on Claude Code across an internal team of 60 developers. Public procurement rules force it to commit a closed annual amount, and changing that amount afterward takes about six months. Mateo, who runs the platform, has three weeks to hand in the figure. He finds a published average of spend per developer per active day in the documentation. What should he do before he commits the number?

options.label: A
options.text: Multiply the published average by the 60 developers and by the working days in the year, then add a fixed margin to absorb the variation.
options.feedback: The published average describes consumption at other organizations with a different work profile. The documentation itself says to start with a small pilot and establish a baseline before you extend the rollout.

options.label: B
options.text: Run a two or three week pilot with a small group, measure the actual spend per active day, and build the annual figure on that baseline.
options.feedback: Correct: the figure you commit to is built on your own measurement, and a short pilot with usage tracking produces that baseline inside the three weeks available.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask each team to estimate how many daily sessions it expects to use over the year and add up the declared estimates before closing the budget.
options.feedback: Declared estimates help line up expectations, but nobody yet knows how much a real working session consumes, so they add uncertainty instead of reducing it.

options.label: D
options.text: Commit the minimum amount the procurement rules allow and request a budget extension as soon as consumption approaches that limit.
options.feedback: Reserving the minimum looks prudent, but an extension takes months to process and the service would run out of budget mid-year.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a spending commitment is built on your own measurement, not on an external reference. The documentation publishes average cost per developer per active day, and on the same page it says the way to commit a number is to start with a small pilot group and use the tracking tools to establish a baseline before a broad rollout. It also warns that a working session, with file contents, tool calls and multi-step reasoning, consumes far more than a conversation. With six months needed to correct the amount, guessing low has no remedy inside the fiscal year. The distinction against extrapolating the average is that the published number describes organizations with a different usage profile, while the pilot answers for your own and fits in the three weeks available.

RULE: A spending commitment is built on your own measurement: the published average describes other organizations, not yours.

TRAP: Treating a published reference figure as if it were an estimate of your own consumption.

TRY IT: Look at your team's spend per active day over the last week, compare it with the average published in the documentation, and compute how far off the published figure would have put your commitment.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs

questions.question: The assistant that serves Zafiro Seguros brokers answers 4,000 messages a day and hands an underwriter the cases the manual reserves for a person. The monthly panel the team presents to the regulator summarizes performance like this: query comprehension 96%, answer relevance 93%, topic adherence 95%, p95 latency 2.1 s, cost per query 0.004 USD. An audit of 300 conversations found that in one out of nine the assistant resolved on its own a case that belonged with the underwriter, and that none of them shows up as a problem on the panel. Why does the panel not show that failure?

options.label: A
options.text: Because latency is reported at the 95th percentile, and the longest conversations, which are the complex ones, fall outside that cut.
options.feedback: The percentile you pick changes what you see of response time, but no latency metric says whether the case belonged with a person.

options.label: B
options.text: Because every metric grades the answers the assistant issued and none compares what it escalated against what it should have escalated.
options.feedback: Correct: escalation accuracy is computed over the cases that should have been escalated, and without it a case resolved in error never counts as one.

options.label: C
options.text: Because relevance is graded by a judge model, and that judge overrates well-written answers even when they resolve what they should not.
options.feedback: An uncalibrated judge inflates relevance and is worth checking against experts, but even well calibrated it would still score only issued answers.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the panel carries no baseline from the earlier manual process, and without one those percentages cannot be interpreted.
options.feedback: A baseline is what makes a target reachable and comparable, but nothing here is missing to read the numbers: what is missing is a number.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that success criteria come from decomposing the interaction into every task the system has to perform, and handing a case to a person is one of them. The panel metrics measure the quality of what the assistant said: whether it understood, whether it was relevant, whether it stayed on topic, how long it took and what it cost. Escalation accuracy is of a different kind, because it is computed over the set of cases that should have been escalated and compared against the ones that actually were. That comparison is the only way an improper resolution counts as an error. The distinction against the miscalibrated judge is that such a defect would move the numbers that already exist, while here the number does not exist.

RULE: Decompose the interaction into tasks and measure each one: if escalating to a person is a task, escalation accuracy is a metric and not a byproduct.

TRAP: Assuming a panel with many metrics is complete, when all of them measure the answer that was issued and none measures the answer that should never have been.

TRY IT: Take 50 conversations from your agent, mark which ones should have escalated according to your own manual, and compute what share actually did: that number appears on no answer-quality panel.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/customer-support-chat https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

questions.question: The merchandising team at Mistral Retail wrote a Skill with the house format for summarizing reviews and uses it daily from claude.ai. That same format now has to apply in the nightly pipeline that summarizes reviews for 30,000 products through the API before every promotional date. One person maintains the format and it changes several times per season, so Camila does not want the guide traveling copied inside every pipeline request. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Call the Skill that already exists in claude.ai from the API using its identifier, so that both surfaces read the same text.
options.feedback: It looks like the lowest-effort option, but custom Skills do not sync across surfaces: what you upload to one is not available on the other.

options.label: B
options.text: Paste the body of the SKILL.md into the system prompt of every request the nightly pipeline sends to the API.
options.feedback: It works on day one, but it brings back the problem the Skill solves: repeating the guide in every request and keeping two texts that drift apart.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the merchandising team to process the reviews of the best-selling listings in claude.ai and leave the remaining products with no summary.
options.feedback: Prioritizing best sellers is reasonable when capacity is short, but it gives up the volume that justifies the pipeline and leaves the format unaligned.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish the same Skill in the API workspace, versioned from the team repository, and attach it to the pipeline requests.
options.feedback: Correct: each surface needs its own published copy, and in the API a custom Skill is scoped to the workspace, so the pipeline uses it without repeating it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a Skill exists so you do not repeat the same guide in every conversation: you publish it once and it loads when it is needed, instead of traveling inside each prompt. What a Skill does not do is move between surfaces on its own, and the documentation says so explicitly: custom Skills do not sync, so one uploaded to claude.ai is not available in the API. The correct action is therefore to publish the same content in the API workspace, where a custom Skill is scoped to the whole workspace, and to attach it to every pipeline request. The distinction against pasting the SKILL.md into the system prompt is that the alternative brings back the per-request cost and the duplication the Skill was meant to remove.

RULE: Publish the Skill on every surface where it will be used: they do not sync with each other, and in the API a Skill is scoped to the workspace.

TRAP: Treating a Skill as a file shared in the cloud, when each surface keeps its own copy and neither one sees the other.

TRY IT: Upload a minimal Skill on one surface and try to call it from the other by the same name: it will not appear, and you will also confirm that in the API it is attached in the container parameter alongside the code execution tool.

questions.question: Andrés rewrote the alert prioritization instructions for the fraud detector and wants approval at Thursday's committee. He ran the 80-case suite once with each version: the new one scored 0.90 and the current one 0.86. The model, the cases and the graders were identical in both arms, and nothing else changed that week at Zafiro Seguros. Every alert the detector discards in error ends up as a fraudulent claim paid out. What should you do before you take the result to the committee?

options.label: A
options.text: Expand the suite to 200 cases drawn from recent files and repeat the comparison on that larger base.
options.feedback: More cases improve coverage and are worth adding, but they do not answer what is open today: whether that difference shows up again on a rerun.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the approval threshold to 0.95 so that only changes with margin against the business risk get through.
options.feedback: A stricter threshold changes what gets approved, not how noisy the measurement is: with one run per case, 0.95 would be just as uncertain.

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the comparison with several runs per case in both arms and decide on the average of those runs.
options.feedback: Correct: the system is not deterministic, so a single run per case cannot tell a real improvement from run-to-run variation.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the new version to a small slice of traffic and compare real outcomes over the next two weeks.
options.feedback: A canary is the right way to promote a change that is already validated, but here it would ship a difference you do not yet know exists.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a single run of a non-deterministic system says very little: the same task can pass or fail between runs, which is why suites are run several times per case and the case score is the average of those runs. With one run per arm, a gap of four hundredths can be entirely run-to-run variation, and there is no way to separate it from an improvement. Repeating the comparison is cheap next to what one wrongly discarded alert costs. The distinction against the canary is one of order: real traffic confirms a change that already showed signal in the suite, and it is not how you find out whether the signal exists.

RULE: One run is not a measurement: confirm any difference with several runs per case in both arms before you believe the delta.

TRAP: Reading the subtraction of two numbers as an improvement, when neither number was measured enough to support a difference.

TRY IT: Run your suite three times without changing a single thing and watch how much the score moves between runs: that spread is the smallest improvement one run can support.

questions.question: The agent that assembles corporate itineraries at Siete Lagos Viajes queries three wholesalers and closes a typical booking in six or seven turns. The cached prefix, which carries the travel policy of each corporate client, weighs about 30,000 tokens and today is read from cache on almost every request. To cut spend before the high-season peak, Bruno turns on server-side context management with this configuration: {"edits": [{"type": "clear_tool_uses_20250919", "trigger": {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 25000}, "keep": {"type": "tool_uses", "value": 3}}]}. What effect will the change have on cost per booking?

options.label: A
options.text: It will fall in proportion to the context removed, because each clearing takes away tokens that stop being billed on the following turns.
options.feedback: That is the saving the mechanism promises, but it only appears in long sessions, where the context really grows and there is much to discard.

options.label: B
options.text: It will not change, because the placeholder text that replaces each cleared result takes up roughly as much room as the original.
options.feedback: The placeholder exists to tell the model that a clearing happened, but it is one short line: the cleared content does stop occupying context.

options.label: C
options.text: It will rise, because the clearing fires on bookings that never grew and invalidates the cached prefix from the point where it deletes.
options.feedback: Correct: in short sessions there is almost no context to save, and every clearing forces a rewrite of what used to be read from cache.

options.label: D
options.text: It will cut cost and raise accuracy, because the model works with less noise and recovers the itinerary data better.
options.feedback: Degradation in long contexts is real, but these bookings are short: there is no accumulated noise to remove and there is a cache to break.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that context levers only pay off in long sessions: in short runs the measured saving was nil, and context editing ended up costing more than not using it. The reason is twofold. First, if the conversation never grows, there is little to clear. Second, and decisive, clearing invalidates the cached prefix from the point where it deletes, and reading from cache costs a fraction of writing it. With a trigger of 25,000 tokens and a stable prefix of 30,000, the clearing fires almost immediately and on nearly every booking, so each one pays for a rewrite. The distinction against the intuition that less context means less cost is that the spend is not in the tokens you delete but in the ones you write again.

RULE: Context levers are for long sessions: in short bookings, clearing context breaks more cache than it saves in tokens.

TRAP: Assuming that every token leaving the context is a token saved, without counting what it costs to rewrite the prefix the clearing invalidated.

TRY IT: Run the same short booking with and without context editing and compare cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens turn by turn: you will see the cache write reappear right after each clearing.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros moved claims triage to the current model generation and cost per claim rose 32% at the same volume of 6,000 claims a day. The prompt was not touched during the migration. Renata then ran the prompt audit, removed the instructions the new model already follows unprompted, and spend barely moved. The share of input read from cache is the same as before, and triage accuracy did not shift. The department's annual budget is already closed. Where should you look to explain what is left?

options.label: A
options.text: In the cached prefix, hunting for the block the migration reordered that now forces a cache rewrite on every claim.
options.feedback: A broken prefix is the most frequent cause of a cost jump, but the measurement already rules it out: the share read from cache did not change.

options.label: B
options.text: In max_tokens, lowering it until spend per claim returns to the level it had before the model migration.
options.feedback: max_tokens is a hard ceiling the model never sees, so it does not lead it to economize: it truncates output that was already generated and billed.

options.label: C
options.text: In the previous model, going back to it while the team works out where the cost difference comes from.
options.feedback: Rolling back looks prudent, but it gives up the measurement that explains the jump and leaves the system on an identifier with an announced retirement.

options.label: D
options.text: In the token count of the same request against the new model, and in the thinking tokens the usage field reports.
options.feedback: Correct: the new tokenizer produces more tokens for the same text and thinking is on by default and billed as output, and both move the cost base.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that after a migration you re-measure the cost base before you look for the cause in the prompt. Two things change without anyone editing a line. The tokenizer in recent models produces more tokens for the same text, so the same request comes in more expensive. And thinking is on by default, with those tokens billed as output even though they are not displayed. The documented procedure is exactly that: count the same request twice, once against the model you left and once against the new one, compare the input_tokens and re-baseline cost and latency. The distinction against reviewing the cache is that the measurement already ruled that hypothesis out, and against lowering max_tokens, that the parameter does not make the model spend less.

RULE: After migrating, count again: the same text does not cost the same tokens in two generations, and thinking on by default is billed as output.

TRAP: Looking in the prompt for an increase that lives in the unit of measure: same text, more tokens, plus thinking tokens that did not exist before.

TRY IT: Count the same request with the counting endpoint against the model you left and against the one you use now, compare the two input_tokens figures, and look at the thinking tokens in the usage field of a real response.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/token-counting https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/opus-5/migration-guide

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud handles 9,000 teleconsultations a day with a triage assistant. Every consultation opens the same fan-out of four subagents today: history, medication, lab results and symptoms. A single search of the clinical record resolves 70% of consultations, and only 15% need all four sources crossed. Medical leadership wants AI cost per consultation down 40% this quarter, without losing depth on the complex cases and with responses still under 90 seconds. Which change to the decomposition fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Give the orchestrator an effort guide keyed to complexity: one call with a few record lookups for simple cases, and the full fan-out only when the case warrants it.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented guidance scales effort to the complexity of the query and avoids overinvesting in the 70% of volume that a single search resolves.

options.label: B
options.text: Cut the fan-out from four subagents down to two on every consultation and split the four sources that are queried separately today between them.
options.feedback: An even cut lowers average cost, but it still opens subagents where none are needed and it takes sources away from the 15% of cases that need them crossed.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the four subagents on every consultation and send them all to the fastest and cheapest model in the family so the fan-out comes out cheaper.
options.feedback: Routing subagents to a cheaper model is a real cost lever, but the token multiplier of the fan-out is still paid on every simple consultation and the complex cases lose depth.

options.label: D
options.text: Group the day's consultations and send them through the Message Batches API to take the 50% discount on standard API pricing.
options.feedback: The batch discount is real and documented, but batch processing is asynchronous and cannot hold up a triage that has to answer within 90 seconds.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that decomposition scales to the complexity of each request instead of being fixed as a constant of the system. The published guidance is explicit: a simple search is resolved by one agent with three to ten tool calls, a direct comparison needs two to four subagents with ten to fifteen calls each, and only complex work justifies more. Embedding that guide in the orchestrator is what prevents overinvestment in simple consultations. With 70% of the volume resolved by a single search, that is where the requested saving sits, and the 15% that does need four sources stays untouched. The distinction against cutting the fan-out evenly is that an even cut degrades the complex cases and still pays coordination on the simple ones.

RULE: Scale decomposition to the complexity of each query: a fixed fan-out overpays on the easy cases and comes up short on the hard ones.

TRAP: Treating the number of subagents as a constant of the architecture instead of a decision taken per query.

TRY IT: Take a hundred real runs of your agent, classify them by how many sources they actually needed, and compute what share of the spend went to subagents whose result did not change the answer.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them

questions.question: Colibrí Pay runs a fraud-alert investigation agent built with the Agent SDK. The regulator requires that no card block execute without an analyst's confirmation, and that control lives inside the canUseTool callback. To cut resolution time, Tomás adds an allow rule that approves the entire accounts MCP server. That server holds the balance-lookup tools and the card-block tool side by side. What will happen to the analyst confirmation after that change?

options.label: A
options.text: It will stop being asked for the block too: the allow rule approves the call before the callback, so the control has no effect.
options.feedback: Correct: a call approved at an earlier step, whether by an allow rule or by the permission mode, never reaches canUseTool, so the check you put there is skipped in silence.

options.label: B
options.text: It will still be asked for the block, because the callback is evaluated before the permission rules and decides every tool call.
options.feedback: The callback is the last step of the evaluation, not the first: hooks, deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode and allow rules all run before it.

options.label: C
options.text: It will stop being asked only on the balance lookups, because an allow rule cannot approve on its own a tool that changes an account.
options.feedback: There is a way for a tool to land in the callback despite an allow rule, but the MCP server has to mark it as requiring user interaction: it does not happen because the tool writes.

options.label: D
options.text: It will still be asked for the block, because irreversible actions fall outside what a permission mode approves on its own.
options.feedback: Some actions no mode approves on its own, but that list rests on explicit ask rules or on server markings, not on the action being irreversible.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a human gate is worth exactly what its attachment point in the evaluation chain is worth. In the Agent SDK the order is hooks, deny rules, ask rules, permission mode, allow rules, and only then the canUseTool callback, so any earlier approval skips the callback entirely. An allow rule that covers a whole MCP server therefore drags along the dangerous tool that lives in that server and disables the confirmation without raising a single error. The distinction against believing the callback always decides is that the callback only sees the calls no earlier step resolved. For a control that must run on all of them, the documented piece is a PreToolUse hook, which runs before the rest.

RULE: A human control only covers the calls that reach it: whatever was approved earlier never passes through the callback.

TRAP: Confusing the last step of the permission chain with a universal checkpoint, and widening the scope of an allow rule without looking at which tools live inside it.

TRY IT: Add an allow rule covering a whole MCP server to a test agent and log every call the callback receives: the tools from that server stop showing up in the log.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions

questions.question: Pehuén Energía generates its predictive-maintenance reports overnight, and the control room needs them before the 6 a.m. shift change. Last night the job started failing at 3:10, and retrying with exponential backoff recovered no request at all. Tomás looks at the error body, which repeats identically: HTTP 429, "type": "rate_limit_error", "details": {"error_code": "enforced_spend_limit_reached"}, and the response carries no retry-after header. What is happening, and what should be done?

options.label: A
options.text: The token bucket has not refilled yet: widen the backoff and raise the number of retries until the refill window moves on.
options.feedback: The throughput limit does refill continuously, and there backoff is the right answer, but a spend 429 does not refill as the minutes pass.

options.label: B
options.text: Priority Tier capacity is exhausted: ask for these calls with service_tier standard_only and retry them right away.
options.feedback: The service tier decides capacity priority and helps against 529 overloaded errors, not against a spend cap that has already been reached.

options.label: C
options.text: The key's limit was used up: split the job across two keys in the same workspace to double the headroom available.
options.feedback: Limits apply per organization and per workspace, not per key: adding keys adds no headroom and scatters the attribution of spend.

options.label: D
options.text: The spending cap for the period was reached: no retry goes through until that cap is raised or the next period starts.
options.feedback: Correct: the enforced_spend_limit_reached code and the missing retry-after header identify a spend limit, and that 429 is not solved by retrying.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that not every 429 means the same thing, and the error body tells you which one you are looking at. A throughput 429 arrives with a retry-after header and describes a token bucket that refills continuously, so retrying with backoff is exactly right. A 429 whose details.error_code is enforced_spend_limit_reached and that carries no retry-after describes a spending cap for the period: the capacity is there and what is missing is budget, so every retry only burns the overnight window. The distinction against widening the backoff is one of time scale: the bucket refills in seconds, the spending cap only in the next period.

RULE: Read the 429 before retrying: with retry-after it is throughput and you wait; without retry-after and with the spend code, retrying only burns your window.

TRAP: Treating every 429 as the same problem and always answering with more retries, without reading the error code or the headers that tell them apart.

TRY IT: Pull last month's 429s out of your logs and sort them into two groups by whether they carry a retry-after header; count how many retries you spent on the ones that were never going to go through.

questions.question: The post-sales agent at Mistral Retail resolves returns and exchanges across 220 stores and the e-commerce channel. When a complaint arrives, internal audit has to answer which operator and which store requested each return the agent executed, within the 48 hours committed to the consumer regulator. Telemetry already reaches the security system with the tool decision events and their results, but every event appears under the same identity, that of the service that runs the agent, and the store appears in none of them. What is the cause and what fixes it?

options.label: A
options.text: The tool decision and result events are missing, and those are the ones that record which action the agent executed at each step.
options.feedback: Those events are the backbone of an audit trail, but they already arrive here: what is missing is not the event but who to attribute it to.

options.label: B
options.text: The identity attributes describe the service credential and not the end user: the store and operator identifiers have to be injected.
options.feedback: Correct: the identity that travels by default is the service's, so a per-person trail comes from adding those attributes on every call.

options.label: C
options.text: Logging of prompt content and tool bodies is not enabled, and that is where the store data would be recorded.
options.feedback: That logging exists and is switched on separately, but it stores the text of the operation: looking for identity there turns an audit into a content search.

options.label: D
options.text: Consumption breaks down only by API key, so a key and a workspace have to be created for each of the 220 stores.
options.feedback: That breakdown exists and does attribute cost, but it cannot tell two operators of the same store apart and multiplies credential management by 220.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an agent's telemetry identifies by default the credential the service runs with, not the person on whose behalf it acted. That is why the events arrive complete and still cannot be audited: they all share one identity. questions.question: The risk team at Banco Altamar extracts data from credit files of 80 to 150 pages, about 6,000 files a month. Internal audit has just required that every figure in the summary be traceable to the page it came from. The last review found that 4 in every 100 summaries carried a figure that appears in no document in the file. Valentina has to fix this without multiplying the cost per file. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask for the verbatim quotes with their location before summarizing, and drop from the summary any figure with no quote.
options.feedback: Correct: for long documents the documented approach is to extract word-for-word quotes first and build the answer on them; forcing a retraction of whatever cannot be cited also leaves the trail audit asked for.

options.label: B
options.text: Reprocess each file three times with the same prompt and keep the figure that comes out the same in two of the three outputs.
options.feedback: Comparing several outputs does help spot inconsistencies, but it triples the cost of 6,000 files a month and still says nothing about which page each figure sits on.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the extraction to the most capable model in the family and keep the same prompt and the same summary format.
options.feedback: A more capable model removes some errors, but traceability is not a property of the model: with no quotes the summary still cannot be located in the file.

options.label: D
options.text: Set temperature to zero so that the extraction becomes repeatable and is documented that way for internal audit.
options.feedback: A low temperature makes the output more conservative, not deterministic: identical inputs can still give different outputs, and that adds no traceability either.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a hallucination is fought with retrievable evidence, not with more model capability. For tasks over long documents the documented technique is to ask for the verbatim quotes first and answer only from them, with the instruction to withdraw any claim that no quote supports. That attacks both problems at once: it lowers the rate of invented figures and it produces the exact location audit demands. The distinction against voting among several outputs is that voting detects discrepancies but generates neither evidence nor location, and the requirement here is to be able to point at the page.

RULE: If you have to be able to point at where a figure came from, make the model quote it first and discard whatever it cannot cite.

TRAP: Treating traceability as a problem of model capability, when it is a problem of how the answer gets built.

TRY IT: Take ten files that have already been reviewed, run the extraction with and without the quoting step, and count in each case how many figures in the summary you can locate on a specific page.

questions.question: Minera Nevado's operational safety assistant is used by 1,200 people, outside contractors among them. Its system prompt carries the internal thresholds the company uses to decide whether a finding gets reported to the authority, and legal treats those thresholds as confidential. In a pre-launch test, a contractor got the assistant to repeat part of those instructions. Launch is two weeks away, and legal wants measures that do not depend on the model's goodwill. Which two documented measures should the team apply? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Add to the system prompt an order never to reveal its instructions, repeated at the start and at the end of the block.
options.feedback: An instruction in the prompt steers the model, but no method is foolproof and this one does not survive a well-built request: it is advice, not a control.

options.label: B
options.text: Filter the output before showing it, with rules or with a filter that detects fragments of the prompt in the response.
options.feedback: Correct: post-processing the output is one of the documented strategies against prompt leak, and it acts even when the model lets itself be talked into it.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the assistant to the most capable model in the family, which better resists requests to reveal internal instructions.
options.feedback: A more capable model may refuse more attempts, but the documentation does not offer that path as a leak mitigation, and the sensitive content still sits in the prompt.

options.label: D
options.text: Take out of the prompt the proprietary details the task does not need in order to answer a worker on site.
options.feedback: Correct: what is not in the prompt cannot leak, and the documentation asks you to avoid unnecessary proprietary details.

options.label: E
options.text: Redesign the prompt with leak-resistant techniques before any other measure, even though it adds complexity.
options.feedback: Hardening the prompt is a real strategy, but the documentation leaves it for after monitoring and post-processing, because the added complexity can degrade the rest of the task.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a secret traveling in the prompt is protected by taking it out or by intercepting it on the way out, not by asking the model to keep it. The documentation orders the strategies against prompt leak: separate context from queries, filter the output by post-processing, avoid unnecessary proprietary details, and audit regularly. It also warns that no method is foolproof. The two measures that act without depending on what the model decides are removing from the prompt what is not needed and screening the response before it is delivered. The distinction against redesigning the prompt with leak-resistant techniques is one of order: that comes after monitoring and post-processing, because it adds complexity that can degrade the task.

RULE: Against prompt leak, remove what is not needed and screen the output; asking the model for discretion is the last measure and the most fragile.

TRAP: Confusing an instruction written into the system prompt with a control applied by code over the response on its way out.

TRY IT: Ask your assistant to repeat its instructions in three different phrasings, save the responses, and check which ones get through your output filter and how many prompt lines you could delete without losing the task.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-prompt-leak

questions.question: Siete Lagos Viajes closed the year with 85% of itinerary assembly automated, and the manual step that remains is about 6% of total handling time. The board approved a budget that has to be allocated this quarter or it is lost, set a target of 40 new corporate accounts, and froze support headcount. The company turns down accounts that demand self-service changes and cancellations today, something no current channel offers. Valentina has to recommend where that budget goes. What should she propose?

options.label: A
options.text: Automate the manual step that remains in itinerary assembly, the only stretch of the current flow with handling time still left to recover.
options.feedback: It is a real improvement, but that stretch is worth about 6% of handling time: even fully automated it moves neither the target for new accounts nor the headcount freeze.

options.label: B
options.text: Build the self-service channel for changes and cancellations, with corporate accounts won and served without added headcount as the committed metric.
options.feedback: Correct: value does not end at cost reduction, and the stated constraint is growth in accounts with headcount frozen, which only a capability that does not exist yet can solve.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the itinerary flow to the most capable model in the family to raise the quality of the proposals and cut the corrections the sales team makes today.
options.feedback: Better proposals can reduce corrections, but they open no new account and they add cost per itinerary just as margin per booking is fixed.

options.label: D
options.text: Measure the return of the current flow for another quarter and only then decide which new capability the approved budget funds.
options.feedback: Measuring before investing is sound, but a year of data on the current flow already exists and the budget expires this quarter: waiting is the same as giving it up.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the technical decision lines up with the explicit business constraint, and that the value of a solution does not end at efficiency. The enterprise guidance names the building of new revenue-generating capabilities, not only cost reduction, and notes that the organizations that get value start from a concrete business problem and measure what matters. Here the approved target is corporate accounts added with headcount frozen, and those accounts are being lost over a capability the company does not offer. The remaining manual stretch has a known and small ceiling, so even solved it does not move the indicator the board will look at. The distinction against optimizing the current flow further is that the extra efficiency is measured against 6% of handling time, while the new capability is measured against the committed target.

RULE: Align the investment with the indicator the business committed to: when the goal is growth, a capability you do not yet offer beats the last point of efficiency.

TRAP: Assuming that optimizing the stretch you already automated pays as well as opening a capability the company does not have.

TRY IT: Write in one line the indicator your sponsor will look at in six months, then file each initiative in your backlog under the indicator it moves; the ones that land under none have no business case.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-ai-agents-for-the-enterprise https://claude.com/blog/driving-ai-transformation-with-claude

questions.question: The environmental authority has opened a review of Minera Nevado and wants to see who viewed and exported each permit file during the two previous quarters. Document search has run across the organization for more than a year, but nobody had enabled the Activity Feed of the Compliance API. Bruno enables it this morning and queries the date range the authority asked for. What should he expect?

options.label: A
options.text: That the feed returns only activity after it was enabled, and that the earlier period has to be rebuilt from logs of your own.
options.feedback: Correct: recording is not retroactive. It starts when the Compliance API is first enabled for the organization, so anything earlier has to be found in your own instrumentation.

options.label: B
options.text: That the feed returns the full period, because activity already recorded for the organization is retained for years.
options.feedback: The feed is retained for years, but that describes how long what was recorded lasts, not how far back recording goes: before it was enabled there was nothing to retain.

options.label: C
options.text: That the audit log export covers the earlier period, with the content of every query that was run.
options.feedback: The audit log export does exist and covers a window backward, but it does not include the content of chats or of projects, only their identifiers.

options.label: D
options.text: That the feed returns the full period, because the query takes a date range and the organization already existed.
options.feedback: The date range filters what is stored; it does not conjure up activity from a period when recording was not yet switched on.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an audit control only produces evidence from the moment it is switched on. The Activity Feed of the Compliance API records authentication, chat, file, project, administrative and platform activity, and its recording begins when the API is first enabled for the organization. The long retention describes how long what was recorded is kept, not how far back it reaches. So, faced with a review that looks at two previous quarters, the only thing that can cover that period is whatever instrumentation the application itself saved. The distinction against the audit log export is that the export covers a limited window and also leaves out the content of chats and projects, carrying only their identifiers.

RULE: Switch the record on before you need it: a recording that is not retroactive has nothing to tell you about the past.

TRAP: Confusing the retention period with how far back the record reaches, and assuming a date range recovers what was never recorded.

TRY IT: Enable the feed in a test organization, run a session, query the range that covers yesterday and today, and compare how many events appear before and after the moment you enabled it.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/compliance-activity-feed https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9970975-access-audit-logs

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud's intake triage proposes an urgency level before a clinician sees the patient, about 18,000 cases a month. An internal audit compared equivalent clinical pictures and found that patients from rural districts are assigned a lower level more often. The agreement with the health plans requires a single documented criterion for each level. The medical committee proposes adding one urgency level to those patients to compensate. What should you propose instead?

options.label: A
options.text: Add one urgency level to patients from rural districts, as the committee proposes, and audit again the following quarter.
options.feedback: Compensating with a fixed adjustment flips the sign of the difference without removing it: the documented methodology surfaces discrimination in both directions, and the positive direction is discrimination too.

options.label: B
options.text: Send every triage from rural districts to immediate clinical review while the source of the difference is studied.
options.feedback: Escalating human review protects in the short term, but it installs different treatment by district, measures nothing, and leaves untouched the criterion that produces the difference.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the model with the most capable one in the family and repeat the audit on the same sample of clinical cases.
options.feedback: Changing model may move the result, but without varying a single attribute over the same cases you will not know whether the difference fell, rose or changed shape.

options.label: D
options.text: Reprocess the same cases varying only the district, and correct with prompt engineering whatever that measurement shows.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented methodology varies the demographic attribute systematically over the same decision scenario, and on top of that measurement careful prompt engineering reduces discrimination.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a difference in treatment gets corrected after it is measured with every other variable held fixed, not compensated by eye. The documented methodology for evaluating discrimination varies demographic information systematically over one same set of decision scenarios, and it surfaces both negative and positive discrimination; on top of that measurement, careful prompt engineering reduces both. Compensating with an extra level introduces positive discrimination, which that same methodology flags as a finding, and it also breaks the single criterion the agreement requires you to document. The distinction against routing those cases to clinical review is that the measure manages the symptom without touching the criterion or producing evidence that the difference went down.

RULE: Compensating in the opposite direction is not correcting a bias: measure with the clinical picture held fixed and correct the criterion, not the result.

TRAP: Assuming that a correction in favor of the affected group does not count as discrimination, and that it therefore needs no measurement.

TRY IT: Take thirty anonymized real cases, duplicate them changing only the district, and compare the distribution of urgency levels between the two copies before touching the prompt.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/news/evaluating-and-mitigating-discrimination-in-language-model-decisions

questions.question: The exam-prep assistant at Grupo Aurora Educación loads the full subject material into every request. The prompt is always built in this order: a system block with the role and the tutoring rules; a user turn with the student's question; a user turn with three model answers as examples; a user turn with the material inside documents tags, about 60,000 tokens. Since the material grew, tutors report that the assistant skips whole sections and answers from memory. The per-student budget is closed and the output is already the expensive part of each answer, so making it longer is not an option. What do you fix first?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the full material to the start of the prompt, above the rules, the examples and the student's question.
options.feedback: Correct: the documentation asks you to place long data above everything else and leave the instruction last, and it measures a clear quality gain with that order.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask it to extract verbatim quotes from the material first and only then write out the answer for the student.
options.feedback: Quote grounding is the documented technique for long documents, but it adds output tokens, which is exactly what the constraint rules out.

options.label: C
options.text: Trim the material to the sections of the current unit until the prompt falls below 20,000 tokens.
options.feedback: Curating context is right when material is surplus, but here it would drop syllabus the student can ask about, and the order would still be inverted.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the number of model answers used as examples to pin down the expected format and level of detail.
options.feedback: Examples pin down format and tone, not attention over a long document, and they grow the prompt without touching the cause of the problem.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for prompts with long inputs is that the long data goes on top: above the instructions, above the examples and above the question. The documentation states it for all current models and measures a substantial quality gain when the instruction comes last. In this prompt the order is inverted, which is exactly the arrangement it advises against, and the effect gets worse as the material grows. Reordering is free: it adds no tokens, adds no calls and changes not one comma of the content. The distinction against quote grounding is that the technique would help too, but it is paid for in output tokens and the budget constraint rules it out.

RULE: The long document goes on top and the question at the end: if the material comes after the instruction, you pay for context the model uses worse.

TRAP: Treating prompt order as a matter of style and looking for the fix in techniques that add steps, when reordering costs nothing.

TRY IT: Take ten real questions and answer each one twice, with the material above and with the material below, changing nothing else: compare against the syllabus how many answers cite the right section.

TRAP: Treating prompt order as a matter of style and looking for the fix in techniques that add steps, when reordering costs nothing.

questions.question: For six months, 40 people from a consultancy join the team that maintains the integration layer with Banco Altamar's mainframe core. Each module carries its own conventions for how changes are written and tested. The platform team is three people, and they cannot keep up with reviewing everything. Internal audit requires those conventions to be versioned alongside the code they govern. Which two documented measures make everyone work from the same configuration? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Write one CLAUDE.md file per directory, maintained by the team that owns that module and versioned with its code.
options.feedback: Correct: the convention lives in the directory it governs, the team that owns it maintains it, and it travels versioned with the code, which is what audit asked for.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish a .claude/settings.json in the repository with the internal marketplace and the team's enabled plugins.
options.feedback: Correct: project settings, carrying the marketplace source and the enabled plugins, install the same set of tools for everyone who works in that repository.

options.label: C
options.text: Point additionalDirectories from each person's user settings at a shared folder that holds the conventions.
options.feedback: That key grants access to the folder's files, but it loads neither its CLAUDE.md, nor its rules, nor its skills: the convention ends up reachable and unapplied.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the conventions skill under each developer's personal directory so as to have it in all of their projects.
options.feedback: The personal directory reaches every project of that one person and nobody else's; to share it with whoever works in the repository you have to version it in the repository.

options.label: E
options.text: Declare relevance in the internal marketplace so that the conventions plugin installs where it is needed.
options.feedback: Declaring relevance only produces suggestions, and not even that until an administrator enables that marketplace in the suggestions list: it never installs anything on its own.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that where you store a configuration decides who it reaches. One CLAUDE.md per directory leaves the convention in the hands of the team that owns that module and versions it alongside the code, which is exactly the audit requirement. Project settings published in the repository, with the marketplace source and the enabled plugins, make anyone who opens that repository work from the same set of tools. The two measures are independent: one distributes instructions and the other distributes tools. The distinction against pointing additionalDirectories at a shared folder is that the key grants access to the files and nothing more: it loads neither the CLAUDE.md nor the skills in that folder.

RULE: Whatever has to reach the whole repository gets versioned in the repository; whatever you keep in your personal directory reaches only you.

TRAP: Confusing granting access to a folder with loading what is inside it: additionalDirectories opens files, not instructions or skills.

TRY IT: Open the repository from a clean machine, run /context and /skills, and check whether the module's CLAUDE.md and the plugins you thought you had distributed actually show up.

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación wants to assist the grading of open-ended answers for 180,000 students. The budget per student only tolerates human review on 5% of the grades, so the acceptance criterion has to be precise enough to decide which ones fall inside that 5%. Camila has three weeks of discovery and access to the academic coordinators who grade by hand today. What sequence should she follow?

options.label: A
options.text: Observe the checks coordinators already run while grading → build 30 to 50 cases from real grades that came out wrong → agree a threshold for each check with them
options.feedback: Correct: the documented source of requirements is the manual checks the team already runs plus real failures, and a set of that size is enough to agree thresholds on concrete cases.

options.label: B
options.text: Send a requirements questionnaire to the academic coordinators at every campus → consolidate the answers into a scope document → validate it with the academic committee before design
options.feedback: A questionnaire collects wishes and priorities, but it returns phrases like fair grading that nobody can measure, and 5% human review needs a threshold, not a description.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a prototype with the most capable model in the family → show it to the coordinators in a demonstration → turn their objections into the list of requirements
options.feedback: An early prototype starts a conversation, but it anchors the discussion on what the prototype already does and turns objections into a fix list rather than acceptance criteria.

options.label: D
options.text: Generate a synthetic set of student answers with the model → measure the accuracy of the automatic grader on it → present that result as the baseline for the project
options.feedback: Synthetic data is useful for filling in edge cases, but a generated set does not reproduce the real distribution of answers, and a baseline on it says nothing about the 5% you will have to review.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that requirements for a system like this come from what someone already checks by hand and from failures that already happened, not from a wish list or from invented data. The evals documentation says it directly: start from the manual checks the team runs before every release, and 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures are a good starting point, as long as the set reflects the real distribution of the work. With those cases in hand, the threshold for each check is agreed with the person who grades and becomes the rule that decides what enters the 5% under human review. The distinction against the questionnaire is that a questionnaire returns intentions, while a real case returns a criterion you can test.

RULE: The first source of requirements is the check someone already runs by hand: turn it into real cases that failed, and only then agree the threshold.

TRAP: Confusing a questionnaire of wishes with a verifiable requirement, or measuring on synthetic data that does not reproduce the real distribution.

TRY IT: Ask whoever does the work by hand today for the last three times they graded something that was wrong, and write each one as a case with an input and an acceptable output: that is the start of your acceptance set.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

questions.question: A platform team decides to send the entire available history on every query, arguing that more context always improves the answer. According to what is documented about long contexts, what should the team expect as the token count grows?

options.label: A
options.text: That quality holds steady as long as the request does not go past the context window limit.
options.feedback: The window limit marks what fits, not how it gets used: the degradation shows up before you reach the ceiling, as the context grows.

options.label: B
options.text: That accuracy improves proportionally, because the model has more evidence to work from.
options.feedback: More evidence helps when it is the relevant evidence; what is documented is the opposite of a proportional improvement, with diminishing returns as the context grows.

options.label: C
options.text: That accuracy at retrieving information from context falls, because attention is a finite resource.
options.feedback: Correct: the more tokens in the window, the lower the ability to retrieve accurately the information sitting there; context is treated as a finite resource.

options.label: D
options.text: That the only effect is cost, because attention is spread evenly across all the tokens.
options.feedback: Cost does rise, but it is not the only effect: attention is not spread evenly, and that is what degrades retrieval and long-range reasoning.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that context is a finite resource with diminishing returns, not a container you can fill without consequence. As the number of tokens in the window grows, the model's ability to retrieve information accurately from that context falls: models remain highly capable over long contexts, but they show lower accuracy in retrieval and in long-range reasoning than they do over short ones. The distinction against thinking the only cost is financial is that the degradation happens inside the window limit and hits quality, not just the bill.

RULE: Treat context as a budget, not a container: every token you add competes for the attention of the rest.

TRAP: Assuming everything that fits in the window gets used equally well, and confusing the window limit with the point where degradation begins.

TRY IT: Run the same question with just the right document and with the full history pasted in front of it, and compare how many concrete facts from the final part each answer retrieves.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Colibrí Pay runs an agent that triages 9,000 fraud alerts a day. For each alert it queries between three and eight internal sources, and the order of those queries changes with what it finds, so two runs over the same case rarely follow the same path. Compliance has asked in writing how the agent is validated before each version ships. About the end-to-end design of that agent, which of these statements is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The loop runs several times within a single alert: every result from a tool feeds the model's next decision.
options.feedback: This statement is correct: the documented loop alternates gathering context, taking action and verifying the work, and each tool result informs the step that follows.

options.label: B
options.text: Explicit stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations, are part of the agent design and not an operational patch.
options.feedback: This statement is correct: stopping conditions are among the controls the documentation asks you to include when designing an autonomous agent.

options.label: C
options.text: Whoever supervises the agent can interrupt the loop at any point to redirect it: supervision is part of the loop and not a stage that comes later.
options.feedback: This statement is correct: the person supervising is part of the loop and can interrupt it at any moment to change the direction of the work.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the agent is not deterministic, validation has to evaluate the path it followed on each alert rather than the end state it reached.
options.feedback: Correct as the answer to a negative question: it is the other way around. Two valid runs can take different paths, so you evaluate the end state reached and whether the process was reasonable; demanding a prescribed path discards correct runs.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for systems where the model decides the steps is to evaluate the outcome and not the route: the multi-agent documentation notes that agents starting from the same point can take completely different valid paths, so you cannot check whether they followed the correct steps prescribed in advance, and it proposes evaluating whether they reached the right outcome by a reasonable process. The other three statements describe the loop as documented: it runs several times per request, it includes explicit stopping conditions, and it admits a person stepping in at any point. The key distinction is between traceability and evaluation criterion: logging the path helps debug one run, but it does not define whether the outcome is acceptable.

RULE: Evaluate the end state the agent reached, not the route: when the model chooses the steps, two different paths can be equally valid.

TRAP: Confusing traceability with evaluation criterion: the record of the path is there to debug, not to decide whether the outcome is correct.

TRY IT: Run your agent twice over the same case, mark the step where the two paths separated, and ask whether both outcomes were acceptable; if they were, your validation criterion cannot be the path.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works

questions.question: Control room operators at Pehuén Energía say the predictive maintenance assistant fails exactly during maintenance windows, which the regulator measures in minutes. No measurement of the assistant exists inside those windows, complaints arrive by chat to different people, and Joaquín's team has capacity for one improvement cycle a month. Which sequence sets up the feedback loop?

options.label: A
options.text: Commit to management the response time the operators are asking for → instrument the measurement in production afterward → review the breaches as they show up
options.feedback: Committing a number before measuring it inverts the order: a target is set on an indicator that already exists, and here there is no measurement at all inside the window that matters.

options.label: B
options.text: Open a feedback form for the whole control room → prioritize each quarter the observations the operators upvote most → take into the backlog the ones that fit next month's improvement capacity
options.feedback: An open channel collects perceptions, but with no agreed indicator and no owner the most upvoted item is not necessarily what breaks the regulatory window.

options.label: C
options.text: Instrument every indicator the assistant exposes → publish an open dashboard for the operators → let each shift set whatever target it considers reasonable for its window
options.feedback: Over-instrumenting scatters attention: too many indicators keep you from attending to the ones that matter, and targets set shift by shift produce goals nobody can compare.

options.label: D
options.text: Agree with the operators the indicator behind the complaint and its window → set a target with a named owner → review monthly what enters the design and tell whoever reported it
options.feedback: Correct: first the indicator and its window, then the target with an owner, and finally a periodic review that decides what gets built and returns that decision to whoever reported it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a target does not exist without an indicator: the indicator is the agreed measurement of an aspect of the service, and the target is a value or a range over that measurement. That is why the sequence starts by agreeing what is measured and in which window, which here is the maintenance window the regulator watches, rather than by committing a number before there is any way to check it. The second half weighs as much: a channel only closes the loop if it has an owner, if observations are prioritized against a criterion, and if the decision goes back to whoever reported it, because a channel that collects and never adjudicates stops receiving reports. The distinction against instrumenting everything is that many indicators with no target guide no decision and compete for the same attention.

RULE: First the indicator and its window, then the target with an owner, and always the reply: a channel that never adjudicates is not a feedback loop.

TRAP: Opening a feedback channel with no agreed indicator and no owner, and calling that alignment of expectations.

TRY IT: Write in one sentence the indicator for your assistant and the window in which you measure it; if you cannot write it, no target you have committed to has anything to check it against.

questions.question: Agencia Nacional de Ingresos classifies filings with an agent that chains five steps per case. The platform has two signals today: an availability alert and the spend report that arrives at month end. Regulation requires reconstructing any automated decision up to 30 days later, and compliance also wants spend closed out per department every month. Andrés has four people on his team and no capacity to run a data pipeline of his own. Which two measures add what is missing? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Store the request-id of every response, so you can later identify the exact call that handled each case.
options.feedback: The request-id identifies one specific call and is the first thing support asks for, but it does not count the five steps or link the calls of a single case to each other.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower the alert threshold so it fires when the agent's error rate goes above 2% within an hour.
options.feedback: Tuning the threshold improves monitoring, which tells you that something is wrong; it does not let you explain what the agent did on one particular case.

options.label: C
options.text: Instrument the loop with traces linked by session, with one span per interaction, per model call and per tool.
options.feedback: Correct: the same case can be resolved in a different number of steps on each run, and only the spans of the loop reconstruct what the agent did.

options.label: D
options.text: Reconcile spend per workspace against the Admin API cost report, which hands back daily buckets.
options.feedback: Correct: the organization cost report groups by workspace in daily buckets and is the reconciliation surface, separate from the tracing one.

options.label: E
options.text: Turn on content logging of prompts and responses on every session to keep the text of each step.
options.feedback: Content logging is optional and meant for debugging: it multiplies volume and risk over taxpayer data without answering either of the two requirements.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that observability for an agent is built in layers, and each layer answers a different question: the usage field says what one call cost, tracing telemetry says what the agent did step by step, and the usage and cost report says what the organization spent per workspace, with a few minutes of delay. Reconstructing a decision needs the tracing layer, because the same case can take a different number of steps on each run and per-request metrics do not show that. Closing out spend per department needs the cost layer, which aggregates by workspace in daily buckets and needs no pipeline of your own. The distinction against tuning the alert is that monitoring warns you something is wrong, while observability lets you tell what happened.

RULE: One layer per question: traces to reconstruct the run, the cost report to close out spend, and usage to explain a single call.

TRAP: Assuming that an availability alert or a per-response identifier is enough to explain a loop whose length changes on every run.

TRY IT: Take a case resolved yesterday and try to answer, with what you store today, how many steps it took, which tools it called and what it cost; note where you run out of data.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/usage-cost-api

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros is replacing its claims triage rules engine with the Claude-based assistant, on a fixed date set by the regulatory calendar. The regulator can ask for the explanation of any automated decision within ten business days, claims in progress cannot be stopped, and the team left running operations is two people. Ximena is drawing up the list of what has to be closed before the cutover. Which two conditions cannot be missing? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Migrate the decision history of the previous engine into the assistant's explanation format, so that the regulator consults a single source for everything.
options.feedback: Rewriting historical decisions in another format does not make them more explainable, and it eats the time before the cutover: what is asked for is the explanation of each decision as it was taken, by the system that took it.

options.label: B
options.text: Write the decommissioning plan for the previous engine: what is turned off, in what order, which decisions and data are kept to answer requests, and who authorizes each step.
options.feedback: Correct: decommissioning a system is a lifecycle phase with a procedure of its own, and it has to happen without raising risk or losing the ability to answer for what that system decided.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave the previous engine running in parallel indefinitely and compare a sample of claims triaged by both systems by hand every week.
options.feedback: A bounded parallel run is a good safety net during the transition, but leaving it open-ended and comparing by hand with two people does not scale and postpones the decommissioning instead of planning it.

options.label: D
options.text: Document the assistant's prompt and its versions on the department wiki, so the two people in operations can consult it when a request arrives.
options.feedback: Documenting the prompt helps whoever operates the system, but it does not answer what the regulator asks about a specific decision and it covers nothing about a failure at the provider.

options.label: E
options.text: Define the contingency procedure for a failure or degradation at the provider: what happens to claims in progress and on what criterion you fall back to the manual path.
