questions.question: Paula wants shipping lines, customs and carriers outside Terminal Puerto Claro to check manifest status through the same MCP server the internal team uses today. The current entry in the ".mcp.json" file is {"mcpServers": {"manifiestos": {"type": "stdio", "command": "node", "args": ["/opt/manifiestos/server.js"], "env": {"API_TOKEN": "${TOKEN_TERMINAL}"}}}}. Each external organization must see only its own shipments, and the audit requires knowing which organization made each query. Which two changes does the design need? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the stdio transport and hand each organization an installation with its own service token in the environment variable.
options.feedback: It is true that a stdio server takes its credentials from the environment, but that forces one process per client, and the server still cannot tell who is calling inside each organization.

options.label: B
options.text: Expose the manifests as resources instead of tools, so each client decides when to read them without going through the model.
options.feedback: Resources are controlled by the application and fit when you want content available without the model deciding; they solve neither the transport nor the identity of the caller.

options.label: C
options.text: Put a coordinating agent in front that delegates to one subagent per organization and filters the results before returning them.
options.feedback: Delegating to subagents multiplies tokens by three to ten times and moves filtering to the model side, which is exactly where an access control must not live.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish the server over Streamable HTTP, which is the transport designed to serve many clients at the same time.
options.feedback: Correct: a stdio server typically serves one client per process, while Streamable HTTP is the transport of the remote servers that serve many.

options.label: E
options.text: Implement the OAuth authorization of the HTTP transport, because a stdio server takes its credential from the environment and identifies no caller.
options.feedback: Correct: MCP authorization is defined at the transport level for HTTP, and it is what lets you require a token issued for this server and decide permissions per organization.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that in MCP the transport is not a deployment detail: it drags the authentication model along with it. A stdio server is launched as a subprocess of the client, typically serves a single client and takes its credentials from the environment, so it cannot tell three external organizations apart or leave a trace of who queried what. Streamable HTTP is the transport of the remote servers that serve many clients, and the specification defines OAuth authorization on top of it: tokens issued for this server, and permissions checked on every request. The distinction against handing out one token per installation is that this identifies the installation and not the caller, and it multiplies the processes you have to operate.

RULE: The transport decides the authentication: stdio takes credentials from the environment for one client, and once the clients are many and external you need HTTP with authorization.

TRAP: Treating the choice of transport as a deployment question and finding out too late that stdio leaves no caller identity to audit.

TRY IT: Open the configuration of one of your own MCP servers and answer two questions: how many clients use it, and how the server knows who is calling; if the answer is the environment variable, there is no identity to audit.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture

questions.question: The document assistant at Pehuén Energía works through a repository of 30 years of technical manuals organized by plant, unit and year: it walks the tree and reads the files it needs, with no index built beforehand. Camila measures that on 40% of queries it opens between eight and twelve files before landing on the right manual, and the field team has eight minutes per query inside the maintenance window. When the assistant starts in the right folder, it gets it right on the first try. Which change attacks the cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Load the complete manuals for the unit being serviced at the start of each session, so the assistant never has to search for a file.
options.feedback: Loading the whole corpus trades an orientation problem for a context problem: it raises the cost per query, and retrieval degrades as the token count grows.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the assistant's step limit so it has room to explore until it finds the manual that applies.
options.feedback: More steps buy more blind exploration: the assistant still does not know where to start, and each extra attempt eats into the eight-minute window.

options.label: C
options.text: Load up front a short map of the repository structure and its naming conventions, and keep reading files on demand.
options.feedback: Correct: agentic search fails when the agent does not know where to look, and that is fixed with input context, not with more exploration or better embeddings.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace the tree navigation with an embeddings index that is rebuilt on every publication of manuals.
options.feedback: An index is the alternative when you need faster results or more variations, but it has to be built and maintained, and here the assistant already succeeds when it starts in the right place.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the choice between loading context up front and discovering it along the way is made per type of content, not for a whole system. Autonomous tree navigation works well over living corpora and avoids maintaining an index, but it has a failure mode of its own: it pays off only when the agent has enough context to know where to look. The evidence points there without ambiguity, because when the assistant starts in the right folder it gets it right on the first try. The initial orientation, meaning the folder hierarchy and the naming conventions, is exactly the context an agent cannot discover by searching, so it goes up front while the manuals keep arriving on demand. The distinction against loading the complete manuals is that this option fixes orientation by paying for context that is almost never used.

RULE: Agentic search does not fail on bad embeddings: it fails on not knowing where to start, and that is fixed with a map, not with more steps.

TRAP: Confusing an orientation problem with a retrieval one and answering it with more context or an index, when what is missing is knowing where to go in.

TRY IT: Take five failed queries from your agent and count how many files it opened before getting it right; then give it a paragraph with the folder structure and repeat the measurement.

questions.question: Assisted grading at Grupo Aurora Educación returns feedback with five sections for every assignment. Internal measurement shows that teachers read and use the first two, and that output is now the most expensive part of each correction. With 180,000 students and a closed per-student budget, Tomás has to cut output spend without losing quality against the rubric the team already applies to a weekly sample. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Set max_tokens to the length you want the feedback to have, so that no answer can go past that ceiling.
options.feedback: max_tokens truncates the answer wherever it lands, even mid-sentence, and since the model never sees it, it does not lead the model to write shorter.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask in the prompt for feedback of at most 120 words, which is what the two sections teachers use add up to today.
options.feedback: It is the intuitive phrasing, but the model counts tokens and not words, so a word limit is followed less reliably than one in sentences or paragraphs.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask for the feedback with a paragraph or sentence limit, keep the two sections that get used, and score it with the rubric.
options.feedback: Correct: length is controlled better by a count of paragraphs or sentences, and the rubric confirms that the trim did not take quality with it.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower the model's effort so that it reasons less and, as a consequence, writes visibly shorter feedback for each assignment.
options.feedback: Lowering effort reduces the volume of thinking and with it the cost, but it does not reliably shorten the visible answer: that has to be asked for.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that output is the most direct cost lever in a high-volume flow: each output token costs several times an input one, and a section nobody reads is billed just like one that gets used. The documented way to shorten it is to ask for the length in units the model handles well: it counts tokens, not words, so a limit in paragraphs or sentences is followed better than a word count. max_tokens does not serve this goal, because it is a ceiling the model cannot see, it does not induce shorter writing, and it truncates only what was already generated and billed. Since the trim could touch quality, the change is closed out by scoring again with the rubric that already exists.

RULE: To shorten output, ask for it in paragraphs or sentences, never in words and never with max_tokens: that ceiling truncates the answer, it does not plan it.

TRAP: Confusing a token ceiling with an instruction to be brief: the first cuts what was already generated and billed, the second changes what the model writes.

TRY IT: Run the same correction asking first for a maximum of 150 words and then for a maximum of two paragraphs, and compare output_tokens and your rubric score across the two versions.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence

questions.question: The Colibrí Pay agent decides in real time whether to block a card on suspicion of fraud, and the regulator requires that decision to be settled in under 6 seconds at the 95th percentile. That percentile sits at 14 seconds today. A typical response comes back with "usage": {"input_tokens": 3100, "output_tokens": 16300, "output_tokens_details": {"thinking_tokens": 15800}}. Ignacio ran the same evaluation set with thinking budgets of 4,000, 8,000, 16,000 and 24,000 tokens: accuracy is the same from 4,000 on. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the thinking budget above 32,000 tokens and send these calls through the Message Batches API to avoid the timeouts.
options.feedback: It is true that above 32,000 thinking tokens batch processing is advisable so you do not run into timeouts, but batch is asynchronous and here a card is waiting on the decision.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower budget_tokens to the point where the evaluation stops improving and measure the 95th percentile again there.
options.feedback: Correct: the thinking budget has diminishing returns that depend on the task, and the evaluation already marked the point past which you only pay latency.

options.label: C
options.text: Move to the fastest model in the family while keeping the same thinking budget, to cut the generation time.
options.feedback: A faster model lowers generation time, but it changes the quality of a decision the regulator audits and leaves untouched the thinking tokens the evaluation showed to be unnecessary.

options.label: D
options.text: Turn on prompt caching over the request prefix to bring down the time to first token on each decision.
options.feedback: Caching is the lever for time to first token with large, stable prefixes; with 3,100 input tokens against 16,300 of output, the time is almost all in generation.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to measure before choosing the lever: the usage field says where the time goes, and here almost every token of a response is reasoning. The thinking budget is a target and not a strict cap, and larger budgets give more thorough reasoning with diminishing returns that depend on the task; when an evaluation shows that accuracy no longer improves past a certain point, everything above it is latency paid for nothing. So you lower the budget to the measured value and re-measure the 95th percentile before touching anything else. The distinction against switching models is that this lever changes the quality of an audited decision, while cutting reasoning already shown to be useless leaves it alone.

RULE: Set the thinking budget where the evaluation stops improving: above that point you are only buying latency.

TRAP: Assuming that a latency problem is solved by switching models or turning on caching, without first looking at how much of the time goes into reasoning tokens.

TRY IT: Run your evaluation set with the thinking budget cut in half and compare accuracy against the 95th percentile; if accuracy does not move, you have just found your cut-off point.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency

questions.question: The data team at Mistral Retail works with Claude Code on the catalog enrichment repository, which holds supplier price lists covered by confidentiality agreements. An external auditor reviews the control next week, and the requirement is that no session be able to send content from that repository to a host outside the approved list. Paula added a deny rule on WebFetch in the managed settings and considers the requirement closed. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add deny rules for Bash(curl *) and Bash(wget *), which are the ways to push content out through the terminal.
options.feedback: Bash rules match the text of the command and not the executable: they miss an absolute path, an sh -c, or any other HTTP client, and that is why they are not a security boundary.

options.label: B
options.text: Turn on the sandbox and declare the list of allowed domains for the network access of commands.
options.feedback: Correct: the sandbox isolates at the operating system level, and its allowed-domain list reaches commands and their child processes, which is exactly what a permission rule does not cover.

options.label: C
options.text: Write the restriction into the managed CLAUDE.md, so that every session receives it at startup.
options.feedback: A managed CLAUDE.md distributes instructions to every session, but it is guidance for the model and not a control enforced by the client: it does not stop a command from reaching the network.

options.label: D
options.text: Rely on the WebFetch domain pre-check, which reviews the host before fetching the page.
options.feedback: That check sends only the host name for a security review; it is not a list approved by the organization, and it covers nothing that leaves through the terminal.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that permission rules and the sandbox are complementary layers: the rule decides whether Claude Code lets a tool run, and the sandbox decides what the process can do once it is running. Denying WebFetch removes that tool but leaves network egress from the terminal untouched, and a Bash rule matches the text of the command rather than the program that executes, so it is not a security boundary. The requirement in this case talks about network destinations, not about tool names, and the documented piece for that is the sandbox with its allowed-domain list. The distinction against adding deny rules for curl and wget is that those rules are sidestepped by writing the same command a different way.

RULE: If the requirement is about where traffic may go, close it in the sandbox: a permission rule only understands tool names and command text.

TRAP: Treating a rule that matches command text as if it were a network control, and calling the requirement closed once WebFetch is denied.

TRY IT: With your current configuration, ask a test session to download a page with curl from a host that is not approved, and see whether the deny rule stops it or whether the sandbox is needed.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions

questions.question: Banco Altamar extracts the data in its credit files with an orchestrator that splits each file among several subagents. Audit requires every extracted field to be traceable back to its source page, and token consumption has already doubled the forecast: two subagents often read the same annexes, and the coordinator ends up with whole pages of quoted text in its context. Tomás is reviewing the design with 4,000 files a day in the queue. Which two changes attack the cause? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Write an explicit assignment for each subagent with its objective, its output format, the sources it may use and where its scope ends.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented delegation guidance asks for an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear boundaries; without that, subagents duplicate work and leave gaps.

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the number of subagents per file so that each one reads fewer annexes and the extraction work finishes sooner.
options.feedback: More subagents spread the pages out but multiply coordination and cost, and they do not touch the cause of the duplication, which is an assignment with no boundaries.

options.label: C
options.text: Have each subagent write its extraction to an artifact and return only the reference plus a short summary to the coordinator.
options.feedback: Correct: leaving the bulky output in an artifact and returning a light reference keeps the coordinator's context from filling with quoted text and preserves the link to the source page.

options.label: D
options.text: Pass the full transcript of every subagent to the coordinator so that it spots the overlapping reads for itself.
options.feedback: Seeing every transcript looks like control, but it cancels the compression that justifies this design: the coordinator's context grows file by file and consumption gets worse.

options.label: E
options.text: Let the subagents consult each other during the run so they can divide up the annexes they come across.
options.feedback: It sounds like fine-grained coordination, but subagents report to the main conversation and do not talk to each other; dividing the work is the job of the assignment each one receives.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a subagent performs only as well as the assignment it receives and what it is asked to return. The delegation guidance is explicit: each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on which tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries, because without detailed descriptions agents duplicate work, leave gaps or fail to find what they need. questions.question: Siete Lagos Viajes answers questions about change and cancellation terms from an index that gathers the policies of eleven wholesalers. To cut down the cases where the assistant could not find the clause, Nicolás raised top_k from 5 to 25. Two weeks later recall on the test set had risen from 0.61 to 0.79, end-to-end accuracy had fallen from 84% to 76%, and cost per query was up 60%, with high season multiplying volume by ten. The wrong answers mix terms from different wholesalers. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The prompt gets twenty-five near-identical chunks from different wholesalers and the model is distracted: recall rose, ranking did not.
options.feedback: Correct: adding chunks raises the chance of including the right one, but more information also distracts the model, and with eleven wholesalers the neighboring chunks look too much alike.

options.label: B
options.text: The chosen model is not enough to reason over twenty-five chunks and you have to move to the most capable model in the family.
options.feedback: A more capable model absorbs some of the noise, but the change that precedes the drop is in retrieval, and papering over it with a bigger model is paid on every high-season query.

options.label: C
options.text: The embeddings fell out of date against the new policies and the index needs a complete rebuild.
options.feedback: A stale index produces confident, wrong answers right after a content refresh; here the decline shows up after a parameter change, not a content one.

options.label: D
options.text: Size-based chunking splits the clauses down the middle, and that is why the assistant ends up combining terms from two different contracts.
options.feedback: Cutting by size with no overlap does split clauses, but that flaw was there before the change and does not explain accuracy getting worse while recall improves.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that recall and answer quality are not the same metric and can move in opposite directions. Raising top_k increases the chance that the right chunk sits in the context, which is why recall rose; but the documentation warns that more information can also distract the model, and with policies from eleven wholesalers the chunks that come in resemble each other and compete with the right one. The documented way to gain accuracy without paying that distraction is to over-retrieve and reorder with a reranker, keeping few chunks in a good order, instead of widening top_k. The distinction against the stale index lies in when the symptom appears: there, after a content refresh; here, after a parameter change.

RULE: Raising top_k improves recall and can worsen the answer: to gain accuracy, over-retrieve and rerank instead of piling up chunks.

TRAP: Treating recall as if it were the quality metric and celebrating that it rises while end-to-end accuracy falls.

TRY IT: Repeat ten queries with top_k 5 and with top_k 25 and count in how many the source behind the answer changes; look as well at how many input tokens each configuration added.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/capabilities-contextual-embeddings-guide

questions.question: Banco Altamar is about to make the complaints classifier available to the 1,200 people in its service department. There is a single communication window agreed with the department and there will be no second announcement. Audit requires the answer on data handling to be available from day one. Paula, who leads adoption, has two weeks to prepare the launch. Which sequence should she follow?

options.label: A
options.text: Test the classifier on a real task from the department and get the data handling answer ready → agree that department leadership signs the announcement → announce with a named owner of the channel for 48 hours
options.feedback: Correct: the pre-announcement checklist asks for a real task already tested, the data answer ready, an owner of the channel for the first 48 hours, and a signature with weight inside the organization.

options.label: B
options.text: Announce the tool to the 1,200 people in the service department → collect the questions that come up in the channel over those days → resolve the most repeated ones one by one
options.feedback: Announcing first turns the launch into an improvised help desk: the data questions arrive the same day, and with no owner of the channel they go unanswered.

options.label: C
options.text: Train the team leads first in a long session → ask them to cascade it to their teams in their own words → measure adoption across the department the following month
options.feedback: Training the leads helps, but a cascade of sessions does not replace the check beforehand and it leaves no channel where questions get resolved in front of everyone.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish the full classifier documentation on the intranet along with a step-by-step how-to → send the announcement from the technology team → open a support channel if questions start arriving
options.feedback: Full documentation is rarely read before people try the tool, and an announcement signed by technology reads as an optional utility rather than a priority of the department.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the announcement is the last step of the preparation and not the first step of the rollout. The pre-launch checklist is short and every item carries its reason: a channel with a named owner for the first 48 hours, because unanswered questions on day one kill momentum; the material on data handling ready, because that is the first question that shows up; a first concrete task from the real work, because generic examples do not convert; and sponsorship with weight, because launches signed by leadership consistently show more first-week activation than those sent by the technical team. With a single communication window the order decides everything: whatever is not settled before the announcement gets no second chance.

RULE: Before the announcement: a real task already tested, the data answer ready and a named owner of the channel; and let whoever sets the priorities sign it.

TRAP: Treating the announcement as the first step of the rollout instead of the last step of the preparation.

TRY IT: Review your team's last internal launch against four points: real task tested, data handling answer, channel owner for 48 hours, and who signed the announcement; the missing one explains where adoption fell.

questions.question: The commercial department at Ceibo Telecom wants the retention assistant to close more cases without handing them to a rep. The contract with corporate accounts commits to a first-response time that the human team misses today in 12% of cases, and every retention offer has a cost cap per customer. Camila has four weeks of discovery before the next commercial cycle. Which sequence produces a usable acceptance criterion?

options.label: A
options.text: Bound with commercial what the assistant decides → set a threshold per decision on quality, offer cost and response time → check each threshold against what is already committed and adjust what is out of reach
options.feedback: Correct: the criterion is written per decision, with a threshold on each dimension that decides, and it is checked against what is reachable and what is already committed before it is accepted.

options.label: B
options.text: Set the monthly retention rate of the corporate segment as the single acceptance criterion → build the assistant against that goal → tune the prompt until the rate climbs
options.feedback: The retention rate is the business outcome, but it depends on price and on the competition; as the only criterion it does not tell which assistant response was acceptable and which was not.

options.label: C
options.text: Measure the current performance of the human team for a month → adopt that performance as the acceptance threshold for the assistant → turn it on when it matches in testing
options.feedback: Taking current performance as the goal is a known mistake, and here it is worse: that performance already misses the contracted response time in 12% of cases, so the threshold would be born in breach.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the sales reps for a list of cases where retention failed → order the list by business priority → write the scope and the acceptance criterion from the first three
options.feedback: Starting from real failures is the right source of cases, but a prioritized list is still not a criterion: it lacks a threshold per dimension and the check that the threshold is reachable.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an acceptance criterion has to be specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and that most use cases need evaluation on several dimensions at once: here response quality, first-response time and offer cost sit together, and they are documented success criteria rather than operational details. The order matters, because until you bound what the assistant decides there is nothing to put a threshold on. What separates this sequence from the more tempting one is the last step: a threshold is checked against what is reachable and against what has already been committed to the outside. Adopting current human performance looks prudent and is the classic trap, because that performance already misses the contracted time in 12% of cases, and freezing it as the goal turns the breach into the acceptance standard.

RULE: Write the criterion per decision with a threshold on every dimension that matters, and check it against what is reachable and already committed before you accept it.

TRAP: Adopting current performance as the acceptance threshold when that performance already misses what the contract promises.

TRY IT: Take the acceptance criterion from your last project and check whether it has a threshold on every dimension that decides and whether anyone verified it was reachable; if it came from current performance, look at which external commitment you were already missing.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/define-success https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/

questions.question: Banco Altamar retrieves internal procedures and circulars for the assistant that classifies complaints. The chunks are embedded as they are and also indexed with BM25. Sofía proposes prepending to each chunk, before embedding it and before indexing it, a short paragraph that places it inside the document it came from. The latency budget for the retrieval step is 900 ms at the 95th percentile, and it consumes 850 today. A complete reindex fits only in one weekend window per quarter. What should you expect from the change?

options.label: A
options.text: An improvement similar to the one from reranking, paying an extra 100 to 200 ms on every query.
options.feedback: Reranking is the other big accuracy lever, and there you do pay those milliseconds per query; contextualizing happens at indexing time and never shows up on the query path.

options.label: B
options.text: No improvement on exact-identifier queries, because the paragraph only affects the semantic leg of retrieval.
options.feedback: The context is prepended before embedding and also before indexing for BM25, so the contextual version of the lexical index is a separate technique that improves as well.

options.label: C
options.text: Fewer retrieval failures on both legs, with an indexing cost that is paid once per document.
options.feedback: Correct: contextualizing cuts retrieval failures on the semantic leg as much as on the lexical one, and its cost is paid a single time, in the reindex window.

options.label: D
options.text: A lower cost per query, because placed chunks let you halve the top_k without losing coverage.
options.feedback: Nothing guarantees you can trim top_k, and saving tokens is not the documented effect of the change: what improves is that the right chunk shows up among those retrieved.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to tell apart where each improvement in a retrieval pipeline is paid for: contextualizing the chunks is a one-time cost, at indexing time and per document, while reranking is a recurring cost per query, in money and in milliseconds. Prepending to each chunk a short context taken from its own document corrects the context the text loses when it is split, and the improvement is documented over the embeddings as much as over the lexical index, because both are built on the same contextualized text. With 850 of 900 ms already consumed, that is the only one of the two levers that fits in the budget. The distinction against reranking is temporal: one is paid at indexing time, the other on every query.

RULE: Contextualizing is paid once at indexing and reranking on every query: with the latency budget spent, only one of the two fits.

TRAP: Assuming that the prepended context only improves the semantic leg, when the lexical index is built on that same contextualized text.

TRY IT: Take twenty chunks from your index and read them without the document beside them: if you cannot say which product or which period they talk about, that is the context to prepend before embedding them.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval

questions.question: Bastión Legal retrieves internal precedents and passes them to the model like this: {"type": "document", "source": {"type": "content", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": ""}]}, "citations": {"enabled": true}}. The citations come back well formed, but they point at the whole block: Lucía, who reviews before signing, has to read all 900 words to find the sentence that supports each claim, and the firm bills by the hour. Internal policy forbids sending the full case file. Which change returns sentence-level citations?

options.label: A
options.text: Also ask for the exact sentence in a structured output field, so the reviewer sees it without opening the block.
options.feedback: Citations and structured outputs are mutually exclusive: asking for both in the same request returns a 400 error.

options.label: B
options.text: Split the precedent into several text blocks inside the same custom-content document, one per paragraph of the ruling.
options.feedback: That is the recommendation for tightening the boundary of a citation and the cited block would be smaller, but custom content is not chunked again: the citation is still block-level.

options.label: C
options.text: Pass each chunk as a plain-text document, where automatic sentence chunking produces the exact location.
options.feedback: Correct: a plain-text document is chunked by sentence and returns a character location, which is the granularity the review needs.

options.label: D
options.text: Trim the retrieved chunk to 200 words so the citation ends up pointing at much less text.
options.feedback: Trimming reduces what has to be read, but it degrades retrieval by cutting the reasoning of the ruling apart and still produces no sentence-level citation.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the granularity of a citation is set by the type of document you send, not by a parameter of its own. Custom content exists precisely so the system does not re-chunk what you already chunked, and that is why the citation points at the whole block; plain text is chunked by sentence and returns a character location. If you want the model to cite specific sentences from your chunks, each chunk travels as a plain-text document. The most tempting alternative, splitting the precedent into one block per paragraph, is documented as good practice and tightens the boundary, but it still produces a block citation rather than a sentence one. Asking for the sentence through structured outputs also runs into a documented incompatibility.

RULE: The type of document picks the citation granularity: plain text cites sentences and custom content cites the block you defined yourself.

TRAP: Treating citation granularity as a configuration setting rather than a consequence of how you packaged the retrieved chunk.

TRY IT: Send the same chunk twice, once as a plain-text document and once as custom content, and compare whether the citation comes back with a character location or a block one.

questions.question: The fault-diagnosis agent at Ceibo Telecom runs the same sequence of checks for every line and returns the subscriber a verdict that is shown as it comes, with no visible retry. The corporate contract penalizes every wrong verdict in that first answer. The suite runs each case three times because the system is not deterministic, and accuracy per run is around 88%. Lucía has to choose which number to commit to the committee that approves next week's launch. Which metric should she commit?

options.label: A
options.text: pass@k with k equal to the number of attempts the platform allows, because one of those attempts hitting is enough.
options.feedback: pass@k is the right metric when a single hit among several attempts settles the case, as in a flow where a person reviews and retries.

options.label: B
options.text: The average of hits per run over the total number of cases, which already reduces the three repetitions to one number.
options.feedback: That average describes typical performance, but it hides the spread: one case at 100% and another at 50% look the same as two cases at 75%.

options.label: C
options.text: The suite score from a single run per case, reporting separately the spread observed across the three repetitions.
options.feedback: Reporting the spread beats hiding it, but the committed number would still come from one run, which is not what the subscriber receives.

options.label: D
options.text: pass^k, the probability that all three runs of the same case hit, because the commitment is to each subscriber.
options.feedback: Correct: when the system has to be consistent and one wrong answer already breaks the commitment, the metric is the probability of hitting on every run.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the metric has to reflect what happens when the system fails in front of the user. pass@k measures the probability that at least one of k attempts succeeds, and it is the right metric when someone can retry or review, as with a coding agent whose output a person validates. pass^k measures the probability that every attempt succeeds, and it is the metric for customer-facing agents that have to be consistent: with accuracy per run near 88%, the probability of hitting three times in a row falls several points below that. Since the contract pays for the first answer per subscriber and there is no retry, that is the number to commit. The distinction against the per-run average is that the average describes the typical case, and what is penalized here is the variation.

RULE: Choose the metric by what failure costs: pass@k if someone can retry, pass^k if every answer reaches the customer and has to be right every time.

TRAP: Reporting the average performance of a non-deterministic system as if it were what each customer receives on their one opportunity.

TRY IT: Take the hit rate per run from your last eval and raise it to the number of runs per case: the drop between that result and the original is what you are not reporting today.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

html.question: The fault-diagnosis agent at Ceibo Telecom runs the same sequence of checks for every line and returns the subscriber a verdict that is shown as it comes, with no visible retry. The corporate contract penalizes every wrong verdict in that first answer. The suite runs each case three times because the system is not deterministic, and accuracy per run is around 88%. Lucía has to choose which number to commit to the committee that approves next week's launch. Which metric should she commit?
options: pass@k with k equal to the number of attempts the platform allows, because one of those attempts hitting is enough.
The average of hits per run over the total number of cases, which already reduces the three repetitions to one number.
The suite score from a single run per case, reporting separately the spread observed across the three repetitions.
pass^k, the probability that all three runs of the same case hit, because the commitment is to each subscriber.
html.explanation:
The general rule is that the metric has to reflect what happens when the system fails in front of the user. pass@k measures the probability that at least one of k attempts succeeds, and it is the right metric when someone can retry or review, as with a coding agent whose output a person validates. pass^k measures the probability that every attempt succeeds, and it is the metric for customer-facing agents that have to be consistent: with accuracy per run near 88%, the probability of hitting three times in a row falls several points below that. Since the contract pays for the first answer per subscriber and there is no retry, that is the number to commit. The distinction against the per-run average is that the average describes the typical case, and what is penalized here is the variation.

RULE: Choose the metric by what failure costs: pass@k if someone can retry, pass^k if every answer reaches the customer and has to be right every time.

TRAP: Reporting the average performance of a non-deterministic system as if it were what each customer receives on their one opportunity.

TRY IT: Take the hit rate per run from your last eval and raise it to the number of runs per case: the drop between that result and the original is what you are not reporting today.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

questions.question: The operational-safety assistant at Minera Nevado writes the risk report at the close of every shift with this configuration: {"stream": false, "max_tokens": 16000, "thinking": {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 4000}}. At the office it never fails. At the mine site, where the link drops several times an hour, one request in six dies without a response after a couple of minutes and the whole generation has to be redone. The shift has ten minutes to issue the report. Renata wants to understand the cause before touching anything. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: A
options.text: The site is going over the requests-per-minute limit and the API answers 429 without the client managing to log it.
options.feedback: A 429 arrives with its error code and its rate-limit headers; here no response comes back at all, which is exactly what separates a transport cut from an API rejection.

options.label: B
options.text: Site queries drag in more retrieved documents, so it would help to lower top_k and shorten the generation.
options.feedback: More retrieved documents make the input more expensive and can distract the model, but that would degrade the office runs too, and there no request fails.

options.label: C
options.text: The request holds a connection open for the whole generation: with no streaming, a link drop loses the entire response.
options.feedback: Correct: without streaming the response arrives complete at the end, so any drop throws the generation away; that is why the documentation advises against generating long responses without streaming, since some networks cut idle connections.

options.label: D
options.text: The thinking budget goes over the 32,000-token threshold, and that is why the request ends up hitting the system timeouts.
options.feedback: The recommendation to process in batch above 32,000 thinking tokens is real, but the budget configured here is 4,000 and comes nowhere near that threshold.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that streaming is not only a user-experience decision: it is also a timeout control. Without streaming, the request keeps a connection open until the whole response has been generated, so with 16,000 output tokens the client waits minutes hanging on a single thread. On a link that drops several times an hour, that means losing the complete generation and paying for it again. The documentation says it directly: do not set a large max_tokens without streaming, because some networks cut idle connections, and for long requests it recommends the Messages API with streaming. The distinction against the thinking threshold is arithmetic, because that limit applies above 32,000 reasoning tokens and the artifact configures 4,000.

RULE: With long outputs, streaming is not cosmetic: it is what keeps a network drop from making you pay twice for the same generation.

TRAP: Reading a transport symptom as if it were a model problem and looking for the cause in retrieval or in the reasoning budget.

TRY IT: Fire one request with a high max_tokens and no streaming, cut the network halfway through the generation and look at what you recover; repeat with streaming on and compare what is left on your side.

questions.question: The platform team at Ceibo Telecom proposes replacing the fixed first-level support flow with an agent that decides its own steps: in testing it resolves 9% more cases without escalation, but it takes longer and cost per case rises about 30%. The service level agreement signed with enterprise customers sets first-response time at the 95th percentile and carries a penalty. Renata takes the proposal to the executive committee next week. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Present the change as an improvement in resolution and propose measuring it in production for a month before the final decision is taken.
options.feedback: Measuring in production is reasonable when nothing is committed; here the trial would run on the traffic that carries the penalty, and the proposal would reach the committee without saying what is being sacrificed.

options.label: B
options.text: Present the decision against the contractual commitment: what it gains in resolution, how much time and cost get worse, and which traffic the agent is limited to.
options.feedback: Correct: agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance, so the decision goes up with all three magnitudes in view and scoped to the traffic where the commitment is not at stake.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the team to cut back the agent's scope until it matches the response time of the current fixed flow, and only then take the proposal to the executive committee.
options.feedback: Cutting until it matches today's performance dissolves the proposal: it turns a decision with tradeoffs into a false comparison and takes current performance as the ceiling.

options.label: D
options.text: Record the change in the architecture decision log and move ahead, because the choice of pattern belongs to the technical team that operates it.
options.feedback: Recording the decision is necessary, but a contractual commitment with a penalty is not a purely technical decision: service level agreements are tied to business and product decisions.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an architecture decision is communicated together with what it sacrifices and against the requirement that makes it significant. The documentation puts it plainly: agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, and it is on you to evaluate when that trade makes sense. Here the requirement that decides is contractual and carries a consequence, so the proposal arrives with all three magnitudes on the table and with a bounded scope: the agent goes where the commitment is not at stake, and the fixed flow keeps covering the committed traffic. The distinction against measuring it in production is that the trial would run precisely on the penalized traffic; and against settling it inside the team, that a service level agreement is a business decision and not an internal technical choice.

RULE: Present the decision with the constraint that decides it: what improves, what gets worse, and how far you limit it while the commitment stays protected.

TRAP: Presenting only the gain from a more autonomous architecture and leaving latency and cost as an implementation detail.

TRY IT: Take your last architecture proposal and write underneath it the two magnitudes it makes worse and the requirement with a contractual consequence that it answers; if you cannot name them, it is not yet a presentable decision.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://adr.github.io/ https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/

questions.question: Bastión Legal gives its clients memos drafted with help from its case law assistant. Under Anthropic's Commercial Terms, whose responsibility is it to decide where human review belongs over those outputs?

options.label: A
options.text: The model provider's, which answers for the accuracy of the citations it generates.
options.feedback: The provider assigns the customer the rights to the outputs, but does not take on assessing whether an output fits the case; factual claims should not be used without checking them.

options.label: B
options.text: The deploying customer's, which also should not use the claims without verifying them.
options.feedback: Correct: the terms put on the customer the assessment of whether outputs are appropriate for its use case, including where human review belongs, and they ask for factual claims to be verified.

options.label: C
options.text: The customer's, but only when the output is shown directly to an end consumer.
options.feedback: Consumer-facing scope triggers a different requirement, the Usage Policy one about high-risk use cases; the contractual duty to assess the output does not depend on it.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither party's, not until a regulator requires it in writing for that particular sector of activity.
options.feedback: Regulatory obligations do stack on top, but the contractual duty to assess the output is already written into the terms and does not wait for a regulator to activate it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that whoever deploys the system answers for the use it makes of the outputs. The Commercial Terms say it directly: it is the customer's responsibility to assess whether outputs are appropriate for its use case, including where human review belongs before those outputs are used or shared, and factual claims should not be taken as good without independently checking their accuracy. That duty is contractual and general. The distinction against the Usage Policy requirement is that the Usage Policy one is triggered by high-risk use cases with consumer-facing outputs and calls for review by a qualified professional: two different sources, with two different triggers.

RULE: Deciding where a human is needed is your job, not the provider's: the contract assigns it to you along with verifying the facts.

TRAP: Assuming the duty to review activates only when an outside rule demands it, or that it travels with the model provider.

TRY IT: Read the Commercial Terms clause on the use of outputs and write in one sentence, for a flow of your own, the exact point where human review enters and who signs off on it.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms

questions.question: Mistral Retail regenerates the review summary for 40,000 products every week and, in the same pass, has to flag the reviews that violate its publication policy; compliance requires that the flagging not depend on the judgment of the same model that writes the summary. The nightly window is six hours and the budget for the process is fixed. 80% of products have fewer than ten reviews and summarize without difficulty, while 5% concentrate the contradictory ones. Which two pattern decisions fit? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Sectioning: run the policy flagging in a parallel call, independent of the one that writes the summary, and compose the two results afterward.
options.feedback: Correct: splitting the work into independent subtasks that run in parallel is sectioning, and the documentation uses as its example one model handling the query while another screens it.

options.label: B
options.text: Routing: classify each product by review volume and spread, and send the simple ones to the fast model and the contradictory ones to the most capable.
options.feedback: Correct: sending the easy and frequent work to a cheaper model and the hard work to a more capable one is the canonical use of routing as a cost optimization pattern.

options.label: C
options.text: Orchestrator-workers: a central model that decides for each product which subtasks are needed and distributes the work across several workers.
options.feedback: Orchestrator-workers buys flexibility when you cannot predict which subtasks are needed; here they are always the same two, so you pay coordination for a freedom you never use.

options.label: D
options.text: Evaluator-optimizer: a second model reviews each summary against a rubric and sends it back to be rewritten until the review approves it.
options.feedback: Evaluator-optimizer pays off with clear evaluation criteria and when iterating adds measurable value; over 40,000 summaries in six hours it multiplies time and cost for a marginal gain.

options.label: E
options.text: An autonomous agent per product, with tools to walk the catalog and the reviews and decide how many steps each case needs.
options.feedback: The autonomous agent is the pattern for open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be predicted; here the path is known in advance and it is the most expensive multiplier on the list.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to choose the pattern from what you already know about the work before it starts. Because the subtasks are fixed in advance and independent of each other, this is parallelization in its sectioning variant, which the documentation illustrates with exactly this shape: one instance of the model processing the query while another screens it, which is what keeps the policy flagging from depending on the same judgment that writes the summary. Because the inputs also have uneven and known difficulty, this is routing, presented in the documentation as the pattern that sends easy and common cases to cheaper models and hard ones to more capable models. The distinction against orchestrator-workers is that the pattern exists for when you cannot predict which subtasks will be needed, and here you can: it is always summarize and flag.

RULE: Choose the pattern from what you already know: subtasks fixed in advance are parallelized, and inputs of uneven difficulty are routed.

TRAP: Paying for the flexibility of a dynamic orchestrator when the set of subtasks is known before the run starts.

TRY IT: Take a batch process in your system, write the list of subtasks it runs on each item, and mark the ones you knew about before the run; if that is all of them, you do not need an orchestrator to discover them.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

questions.question: Minera Nevado checks every environmental permit application against the commitments recorded in 400,000 technical documents. The process launches 60 subagents at once, one per family of commitments. Since volume grew, part of that fan-out ends in rate limit errors, the orchestrator retries the whole run, and the review no longer fits in the eight-hour nightly window that leaves the filing ready for the regulatory deadline. What should change?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the concurrency limit of the orchestrator so that no subagent waits its turn and the fan-out finishes its work sooner.
options.feedback: More concurrency against a provider rate limit produces more rejections, not more speed: the bottleneck is not the orchestrator but the rate the provider accepts.

options.label: B
options.text: Split the dispatch into smaller batches and chain them, keeping the result of each batch before the next one is launched.
options.feedback: Correct: for large fan-outs the documented recommendation is to split the work into batches rather than issue one wide dispatch, and keeping what is done avoids repeating what already succeeded.

options.label: C
options.text: Retry the whole run every time a subagent fails, so that the result always comes out of a single consistent pass.
options.feedback: Retrying everything gives consistency, but agents accumulate state and errors compound: the documented practice is to resume from the point of failure, with checkpoints, instead of starting over.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the review to a single agent with more turns, since the benefit of parallelizing is thoroughness and not speed.
options.feedback: It is true that the main benefit of parallelizing is thoroughness rather than speed, but a single agent does not cover 400,000 documents inside an eight-hour window.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a fan-out that is too wide does not get fixed by widening it. The hosting documentation says so directly: large parallel dispatches of subagents run into rate limits, and the recommendation is to break the work into smaller batches instead of issuing one wide dispatch. The second half of the answer comes from the published experience with multi-agent systems: agents accumulate state and errors compound, so you want to resume from where the failure happened, with retries and checkpoints, rather than repeat the entire run. The distinction against raising concurrency is that the limit holding the process back belongs to the provider and not to the orchestrator, and asking for more in parallel only multiplies the rejections.

RULE: A fan-out that is too wide runs into the rate limit: split the dispatch into batches and keep what is done so you never repeat it.

TRAP: Believing that raising concurrency speeds up work that is already bounded by the rate the provider accepts.

TRY IT: Look at the log of your last parallel run and count how many subagents ended with a rate limit error; then repeat the work in batches a third of the size and compare total time.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hosting https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

questions.question: The medical-record summary suite at Red Vicuña Salud has 120 cases, grades each summary by its similarity to a reference written by physicians, and has been scoring above 0.97 for five months. Over those same five months the quality committee logged eleven summaries that omitted a declared allergy, a field the protocol always requires, and not one of them pushed the score down. The team has two days of clinical time per month to work on the suite. What are the two most likely reasons the suite does not see the problem? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The suite is saturated: pinned near its ceiling for months, it works as a regression alarm but gives no signal on new cases.
options.feedback: Correct: an eval living at its maximum has stopped discriminating, and the documented answer is to build new and harder tasks out of real failures.

options.label: B
options.text: The set is too small for a clinical system: below several thousand cases no result is representative.
options.feedback: Volume helps when grading is automatic, but no documented minimum exists, and adding similar cases would not make the omission appear.

options.label: C
options.text: The physicians who wrote the reference summaries did not measure agreement among themselves before using them as the standard.
options.feedback: Agreement between raters matters when the reference is debatable, but the omission of a declared allergy admits no second reading.

options.label: D
options.text: The only measure is global similarity to the reference text, which barely moves when one mandatory line is missing.
options.feedback: Correct: a criterion that must always hold needs its own deterministic presence grader, one that passes or fails the case on its own.

options.label: E
options.text: The platform updated the model over those five months and the suite does not pin it, so it compares different systems.
options.feedback: Pinning the model avoids mistaking an update for a regression, but it does not explain why the suite never caught the omission in five months.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an eval measures only what you asked it to measure, and that a high, stable score over months is a symptom rather than an achievement: a saturated eval still catches regressions but has no headroom left to flag anything new, and the documented answer is to build harder tasks out of the failures users report. The second cause is a grading-method problem. Similarity to a reference text scores global resemblance, so the absence of one mandatory line barely moves it. A criterion that can never be missing is graded apart, with a deterministic presence check that decides the case on its own, because scoring each dimension separately beats compressing everything into one number.

RULE: An eval pinned at its ceiling has stopped measuring: add hard tasks taken from real failures, and give every mandatory criterion its own check.

TRAP: Assuming a global resemblance metric covers an absolute requirement: the text has resemblance to spare even when the one line that matters is gone.

TRY IT: Take one case from your suite, delete by hand the line that can never be missing from the summary, and grade it again: if the score barely drops, you know which grader you lack.

questions.question: Yaguareté Logística classifies 12,000 shipments a day with an agent whose stable prefix weighs 40,000 tokens between the tariff guide and the house criteria, and today that prefix is read from cache on almost every request. To simplify the code, Ximena decides to assemble the tools array per request according to the destination country: the four customs authorities share eight tools and each adds two of its own, so the array changes from one request to the next. Cost is controlled per shipment. What effect will that change have?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the messages part will be invalidated, because tool definitions are cached in a separate space of their own.
options.feedback: That is what happens when you change tool_choice, which affects the messages alone; changing the definitions reaches quite a bit further.

options.label: B
options.text: There will be no impact on the cache, because the prefix is identified by the content of the system prompt and tools stay outside it.
options.feedback: The hashed prefix spans tools, system and messages in that order, so the tool definitions are part of the cache key.

options.label: C
options.text: Cost per shipment will fall, because each request carries fewer tool definitions and therefore fewer input tokens.
options.feedback: The prompt does carry fewer tokens, but that reduction is tiny next to what it costs to rewrite a 40,000-token prefix on every shipment.

options.label: D
options.text: Cost per shipment will rise, because changing the tool definitions invalidates the whole cache and every request writes it again.
options.feedback: Correct: tools head the prefix, so touching them invalidates that level and every level after it, and the stable prefix stops being read from cache.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of prompt caching is that the prefix is hashed in a fixed order, tools first, then system and finally messages, and that a change at one level invalidates that level and all the ones behind it. Varying the tools array by country touches the first level, so no request shares a prefix with the one before: the 40,000 stable tokens are written again every time, at write price, instead of being read at a fraction of the cost. The saving from carrying two fewer definitions is negligible next to that. The way to vary what tools are offered without breaking the cache is to declare the full set once and leave the array identical across requests.

RULE: The tools array heads the cached prefix: if it changes between requests there is no cache, so declare the full set once and vary by other means.

TRAP: Confusing fewer tokens with less cost: dropping two definitions saves cents and breaks a prefix that was far cheaper to read than to write.

TRY IT: Send two requests back to back with different tools arrays and look at cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens in both: you will see writes in both and reads in neither.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages

questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro runs its own MCP server that acts as an intermediary in front of the customs API. In the penetration test, Malena demonstrated two things: a client she registered from outside the terminal obtained an authorization code in the name of a customs broker without the customs consent screen ever appearing, and an agent whose token carried no write permissions managed to run the file-declaration operation. A misattributed declaration blocks clearance for 72 hours. What are the two causes? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The server requires the Authorization header on every HTTP request instead of opening an authenticated session and reusing it.
options.feedback: The specification requires exactly that: the token travels on every request even when they belong to the same logical session, and an MCP server must not use sessions to authenticate.

options.label: B
options.text: Tokens travel in the header and not in the query string, so the load balancer cannot log them for the audit.
options.feedback: That is also the correct behavior: access tokens must not be included in the query string of the URL, precisely so they do not end up in intermediate logs.

options.label: C
options.text: The intermediary uses a static client_id with customs, lets clients register dynamically and asks for no consent of its own per client.
options.feedback: Correct: with a static client_id, dynamic registration and a consent cookie already issued, the authorization server skips the screen and the code lands in the attacker's client.

options.label: D
options.text: The server checks that the token was issued for itself and rejects those carrying another audience before serving the request.
options.feedback: Validating the audience of the token is mandatory and is what prevents accepting credentials issued for a different recipient; it describes a control that is present, not a hole.

options.label: E
options.text: The server takes a valid token as sufficient and runs no permission check of its own on each operation.
options.feedback: Correct: a valid, well-addressed token proves who is calling, but authorization of each operation has to be applied by the server with logic of its own.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that authenticating the caller and authorizing the operation are two different controls, and that an MCP server acting as an intermediary in front of a third party also takes on the responsibility for consent. The confused deputy needs four conditions at once: a static client_id with the third party's authorization server, clients that can register dynamically, a consent cookie already present from an earlier authorization, and no per-client consent at the intermediary. When all four hold, the consent screen is skipped and the authorization code ends up in the attacker's client; the mitigation is to keep a record of the client_ids each person approved and to ask for consent before starting the flow. The second finding is independent: accepting a valid token does not relieve the server of checking permissions operation by operation.

RULE: The intermediary asks for its own per-client consent before forwarding the flow and checks permissions on every operation, even when the token is valid.

TRAP: Assuming that a well-issued token with the right audience already authorizes the operation, and that the third party's consent screen protects the intermediary.

TRY IT: Check whether your intermediary server records which client_id each person approved, and whether any write operation is decided on token validity alone; one of the two is almost always missing.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/security_best_practices https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization

questions.question: Pampero Agro closes the season with one agronomic report per plot: 2,400 plots, twenty days to deliver, and sections that lean on the one before, because the final diagnosis cites the deviations detected earlier. Each report means reading the weekly field notes, the sensor series and the lab results for the whole season, far beyond what fits in a single run. Connectivity out on the farms drops often and cuts any run longer than fifteen minutes. Which decomposition fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Split the report into sections, run one session per section, and leave a progress file with the state of each one for the next session to read.
options.feedback: Correct: work that does not fit in one run is split into discrete sessions that leave artifacts behind, because each new session starts with no memory of the last and has to read the state to resume.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep a single long session per plot and rely on the automatic compaction of the context every time the conversation approaches the limit of the available window.
options.feedback: Compaction keeps the conversation alive, but on its own it does not sustain long work: it summarizes and discards, and what it discards is usually the detail the next section has to cite.

options.label: C
options.text: Launch one subagent per section in parallel and have the coordinator assemble the report by joining the results once they have all finished.
options.feedback: Parallelizing pays off when the context can genuinely be isolated; here each section needs the result of the previous one, and a connectivity drop leaves the fan-out half done with no way to resume it.

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce the scope of the report until the season's data fits complete into a single run, avoiding the continuity problem altogether.
options.feedback: Cutting the scope solves the technical problem by deleting the deliverable: the closing report is what the grower contracted, and its value is precisely in crossing the whole season.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that work which does not fit in a single run is decomposed into discrete sessions that leave a trace, because every new session starts with no memory of the previous one and compaction alone is not enough. The documented pattern separates preparing the environment from making incremental progress, has each run work on one unit at a time, and leaves explicit artifacts, a progress file and a list of units with their state, that the next session reads before it starts; an interrupted run then costs one section instead of the whole report. The distinction against parallelizing by section is that work is only split when the context can truly be isolated: when step two needs the output of step one, a single chained line of work comes out cleaner and cheaper.

RULE: When the work does not fit in one run, split it into steps that leave a trace: the next session resumes from the artifact, not from memory.

TRAP: Trusting compaction to sustain long work, or parallelizing steps that depend on the result of the one before.

TRY IT: Interrupt a long run of your agent halfway on purpose and start a fresh session: if it cannot tell you what is done and what is left, you are missing the progress artifact.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents https://claude.com/blog/subagents-in-claude-code

questions.question: At Agencia Nacional de Ingresos, the three production systems and the test environment share this credential: {"name": "agentes-ani", "scope": {"type": "organization"}, "expires_at": null}. Ximena, from audit, raises two requirements: attribute every automated decision to the system that made it, and cut off a compromised credential without stopping the other three services. The monthly cost report arrives today as a single line. What is the gap, and what should be done?

options.label: A
options.text: The credential does not expire: rotate it every 90 days and audit its expires_at while keeping the current scope.
options.feedback: Rotating and watching expiry is recommended hygiene and shortens the window of a leaked credential, but a rotated, shared key still attributes nothing and still cannot be cut off alone.

options.label: B
options.text: Static credentials are unnecessary: migrate to Workload Identity Federation and leave this key in the environment as a fallback.
options.feedback: Federation with short-lived tokens is the deep answer to long-lived keys, but a key left in the environment silently takes precedence over federation and cancels out the change.

options.label: C
options.text: A cap per system is missing: declare in each agent's system prompt how much it may spend during the month.
options.feedback: A limit written into the prompt is advice, not a control: spend is bounded with workspace limits, which apply outside the model and do not depend on the response.

options.label: D
options.text: The scope is organization-wide and shared: issue one credential per workspace, one for each of the systems.
options.feedback: Correct: an organization-scoped credential reaches any workspace, and separating them by workspace is what gives spend attribution and independent revocation.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the scope of a credential defines both the blast radius and the unit of attribution. An organization-scoped key works in any workspace the account reaches, so sharing it across four systems makes it impossible to know which one made each call and forces you to cut all of them off when one is compromised; a workspace key stays tied to that space and is revoked on its own. Usage and cost are also reported grouped by workspace, so the separation fixes the single line in the monthly report as well. The most tempting alternative, federating identities with short-lived tokens, is better in the long run, but leaving the old key in the environment puts it ahead of federation and the change has no effect.

RULE: One credential per system and per workspace: the scope is at once the blast radius, the unit of revocation and the line in the cost report.

TRAP: Confusing rotating a credential with narrowing it: changing its value does not reduce what it reaches or let you shut down a single system.

TRY IT: List your active keys with their scope and note beside each one which systems use it; any key that shows up in more than one system is the one you cannot revoke without shutting down too much.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/administration-api https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/workload-identity-federation

questions.question: Yaguareté Logística classifies 12,000 shipments a day with a single call that pulls the candidate tariff headings from the nomenclature plus a few examples. Customs in one of the four countries now requires that, on any query, the company show the heading considered and the nomenclature rule that supports it. Nothing records that today, and every unsupported classification costs a fine and a delay at the border. The team proposes making the classification agentic. Which design fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn the classifier into an autonomous agent with access to the nomenclature and the customs tools, so that it decides for itself what to query on each shipment.
options.feedback: The autonomous agent fits when you cannot predict the steps; here the path is known, and giving it freedom complicates exactly what customs asks for, an intermediate step you can record.

options.label: B
options.text: Chain two calls with a programmatic check between them: the candidate heading with its rule, the check against the nomenclature, and then the classification.
options.feedback: Correct: chaining serves when you need to inspect the intermediate output or impose a fixed pipeline structure, and because each step is a separate call you can log it, evaluate it or block it.

options.label: C
options.text: Run the same classification three times and keep the heading that gets the most votes across the three runs to raise confidence in the result.
options.feedback: Voting across runs raises confidence when there is no way to verify the answer, but it triples cost over 12,000 shipments a day and still produces no rule to exhibit.

options.label: D
options.text: Move to the most capable model in the family on every classification to reduce the number of wrong headings that reach the border.
options.feedback: A more capable model can reduce errors, but the stated problem is support and traceability: with no intermediate step on record, customs still cannot see which rule was applied.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to choose the pattern from what the problem requires and not from what sounds most advanced. Here the requirement is to show the heading considered and the rule that supports it, which means inspecting and keeping an intermediate output, and that is exactly the criterion the current documentation gives for explicit prompt chaining: it serves when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or impose a particular pipeline structure, and because each step is a separate call you can log, evaluate or branch at any point. The programmatic check between steps is what turns the chain into a guarantee rather than a suggestion. The distinction against the autonomous agent is that the pattern is reserved for problems where you cannot predict how many steps are needed, and here the sequence is fixed by the customs procedure.

RULE: Chain when you need to see or validate the intermediate step: every link is a separate call you can log, evaluate or block.

TRAP: Confusing a traceability problem with a problem of model capability.

TRY IT: Take a classification your system made yesterday and try to reconstruct from what was logged which alternative it considered and on what grounds; if you cannot, that step is not yet a separate call.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/chain-prompts https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
