questions.question: AndesWare standardized on Claude Code across its 400 developers. The monorepo merges about 300 change requests a day, and 40 of its packages have access restricted by team. Today the assistant locates code by walking the tree and reading files with the permissions of whoever is asking. Joaquín, a tech lead, proposes building a semantic index of the repository because some searches feel slow. The platform is maintained by three people. What should you propose?

options.label: A
options.text: Build the index and replicate the per-team permissions inside it, rebuilding it every night to bound the drift.
options.feedback: Replicating permissions is possible, but no documented mechanism keeps them in sync with the source, and every drift of that copy is a leak someone has to watch.

options.label: B
options.text: Build the index and add a lexical leg to it, so that searches by exact function name do not fail.
options.feedback: The lexical leg fixes semantic retrieval losing exact identifiers, but walking the tree already matches exactly, and that touches neither the permissions nor the maintenance.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the agentic search, which reads with the permissions of whoever is asking and leaves no second copy of the code to protect.
options.feedback: Correct: walking the tree needs no index to build, maintain or host, so no second set of permissions appears that has to be kept in sync with the repository's.

options.label: D
options.text: Spread the exploration across subagents in parallel, which lowers the wall-clock time of the broadest searches.
options.feedback: Exploring in parallel does lower wall-clock time on broad tasks, but it multiplies tokens per query and does not address the restricted access on the 40 packages.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that semantic search is usually faster than agentic search, but less exact, harder to maintain and less transparent, which is why the recommendation is to start with agentic search and add an index only if you need faster results or more variations. An index also creates a copy of the corpus outside the system of record: it has to be built, maintained and protected, and its permissions have to follow the repository's without any standard mechanism to make that happen. Walking the tree reads with the permissions of whoever is asking and leaves no such copy, and that is what decides the comparison with 40 restricted packages and a team of three. The distinction against the nightly index is that the design arrives late not only to the state of the code but also to changes in permissions.

RULE: An index is one more copy of the corpus: you have to keep it fresh and under the same permissions as the source, and nobody hands you that sync for free.

TRAP: Comparing an index against navigation on speed alone, forgetting that the index adds a copy of the data with an access control of its own to maintain.

TRY IT: List which folders your agent can read and compare that with what the person asking can read; if you already have an index, find out who keeps that list in sync.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk https://claude.com/blog/how-claude-code-works-in-large-codebases-best-practices-and-where-to-start

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom's technical support agent queries the ticketing system through an in-house MCP server, declared in the .mcp.json file at the root of the repository: {"mcpServers": {"tickets": {"type": "stdio", "command": "node", "args": ["./scripts/tickets-mcp.js"]}}}. People who open the session at the root see the server connected; people who open it inside the diagnostics module folder get Failed to connect, and that team carries the contractual first-response commitment. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The relative path in args resolves against the directory the session was launched from, not against the file's location.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the frequent cause of a stdio server not starting, and it explains why the result depends on the folder the session is opened from; a path that does not depend on the launch is the fix.

options.label: B
options.text: The project-scope server is still waiting for the one-time approval that is granted from /mcp in the first session.
options.feedback: A project-scope server does need that approval, but then it shows as pending approval, and for everyone alike, not only for whoever opens the session in a subfolder.

options.label: C
options.text: The server's startup time exceeds the default limit and has to be raised with the MCP_TIMEOUT variable.
options.feedback: A slow startup gives the same failure from any folder; here the result changes with where the session is launched, and that rules out the timeout.

options.label: D
options.text: The entry does not declare the transport, so it is skipped as an error when the configuration file loads.
options.feedback: An entry that carries url but declares no type is a configuration error, because Claude Code reads it as a stdio server; the one in the artifact declares stdio explicitly, so reading the entry rules this cause out before you test anything.

questions.explanation:
The general rule in configuration troubleshooting is to separate what depends on the environment from what depends on the file. An MCP server that connects from one folder and fails from another points at a path that resolves against the working directory: relative paths in command and in args resolve against the directory Claude Code was launched from, not against the location of the .mcp.json file, and that is a frequent cause of a stdio server never starting. The distinction against the pending approval of a project-scope server is in the symptom: that one appears as a pending approval state and affects every session alike.

RULE: When something fails depending on where you launch it, suspect a relative path: it resolves against the working directory, not against the file that declares it.

TRAP: Reading a relative path as if it were relative to the file that contains it, and looking for the cause in the server instead of in the launch directory.

TRY IT: Open a session in a subfolder of the repository and run claude mcp list; then change args to the absolute path of the script, repeat from the same subfolder and compare the two states.

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación enabled Zero Data Retention across its organization, as its agreement with the schools requires, and the 25 people who build the automated tutors run Claude Code on that organization. The board approved the tool's cost for one semester on the condition of receiving a monthly impact report. While preparing the first one, Malena finds that the analytics dashboard shows no contribution metrics. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn off Zero Data Retention during the trial semester so that the dashboard completes the contribution metrics.
options.feedback: It does bring the dashboard back in full, but it trades a data control the agreement requires for a report: the requirement that decides here is the one that cannot be negotiated.

options.label: B
options.text: Install the GitHub app and switch on the GitHub analytics toggle so that the metrics start showing up.
options.feedback: Those two steps are the right ones for enabling contribution metrics in an ordinary organization, but in an organization with ZDR the dashboard shows usage metrics only.

options.label: C
options.text: Request an analytics API key from the Enterprise plan and rebuild the contribution metrics from it.
options.feedback: That API delivers interaction, usage and cost per person across the Claude surfaces; it does not bring back the attribution of lines and pull requests that ZDR leaves out.

options.label: D
options.text: Report with usage metrics and your own OpenTelemetry telemetry, and state that contribution is missing.
options.feedback: Correct: usage metrics stay available and OpenTelemetry carries cost and tokens per person to your own stack, which is what sustains a monthly report without touching the data control.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a metric you cannot obtain does not belong in a reporting commitment. In an organization with Zero Data Retention the analytics dashboard shows usage metrics only: contribution metrics, which attribute lines and pull requests to assisted work, are not available. Since ZDR comes from a contractual requirement, what gets adjusted is the report and not the data control. The distinction against enabling the GitHub integration is that those steps are the right ones in an organization without ZDR and change nothing here, while OpenTelemetry works in any configuration and carries cost and tokens per person to your own stack.

RULE: Promise only the metric your configuration can produce: look first at what the data control you already signed lets you measure.

TRAP: Loosening a contractually required data control to complete a dashboard, or repeating the enablement steps that ZDR leaves without effect.

TRY IT: Open your organization's analytics dashboard and note which sections bring back data and which come up empty; then check in the settings whether ZDR is enabled.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/analytics https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs

questions.question: The internal incident agent at AndesWare loads the tools of the platform's six MCP servers: 180 definitions that take up 38,000 tokens of the input. A typical run resolves in four or five turns, the usage field of one turn returns input_tokens 96,300 and output_tokens 1,200, and the tool that searches the monorepo returns the whole file every time. The team's measurement shows that twelve tools cover 90% of the calls and that accuracy is the same with the full catalog or the trimmed one. Cost per team has a monthly cap. Which two measures lower the input without losing capability? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Turn on tool search with deferred loading so that only the definitions a request needs enter the context.
options.feedback: Correct: with a deferred catalog the cost per run drops noticeably at this scale and accuracy stays in the same range.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the agent to the family model with the largest context window so that 96,300 tokens stop being a problem.
options.feedback: A bigger window admits more tokens, but it does not make them cheaper or improve retrieval: accuracy degrades just the same as the context grows.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on compaction with a low threshold so that the history is summarized before the run reaches its fifth turn.
options.feedback: Compaction sustains long conversations, but these runs end in four or five turns and the summarization step saves nothing here.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the runs through the Message Batches API to take the 50% discount on every token type.
options.feedback: The batch discount is real, but the agent resolves incidents interactively and batch is asynchronous: it does not apply to this workload.

options.label: E
options.text: Make the monorepo tool return paginated and filtered results, with sensible defaults, instead of the whole file.
options.feedback: Correct: sizing each tool response is the other half of the problem, because every full dump comes back as input on all the following turns.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to look for the smallest set of high-signal tokens that gets the result, and here the input is inflated by two independent causes. The first is the catalog: at this scale tool definitions cost money and not accuracy, and the team's own measurement confirms it, so the documented lever is tool search with deferred loading, which keeps the catalog available without putting all of it in the context. The second is the size of the responses: a tool that returns the whole file leaves that dump in the conversation and drags it along on every later turn, and the recommendation is to paginate, filter or truncate with sensible defaults. The distinction against a bigger window is that more room makes nothing cheaper and retrieval degrades all the same.

RULE: Lower the input from both sides: defer the definitions almost nobody calls, and return paginated results instead of whole dumps.

TRAP: Treating an inflated context as a window-size problem, when what is in excess are definitions nobody uses and results nobody reads in full.

TRY IT: List the tools your agent exposes and mark which ones 90% of the traffic uses; then measure how many tokens your noisiest tool returns and compare that with a paginated version.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

questions.question: The control-room assistant at Pehuén Energía exposes eight tools, and three of them overlap: consultar_alarma_activa returns the alarm in progress, listar_alarmas returns the ones from the shift and buscar_evento searches the history by text. During an alarm the operator needs the answer in under 20 seconds, and each call adds a full round trip. Facundo measures that on one alarm in four the assistant chains all three before answering, and that two engineers on the team do not agree on which one applies either. What is the cause, and what should be done first?

options.label: A
options.text: The catalog takes up too much context: turn on tool search so only the tools that are needed arrive.
options.feedback: Deferring definitions pays off from around ten tools on, or with large definitions; with eight, loading them up front is faster, and the ambiguity would be left untouched.

options.label: B
options.text: The descriptions are too brief: expand them to three or four sentences explaining when to use each one.
options.feedback: Detailed descriptions are the factor with the most influence on selection, but if two engineers do not know which one applies, the problem is in the catalog and not in the text.

options.label: C
options.text: The agent carries too many responsibilities: split it into one agent for alarms and another for trends.
options.feedback: Splitting agents is justified by context, parallelism or genuinely different tool sets and costs several times more tokens; here the overlap would travel to the alarm agent all the same.

options.label: D
options.text: The three tools do not have distinct purposes: consolidate them into a single query with a scope parameter.
options.feedback: Correct: overlapping tools create ambiguous decision points, and grouping related operations into one tool with a parameter cuts both the ambiguity and the round trips.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for capability bloat is to look first at what kind of excess you have: when there are too many definitions you defer them, when there are too many results you process them outside the context, and when tools overlap what is short is not volume but clarity. The qualitative test is documented: if an experienced person cannot say which tool applies in a situation, the agent should not be expected to either, and here two engineers disagree. With eight tools the catalog does not justify deferring definitions, so the fix is to consolidate the related operations into a single tool with a parameter that covers the three cases, which also removes two round trips from the twenty-second window. The distinction against improving the descriptions is that longer text does not separate two tools that do the same thing.

RULE: If an experienced engineer cannot tell which tool applies, neither can the agent: that is not fixed by writing more, it is fixed by consolidating.

TRAP: Confusing an ambiguous catalog with a large one and answering with deferral or with more agents, when what is in excess is overlap.

TRY IT: Take your tool list and ask two people on the team, separately, which one they would use for the five most frequent queries; the ones they disagree on are candidates for consolidation.

questions.question: Bastión Legal extracts the parties, the dates and the amounts from 3,000 scanned contracts every night, and a deterministic validator compares each field against the document and flags whatever does not match. That extraction already goes through the Message Batches API and runs at the lowest effort of the same capable model the long contract review uses. Lowering the effort did not change accuracy, and the firm is still over its monthly budget. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the long contract review to the fastest and cheapest model as well, so that the whole flow runs at one cost.
options.feedback: It would unify spend, but that model fits high-volume work with checkable output, not long loops, where it falls clearly behind.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the extraction with the fastest and cheapest model in the family and leave the long review on the capable model.
options.feedback: Correct: extraction is high-volume work with output a validator can check, which is exactly the profile where the cheap model pays off.

options.label: C
options.text: Split each contract across several subagents in parallel so that each one processes less text and the night ends sooner.
options.feedback: Delegation helps when the work splits into independent pieces, but it multiplies tokens, and the bottleneck here is cost and not the clock.

options.label: D
options.text: Turn on fast mode for the nightly run to close the window earlier and free capacity for the next day.
options.feedback: Fast mode raises tokens per second at a premium price and cannot be combined with the Batches API, so it does not fit this workload.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for choosing a model is to decide by criteria rather than by catalog: capability, speed, cost and effort. The criteria are clear in this workload. Extraction is high-volume work with checkable output, because a deterministic validator reviews every field and catches the error with no human intervention, and that is the documented profile of the fast, cheap model, which in exchange falls behind in long agentic loops such as contract review. The correct decision therefore routes each task to its own model instead of unifying them. Lowering the effort further is already exhausted here: it was swept down to the minimum with no loss of accuracy and the budget still does not close, so the next lever is the model.

RULE: Route by task: high volume with checkable output goes to the cheap model, and long loops stay on the capable one.

TRAP: Choosing one model for the whole flow and ending up paying frontier capability on the most repetitive and most easily verified task.

TRY IT: Take 100 contracts you have already extracted, run them again with the cheapest model, and pass both outputs through your validator: compare the share of flagged fields and the cost per document.

questions.question: The assisted-grading suite at Grupo Aurora Educación is scored by an automatic judge that applies a five-criterion rubric. Since Monday's run the judge has been failing 30% of the feedback. Two teachers reviewed thirty of those failed items by hand and agree they are fine: they differ from the rubric example only in the order of the sections and in the heading. To fit the whole suite inside the weekly budget, the judge runs on a small, fast model. What is the most likely cause and what fixes it?

options.label: A
options.text: The grading assistant changed behavior: its prompt has to demand the same section order and the same heading as the rubric.
options.feedback: Tuning the assistant to the format the judge expects raises the score, but it optimizes the system against a quirk of the grader rather than against quality.

options.label: B
options.text: The judge is the defect: a small model penalizes format, so raise the judge's model and adjust the rubric.
options.feedback: Correct: if expert review passes the answers the judge fails, the problem sits in the grader, and format must not decide the verdict.

options.label: C
options.text: Automatic scoring is not enough for this criterion: the evaluation of feedback should move to permanent human review.
options.feedback: Human review is the highest-quality option, but the documentation asks you to avoid it where you can, and with 180,000 students it neither scales nor fits the budget.

options.label: D
options.text: The case set has become small and unbalanced: recent feedback has to be added until the suite doubles in size.
options.feedback: More cases improve coverage, but a judge that punishes format will fail the same proportion of feedback in a suite twice the size.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the grader is also a component that can fail, and the way to check it is to read the transcripts and contrast its verdicts with expert people. Here the contrast already happened: two teachers pass the feedback the judge fails, and the only difference is format. That is the documented failure mode of a small judge, which marks a correct answer as incorrect because it does not look like what the rubric describes. The documented corrections are to use a more capable model to judge and to rewrite the rubric so that format does not decide. The distinction against tuning the assistant that writes the feedback is that this option makes the suite pass without improving anything real: it adapts the system to the grader's defect.

RULE: Before you believe a drop in the score, audit the judge: if experts pass what the judge fails, the defect is in the grader.

TRAP: Fixing the system to please the grader: the score goes up, quality does not move, and the rubric ends up measuring format.

TRY IT: Take twenty cases your judge failed, have an expert grade them, and count how many they agree on: if disagreement is high, change the judge's model before you touch the system prompt.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: A team documents what information will be available about its system and its outputs to the people who interact with it. Under the trustworthy AI characteristics of the NIST AI RMF, which characteristic is that team working on?

options.label: A
options.text: Explainability, that is, a representation of the mechanisms underlying how the system operates.
options.feedback: Explainability describes the mechanism by which the system operates; it is a neighboring characteristic, but it answers how it works, not how much information is made available.

options.label: B
options.text: Interpretability, that is, the meaning of the system's output in its context of use.
options.feedback: Interpretability deals with the meaning of the output for whoever receives it; also a neighbor, but it is not the availability of information about the system.

options.label: C
options.text: Security and resilience, that is, maintaining function and structure in the face of external change.
options.feedback: That characteristic covers confidentiality, integrity and availability, and the ability to maintain function and structure under internal and external change; it does not speak to what is communicated.

options.label: D
options.text: Transparency, that is, how much information is available about the system and its outputs.
options.feedback: Correct: transparency is the degree to which information about the system and its outputs is available to those who interact with it, whether or not the mechanism is explained as well.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that transparency, explainability and interpretability answer different questions, and the framework separates them on purpose. Transparency measures how much information about the system and its outputs is available to those who interact with it; explainability is a representation of the mechanisms underlying its operation; interpretability refers to the meaning of the output. Documenting what is made available, to whom and at what moment is transparency work. The distinction against explainability is that a system can be very transparent about its data, its limits and its purpose without yet offering an explanation of the mechanism that produces each result.

RULE: Transparency is what is known about the system, explainability is how it works, and interpretability is what its output means.

TRAP: Using transparency and explainability as synonyms, and promising an explanation of the mechanism when what was delivered was available information.

TRY IT: Write one line for each of the three for a system of your own: what information you publish, what mechanism you can describe, and what one concrete output means; you will see which one is missing.

questions.question: A platform team needs its internal assistant to stop producing a format that breaks the text reader of the system that consumes the answers. According to documented prompting practice, which wording of that rule in the system prompt works best?

options.label: A
options.text: The prohibition written in capitals and repeated at the beginning and at the end of the system prompt to reinforce it.
options.feedback: Repeating and emphasizing a prohibition spends tokens without adding information: the model still does not know what to produce instead, or why.

options.label: B
options.text: The prohibition together with an example of the format that must not be generated, so that what to avoid is clear.
options.feedback: Examples are a powerful technique, but an example of what you do not want puts precisely that format in front of the model.

options.label: C
options.text: The instruction of what to do instead of what to avoid, together with the reason that format causes problems.
options.feedback: Correct: saying what is expected and explaining why works better than prohibiting, because the model generalizes from the explanation to cases you did not list.

options.label: D
options.text: The prohibition placed at the end of the system prompt, as close as possible to the turn where the model writes.
options.feedback: Position weighs in long blocks of data, not in a short rule: moving it does not change that it still says only what not to do.

questions.explanation:
The documented general rule is to tell the model what to do instead of what not to do, and to give it the reason. The documentation shows it with a concrete case: a flat prohibition performs worse than the same rule explained, because the model generalizes from the explanation toward situations nobody listed. A prohibition in capitals or repeated adds no information, and an example of what you do not want introduces that very format into the context. The key distinction is that the positive instruction describes the desired output, which is what the model has to produce.

RULE: Say what to do, not what to avoid, and explain the reason: the explanation is what lets the model generalize to the cases you did not list.

TRAP: Assuming a more emphatic prohibition is followed better, when what is missing is not emphasis but the expected behavior and its reason.

TRY IT: Take the most repeated rule in your system prompt, rewrite it in the positive with one sentence of reason, and run twenty cases with each version to count how often it is followed.

questions.question: The fault diagnosis assistant at Ceibo Telecom builds every response from the line status, the incident history for the area and the complete procedures manual: about 45,000 tokens per request. At 60,000 diagnoses a day the 95th percentile is over the agreed time, which is measured on the complete diagnosis delivered to the technician and not on the first token, and 30% of responses cite procedures from a different fault family. Which change attacks both at once?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn on streaming so that the technician starts reading the diagnosis while the rest of the response is still being generated.
options.feedback: Streaming improves perceived latency and time to first token, but the commitment is measured on the complete diagnosis, and none of this touches the cause of the wrong citations.

options.label: B
options.text: Cache the static prefix of the prompt so that the procedures manual stops being billed as new input on every single request.
options.feedback: Caching makes repeated input cheaper and it is a real lever, but the model is still attending to 45,000 tokens per request and the whole manual still competes for its attention.

options.label: C
options.text: Retrieve at run time only the procedures for the fault family of the case, instead of sending the complete manual on every request.
options.feedback: Correct: when the static and dynamic context is large, putting all of it in the prompt raises cost, lengthens the response and exhausts the window; retrieving what is relevant improves accuracy, time and cost at once.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace the model with the fastest and cheapest in the family to bring down the generation time of each diagnosis delivered.
options.feedback: A faster model lowers generation time, but the documented guidance is to tune the prompt and the length of the context first; with 45,000 mostly irrelevant tokens the cross-family citations keep appearing.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that context is a finite resource with diminishing returns: as the number of tokens grows, the model's ability to recall precisely what is inside it drops, and the criterion is to keep the smallest set of high-signal tokens. The support assistant guidance frames it as an architecture decision: with a lot of static and dynamic context, putting all of it in the prompt leads to high cost, slower responses and window limits, while retrieving what is relevant at run time improves accuracy, reduces response time and lowers cost. That is why a single change corrects both symptoms. The distinction against caching is that caching makes the repeated part cheaper but does not reduce what the model has to attend to, which is what produces the citations from another fault family.

RULE: Do not put the whole manual in every request: retrieve at run time only the procedure the case needs, and cost, time and accuracy improve together.

TRAP: Treating an overloaded context as if it were a problem of model speed or of input price.

TRY IT: Take ten real requests and mark what share of the prompt tokens had anything to do with the case; then run those same ten with only that part and compare response time and accuracy.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/customer-support-chat https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Operations leadership at Terminal Puerto Claro wants truck waiting time at the gate down 30% this quarter. The 1,800 trucks a day wait mostly because their paperwork arrives incomplete and the gate turns them away. The terminal's central system can only accept or reject an entry, and any change inside that system takes six months through its vendor. Valentina has to translate the request into a solution. What should she propose?

options.label: A
options.text: An agent that negotiates the arrival window with each carrier and reschedules the unloading plan in real time according to what happens on the dock.
options.feedback: It is the most ambitious reading of the request, but it needs to write into the central system, which takes six months to change, and an open negotiation with people leaves no measurable success signal per case.

options.label: B
options.text: Validate and complete the truck's paperwork before it arrives, taking acceptance at the gate as the objective success signal for each case.
options.feedback: Correct: it narrows the problem to the stretch the solution can actually decide and that produces an objective, automatable signal, acceptance at the gate, inside the committed deadline.

options.label: C
options.text: A dashboard that predicts the expected queue by hour, so that operations reassigns gate staff according to the load forecast for each day.
options.feedback: Predicting the queue helps staff the gate, but it prevents no rejection: the committed indicator does not move while trucks keep arriving with incomplete paperwork.

options.label: D
options.text: Digitize all the historical manifests first, so there is enough data before deciding which part of the process is worth automating.
options.feedback: Historical data is useful for other questions, but digitizing it consumes the whole quarter, and the cause of the rejections is already identified without that set.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to translate the business problem into the stretch where the system can decide and where an objective, automatable success signal exists: that is what makes a use case a good candidate, the same way support is measured by user-defined resolutions and code by tests that pass. Here the gate accepts or rejects, and that acceptance is a criterion measurable case by case and available without touching the central system. The six months needed to modify that system and the one-quarter deadline rule out the most ambitious alternative, and the committed target rules out stopping at observation. The distinction against the agent that negotiates windows is that the design needs to write where writing is not possible and has no success criterion per interaction.

RULE: Translate the business request into the stretch you can decide and measure with an objective signal inside the deadline: the rest is another project.

TRAP: Accepting the problem as the business states it and designing against a goal your system can neither decide nor measure.

TRY IT: Write down the goal the business gave you and, next to it, which signal available today without human intervention tells you case by case whether you achieved it; if none exists, the scope is cut wrong.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/define-success

questions.question: The conventions file at the root of the AndesWare monorepo has reached 700 lines and loads in every session of all 400 developers. Nearly 60% of it describes practices that apply to only two subdirectories, the platform team is three people who field requests to add more every week, and the per-team cost controls already show what that context weighs in each session. Nicolás has to reorganize it. What should he do?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep a single file at the root, add one section per team and an index at the top so that everyone quickly finds their part.
options.feedback: An index helps people, but the file is still loaded whole in every session: everyone pays for conventions that do not apply to them and nobody owns the sections of others.

options.label: B
options.text: Move all the content into a skill that the developer invokes when they need to look up the convention for their area.
options.feedback: A skill is the right shape for a multi-step procedure used now and then; a convention that has to govern a directory at all times needs to be loaded, not wait for someone to invoke it.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave at the root only what applies to the whole monorepo, move each convention to the file of the subdirectory that uses it, and let its owner keep it.
options.feedback: Correct: the guidance for large codebases separates what applies everywhere, which goes at the root, from what is specific to each area, which goes in the file of its subdirectory and is maintained by the owner.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish the conventions on the wiki of the platform team and leave a link at the root, so that the documentation has a single place to be edited and consulted.
options.feedback: A wiki is good for durable patterns and examples, but a link never reaches the session context: what has to guide the work is versioned in the repository, next to the code it governs.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a convention lives next to the code it governs and is maintained by whoever owns that code. The guidance for large codebases explicitly separates the root file, with the instructions that apply everywhere, from the per-subdirectory files, with the conventions specific to each area's stack, and it notes that these are versioned in the repository so teammates inherit them and that each file is maintained by the owner of that directory. Against aging it proposes reviewing them in pull requests like any other documentation change, which is exactly what prevents the situation described: conventions that drift, stale files, and nobody owning the root. The distinction against moving everything into a skill is that a skill loads when it is invoked, while a convention that always governs an area has to be present without anyone asking for it.

RULE: A convention lives next to the code it governs and is maintained by the owner of that directory; what gets reviewed in every pull request does not go stale.

TRAP: Leaving conventions that apply to only two areas in the root file: everyone pays for that context and nobody owns that content.

TRY IT: Open your repository's conventions file, write next to each line the directory it really applies to, and count how many apply to the whole monorepo: the rest have another owner.

questions.question: Pampero Agro runs the assistant that its field advisors consult during farm visits. Since the campaign started, several of them say the recommendations are worse than what they would write themselves, and the platform lead proposes moving the whole workload to the most capable model in the family. The assistant answers 4,000 consultations a day at harvest, the year's budget is already closed, and the campaign ends in six weeks, so a change made now is paid on every consultation until then. Nothing is measured today beyond those comments. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the whole workload to the most capable model in the family and watch whether the comments stop over the coming weeks.
options.feedback: A more capable model may turn out to be the answer, but nothing so far says the model is what fails, and the change is paid on 4,000 consultations a day against a closed budget.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a rule to the prompt for each case the advisors complained about, which costs nothing extra per consultation.
options.feedback: Patching rule by rule from anecdotes fixes the cases you happened to hear about and says nothing about the rest, while the prompt grows with every complaint.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the advisors to flag every bad answer for a month and decide with that evidence once the campaign is over.
options.feedback: Real failures are the right raw material for an evaluation set, but a month of flagging delivers the evidence after the campaign, when the decision it should have informed is already made.

options.label: D
options.text: Build a benchmark of real consultations with their expected answer and run both models on it with the current prompt.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented way to find out whether the model is what fails is a benchmark specific to your use case, run with your actual prompts and data and then weighed against cost.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for a suspected model mismatch is that the comparison comes before the migration, and the documented procedure names the order: create benchmark tests specific to your use case, because a good evaluation set is the most important step; test with your actual prompts and data; compare the candidates on accuracy, response quality and edge cases; and only then weigh performance against cost. That is what turns a complaint into a difference you can attribute to the model rather than to the prompt, the retrieval or a harder set of cases this season. The constraint decides the rest: the benchmark is built once, while a migration is paid on every one of 4,000 daily consultations for six weeks against a budget that is already closed. The distinction against collecting complaints for a month is timing, not method: the cases are the right material, but the evidence has to exist before the decision, not after it.

RULE: Compare before you migrate: a benchmark of your own cases run with your real prompts is what says whether the model is what fails.

TRAP: Attributing a failure to the model on the strength of comments, without having run a single case against the alternative.

TRY IT: Take ten consultations the advisors called bad, write the answer each one should have produced, and run your current setup and one alternative on them before deciding anything.

questions.question: AndesWare spent two weeks testing a two-model scheme for the agent that modernizes legacy modules: a cheap executor that consults a frontier advisor when it gets stuck. The measurement shows that the executor consults on 80% of tasks, that almost every step of a migration demands frontier reasoning, and that cost per completed task landed 2.4 times above the baseline. Cost control per team is monthly, and Nicolás has to decide before the next cycle. What is the best move?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the advisor model on its own at low effort and compare its cost per completed task against the current scheme.
options.feedback: Correct: with a consultation rate that high you pay frontier rates on almost the whole workload, and that model alone usually comes out cheaper at the same score.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the effort of the cheap executor so that it gets stuck less and the number of advisor consultations falls on its own.
options.feedback: Restoring the executor's effort is the fix when the consultation rate collapses, not when almost every task needs frontier capability.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the scheme with a frontier orchestrator that spreads the work across several cheap workers in parallel.
options.feedback: An orchestrator pays off when the work opens into independent pieces or exceeds a context window, and a migration is a chain of dependent steps.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the scheme and cap consultations at two per task through the prompt, to bound the frontier model's spend.
options.feedback: Fixing the number of consultations through the prompt is how you lift a low rate, but here it would cut back exactly where the executor does need help.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for any multi-model architecture is that it first has to beat the simple alternative: you sweep the effort of the current model and, if a gap remains, you put a price on the more capable model running alone at low effort. That number is what the architecture has to beat. An advisor pays off when there is a real capability gap and the executor consults rarely. If it consults on almost every task, you are paying frontier rates across the whole workload, and running the advisor model on its own turns out to be the cheaper route to the same result, which is what the measurement suggests. The distinction against capping consultations through the prompt is that this lever is for an executor that consults too little: here it would cut back help in work where almost every step needs it.

RULE: Before you build a two-model scheme, price the strong model running alone at low effort: that is the number you have to beat.

TRAP: Assuming a cheap executor makes the workload cheaper, when it consults on almost every task and you end up paying two models to do one job.

TRY IT: Measure your scheme's consultation rate over a hundred real tasks and run those same tasks with the advisor model alone at low effort: compare score and cost per completed task.

TRY IT: Measure your scheme's consultation rate over a hundred real tasks and run those same tasks with the advisor model alone at low effort: compare score and cost per completed task.

questions.question: The procurement team at the Agencia Nacional de Ingresos is drafting the tender for the taxpayer assistant and takes the FedRAMP program as a reference, because several bidders cite it in their proposals. Every statement in the tender has to hold up against documentation from the body that issues it, and one false statement invalidates the process. Renata reviews the draft before it goes out. Which of these statements is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The program authorizes cloud service offerings, and an AI model is a software component, not a cloud service in itself.
options.feedback: True: the program evaluates cloud service offerings, which is why a question about a model is answered by looking at the service it is consumed through.

options.label: B
options.text: A designation from the program is not the authorization to operate that each agency grants after reviewing the package.
options.feedback: True: the program packages the security information for each agency to review and decide; the authorization to operate is still granted by the agency.

options.label: C
options.text: The level of the designation describes how secure the evaluated service is, so a higher level means a more secure service.
options.feedback: Correct as the false statement: the level does not describe the security of the service as a whole, but the coverage and depth of the evaluation material available to agencies.

options.label: D
options.text: Defining the authorization boundary badly is a frequent barrier, because that boundary sets which components fall under review.
options.feedback: True: defining that boundary badly is among the frequent barriers to obtaining authorization, and it is what determines which components enter the review.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a compliance instrument is read by what it evaluates and by what it leaves out, never by the label. The program evaluates cloud service offerings and publishes a package of security information; the level of a designation indicates the coverage and depth of that evaluation material available to agencies, and it does not say how secure the service is as a whole. Nor does it replace the authorization to operate, which each agency grants after reviewing the package. The distinction that decides this item is between the depth of an evaluation and the security level of what was evaluated: only the first is what that level communicates.

RULE: A designation level says how much was reviewed, not how secure the reviewed service is, and it never replaces the agency's own authorization to operate.

TRAP: Reading the level of an evaluation as if it were a security grade, and copying that reading into a tender where every statement has to hold up.

TRY IT: Take a tender or a proposal that cites a certification and mark, sentence by sentence, which ones claim what was evaluated and which claim how secure the evaluated thing is: the second column usually ends up with no backing.

questions.question: The platform team at Terminal Puerto Claro is writing the implementation guide that three squads, in three countries, will build the manifests pipeline from. They start in two weeks, the guide is published on the internal wiki, and the project calendar means nobody will review it for a quarter. The draft mixes design decisions with field names, flags and values that the vendor changes every few weeks. What should Ignacio do with that guide?

options.label: A
options.text: Write down what does not change, what gets validated, what gets logged and what must never happen, and link each version-dependent detail to its official page.
options.feedback: Correct: the stable criterion is written down and the version-dependent detail is linked and checked against the official documentation before anything is distributed internally.

options.label: B
options.text: Copy the current official documentation into the wiki in full so that the three squads all work from a stable version, and set an annual review of that content.
options.feedback: Copying freezes into the wiki a detail the vendor changes every few weeks; with an annual review the squads will work for a quarter from instructions that have stopped being true.

options.label: C
options.text: Publish a minimal guide with the goals of the pipeline and let each squad document its own implementation once it finishes the part that falls to it.
options.feedback: Documenting afterward produces three different implementations of the same pipeline and no common guide, which is exactly what has to be settled before the squads start.

options.label: D
options.text: Write the guide as a decision record with its alternatives and consequences, with no implementation instructions that could go out of date.
options.feedback: A decision record is valuable and complementary, but it captures a decision with its rationale; the squads also need the implementation guidance that format does not deliver.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for internal documentation derived from product documentation is to separate the stable from the volatile: you write the criterion, what gets validated and where, what is logged and what must never happen, and you link the detail that depends on the version. The material this guide comes from carries the warning that the product ships often and that version-specific details have to be checked against the official documentation before they are distributed internally. With a quarter without review and three squads working in parallel, a guide that freezes flags and field names ages before they finish. The distinction against the decision record is one of purpose: that format captures a decision with its rationale and its alternatives, while the implementation guide says how to build; they complement each other, but neither replaces the other.

RULE: In an internal guide write what does not change and link what does: version-dependent detail is checked at the source before you hand it out.

TRAP: Freezing into an internal document a detail the vendor changes every few weeks and that nobody will review again.

TRY IT: Take the last internal guide your team handed out, mark every line that depends on a specific version, and check today in the official documentation how many of them are still true.

questions.question: Bastión Legal answers questions about its internal clause manual: about 60,000 tokens, stable, revised once a quarter. Today the whole manual travels in every request behind a cache breakpoint, with a 90% hit rate. Tomás, the technical lead, proposes replacing it with a retrieval pipeline that uses chunking and embeddings and pulls five chunks per query, aiming to cut the assistant's monthly bill by 40%. The firm bills by the hour, and half the queries are resolved by reading two or three different sections of the manual. Which two effects should you expect from that change? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Accuracy rises on every query, because a shorter prompt removes the recall degradation of long contexts.
options.feedback: Context rot is real and grows with the token count, but the documented threshold for skipping retrieval is around 200,000 tokens: at 60,000 the manual is exactly the case worth keeping whole.

options.label: B
options.text: The 95th percentile improves, because the cache write disappears, and that write is the priciest step per request.
options.feedback: Writing the cache does cost more than reading it, but you pay that once per entry lifetime, not on every request; in exchange, each query now adds a retrieval step before the model call.

options.label: C
options.text: The saving is far smaller than the token difference, because the cached prefix was already billed at a fraction of normal input.
options.feedback: Correct: a cache read is billed at 0.1x base input, so the manual's 60,000 tokens already cost about 6,000 uncached; a 40% cut does not come from there.

options.label: D
options.text: Consumption against the input tokens per minute limit drops in the same proportion and leaves room for the morning peaks.
options.feedback: Tokens read from cache do not count against the input tokens per minute limit, so the cached manual barely used that quota; retrieved chunks are ordinary input and do count.

options.label: E
options.text: Queries resolved from several sections now depend on retrieval recall, which carries a new failure rate.
options.feedback: Correct: with the whole manual in context nothing could lose the right section; pulling five chunks introduces that failure mode in exactly the half of traffic that needs more than one section.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that below roughly 200,000 tokens you put the whole corpus in the prompt and cache it instead of building retrieval. The manual fits inside that threshold with room to spare, and the cached prefix is already billed at a fraction of normal input, so cutting tokens does not cut the bill by the same amount. At the same time, replacing the full context with five chunks adds a step that can fail: the queries that cross two or three sections now depend on the recall of the index. The distinction against the long-context argument is one of scale, because the degradation shows up when the token count grows a great deal, not at 60,000 with material the model needs.

RULE: Below roughly 200,000 tokens, cache the whole corpus instead of building retrieval: the index is not free and adds a step that can lose the right section.

TRAP: Confusing a cut in tokens with a cut in the bill, when the prefix you remove was already billed at a tenth for being read from cache.

TRY IT: Take a prompt with a large stable prefix, send two requests back to back and add cache_read_input_tokens times 0.1 to input_tokens: compare that total with what sending only five retrieved chunks would cost.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

questions.question: Pehuén Energía evaluates a new retrieval configuration for the control-room assistant with a suite of 300 cases, 40 of which are emergency procedures the regulator audits. With the change, the suite average rises from 0.82 to 0.89. There is only one maintenance window per quarter to promote it, and any correction would have to wait for the next one. Facundo, the tech lead, wants to take the change into that window. What should you do before promoting?

options.label: A
options.text: Promote the change: seven points of improvement in the average over 300 cases is enough evidence for a window that does not come around again until next quarter.
options.feedback: The average can rise while a critical subset gets worse, and what the regulator audits is those 40 cases, not the mean of the 300.

options.label: B
options.text: Review the delta case by case and hold the promotion if any emergency-procedure case fell below the threshold, even though the average rises.
options.feedback: Correct: the report gives the delta of each case alongside the aggregate, and a case passes when its score reaches the threshold, so a single regression can block promotion.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the pass threshold for the whole suite to 0.95 and run it again, so that a high average cannot hide weak cases.
options.feedback: A stricter global threshold makes the whole suite fail without telling you which case broke, and it penalizes cases with no regulatory consequence just as hard.

options.label: D
options.text: Extend the suite with 200 new cases taken from recent traffic and decide on the average of the 500, which will be a good deal more stable.
options.feedback: More cases stabilize the measurement, but an average over 500 still does not show which ones got worse: the problem is not sample size but the level at which you read the result.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a suite is read at two levels: the aggregate says whether the system improved, and the per-case delta says for whom it improved and for whom it got worse. The documented harness report carries the overall score together with the delta of each case, and a case passes when its score reaches the threshold, so a single regression can fail the promotion even when the average rises. Here the subset that decides is emergency procedures, because that is what the regulator audits and the maintenance window leaves no room to correct until next quarter. The difference against raising the global threshold is that such a threshold does not distinguish cases with regulatory consequence from cases without it: it blocks everything or it blocks nothing.

RULE: Promote on the delta of each case, not on the average: a mean that rises can hide a regression in the one subset you cannot afford.

TRAP: Treating an improvement in the aggregate as an improvement in every case, when the average offsets one regression with several smaller gains.

TRY IT: Take the last report from your suite, sort the cases by delta from lowest to highest and count how many got worse while the average rose; then mark which of those carry a contractual or regulatory consequence.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals

questions.question: The Ceibo Telecom team evaluates the first-level support assistant with 400 cases that run every night, and each case is scored by a single llm grader whose rubric reads: "Is the answer good and useful for the customer? Yes/No". Runs give different results from one night to the next on the same cases, nobody can explain why a case passed, and reviewing all 400 by hand is not viable. Which change makes that score usable?

options.label: A
options.text: Swap the judge for the most capable model in the family, so that it interprets the rubric question better in each of the cases.
options.feedback: A more capable judge helps when the rubric is demanding and the judge falls short; here no model can apply a criterion that is not written down in a stable way.

options.label: B
options.text: Run each case three times and keep the result that repeats most often, to absorb the variation that shows up between one night and the next.
options.feedback: Repeating runs reduces the noise of a grader that already measures something defined, but averaging three opinions on a vague question still does not tell you what was evaluated.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the same question but ask for a score from 1 to 5 instead of a binary answer, in order to gain resolution.
options.feedback: A 1 to 5 scale is a documented way to make scoring empirical, but resolution does not fix ambiguity: with no criteria, the judge weighs different things each night.

options.label: D
options.text: Write a rubric with the concrete requirements of an acceptable answer and ask the judge to reason before emitting correct or incorrect.
options.feedback: Correct: a detailed rubric fixes what counts as acceptable, and asking for the reasoning before the score, then discarding it, improves grading on complex judgments.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an LLM judge can only be as consistent as the rubric you give it: the documentation asks for detailed, clear rubrics, empirical outputs such as correct or incorrect or a bounded scale, and for the model to reason before scoring and then discard that reasoning. A question about whether the answer is good leaves the criterion in the judge's hands, which is why the same cases change result between runs. Listing the concrete requirements turns the score into something auditable and repeatable. The difference against upgrading the judge model is that a more capable model applies a written criterion better, but it cannot invent the criterion that is missing.

RULE: A rubric says what has to be in the answer, not whether the answer is good: with no written requirements, the judge improvises a different one every run.

TRAP: Confusing the resolution of the scale with the clarity of the criterion: going from yes or no to five points does not define what is being measured.

TRY IT: Take ten answers your judge has already scored, hand them to two people with the current rubric and compare their verdicts with each other and with the judge's; if they disagree, the problem is the rubric and not the model.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

questions.question: Bastión Legal runs a precedent-search assistant that answers about 4,000 queries a month. The partners promised clients an answer in under six seconds, and the firm bills by the hour, so every minute of waiting comes out of margin. Tomás found three answers that cited a ruling that does not exist. He proposes running each query three times with the same prompt and releasing the answer only when all three agree. What should you expect from that change?

options.label: A
options.text: It will eliminate the fabricated citations: a false claim cannot hold up across three independent runs of the same prompt, so the disagreement between them always exposes it.
options.feedback: Verification by repeated sampling is a documented technique, but it detects inconsistency rather than falsehood: nothing stops the model from confidently repeating the same invention.

options.label: B
options.text: It will catch the answers where the model varies, but a stable false citation will appear in all three and pass the filter, at triple the cost.
options.feedback: Correct: comparing runs only reveals what changes, and the documentation warns that these mitigations reduce hallucinations without eliminating them, so anything critical still gets verified.

options.label: C
options.text: Nothing observable will change: with the same prompt and temperature at 0, the three runs return exactly the same text by definition.
options.feedback: A low temperature produces more conservative output, not identical output: the documentation warns that even at temperature 0, identical inputs can give different outputs across calls.

options.label: D
options.text: It will improve in proportion to the number of runs, so going from three to five closes the problem inside the latency budget.
options.feedback: More runs raise the chance of seeing a discrepancy, but they do not turn consistency into truth, and each extra run competes with the six-second commitment.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that anti-hallucination techniques lower the probability of the error without driving it to zero, and each one catches a different kind of failure. Verification by N runs measures dispersion: if the outputs differ, that is a sign of invention. If the model holds the same nonexistent citation across all three, the method has nothing to compare and the answer ships with a confidence stamp it never earned. The distinction against the option that promises to eliminate the problem is that consistency is a property of the model, not of the source. To attack the false citation you have to ground it, asking for the verbatim text of the ruling and discarding the claim when that text does not appear.

RULE: Verification by repetition catches what varies, not what the model repeats with confidence.

TRAP: Confusing consistency with truth: three identical answers prove the model is stable, not that the cited ruling exists.

TRY IT: Pick a question your corpus cannot answer and run it five times; count how often the model repeats the same invented claim and how often it changes it, then see what your agreement filter would have done.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/glossary

questions.question: Mistral Retail's after-sales agent handles 60,000 conversations a day outside campaign periods, and that volume quadruples during the promotional week. Camila, who runs the platform, is working against two numbers: a daily API spend cap that cannot be exceeded that week, and an internal commitment of 3 seconds to first response. Measurement of the previous peak shows that 70% of conversations are repeat questions about order status and exchanges, and that 4% of cases run into long tool chains that concentrate most of the spend. Which two measures attack both constraints without degrading resolution? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Classify the query on arrival and let the fast model resolve the frequent repetitive categories, reserving the more capable model for the hard minority.
options.feedback: Correct: routing the easy, common questions to a smaller model and the hard ones to a more capable one is the documented cost lever for a traffic mix like this.

options.label: B
options.text: Serve all after-sales traffic with the most capable model during the promotional week, so that it resolves in fewer turns and offsets its price per case.
options.feedback: Fewer turns help when reasoning is the bottleneck. Here 70% of the traffic is repetitive, and paying for it at the highest price pushes the very number that has to be held down.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a supervisor subagent that reviews every answer before it reaches the customer and corrects it whenever it spots a commercial policy error.
options.feedback: Verification by a second agent pays off when quality outranks time. In series and on every answer it adds tokens and latency exactly where 3 seconds are committed.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the customer's full history and the entire catalog into every request, so that the agent never has to call a tool during the conversation.
options.feedback: Avoiding tool calls sounds like a saving, but a large context is billed on every request, it degrades retrieval of what matters, and it does nothing about the tail of long cases.

options.label: E
options.text: Set an iteration cap and a spend ceiling per conversation, so that a pathological case goes to a person before it exhausts the day's quota.
options.feedback: Correct: stopping conditions are the documented control for the 4% that concentrates the spend, and they turn an open-ended loop into a cost bounded per conversation.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the architecture lines up with the business constraint that is written down, and here two different constraints ask for two different levers. Routing by difficulty attacks the unit cost of repetitive traffic, which is where the volume sits. A cap on iterations and budget per conversation attacks the tail of long cases, which is where the spend is concentrated. The two are independent: one lowers the price of the average case, the other bounds the worst case. The distinction against moving up a model is that the more capable model improves the difficult 4% but multiplies the price of the 70% that never needed it; and against the supervisor subagent, that it adds a serial stage on top of an answer that already has 3 seconds committed.

RULE: When the commitment is double, use two levers: route by difficulty for the cost of the average case, and set stopping conditions for the cost of the worst case.

TRAP: Assuming that a more capable model lowers spend because it resolves in fewer turns, when the volume sits in the queries that never needed that model.

TRY IT: Take a week of your own traffic, sort the conversations by cost, and see what share of the spend sits in the most expensive 5%; then review the 100 cheapest cases and count how many the fast model would have resolved.

questions.question: AndesWare has six weeks to close the scope of an assistant that a client in a regulated sector wants to put into production, and the client's compliance team has calendar time for only two meetings. Ignacio, the solutions architect, receives a list of 40 mixed requests, from the color of a button to the requirement that no response leave the system without being logged. His team proposes starting by measuring the cost and latency of a prototype, so there is data for the first meeting. Which order of work makes the best use of those two meetings?

options.label: A
options.text: Separate out the requests with a measurable effect on the architecture → frame context and risks for those few with the client → define the indicators that measure them
options.feedback: Correct: only a requirement with a measurable effect on the architecture belongs in an architecture decision, and framing context and risks is what precedes any measurement.

options.label: B
options.text: Measure the cost and the latency of a prototype → choose the architecture that scores best on that measurement → document the requirements that were left out
options.feedback: Measuring early is a good habit, but a measurement with no framed context describes what the prototype does, not what the client has to decide, and it burns the first meeting.

options.label: C
options.text: Write the proposed architecture document with all of its alternatives → circulate it among the affected areas for comment → adjust the requirements to the objections that arrive
options.feedback: Arriving with a closed proposal turns the meeting into a review of the text. With only two meetings available, that leaves discovery for when there is no calendar left.

options.label: D
options.text: Rank the 40 requests by how many stakeholder votes each one gets → take the top ten → turn those into the acceptance criteria for the project
options.feedback: Voting prioritizes what is popular, not what changes the design: the requirement that no response leave without a log may carry a single vote and decide the whole architecture.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of discovery is to frame before you measure: context and risks are established first, and measurement comes afterward, against indicators already agreed. Not every request is an architecture requirement either. The ones that are have a measurable effect on the architecture and on system quality, and that filter is what turns a list of 40 requests into the three or four conversations that justify a meeting with compliance. The distinction against starting by measuring the prototype is that a number with no agreed criterion decides nothing: it says what the thing you already built costs, not whether it solves what the client is going to sign.

RULE: Frame before you measure, and call a request an architecture requirement only when it changes the architecture in a measurable way.

TRAP: Confusing having data with having criteria: measuring a prototype before framing the context produces numbers that settle none of the open questions.

TRY IT: Take the requirement list from your current project and mark which ones would change the design if they were reversed; the ones that change nothing do not belong in the architecture conversation.

SOURCE: https://adr.github.io/ https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/

questions.question: The taxpayer assistance channel of the Agencia Nacional de Ingresos handles about 60,000 conversations a day. Since the season changed, a small group of accounts keeps pushing the assistant to draft instructions for faking addresses and splitting income among third parties: 0.4% of the accounts produce 80% of those attempts. The agency's audit function wants evidence, conversation by conversation, that a control acted before the assistant replied, and the budget does not allow human review at that volume. Which two controls should you implement? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Extend the system prompt with a section that forbids the request and spells out how the assistant should refuse each variant.
options.feedback: Writing explicit limits into the system prompt is one of the documented layers, but it shapes what the model tries to do and leaves no per-conversation record that anything was applied.

options.label: B
options.text: Deliver the taxpayer message inside a tool_result block and tag its origin so the model treats it with skepticism.
options.feedback: That is the control for third-party content the agent reads, where the instruction hides inside a document; here the request arrives head-on in the user turn.

options.label: C
options.text: Pre-filter every message with a fast, cheap model before the main conversation, with structured output returning a classification.
options.feedback: Correct: the harmlessness screen is a documented control that runs on every message, costs little at this volume, and produces the recordable decision the audit asks for.

options.label: D
options.text: Rate-limit or block the accounts that keep trying to get around the channel guardrails, and adjust the response they receive.
options.feedback: Correct: responding to repeat offenders is a documented layer, independent of the previous one, and here it solves most of the problem because the attempts sit in very few accounts.

options.label: E
options.text: Log every flagged attempt and review it at the monthly meeting of the agency's internal audit committee.
options.feedback: Continuous analysis of outputs is part of the design, but it is after-the-fact monitoring: it does not stop the reply from going out and does not replace a control that acts in the conversation.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that jailbreak defense is built in layers and that each layer has to act where the attack happens. Here the attempt comes from the user, so the place for the control is the input, before the main conversation: a small model with structured output classifies the message, decides for every conversation, and leaves the evidence the audit demands at a cost that works at 60,000 a day. The second layer is different and complementary: adjusting the response and limiting repeat offenders attacks the concentration of abuse in 0.4% of the accounts. The distinction against putting the content in a tool_result is that this control exists for outside content the agent reads, not for a user attacking head-on.

RULE: A guardrail written into the prompt is advice; the control an audit can see runs outside the model and leaves a recorded decision.

TRAP: Treating the user turn as if it were third-party content: tool_result protects you from the document the agent reads, not from whoever types in the chat.

TRY IT: Take 20 real messages from your channel, run them through a classifier with structured output that returns a single boolean field, and compare its decision with what your main prompt does with those same messages.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup

questions.question: The European group that controls Minera Nevado applies to every subsidiary the same risk-level classification that the European AI regulation requires of it. Nevado is about to deploy two uses of the same assistant: one answers operator questions about site procedures, and the other scores applicants for heavy-equipment operator to decide who gets an interview. The committee has granted a single eight-week window with two people to assemble the compliance file before go-live. Where should Andrés concentrate that window?

options.label: A
options.text: On both equally: they run on the same model and the same integration, so the compliance file should cover them with identical rigor and documentation.
options.feedback: Treating both the same looks prudent, but the classification looks at what each use decides rather than at shared technology; spending the window on the one that owes only a notice leaves the other with no file.

options.label: B
options.text: On neither: the obligations on general-purpose models fall on whoever supplies the model, not on the subsidiary that deploys it.
options.feedback: Providers of general-purpose models do carry their own obligations, but those do not absorb the obligations of whoever deploys a system in a concrete use; they are separate layers of the same framework.

options.label: C
options.text: On the one that scores applicants: recruitment falls in the high-risk tier, which demands logging, documentation, data quality and human oversight.
options.feedback: Correct: recruitment appears among the high-risk examples, and that tier is where the heavy work sits: activity logging, documentation, data quality and human oversight.

options.label: D
options.text: On the procedures assistant: it is the one that talks to people every day, and telling them a machine is answering is the most visible duty of all.
options.feedback: That use falls in the transparency tier, whose duty is that the person knows a machine is involved: real, but far lighter than the duty on a high-risk system.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the European framework classifies by use and not by technology: the same model can sit under a transparency-tier system and a high-risk one, and each tier owes different things. The use that scores applicants falls among the high-risk examples, where the provider owes a risk assessment, quality data, activity logging, detailed documentation, information for the professional user, human oversight measures and robustness. That is the file eight weeks with two people can barely assemble. The procedures assistant, by contrast, essentially owes the person the knowledge that a machine is answering. The distinction against treating both the same is that the effort is not split per system, it is split per tier.

RULE: AI regulation classifies by use, not by model: the same assistant can land in two tiers and owe very different things in each.

TRAP: Classifying by the technology two uses share instead of by what each one decides about a person.

TRY IT: List your organization's AI uses and place each one in a risk tier; for the ones that land in high risk, write down who produces the activity log and who exercises the human oversight.

SOURCE: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai
