questions.question: Banco Altamar has six weeks to show internal audit that its credit documentation extractor meets the agreed criterion. The three risk analysts who know the real cases have four hours a week available between them, and the archive holds 9,000 files already reviewed by hand with their correct outcome. Malena, the tech lead, has to decide how the set of acceptance cases gets built on that budget of hours. Which order of work produces the best set within the deadline?

options.label: A
options.text: Bring the three analysts together in a series of workshops → have them jointly write thirty cases graded by hand → use those as the acceptance criterion
options.feedback: Thirty careful cases look sturdier, but they consume exactly the scarce hours and leave a small set: for the same effort, more cases graded by code give more signal.

options.label: B
options.text: Give the analysts a simple way to contribute cases → automate grading against the history already reviewed → save their hours for reading a sample of transcripts
options.feedback: Correct: the history already reviewed lets you grade many cases by code, and the scarce hours go to the one thing that cannot be automated, judging whether a failure is fair.

options.label: C
options.text: Generate synthetic cases with the model itself to cover gaps → validate them one by one with the analysts → fill in later with the files that fail in production
options.feedback: Synthetic cases do cover gaps, but validating them one by one spends the same hours, and the real history already holds the failures audit is going to want to see.

options.label: D
options.text: Commission an external review of the extractor → fold its findings in as acceptance cases → ask the analysts to sign off on the final result
options.feedback: An external review brings another pair of eyes and it does not replace the acceptance criterion: what audit asks for is a set of your own that can be rerun when the system changes.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for building acceptance cases is to prefer volume with automated grading over a handful graded by hand, and to draw the cases from real failures instead of imagining them. Here the archive of files already reviewed is the reference set: it lets grading be automated and the number of cases multiplied without spending the scarce hours. Someone who knows the domain also does not need to be an engineer to contribute a case, so it is worth opening that path instead of calling them into workshops. The distinction against the thirty cases graded by hand is that such a set is small, discriminates less, and every new run asks for the same scarce hours again.

RULE: Many cases graded automatically beat a few graded by hand: save the expert hours for judging a sample, not for labeling.

TRAP: Assuming that a small, very careful set measures better, when the scarce resource is precisely the time of the people who would have to care for it.

TRY IT: Count how many of your acceptance cases are graded by code today and how many by hand, and work out how many hours it costs to rerun the whole set.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: The coordination agent at Terminal Puerto Claro brings together four MCP servers (customs, shipping lines, carriers and yard) and exposes 140 tools whose definitions take up some 48,000 tokens. To free context before the export season, Ignacio configures tool search like this: tools: [{"type": "tool_search_tool", "name": "tool_search", "defer_loading": true}, {"name": "consultar_manifiesto", "defer_loading": true}, {"name": "liberar_contenedor", "defer_loading": true}, and 137 more definitions, all with defer_loading true]. What does this configuration produce?

options.label: A
options.text: It loads only the three to five tools each query needs and cuts more than 85% of the definition tokens.
options.feedback: That is the documented effect of deferring when the search tool stays loaded: more than 85% fewer definition tokens and better selection. Here the very piece that makes it possible is missing.

options.label: B
options.text: It leaves the agent with no entry point: the one tool able to find the others was deferred too.
options.feedback: Correct: deferring takes definitions out of the context and leaves them reachable through the search tool, so deferring that tool breaks the chain. The documentation says never to defer it.

options.label: C
options.text: It has no effect until the definitions pass 10% of the context window, the threshold where deferring starts.
options.feedback: That 10% threshold exists, but it describes the automatic mode in Claude Code, which decides for you when to defer. Here deferring is declared tool by tool and applies exactly as written.

options.label: D
options.text: It doubles the startup cost, because each deferred definition is billed on discovery and again on use.
options.feedback: Deferring changes what occupies Claude's context, not how a definition is billed, and there is no charge for discovering plus another for using. Full definitions are in fact still sent in every request.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of progressive disclosure is that something can leave the context only if a mechanism remains for finding it again. The search tool is that mechanism: with it loaded, the rest of the catalog is discovered on demand and definition tokens fall by more than 85%. Deferring the search tool itself breaks the chain, which is why the documentation advises against it explicitly. The distinction against the optimistic reading is that the saving does not come from deferring more things, but from deferring everything except the entry point and the three to five tools that are used almost always.

RULE: Defer the catalog, never the finder: what leaves the context has to stay discoverable, and the three to five tools in constant use stay loaded.

TRAP: Assuming the saving grows with how much you defer, until you also defer the piece that let you find what was deferred.

TRY IT: List your agent's tools, mark the ones that show up in 90% of runs and leave those undeferred; then send a typical query and check in the response that the search tool was invoked exactly once.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool

questions.question: The inconsistency-detection agent at Agencia Nacional de Ingresos returns a long report per taxpayer that the analyst reads on screen while it is generated, and the department set a target of having it complete in under 12 seconds. This week's measurement came out like this: stream true, first character at 0.8 s, output_tokens 2,800 completed in 26 s, cache hits of 92% on the instruction prefix. Joaquín has to pick one change before the quarterly close. Which change attacks the number that is missed?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the thinking budget so the model settles the case sooner and writes the whole report in one go.
options.feedback: A larger budget gives more complete reasoning and adds latency instead of removing it: thinking tokens are generated before the answer and stretch exactly the wait you need to shorten.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the reports through the Message Batches API and take the 50% discount on the price.
options.feedback: The batch discount is real and it is the right lever when nobody is waiting for the result. Here an analyst is watching the screen, and batch does not accept the speed field either.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on fast mode with the speed field, which raises output tokens per second where available.
options.feedback: Correct: the bottleneck is generation speed, and fast mode is the documented lever for that indicator, with up to 2.5 times more output tokens per second.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower max_tokens so the report finishes sooner and the analyst does not wait for the final part.
options.feedback: Shortening the output cuts total time, but it changes the product: the report loses content the analyst needs, and the speed at which it is written stays the same.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to read which indicator is being missed before you move a lever. questions.question: The regulator has asked Colibrí Pay for evidence of how it governs the support agent that checks balances, issues refunds and blocks cards. The request falls due in twenty business days, and an incomplete answer opens a sanction proceeding. Sofía, the compliance lead, proposes answering with the certificates and audit reports that the model provider publishes on its trust portal. What is most likely to happen?

options.label: A
options.text: It will close the request: what the provider certifies also reaches the workloads that run on its platform, Colibrí Pay included.
options.feedback: That inheritance does not exist: a certificate describes the scope of the provider's products and management system, and says nothing about the decisions the application built on top makes.

options.label: B
options.text: It will stay open: those reports cover the provider's platform, and the regulator expects Colibrí's own risk analysis, controls and records.
options.feedback: Correct: evaluating whether the outputs are appropriate for the use case is the customer's responsibility under the terms, so the part the regulator is asking about is still unanswered.

options.label: C
options.text: It will close the request if you also turn on Zero Data Retention, because with nothing stored at rest there is no processing left to answer for.
options.feedback: ZDR describes what is not stored after the response; it does not remove the processing and does not replace evidence of how the agent decides and how it is controlled.

options.label: D
options.text: It will stay open until the contract moves to the provider the liability for what the agent decides about each customer.
options.feedback: Splitting risk by contract between companies does not move regulatory responsibility: before the supervisor, the entity operating the service still answers.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a provider's certifications and audit reports describe the scope of its own products and management system, not the system a customer builds on top. Under the commercial terms, evaluating whether the outputs are appropriate for the use case, including deciding where human review belongs, sits with the customer. So the agent's risk analysis, the limits on what it may execute and the records of what it did are evidence only Colibrí can produce. The distinction against the option that declares the request closed is one of scope: the provider package answers which platform you use, not how you govern what that platform executes on your behalf.

RULE: What the provider certifies is its platform: responsibility for what your application decides is not subcontracted by attaching a report.

TRAP: Assuming a provider certification is inherited upward and covers the application built on top of it.

TRY IT: Take the last compliance questionnaire you answered and mark each question as answered by the provider or answered by me; count how many sit in the second column with no evidence of your own behind them.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/10015870-what-certifications-has-anthropic-obtained

questions.question: AndesWare runs an agent that triages the issues from its public reporting portal: it reads the issue text, classifies it, opens a branch and leaves a comment in the monorepo. Some reports carry, inside the body, sentences addressed to the agent. Volume is 60,000 issues a month with cost control per team, so there is no room for an extra call to the most capable model per issue, and rewriting the twelve internal tools would take a quarter. Which two measures attack the risk within those constraints? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Pass the issue body into the system prompt as task context, preceded by a line clarifying that it is third-party content.
options.feedback: Content in the system prompt is treated as operator instruction, so putting it there gives maximum authority to someone else's text no matter what warning precedes it.

options.label: B
options.text: Deliver the issue body only inside tool_result blocks, never in the system prompt or in user text, and encode it as JSON.
options.feedback: Correct: the model is trained to treat instructions that appear inside tool_result with skepticism, and encoding the text stops it from closing a quote or a tag to escape into the instruction context.

options.label: C
options.text: Screen the tool result with the cheapest model and structured outputs, which return a single suspicion boolean before that text reaches the agent.
options.feedback: Correct: the documentation describes that screen with a lightweight model and a structured output of a single field, which costs a fraction of a frontier call and touches none of the existing tools.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the triage agent to the most capable model in the family, which resists adversarial instructions embedded in content better.
options.feedback: A more capable model is still a model that reads text: the documented defense is where the content enters and what filters it, not how good the reader is.

options.label: E
options.text: Add to the end of the tool_result itself the instruction to ignore any order that appears in the text above.
options.feedback: Your instructions inside a tool_result read as part of the untrusted content, so they can be ignored or flagged as suspicious; they belong in the user turn after the result.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the block where you place a text decides how much authority it carries: the system prompt is operator instruction, the user turn is the request, and tool_result is untrusted data the model is trained to view with skepticism. Against indirect injection the documentation combines two independent things: isolating third-party content in tool_result, encoded so it cannot break the structure, and filtering that content with a lightweight model whose output is restricted to a minimal classification. Both fit the budget because neither adds a frontier call per issue. The difference against upgrading the model is that the attack does not depend on the capability of the reader, but on where the text is placed and what reviews it first.

RULE: Someone else's content enters through tool_result and is screened by a cheap classifier: the defense is in the architecture of the message, not in the capability of the model.

TRAP: Assuming a more capable model resists indirect injection, when what decides it is which block the text travels in and whether anything filters it before it reaches the agent.

TRY IT: Write a test issue that includes an order addressed to the agent, run it through your current flow and look at which block of the request that text ends up in; then repeat with the body delivered in tool_result and encoded as JSON.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks

questions.question: The operational safety assistant at Minera Nevado answers questions over a corpus of 400,000 technical documents and environmental permits. The authority requires every limit value the assistant states to be traceable to the document and its version. A review of 500 answers found that in 2% of them plausible values appear that are in no retrieved passage. The system handles 9,000 queries per shift on a budget that does not allow a second model pass over every answer. Which change to the design closes that gap?

options.label: A
options.text: Assemble the answer from the retrieved fields and block, before sending, any answer whose values do not appear verbatim in a passage, routing the case to the document.
options.feedback: Correct: the control sits in the code, it applies to every answer, and it adds no second model call; what the rule cannot resolve is routed on instead of being stated.

options.label: B
options.text: Add an explicit instruction to the system prompt never to state a value that is not present in the retrieved sources, and to answer that it was not found in every other case.
options.feedback: An instruction in the prompt steers behavior but does not guarantee it: the model still decides, and the 2% that fails today is exactly the case where it did not follow.

options.label: C
options.text: Put every answer through a second call that acts as a judge and checks that the cited values appear in the retrieved passages before the answer is shown.
options.feedback: A judge built on another model is the weakest form of verification, and it adds latency and cost on every answer, which is precisely what the per-shift budget rules out.

options.label: D
options.text: Widen retrieval by raising the number of passages per query, so that the model always has in view the document where the value it needs is written.
options.feedback: More passages help when the value was not being retrieved. Here the problem is not coverage: the answer states values that no passage contains at all.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the best feedback on an output is the kind built on clear rules, which say what failed and why, and that a control which must hold every time lives in the code and not in the prompt. A deterministic check requiring every limit value to appear verbatim in a retrieved passage is cheap, applies to 100% of traffic, and adds no model call. The distinction against the system prompt instruction is the one that separates advice from a guarantee: the prompt influences most cases, and the remaining 2% is precisely where it did not. Against the model-based judge, the documentation is explicit that it is not a robust method and that it carries a high latency cost.

RULE: What must hold every time is checked by a rule in the code: the prompt steers, deterministic verification guarantees.

TRAP: Treating a system prompt instruction as if it were an enforced control, when what decides is who runs the check.

TRY IT: Take 50 answers from your system and write a check that every figure cited appears in some retrieved passage; count how many fail and compare that with what you assumed.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/commerce-agents

questions.question: The change agent at Siete Lagos Viajes has to recall, before touching each booking, the cancellation window of the wholesaler that issued it, which differs from one booking to the next. Today the team rewrites the system field with that value on every turn, and the stable 30,000-token prefix is written again in full. One case reaches 35 turns, and high season multiplies traffic by ten. Camila needs the reminder to appear on the turn where it applies, without piling up or breaking the cache. Which design does she choose?

options.label: A
options.text: Append the reminder as a mid-conversation system message, which stays in the array and is sent again on every later turn.
options.feedback: This is the right option when the instruction has to keep applying from then on; here the reminder is good for one turn and thirty-five of them would stack up in the context.

options.label: B
options.text: Rewrite the system field at the start of each turn with the window of the booking in hand, which is what guarantees the value is present today.
options.feedback: Editing the system field leaves the value where the model reads it, but the cache hashes the prefix in the order tools, system and messages, so changing it invalidates system and everything after it.

options.label: C
options.text: Append the reminder as a system message scoped to the turn, which stops being rendered once the next user message arrives.
options.feedback: Correct: a turn-scoped message renders only until the next user message, after that it costs no tokens even though it stays in the array, and the cached prefix is never touched.

options.label: D
options.text: Return the reminder inside the tool_result of the booking lookup, alongside the wholesaler data that already travels there.
options.feedback: The content of a tool_result is treated as untrusted data, so an instruction of yours written there can be ignored or flagged as an injection attempt.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that instructions arriving mid-conversation are appended to messages instead of rewriting the system field, because the cache hashes the prefix in the order tools, system and messages, and a change at one level invalidates that level and every one after it. Within that family there are two variants, and the constraint picks one: an ordinary system message is sent again on every later turn, while the turn-scoped variant switches off as soon as the next user message arrives, stays in the array unrendered and stops costing tokens. Since the reminder applies only to the booking being touched and one case reaches thirty-five turns, the second keeps thirty-five reminders from stacking up in the context.

RULE: If the instruction is good for one turn, append it scoped to that turn; if it holds from then on, append it permanently; never rewrite the system field.

TRAP: Treating every reminder as if it had to persist, and paying on every later turn for a value that stopped applying on the previous one.

TRY IT: Run a ten-turn conversation appending one reminder per turn and watch how the input_tokens grow; repeat with the variant that clears on the next user message and compare the two curves.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages

questions.question: Mistral Retail enriches the catalog before each campaign with a stable 25,000-token prefix that carries the categorization rules and the mandatory attributes, with the product record at the end. As the campaign starts, Bruno fires twenty requests in parallel, all with that same prefix marked with cache_control, expecting only the first to pay for the write. What he wants to bring down is precisely the cost of that first batch, and the campaign opens with 40,000 records. What will the usage field of those twenty responses show?

options.label: A
options.text: The first records a cache write and the remaining nineteen record reads, so the saving shows up in that first batch already.
options.feedback: That is what happens when the requests go out one after another within the TTL; in parallel none of them gets to see the entry the others are writing.

options.label: B
options.text: All twenty wait for the first one to finish writing the cache and then read, with a little more latency but at the cost of one read.
options.feedback: The API does not serialize requests for you: each one is processed without waiting for the rest, so there is no queue to join and no read to take advantage of.

options.label: C
options.text: All twenty are billed as uncached input, with no write and no read, because the prefix did not yet exist when they went out.
options.feedback: Marking cache_control does produce a write as long as the prefix exceeds the model's minimum cacheable length; what this batch lacks is not the write but the read.

options.label: D
options.text: All twenty record a cache write and none of them a read, because the entry exists only once the response of the first one starts.
options.feedback: Correct: in a simultaneous burst they all write, and since writes are billed above base input, that first batch ends up costing more than it would with no caching.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that prompt caching pays off when a prefix that is already written gets reused, and an entry becomes available only after the response of the request that wrote it begins. In a simultaneous burst none of the twenty sees the entry of the others yet, so all twenty write: because the five-minute write is billed above base input, that first batch comes out more expensive than it would with no caching. The documented pattern is to send the first request, wait for its response and only then open up the parallelism, so that the rest read. The difference against assuming one writes and nineteen read is that the split depends on when each request goes out, not on all of them sharing the same prefix.

RULE: In parallel nobody reads what another is writing: send one request, wait for its response and only then fan out.

TRAP: Assuming that sharing the prefix is enough to hit the cache, without looking at whether the entry already existed at the moment each request went out.

TRY IT: Send five identical requests in parallel and add up cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens across the five; repeat sending the first alone and the other four after its response, and compare the two sums.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación is weighing an extra verification pass over the answers of its automated tutor: it improves correctness and raises cost per student. Valentina has to take the decision to the academic committee, which follows two numbers, monthly cost per student and wait time on a query, and which already rejected an earlier proposal for arriving full of technical jargon. Which two elements must the communication of this decision include? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The effect of each option stated in the units the committee already follows: monthly cost per student and wait time on a query.
options.feedback: Correct: a decision is communicated in the unit of whoever decides, and that translation turns a technical discussion into a choice the committee can actually make.

options.label: B
options.text: Published benchmark results for the chosen model, as outside backing that the extra verification is the best alternative available.
options.feedback: Benchmark numbers describe performance on someone else's tests and say nothing about cost per student or about the wait, which are this committee's two indicators.

options.label: C
options.text: The full thread of the technical discussion where each alternative was compared, so the committee can review the context of the decision itself.
options.feedback: The thread preserves the context, but a decision record exists precisely so that nobody has to reconstruct the decision by reading the whole discussion.

options.label: D
options.text: The condition that would force a review of the decision, a model change or a rise in volume for instance, and the moment that review happens.
options.feedback: Correct: writing down what would change it and when it gets reviewed keeps the record from aging in silence, and it turns the review into a date rather than another debate.

options.label: E
options.text: A commitment not to modify the architecture during the school year, so as to give the committee predictability over cost per student.
options.feedback: Promising that nothing will change gives predictability and ties your hands: if an option appears that lowers cost per student, the commitment blocks it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a decision record captures the decision, the requirement that makes it significant, and its consequences, and that the consequence is expressed in the terms of whoever pays for it. Translating the effect into cost per student and wait time is what lets a committee with no technical profile choose on its own criteria. Writing down which condition would force a review, with a concrete moment, keeps the record alive when the model or the volume changes. The two elements are independent: one is the content of the consequence, the other is its expiry. The distinction against attaching benchmarks is that those numbers answer a question the committee did not ask and connect to neither of its two indicators.

RULE: State the decision in the unit of whoever decides and write down what would change it: with no consequence and no expiry, a record ages unnoticed.

questions.question: During a maintenance window with a regulatory deadline, the control room assistant at Pehuén Energía started returning procedures for a turbine model other than the one installed. The on-call engineer rolled the version back in 20 minutes, the window closed on schedule, and no operator got as far as applying a wrong procedure. The team lead proposes closing the case: there was no loss, there was no complaint, and the week ahead is full. What is the right thing to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Close the case with no report, because the rollback worked, the window was met on time, and no operator got as far as applying the wrong procedure.
options.feedback: With no visible impact it looks as though there is nothing to learn, but a rollback performed by the on-call engineer is by itself one of the criteria that trigger the analysis.

options.label: B
options.text: Write the incident report and file it without review, so as not to occupy a team that already worked extra hours during the maintenance window.
options.feedback: Writing it is half the work: a report nobody reviews amounts in practice to not having written it, and its follow-up actions reach no one at all.

options.label: C
options.text: Write the report because there was an on-call intervention with a rollback, center it on the contributing causes, and put it through review by the team.
options.feedback: Correct: the on-call intervention triggers the analysis, the focus goes on causes rather than people, and the review is what turns the document into shared learning.

options.label: D
options.text: Log the case on the quality board and assign the correction to whoever shipped the version, so that it is closed before the next maintenance window arrives.
options.feedback: Assigning the finding to whoever shipped turns the analysis into blame, and it guarantees that next time the uncomfortable detail appears in no report at all.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a postmortem is triggered by criteria agreed in advance and not by the size of the damage. Those criteria include degradation visible to whoever uses the service, data loss of any kind, an on-call intervention such as a rollback or a traffic diversion, a resolution time above the threshold, and a failure of monitoring. Here there was a rollback performed by the on-call engineer, so the criterion is met even though the window closed on schedule. The document has to be blameless, centered on the contributing causes, and it has to be reviewed. The distinction against closing the case is that the criterion which triggers the analysis is fixed beforehand and is not renegotiated according to how things ended.

RULE: A postmortem is triggered by an agreed criterion, not by how much it hurt: write it blameless and have someone review it, or it may as well not exist.

TRAP: Confusing an outcome with no damage with a cause of no importance, and leaving unexamined the failure the on-call engineer managed to cover in time.

TRY IT: Write down the list of criteria that trigger an incident report on your team and review your last three cases: count how many met a criterion and ended with no document.

questions.question: The Pampero Agro field assistant accompanies the adviser through visits of two or three hours: it looks up earlier reports, records observations by plot and agrees on a management plan. Connectivity drops several times per visit, the app restarts the session from scratch and what was agreed is lost, and the history is sent again in full once there is signal. At harvest there are 300 visits a day with a cost per visit already committed. What should you do so the session survives the dropouts without inflating the context?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn on server-side compaction so that the conversation summarizes itself on its own as it grows during the visit.
options.feedback: Compaction keeps the thread when the conversation is long but continuous; here the process dies and the summary dies with it, because it lives inside the conversation itself.

options.label: B
options.text: Move to the model with the largest context window, so that the whole visit fits without anything having to be summarized.
options.feedback: A larger window gives you room, not persistence: the dropout still wipes the session and the context still grows with everything you drag along.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the agent write structured notes outside the context at each milestone of the visit, and have the new session start by reading them.
options.feedback: Correct: notes persisted outside the window survive the dropout, and the next session rebuilds itself by reading what matters instead of resending everything that was said.

options.label: D
options.text: Cache the conversation with the one-hour TTL so that, on reconnect, the resent history is read from cache instead of being reprocessed in full.
options.feedback: A long TTL makes it cheaper to resend a history you still have, but it does not give back what the app lost and it does not stop the context from growing.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that information that has to survive an interruption cannot live only in the context window: it is written outside, in structured notes the next session reads back. That is the documented technique for iterative work with clear milestones, as opposed to compaction, meant for long continuous conversations where the thread does not break, and to subagents, which serve to explore in parallel with clean contexts. Here the session dies several times per visit, so a summary that lives inside the conversation is lost along with it. The difference against enlarging the window is that the problem is not how much fits, but what is left when the session disappears.

RULE: What has to survive the dropout is written outside the window: context is working memory, not storage.

TRAP: Confusing summarizing the conversation with preserving it: compaction reduces what you drag along, but it disappears together with the session that contains it.

TRY IT: Cut the connection halfway through a test session and write down what you would need to resume: write those four or five lines as milestone notes and measure how many tokens you have to resend to get back to the same point.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool

questions.question: The platform team at Ceibo Telecom maintains the internal support tooling, where the contract with corporate customers fixes the first-response time. To keep anyone from breaking the pipeline during closing week, Bruno added this line to the repository CLAUDE.md: "Never edit the generated files under dist/ and always run the regression suite before calling a change done." Two weeks later, two merges touched dist/ and three changes closed without the suite being run. What should be done with that line?

options.label: A
options.text: Move it to the organization's managed CLAUDE.md, so it reaches every session on the team and no developer can remove it from their copy.
options.feedback: The managed path guarantees the instruction arrives and that nobody deletes it, but it is still text for the model: it changes who delivers it, not whether the client enforces it.

options.label: B
options.text: Rewrite it more precisely and repeat it at the end of the file, since adherence drops when an instruction admits more than one reading.
options.feedback: It is true that adherence falls with vague instructions and long files, and tightening them is worth doing; even so, a better-written instruction is still guidance and does not prevent the edit.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the convention in CLAUDE.md and move the prohibition to a deny rule on that path and the check to a hook that runs before closing.
options.feedback: Correct: permission rules and hooks are enforced by the client whatever happens, while CLAUDE.md is left for how we do things here, which is what it does know how to convey.

options.label: D
options.text: Turn it into a path rule under .claude/rules/ so that it loads only when someone is working on that directory of the repository.
options.feedback: Path rules keep conventions tidy and save context, but they also enter as instructions to the model: they narrow when the text is read, not turn the prohibition into a control.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that CLAUDE.md is guidance while permission rules and hooks are guarantees: configuration rules are enforced by the client no matter what the model decides to do, whereas the memory file only shapes what it tries. Bruno's line therefore has two halves that belong in different places: the prohibition on the generated path is written as a deny rule, and the pre-close check is written as a hook, which always runs and can block. The distinction against promoting it to the managed level is that managed policy guarantees delivery, not enforcement: a managed CLAUDE.md is still instruction text, which is why it does not even require the security approval that settings which execute commands do.

RULE: CLAUDE.md says how we do things here; whatever cannot be allowed to fail is written as a permission rule or as a hook.

TRAP: Believing that promoting an instruction to the managed level turns it into a control: it is still text for the model, not a rule the client enforces.

TRY IT: In a test repository, write an Edit deny rule over a generated directory and ask for a change there; compare what happens with what happens when the same prohibition lives only in CLAUDE.md.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud produces the clinical record summary at the moment of the consultation across its 40 clinics: 12,000 summaries a day, with a target of under 20 seconds from the moment the clinician asks for one. Confidentiality agreements with the provider networks limit which fields may leave each clinic. Today the system sends the patient's entire record in every request, and the medical team reports summaries that are correct yet omit what changed at the last consultation. Which two design changes are worth making? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Serve the summaries with the most capable model in the family, so that it picks out what is relevant inside the patient's complete clinical record.
options.feedback: A more capable model helps when the task exceeds the model. Here the summary already comes out correct: what fails is what goes into the request, and time rises across 12,000 summaries a day.

options.label: B
options.text: Add one subagent per specialty that reviews each summary before it is shown and fills in whatever is missing by that specialty's clinical criteria.
options.feedback: Review by another agent adds judgment, and it also adds tokens and seconds in series, over sequential dependent work that gains nothing from being split up.

options.label: C
options.text: Widen the context with the patient's last fifty consultations, so that the summary always has every available antecedent in view.
options.feedback: More history looks like more useful information, but context is a finite resource: past a point retrieval of what matters gets worse, and here what matters is precisely the latest entry.

options.label: D
options.text: Normalize the input and send only the fields the summary needs, instead of dumping the patient's complete record into every request.
options.feedback: Correct: the input stage decides what the model sees; narrowing the fields cuts the dilution, shortens the time, and respects the limit on what may leave each clinic.

options.label: E
options.text: Store the difference between the draft and the text the clinician signs, and turn those corrections into the cases of the evaluation set.
options.feedback: Correct: the correction the clinician already makes is the signal of the feedback stage, and turning it into cases closes the loop with real data at no extra work.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of an end-to-end design is that every stage is decided on purpose: what goes in, how it is processed, what comes out, and what returns as feedback. The symptom described is not a model capability problem but an input problem: dumping the complete record dilutes what matters, and context is a finite resource with diminishing returns. Curating the input also shortens the time and respects the contractual limit on which fields leave the clinic. The second measure is independent of the first: the difference between the draft and the signed text is a real signal already produced every day, and it turns usage into evaluation cases. The distinction against moving up a model is that the summary already comes out correct; what fails is what it is being given to summarize.

RULE: Design the input before you touch the model, and take the correction the person already makes as the signal that closes the loop.

TRAP: Assuming that more context is more useful information, when the one datum that decides ends up buried among the ones that decide nothing.

TRY IT: Measure the average size of what you send per request, drop the fields that appear in no answer from the last day, and rerun twenty cases to compare what changed.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Colibrí Pay grew threefold year over year, and support cost per contact is climbing at the same rate. Management wants it down 30% in two quarters. The regulator requires that every decision that moves a customer's money have an identifiable person accountable for it. The traffic mix is already measured: 70% are informational queries about balances, transactions and card delivery status, and 30% are cases that end in a refund, a block or a reversal. Renata has to choose the shape of the solution. Which one fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Deploy an agent that resolves both families end-to-end and record in the history every action that moves money, so that it can be audited afterward.
options.feedback: Recording afterward does not meet what the regulator asks: the trace explains what already happened, but the requirement is that someone answer for the decision before the money moves.

options.label: B
options.text: Deploy an assistant that drafts the reply so that the human agents review it and send it, across both families of traffic alike.
options.feedback: Assistance improves quality and it is the right shape where judgment rules, but if a person still touches 100% of contacts, the 30% reduction never shows up.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the current process and spend the first quarter measuring cost per contact for each family before building any solution at all.
options.feedback: Measuring before building is prudent, and here the measurement that decides already exists: the traffic mix is taken and the target has a date, so the quarter would go by without progress.

options.label: D
options.text: Automate the informational queries end-to-end and design the money-moving family as assistance: the system prepares the case and a person decides.
options.feedback: Correct: the informational 70% admits full automation and that is where the saving is, while the money-moving family keeps the accountable person the regulator requires.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when translating a business problem is to separate the part that admits automation, where the system completes the task, from the part that calls for augmentation, where the person decides and the system assists. The two constraints in this case point at different places in the traffic: the cost target is only reached if the informational majority resolves without intervention, and the regulator's requirement falls on the minority that moves money. The distinction against assisting everywhere is that augmentation improves quality and preserves cost per contact, because a person still touches every case. And against automating everything with a trace, that an after-the-fact record documents the action but puts nobody in place to answer for it before it executes.

RULE: Automate where the outcome completes itself and assist where someone has to answer for the decision: the traffic mix tells you how much you will save.

TRAP: Confusing leaving a trace of an irreversible action with having someone answer for that action before it executes.

TRY IT: Classify a week of your contacts into the ones a system could close on its own and the ones someone has to sign off, and compute the maximum saving the first group can yield.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/research/anthropic-economic-index-january-2026-report https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

questions.question: The Mistral Retail after-sales agent resolves the median conversation for a few cents, but the most expensive 3% takes 40% of the monthly spend. Renata lowered max_tokens from 32,000 to 8,000 to contain that tail: the next month's spend fell by just 4% and answers started getting cut off in the middle of a returns explanation. The quarter's budget is already closed and the promotional season starts in three weeks. What is the most likely cause of the cut not having saved anything?

options.label: A
options.text: The saving was eaten by the long conversations, whose cache writes dominate the spend and do not depend on how much the model writes.
options.feedback: Cache writes weigh heavily when the prefix breaks on every turn, but that would explain a high spend spread evenly across all conversations, not a tail concentrated in 3%.

options.label: B
options.text: The cap applies to each response and not to the conversation, so every turn starts over from zero and the total does not move.
options.feedback: The cap does bound one response rather than the whole conversation, but even summed turn by turn it would still not change how much work the model decides to do.

options.label: C
options.text: The tail comes from the model, which needs more turns than the task deserves; with the most capable family the cost per finished task would drop.
options.feedback: Comparing by cost per finished task is the right metric and sometimes a more capable model comes out cheaper, but that does not explain why lowering the cap saved nothing.

options.label: D
options.text: The model does not see that cap: it cuts the response after generating it, so it never economizes and what gets discarded was already billed.
options.feedback: Correct: max_tokens is a limit that is invisible to the model, whereas a task budget is communicated to it and leads it to adjust the work it plans.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that there are three spend controls doing three different things. Effort and the task budget are signals the model sees and that change how much work it plans; max_tokens is a hard, invisible cap that truncates a response already generated and billed; and the workspace spend limit is the final brake in dollars. Lowering max_tokens cuts the text without changing behavior, which is why the saving was marginal and truncated answers appeared. For a tail of expensive conversations the documented path is to declare a task budget, which the model does see, with a spend limit behind it. The difference against switching models is that the tail is not explained by incapacity, but by nothing telling the model how much it may spend.

RULE: max_tokens trims what you already paid for; to make the model economize you have to give it a budget it can see.

TRAP: Confusing an output cap with a signal to economize: the model does not know max_tokens exists and plans its work just the same.

TRY IT: Take the ten most expensive conversations of the month, count how many ended with stop_reason max_tokens and how many output tokens were billed in them; then run those same ones with a declared task budget and compare.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence

html.question: The Mistral Retail after-sales agent resolves the median conversation for a few cents, but the most expensive 3% takes 40% of the monthly spend. Renata lowered max_tokens from 32,000 to 8,000 to contain that tail: the next month's spend fell by just 4% and answers started getting cut off in the middle of a returns explanation. The quarter's budget is already closed and the promotional season starts in three weeks. What is the most likely cause of the cut not having saved anything?
options: The saving was eaten by the long conversations, whose cache writes dominate the spend and do not depend on how much the model writes.
The cap applies to each response and not to the conversation, so every turn starts over from zero and the total does not move.
The tail comes from the model, which needs more turns than the task deserves; with the most capable family the cost per finished task would drop.
The model does not see that cap: it cuts the response after generating it, so it never economizes and what gets discarded was already billed.
html.explanation:
The general rule is that there are three spend controls doing three different things. Effort and the task budget are signals the model sees and that change how much work it plans; max_tokens is a hard, invisible cap that truncates a response already generated and billed; and the workspace spend limit is the final brake in dollars. Lowering max_tokens cuts the text without changing behavior, which is why the saving was marginal and truncated answers appeared. For a tail of expensive conversations the documented path is to declare a task budget, which the model does see, with a spend limit behind it. The difference against switching models is that the tail is not explained by incapacity, but by nothing telling the model how much it may spend.

RULE: max_tokens trims what you already paid for; to make the model economize you have to give it a budget it can see.

TRAP: Confusing an output cap with a signal to economize: the model does not know max_tokens exists and plans its work just the same.

TRY IT: Take the ten most expensive conversations of the month, count how many ended with stop_reason max_tokens and how many output tokens were billed in them; then run those same ones with a declared task budget and compare.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence

questions.question: The Ceibo Telecom fault diagnosis is built as a chain of six steps: it normalizes the complaint, identifies the service, checks the line status, proposes a test, interprets the result and drafts the answer. Each step is measured separately against its own set and none falls below 97%. End-to-end resolution, in contrast, stays at 83%, and the contract with the corporate customer fixes a first-contact resolution rate. The team proposes moving all six steps to the most capable model. What is the most likely explanation for the gap?

options.label: A
options.text: One step in the chain drags the rest down and its isolated measurement hides it, so it has to be found before anything else is touched.
options.feedback: That is the right hypothesis when the per-step measurement shows a weak link; here all six give the same number and the arithmetic explains the gap without needing a culprit.

options.label: B
options.text: The sets for each step are overfitted and that 97% does not hold up against the real inputs of support traffic.
options.feedback: Overfitting a set is a real cause of per-step numbers that look too good, but then you would expect spread between steps and not six even values.

options.label: C
options.text: The model falls short for the whole task: it is enough for each isolated step, but not to sustain the criterion across all six.
options.feedback: Upgrading the model improves each step and with it the product, but the gap does not come from the task exceeding the model: it comes from the number of dependent steps.

options.label: D
options.text: 83% is what six dependent steps at 97% predict: the error compounds along the chain without any step failing.
options.feedback: Correct: 0.97 to the sixth power is about 0.83, so the observed resolution is exactly what the chain predicts and the problem is its length, not its quality.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that in a chain of dependent steps accuracy multiplies: six steps at 97% give about 83% end-to-end, which is precisely what the team observes. It is the documented flip side of decomposing, the compounding-error risk of agentic systems, and it is not fixed by improving a link that is already at its ceiling. What moves that number is reducing the number of dependent steps or inserting programmatic checks between them, so an error is caught before it propagates. The difference against upgrading the model is that gaining two points per step leaves the chain still far from the target, while removing two steps changes the exponent.

RULE: In a dependent chain accuracy multiplies: before blaming the model, raise per-step accuracy to the number of steps and compare it with what you see.

TRAP: Reading an end-to-end gap as a capability problem, when it is the arithmetic of chaining steps that are individually fine.

TRY IT: Take your multi-step flow, multiply the measured accuracy of each step and compare the product with your real success rate; if they match, your problem is the length of the chain and not the model.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

questions.question: The taxpayer-support assistant at Agencia Nacional de Ingresos queries the registries of three partner agencies through their MCP servers, on top of its own. Internal audit raises two findings: the agent can invoke the cancellation of a registration, an operation its mandate does not cover, and in a sample of 200 cases it twice picked another agency's registry lookup when the internal one applied. Andrés answers that tool search already covers both, since only three to five definitions are loaded per query, and the audit closes in four weeks. Which two things explain why that answer falls short? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Selection accuracy degrades above 30 or 50 loaded tools, and with search active only three to five are loaded.
options.feedback: That is true and it is exactly what tool search improves, which is why it sounds like an answer. But it explains why the agent chooses better, not why it keeps a capability its mandate does not cover.

options.label: B
options.text: Deferring a definition is a context optimization and not a scope control: the tool stays invocable.
options.feedback: Correct: deferring takes definitions out of the context and leaves them available on demand. Removing a capability is a different thing, done by narrowing the agent's tool set or denying it by permissions.

options.label: C
options.text: The reasoning budget fell short for telling apart agencies whose procedures have similar names.
options.feedback: Widening the reasoning helps on hard tasks, but both findings are configuration: one is about scope and the other about how the tools the agent gets to see are described.

options.label: D
options.text: The server descriptions from the other agencies have a quality the agency does not control.
options.feedback: Correct: with third-party MCP servers the agent runs into descriptions of uneven quality, and a poor description sends it down the wrong path even when the loaded catalog is small.

options.label: E
options.text: The results returned by the registry lookups fill the window, and that is why the agent queries again.
options.feedback: Large results do crowd the context and have their own fix, but here the detour happens when choosing the tool, with two cases in two hundred and no sign of a saturated context.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that behind an inflated catalog sit two different questions: how much it occupies and what it permits. Tool search answers the first, because it takes definitions out of the context and loads them on demand, and that improves selection. It does not answer the second: a deferred tool is still invocable, so the ability to cancel a registration remains until it is removed from the agent's set or denied by permissions. The second finding has another root, because consuming third-party servers puts the agent in front of descriptions of uneven quality that the agency does not control. The distinction against the team's answer is between a context optimization and a scope control.

RULE: Deferring a tool takes it out of the context, not out of scope: what the agent should not be able to do is removed, not hidden.

TRAP: Treating a context optimization as if it were a permission control, and closing a scope finding because the definition is no longer loaded.

TRY IT: List the tools your agent can invoke today, mark the ones its mandate does not cover and remove them from the set instead of deferring them; then count how many of the rest come from servers you do not maintain.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación grades 40,000 short answers a week. The batch already goes through the Message Batches API with its 50% discount and the prompt prefix is cached, and even so the spend sits 30% above the budget per student. Each answer is then checked against an answer key, so the system knows which ones came out wrong. Grades are published six hours after the deadline and a full pass takes about forty minutes. The academic area will not accept losing accuracy. What cuts the most spend under those conditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower effort to the lowest level for the whole batch and accept the accuracy points that are lost in exchange for the saving.
options.feedback: That is half the idea: low effort does save, but applied to the whole batch it delivers exactly the accuracy drop the academic area will not accept.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the whole batch at the lowest effort level and rerun, at the default level, only the answers the key marked as failed.
options.feedback: Correct: with a failure signal and clock headroom, running everything low and retrying only the failures reaches the same success rate for around half the cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the whole batch to the cheapest model in the family, since this is high-volume work with verifiable output.
options.feedback: The cheapest model fits high volume with verifiable output, but it trades accuracy for price, which is what the constraint forbids, and it skips the effort sweep as well.

options.label: D
options.text: Buy the one-hour TTL for the prompt prefix, so that it survives between the batches of the different subjects.
options.feedback: The long TTL pays off when the pauses fall between five minutes and one hour; between weekly runs they are far longer and you would pay double for every write.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that when the result can be checked, the effort level does not have to be the same for all the work: you run everything at the lowest level and rerun at the default level only the cases the check marked as failed. The published measurement gives the same success rate for close to half the cost. The strategy demands two conditions that hold here: a failure signal, which the answer key provides, and clock headroom, because each failure consumes two passes and there are six hours for forty minutes of processing. The difference against lowering effort for the whole batch is that that version saves about as much but delivers the accuracy drop the academic area has already rejected.

RULE: If you can check the result, run everything at the cheap level and pay for the expensive one only on what failed.

TRAP: Applying a cost lever uniformly when a failure signal exists that lets you apply it only where it does not hurt.

TRY IT: Take a thousand cases with automatic verification, run them all at the lowest effort level, count how many fail, rerun only those at the default level and compare total cost and accuracy against running everything at the default level.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence

questions.question: At two in the morning the manifest validator at Terminal Puerto Claro starts assigning the wrong berth positions. Two shipping lines have already called, customs is asking about a held clearance, and the shift changes in 90 minutes. Bruno, the on-call engineer, has spent 70 minutes going through logs on his own while answering messages in three channels at once. How should the response be organized from this point on?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep digging into the analysis until the cause turns up → apply the correction → tell the shipping lines and customs once the problem is already solved
options.feedback: Fixing first and telling afterward works when nobody outside noticed. Here the problem is already visible, and the silence is paid for in calls that also interrupt the analysis.

options.label: B
options.text: Call the whole team onto a single bridge → split the analysis among whoever connects → write the report once the night shift has ended
options.feedback: Adding people without structure multiplies the conversation, not the capacity: with nobody in command and no roles assigned, the bridge is one more channel to attend to.

options.label: C
options.text: Roll back the last version → wait and see whether the manifests return to normal → escalate only if the problem persists after the rollback
options.feedback: A rollback is often the right first technical action and it does not replace declaring the incident: external visibility and the shift change already force a structured response.

options.label: D
options.text: Declare the incident and name who commands it → separate external communication from the technical work → keep the document live → hand over with explicit acknowledgment
options.feedback: Correct: two criteria for declaring are already met, the failure is visible to the customer and it has gone unresolved for a while, and the shift change demands an acknowledged handover.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to declare the incident when any of the agreed criteria is met: another team is needed to resolve it, the failure is visible to whoever uses the service, or it is still unresolved after an hour of focused analysis. Once declared, the response splits into separate responsibilities: the commander holds the overall state, the operations role applies the changes, and the communications role talks to the outside, over a document updated while it happens rather than afterward. The shift change is the other reason the order matters: a handover closes when the person handing off states the transition and receives explicit acknowledgment before disconnecting. The distinction against rolling back and waiting is that a rollback is a technical action and settles neither the communication nor the handover this shift already has on it.

RULE: Declare by criterion, separate command, operations and communication, and never disconnect without an explicit acknowledgment from whoever relieves you.

TRAP: Treating an incident visible to the customer as personal debugging, and finding out at the shift change that nobody else knows what was tried.

TRY IT: Take your last incident and answer three questions: who was in command, who spoke to the outside, and where is the document that was updated during it rather than after.

SOURCE: https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/

questions.question: Banco Altamar is about to expose its core banking system, which already has an API, to three different assistants: digital banking, complaint classification and credit documentation extraction. The team is comparing wrapping it in an MCP server, calling the API directly from each assistant, or delegating the work between agents. Which of the following statements about that choice is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: An MCP server provides a standardized integration that handles authentication and the API calls, and it is reused from several clients.
options.feedback: This statement is true: the documented advantage of MCP is a standardized integration that takes care of authentication and of the API calls, and that makes the same integration reusable across clients.

options.label: B
options.text: A local server over stdio usually serves a single client, while a remote one over streamable HTTP serves many.
options.feedback: This statement is true: that is the usage difference the protocol architecture describes, and it drags along how each transport authenticates.

options.label: C
options.text: Wrapping the API in an MCP server lowers the latency of each call, because the protocol holds the connection to the core open.
options.feedback: Correct as the false statement: MCP is chosen for standardization and reuse, not for speed. A server in the middle does not shorten the path to the core; if anything it adds a hop and one more startup dependency.

options.label: D
options.text: Delegating the work between agents costs on the order of 3 to 10 times more tokens than one equivalent single agent.
options.feedback: This statement is true: that is the documented multiplier for multi-agent implementations against a single-agent approach on equivalent tasks.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for choosing an integration mechanism is to ask how many consumers there are and who controls both ends. MCP is chosen when several clients will consume the same capability and the heavy work is authentication and transport, because that is what the protocol standardizes. What no official page promises is performance: an MCP server in front of an API that already exists adds a component, it does not remove one. The key distinction is between reuse and speed, because the first justifies the protocol and the second points at calling the API directly when there is a single consumer.

RULE: Choose MCP for standardization and reuse across clients, never for latency: a server in the middle adds a hop, it does not save one.

TRAP: Treating an integration protocol as if it were a performance optimization, and justifying with speed a decision that is made for reuse.

TRY IT: Take one of your own integrations and count how many different clients consume it; with a single one and both ends your own, write in two lines what MCP would give you that the direct call does not.

questions.question: The Grupo Aurora Educación automated tutor runs as a short process per query, a few seconds long, and exports telemetry to its own collector. The monthly dashboard shows 1.1 million executions, while billing corresponds to close to 1.8 million, and Aurora splits the cost among the schools using the dashboard count. The collector recorded no errors. Ignacio has to close this month's split. What should you do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Reconcile the month against the usage and cost API, which is the authoritative billing source, and split by school with those numbers.
options.feedback: Reconciling with that API is worth doing because it is the authority for billing, but it groups by key, workspace and model: it does not return the per-session count Aurora splits by, nor does it fix the missing telemetry.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the export interval so the collector receives fewer batches per minute and stops dropping data when bursts arrive.
options.feedback: A longer interval eases the load on the collector, but here the problem is the opposite: the further apart the exports, the more short executions finish before the buffer is flushed.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on logging of prompt and tool content so you can identify which of the executions never reached the dashboard.
options.feedback: Logging content puts student data into a pipeline that may not be approved to store it, and it changes nothing if the export never leaves the process.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower the export interval and turn on exporter diagnostics: short processes end before flushing the buffer and failures are dropped silently.
options.feedback: Correct: the exit flush is bounded by a short deadline and failed exports neither interrupt the run nor surface as an error, so diagnostics is the only thing that shows them.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that telemetry is sent in batches and process exit only triggers one last flush bounded by a short deadline, so very brief executions can finish before exporting. On top of that, export failures are silent by design: the agent keeps working and the tool drops the data without raising an error in your application, which is exactly the picture of a dashboard with no errors and fewer executions than were billed. That is why the first move is to shorten the export interval and turn on the exporter's diagnostic output. The difference against reconciling with the usage and cost API is that the API is the authority for the invoice, but it does not return the per-session detail Aurora splits among the schools.

RULE: A dashboard with no errors is not a complete dashboard: exporters fail silently and short processes die with the buffer full.

TRAP: Reading the absence of errors in the collector as evidence that everything arrived, when silent dropping is the default behavior.

TRY IT: Run twenty executions of a few seconds with the default export interval and count how many appear in your collector; repeat with a low interval and diagnostics turned on, and compare the two counts.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/observability

questions.question: Fraud detection at Zafiro Seguros flags about 120,000 claims a year for investigation, and the regulator requires a quarterly report with the flag rate by policyholder group. An internal review found that policyholders in two regions are flagged more often than others with equivalent claims. The committee decides to strip gender, age and postal code from the file that reaches the model, and to treat the finding as corrected. What should you expect?

options.label: A
options.text: The disparity will disappear: without those fields the model can no longer condition its output on the attribute that was producing it.
options.feedback: Dropping the field removes the most direct route, but the attribute rarely travels alone: the correlation is still available in other data in the same file.

options.label: B
options.text: Discrimination will fall in one direction but not the other, because suppressing the field only corrects the bias that harms one group.
options.feedback: The documented measurement reveals patterns of both positive and negative discrimination, and suppressing a field does not act selectively on one of the two directions.

options.label: C
options.text: The signal will keep arriving through proxies in the free text and the history, so the disparity can persist and shows up only by measuring.
options.feedback: Correct: occupation, locality, the claim narrative and the history carry the same information, and the only way to know whether the bias is still there is to vary one attribute in a controlled way and compare.

options.label: D
options.text: The system will fall outside the quarterly report, because with no demographic attributes there is no group left to compare flag rates across.
options.feedback: The duty to report does not depend on which fields enter the model: the regulator compares outcomes by group, and those groups are known from the policyholder register.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that not receiving an attribute is not the same as not using it: systemic bias lives in the data, in the practices of the organization and in the society that produced them, so the signal reappears through correlated variables. The documented way to find out whether there is discrimination is to build decision scenarios and vary the demographic information systematically while holding everything else constant, which also reveals discrimination in both directions. Careful prompt engineering against that baseline is what then reduces the effect. The distinction against the option that declares the problem closed is that suppressing the field changes what the system sees, not what the system does, and without measurement that difference stays invisible.

RULE: Removing the attribute does not remove the correlation: if you do not measure by varying one field, you do not know whether the bias left or just stopped showing.

TRAP: Confusing not receiving an attribute with not using it, when the proxy comes in through the free text and the history.

TRY IT: Take 30 real files, duplicate each one changing only the region and leaving everything else identical, and compare the flag rate between the two copies before and after the fields are removed.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/news/evaluating-and-mitigating-discrimination-in-language-model-decisions https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/

questions.question: Yaguareté Logística reads shipping documentation from photos the customs brokers take on the dock. The field it gets wrong most is the seal number, printed in small type inside the customs stamp: it fails on 9% of shipments and every error forces the filing to be redone. Today each photo travels whole, resized to fit the token budget per clearance, which is already committed for the quarter. Sofía wants to raise the reading of the stamp without enlarging the spend per image. What is worth trying first?

options.label: A
options.text: Give the model a cropping tool so that it can zoom into the stamp area and read it again when it needs to.
options.feedback: Correct: the prompting guide reports consistent gains on image tasks when the model can get close to the relevant region instead of always looking at the whole photo.

options.label: B
options.text: Send each photo at its original resolution, without resizing, so that the seal arrives with a good deal more detail.
options.feedback: More resolution across the whole photo multiplies image tokens on every clearance and spreads attention evenly between the stamp and the rest of the dock.

options.label: C
options.text: Route to the most capable model in the family the clearances whose stamp is illegible, and leave the rest where they are today.
options.feedback: Routing to the most capable model helps when the difficulty is in the reasoning, and it also requires a prior detector of an illegible stamp, which is exactly what is missing.

options.label: D
options.text: Add three examples of correctly read stamps to the prompt, each one with its seal number already transcribed alongside.
options.feedback: Examples fix format and criteria, but they do not change what the model can make out inside a small region of an image.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that on image tasks what moves accuracy most is not how much image you send, but whether the model can look closely at the region that matters: the documentation recommends giving it a cropping tool or an equivalent Skill to zoom in, and reports consistent gains on image evaluations. That lever fits the constraint because the crop is requested only when it is needed, whereas raising the resolution of the whole photo pays image tokens on every clearance, blurry stamp or not. The difference against upgrading the model is that the problem is not reasoning but what the model can make out in a small region.

RULE: When a small detail of an image fails, give the model a way to get closer before you send it more pixels or a more expensive model.

TRAP: Treating an attention problem inside the image as if it were one of resolution or capability, and paying for it on every photo.

TRY IT: Take thirty photos with a difficult stamp, measure the accuracy of the seal number with the whole photo and with a manual crop of the stamp area, and compare the image tokens of each variant as well.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

questions.question: The anti-money-laundering desk at Colibrí Pay is about to connect its agent to an MCP server from a sanctions-list provider that appears in Anthropic's connectors directory. What does that presence in the directory guarantee?

options.label: A
options.text: That Anthropic audited the security of that server before listing it and keeps monitoring how it operates.
options.feedback: That is the most common reading and it is exactly the one the documentation denies: Anthropic does not security-audit or manage any MCP server.

options.label: B
options.text: That Anthropic reviewed it against its listing criteria, without auditing or managing it: the security review stays yours.
options.feedback: Correct: the directory applies listing criteria, and the documentation states that Anthropic does not security-audit or administer the MCP servers that appear there.

options.label: C
options.text: That the server implements the authorization part of the specification, including the audience validation required for tokens.
options.feedback: The specification does require validating that the token was issued for that server, but that is a protocol requirement, not something the listing verifies for you.

options.label: D
options.text: That the annotations the server declares can be treated as trustworthy by the client that consumes it.
options.feedback: Annotations are hints the server itself declares, and the client should treat them as untrusted unless the server is trusted; the listing does not change that.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that curating a catalog is not a security audit. The Claude Code documentation says so explicitly: Anthropic reviews connectors against its listing criteria before adding them to the directory, but does not security-audit or manage any MCP server. The client-side work the specification assigns therefore remains yours: validating results before passing them to the model, asking for human confirmation on sensitive operations, logging tool use, and treating server annotations as untrusted. The distinction against reading it as a certification is about who carries the risk: the directory filters by publication criteria, and the technical review of the server you are about to connect stays on your side.

RULE: Being in the directory is a listing criterion, not a security audit: you answer for the server you connect.

TRAP: Reading a catalog curation as if it were a security certification of the server you are about to connect.

TRY IT: Pick an MCP server you already use, list its tools and mark which ones can write or move money; for each one, note which control of yours limits it today, without counting the catalog it came from.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/security https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools
