questions.question: Minera Nevado runs an operational safety assistant on site, built on the Agent SDK. After an incident, internal audit requires reconstructing within 24 hours which tools the agent invoked on each turn and what the operator decided on each permission. Telemetry was enabled like this: {"CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY": "1", "OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER": "otlp", "OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER": "none", "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT": "https://colector.faena:4318"}. What is missing to be able to answer that question?

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing: the metrics for sessions, tokens and cost already reconstruct what the agent did on each turn.
options.feedback: Metrics answer whether something changed and what it cost, which is monitoring. The audit's question is one of observability, that is, what the agent did step by step, and that is not in an aggregate counter.

options.label: B
options.text: The logs exporter, which is the channel where the decision and result events of each tool travel.
options.feedback: Correct: tool decision events, tool result events and API request events go out through the logs exporter; with that exporter set to none not one is emitted, however well the metrics flow.

options.label: C
options.text: The content-logging variables, which are the ones that store what each tool did in the run.
options.feedback: Those variables exist and control how much content the events carry, but the events still travel through the logs exporter: with it off they change nothing, and storing full prompts is a separate privacy decision.

options.label: D
options.text: A query to the Admin API cost report grouped by key identifier, to see the detail per turn.
options.feedback: The cost report closes out spend per key and per workspace, in daily buckets and with about five minutes of delay. It has no per-tool or per-turn detail, so it does not reconstruct the run.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that each observability layer answers a different question: metrics say that something changed, events say what the agent did, and the usage and cost report closes out the organization's spend with several minutes of delay. Reconstructing a run step by step is a question for events, and in this instrumentation the events are off, because the logs exporter is the one that emits the tool decision, the tool result and the API request. The distinction against raising the content detail is one of channel: those variables regulate how much of each event is stored, not whether the event gets out at all.

RULE: Metrics tell you that something changed and events tell you what the agent did: with the logs exporter off there is no tool trace, however much content you configure.

TRAP: Confusing monitoring with observability and believing a dashboard of tokens and cost can tell what the agent did at each step.

TRY IT: Turn the logs exporter on in a test environment, run a query that uses two tools and look in your collector for the tool decision and tool result events; count how many show up per run.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/usage-cost-api

questions.question: Pampero Agro generates 3,000 agronomic reports a week and multiplies that volume eightfold during the six weeks of the campaign, on a cost per report the business has already fixed. An audit of the rejected reports shows that 60% of the errors correspond to data the field sheet never recorded. The team proposes running the same extraction three times over each field sheet and keeping the majority value. What effect will that change have?

options.label: A
options.text: Cost per report approaches three times what it is today and accuracy barely moves, because the three passes share the same gap in the input.
options.feedback: Correct: voting adds attempts, not information; when the datum is not on the field sheet, three readings arrive at the same place and only the bill is multiplied.

options.label: B
options.text: Accuracy rises appreciably, because taking three samples of the same field sheet reduces the variability inherent in the model's own response.
options.feedback: Voting improves confidence when the error comes from variability between runs. Here the cause is measured in the input, so the majority value does not correct it.

options.label: C
options.text: Latency per report triples, because the three passes are executed one after another over each field sheet instead of all at the same time.
options.feedback: Voting is a form of parallelization: the passes run at the same time and the total is close to the slowest of them, not the sum of the three.

options.label: D
options.text: The system will be able to flag the reports with missing data on its own, because the three passes will disagree on exactly those fields.
options.feedback: Disagreement is a useful signal when the model is unsure; the problem is that faced with an absent datum the three passes tend to fill it in just as plausibly and agree.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that voting, meaning running the same task several times and keeping the most frequent result, is for when several attempts or several perspectives are needed to gain confidence, and its cost is proportional to the number of attempts. Here the audit has already located the cause outside the model: 60% of the errors are data the field sheet never recorded, and rereading the same sheet does not make them appear. So cost per report approaches three times what it is while accuracy barely moves, in exactly the campaign where volume multiplies eightfold. The distinction against expecting a gain in accuracy is the origin of the error: voting corrects variability between runs, not missing information in the input.

RULE: Repeating the same task buys confidence against variability, never against a datum that is not in the input.

TRAP: Extrapolating the benefit of voting to an error already measured in the input, and paying three times for the same incomplete reading.

TRY IT: Take twenty cases your system got wrong, run each one three times, and count how many produce three identical answers: that tells you whether the error is variability or missing information.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

questions.question: The support agent at Colibrí Pay uses the policy manual to answer questions about fees and refund times, and the regulator requires every automated answer to point at the clause that supports it. Retrieved chunks reach the model like this: {"role": "user", "content": "Retrieved chunks: [1] refund fee ... [2] crediting times ... [3] exceptions ... Answer citing the clause number."}. In an audit of 400 cases, 22% cite a clause number that does not exist in the manual, even though the content of the answer was right. Which change fixes the cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise top_k from three to ten chunks so the model has more material to take the clause from.
options.feedback: More chunks raise the odds of including the right one, but the answer was already right: what fails is not what was retrieved, but that the model writes the reference. More material can also distract it.

options.label: B
options.text: Add reranking over the candidates so the right chunk comes first and the citation is reliable.
options.feedback: Reranking is the improvement with the most leverage when the right chunk arrives badly positioned, and it costs between 100 and 200 ms per query. Here that chunk already arrived and the model used it well.

options.label: C
options.text: Pass each chunk as a search_result block with its source and its title, and enable citations.
options.feedback: Correct: search_result blocks are the container meant for your own search results, and with citations enabled the reference comes back as a verifiable pointer to the document instead of text the model composes.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask in the system prompt for the source sentence to be quoted before each answer is written.
options.feedback: Asking for the citation in the prompt is exactly what is failing already: the documentation notes that native citations cost less, guarantee valid pointers to the documents and improve the relevance of the cited passage.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to separate two problems that look alike: if the answer is wrong, look at retrieval; if the answer is right but you cannot show where it came from, look at the grounding format. Here the content is right and the index works, so what fails is that the reference is text written by the model, and an invented number looks exactly like a real one. Passing each chunk as a search_result block with citations enabled turns that reference into a pointer to the document, with its source and its title, and the quoted text does not even count as output tokens. The distinction against reranking is what is being fixed, because reranking moves the order of the candidates and not the traceability of the answer.

RULE: When the answer is right but you cannot show where it came from, the problem is the container and not retrieval: move the chunks into search_result blocks with citations.

TRAP: Treating a citation written by the model as if it were a verifiable reference, and fixing retrieval when what is missing is the grounding format.

TRY IT: Take three chunks you paste as text today, send them again as search_result blocks with citations enabled and compare the citations that come back with the clause numbers the model used to write.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/search-results https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations

questions.question: AndesWare sized its quota using the per-user recommendation for an organization of 400 developers, and day to day there is room to spare. Training has announced a live session: all 400 connected at once, one single afternoon, with the date already communicated to clients. Paula, who administers the platform, has to tell the organizer what to expect before the invitation goes out. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Request a larger allocation for that afternoon, because the per-user recommendation assumes low concurrency and the training brings everyone together at once.
options.feedback: Correct: limits are consumed at the organization level, and the per-user recommendation falls as the team grows precisely because it assumes few people work at the same time.

options.label: B
options.text: Explain that the limit is applied at the user level, so that each one of the 400 developers connected has a quota of its own available for the whole training afternoon.
options.feedback: This is the most frequent confusion: the quota is agreed and consumed at the organization level, so 400 simultaneous sessions compete for one quota, not for 400 separate ones.

options.label: C
options.text: Choose the fastest model in the family for the exercises, so that each one finishes sooner and total consumption spreads better across the afternoon.
options.feedback: A faster model shortens each exercise and does not change the quota available in that window: what pinches is how many requests land in the same minute.

options.label: D
options.text: Wait for the first rate limit errors to appear during the session and request the quota increase at that point, with the evidence of real consumption.
options.feedback: Reacting to telemetry is reasonable when the event repeats. With a fixed date and a single afternoon, the adjustment arrives once the training is already spoiled.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for aligning capacity expectations is that rate limits apply at the organization level and not per person, and that the recommended tokens per user falls as the team grows precisely because it assumes few people use the tool at the same time. A live training with the whole team breaks that assumption: it is the unusually high concurrency scenario the documentation names as an exception, and the one for which a larger allocation should be requested in advance. The distinction against waiting for the errors is the date: a quota adjustment is not resolved inside the same afternoon, so the expectation is agreed beforehand with whoever is organizing.

RULE: Quota is consumed at the organization level and sized assuming low concurrency: a live event with the whole team is requested in advance.

TRAP: Assuming that the limit travels with each user, when what is shared out is a single organization quota across all the simultaneous sessions.

TRY IT: Look at how many active users you have in your peak hour and compare that with your total licenses: that ratio is the concurrency assumption your quota is sized on.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs

Explain that the limit is applied at the user level, so that each one of the 400 developers connected has a quota of its own available for the whole training afternoon.
Choose the fastest model in the family for the exercises, so that each one finishes sooner and total consumption spreads better across the afternoon.
Wait for the first rate limit errors to appear during the session and request the quota increase at that point, with the evidence of real consumption.
html.explanation:
The general rule for aligning capacity expectations is that rate limits apply at the organization level and not per person, and that the recommended tokens per user falls as the team grows precisely because it assumes few people use the tool at the same time. A live training with the whole team breaks that assumption: it is the unusually high concurrency scenario the documentation names as an exception, and the one for which a larger allocation should be requested in advance. The distinction against waiting for the errors is the date: a quota adjustment is not resolved inside the same afternoon, so the expectation is agreed beforehand with whoever is organizing.

RULE: Quota is consumed at the organization level and sized assuming low concurrency: a live event with the whole team is requested in advance.

TRAP: Assuming that the limit travels with each user, when what is shared out is a single organization quota across all the simultaneous sessions.

TRY IT: Look at how many active users you have in your peak hour and compare that with your total licenses: that ratio is the concurrency assumption your quota is sized on.

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom has one quarter to show a 25% reduction in cost per first-level support contact, without touching the contractual SLA of 30 seconds to first response. Three candidates compete: technical faults, which are the longest and most expensive calls; retention, where the revenue is; and service status and billing queries, which are 55% of the volume and whose outcome is confirmed by the network test that already runs on its own. Ximena has to choose where to start. What fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Start with the status and billing queries, where the volume is high and the outcome is confirmed by an automated test that already exists.
options.feedback: Correct: the first use case is chosen on measurable metrics and abundant data, and here volume multiplies the saving while the network test proves the result inside the quarter.

options.label: B
options.text: Start with the technical faults, because every case resolved saves far more operator minutes and the impact per contact is the highest of the three.
options.feedback: The most expensive case looks like the biggest return and it is also the noisiest signal: a fault is sometimes confirmed by a site visit, so the effect is not demonstrable in time.

options.label: C
options.text: Start with retention, because it is the highest-value case for the business and the one that best justifies the investment to company management.
options.feedback: Retention is where the revenue is and also where the result takes weeks and depends on factors outside the system: it is not the first case for a dated cost target.

options.label: D
options.text: Build a single agent covering all three cases, to avoid maintaining three systems and to spread the cost of the shared platform across them.
options.feedback: One agent for three different families sounds efficient and it multiplies the reach of the first mistake, besides mixing the low-risk case with the one that touches customer retention.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for choosing the first use case is to look for measurable success metrics, abundant data, clear return and low risk, not for the case with the highest unit cost. Here the volume is what turns a small saving per contact into the 25% committed, and the network test already running supplies the objective, automatic signal that lets the result be demonstrated within the quarter. The distinction against starting with technical faults is in the signal: they are the most expensive cases, but their resolution is sometimes confirmed by a visit to the customer's premises, so the effect is neither observable nor attributable inside the deadline. Against retention, that its result is measured in weeks and depends on factors the system does not control.

RULE: Choose the first use case on volume multiplied by certainty of the signal, not on the unit cost of the most expensive case.

TRAP: Confusing the case that costs the most with the one that pays back first, and choosing the one that cannot demonstrate its result inside the committed deadline.

TRY IT: List your candidates and note for each one the monthly volume and which existing signal would confirm the result with no extra human work: the one with both goes first.

questions.question: The itinerary assistant at Siete Lagos Viajes needs the rules of fourteen wholesalers: cancellation penalties, change windows and refund conditions. Today all fourteen rulebooks travel complete in the system prompt. In high season the volume multiplies tenfold and cost per query is already at the limit of the budget; measurement also shows the assistant mixing one wholesaler's conditions with another's. Two of the fourteen account for 80% of bookings. Which decomposition fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Leave the fourteen rulebooks in the prompt and turn on caching over that block, so that the repeated content costs much less on every query.
options.feedback: Caching does make repeated content cheaper and it does not reduce what the model has to attend to: the fourteen sets of conditions still compete, and the mixing continues.

options.label: B
options.text: Create one subagent per wholesaler and have the assistant delegate to the right one every time it has to apply a cancellation or change rule.
options.feedback: Fourteen subagents isolate context and add a token multiplier and a coordination cost that this work, sequential and one booking at a time, does not need.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn each rulebook into a modular capability of which only a short description is always loaded, pulling in the full text when a case invokes it.
options.feedback: Correct: the short description takes up very little permanently and the full text enters only when needed, so cost per query and interference between wholesalers fall together.

options.label: D
options.text: Summarize the fourteen rulebooks into a single page of common conditions and consult the original text only when a customer files a complaint.
options.feedback: A common summary saves tokens and erases exactly what decides: each wholesaler's specific penalty is the difference the itinerary has to apply.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that when the problem is context and not work, what gets decomposed is the context: a minimal description of each capability stays loaded, the full instructions enter when a case activates it, and additional resources cost nothing until they are read. That attacks both constraints at once, cost per query in high season and interference between similar conditions, because the model stops having fourteen rulebooks competing for its attention. The distinction against caching is that caching makes repeating the same content cheaper, but the content still enters on every query. And against the subagents, that there is no parallel work to isolate here, only text that is better loaded on demand.

RULE: When the excess is context and not work, keep loaded the minimum that lets you decide and pull in the rest only when the case invokes it.

TRAP: Confusing making repeated content cheaper with getting it out of the way: caching changes the price of context, not its effect on the model's attention.

TRY IT: Count how many tokens of your prompt are used in under 10% of queries and work out what you pay for them each month: that is the budget loading them on demand frees up.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Pampero Agro changed the prompt for the agronomy reports and the evaluation suite went from 0.71 to 0.78 over 240 cases, each one run three times and with the model pinned in the pipeline. With the change already in production, advisers send back more reports than before, above all the ones produced from incomplete field notes and those for plots outside the core zone. The failures do not always fall on the same cases in the suite. Which two reviews best explain that difference? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The case set does not mirror the real distribution: it was built from typical full-season reports, with no incomplete notes and no atypical plots.
options.feedback: Correct: the first principle of evaluation design asks for cases that mirror the real distribution of the task, edge cases included; a set that omits them rewards changes that get worse exactly there.

options.label: B
options.text: The suite has hit its ceiling and no longer tells two versions apart, so any difference it shows is just noise.
options.feedback: A saturated suite does stop giving signal for improvement, but the stem puts it at 0.78, with plenty of room for a real improvement to show.

options.label: C
options.text: The improvement was declared with one layer only: no production monitoring, no human review of transcripts against what the suite said.
options.feedback: Correct: no evaluation layer catches everything, which is why automated evaluations are combined with production monitoring, A/B tests and human review of transcripts.

options.label: D
options.text: The model was updated during the test, so what got measured was that update and not the change to the prompt.
options.feedback: Changing two variables at once ruins attribution, which is why the model is pinned in the pipeline; the stem says it already was.

options.label: E
options.text: The runs share state with one another, so execution order decides which case fails and the average comes out inflated.
options.feedback: Shared state produces failures that correlate across runs, which the stem rules out by saying the failures do not always land on the same cases.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a suite measures what it contains and nothing more, and that no single layer is enough. A set built from typical cases can rise while the system gets worse exactly at the edges that are not represented, because the first design principle asks it to mirror the real distribution of the task including its edge cases. On top of that the improvement was declared with automated evaluations alone: the documented practice is to stack layers, with production monitoring, A/B tests and human review of transcripts, so that what escapes one is caught by another. The other three hypotheses are ruled out by data in the stem itself: the suite is not saturated, the model was pinned and the failures do not repeat case by case.

RULE: Your suite can only reward what it contains: check which cases are missing before you believe it, and test its verdict against at least one more layer.

TRAP: Reading an improvement in the suite as an improvement in production, when the cases that broke were never in the set.

TRY IT: Take the last twenty reports the advisers sent back and look for how many have an equivalent case in your suite; the ones that do not are the first batch of new cases.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: AndesWare standardized on Claude Code across its 400 developers. The most used flow compiles the monorepo with the Bash tool and opens a ticket against a remote MCP server; its 95th percentile went from 4 to 9 minutes, and management wants to know how much of that is the build and how much is the ticket server. What the collector shows today is this: claude_code.interaction → claude_code.llm_request → claude_code.tool (Bash) with no children → claude_code.tool (mcp__tickets__crear) with no children. Paula proposes enabling distributed tracing before the next cost review. What will the team get?

options.label: A
options.text: The full tree, including the build's internal steps, because subprocesses inherit the exporter configuration.
options.feedback: Subprocesses do not inherit that configuration: it is documented that the OTEL variables are not passed to the Bash tool, to hooks or to MCP servers, so their insides stay dark until you instrument them.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the time of the model calls, because traces do not cover the execution of the tools.
options.feedback: The span hierarchy covers the interaction, the model request, the hooks and the tools, with one span for the approval wait and another for the execution. Time per tool is visible.

options.label: C
options.text: The time the agent spends in each tool, but the build's insides appear only if that process exports its spans.
options.feedback: Correct: the agent's spans cover every tool and its execution, and subprocesses inherit the trace context, so they can join the same tree; but they emit spans of their own only when you instrument them.

options.label: D
options.text: Nothing new: it will have to be estimated from the usage report grouped by key, which is where per-step time sits.
options.feedback: The usage and cost report reconciles spend per key and per workspace, in daily buckets and with a few minutes of delay. It has no per-step or per-tool times, so it does not answer the question.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the trace shows you what the agent does, not what the processes it launches do. Enabling distributed tracing brings up the hierarchy of the interaction, the model request, the hooks and each tool with its execution, so the team will be able to say how many minutes of the 95th percentile go inside the Bash tool and how many inside the call to the ticket server. What does not appear is the build's internal breakdown, because Claude Code does not pass the OTEL variables to subprocesses; the trace context is propagated, so instrumenting that tool is enough for its spans to hang from the same tree. The distinction against the optimistic reading is between inheriting the trace context and inheriting the exporter configuration.

RULE: The agent's trace reaches the edge of each tool: the processes it launches inherit the trace context, not the exporter configuration.

TRAP: Assuming a subprocess ends up instrumented by inheritance, when the only thing it inherits is the trace identifier.

TRY IT: Enable distributed tracing in a session, run a flow that uses the Bash tool and a remote MCP server and count how many tool execution spans appear; then instrument the build script and check that its spans hang from the same trace.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage

questions.question: The Agencia Nacional de Ingresos is about to put its inconsistency detector into production over 4 million filings a year; when it flags one, the taxpayer receives a demand notice. Internal audit will not clear go-live without a documented risk management program against the NIST framework the agency adopted as its reference, and any external tool takes nine months to clear procurement. Valentina has eight weeks and a team of three. What should be done in that window?

options.label: A
options.text: Buy a bias-testing platform and walk the seven characteristics of trustworthy AI as a checklist to complete before go-live.
options.feedback: The seven characteristics describe what makes a system trustworthy, but they are not a pre-launch checklist, and nine months of procurement puts this option outside the window.

options.label: B
options.text: Draft the ethics policy and stand up the governance committee, and postpone the rest of the risk work until that committee is formally constituted and operating.
options.feedback: The govern function is cross-cutting and infused continuously, not a stage that finishes: waiting for it to close leaves the system with no mapped context and no measurement at go-live.

options.label: C
options.text: Frame the context (what it is for, who it affects and what a wrong flag costs) and let that map decide what to measure, with governance in parallel.
options.feedback: Correct: the map function establishes the context that frames the risks, and it is that map that decides what to measure afterwards; governance runs above the whole process.

options.label: D
options.text: Assign a person to review every flagged filing before the notice goes out, and leave risk measurement for after go-live.
options.feedback: Human review is a valuable control, but it is not a risk management program, and at four million filings a year it is not sustainable as the only control either.

questions.explanation:
The general rule in the framework is that governing is cross-cutting and continuous, and that after governance the work starts by mapping: the map function establishes the context that frames the risks of the system, and only with that context do measuring and managing mean anything. Framing what the detector is for, who a wrong flag hurts and what that demand notice costs is what defines which metric means something, and it is work three people can do in eight weeks without going through procurement. The distinction against starting from measurement is that with no map you buy metrics that answer no identified risk. The distinction against waiting for the committee is that governance is not a preliminary stage that closes.

RULE: Governing is continuous, not a stage: frame the context before you measure, because the map is what decides which metric means anything.

TRAP: Treating the govern function as a formality that gets finished, or running out to measure without having framed who the system affects.

TRY IT: Write the map of your system on one page: purpose, people affected, what happens on a false positive and on a false negative, and which indicator shows each one; then see which of your current metrics answer none of that.

SOURCE: https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/ https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros estimated the monthly cost of the broker assistant by running each saved prompt through the token counting endpoint, adding a generous output per answer and multiplying by the forecast volume. The commitment to finance was signed with that number and the invoice came in four times higher. The measurements were taken against the same model that is in production, and the assistant resolves each query with an agent that chains between ten and thirty turns with tools. Where should you look first?

options.label: A
options.text: The calculation counts each prompt once, but the agent resends the whole conversation on every turn and billed input grows much faster than volume.
options.feedback: Correct: in an agentic loop every turn resends everything accumulated, so a forty-turn task sends its first turn forty times and cost grows close to the square of the number of turns.

options.label: B
options.text: The estimate ignored that output costs several times more than input, and a long answer ends up being paid for many times over.
options.feedback: Output does cost several times what input costs, but the stem states that the estimate already included a generous output per answer.

options.label: C
options.text: The endpoint returns an estimate and also counts tokens added by the system, so the count drifts away from what is actually charged.
options.feedback: It is true that the count is an estimate and that it includes system-added tokens that are not billed, except that this pushes the number up and here it fell short.

options.label: D
options.text: The tokenizer of the model produces around 30% more tokens for the same text than the previous generation of the family.
options.feedback: A tokenizer change explains surprises when you migrate, but the measurements were made against the same model that is running in production.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that in an agent the unit of cost is not the prompt but the task: every turn resends the whole accumulated conversation, so a forty-turn task sends its first turn forty times and spend grows roughly with the square of the number of turns. Counting each prompt once describes a single-turn system, not one that chains between ten and thirty. The other three statements are true as facts and do not explain this invoice: expensive output was already accounted for, system-added tokens push the estimate up rather than down, and the tokenizer changes only if you change generation. The distinction that decides is whether the loop resends context, not whether the count is exact.

RULE: Estimate by task and not by prompt: in an agent, every turn pays again for everything the conversation has already said.

TRAP: Extrapolating the cost of an agentic system from the count of an isolated prompt, as if each query were a single call.

TRY IT: Run one representative query end-to-end and add up the input_tokens of all its turns; divide that total by the count of the first prompt and apply that factor to your estimate.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/token-counting

TRAP: Extrapolating the cost of an agentic system from the count of an isolated prompt, as if each query were a single call.

TRY IT: Run one representative query end-to-end and add up the input_tokens of all its turns; divide that total by the count of the first prompt and apply that factor to your estimate.

questions.question: In the human-in-the-loop pattern with a sandbox that Anthropic documents from its own experience, approval fatigue appears as a failure mode of the human control. What does that term describe?

options.label: A
options.text: That the gate denies by default when the reviewer does not answer within the time configured for it.
options.feedback: An expiry that denies is a reasonable design decision, but it describes what happens when nobody answers, not what happens when the person always says yes.

options.label: B
options.text: That the requests pile up and the agent stays blocked while it waits for a human answer.
options.feedback: Queue blocking is a real operational problem with synchronous gates, but it is the opposite of what fatigue describes: there the problem is that nothing stops.

options.label: C
options.text: That the reviewer loses context because the request does not show the arguments the tool will be called with.
options.feedback: Showing the user the tool inputs before the server is called is an explicit recommendation of the protocol, but it is a presentation defect distinct from fatigue.

options.label: D
options.text: That the reviewer approves almost everything by volume, and the gate suggests more safety than the review gives.
options.feedback: Correct: when the approval rate approaches the total, the gate stops filtering and only sustains the impression that somebody is reviewing.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a human control is worth something only while the person exercises judgment, and that degrades with volume: the documented experience of the sandbox with human approval shows users with approval fatigue, where a very high approval rate creates a false sense of safety. The design consequence is that the number of confirmations is a safety parameter: if you ask about everything, review becomes a reflex click. The distinction against the queue and presentation problems is where the failure sits: there the gate works and annoys, here the gate works, annoys nobody, and for that reason protects nobody.

RULE: Measure your approval rate: if it is close to 100%, the gate is no longer reviewing, it is only recording.

TRAP: Taking the existence of the gate as evidence of control, without looking at the rate at which the people staffing it approve.

TRY IT: Count how many confirmations your agent asked for last week and how many were denied; if the denial rate is near zero, look for actions to take out of scope instead of asking more often.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros fraud detection returns two things per claim: a verdict among four fixed categories and a written justification of a few lines that the regulator requires to be reviewable. The suite has 3,000 labeled cases and is rerun in full with every prompt change, once a week. The evaluation budget does not stretch to a judge over the 3,000 cases on both dimensions, and the team has six hours a week from two analysts. How should the scoring be divided?

options.label: A
options.text: Score both dimensions with a judge and a 1 to 5 scale, which is flexible enough for the verdict and for the justification.
options.feedback: A judge is the right tool for what requires judgment, but applying it to a four-value category adds cost and variance where a string comparison is exact and free.

options.label: B
options.text: Score the verdict with exact match and leave the justification unscored, since it is free text and does not lend itself to automation.
options.feedback: Automating the verdict is fine, but leaving the justification unmeasured leaves unmeasured exactly the dimension the regulator reviews, and a judge over short text does scale.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the judge with the analysts reviewing 200 cases a week, which is the highest-quality scoring available.
options.feedback: Human review is the highest quality and the documentation asks you to avoid it where you can: two hundred cases do not cover the suite and they consume the hours that should be calibrating the judge.

options.label: D
options.text: Score the verdict with exact match on the 3,000 cases and reserve the judge, with an explicit rubric, for the justification, which is short.
options.feedback: Correct: for each thing you measure you pick the fastest, most reliable and most scalable method that works, and the judge is left for short outputs where judgment is genuinely needed.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for choosing a grader is to keep the fastest, most reliable and most scalable method that works for what you are measuring. A verdict among four categories is an exact comparison, so code-based scoring is the fastest and most reproducible and costs nothing per case. A written justification requires judgment, and that is where the judge comes in, and it is more stable the shorter the text it has to read. Splitting it this way frees the analysts' hours to calibrate the judge against human verdicts, which is where expert time pays off. The difference against scoring everything with a judge is that on the categorical part it adds nothing and brings cost and variance between runs.

RULE: Each dimension gets its own grader: code where the answer is categorical, a judge where judgment is needed and the text is short, people to calibrate.

TRAP: Choosing a single method for the whole suite, and paying judge variance on the part an exact comparison settled without error.

TRY IT: Take a hundred already scored cases, compare the verdict with an exact comparison and with your judge, count how many they differ on and note what each method cost.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals

questions.question: The Grupo Aurora Educación tutor receives nine documents from the unit on every query, about 35,000 tokens in all: the base text, the current syllabus, the rubric, three past exams and two FAQ sheets. They are concatenated with a line of dashes between one and the next, and the student's question goes at the end. The tutor mixes criteria from a past exam with the current rubric and cannot say where it got each rule. Valentina proposes wrapping each document in tags with its index and its source, touching neither the content nor the order. What effect do you expect?

options.label: A
options.text: Attribution will improve, and so will the answers that depend on which document takes precedence, at a token cost almost equal to today's.
options.feedback: Correct: the guidance for long inputs asks you to structure the documents with tags that declare index and source, and those tags add a few tokens on top of thirty-five thousand.

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing will change, because the content and the order are the same and the model already has the nine documents in view.
options.feedback: Separating is not the same as concatenating: with no declared boundaries, the model has nothing to tell where one source ends and the next begins.

options.label: C
options.text: It will improve, but only if you also move the documents after the question, so that they sit closer to the answer.
options.feedback: The recommended order is the one the prompt already has: long documents at the top and the query at the end, which is what improves quality; inverting it makes things worse.

options.label: D
options.text: Attribution will improve and cost will drop as well, because the model will be able to skip the documents it does not need.
options.feedback: Everything that enters the window is processed and billed: tags help reference the source, they do not let the model skip content or lower the spend.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that from around 20,000 tokens onward the structure of the prompt starts to decide the quality of the answer, and the documentation gives three pieces for long inputs: documents at the top and the query at the end, each document wrapped in tags that declare its index and its source, and answers grounded in quotes. Here the order is already right, so what is missing is the second piece: with no declared boundaries, nine concatenated sources read as a single block and the model has nothing to tell which rule came from which. The tags cost a few tokens on top of thirty-five thousand. The difference against expecting a saving is that context is not skipped: everything that enters the window is processed and billed.

RULE: On long inputs each document is wrapped and named: the model can only cite the source whose beginning and end it can recognize.

TRAP: Assuming a line of dashes is equivalent to declaring sources, or that tagging lets the model read less.

TRY IT: Take twenty questions whose answer depends on which document takes precedence, run the current prompt and then a copy of it with each document tagged with index and source, and count how many times the tutor names the right source.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

questions.question: The maintenance assistant at Pehuén Energía combines two sources in the same request: its own index over 30 years of manuals, which arrives as search_result blocks, and the web search tool for the service bulletins the manufacturer publishes every week. The regulator requires every procedure handed over during a maintenance window to be traceable back to its source. Each internal block is built like this: {"type": "search_result", "source": "kb://manual-3412", "title": "Emergency stop", "content": [...], "citations": {"enabled": false}}. What is wrong with this configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing about the mix: it is enough to turn the web search citations off so that both sources match.
options.feedback: Citations from the web search tool are always enabled and cannot be turned off; uniformity is reached the other way around, by turning them on in your own blocks.

options.label: B
options.text: The search_result blocks sit in the user message and belong in the assistant one, where they are allowed.
options.feedback: It is the other way around: search_result blocks can appear only in user messages or in tool results, never in assistant messages. Where they sit is one of the two valid places.

options.label: C
options.text: The problem is cost, because web search results are billed per search and do not count again as input.
options.feedback: Results retrieved by web search do count as input tokens in that turn and in the following turns as well, on top of the per-search rate. Cost matters, but it is not the flaw in this configuration.

options.label: D
options.text: With web search enabled in the same request, every search_result block has to carry citations enabled.
options.feedback: Correct: all search results in one request share the same citations setting, and with the web search tool present that setting can only be enabled.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the citations setting is uniform within a request: either it is enabled on every document and search result, or on none of them. The web search tool does not offer that second option, because its citations are always on, so the moment it shares a request with your own search_result blocks the only possible state is to enable them there too. That is also what the regulator asks for, because with citations off on the internal index half the answers would be left with no pointer to their source. The distinction against the symmetric reading is that uniformity is not reached by lowering the source you cannot lower, but by raising the one you do control.

RULE: The citations setting is one per request: if web search is in, and it always brings citations on, your own search_result blocks have to turn them on too.

TRAP: Assuming two sources are matched by lowering the stricter one, when the source that always brings citations on cannot be lowered.

TRY IT: Build a request with a search_result block with citations disabled and the web search tool enabled, save what comes back, and repeat it with citations enabled, comparing the references each source brings.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/search-results https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/web-search-tool

questions.question: The integration team at Terminal Puerto Claro uses Claude Code on the repository that connects with the shipping lines and customs. The proposal that reached the security committee claims that denying the web fetch tool leaves the assistant with no way out to the internet. The security lead wants a written answer before he approves the deployment. What should that answer say?

options.label: A
options.text: That the rule is enough, because denying the web fetch tool blocks every route to the internet the assistant could ever attempt to take.
options.feedback: Denying the tool closes one real route and leaves the other one open: the rule acts on that tool, not on the commands the interpreter is able to run.

options.label: B
options.text: That it is enough to add to the project instructions file a line that forbids the assistant to download external content while it is working.
options.feedback: The instructions file steers the behavior of the assistant; a limit that has to hold every time needs an enforced control, not a written note.

options.label: C
options.text: That it is also worth logging every attempt the assistant makes to reach the internet, so you can review afterward whether it reached an unauthorized address.
options.feedback: The log lets you explain afterward what happened and it does not stop it from happening: what the committee is approving is a preventive control, not an audit after the fact.

options.label: D
options.text: That the rule covers the tool and not the command interpreter: with Bash allowed, curl or wget still reach any address, and the sandbox is what closes it.
options.feedback: Correct: permission rules and the sandbox cover different layers, and it is the allowed-domain list enforced by the operating system that closes the interpreter's route.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when communicating a security control is to say which layer it covers and which one it leaves open. Denying the web fetch tool blocks that tool, but if the command interpreter is allowed, utilities such as curl or wget still reach any address; that gap is closed by an allowed-domain list applied at the operating system level by the sandbox. The distinction against logging the attempts is one of timing: a log explains afterward and does not prevent beforehand, and what the committee approves is a preventive control. Presenting the proposal without naming the layer left uncovered turns a partial measure into a guarantee nobody can stand behind.

RULE: Always say which layer each control covers: denying a tool closes its route, and only the sandbox domain list closes the one the command interpreter opens.

TRAP: Assuming that denying a tool amounts to cutting off network access, when the command interpreter is still an open route.

TRY IT: In a test environment deny the web fetch tool, leave the command interpreter allowed, and ask the assistant to bring you a page: you will see which way it goes out.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/admin-setup

questions.question: Mistral Retail routes Claude Code for its 80 developers through Amazon Bedrock, on the corporate cloud account. Last month's spend tripled and finance set a monthly cap for the promotional quarter. Paula, who leads the platform, needs two things before the next campaign: to know which team consumes how much, and to have the cap actually take effect. Which two measures fit this deployment? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Set spend limits per organization and per member in the organization's administration settings.
options.feedback: Those limits govern seat allocation and usage credits on team plans; traffic that leaves through your own cloud never passes through them.

options.label: B
options.text: Open the analytics dashboard and sort the leaderboard by user to identify who consumes the most.
options.feedback: The dashboard is useful for adoption and contribution, but it does not cover usage running through a cloud provider, and the money lives in the spend report rather than in that dashboard.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the team to run /compact before every task so that context does not grow between requests.
options.feedback: Compacting is a real lever on tokens, but compacting a large context is itself a large request; to start from nothing, /clear costs nothing.

options.label: D
options.text: Export metrics over OpenTelemetry with OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES carrying team and cost center.
options.feedback: Correct: in this deployment OpenTelemetry is the only path that carries cost and tokens per user into your own stack, and those attributes are what let you split the bill by team.

options.label: E
options.text: Put the cap in the cloud's budget controls, which is where this traffic is billed.
options.feedback: Correct: with Bedrock the consumption is billed to your cloud account, so that cloud's budget control is what actually stops the spend.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the cap goes where the billing happens and the attribution is built where the traffic runs. With Claude Code on a cloud provider, the spend shows up in that cloud's billing console, the brake is its budget controls, and visibility comes from OpenTelemetry or from a gateway, because the analytics dashboard and the analytics API do not cover that usage. Resource attributes are the documented mechanism for tagging every session with department, team and cost center, and that is how you answer who consumes what. The distinction against setting limits in the organization administration is the billing channel: that control exists and works, but over seat allocation and usage credits, not over an invoice your cloud issues.

RULE: The cap goes where the billing happens and attribution is built where it runs: on a third-party cloud, that means cloud budgets plus OpenTelemetry.

TRAP: Looking for the spend in the model provider's dashboard when the traffic leaves through your own cloud: that dashboard does not see that usage.

TRY IT: Look at where the invoice for your deployment comes from, then open the dashboard you were planning to control it with; if they do not match, that dashboard is not your spend control.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage

questions.question: Ahead of an audit, Tomás has to review the customs documentation validation rules at Terminal Puerto Claro, spread across fourteen configuration files in different formats. Each file is read and summarized on its own, and afterward someone compares the summaries with each other. Tomás works with an agent and needs the main conversation to keep room for that final comparison. What should he do?

options.label: A
options.text: Paste the fourteen files into the main conversation and ask for the complete analysis in one go, so that the agent has all of them in view at the same time.
options.feedback: Having it all in view looks simplest and it fills the window with content that then competes with the analysis: ten or more files is exactly the threshold for delegating.

options.label: B
options.text: Split the work across three subagents by stage: one that reads the files, another that summarizes what was read, and a third that compares the summaries.
options.feedback: Splitting by stages of the same work is the worst split there is: each handoff loses what the previous link knew, and more is spent coordinating than advancing.

options.label: C
options.text: Work with the most capable model in the family, so that it handles the volume of the fourteen files better inside one single long conversation.
options.feedback: A more capable model does not change the fact that the content of fourteen files takes up the window: the problem is what enters the context, not who processes it afterward.

options.label: D
options.text: Delegate the reading to subagents, one per group of files, and ask each of them to return only the summary that the final comparison needs.
options.feedback: Correct: exploring ten or more files is the documented threshold for delegating, and each subagent works in its own window and returns a summary, not everything it read.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to delegate when the task requires exploring ten or more files or brings together three or more independent pieces of work, and to do it by isolatable context: each subagent works in its own window and only its final message returns to the main conversation, which grows by the summary and not by everything read. Reading fourteen independent files clears that threshold comfortably and leaves the space free for the comparison. The distinction against splitting by stages, a reader, a summarizer and a comparer, is that those are phases of the same work and not separable contexts: each handoff discards what the previous step had understood.

RULE: Delegate when there are ten or more files to explore or three or more independent pieces, and ask for the summary back, never the whole reading.

TRAP: Splitting by phases of the same work instead of by isolatable context, and paying in coordination what you thought you were saving in context.

Each file is read and summarized on its own, and afterward someone compares the summaries with each other. questions.question: The Red Vicuña Salud triage assistant classifies patient messages into three urgency levels. The monthly dashboard shows classification accuracy of 96%, p95 latency of 1.4 s and cost per message. Two facts do not appear there: two urgent messages answered as routine queries that nobody caught until the patient called back, and a summary that reproduced identifiable data of one patient in a message addressed to another clinic, which the agreements with the providers prohibit. Which two metrics are missing? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The severity of errors, measured as what share of them causes an annoyance and what share leaves an urgent case unattended.
options.feedback: Correct: the canonical example of success criteria includes the breakdown of error severity, because a global accuracy figure does not tell an innocuous error apart from one that leaves an urgency unattended.

options.label: B
options.text: Privacy preservation, measured with a binary classifier over the outputs and a set that includes cases carrying identifiable data.
options.feedback: Correct: that is the documented method for this dimension, because a classifier recognizes implicit forms of identifiable data that a fixed rule lets through.

options.label: C
options.text: Semantic consistency between answers to paraphrased messages, measured with cosine similarity over embeddings.
options.feedback: Consistency measures whether similar messages get equivalent answers, which is a real criterion, but neither of the two facts is a discrepancy between similar answers.

options.label: D
options.text: Time to first token, to find out whether the perceived wait explains the complaints coming from patients.
options.feedback: It is a valid operational metric and the dashboard already reports latency; neither of the two problems described is about waiting.

options.label: E
options.text: Deflection rate, to find out what share of the messages is resolved without a person having to step in.
options.feedback: Deflection is a business impact metric and tells you how much is resolved without a person, not whether what was resolved was resolved correctly.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that most use cases need a multidimensional evaluation, because a single aggregate figure hides exactly what matters. The canonical example of success criteria combines accuracy with a breakdown of error severity and with a safety measurement, and here that is decisive: 96% accuracy is perfectly compatible with failing systematically on the least frequent class, which is the urgent one. The second absence is privacy preservation, measured as the share of answers free of identifiable data using a binary classifier over the output, able to recognize implicit forms a fixed rule does not see. The other three metrics are real and measure other things: consistency, perceived waiting and business impact.

RULE: An aggregate number is not a criterion: alongside accuracy go the severity of errors and an explicit measurement of privacy.

TRAP: Reading high accuracy as coverage of every risk, when neither the rare class nor a data leak moves that average.

TRY IT: Take the last hundred errors from your system and sort them into annoyance and serious harm; then pass a hundred outputs through a binary classifier for identifiable data and see what percentage comes out clean.

questions.question: The catalog enrichment team at Mistral Retail works with Claude Code on its own repository. After an incident in which a skill copied from a blog wrote to the production index, the auditor requires that, from the November review on, every skill, subagent, hook and MCP server a session loads come from a source the company has reviewed. The company already publishes its plugins in an internal marketplace and manages the team's machines. What should you configure?

options.label: A
options.text: The "allowManagedHooksOnly" key in the managed settings, so that only the hooks the organization publishes are executed.
options.feedback: It closes half the problem and also blocks plugins sourced from commands, but it still lets in skills, subagents and MCP servers defined at the user or project level.

options.label: B
options.text: The "strictPluginOnlyCustomization" key in the managed settings: skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers can come only from plugins or managed policy.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the key that blocks the four forms of customization from user and project sources, which is exactly the scope the auditor is asking for.

options.label: C
options.text: The "strictKnownMarketplaces" key with an empty list in the managed settings, to block any marketplace outside the internal one.
options.feedback: With an empty list the block is total and shuts out the internal marketplace as well; and even well populated it governs where plugins come from, not whether someone defines a local skill.

options.label: D
options.text: A versioned ".claude/settings.json" file with "extraKnownMarketplaces" and "enabledPlugins", so that everyone receives the approved plugins from the marketplace.
options.feedback: That is the documented way to distribute the team's plugin set, but distributing what is approved does not prevent loading anything else, and anyone with access to the repository can edit that file.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to pick the key by what has to stay out, not by what you want to hand out. The requirement names four forms of customization, so the setting that satisfies it is the one that blocks all four from user and project sources and forces them to arrive through a plugin or through managed policy; that is exactly the description of this key, the one that turns a permissive team into a plugin-only team. The marketplace keys are complementary and govern where those plugins may come from. The distinction against the managed-hooks key is one of scope: it closes hooks and command sources, and leaves skills, subagents and MCP servers open.

RULE: Pick the key by what has to stay out: distributing the approved configuration does not stop anyone from loading the configuration that is not.

TRAP: Confusing distributing the right thing with preventing the wrong one: a versioned settings file hands out, it does not restrict.

TRY IT: With your current policy, create a skill under ".claude/skills" in a test project and see whether the session loads it; repeat with a hook declared in the project settings.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/admin-setup https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud generates the summary of each medical record three times and compares the outputs before showing it. On 7% of the notes the three summaries differ on the dose of a medication. A resident proposes keeping the version that two of the three agree on and moving ahead, because the process is already running in the 40 clinics and the clinical committee reviews the dashboard on Monday. What conclusion follows from that 7%?

options.label: A
options.text: That the model falls short on long notes and those records are worth sending to the most capable model in the family.
options.feedback: Capability helps with difficult notes, but the signal you have does not say the model falls short: it says that on those notes the statement is not supported by the source.

options.label: B
options.text: That variation between runs is expected and is fixed by pinning the sampling parameters so that the three outputs match.
options.feedback: On current models those parameters are no longer adjustable, and even if you forced three identical outputs you would have the same error repeated three times and no signal.

options.label: C
options.text: That on those notes the dose is not supported by the source text: comparing runs detects the problem, but majority voting does not correct it.
options.feedback: Correct: running the same prompt several times and comparing is documented as a way to detect hallucinations; the fix is to ground the dose in a quote and to allow saying it is not recorded.

options.label: D
options.text: That the flaw is in the comparison: three different summaries can all three be correct, and comparing them word by word does not tell that apart.
options.feedback: That is a valid observation in general, because comparing long texts is noisy, but the difference here falls on a specific value that can be checked against the note.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that running the same prompt several times and comparing the outputs is a hallucination detector: inconsistency between runs marks where the answer is not supported by the source. It is not a correction mechanism, and keeping the majority version also hides the worst case, which is when all three agree on the same error. What does fix the problem are the grounding techniques: first extract the verbatim quote where the dose appears, require every statement to be backed by a quote and retract any that is not, and give explicit permission to answer that the value is not recorded. The difference against upgrading the model is that the signal points to missing grounding and not to missing capability.

RULE: Comparing several runs tells you where to look, not what to write: inconsistency detects the hallucination and grounding in the source corrects it.

TRAP: Treating a vote between runs as a correction, when it cannot tell a right answer from an error all three repeat identically.

TRY IT: Take twenty notes where the runs disagree, ask for a verbatim extraction of the dose line before the summary, and see in how many the disagreement disappears or turns into a value that is not recorded.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations

questions.question: Complaint classification at Banco Altamar started attaching the documentation the complainant uploads: each case arrives with two or three PDFs of 20 to 60 pages, with transaction tables and screenshots. Before, only the text extracted by an in-house service was sent. Since the change, cost per complaint has multiplied by five, one in six cases exhausts the context window before reaching the page limit per request, and classification quality has not improved. The department's monthly budget is closed. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Every PDF page is turned into an image and has its text extracted too, so a dense page costs thousands of tokens.
options.feedback: Correct: a PDF is processed page by page as image plus text, on the order of 1,500 to 3,000 text tokens per page plus the image ones, which is why a dense document fills the window before the page limit.

options.label: B
options.text: The files go over the 32 MB limit per request, and that is why the largest cases fail before being processed.
options.feedback: That limit exists and does make requests fail, but it produces a request size error; it does not explain consumption five times higher with the same number of complaints.

options.label: C
options.text: The model reads tables poorly and goes back over the whole document several times until it settles the case.
options.feedback: Dense tables do complicate reading and make documents with a lot of graphic content pricier, but the model does not reread the attachment on its own: the cost is in the attachment itself.

options.label: D
options.text: What is missing is reusing the Files API file_id, which is what avoids paying for the content on every request.
options.feedback: The Files API avoids uploading the file again and is the right way to reuse large documents, but its content still counts as tokens in every request that references it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a PDF is paid for by the page and not by file size: every page is turned into an image and has its text extracted as well, so a dense page costs on the order of 1,500 to 3,000 text tokens plus the image tokens. Two or three documents of up to 60 pages per complaint reach hundreds of thousands of tokens that way, which explains both the jump in cost and the window running out before the page limit per request. The right ingestion decision is the one that already existed: extract the text and pass only what the case needs. The distinction against the Files API is between uploading a file again and paying for it again, because the file_id saves the upload and not the tokens.

RULE: A PDF is billed per page turned into image plus text, not per megabyte: with dense material, extract the text and pass only what the case needs.

TRAP: Confusing not uploading a file again with not paying for it again, and believing that a file_id reference discounts content that still enters the context in full.

TRY IT: Take a dense ten-page PDF, count its tokens with the counting endpoint by attaching it in base64 and compare that with the plain text of those same pages; multiply the difference by your monthly volume.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/pdf-support https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files

questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro committed to the hauliers a response in under 8 seconds at the 95th percentile for slot assignment, measured until the response is complete. That percentile sits at 11 seconds today and the monthly budget does not move. The response carries an eight-line justification the driver's screen never shows, and the prompt drags along instructions accumulated from three earlier versions of the service. Facundo has to recover the 3 seconds. Where should he start?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to the fastest model in the family, which is the lever with the largest effect on the total generation time of each response.
options.feedback: Changing model is one of the three latency levers and it comes afterward: applied over a bloated prompt, the lever is spent compensating for something that was surplus.

options.label: B
options.text: Clean up the inherited prompt and cut the output back to what the screen shows, leaving the model change for the case where time is still missing.
options.feedback: Correct: first you get the prompt into its best shape and then you apply the latency levers, and output that nobody reads is pure generation time.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on streaming so that the response starts arriving sooner and the driver perceives the system as far quicker during slot assignment.
options.feedback: Streaming improves time to first token and the feeling of speed. The commitment is measured on the complete response, and that number does not move.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the assignments grouped through the Batches API, which charges half and relieves the busiest window of demand at the terminal.
options.feedback: Batch costs half and is asynchronous, with a window of up to 24 hours: it is for work nobody is waiting on, not for a slot that is assigned in minutes.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is one of order: first get to a prompt that works well with no model and no format constraints, and only then apply the latency reduction strategies, which are choosing the right model, optimizing the length of prompt and output, and streaming the response. Here two excesses are already measured, they fall in that second step and they cost nothing in quality: instructions inherited from old versions, and eight lines of justification that no screen displays, which are pure generation time. The distinction against changing model is the order: optimizing over a bloated prompt moves the problem instead of removing it, and it burns the only lever left if the target is still missed at the end.

RULE: Get the prompt and the output to their useful minimum first: the latency levers are applied afterward, never over text that nobody reads.

TRAP: Jumping to the most visible lever, changing model, before removing the inherited prompt and the output that no screen displays.

TRY IT: Measure how many output tokens your system returns and how many are actually displayed on screen; trim the difference and measure the 95th percentile again before you touch the model.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing

questions.question: At Banco Altamar, the design of the claims flow proposes two subagents: one classifies the claim and another extracts the data from the associated credit file. The diagram draws an arrow between them: when the classifier detects a credit claim, it asks the extractor directly for the document it needs in order to settle the category. Nicolás reviews the design before implementation starts. What should he correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the limit on concurrent subagents, so that the two of them can be active at the same time and the exchange between them is not blocked.
options.feedback: The concurrency limit decides how many subagents run at once, not whether they can talk to each other: even with both active, no channel exists between them.

options.label: B
options.text: Mark both subagents as foreground, so that the classifier sees the tool results of the extractor while the two of them are working.
options.feedback: Foreground and background decide whether the main conversation waits and which tools each one gets, not what one subagent sees of another one's work.

options.label: C
options.text: Give both subagents a shared messaging tool so that they can exchange documents with each other without having to pass through the main thread of the flow.
options.feedback: There are architectures where several agents share a queue or an event bus, but that is a different pattern: here subagents report only to the main conversation.

options.label: D
options.text: Have the main thread receive the result of the extractor and hand it to the classifier inside its assignment, since subagents do not talk to each other.
options.feedback: Correct: all a subagent receives is the text of its assignment, so the dependency is resolved in the main thread, which carries the result of one over to the other.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a subagent starts with a fresh window, receives only the text of the assignment the main thread passes it, and returns only its final message: it does not see the parent conversation or the tool results of its peers, and there is no direct channel between subagents. That is why a dependency between two of them is resolved in the main thread, which takes the result of the first and writes it into the assignment of the second. The distinction against giving them a messaging tool is that coordination patterns where several agents share a queue or an event bus do exist, but with subagents everything one needs to know about the other has to be written into its assignment.

RULE: Subagents report to the main thread and do not talk to each other: what one needs from the other goes written into its assignment.

TRAP: Drawing an arrow between two subagents and assuming that the channel the arrow represents exists.

TRY IT: Ask one subagent to consult another subagent and watch what comes back: it has nobody to ask, because all it has is the text of the assignment you gave it.

TRY IT: Ask one subagent to consult another subagent and watch what comes back: it has nobody to ask, because all it has is the text of the assignment you gave it.

questions.question: Bastión Legal has to review the contract repository of an acquisition and deliver a single risk memo. The work order reads: {"trabajo": "due_diligence", "documentos": 1240, "tokens_totales": 21000000, "revisiones_independientes": true, "plazo_horas": 48}. Each contract is reviewed separately and afterwards clauses that contradict each other across documents have to be reconciled. The previous review ran past the deadline precisely at the synthesis stage. Which model architecture is the right one?

options.label: A
options.text: A frontier coordinator that plans, splits the 1,240 contracts among workers on a cheaper model and synthesizes the memo.
options.feedback: Correct: the work opens into genuinely independent pieces and far exceeds a single context window, which are the two documented conditions for delegating to cheaper workers.

options.label: B
options.text: A single long session on the most capable model, with compaction as the context fills, so that one thread sees the whole repository.
options.feedback: A single thread suits work that is a dependent chain fitting inside one window; twenty-one million tokens in series do not fit the deadline even if compaction keeps the thread.

options.label: C
options.text: A cheap executor that runs the whole job and consults a frontier advisor whenever a clause is beyond it.
options.feedback: The advisor fits serial work that gets hard at specific points and its cost grows with how often the executor gets stuck; here the problem is parallel volume.

options.label: D
options.text: The 1,240 contracts through the Message Batches API on the most capable model, with the memo synthesis handled by the lawyers.
options.feedback: The batch captures the discount and the reviews are independent, but it leaves the cross-document reconciliation unsolved, which is exactly where the previous review ran past the deadline.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the choice between a single model, an advisor and an orchestrator comes down to one question: whether the work opens into independent pieces or is a chain of dependent steps. Here it opens into 1,240 independent reviews and the material exceeds a context window many times over, which are the two situations where delegating to cheaper workers is documented as a gain, with a frontier model that plans, distributes and synthesizes. The advisor serves the opposite case: serial work that gets difficult at isolated points. The difference against the asynchronous batch is in the output: the deliverable is a single memo that reconciles contradictions, and that synthesis has to be done by the coordinator, not by the team by hand against the deadline.

RULE: Ask whether the work opens into independent pieces or is a chain: the first calls for orchestration with cheap workers, the second for one well-tuned model.

TRAP: Choosing the two-model scheme by its name and not by the shape of the work: the advisor is paid for stalls and the orchestrator for coordination.

TRY IT: Take ten contracts from the repository, review them with the cheap model and with the capable one, compare findings and cost per document, and use those numbers to estimate the clock and the spend of all 1,240 under each architecture.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence
