questions.question: AndesWare moved its 400 developers behind the corporate gateway last night. The smoke tests pass, but real sessions cut off as soon as anyone sends the first long prompt. The network team shows two lines from the same minute: POST /v1/messages status=403 bytes_in=48210 rule=XSS_BODY action=BLOCK, and a test against the same endpoint with 12 tokens: status=200. None of the failing requests appear in the gateway log. Where should you look first?

options.label: A
options.text: At the inspection sitting in front of the gateway: the prompt body carries code and XML-shaped tags and trips its cross-site scripting rules.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the documented pattern of a WAF in front of the gateway, and it fits both clues, that the short test passes and that the blocked request never reaches the gateway log.

options.label: B
options.text: At the provider credential the gateway uses: a rejection like this shows up when the gateway cannot authenticate against the model endpoint.
options.feedback: That failure exists, but it presents as a 401 that names the provider endpoint and does get logged by the gateway, which is exactly what is not happening here.

options.label: C
options.text: At the base URL variable on the workstations: if it does not point at the gateway, requests leave for another destination and never show up in its log.
options.feedback: That also leaves the log empty, but its symptom is a session hanging with no traffic for minutes, not an immediate rejection carrying the code of an inspection rule.

options.label: D
options.text: At the console roles: without the Claude Code role assigned, the session gets a permission rejection as soon as the developer authenticates.
options.feedback: That rejection arrives with a provider error body and affects the person from sign-in onward, not only the long prompts of the whole team at once.

questions.explanation:
The general rule in a routed deployment is to isolate by layer before touching anything: the pair that decides is which code comes back and which log recorded the request. Here the rejection is a 403 carrying the name of an inspection rule, the blocked body weighs tens of kilobytes, and the gateway never saw the request, so something cut it earlier. This is the documented case of a WAF in front of the gateway: Claude Code prompts carry source code and XML-shaped tags that trigger cross-site scripting rules on the body, so real sessions get 403 while short test requests pass. The distinction against the gateway credential is the code and the log: a credential problem is a 401 that the gateway does record.

RULE: In a routed deployment, the error code and the log that did record the request tell you which layer cut it before you touch any credential.

TRAP: Assuming a rejection in a new deployment is authentication, when the one that never appears in the gateway log was cut before it arrived.

TRY IT: Send one short request and one carrying a code file of several tens of kilobytes through your gateway, and compare the response code and whether each one was recorded in the gateway log.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-rollout

questions.question: The production readiness criterion for Zafiro Seguros claim triage is written like this: accuracy >= 99.9% on claim classification; set: 4,000 cases labeled by two adjusters; method: exact match. Four months later the team is still between 96% and 97%, adds rules to the prompt on every iteration and cannot move. Reviewing the set, Tomás finds that in one out of every twelve cases the two adjusters had chosen different categories and the label was settled by taking the one from the more senior adjuster. What is the underlying flaw in the criterion?

options.label: A
options.text: The set is too small: with 4,000 cases you cannot tell 99.9% from 99% and it has to be enlarged before deciding anything.
options.feedback: More cases narrow the interval of the measurement, but they do not fix the label: if the reference disagrees with itself, measuring more cases does not make it more accurate.

options.label: B
options.text: The target is not achievable against that set: if two adjusters disagree on one case in twelve, the label cannot sustain 99.9%.
options.feedback: Correct: an achievable criterion rests on a baseline, on earlier experiments or on expert knowledge, and a reference the adjusters do not agree on cannot sustain a three-nines target.

options.label: C
options.text: What is missing is a statement of how each case is scored, which is why measurements from different weeks do not end up comparable.
options.feedback: Declaring the scoring method is essential and is a frequent omission, but the criterion already says exact match: that is not what has the team stuck.

options.label: D
options.text: The criterion measures the task but not the impact: it should add the referral rate to an adjuster and the cost per claim classified.
options.feedback: Adding impact metrics is a real improvement and almost every use case needs multidimensional evaluation, but it does not explain why the team cannot get past 97%.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a success criterion has to be specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and what makes it achievable is a baseline, earlier experiments or expert knowledge, never a round number picked by eye. Here the reference the system is measured against carries expert disagreement on one case in twelve, so on that one case in twelve the label is not a truth but the preference of the more senior adjuster: chasing 99.9% forces the system to reproduce that person's criterion exactly where the experts do not agree, and in that band the measurement no longer separates accuracy from imitation of the labeler. The guidance on designing sets already warns that ambiguous cases, the ones where people themselves reach no consensus, are handled separately. The difference against enlarging the set is that size changes the precision of the measurement, not the ceiling the label imposes.

RULE: Set the target against what the reference can sustain: where experts disagree, the label stops being truth and the target measures obedience to a labeler.

TRAP: Treating the human label as perfect truth and reading the gap that is left as a failure of the system.

TRY IT: Take a hundred cases from your set, have two people label them separately and measure the percentage on which they agree: the part where they do not agree is the band of your set where no accuracy target means anything.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom is about to route all the traffic of the self-service assistant in its mobile app through a corporate gateway. The assistant is already in production with a 30-second commitment for first response. Renata is drafting the handover document for the operations team, which has signaled three intentions: translate the provider's error messages into the internal format, inspect the body of the responses at the WAF, and allow only the headers it knows today. What must the document establish?

options.label: A
options.text: That the provider's errors are returned unmodified and that the responses pass through as they arrive, because the client's automatic recovery depends on both things.
options.feedback: Correct: automatic recovery recognizes the error by its original text, and holding the response back to inspect it cancels the progressive streaming the SLA needs.

options.label: B
options.text: That the errors are translated into the internal format and their equivalences documented, so that operations can correlate them with the rest of the support platform.
options.feedback: Normalizing errors is good practice on a platform of your own and here it breaks automatic recovery, which decides whether to retry from the text the provider returns.

options.label: C
options.text: That the WAF inspect the complete body of every response before delivering it, and that the time that inspection adds to the committed total be documented.
options.feedback: Inspecting the body forces the whole response to be held back before delivery, which cancels progressive streaming and adds seconds where 30 are committed.

options.label: D
options.text: That the list of allowed headers be reviewed every quarter, so as to take in the new ones that appear in the later versions of the mobile client.
options.feedback: A list reviewed every quarter arrives late: when the client ships a new header, requests fail until the next review, and that is why headers are forwarded as they are.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the handover document for an integration writes down what the other side has to guarantee, not what would be tidy. For a gateway in front of the API, that list includes streaming the response as it arrives instead of holding it back, forwarding headers and body without altering them, returning the provider's errors unmodified, because the client's automatic recovery leans on the text of the error, and exempting that route from body inspection. The distinction against translating the errors is that these are correct practices on a platform of your own which here break a mechanism of the client: the gateway is a transparent segment, not the place to improve the format.

RULE: A gateway is a transparent segment: stream without holding back, forward the headers as they are, and return the provider's errors with their original text.

TRAP: Applying the good practices of your own platform to a transparent segment, and breaking the client's automatic recovery with them.

TRY IT: Trigger a rate limit error through your gateway and compare the body it returns with the one the provider returns directly: if they differ, you have already broken automatic recovery.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-rollout

questions.question: At Minera Nevado, the permit compliance assistant cross-checks up to thirty documents per file: the permit, its addenda, the monitoring reports and the authority's records. Joaquín proposes that it run in a single autonomous pass of up to sixty turns and hand over the conclusion, because the site only has twenty-minute connectivity windows. The resulting report is signed by the safety manager, who is legally answerable for it. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Move to the most capable model in the family for the whole pass, because across sixty chained turns the margin of error depends mostly on reasoning capability.
options.feedback: A more capable model improves each step, but it does not change that step fifty rests on what step ten took as true without anyone looking at it.

options.label: B
options.text: Shorten the pass and put a human checkpoint before the conclusion is written, because each step rests on the ones before it and error accumulates.
options.feedback: Correct: autonomy brings cost and compounding errors, and the documented design is to stop at checkpoints, above all when somebody signs the result.

options.label: C
options.text: Load all thirty full documents into a single request so that the model has the whole context and does not depend on what it summarized in earlier turns.
options.feedback: It avoids one kind of loss and adds another: context is a finite resource with diminishing returns, and retrieval precision drops as the window fills.

options.label: D
options.text: Split the thirty documents across parallel subagents and merge the conclusions, so that the pass fits whole inside the connectivity window.
options.feedback: Parallelism works when the subtasks are independent; here each cross-check depends on what the previous one established, so merging partial conclusions does not rebuild the reasoning.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that autonomy has a documented price: more cost and the possibility of compounding errors, because each turn works on what the agent itself concluded earlier. That is why the recommended design includes stopping conditions and pauses for human intervention at checkpoints, and the test for when one is needed comes from the use: here a person with legal responsibility signs the result, so the checkpoint goes before the conclusion is written, not after. The twenty-minute window pushes toward fewer round trips, but a checkpoint is one more exchange and a wrong conclusion is a signed document. The distinction against parallel subagents is the dependency between steps.

RULE: The more turns it runs alone, the more the agent leans on its own errors: put the checkpoint before the conclusion is written.

TRAP: Confusing autonomy with efficiency: stretching the pass does not reduce the error, it compounds it.

TRY IT: Take a long run of your agent and mark in the trace the first step whose conclusion was already wrong; count how many later steps used it as fact and where you would have placed the checkpoint.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

questions.question: The itinerary agent at Siete Lagos Viajes books against three wholesalers through their MCP servers. In high season, at ten times the usual volume, the agent abandons the booking and tells the traveler the provider is unavailable instead of retrying with the corrected date; turns per booking have doubled, and Malena's team handles those cases by hand under a two-hour response commitment. One wholesaler's log repeats this response: {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 42, "error": {"code": -32602, "message": "Invalid params"}}. Which two things explain the agent's behavior? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The connection to remote MCP servers times out at 30 seconds by default, and in high season that time is exceeded.
options.feedback: That timeout exists and every remote server is a real dependency of the turn, but a cut for time does not return an invalid parameters error: what repeats here is an input validation.

options.label: B
options.text: The input validation comes back as a protocol error instead of coming back in the tool result with isError true.
options.feedback: Correct: the specification asks for input validations to be returned as execution errors, because protocol errors describe request problems the model can hardly fix and clients do not always pass them on.

options.label: C
options.text: Availability should be exposed as a resource and not as a tool, so the application loads it without the model deciding.
options.feedback: Telling tools from resources is a real design decision, between what the model chooses to invoke and what the application loads. But booking here is an action, and the failure happens while executing it, not while choosing it.

options.label: D
options.text: Each wholesaler is better delegated to a subagent, to isolate each provider's context and be able to retry in parallel.
options.feedback: Delegating between agents costs on the order of 3 to 10 times more tokens and is justified by context isolation, parallelism or specialization. Retrying a call that failed on a badly formed date is none of those.

options.label: E
options.text: The message does not say which parameter failed or what format is expected, so nothing is left to correct and retry with.
options.feedback: Correct: the guidance asks for instructive errors that say what went wrong and what to try next, with the right format and an example; without that the model has nothing to correct itself with even when the error reaches it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a tool error carries two independent decisions: which channel it comes back on and what it says. The specification separates protocol errors, for request problems such as an unknown tool or a malformed message, from execution errors, which come back in the result with isError true and exist precisely so the model can correct itself and retry; input validations belong to the second group. This wholesaler uses the first, so the agent is left with nothing to act on and closes the case. The content fails just as hard, because a message that only says the parameters are invalid does not say which format to use. The distinction against the timeout is direct: a cut for time does not return a parameter error.

RULE: What the model can fix comes back in the result with isError true and with instructions; what it cannot fix comes back as a protocol error.

TRAP: Treating an input validation as a protocol failure, and leaving the agent without the text that would let it correct the parameter and retry.

TRY IT: Trigger a validation error in your own server and look at what the model receives; then return it in the result with isError true, naming the field, the expected format and an example, and count how many retries succeed.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

questions.question: The maintenance-order MCP server at Pehuén Energía serves four clients: the control-room assistant, two internal applications and one contractor. The server already validates that each token was issued for it, and it checks the permissions of every operation before running it. Reviewing the authorization flow, Bruno finds that the metadata publishes all nine scopes that exist, that the four clients request them all in the first authorization, and that the initial challenge always returns the full catalog. The regulator's audit, six weeks away, assesses the blast radius of a leaked credential. Which finding has to be fixed?

options.label: A
options.text: The tokens last too long: their lifetime has to be shortened and refresh tokens rotated on every client use.
options.feedback: Short-lived tokens and rotating refresh tokens are recommendations of the specification and they shorten the window of a leaked credential, but they do not change what that credential can do while it is valid.

options.label: B
options.text: The metadata publishes all nine scopes and clients ask for them together: publish the minimum and escalate the rest.
options.feedback: Correct: the published set is meant to be the minimum needed for basic functionality, and the rest is requested in steps when an operation needs it.

options.label: C
options.text: Permission checks per operation are missing on the server, instead of trusting the scopes that the token declares.
options.feedback: Taking the declared scopes as sufficient without authorization logic of your own is a frequent and serious mistake, but this server already checks every operation: that control is in place.

options.label: D
options.text: The server answers 403 when a permission is missing and should answer 401, so that the client repeats the authorization.
options.feedback: It is the other way around: a 401 signals a missing or invalid token, and a 403 with insufficient scope is exactly the signal that triggers step-up authorization to ask for the missing permission.

questions.explanation:
The general rule of least privilege in MCP is that a token should be able to do what the task needs now, not everything the server knows how to do. The specification describes the published scope set as the minimum needed for basic functionality and provides for requesting the rest incrementally: when an operation needs a permission the token does not carry, the server answers 403 with an insufficient scope challenge and the client steps up. Publishing all nine and granting them together in the first authorization turns any leaked credential into the largest possible incident, which is exactly what the audit measures. The distinction against checking permissions per operation is that the two controls add up: one prevents running what should not run, the other reduces what the credential can ask for.

RULE: Publish the minimum scopes needed to work and grant the rest in steps: the full catalog in the first authorization is the blast radius of every credential.

TRAP: Treating the published scope set as a menu the client can order whole, when it is meant as the minimum for basic functionality.

TRY IT: Open your MCP server's protected resource metadata, count how many scopes it publishes and mark which ones a client needs for its first useful operation; if there are extras, move them behind an insufficient scope challenge.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/security_best_practices https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization

questions.question: Yaguareté Logística is evaluating a multi-agent architecture for tariff classification: a coordinator distributes the work among subagents that query the customs systems of four countries and return their finding. Before approving it, the technical committee goes over what this architecture offers and what it costs. Which of the following statements about it is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Parallelism between subagents lowers the total cost in tokens, because each one explores a smaller portion of the problem.
options.feedback: Correct as the false statement: splitting the work multiplies consumption, because each subagent keeps its own window and adds coordination on top.

options.label: B
options.text: Each subagent works in its own context window, and only its final message returns to the coordinator, not everything it read.
options.feedback: True: context isolation with a summary returned is precisely the benefit that is sought when delegating to a subagent.

options.label: C
options.text: Each subagent follows its own exploration path, which reduces path dependence and allows for independent investigations.
options.feedback: True: separate tools, prompts and trajectories are what keep a subagent from dragging along the path bias of the coordinator.

options.label: D
options.text: A parallel dispatch that is too wide can run into the rate limits, so it is better to break it up into smaller batches.
options.feedback: True: very wide fan-outs of subagents run into rate limits, and the documented recommendation is to split the work into batches.

questions.explanation:
The false statement is the one about saving. Splitting the work among subagents does not reduce token consumption; it multiplies it several times over a single well-designed agent, because each subagent keeps its own window, repeats instructions and adds the cost of coordinating and synthesizing. What parallelism does buy is breadth of exploration and context isolation, which is why the architecture is justified when the value of the task covers the bill. The other three statements are correct: the subagent returns only its final message, each independent trajectory reduces path dependence, and a parallel dispatch that is too wide runs into the rate limits.

RULE: Parallelism between agents buys breadth, not savings: multi-agent costs several times what one well-designed agent costs.

TRAP: Confusing splitting the work with splitting the cost, when each subagent pays for its own window and its own coordination.

TRY IT: Run the same task with a single agent and with a coordinator plus three subagents, and compare the total tokens of the two runs before you decide the architecture.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

questions.question: Colibrí Pay runs one support agent for card disputes. A single step of that flow, the transaction investigation, reads up to nine months of movements and pushes the conversation past the context limit about twice a day; every other step is short. Volume has grown threefold this year and Mateo, the platform lead, has a monthly token budget he cannot exceed. He wants to move the investigation into a delegated agent. Which TWO decisions keep that split inside the budget? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Launch one delegated agent per month of history in parallel, so the investigation finishes in the time of the slowest branch.
options.feedback: Fan-out is real and it does cut wall-clock time on independent work, but here it multiplies tokens across months that mostly hold nothing, and wide dispatches run into rate limits.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the whole dispute flow into the delegated agent, so that every step of it benefits from a separate context window.
options.feedback: A separate window does protect the main conversation, yet the short steps never needed it and the overhead of delegation is then paid on every single request.

options.label: C
options.text: Delegate only the investigation, whose context can be isolated, and have it return a distilled summary rather than the movements it read.
options.feedback: Correct: work should be split only where context can be truly isolated, and the parent conversation then grows by the summary instead of the whole transcript.

options.label: D
options.text: Let the delegated agents exchange partial findings with each other, so the investigation converges before the customer is answered.
options.feedback: Cross-talk sounds efficient, but delegated agents report back to the conversation that spawned them and cannot talk to one another, so it would route through the parent anyway.

options.label: E
options.text: Cap each delegated run with a maximum number of turns and a spend ceiling, so an investigation that does not converge stops on its own.
options.feedback: Correct: stopping conditions are the documented control for a loop whose number of steps is not known in advance, and they bound the worst case against the budget.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that multi-agent designs buy isolation at a token multiplier of three to ten times a single agent, so the split has to be justified by context that can genuinely be isolated and bounded once it runs. The investigation is the only step whose context overflows, and what returns to the parent is a distilled summary rather than nine months of movements, which is exactly the shape the guidance describes. A run whose step count is unknown also needs an explicit stopping condition, because a stateful agent that cannot converge keeps spending. The distinction against fanning out by month is that slicing the same dependent task across agents isolates nothing: each branch still needs the others to answer, and the tokens are spent several times over.

RULE: Split where the context can be isolated and bound every delegated run: delegation pays only when the parent inherits a summary instead of a transcript.

TRAP: Confusing delegation with parallelism, so one agent per slice of data multiplies tokens without isolating any context at all.

TRY IT: Take one real dispute, count the tokens the investigation adds to the main conversation today, and compare that with the length of the summary you would be willing to accept back from a delegated agent.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

questions.question: AndesWare runs an internal code-review agent for its 400 developers. Every request sends, in a single user turn, the pull request diff, the company coding standard, three past reviews used as examples and the reviewer's question, concatenated as plain text with capitalized headings. Two failures repeat: the agent sometimes reviews the coding standard as if it were submitted code, and sometimes returns one of the three past reviews almost verbatim. Every bad review is re-run by hand, and each squad has a fixed monthly token budget that a second call per review would break. Tomás has one prompt change to spend. Which change should he make?

options.label: A
options.text: Split the work into two calls, one that summarizes the diff and a second that writes the review against the standard.
options.feedback: Prompt chaining is a real technique and each call would be an easier task, but it doubles the tokens billed per review and the squad budget has no room for a second pass.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a sentence telling the agent never to review the coding standard and never to copy an example verbatim from the block of past reviews.
options.feedback: Prohibitions are the weakest form of instruction, and the guidance is to say what the output should be instead; the four materials would still arrive as one undifferentiated block.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the agent to the most capable model in the family, which separates the four kinds of material without any change to the prompt.
options.feedback: A stronger model does read ambiguous input better, but the ambiguity is in your prompt, and you would pay more on every review for a defect a pair of tags removes.

options.label: D
options.text: Wrap each part in named XML tags, one for the diff, one for the standard and one for the examples, and put the question last.
options.feedback: Correct: XML tags tell the model which block is which, examples belong inside example tags so they read as illustrations, and the edit costs no extra call.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that structure inside the prompt is what tells the model which part of the input is which. Structuring prompts with XML tags is listed among the general prompting principles precisely for prompts that carry several kinds of material at once, and the examples convention wraps them in example tags so they read as illustrations rather than as content to act on. Tagging is one edit inside one call, so the squad budget is untouched. The distinction against chaining is that decomposition buys accuracy by making each call an easier task, which the budget cannot pay for, while the failure here is not difficulty but ambiguity about what each block is.

RULE: When one turn carries several kinds of material, name each one with a tag: the model cannot separate a diff from a standard you pasted as one block.

TRAP: Treating a prompt-structure defect as a capability gap, and buying a stronger model or a second call to do the work a pair of tags does.

TRY IT: Take a prompt of yours that pastes two kinds of material together, tag each block, and run both versions over ten inputs counting how often the model acts on the wrong block.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

questions.question: Minera Nevado is indexing 400,000 technical documents for search. About 9,000 of them are community-consultation records that carry names, national identity numbers and home addresses, and the company reports into a European Union parent, so GDPR applies to that material. Valentina, the solutions architect, has the Commercial Terms accepted and a working assistant, and the group data protection officer has given her eight weeks to hand over the compliance file before 1,200 field users get access. What should she do first so the processing of that personal data is defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: Record a lawful basis under Article 6 for that specific purpose and strip from the indexed text the personal fields that engineers never search on.
options.feedback: Correct: the controller has to be able to demonstrate a basis and a purpose, and to keep the data adequate, relevant and limited to what that purpose needs.

options.label: B
options.text: Rely on the Data Processing Addendum with its Standard Contractual Clauses, which is already incorporated once the Commercial Terms have been accepted.
options.feedback: The addendum really is incorporated without a separate signature, but it governs the processor relationship. It never supplies the controller's own lawful basis.

options.label: C
options.text: Collect explicit consent from every individual named in the consultation records before any of that material is indexed for search.
options.feedback: Consent is one of the six lawful bases, not the default one, and it has to be freely given and specific, which it rarely is for records gathered years earlier.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace each name and identity number with a reversible code kept in a separate key store, so the indexed corpus falls outside the regulation.
options.feedback: That is pseudonymization, a safeguard that reduces linkability without cutting it. The data can still be attributed with the additional information, so it stays personal data.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a controller must be able to demonstrate a lawful basis and a specific purpose for every processing operation, and must limit the data to what that purpose actually needs. Anthropic acts as processor here and its addendum governs that relationship, but a processor contract never answers the controller's own question of why this material may be processed at all. Consent is one of six bases rather than the default one, and it is rarely workable for records collected for a different purpose years earlier. The distinction against replacing names with a reversible code is that pseudonymization reduces linkability without aiming to cut it, so the corpus stays personal data and stays in scope.

RULE: A processor contract is not a lawful basis: you still choose the basis, name the purpose, and index only the fields that purpose needs.

TRAP: Treating the provider's addendum as if it answered the controller's own question of why this personal data may be processed in the first place.

TRY IT: Take one document type your system indexes, write the purpose in one sentence, name the Article 6 basis it rests on, then list the fields nobody ever queries: those are the ones to drop before indexing.

SOURCE: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32016R0679 https://www.edpb.europa.eu/topics/ai-and-technology/anonymisation-pseudonymisation_en https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/7996862-how-do-i-view-and-sign-your-data-processing-addendum-dpa

questions.question: Agencia Nacional de Ingresos runs a taxpayer-assistance agent that aggregates six internal MCP servers, 140 tool definitions in total. Public procurement has frozen the platform budget until next year, so Mateo enabled compaction to cut tokens per interaction without buying anything new. Conversations now survive much longer, but every fresh context window still opens with roughly 34,000 input tokens billed before the agent does any work, and spend per interaction has barely moved. What explains that result?

options.label: A
options.text: Compaction only fires once the conversation passes its trigger, so lowering that threshold is what will bring the opening cost down.
options.feedback: The trigger is configurable and does decide when summarization happens, but it only governs conversation content, never what is sent ahead of the conversation.

options.label: B
options.text: The summary keeps the oldest tool results, so context editing has to be enabled alongside it to clear them out of the window.
options.feedback: Context editing really does clear the oldest tool results, which is the right fix for result bloat, but results accumulate during a session and are not what a window opens with.

options.label: C
options.text: Tool definitions travel in the tools block of every request, which compaction never rewrites, so only deferring them lowers that floor.
options.feedback: Correct: compaction summarizes conversation content and restarts from the summary, while the definitions are re-sent ahead of it on every call.

options.label: D
options.text: The six servers each reload their instructions on reconnect, so merging them into one server removes the duplicated preamble.
options.feedback: Server instructions do cost tokens and are worth trimming, but merging servers leaves the same 140 definitions in context, so the floor stays where it is.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that progressive discovery prevents context from growing, while compaction and context editing recover a context that already grew. Compaction summarizes the conversation and reinitiates the window from that summary, so everything sent ahead of the conversation is untouched by it, and tool definitions are the first thing in that order. With 140 definitions the opening cost is a floor paid on every request, which is exactly the symptom Mateo measured. Tool search is the lever that matches it: definitions leave the context window and only the few tools a request needs are loaded, which is where the reported saving of more than eighty-five percent comes from. The distinction against lowering the compaction trigger is that the trigger changes when summarization happens, not what a window starts with.

RULE: Compaction shrinks what a conversation accumulated; only deferral shrinks what every request starts with.

TRAP: Treating compaction as a discovery mechanism, when it rewrites conversation content and never the tool definitions sent ahead of it.

TRY IT: Record the input tokens billed on the first request of a session, turn on the tool search tool while leaving your three most-used tools loaded, and compare that same first-request figure.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool

questions.question: Colibrí Pay's compliance agent helps analysts review flagged transfers. Its tool block is {"tools": [{"type": "web_fetch_20250910", "name": "web_fetch"}, {"name": "get_account_ledger"}, {"name": "get_kyc_file"}]}. Analysts paste customer-supplied statements and follow the links inside them, so the fetch target cannot be reduced to a fixed list of sites. The regulator supervising the fintech requires that customer identity data never reach systems the company does not control, and the audit is in three weeks. Which change should Valentina make?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep one agent and restrict the fetch tool with an allowed_domains list of the regulator bulletin sites analysts cite most often.
options.feedback: Domain filtering is a real control, but an allowlist blocks precisely the customer-supplied links the review depends on, and the identity data stays in the same context either way.

options.label: B
options.text: Move fetching and summarizing to a separate agent thread that carries the fetch tool but no ledger or file tools, and return its summary.
options.feedback: Correct: each agent runs in its own context-isolated thread and tools are not shared between them, so untrusted page content never sits beside customer identity data.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the fetch tool with the web search tool, whose citations are always enabled, so that every claim the agent makes points at a source.
options.feedback: Citations are indeed always on for web search and that helps attribution, but the retrieved content still lands in the same context window as the customer file.

options.label: D
options.text: Wrap the fetch behind an internal MCP server so every outbound URL is logged and leaves through infrastructure the company controls.
options.feedback: Logging is worth having and MCP standardizes the integration, but the fetched page still enters the same context; MCP does not isolate one capability from another.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the integration mechanism has to match the trust boundary, not only the capability. The documentation is explicit that enabling the fetch tool where the model processes untrusted input alongside sensitive data poses data exfiltration risks, and the mitigation offered is to keep it to trusted environments or non-sensitive data. Splitting the work across agent threads implements that separation in the architecture: threads share the sandbox and credentials but not context, tools or MCP servers, so the thread that reads customer-supplied pages has no ledger or identity tool to reach for. The distinction against the domain allowlist is the stated requirement itself: the review depends on following links the customer supplied, which an allowlist can only block.

RULE: Untrusted content and regulated data belong in different contexts: isolate them by thread, not by an allowlist the task cannot live with.

TRAP: Treating a domain filter or an audit log as an isolation boundary, when both leave the untrusted page in the same context as the customer data.

TRY IT: List the tools of your most exposed agent, mark the ones that read content you do not control, and check whether any of them shares a context with a tool that reads regulated data.

questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro is deciding how its berth-planning assistant should call the two tools that return stowage plans, several thousand lines each. The integration team wants programmatic tool calling, so those results never enter the context window. The desk team wants every answer returned in a fixed JSON shape with structured outputs, because the coordination screen the shipping lines signed off renders fields, not prose, and the coordination window lasts minutes. Rodrigo has to close the argument with a decision record for both teams. What should that record say?

options.label: A
options.text: The two cannot be enabled on the same call, the signed screen contract decides for the fixed shape, and what the rejected option would have saved.
options.feedback: Correct: a record carries one decision, the requirement that settles it and the consequence of the alternative that was dropped, which here is the result tokens that will now stay in the context.

options.label: B
options.text: Both can be enabled on the same call as long as the schema stays shallow, so each team keeps the behavior it asked for on this service.
options.feedback: A shallow schema does keep the grammar cheap to compile, and it changes nothing about the exclusion: the two features are documented as incompatible on one call.

options.label: C
options.text: The fixed shape is chosen, with the rejected option left out so the page stays short enough for the coordination committee to read in one sitting.
options.feedback: Brevity is worth protecting, and a record that names no discarded alternative documents a preference rather than a decision anyone can revisit.

options.label: D
options.text: The decision belongs to whoever writes the integration, so the record states the requirement and leaves the mechanism to be settled at build time by that team.
options.feedback: Handing the mechanism to build time reads as delegation, and here the mechanism is the decision: only one of the two can run, so the choice cannot be deferred.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for communicating an architectural decision is that a record captures one decision, the requirement that makes it significant, the alternatives discarded and the consequence accepted. The technical fact underneath is an exclusion rather than a preference: programmatic tool calling is documented as incompatible with structured outputs and with forced tool choice, so no configuration gives both teams what they asked for on the same call. The requirement that settles it is contractual, because the screen the shipping lines signed renders fields. What the record still owes the integration team is the consequence: the stowage plans now land in the context window, so their size has to be attacked inside the tools, with filtering and pagination, rather than by the mechanism that was ruled out. The distinction against deferring to build time is that there is nothing left to design, only a trade to record.

RULE: When two options exclude each other, record the exclusion, the requirement that decides and the cost of what you dropped: that is a decision, not a preference.

TRAP: Treating two optimizations as additive when the documentation lists them as mutually exclusive, and calling the choice an implementation detail.

TRY IT: List the features enabled on your busiest call, check each one against the documented compatibility notes of the others, and write two lines naming which requirement would decide if two of them collide.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/programmatic-tool-calling https://adr.github.io/

questions.question: Pehuén Energía books maintenance windows from its control-room assistant through an internal MCP server. Regulation requires 72 hours of notice and the server enforces that rule. Operators report that when they ask for a window inside the notice period, the assistant answers that the scheduling tool is unavailable and stops, instead of offering the first legal date; the same request typed into the scheduling console returns a clear message naming the rule. Traces show one tool call and no retry. With one window a week available, where should Joaquín look first?

options.label: A
options.text: At the tool description, which is probably too short for the model to build a valid request on its first attempt.
options.feedback: Thin descriptions do produce invalid inputs and the guidance asks for at least three or four sentences, but here the call reaches the server and the rule is evaluated.

options.label: B
options.text: At the connection timeout, since an MCP server that does not answer within thirty seconds is surfaced to the model as unavailable.
options.feedback: The default connect timeout is real and worth checking, but it would fail whatever date was asked for, not only requests inside the notice period.

options.label: C
options.text: At the transport, because a server launched over stdio writes its diagnostics to standard error, where the model never sees them.
options.feedback: Stdio servers do log to standard error and that stream is not protocol traffic, yet a refused business rule is a result the server chose to return, not a log line.

options.label: D
options.text: At how the server reports the violation: a business rule refused at the protocol level leaves the model nothing it can act on.
options.feedback: Correct: execution failures belong in the tool result with isError set to true and actionable text, so the model can retry with a date that satisfies the rule.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that MCP separates two kinds of failure on purpose. Protocol errors describe problems the model cannot fix, such as an unknown tool or a malformed call, while execution errors are reported inside the result with isError set to true and carry feedback the model can use to self-correct. A date rejected by a notice rule is business logic, so answering with a JSON-RPC error removes the only thing that would have helped: the reason and the first acceptable date. Clients are expected to hand execution errors to the model precisely so this recovery can happen. The distinction against the timeout reading is the shape of the symptom: the failure appears only when the requested date breaks the rule, which means the server evaluated it and then replied in the wrong channel.

RULE: Failures the model can fix belong in the tool result with actionable text; only problems finding or forming the call belong at the protocol level.

TRAP: Reading unavailable as a transport fault, when the server answered normally and reported a business rule where the model cannot see it.

TRY IT: Force a business-rule violation on one of your own tools and check whether the refusal arrives as a protocol error or as a result with is_error true and a sentence saying what to try next.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

questions.question: Banco Altamar extracts fields from the documentation borrowers submit with a credit application: payslips, tax statements, property deeds and eleven other document types, each with its own rules. Today all fourteen rule sets travel in one system prompt, the prompt keeps growing with every new product, and accuracy on the rarer document types has been falling. Internal audit also asks the team to show which rules were applied to a given file. Which TWO changes should the team make? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the single prompt and add an instruction telling the model to apply only the rules for the document type in hand.
options.feedback: Instructions do steer behavior, but every rule set still occupies the context window on every request, and recall degrades as that window fills: the problem is what is loaded, not what is said.

options.label: B
options.text: Split the pipeline into fixed steps with a programmatic check between them, so the document type is settled and logged before extraction runs.
options.feedback: Correct: fixed subtasks with a gate between them is the documented shape when the steps are known, and each step is a separate call you can log, evaluate or branch on, which is what audit is asking for.

options.label: C
options.text: Spawn one delegated agent per field on the form, so that each field is extracted inside its own clean context window.
options.feedback: A delegated agent per field pays the overhead of delegation on tasks far too small to justify it, and it does nothing about the rule sets traveling in every prompt.

options.label: D
options.text: Move each document type's rules into a capability loaded on demand, leaving only its short description in context until it is triggered.
options.feedback: Correct: progressive disclosure keeps roughly a line of metadata in context and loads the full instructions only when the document type triggers them, so the prompt stops growing with the catalog.

options.label: E
options.text: Split the work by phase, with one agent reading, one validating and one filing, so that each phase carries its own prompt.
options.feedback: Sequential phases of the same work are the documented bad boundary: every handoff re-explains the case and coordination starts costing more than the work it coordinates.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to decompose the context before decomposing the work, because context is a finite resource with diminishing returns and a prompt that carries every rule set degrades on the cases it rarely sees. Loading a document type's rules only when that type is present is progressive disclosure: metadata stays resident, the full instructions arrive on trigger, and nothing is paid for the twelve types that are not in the file. Settling and logging the type in a separate gated step gives the auditor the record of which rules applied. The distinction against splitting by phase is that reading, validating and filing are stages of one case: each handoff re-explains it, which is the boundary the guidance warns against.

RULE: Decompose the context before the work: load the rules the case triggers, and split into fixed steps you can gate and log.

TRAP: Treating a growing prompt as a wording problem, so more instructions go into a context already too full for the model to attend to all of it.

TRY IT: Count the tokens your prompt spends on rule sets the current document type does not use, move one type behind an on-demand load, and measure what the request costs afterwards.

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros added a policy-clause lookup step to the agent that answers brokers. The step adds about 900 milliseconds and a call to every reply, and the steering committee keeps only changes that show a measured gain. The eval suite runs each case in two arms, with the lookup and without it, and reports the difference between them; the report showed plus 0.41 and the change was approved on that number. Six weeks later the brokers' resolution rate is unchanged and the supervisors who read replies see no improvement. Each case carries two graders: one checks that the reply names the applicable clause, one checks that the lookup step was called. Where should Ximena look first?

options.label: A
options.text: At the number of runs per case, because two runs of a non-deterministic agent tell you very little and the difference may be noise around zero.
options.feedback: Repeating each case is how you separate a result from variance, and two runs is thin; noise, though, would not have produced a difference this large and this stable.

options.label: B
options.text: At the judge model, because a small judge can mark a correct reply wrong when its wording differs from the rubric and depress one of the arms.
options.feedback: A weak judge penalizing formatting is a documented cause of suspicious verdicts, but it would depress both arms equally here, since both are scored by the same graders.

options.label: C
options.text: At the case mix, because a suite written before the current clause catalog can show a gain offline that today's broker questions no longer produce.
options.feedback: Stale cases are worth auditing and would explain a gain that does not transfer; they would not explain a difference that the suite itself manufactures.

options.label: D
options.text: At how the second grader scores the control arm: only a run with the lookup can pass it, which drags that arm toward zero and inflates the gap.
options.feedback: Correct: a grader that only the treatment arm can satisfy has to be excluded from scoring in both arms, or it pushes the control toward zero and the difference stops measuring the outcome.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an ablation difference is only meaningful when both arms are scored on graders that either arm could pass. A grader asserting that the new step was called is a check on the mechanism, not on the answer, and counting it in both arms pushes the arm without the step toward zero and inflates the difference. What the committee bought was the reply quality, which the first grader measures and which apparently did not move. The distinction against the noise explanation is that re-running more trials would tighten an estimate of a number that is measuring the wrong thing.

RULE: Score both arms only on graders that both arms could pass; a grader that asserts the new step ran measures the change, not the outcome.

TRAP: Reading a difference produced by a grader the control arm could never satisfy as if it were the value the change added.

TRY IT: Take your last comparison report, list every grader, mark the ones the control arm could not pass even in principle, and recompute the difference without them.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals

options.feedback: True and documented: past that range the model's ability to pick the right tool falls, which is one of the signals for turning tool search on.

options.label: B
options.text: Turning tool search on is advised once definitions pass about 10,000 tokens or when several MCP servers are aggregated.
options.feedback: True: ten or more tools, definitions above ten thousand tokens, falling selection accuracy or an aggregated catalog each justify deferral.

options.label: C
options.text: Programmatic tool calling attacks a different kind of bloat, because results from those calls stay out of the context window.
options.feedback: True: it shrinks tool results rather than tool definitions, which is why the two levers answer different symptoms.

options.label: D
options.text: Marking a tool as deferred also drops it from the request payload, so the tools array carries only what is loaded.
options.feedback: This is the statement that fails: every definition still travels in the tools array on every request because the API needs it server-side; deferral removes it from Claude's context only.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that deferred loading changes what Claude reads, not what you send. The thresholds are worth memorizing: under ten tools that are used on every request, load everything up front, since discovery costs a round trip; from about ten tools, or once definitions pass ten thousand tokens, or when you aggregate servers, defer them and keep the three to five most used tools loaded. What deferral buys is context, and the documented effect is that only the few tools a request needs are loaded. What it does not buy is a smaller request body, and a team that plans a payload budget around that assumption will be surprised when the wire format does not change.

RULE: Deferral takes tool definitions out of the context window, not out of the request: the payload keeps its size.

TRAP: Reading the field "defer_loading" as if it removed the definition from the request, when it only removes it from what the model reads.

TRY IT: Measure your current definitions with the token-counting endpoint, enable tool search, and compare the counted request against the input tokens the response reports.

questions.question: Bastión Legal drafts client memos with an assistant that searches internal precedents. Two partners have found citations to cases that do not exist in the firm's archive. Interactive search has to stay under two seconds because time is billed by the hour, but the memo draft runs overnight in a batch, so extra calls in that step are affordable. Malena, the technical lead, has to show a measurable reduction before the next release. Which two changes address this failure mode? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Set temperature to 0 on the drafting call so that identical inputs return identical text and the fabricated citations stop appearing.
options.feedback: A low temperature makes wording more conservative, but identical inputs may still produce different outputs, and nothing about it stops the model inventing a case.

options.label: B
options.text: Restrict the assistant to the retrieved precedents and let it answer that the archive does not cover the question instead of inventing a citation.
options.feedback: Correct: restricting it to the provided material and allowing an explicit non-answer removes the pressure to fill a gap, which is the documented first move.

options.label: C
options.text: Load the whole precedent archive into the context of every drafting call so the model stops depending on what the search step retrieved.
options.feedback: More context is not more accuracy: recall precision drops as the window fills, and the drafting step would pay for the whole archive on every memo.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the drafting step to the most capable model in the family, since fabricated citations are a capability limit that a stronger model removes.
options.feedback: A stronger model helps with hard reasoning, but hallucination is a documented limitation of the technique rather than a gap that capability closes.

options.label: E
options.text: Generate the draft several times in the overnight batch and route to human review every assertion that is not consistent across the runs.
options.feedback: Correct: inconsistency across repeated runs is a documented hallucination signal, and the overnight window is exactly where the extra calls are affordable.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that hallucination controls come in two independent kinds and a production system needs both: one that lowers the chance of inventing a source, and one that detects the invention when it happens anyway. Restricting the assistant to the retrieved precedents and giving it an explicit way to say the archive does not cover the question removes the pressure to produce something. Sampling the same draft several times and sending the assertions that differ between runs to a reviewer turns inconsistency into a signal, and the batch window is what makes those extra calls affordable. The distinction against setting temperature to 0 is that identical inputs may still produce different outputs, so it buys neither reproducibility nor factual grounding.

RULE: Let the model say the source does not cover it, then sample twice: what changes between runs is what the reviewer should read first.

TRAP: Confusing a lower temperature with a factual guarantee, when it narrows variation in wording and not the willingness to supply a citation the model does not have.

TRY IT: Ask a question your corpus cannot answer, run it three times, and count how many runs invent a source; then add the instruction that allows an explicit non-answer and run the same three.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/glossary

questions.question: Minera Nevado runs an agent that reads permit files uploaded by contractors, extracts the obligations and can call a tool that mails a summary to an external distribution list. Last month one file carried hidden text instructing the agent to attach a restricted environmental report, and the mail went out. Internal audit will not accept a remedy whose effect depends on the model reading the document correctly, and the team has a single maintenance window left this quarter. What should Joaquín, the platform engineer, put in place?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a paragraph to the system prompt stating that text inside uploaded files is data to report, never instructions to follow.
options.feedback: This is a documented control and worth keeping, but it shapes what the agent tries to do rather than what the system permits, which is what audit ruled out.

options.label: B
options.text: Take the mail tool away from the agent and have it write summaries to an internal queue that a person releases, so an injection has no path out.
options.feedback: Correct: scoping permissions as narrowly as possible means a successful injection does minimal damage, and removing the outbound path does not depend on any judgment.

options.label: C
options.text: Screen every uploaded file with a small classifier that reports whether an injection is suspected, and discard the ones it flags before the agent reads them.
options.feedback: Screening tool input is documented and useful as a layer, but a classifier is another probabilistic judgment, so its effect still depends on reading the document correctly.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the extraction step to the most capable model in the family, which resists instructions injected into documents better than the faster one.
options.feedback: Capability shifts the odds and nothing more: protection at the model layer is never fully effective, which is exactly why it cannot be the enforcement boundary.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that model-layer defenses are probabilistic while the environment is the boundary, because protection in the model layer will never be fully effective and cannot stand alone. In the incidents Anthropic has published, data left through a permitted path and the only effective safeguard was environmental restriction, so a requirement phrased as no dependence on the model points at removing the path rather than at improving the refusal. Routing summaries to a queue that a person releases means a successful injection still has nothing to send anything out with. The distinction against screening uploads with a classifier is that a classifier is one more probabilistic layer: worth having, but its effect still rests on a judgment about the document.

RULE: Close the path, do not only warn the model: an injection can take data out only through a tool you left within reach.

TRAP: Treating a sentence in the system prompt as a control, when it shapes what the agent attempts and not what the surrounding system allows it to do.

TRY IT: List the tools your agent can reach after it reads third-party content, mark the ones that can move data outside your network, and ask for each what a single injected instruction could do with it.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks

questions.question: Pehuén Energía put Claude Code in the hands of its forty internal software engineers two quarters ago, and the steering committee decides in three weeks whether to renew the budget line. That committee has tracked delivery for years with two indicators of its own: pull requests merged per engineer and cycle time. Joaquín opens the analytics view and finds contribution figures noticeably lower than what the engineers describe in their own reports. What should he take to the committee?

options.label: A
options.text: The contribution figures from the company's own repositories, next to the two indicators the committee already tracks, flagged as a deliberate undercount.
options.feedback: Correct: contribution metrics answer the investment question from your own codebase, they are documented as deliberately conservative, and pairing them with existing delivery indicators is the documented framing.

options.label: B
options.text: The published results of another organization that standardized on the same tool, which report a large reduction in time to market for a comparable engineering group.
options.feedback: A published customer outcome supports a business case and describes somebody else's codebase and staffing, so it cannot stand in for the committee's own indicators.

options.label: C
options.text: The active user count from the adoption chart, which shows how much of the engineering group has taken the tool up and therefore how much value it returns.
options.feedback: Adoption tells you who is using it and is documented for spotting dips that signal friction; how many people opened a tool is not a statement about delivery.

options.label: D
options.text: A survey in which every engineer estimates the hours saved each week, which converts into an annual figure in the units the finance team prefers.
options.feedback: Self-reported savings are quick to collect and just as quick to challenge, and the committee would be asked to renew a budget on a number nobody measured.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for expectation alignment is to report the benefit in the units the audience already trusts and to say out loud what the number cannot see. The documented framing for contribution metrics is exactly that: track pull requests per user as adoption grows, compare work shipped with and without the tool, and use the result alongside the delivery indicators the organization already follows. The same page states that these metrics are deliberately conservative and represent an underestimate, because only changes with high confidence of involvement are counted, which is why the figures look low beside what the engineers report. A committee that discovers that caveat later discounts the whole report, so it belongs in the first one. The distinction against the published result of another organization is that it describes a different codebase and a different team, and it answers none of the committee's two indicators.

RULE: Report the benefit in the indicators your audience already tracks, and say plainly that the tool's own attribution is a floor rather than the whole effect.

TRAP: Presenting a deliberately conservative attribution count as the total impact, or borrowing another organization's published outcome as evidence about your own.

TRY IT: Pull last month's contribution figures for your team, then ask two engineers what they shipped with the tool in that period and see how much of it those counts captured.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/analytics

questions.question: Minera Nevado's operational safety assistant answers questions about permit conditions over 400,000 technical documents. The environmental authority audits the operation, and every condition the assistant states has to be traceable to the document it came from. Ximena's team sees answers that are correct in substance but written as general mining practice, with no document behind them. Adding a line to the system prompt asking for citations improved things, and roughly one answer in twelve still arrives without one. What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise top_k so that more passages reach the model and there is always some retrieved document available for the answer to cite.
options.feedback: More passages usually helps recall, but the failure here is that the model answers from general knowledge; passing more context does not make it use what it was passed.

options.label: B
options.text: Require every answer to carry the identifier of each passage it used, and reject at the output stage any answer whose conditions are not backed by one.
options.feedback: Correct: the answer states conditions only from tool results, and a deterministic check at the output stage turns that requirement into something that either passes or fails.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the instruction about citations to the end of the prompt, where the model is more likely to follow it once the retrieved passages are long.
options.feedback: Placement does matter in long prompts, yet a written instruction is guidance; an audit requirement needs a control that fails the answer, not a better-placed request.

options.label: D
options.text: Route the answers that arrive with no citation to a second model that judges whether each stated condition looks properly grounded in the retrieved passages.
options.feedback: A judging model is a real verification tier, and the documented ranking puts it last: it costs latency on every reply and returns an opinion, where the audit needs only a presence test on a field.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an output property somebody will audit belongs in the output contract and its check, not in the prompt. The reference design for grounded agents states facts only from tool results, and the ranking of feedback puts clearly defined rules first, because they say which rule failed and why, with a judging model explicitly last and described as not very robust. Binding each stated condition to the identifier of the passage it came from makes the audit requirement mechanically testable at the moment the answer leaves the system. The distinction against the judging model is that asking whether an identifier is present is a rule, while asking whether an answer looks grounded is an opinion that costs latency on every reply.

RULE: What an auditor will ask for has to be checkable: bind the answer to the passages it used and fail the answer that cites nothing.

TRAP: Treating a prompt instruction as a control, so compliance goes up but the guarantee the audit asks for never exists.

TRY IT: Take fifty recent answers, count how many state a condition with no identifier attached, and write the ten-line check that would have failed them before a user saw them.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/commerce-agents https://claude.com/blog/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación charges each academic program for its share of the Claude bill, and the per-student budget leaves no room for an error of a few percent. Finance builds the chargeback today by adding up the cost figure the agent SDK reports at the end of every tutoring session. Two months running, the invoice has arrived above the sum of those figures, and nobody can say which program spent the difference. Valentina has to produce a number the finance director will sign, without waiting for a rebuild of the tutoring service. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Count the tokens of each request before it is sent, using the token counting endpoint, which is free and needs no admin credentials, and price those counts per program.
options.feedback: The endpoint is free and useful for sizing a prompt, but it returns an estimate, applies no caching logic and says nothing about output, so it cannot reconcile against an invoice.

options.label: B
options.text: Export the Console usage report once a month and split the organization total across programs by the number of students each one enrolled.
options.feedback: Splitting a total by enrollment invents the attribution instead of measuring it, and a program that runs longer sessions quietly subsidizes one that does not.

options.label: C
options.text: Give each program its own API key, then pull the Usage and Cost API grouped by key and reconcile the daily cost figures against the invoice.
options.feedback: Correct: usage and cost are reported by API key and workspace, with cost in daily buckets, which is the authoritative figure to put next to the invoice.

options.label: D
options.text: Poll the cost endpoint every five minutes with hourly buckets so that finance can watch spend per program as it accumulates during the day.
options.feedback: The cost report supports daily granularity only, and polling is documented as once a minute at most; intra-day signal comes from the usage endpoint's token counts, not from money.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that client-side cost fields are development insight and the Usage and Cost API is the accounting record. The SDK documentation says so explicitly, and warns against billing anyone from those fields, which are estimates and which also miss tokens once subagents are involved. The admin endpoints report usage and cost grouped by API key, workspace, model and service tier, so attribution is a consequence of how you issue keys rather than a spreadsheet exercise. The distinction against polling the cost endpoint faster is that cost is published in daily buckets, so a live money dashboard is not on offer; what is on offer is a daily figure that reconciles.

RULE: Bill from the Usage and Cost API and let the SDK cost fields be what they are: a development estimate no invoice is built on.

TRAP: Treating a client-side cost estimate as an accounting record, and discovering the gap only when the invoice arrives.

TRY IT: Sum your SDK cost estimates for one past day, pull the same day from the cost report, and measure the gap before you promise anyone a chargeback number.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/cost-tracking https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/usage-cost-api

questions.question: Banco Altamar's credit-documentation assistant answers questions that normally need three or four clauses from different sections of a policy. Its retrieval stage reads: chunk_size 800 tokens, over-retrieve 150 candidates per leg, rerank on, top_k 20. To hold cost per query inside the ceiling the finance committee set for the year, Tomás proposes cutting top_k from 20 to 5 and changing nothing else. What should he expect?

options.label: A
options.text: Precision and recall both fall, because the pipeline now scores far fewer chunks before the answer is written.
options.feedback: Scoring is unchanged: the reranker still ranks the over-retrieved candidates, and keeping the top five of a ranked list usually raises precision while recall drops.

options.label: B
options.text: Accuracy holds and only input tokens drop, since reranking already places the single best chunk at the top.
options.feedback: That holds for questions answered by one chunk; here the answer is assembled from several sections, so the chunks cut away were carrying part of it.

options.label: C
options.text: Latency at the ninety-fifth percentile falls in proportion, because the reranker now has fewer candidates to score.
options.feedback: The reranker still scores the whole over-retrieved set; top_k only decides how many survive it, so the per-query reranking cost stays where it was.

options.label: D
options.text: Input tokens per query fall and end-to-end accuracy falls with them on multi-section questions, while ranking quality is untouched.
options.feedback: Correct: recall drops for answers that span sections, and that loss shows up in end-to-end accuracy rather than in the ranking metric.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to set the number of passed chunks by how many the answer needs, not by the budget alone. Anthropic's retrieval work over-retrieves a large candidate set and passes a generous number of chunks precisely because its evaluation questions require synthesis across several of them, while warning in the same place that more chunks can distract the model, so the parameter trades in both directions. Cutting from twenty to five is a real and immediate token saving, and on single-fact questions it costs almost nothing. Here the removed chunks carry part of the answer, so the loss lands in recall and in end-to-end accuracy.
