questions.question: Pampero Agro's advisors spend three to five days at a time in fields with no connectivity, and deliver an agronomic report within twenty-four hours of coming back. During the ten-week peak the volume of reports is eight times the off-season. The product lead wants an agent on the advisor's tablet that decides on its own what to look at, queries the sensor history and drafts the report while the advisor is still in the field. Nicolás has to size that against the constraints before the season starts. What should he propose?

options.label: A
options.text: A guided capture flow offline, with the agentic work run once the tablet reconnects, since in the field the agent cannot check any step against the sensor history.
options.feedback: Correct: an agent needs ground truth from the environment at each step to judge its own progress, and offline there is no tool result to check against, so the field stage captures and the agentic stage runs where the environment answers.

options.label: B
options.text: The agent on the tablet with a high iteration limit, so that it keeps working through the steps it cannot confirm until the advisor is back in range.
options.feedback: Raising the limit lets it try more times, and a stateful agent compounds its errors: every extra step is taken with no signal that the previous one was right.

options.label: C
options.text: The agent on the tablet with last season's sensor history cached locally, so that it works from stored data rather than from the advisor's field notes alone.
options.feedback: A local cache removes part of the problem and not the deciding part: last season is not this visit, so the readings the report depends on are exactly the ones the tablet lacks.

options.label: D
options.text: A second model on the tablet that reviews each drafted section, so that mistakes are caught before the report ever leaves the field.
options.feedback: A reviewing model adds a second opinion, not a fact: both are working from the same unverifiable notes, and the review costs time for a check that cannot reach the data.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when turning a business problem into a design is to ask what signal the environment can return before choosing how autonomous the system should be. Agents suit open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be predicted, and the non-negotiable element is that the agent gains ground truth from the environment at each step, such as a tool result, to assess its progress. A tablet with no connectivity returns nothing to check against, so the autonomy buys only compounding errors, at four times the tokens of a plain call and during a peak that is eight times normal volume. The distinction against caching last season is that the cache answers a latency question, while what is missing is the feedback the agent needs about this visit.

RULE: Put the agentic step where the environment can answer it: with no tool result to check against, autonomy only buys compounding errors.

TRAP: Reading offline as a latency problem to be cached away, when what is absent is the feedback the agent needs to judge its own step.

TRY IT: List the steps your agent takes on one real task and mark which of them end in a tool result it can check; if most do not, the loop is running blind.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

questions.question: Mistral Retail regenerates the review summary of every catalog item in a nightly window of four hours; the job takes three today and the catalog grows around fifteen percent before each promotional season. The product lead proposes splitting each item's summary across delegated agents, one per review source, so that the window stops being a risk. The token spend of the job is capped for the year. Paula has to decide before the next catalog load. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Split each summary by review source as proposed, since independent branches finish in the time of the slowest one rather than the sum.
options.feedback: Fan-out is real, but the sources for one item feed a single synthesis: splitting them multiplies tokens and adds a coordination step over branches that are not independent in the first place.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the whole job to the most capable model in the family, so that each summary needs fewer passes and the window shortens.
options.feedback: A more capable model can shorten the reasoning on hard items; it is the slowest and most expensive lever for a job whose problem is throughput rather than difficulty.

options.label: C
options.text: Generate each summary three times and keep the version that two of the runs agree on, so that quality does not fall as the job speeds up.
options.feedback: Running the same task repeatedly buys confidence when attempts disagree, and it triples the spend of a capped job to solve a problem the window does not have.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep one agent per item and run more items at a time, since the items are independent of each other and the sources for one item are not.
options.feedback: Correct: the independent unit here is the item, so concurrency at that level uses the parallelism the work really has without paying a multi-agent multiplier on every summary.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to parallelize the unit that is genuinely independent. Multi-agent designs use three to ten times the tokens of a single agent, and the wall-clock gain that fan-out buys applies only to branches that are genuinely independent, while total end-to-end time and token cost usually rise. The review sources for one item are not independent: they all feed one synthesis, so splitting them creates the tightly coupled boundary the guidance warns against, while the catalog items are independent by construction. The distinction against the proposal is that both designs run things at the same time, but only one of them runs things that do not need each other.

RULE: Parallelize the unit that is independent, not the steps inside it: fan-out inside one dependent task multiplies tokens without shortening the window.

TRAP: Reading multi-agent as a free speed lever, when the branches being fanned out all feed one synthesis and the documented cost is a token multiplier.

TRY IT: Time one item summary end to end, then run twenty items concurrently and compare the throughput with the same twenty run as one fan-out per source.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

questions.question: Bastión Legal runs an assistant that answers associates' questions about an open matter, with one tool that searches the firm's precedent database. Its system prompt ends with the line: CRITICAL: You MUST search the precedent database before answering, and if in doubt, search again. A week of measurement shows 3.4 searches per question at about 1.2 seconds each, and the partners have capped the assistant at four seconds per answer because the time sits inside billable work. Quality review finds that on a third of the questions none of those searches returned anything the answer ended up using. What should Ignacio change first?

options.label: A
options.text: Rewrite the instruction in ordinary language and name the cases where a search applies, since emphatic wording and an if in doubt clause cause overtriggering.
options.feedback: Correct: the guidance is to dial back aggressive tool instructions and to state when a tool applies, and it names an if in doubt instruction as a cause of overtriggering.

options.label: B
options.text: Force the search tool on every request so the behavior is uniform, then shorten the answer text so that the total time comes back under the four second cap.
options.feedback: Forcing the tool does remove the variance, and it guarantees a search on every question including the ones that needed none, which raises the floor instead of the ceiling.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the assistant to the fast and economical model of the family, which shortens each search round trip enough to bring the four second cap within reach again.
options.feedback: A faster model shortens generation, and the time being spent here is three round trips the prompt asked for, which a faster model still has to make.

options.label: D
options.text: Cap the tool at one call per question in the application code, which holds the four seconds and leaves the prompt exactly as the partners approved it.
options.feedback: The cap does hold the time, and it also cuts the second search in the cases that deserved one, while the instruction producing the extra calls stays in place.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that how often a tool fires is steered by the words that describe it, and that emphatic, unconditional wording steers it upward. The documentation names both halves of this failure: language of the form CRITICAL, you MUST use this tool can be replaced by ordinary phrasing such as use this tool when, and an instruction of the form if in doubt, use the tool is called out as producing overtriggering. Rewriting the instruction to name the cases that need a precedent costs nothing at request time, which is what a four second cap on billable work requires. The distinction against capping the calls in application code is that the cap hides the behavior rather than changing it: the prompt still asks for a search on every question, and the cases that genuinely needed a second search lose it.

RULE: Say when a tool applies, in ordinary words: emphasis and an if in doubt clause buy you calls nobody needed and seconds you have to pay for.

TRAP: Reading extra tool calls as model behavior when the prompt ordered them, and answering with a hard cap instead of a clearer instruction.

TRY IT: Count tool calls per request over one day, then rewrite the tool instruction without the emphasis and without the if in doubt clause and count the same day of traffic again.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

questions.question: A platform team is sizing the context budget of a long agent session and wants to know which tokens occupy the window. Which statement is accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Tool definitions sit outside the window because they are configuration, so only the system prompt and the messages consume the budget.
options.feedback: Tool definitions are part of the request prefix and count toward the window along with the system prompt and every message, tool results included.

options.label: B
options.text: Tokens read from the cache do not occupy the window, which is how a cached session can run past the model's limit.
options.feedback: Caching lowers the price of a repeated prefix; those tokens are still sent and still counted, so a well-cached session hits the limit at the same point.

options.label: C
options.text: Cached tokens still occupy the window; caching changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count.
options.feedback: Correct: the documentation states that prompt caching changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count toward the context window.

options.label: D
options.text: The output the model generates is billed but does not consume the window, which is reserved for what you send.
options.feedback: The window covers the response too, including the reasoning for that turn, which is why a large answer on top of a large input is what pushes a request over the limit.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that the window holds everything the model must read and write for a turn: the system prompt, every message in the array including tool results, images and documents, the tool definitions, and the output it generates, its thinking included. Caching and the window are two separate accounts. The cache decides the price of a repeated prefix; the window decides whether the request fits at all. That is why a session with a healthy cache reaches the limit at the same point as one without it, and why curating what travels, rather than caching it, is the lever for a session that keeps growing.

RULE: Caching is a price, not a place: cached tokens are still sent, still read and still counted against the context window.

TRAP: Reading a low bill for a cached prefix as evidence that those tokens left the context window.

TRY IT: Send a request with a large cached prefix and add its usage fields together, cache reads plus cache writes plus uncached input, then compare the total against the model's window.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows

questions.question: Siete Lagos Viajes runs an itinerary assistant whose prompt carries a long, stable block of supplier rules ahead of each traveler request. High season brings peaks of ten times the usual traffic, and the corporate contract caps cost per booking. Paula samples one response and reads: input_tokens 6100, cache_read_input_tokens 0, cache_creation_input_tokens 0, output_tokens 240. Which monitor should the team add first?

options.label: A
options.text: A daily alert on the cost report that raises a ticket on any day whose spend per booking passes the contracted cap.
options.feedback: The cost report is the right surface for reconciling spend, but it is daily and expressed in currency, so it says the bill grew and never that caching stopped working.

options.label: B
options.text: A panel tracking cache reads as a share of input tokens per route, because a prefix below the cacheable minimum fails silently.
options.feedback: Correct: nothing is cached when the prefix is under the model minimum and no error is returned, so both cache fields sitting at zero is the only evidence you get.

options.label: C
options.text: An alert on the rate-limit headers, since the remaining input-token budget is the first signal that peak traffic is about to throttle.
options.feedback: Those headers are the cheapest capacity telemetry available and deserve an alert, but they describe throughput, not whether the stable prefix is being reused.

options.label: D
options.text: A log entry whenever the supplier rules block changes, because a cache miss always follows an edit to the cached content.
options.feedback: Edits do invalidate that level and every level after it, so the log helps, but zeros like these can equally mean the prefix never qualified for caching at all.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that prompt caching fails quietly. When the prefix is shorter than the model's minimum cacheable length nothing is cached, no error is raised, and the only symptom is that both cache fields come back at zero. That makes a cache-hit-rate panel a required monitor rather than a nicety when the cost per unit of business is contractual and traffic multiplies in season. Reading cache reads as a share of total input also protects you from the classic accounting mistake, since the reported input tokens count only what follows the last breakpoint. The distinction against watching the cost report is resolution and delay: daily spend in currency will eventually show that something changed, but never that the prefix stopped being reused.

RULE: Monitor the cache hit rate directly: a prefix that never gets cached raises no error and appears only as two zeros in usage.

TRAP: Waiting for a spend report to reveal a caching problem, when the per-response usage fields name it immediately and the report is daily and in currency.

TRY IT: Take one production route, read the two cache fields on twenty consecutive responses, and work out what share of input tokens was served from cache.

questions.question: Mistral Retail shipped version 7 of the post-sale agent's prompt two weeks before the November promotion. The offline suite ran every case three times on a pinned model, version 7 beat version 6 on the difference between arms, and the change went live. During the promotion, volume rose about tenfold, escalations to human agents rose by a third and the store managers say the agent has got worse. The escalation desk is staffed for the season and cannot absorb another week like this. Facundo re-runs the suite and version 7 still wins. Where should he look first?

options.label: A
options.text: At production transcripts from the promotion, because the suite holds no case of the kind the peak produces and cannot show a regression those inputs cause.
options.feedback: Correct: an eval answers only for the cases it contains, so a suite that keeps winning while production degrades is telling you that the failing traffic is not in it.

options.label: B
options.text: At the number of runs per case, because three runs on each case is too few to separate a real gain from the variance of a non-deterministic agent.
options.feedback: Repeated trials are how you tell a result from noise, and three is the documented starting point; a suite that reproduces its own verdict on re-run is not what noise looks like.

options.label: C
options.text: At the judge model that scored the suite, because a small judge can pass a reply whose wording matches the rubric while the people reading the same reply find it unhelpful.
options.feedback: A judge that rewards format over substance is a real defect and worth auditing, but it would have been just as wrong before the promotion, when the agent was fine.

options.label: D
options.text: At the volume, because at ten times the traffic the agent is rate limited and truncated replies read as unhelpful even when the prompt is better.
options.feedback: Rate limiting is worth ruling out, and it shows up as 429 responses and retries rather than as complaints about the content of replies.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that no single evaluation layer catches every issue, which is why automated evals, production monitoring, comparisons on live traffic and human review of transcripts are stacked. An offline suite speaks only for its own task distribution, and evals are supposed to mirror the real distribution including its edge cases; a peak that multiplies volume tenfold brings inputs nobody wrote a case for, such as stockouts, delayed shipments and canceled promotions. Reading real conversations from the peak is what turns those into cases. The distinction against the trial-count answer is that the suite agrees with itself on re-run, so what changed is the traffic, not the measurement.

RULE: An eval answers only for the cases it contains: when production disagrees with a suite that keeps winning, go and read the traffic the suite never had.

TRAP: Treating a passing offline suite as coverage, when the season that broke the agent is not represented by a single one of its cases.

TRY IT: Sample twenty conversations from your busiest hour last month and check how many have a matching case in your eval suite; add the ones that do not.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

An offline suite speaks only for its own task distribution, and evals are supposed to mirror the real distribution including its edge cases; a peak that multiplies volume tenfold brings inputs nobody wrote a case for, such as stockouts, delayed shipments and canceled promotions. Reading real conversations from the peak is what turns those into cases. The distinction against the trial-count answer is that the suite agrees with itself on re-run, so what changed is the traffic, not the measurement.

RULE: An eval answers only for the cases it contains: when production disagrees with a suite that keeps winning, go and read the traffic the suite never had.

TRAP: Treating a passing offline suite as coverage, when the season that broke the agent is not represented by a single one of its cases.

TRY IT: Sample twenty conversations from your busiest hour last month and check how many have a matching case in your eval suite; add the ones that do not.

questions.question: AndesWare ships a standard Claude Code setup per squad directory in its monorepo, and the rollout to the remaining eleven squads is on hold until the pilot is known good. In apps/payments the platform team committed .claude/settings.json holding {"mcpServers": {"billing": {"type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.internal/billing"}}, "permissions": {"deny": ["Bash(rm *)"]}} and saved the release checklist at apps/payments/.claude/skills/release-check.md. Squad members report that /mcp lists no billing server and /skills does not show the checklist, while the deny rule is clearly in effect. Which two changes fix this? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Choose Reconnect from /mcp and, if the tool count stays at zero, read the server stderr in the session debug log.
options.feedback: That is the right ladder for a server that connected but exposed no tools. This one was never registered at all, so there is nothing to reconnect to.

options.label: B
options.text: Relaunch with safe mode to confirm that no plugin or hook is suppressing the server and the checklist for these squads.
options.feedback: Safe mode is a sound bisect when something loads inconsistently, but it only disables customizations; it cannot repair a key or a path written in the wrong shape.

options.label: C
options.text: Declare the billing server in a .mcp.json file outside .claude, because a settings file does not read an mcpServers key.
options.feedback: Correct: MCP servers are configured in .mcp.json, and an mcpServers key placed in a settings file is ignored while the rest of that file still applies.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete the squad settings file and declare everything in the repository root settings, since subdirectory files layer on top of the root one.
options.feedback: Project settings are not inherited from parent directories the way memory files are, so each file has to be self-contained, and moving the same two keys would change nothing.

options.label: E
options.text: Move the checklist to apps/payments/.claude/skills/release-check/SKILL.md, because a lone Markdown file in that folder never loads.
options.feedback: Correct: a skill is a directory containing SKILL.md, so a file saved directly under the skills folder is never picked up as a skill.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when a configuration never appears is to check its shape before its behavior: every customization has one file name and one path that Claude Code reads, and anything else is ignored in silence. A settings file carries permissions, hooks and environment variables but does not read an mcpServers key, so the billing entry belongs in .mcp.json; and a skill is a directory containing SKILL.md, so a lone Markdown file in the skills folder is never loaded. The deny rule taking effect is the clue that settles it: the file is valid and is being read, so this is not a loading problem but two keys in the wrong place. The distinction against reconnecting from /mcp is that reconnect helps a server that registered and listed zero tools, not one that was never registered.

RULE: When only part of a settings file takes effect, the file is fine and the key is wrong: MCP servers live in .mcp.json, and a skill is a folder with SKILL.md.

TRAP: Debugging a configuration that was never read as if it were a runtime failure, and reconnecting a server Claude Code never registered in the first place.

TRY IT: Open a session in that directory, run /context to see whether the skill and the MCP tools are present at all, then run /mcp and compare a server that is connected with zero tools against one that is simply absent.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/debug-your-config https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud approved a first tranche of budget for clinical documentation work across its forty clinics, and will release the second tranche only against a measured result on one real workflow. Camila has watched neighboring organizations choose a platform first and then look for a problem to apply it to. She has to put the order of work in the plan the board will approve. Which sequence should she propose?

options.label: A
options.text: Set the strategy and pick the use case → create measurable value on that case → build it for production → deploy and expand to the other clinics.
options.feedback: Correct: the published stages run from strategy, to creating business value on a concrete case, to building for production, to deploying, with iteration between them.

options.label: B
options.text: Choose the platform and the tooling → build the production integration → find the clinical workflows that fit it → measure the value once the clinics are live.
options.feedback: Tooling first is the common order and the one the guidance argues against: organizations that get value start from concrete business problems, not from the platform they bought.

options.label: C
options.text: Run a pilot in every clinic at once → compare the results between them → derive the strategy from whatever worked → industrialize the winner.
options.feedback: Parallel pilots everywhere spend the first tranche before anything is measured, and a strategy derived afterwards has no baseline to compare the result against.

options.label: D
options.text: Write the compliance and security framework → deploy to all forty clinics → collect usage data → decide which use cases deserve the investment.
options.feedback: Governance is a genuine requirement that runs through every stage rather than replacing the first one; deploying before any case has shown value inverts what the board is funding.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that value is demonstrated on one concrete case before the solution is industrialized. The published enterprise adoption stages are strategy, then creating business value, then building for production, then deploying, with iteration and expansion between them, and the organizations that get value are described as the ones that start with concrete business problems and measure what matters. The board's condition, a measured result on one workflow before the second tranche, is exactly the second stage. The distinction against the tooling-first order is that it postpones the first measurable result until after the money has been spent on an integration nobody has justified yet.

RULE: Strategy, then value on one real case, then production, then deployment: the tool is chosen for the problem and never the other way round.

TRAP: Starting from the platform and looking for a workflow afterwards, so the first measurable result arrives after the budget is committed.

TRY IT: Write down the one workflow you would measure first and the number that would prove it worked, then check whether anybody measures that number today.

SOURCE: https://assets.anthropic.com/m/66daaa23018ab0fd/original/Anthropic-enterprise-ebook-digital.pdf https://claude.com/blog/driving-ai-transformation-with-claude

questions.question: Siete Lagos Viajes is redesigning the agent that handles changes and cancellations against eleven wholesale suppliers, each behind its own MCP server. Bruno is evaluating file-based tool discovery through a code-execution container, since peaks of ten times the usual volume make the token bill per request the binding constraint. Which statement about that approach is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Presenting tool definitions as files an agent reads on demand lets it load only the ones a request needs instead of all of them.
options.feedback: True: models navigate a filesystem well, and reading definitions on demand is what turns a very large catalog into a small amount of context.

options.label: B
options.text: Intermediate results can stay inside the execution environment, so a large document a tool returns need not pass through the model twice.
options.feedback: True, and it is the less obvious saving: filtering and transforming in code keeps whole transcripts and documents out of the context window.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the definitions become files, the approach removes the infrastructure a team would otherwise operate to call tools.
options.feedback: This is the statement that fails: code execution adds a secure sandbox, resource limits and monitoring, which is operational overhead that direct tool calls avoid.

options.label: D
options.text: Agentic search defers the data itself, while deferring definitions only postpones what the catalog costs to load.
options.feedback: True: the mechanisms defer different things, and the one you pick follows what is actually crowding the window.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that progressive discovery moves a cost, it does not delete it. Reading tool definitions from a filesystem on demand is the most aggressive version of the idea and the reported savings are large, and keeping intermediate results inside the execution environment removes a second, less visible load from the context window. What the same documentation states just as plainly is the price: a secure execution environment with sandboxing, resource limits and monitoring, none of which a direct tool call needs. For a team whose constraint is the token bill at peak, that trade may well be worth paying, but it has to be decided knowing that infrastructure is added rather than removed.

RULE: Progressive discovery buys context back and charges you in infrastructure: sandbox, limits and monitoring are part of the price.

TRAP: Hearing a large token saving and assuming it comes for free, when the same page lists the sandbox and monitoring it requires.

TRY IT: Write down what your team would have to run to host tool definitions as files in a sandbox, then compare that list against the token saving you estimate for one peak day.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool

questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro runs the haulier appointment service on the default service tier and has measured a median answer under two seconds for four months. Commercial wants that number in the coordination agreement with the shipping lines, with a credit for every month it is missed. The pre-harvest week triples request volume across the whole terminal. Rodrigo is asked what will actually give way first if the agreement is signed as drafted. What should he expect?

options.label: A
options.text: Answer time will drift up in proportion to the extra volume, so the commitment is missed by a predictable margin that capacity planning can absorb.
options.feedback: Load does raise latency, but what a best-effort tier does under pressure is not a smooth slope: it is refusals and waiting, which a linear plan will not have budgeted for.

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing will give way, because the commitment is measured as a monthly median and one slower week moves a month of measurements very little.
options.feedback: Choosing a window that hides the bad week is how a measurement stops describing the experience the customer has, and the credits will be argued over the week, not the month.

options.label: C
options.text: Overload and queueing during the peak will produce the misses, because the default tier serves requests on a best-effort basis rather than against a commitment.
options.feedback: Correct: the default tier prioritizes requests alongside everyone else's with best-effort availability, so the peak takes availability first; a penalty clause has to sit on measured behavior with margin.

options.label: D
options.text: Token cost will rise faster than volume, so the commitment holds while the peak month turns unprofitable at the price already agreed.
options.feedback: Spend does grow with volume, and the clause that triggers is written on answer time; cost is a separate problem that no credit in this agreement pays for.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an external commitment can never be stronger than the guarantee underneath it. The default tier is documented as best-effort availability, with requests prioritized alongside every other request, while a capacity commitment is what targets a published uptime figure. Under a tripled peak, therefore, the first thing to give way is availability, not a few milliseconds of generation time, and the misses arrive as overload and waiting. A target should also not be set from current performance, because it leaves no room for the variation nobody has observed yet. The distinction against the proportional-drift answer is that it assumes a graceful degradation the tier does not promise.

RULE: You cannot promise more than the tier beneath you commits to: on best-effort capacity, a peak takes availability first, not milliseconds.

TRAP: Reading a comfortable median as a guarantee, when the number describes months in which nothing else was competing for capacity.

TRY IT: Pull your busiest hour of the last quarter, compute over that hour alone the percentile you were about to promise, and see whether the commitment would have survived it.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/service-tiers https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación is building the first eval suite for its automatic tutor. Three things matter to the academic board: answers to exercises that have a single right answer must be right, the tone must stay encouraging, and two students who ask the same question in different words must get the same guidance. The suite will run on every prompt change, which is roughly weekly, and the per-student budget cannot absorb a human grading pass on each release. Renata has to decide how each of the three is graded. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Score all three with one LLM judge and a single rubric that asks whether the answer is correct, encouraging and consistent, returning one verdict per case.
options.feedback: One verdict over three qualities hides which of them moved, and the guidance is to build a structured rubric per dimension rather than a single holistic judgment.

options.label: B
options.text: Score all three by exact match against a reference answer written by a teacher for every case in the suite, which is deterministic and costs nothing to run.
options.feedback: Exact match is the fastest and most reliable grader and it is the right one for the exercises, but it cannot see tone, and two differently worded answers that mean the same thing both fail it.

options.label: C
options.text: Have teachers grade a sample of thirty responses per release on a five point scale, since human judgment is the gold standard for all three qualities.
options.feedback: Human grading is the highest quality and the slowest, and the documented advice is to avoid it where possible; thirty cases a week cannot follow a suite that runs on every change.

options.label: D
options.text: Grade the exercises by exact match, the tone with an LLM judge on a one to five scale, and consistency by the similarity between answers to paraphrased questions.
options.feedback: Correct: each criterion gets the fastest reliable method that can actually see it, which is what the documentation prescribes for a suite that has to run often and automatically.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to pick, for each criterion, the fastest, most reliable and most scalable method that can detect a failure of it. The documentation pairs task fidelity with exact match, tone and style with an LLM judge on a Likert scale, and consistency with the similarity between answers given to paraphrased versions of the same question, and it prefers many automatically graded cases over a few hand-graded ones. Mixing methods inside one suite is what a mixed methodology means, not a compromise between them. The distinction against a single judge is that one verdict over three qualities cannot say which one regressed, and it pays a model call for a comparison a string match already settles.

RULE: One criterion, one method: exact match where the answer is categorical, a judge where only judgment can see it, similarity where wording may vary but meaning may not.

TRAP: Collapsing several criteria into one rubric, so a single verdict hides which quality moved and the suite stops telling you what to fix.

TRY IT: Write your success criteria one per line and put beside each the grader that would detect a failure of it; any criterion left without a grader is not being measured.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud runs consultation triage as a five-step pipeline, each step a separate call. The quality team measured every step against a nurse-labeled sample and reported one line: intake parse 96%, symptom extraction 95%, protocol lookup 97%, triage decision 95%, note write 98%, end-to-end correct 78%. The clinical committee will not let the pipeline triage without nurse review until end-to-end reaches 90%, and every step already runs on the most capable model the budget allows. Which TWO actions address what this line shows? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Add programmatic checks between the steps so a malformed or empty intermediate result is caught and retried before the next step consumes it.
options.feedback: Correct: a chain of calls compounds the errors of its steps, and the documented control is a gate between steps that stops a bad intermediate result from traveling.

options.label: B
options.text: Move every step to a more capable model, since five steps in the mid nineties are the ceiling the current model can reach.
options.feedback: Five steps at those numbers multiply out to about 82% even when nothing else goes wrong, so the loss lives in the composition rather than in any one step's capability.

options.label: C
options.text: Make end-to-end correctness the number the committee tracks, and keep the per-step figures as diagnostics that say where the chain loses cases.
options.feedback: Correct: what the committee is buying is the outcome of the whole pipeline, and per-step accuracy read on its own hides how a chain multiplies.

options.label: D
options.text: Raise the number of labeled cases per step so the per-step numbers stop moving between measurements and the ceiling becomes visible.
options.feedback: A bigger sample tightens each estimate, which is worth doing, but the gap between 82% and 78% is not a measurement error you can sample away.

options.label: E
options.text: Merge the five steps into a single call so there is one place to fail instead of five places where an error can enter.
options.feedback: One call is one failure point and also one call carrying five concerns; the documented direction is the opposite, decomposing so each subtask gets full attention.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a chain multiplies the error rates of its steps, so a pipeline whose parts all sit in the mid nineties can land well below any of them: these five cap the chain at roughly 82% before any interaction effect. Agentic and multi-step designs are documented as trading cost and compounding errors for capability, and the recommended controls are programmatic checks between steps and testing of the whole path rather than of its parts. Reporting the end-to-end outcome keeps the committee's target honest and turns the per-step numbers into a diagnostic that says which link leaks. The distinction against upgrading every step is that no per-step gain the budget can buy closes a gap created by composition.

RULE: Multiply your steps before you promise a number: a chain is worth the product of its links, never the average of them.

TRAP: Reading five reassuring per-step numbers as if they described the pipeline, when the pipeline is their product.

TRY IT: Multiply the per-step accuracies of one pipeline of yours and compare the product against the end-to-end number you measure; the gap is what your gates have to catch.

RULE: Multiply your steps before you promise a number: a chain is worth the product of its links, never the average of them.

TRAP: Reading five reassuring per-step numbers as if they described the pipeline, when the pipeline is their product.

TRY IT: Multiply the per-step accuracies of one pipeline of yours and compare the product against the end-to-end number you measure; the gap is what your gates have to catch.

questions.question: The catalog squad at Mistral Retail works in Claude Code all day and keeps one session open from morning to evening, running /compact whenever the context warning appears. Their seat allowance resets on a rolling window shared with chat, and four of the eight developers now exhaust it by Thursday, which stalls the enrichment backlog before the weekend release. Tomás, the team lead, wants the change that cuts consumption without asking anyone to work differently on the code itself. What should he tell the squad to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Start a new session with /clear when they move on to an unrelated task, renaming the old one first if they may want to resume it later.
options.feedback: Correct: clearing costs nothing and drops the history that every later request was paying for, and renaming first keeps the session available to resume.

options.label: B
options.text: Run /compact more frequently so that the context window never grows large enough to trigger the warning in the first place.
options.feedback: Compacting a large context is itself a large request, so compacting more often adds cost rather than removing it and only defers the window filling again.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the individual spend limit in the admin console so that nobody is interrupted before the weekend release ships.
options.feedback: Spend limits only bite once usage credits are on, and raising a ceiling changes what a team is allowed to consume, not what it actually consumes.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch models from the picker as soon as the limit message appears, so the remaining work runs outside the exhausted family.
options.feedback: That works for a message naming one model family, but a session or weekly allowance is shared across models, so the picker cannot rescue it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that spend follows the context you keep carrying, so the cheapest lever is to stop carrying it. Compaction is not free: compacting a large context is itself a large request, which means a squad that compacts all day keeps paying for the same history, while clearing costs nothing at all. Renaming before clearing is what makes this acceptable in practice, because the session can still be resumed if the task comes back. The distinction against switching models is that a seat allowance is shared across models and chat, so the picker rescues only a limit that names one model family.

RULE: Compaction is a large request and clearing is free: compact when you need continuity, clear when what you really want is a fresh start.

TRAP: Reading compaction as a saving, when it re-sends the very history it is summarizing and only postpones the moment the window fills again.

TRY IT: Over one working day, note your usage totals just before and just after a compaction, then begin the next unrelated task with a clear and compare what the first request of each session costs.

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom wants its fault diagnosis agent to cost less per conversation, and the platform team has proposed a two model scheme in which a cheaper model runs the loop and escalates the hard cases. The contract with corporate accounts sets a first response time and carries a penalty, and the team would like to switch the whole service over on the next maintenance night. Malena owns the lifecycle of the agent and has six weeks. Which sequence should she follow?

options.label: A
options.text: Cut the whole service over on the maintenance night → watch the dashboards for a week → keep the change if no penalty is triggered → write the record of the decision afterward.
options.feedback: Cutting over first makes the penalized traffic the experiment, and a record written after the fact keeps the outcome while losing the reasons the change was made.

options.label: B
options.text: Estimate what the new scheme would save → take the number to the contract owner → cut over once the saving has been approved → build the measurement during the following quarter.
options.feedback: An estimate is the right thing to discuss with the contract owner, and approving it as evidence commits a contractual penalty to a projection nobody has tested.

options.label: C
options.text: Build cases weighted like production with outcome checks → baseline today's configuration across effort levels → adopt the new scheme only if a gap remains → shadow it before cutover.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented protocol measures production weighted tasks with outcome checks, plots the current configuration across effort levels rather than only its default, and shadows the winner on a traffic slice before any cutover.

options.label: D
options.text: Run both configurations over the evaluation set the team already has → pick the cheaper one → tell the contract owner what will change → cut over on the next maintenance night and watch the dashboards.
options.feedback: The existing set is built to iterate rather than to mirror production traffic, and choosing on it and cutting over skips the shadow run the penalty makes necessary.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for changing a system that already carries a commitment is that the evidence arrives before the cutover, and the cutover arrives in a slice. The documented measurement protocol is ordered: pull tasks weighted like production traffic with outcome checks and record cost per task, baseline the model tiers across effort levels rather than only at the default because a multi model configuration has to beat the whole curve, add the new strategy only if a gap remains after that, and run the winner in shadow on a traffic slice before cutover. Following it in this order also protects the contract, since the shadow run produces the first response times of the new scheme without any customer depending on them. The distinction against measuring on the team's existing evaluation set is that the set was assembled to iterate on the agent, not to describe the traffic that carries the penalty.

RULE: Measure on traffic shaped like production, baseline the curve you already run, adopt only if a gap survives, and shadow the winner before it carries the contract.

TRAP: Treating the cutover as the experiment, so the traffic that proves the change is the same traffic that pays the penalty when it fails.

TRY IT: Take your last configuration change and answer two questions: whether the cases it was measured on were weighted like production, and whether it ran in shadow before it carried live traffic.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence

questions.question: Mistral Retail pushed managed policy to 90 Windows laptops through the registry, and security signed the rollout on the condition that no session runs outside that policy. The store-systems developers do their work inside WSL on those same laptops. The deployment reads: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode carries permissions.deny and sandbox.enabled, and /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json exists on none of the machines. Sessions opened from PowerShell show the policy in effect; sessions opened inside WSL show none of it. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The managed arrays failed to merge, because permissions.deny replaces the lower layers instead of combining entries with them.
options.feedback: Allow and deny lists merge entries from every source, which is why developers can extend them but not remove from them, and that would not split by shell anyway.

options.label: B
options.text: The developers overrode the policy in their project settings file, which takes precedence over the registry inside the Linux environment.
options.feedback: User and project settings cannot override managed settings in any environment, and an override would show a different policy rather than no policy at all.

options.label: C
options.text: WSL reads only the Linux managed path by default, so the Windows policy reaches it only when the inheritance key is set in an admin source.
options.feedback: Correct: the registry and the Linux managed file are two delivery channels, and WSL follows the Windows one only when an admin-only source turns on inheritance.

options.label: D
options.text: The WSL sessions go out through a gateway, so the delivery that needs a direct connection to the API was skipped for those developers.
options.feedback: A gateway does block the server-managed channel, which needs a direct connection. This rollout uses registry policy, which never depends on that fetch.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that managed policy arrives through a channel, and each channel has its own reach: an administrator source on Windows covers Windows sessions, while WSL by default reads only the Linux file path. That split is exactly the symptom, and it is how one laptop can be compliant in one shell and completely unmanaged in the other. The remedy is either to set the inheritance key in one of the admin-only Windows sources so the registry policy follows into WSL, or to deploy the managed file at the Linux path as well. The distinction against a precedence problem is that user and project settings cannot override managed settings at all, so an override would never produce a shell with no policy whatsoever.

RULE: Managed policy reaches only the platform whose channel you deployed: WSL reads the Linux path unless you tell the Windows policy to follow it in.

TRAP: Assuming one endpoint means one policy surface, when the Windows registry and the Linux managed file are two separate delivery channels on the same machine.

TRY IT: On one managed laptop run /status in a PowerShell session and again inside WSL, and compare which settings sources each one reports as active: the difference names the channel that is missing.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/admin-setup

questions.question: Banco Altamar screens every incoming message to its complaint-classification channel with a small model before the main call, and throttles accounts that repeatedly probe the assistant's limits. The screen adds about 180 milliseconds, and the channel has a contractual response target of two seconds at the ninety-fifth percentile that it now misses on peak days. Nicolás proposes dropping both the screen and the throttling and leaning on the provider's deployed classifiers instead. Internal audit requires evidence of how repeated abuse attempts are handled. What is the most likely outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: Risk stays where it is, because the deployed classifiers are the enforcement boundary and an application screen only duplicates work they already do.
options.feedback: Protection at the model layer is never fully effective and is documented as unable to stand alone, so removing a layer does change the residual risk.

options.label: B
options.text: Most attempts keep being refused, but the ones that get through leave no application record, and the evidence about throttling that audit asked for disappears.
options.feedback: Correct: the deployed classifiers filter the overwhelming majority yet may not catch every attempt, and the removed layer was the one producing Altamar's own evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: Jailbreak attempts begin succeeding at scale, since the deployed classifiers act only on the output and never inspect what the user actually sent.
options.feedback: The deployed guardrail is made of input and output classifiers, and it refuses the overwhelming majority of attempts, so a collapse of this size is not what follows.

options.label: D
options.text: Response times improve and the deployed classifiers additionally keep the assistant from disclosing its internal escalation thresholds in answers.
options.feedback: Latency does improve, which is what makes this tempting, but prompt leakage is a separate concern addressed by output filtering and by trimming the prompt.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that these defenses are layered deliberately: classifiers deployed by the provider refuse the overwhelming majority of jailbreak attempts, yet they may not prevent every one, and protection at the model layer cannot stand alone. Removing the application screen therefore does not open the floodgates, which is exactly what makes the proposal tempting; what it removes is the layer that belonged to the bank, namely the record of what was attempted and the response to users who keep attempting it. That record is precisely the evidence internal audit asked for. The distinction against predicting no change in risk is that residual risk does not vanish because somebody else runs a filter, and the duty to detect and act on repeat offenders stays with the bank.

RULE: Layer the defenses and keep one of them yours: someone else's filter catches most attempts, but only your layer can log, throttle and prove it.

TRAP: Reading a very high refusal rate as a boundary, and dropping the only layer that produced evidence because it was not the one doing most of the filtering.

TRY IT: Take one week of traffic and count how many requests your own screen rejected and how many accounts it throttled; that count is exactly what you would stop being able to show after removing it.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/news/constitutional-classifiers https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks

questions.question: A new squad of eight joins the payments area at AndesWare, where the platform team spent four months tuning skills, commands and MCP servers for that part of the monorepo. Bruno, who set most of it up, moves to another area in two days and wants the squad productive without a week of pairing that nobody has time for. What should he do before he leaves?

options.label: A
options.text: Write a wiki page from memory that lists the skills, commands and servers the area uses, and link it in the squad channel.
options.feedback: A written page is the right destination, and written from memory it misses what he actually ran; the guide generated from real sessions is the one a newcomer can replay.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the team onboarding command in the project where he worked, and pin the guide it produces from his own sessions and servers.
options.feedback: Correct: it scans recent sessions, commands and MCP servers in a project with real use behind it and produces a guide the newcomer can paste as a first message.

options.label: C
options.text: Record a two-hour walkthrough of his setup so that the squad can follow it at their own pace during their first week in the area.
options.feedback: A recording shows the setup and cannot be replayed by the tooling, and it is out of date the first time a server or a command changes.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the squad the vendor enablement material together with the documentation links for the tools the payments area depends on.
options.feedback: Vendor material is published as draft copy meant to be rewritten with the organization's own cases, and it says nothing about this area's servers or commands.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for a handoff is that the document should be generated from what was actually done, not from what someone remembers doing. The documented artifact for this is the team onboarding command: run in a project where you have spent real time, it scans recent sessions, commands and MCP servers and produces a guide a new teammate can paste as their first message, which is then pinned in the channel. Vendor communication material is explicitly draft copy to be rewritten with your own tasks and modules before it is sent. The distinction against the wiki page is not the format but the source: one is written from memory two days before leaving, the other from the sessions themselves.

RULE: Hand over the setup you actually used: generate the guide from real sessions and pin it, instead of describing it from memory.

TRAP: Confusing a description of a setup with something the next person can replay on their own machine.

TRY IT: Run the team onboarding command in a project you have used for weeks and check whether the guide mentions a server or a command you would have forgotten to write down.

questions.question: The support agent at Colibrí Pay reads balances, issues refunds and blocks cards. Volume has tripled year on year and the team wants the agent to run a whole investigation on its own, so that first responses stay inside the published target. The regulator supervising fraud and money laundering requires every card block to be traceable to a verified condition. Renata, the solutions architect, is asked what has to be in place before autonomy is switched on. What should she propose?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the agent to the most capable model in the family, so that longer chains of reasoning hold their accuracy across an entire investigation.
options.feedback: A stronger model follows a longer chain, but autonomy brings higher cost and compounding errors, and capability does not stop an error propagating step by step.

options.label: B
options.text: Define stopping conditions and a checkpoint before any state-changing call, and exercise the whole loop in a sandbox before enabling it.
options.feedback: Correct: stopping conditions and checkpoints are the documented way to bound an autonomous loop, and sandboxed testing is what earns the trust it needs.

options.label: C
options.text: Feed the customer's complete history into every turn, so the agent has all the context it needs and never has to stop and ask.
options.feedback: A fuller window buys less than it seems: recall precision drops as the context grows, and nothing in it prevents the agent from acting on a wrong conclusion.

options.label: D
options.text: State in the system prompt that the agent must never block a card without evidence, and list the conditions that count as evidence.
options.feedback: Worth writing, but a prompt shapes what the agent tries to do. The irreversible call stays reachable on the turn where the agent has already drifted.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that autonomy buys scale and pays for it in cost and compounding errors, so an agent that acts alone needs an explicit boundary rather than a better model. The documented design answers are stopping conditions, pausing for human feedback at checkpoints, and extensive testing in sandboxed environments with the appropriate guardrails before the loop is trusted in production. A checkpoint before the state-changing call is also what makes each block attributable to a verified condition, which is what the regulator asked for. The distinction against writing the rule into the system prompt is that the prompt shapes intent while leaving the irreversible call reachable on any turn where the agent has drifted.

RULE: Autonomy compounds errors: before you let an agent act alone, write down where it must stop and rehearse the whole loop in a sandbox.

TRAP: Confusing a capable model with a bounded one: capability lengthens the chain the agent can follow, it does not stop that chain going wrong one step at a time.

TRY IT: Take one investigation your agent would run end to end, list every call it makes, mark the first one that cannot be undone, and check what stops the run before that point today.

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros triages claims with an agent that delegates to subagents: one reads the loss documents, another checks the fraud flags. The regulator requires that any automated decision be explained on request within ten business days, and the explanation has to show which step produced what. The metrics and logs exporters have run since launch, so the team can list the tool calls of a run and what it cost, and cannot tell which subagent made which of them. The observability pipeline is not approved to hold claim content. What should Bruno enable?

options.label: A
options.text: The content logging variables, so every prompt and tool argument is stored and any decision can be reconstructed from the text of the run.
options.feedback: Content logging would certainly explain a decision, and it would put loss documents into a pipeline that is not approved to hold them; those variables are documented as staying off until it is.

options.label: B
options.text: A daily export of the usage and cost figures per run, which carries the tokens and the cost of each step of the agent in the order they ran.
options.feedback: Those figures are aggregated for platform and finance use and carry no per-step ordering, so they answer what a run cost rather than what it did.

options.label: C
options.text: The traces signal, exported apart from metrics and logs, which nests each subagent's calls under the parent tool span as one trace per run.
options.feedback: Correct: telemetry is enabled signal by signal, and the documented span hierarchy nests a subagent's model calls and tool spans under the parent agent's tool span, so the delegation chain arrives as one trace.

options.label: D

questions.question: Bastión Legal opens each matter by firing forty requests at once, one per contract section, all sharing a 30,000-token prefix of firm precedent and review policy. The prefix carries a cache breakpoint and is byte for byte the same in all forty. Every one of them returns the same shape of usage: input_tokens 1,240, cache_creation_input_tokens 30,050, cache_read_input_tokens 0. Matter opening is billed to the client at a fixed fee, so the firm wants that prefix paid for once. Ignacio cannot reduce the number of sections. What should he change?

options.label: A
options.text: Buy the one-hour cache duration for the prefix so that the entry survives the burst and the later requests find something to read.
options.feedback: A longer duration extends an entry that already exists; nothing survives this burst because there was no entry to read when the forty requests arrived together.

options.label: B
options.text: Send one request first and wait for its response to begin, then fan out the other thirty-nine, which now share the entry it wrote.
options.feedback: Correct: a cache entry becomes available only once the first response begins, so serializing one request turns thirty-nine writes into thirty-nine reads.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the breakpoint to the end of each section's text so that every request caches its own prefix instead of competing for a shared one.
options.feedback: A breakpoint after per-request content is the classic mistake: it buys a fresh write on every call and never a read, which is what the usage already shows.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the forty sections as one batch so that the discount applies and the identical prefix is written to the cache once for the whole job.
options.feedback: The batch discount is real, but cache hits inside a batch are best effort and the queue is asynchronous, which is not where a partner waits to open a matter.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a cache entry only becomes readable after the response that writes it has begun, so requests fired at the same instant cannot share one: each finds nothing, each writes, and the firm pays the write multiplier forty times over. The documentation states the remedy directly, which is to wait for the first response before sending the rest when you need cache hits across parallel requests. Neither the content nor the breakpoint is at fault here, since the prefix is already identical and already marked; the defect is timing. The distinction against the one-hour duration is that a longer life extends an entry that exists, and this burst never created one.

RULE: Warm the cache with one request before you fan out: an entry can only be read after the response that wrote it has started.

TRAP: Assuming an identical prefix is enough for a cache hit, when forty simultaneous requests each arrive before any of them has written anything.

TRY IT: Fire five identical requests at once and read their usage, then send one, wait for its first token and fire the other four, and compare cache_read_input_tokens.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

questions.question: The Agencia Nacional de Ingresos answers taxpayers at its service windows with an assistant that classifies each question into one of forty case types and then calls the matching lookup tool. The service standard gives the clerk an answer within four seconds. A month of measurement isolates two costs: the model writes a short explanation before it calls the classification tool, and about 7 percent of those calls arrive with a missing or mistyped field, each one paying for a corrective round trip. The agency will not trade classification accuracy for either of them. Which TWO configuration changes address that? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Force the classification tool with the tool choice parameter, which prefills the call so that no explanatory text is generated before it.
options.feedback: Correct: with the choice forced, the API prefills the assistant turn, so the model emits the tool call without the natural-language explanation that is costing time on every question.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the output cap so that the explanation and the tool call both fit, which stops the answers that arrive truncated today.
options.feedback: A higher cap is the fix when answers end mid-sentence, and nothing here is being truncated; it would give the explanation more room instead of removing it.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn off parallel tool use so the lookups are issued one at a time and the clerk sees a single result on the screen.
options.feedback: Serializing calls is a real control and the wrong direction here: it adds round trips to a path with four seconds, and it touches none of the invalid fields.

options.label: D
options.text: Set strict on the classification tool, so that its inputs are constrained to the schema and the corrective round trips disappear.
options.feedback: Correct: strict tool use constrains sampling to schema-valid inputs and is documented as removing the validate-and-retry cycle those malformed calls are paying for.

options.label: E
options.text: Move the classification to the most capable model of the family, which makes fewer field mistakes across forty case types.
options.feedback: A more capable model would misclassify less and would spend more time doing it, and the schema violations it still produced would keep their corrective round trip.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to separate the two things a response time is spent on: tokens generated before the useful output, and round trips spent recovering from a malformed one. Forcing the tool through the tool choice parameter makes the API prefill the assistant turn, so the tool call arrives with no natural-language preamble in front of it, and the documentation notes that testing has not shown this to reduce performance. Strict tool use answers the second cost: constraining sampling to schema-valid outputs guarantees the tool name and the shape of its input, which is documented as removing the need to validate and retry, at the price of compiling the grammar the first time a schema is used. The two are documented as a pair, forced choice plus strict, and the distinction against a stronger model is that neither cost measured here is a capability problem.

RULE: Force the call when you are paying for prose in front of it, and constrain the inputs when you are paying for retries: one buys the turn, the other buys the shape.

TRAP: Answering a latency measurement with a bigger output cap or a stronger model, when what is being paid for is a preamble and a corrective round trip.

TRY IT: Take fifty of yesterday's requests, count the characters generated before the tool call and the share of calls that failed validation, then measure both again with the tool forced and strict enabled.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud exposes a tool through its own MCP server that finalizes the urgency level of a triage case. Which mechanism makes that tool always reach the human confirmation, even in a client where an allow rule already matches it?

options.label: A
options.text: Mark the tool with a destructive annotation, so that every client knows it needs a confirmation before it runs.
options.feedback: Annotations are hints supplied by the server about itself, and clients must treat them as untrusted unless the server is trusted, so they authorize nothing.

options.label: B
options.text: State the requirement in the system prompt and in the memory file that the client loads at startup.
options.feedback: Instructions shape what the model tries to do. They do not change what the harness allows, which is where an approval gate is actually enforced.

options.label: C
options.text: Give the tool a name that no allow rule in the client's configuration can match by pattern, so the call falls through.
options.feedback: Renaming around a rule survives until somebody widens the pattern, and text matching is not a security boundary in the first place.

options.label: D
options.text: Set the tool metadata flag "anthropic/requiresUserInteraction", which sends every call through to the permission callback.
options.feedback: Correct: tools carrying that flag prompt even when an allow rule matches, and they are denied outright in the mode that never asks.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a human gate is enforced by the client and the harness, not described by the server. Tool annotations travel as the server's own claims about itself, and clients are required to consider them untrusted unless the server is trusted, so a destructive hint cannot guarantee a prompt. The documented mechanism is the tool metadata flag that marks a tool as requiring user interaction: those calls always fall through to the permission callback even when an allow rule matches, and they are denied in the mode that never asks. The distinction against writing the requirement into the prompt or a memory file is that instructions shape what Claude tries to do and never change what the harness permits.

RULE: A gate you can rely on is declared in metadata and enforced by the harness; an annotation is the server describing itself, and a prompt is only advice.

TRAP: Treating a server-supplied annotation as an authorization mechanism, when clients are told to consider annotations untrusted unless the server itself is trusted.

TRY IT: Add an allow rule for one of your own MCP tools and call it to see it run without a prompt, then set the interaction flag on that tool and watch the same call stop for confirmation.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools

questions.question: Siete Lagos Viajes lets an agent apply itinerary changes through the wholesalers' APIs. In high season the volume is ten times the baseline, and the contract with the wholesalers says a change exists only once their confirmation code has been issued. Last week six travelers were told their change was done for changes no wholesaler had registered; in each case the agent had reported the step as complete. Sofía has to change the design rather than the prompt. What should she change?

options.label: A
options.text: Have the agent restate at the end of each run which steps it completed, so that any discrepancy becomes visible in the transcript.
options.feedback: A self-report is what already failed: an agent summarizing its own steps is judging itself, and the summary is precisely where the error entered.

options.label: B
options.text: End the turn only once the wholesaler's confirmation code has come back, and escalate the change when it has not.
options.feedback: Correct: the loop closes on a signal the environment produces, so the code either exists or the run is not finished, and nothing depends on the agent's own account.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a second model that reviews each transcript and flags the runs where a confirmation appears to be missing from the steps.
options.feedback: A reviewing model catches some of these, but it is the weakest verification tier and it adds latency, when the check that is missing is simply whether the wholesaler's confirmation code came back.

options.label: D
options.text: Retry the wholesaler call three times with backoff and treat the change as applied when the last attempt comes back without an error.
options.feedback: Retries with backoff are the right handling for a transient failure, and an absent error is not a confirmation: the contract is written on the code, not on the call.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for the feedback stage of an end-to-end design is that the signal has to come from the environment, not from the model. An agent needs ground truth at each step, such as a tool result, to assess its progress, and a verification loop is a check it can run that returns a pass or a fail; without one, the only thing deciding that the work is done is the agent itself, which is exactly what produced six wrong confirmations. The wholesaler's code is that check, and it is already the definition of done in the contract. The distinction against retrying is that backoff handles a call that failed, while the failure here is a call that succeeded and changed nothing.

RULE: Close the loop on what the outside world returns: an agent that reports its own success has no verification loop at all.

TRAP: Treating a call that did not fail as a confirmation, when the contract defines done as the identifier the other system issues.

TRY IT: Take one completed change from yesterday and try to match it to a wholesaler confirmation code with a single query; if you cannot, your loop is closing on the agent's word.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/glossary https://claude.com/blog/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk

questions.question: Minera Nevado searches 400,000 technical documents and environmental permits, and the permits are produced in-house with numbered sections. The pipeline reads: chunking size-based, chunk_size 2000 tokens, overlap 200, embeddings only, top_k 3, index rebuilt every 30 days. Connectivity at the mine site is intermittent, so an engineer gets one round trip per question. Camila's review finds two patterns among the failures: answers cite the right permit family but attribute a clause to the wrong mine site, and a long clause sits in one chunk while its exception sits in the next. Which TWO changes should the team make first? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Raise top_k from 3 to 30 so that many more candidate chunks reach the prompt on the single round trip available.
options.feedback: Recall does rise, but more chunks can distract the model, and neither failure pattern comes from having too few candidates in the prompt.

options.label: B
options.text: Chunk the permits by their numbered structure rather than by a fixed length, since the team controls how those documents are produced.
options.feedback: Correct: structure-based chunking is the recommended choice when you control the document format, and it keeps a clause and its exception together.

options.label: C
options.text: Prepend to each chunk, before it is embedded, fifty to a hundred tokens of document-aware context naming the permit and the site.
options.feedback: Correct: contextual embeddings exist for chunks that are topically right but ambiguous once they are lifted out of the document they came from.

options.label: D
options.text: Shorten the index rebuild cycle from thirty days to twenty-four hours so retrieval always reflects the current permit set.
options.feedback: A stale index does cause confident wrong answers, but its signature is language that no longer exists in the source, which is not what this review found.

options.label: E
options.text: Lower the similarity threshold so that fewer questions come back with no chunk at all on the first attempt.
options.feedback: A looser threshold admits weaker matches and can help with empty results, yet it changes neither the chunk boundaries nor the missing document context.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to choose the chunking strategy from the shape of the data and to give each chunk back what indexing took away from it. Structure-based chunking is the documented choice when you control the format, as this team does for its own permits, and it directly fixes a clause separated from its exception by a fixed-length cut. The second failure is the classic case for contextual embeddings: a chunk that is topically right but ambiguous on its own, because nothing in it says which permit or which site it belongs to, so fifty to a hundred tokens of document-aware context are prepended before embedding. Note that this cost is paid once at index time, which matters when every query has to survive one round trip. Raising top_k or loosening the threshold changes how many candidates arrive, which is not what is broken.

RULE: Chunk along the structure you control, and give every chunk back the document context that indexing removed.

TRAP: Answering a chunk-boundary problem with retrieval knobs, when no value of top_k restores context that was never indexed.

TRY IT: Take ten failing questions, print the chunks that were retrieved, and mark for each one whether it names its own document and whether an obligation and its exception stayed together.

SOURCE: https://academy.claude.com/courses/building-with-the-claude-api/text-chunking-strategies https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval
