questions.question: Pampero Agro's field advisor assistant holds long sessions with agronomists and keeps reaching the context limit halfway through the day. The platform team switches on server-side compaction with the documented default trigger. Finance tracks the assistant on a dashboard that sums input_tokens and output_tokens from every response, and the seasonal budget is approved and closed against that dashboard. Joaquín is asked what will change once compaction is running. What should he expect?

options.label: A
options.text: Sessions stop reaching the limit, and the dashboard under-reports, because the compaction pass is billed and reported only inside the iterations of the response.
options.feedback: Correct: compaction adds a sampling step that counts toward billing and rate limits, and its tokens appear in the iterations array rather than in the top-level totals.

options.label: B
options.text: Sessions stop reaching the limit and the dashboard is unaffected, because compaction happens on the server and adds no sampling step of its own to the request.
options.feedback: Compaction does run on the server, but it summarizes the conversation with an additional model call, and that call is billed like any other.

options.label: C
options.text: Sessions stop reaching the limit and the dashboard over-reports, because the summary is billed once when it is written and again on every request that carries it.
options.feedback: The compaction block is carried forward and paid as input on later requests, which is ordinary prefix cost rather than double counting of the write.

options.label: D
options.text: Sessions keep reaching the limit until the trigger value is lowered below the model's window, and the dashboard reports exactly the same totals as before.
options.feedback: The trigger has a documented default and a minimum and fires on input size inside the window, so leaving it alone does not leave the session unbounded.

questions.question: The security and finance leads at AndesWare ask Ximena for one page on the standard Claude Code configuration that reaches four hundred developers in two countries, half of them on machines the company manages and half on machines it does not. They want to know what that configuration settles for everyone and where it stops. Which TWO statements belong in that page? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Policy delivered from the server applies uniformly across the organization, so a squad that needs different rules is not served by that channel.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented limitation is that these settings apply to every user in the organization, with per-group configuration not supported, and a page that leaves that out promises something the channel cannot do.

options.label: B
options.text: The prices shown in the model picker move to the negotiated rates once the pricing setting is deployed, so developers read the same figures finance does.
options.feedback: The setting does change the total the tool reports, while the per-million-token prices in the picker are documented to stay at list price, so the two views will not agree.

options.label: C
options.text: Per-squad differences are handled by each squad keeping its own rules in a project settings file, which the delivered policy merges in.
options.feedback: Developers can extend managed lists from their own files and cannot remove from them, so a project file gives a squad more rules rather than different ones.

options.label: D
options.text: The configuration holds on every machine whatever the sign-in, because the policy travels with the developer's account rather than with the device.
options.feedback: Which channel reaches a machine depends on how the session authenticates and on who administers the device, which is exactly why half of this fleet needs a different mechanism.

options.label: E
options.text: Reported cost can be aligned with the negotiated contract through a managed-only setting, which changes what the tool reports and not what is billed.
options.feedback: Correct: the pricing key is honored only from managed settings and is documented as changing what Claude Code reports rather than what Anthropic charges, which is the distinction finance needs in writing.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when you put a configuration decision on paper is to state what it guarantees and where it stops, because the page will be read afterward as a commitment. Two documented limits belong in this one. Settings delivered from the server apply uniformly to every user in the organization, and per-group configuration is not supported, so a squad with different needs has to be served by another channel rather than by an exception nobody can grant. And the managed-only pricing setting exists so the cost the tool displays matches a negotiated contract: the documentation is explicit that it changes what Claude Code reports rather than what Anthropic charges, and that the model picker keeps showing list prices. The distinction against the project settings answer is that managed arrays merge downward, so a developer adds rules and never removes them.

RULE: Write down where the policy stops: one configuration for the whole organization, and a pricing setting that changes the report rather than the invoice.

TRAP: Reading a reporting setting as a negotiated discount, or promising per-team policy through a channel documented to apply to everyone alike.

TRY IT: Ask whether any team in your organization needs rules different from the standard set, then check which delivery channel could carry that difference today.

questions.question: Yaguareté Logística classifies tariff codes for twelve thousand daily dispatches and wants the assistant working with a fourth country's customs system before the quarter closes. Classification accuracy on the three live countries already meets the target. The new country publishes its tariff tables as scanned annexes, and its customs API has no test environment. Tomás is asked what will decide the launch date. What should he answer?

options.label: A
options.text: Turning the annexes into usable data and working against a system with no test environment, which is where programs of this kind stall.
options.feedback: Correct: integration with existing systems and data access and quality are the blockers organizations report most often when taking agents to production, ahead of anything about model capability.

options.label: B
options.text: The accuracy of the classification on the new country's codes, which has to be measured before any other part of the plan can be committed.
options.feedback: Accuracy does have to be measured, and it is the part this team already knows how to do; it is not what holds a date when the source is a scan and the counterpart has no test environment.

options.label: C
options.text: The cost per dispatch of the fourth integration, since a fourth country multiplies the token spend of the pipeline that is already running.
options.feedback: Spend does grow with another country, and the pipeline is the same one in production today; cost is a planning input here rather than the thing that sets the date.

options.label: D
options.text: The latency of the fourth customs API, since the assistant has to answer inside the same window it meets for the other three countries.
options.feedback: The counterpart's latency matters for the design once that system is connected, which makes it a consequence of an integration that does not exist yet.

questions.explanation:
The general rule when translating a business problem into a deployed solution is to budget for where the work actually goes. Enterprises deploying agents report integration with existing systems and data access and quality as the leading implementation blockers, with change management next, and model capability is not on that list. This case makes both concrete: a source published as scanned annexes is a data-quality problem, and a counterpart with no test environment means every integration defect is discovered in production. The distinction against measuring accuracy first is that accuracy is the part the team has already solved three times, so it is the least likely thing to move the date.

RULE: Plan for the integration and the data, which is where production programs stall; model capability is rarely what holds the date.

TRAP: Sizing a rollout by the part you already know how to measure, so the scanned source and the missing test environment appear as surprises.

TRY IT: List the last three integrations your team shipped, write down what actually delayed each one, and count how many of those delays were about the model.

SOURCE: https://claude.com/blog/how-enterprises-are-building-ai-agents-in-2026

questions.question: Pampero Agro produces agronomic reports from sensor series and field notes with an agent loop that can run for several minutes. In the peak month the number of reports rose by about a fifth while the bill doubled. The median cost per report is where it was last season, the share of input read from the cache is steady at 90%, and neither the model nor the prompt changed. Six percent of the runs account for close to half of the month's spend. The finance lead proposes lowering effort on every report. Where should Sofía look first?

options.label: A
options.text: At the tokenizer, because the same report text can cost more tokens after a change of model generation and totals rise without anything else moving.
options.feedback: A tokenizer change does raise the token count of identical text, but it would lift the median report as well, and no model change happened here.

options.label: B
options.text: At the tail of long runs, because a small share of tasks that keep going carries the increase, and a budget the model can see caps them.
options.feedback: Correct: spend on agent loops concentrates in a few very costly runs, and the documented control is a task budget the model can see, backed by a session or workspace spend limit.

options.label: C
options.text: At the cache, because an agent loop that pays full price on part of its input doubles quickly, and a healthy read share alone does not prove the breakpoint is right.
options.feedback: Checking the cache first is the right instinct on an agent loop, and here it is already checked: a read share at 90% is what a well-built loop looks like.

options.label: D
options.text: At the volume, because a fifth more reports in a season with longer field notes is enough on its own to explain a bill of that size.
options.feedback: A fifth more work explains a fifth more spend, not twice as much; the figures in the stem are what rule this explanation out.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for cost diagnosis on agent loops is to read the distribution before touching the defaults, because spend concentrates in a tail: published measurements show two problems out of twenty carrying nearly half the cost of a run. Here the median is unchanged and the cache is healthy, so the increase lives in the six percent of runs that keep going, and the documented control for a few very costly runs is a task budget the model can see, with a session budget and a workspace spend limit behind it. Lowering effort everywhere pays for that tail with quality on the ninety-four percent that were never the problem. The distinction against the volume explanation is arithmetic: a fifth more work does not double a bill.

RULE: Price the tail before you touch the defaults: when a few runs carry half the bill, cap those runs instead of degrading all of them.

TRAP: Treating a bill that a tail created as an average problem, and paying for it with quality across the whole workload.

TRY IT: Sort last month's runs by cost and add up the most expensive five percent; if they carry a third or more of the bill, you have a tail problem, not a default problem.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom absorbed a smaller operator, and eight of its engineers joined the team that maintains the fault-diagnosis tooling. Three of them hit API Error 400 saying the organization has been disabled, although their Enterprise seats are active. After signing out and back in, their interactive sessions work, but every run launched with the -p flag in the nightly pipeline still fails the same way, and that pipeline gates the release that protects the contractual first-response target. What should the platform team check first?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the administrator to re-provision their seats, since the message points at an account without Claude Code access.
options.feedback: A seat that lacks Claude Code access announces itself differently, with a message about not having been added to the organization yet.

options.label: B
options.text: Have them sign out and sign in once more, which clears most login failures and restores the organization binding.
options.feedback: A clean re-authentication does resolve most login problems, and it already half worked here. It cannot beat a variable that outranks the sign-in.

options.label: C
options.text: Check whether the corporate proxy is interfering with the requests, a documented cause of calls being refused after login.
options.feedback: A proxy is one of the documented causes, but of a forbidden response rather than of this message about a disabled organization.

options.label: D
options.text: Look for an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY exported in their shell profiles, unset it, and confirm the active authentication method.
options.feedback: Correct: this message with an active subscription means a stray key is overriding the sign-in, and with the -p flag the key is always used when present.

questions.explanation:
The general rule during a rollout is to read the error string as a pointer to the credential path rather than to the person's entitlement. This message alongside an active subscription means an environment variable holding an API key is overriding the sign-in, which usually arrives in a shell profile inherited from a previous employer or project. In non-interactive mode with the -p flag the key is always used when present, which is exactly why the interactive sessions recovered after signing in again and the pipeline did not. The distinction against re-provisioning the seat is that a missing seat produces its own message about not having been added to the organization yet.

RULE: Read the error before the org chart: a disabled organization on an active seat means a stray API key is winning, and in a headless run it always wins.

TRAP: Reading a credential collision as an entitlement problem, and re-provisioning a seat that was never the thing rejecting the request.

TRY IT: Print the environment your pipeline runs with on one affected machine and look for ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, then run /status in an interactive session and compare the authentication method it reports.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/troubleshoot-install

questions.question: Yaguareté Logística files customs declarations through a remote MCP server shared by the systems of four countries. A request line from its client log reads: POST /mcp, Mcp-Session-Id: 9f21c0a4, Accept: application/json and text/event-stream, no Authorization header after the first call of the session. Every declaration has to be attributable to the individual broker who filed it, and the four customs authorities audit that trail in six weeks. Which gap should Andrés close first?

options.label: A
options.text: Every inbound request has to carry and be verified against its own access token, because a session identifier is not a credential.
options.feedback: Correct: servers that implement authorization must verify all inbound requests, and the specification states that sessions must not be used for authentication.

options.label: B
options.text: The session identifier has to be bound to the user, in a form such as user id joined to session id, so a leaked value cannot be replayed.
options.feedback: That binding is genuinely recommended and worth doing, but it hardens an identifier that should not be carrying the identity of the caller at all.

options.label: C
options.text: The token should leave the Authorization header and travel as a query parameter, so one logical session is not re-authenticated on every call.
options.feedback: The requirement runs the other way: the bearer token goes in the header on every request, and access tokens must never appear in the URI query string.

options.label: D
options.text: The server should answer an unknown session with 403 rather than 401, so that clients can tell a missing session from a missing permission.
options.feedback: The mapping is the opposite: 401 means authorization is required or the token is invalid, while 403 signals invalid scopes or insufficient permissions.

questions.explanation:
The general rule in MCP authorization is that identity travels with every request and never with a session. The specification says both halves plainly: servers that implement authorization must verify all inbound requests and must not use sessions for authentication, and the bearer token belongs on every HTTP request even when those requests are part of one logical session. The audit requirement makes the consequence concrete, because with no token after the handshake nothing in the later calls identifies the broker who filed the declaration. Binding the session identifier to a user is real advice and worth applying afterwards, but the difference in force is what decides the item: that binding is a recommendation for an identifier, while verifying every request is a requirement for the credential.

RULE: Authenticate every request, not the session: a session identifier is a routing key and never a credential.

TRAP: Treating a session established once as proof of identity for all the calls that follow it.

TRY IT: Capture ten consecutive calls your client makes to a remote MCP server, check that each one carries its own Authorization header, and confirm the server rejects the same call without it.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/security_best_practices https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization

questions.question: A team is rewriting the system prompt of an agent that has grown one hardcoded rule per case the team has met. Which TWO statements match the documented guidance on the altitude of a system prompt? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: Rules hardcoded for every case are one of the two failure modes, because the prompt then has to be extended for each new situation.
options.feedback: Correct: hardcoding brittle logic for every case is named as one of the two failure modes, and it makes the prompt fragile as new cases arrive.

options.label: B
options.text: Guidance so general that it assumes context the model does not have is the other failure mode, and it reads as vague rather than flexible.
options.feedback: Correct: the opposite failure is a prompt so vague that it falsely assumes shared context, which leaves the model no heuristic to work from.

options.label: C
options.text: The rule list is the safer extreme of the two, since anything written down explicitly leaves the model no room to misread it.
options.feedback: Explicit rules do remove ambiguity on the cases they name, and the guidance treats that extreme as a failure mode too, not as the cautious side.

options.label: D
options.text: Altitude is a length target, and the guidance names a system prompt of about one page as the point between the two failure modes.
options.feedback: Length is a consequence rather than the target: the aim is guidance specific enough to steer behavior and flexible enough to leave strong heuristics.

options.label: E
options.text: The way out of both failure modes is to move every rule into examples, because examples stop being instructions once there are enough of them.
options.feedback: Examples are a documented technique and they do not settle altitude: a set of examples can be just as brittle as the rule list it replaced.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for a system prompt is to aim at the right altitude, described as the Goldilocks zone between two common failure modes. Below it sits hardcoded, brittle logic: a branch for every case the team has met, which has to be extended the first time a case arrives that nobody wrote a rule for. Above it sits guidance so vague that it falsely assumes shared context, leaving the model to guess what the team already knows. The target between them is guidance specific enough to guide behavior effectively and flexible enough to give the model strong heuristics. The distinction against reading the rule list as the safer extreme is that both ends are failure modes: one is fragile and the other is empty, and neither is the cautious choice.

RULE: Write the system prompt at the altitude between a rule for every case and a slogan for none: specific enough to steer, general enough to leave heuristics.

TRAP: Assuming the more explicit prompt is always the safer one, when a branch for every case is one of the two documented failure modes.

TRY IT: Take your longest system prompt, count the rules that name one specific case, and ask for each whether the model could have reached the same behavior from a heuristic.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

Altitude is a length target, and the guidance names a system prompt of about one page as the point between the two failure modes.
The way out of both failure modes is to move every rule into examples, because examples stop being instructions once there are enough of them.
html.explanation:
The general rule for a system prompt is to aim at the right altitude, described as the Goldilocks zone between two common failure modes. Below it sits hardcoded, brittle logic: a branch for every case the team has met, which has to be extended the first time a case arrives that nobody wrote a rule for. Above it sits guidance so vague that it falsely assumes shared context, leaving the model to guess what the team already knows. The target between them is guidance specific enough to guide behavior effectively and flexible enough to give the model strong heuristics. The distinction against reading the rule list as the safer extreme is that both ends are failure modes: one is fragile and the other is empty, and neither is the cautious choice.

RULE: Write the system prompt at the altitude between a rule for every case and a slogan for none: specific enough to steer, general enough to leave heuristics.

TRAP: Assuming the more explicit prompt is always the safer one, when a branch for every case is one of the two documented failure modes.

TRY IT: Take your longest system prompt, count the rules that name one specific case, and ask for each whether the model could have reached the same behavior from a heuristic.

questions.question: A configuration change at Terminal Puerto Claro left the manifest filing assistant serving stale berth data for forty minutes, visible to the hauliers, until the team rolled it back. The platform team is four people and the pre-harvest peak starts in nine days. The team lead proposes skipping the write-up, since the cause is understood and the fix is already in production. What should the architect propose instead?

options.label: A
options.text: Skip the write-up as proposed and record the rollback in the change log, since the cause is understood and the fix is already deployed.
options.feedback: A change-log line records what happened and not why the system allowed it; an incident with user-visible impact that needed a rollback meets the criteria for a written record.

options.label: B
options.text: Write it after the peak, when the team has the time to do it properly and the incident can be looked at with some perspective.
options.feedback: Deferring is the usual compromise, and the peak is when the same failure would cost most; a record written weeks later is reconstructed rather than remembered.

options.label: C
options.text: Write it now inside a timebox that protects the peak preparation, keep it focused on contributing causes rather than on people, and have it reviewed.
options.feedback: Correct: the triggers are met, the value comes from the contributing causes, the review is what makes the record count, and a timebox keeps it proportionate for four people.

options.label: D
options.text: Write it now and record which engineer approved the change, so that the approval step can be tightened before the peak begins.
options.feedback: Naming the approver turns the record into an attribution of blame, which is what stops the next one being reported; the approval step can be tightened without a name in the record.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a postmortem is a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken, the causes and the follow-up, and the documented triggers include user-visible degradation and on-call intervention such as a rollback, both of which happened here. Blameless means focusing on contributing causes without indicting an individual or a team, which is what keeps people reporting incidents at all. The review is not optional either: an unreviewed postmortem might as well never have existed. The distinction against deferring it is that a four-person team is a reason to timebox the write-up, not to postpone it past the week in which the same failure would hurt most.

RULE: An incident that needed a rollback and that users could see earns a record: write it while it is fresh, keep it about causes, and have it reviewed.

TRAP: Treating a known cause as a finished investigation, so the conditions that let the change reach production are never written down.

TRY IT: Check your last three incidents: which produced a written record, which of those was read by someone who was not on the call, and which of them named a person.

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom answers retention chats with a pipeline that first classifies the customer's intent in one model call and then answers with the prompt specialized for that intent. The contract commits the company to a complete first reply within three seconds at the ninety-fifth percentile. Before the classifier that percentile sat at 2.4 seconds; it now sits at 4.1, while the answering prompts and their inputs are the same length as before and the error rate has not moved. Nicolás has to get back under the commitment. Where is the time going?

options.label: A
options.text: Into the queue, because two calls per conversation double the request rate and the account is hitting its limits at peak.
options.feedback: Contention is worth ruling out, and it would appear as 429 responses and retries in the logs; the error rate here has not moved at all.

options.label: B
options.text: Into the first token, which streaming would deliver sooner, bringing the measured percentile back under the commitment.
options.feedback: Streaming improves perceived responsiveness and the time to the first token, but what is promised is a complete reply, and the classifier still runs before anything streams.

options.label: C
options.text: Into the extra model call, which the classifier adds to the critical path of every conversation before the answer can start.
options.feedback: Correct: routing with a classifier is an additional call to Claude, documented as increasing latency, and it must finish before the answering call begins.

options.label: D
options.text: Into the network, because the pipeline makes two round trips to the API instead of one and the extra transport shows at the tail.
options.feedback: Two round trips do add their transport time, but what dominates is generation: a full model call has to complete before the answer starts.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that every step placed in front of the answer is latency the user pays, and a router is a model call like any other. The customer support guidance says exactly that about putting an intent classifier in front of specialized conversations: it requires an additional call to Claude that can increase latency. Because the commitment is a complete reply, the levers that move perceived responsiveness or the speed of output tokens do not help while a classification call runs first. The real choice is to accept the added call knowingly and buy the time back elsewhere, or to fold the routing into the single call that answers. The distinction against the queueing explanation is that contention would show up as errors and retries, and it has not.

RULE: A router is a model call: put it in the latency budget, or fold the routing into the call that has to run anyway.

TRAP: Reaching for streaming or a faster serving option when the clock started on a step you added yourself, before the answering call.

TRY IT: Time your router and your answering call separately over a hundred conversations and put the two percentiles side by side before deciding which one to optimize.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/customer-support-chat https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency

questions.question: Banco Altamar routes its engineering tooling through an internal gateway. Internal audit requires every request to be attributable to a person and access to be revoked the day someone leaves. The platform team ships one shared credential together with the gateway address in the managed configuration, and Andrés is writing the implementation guidance that goes out with the rollout to two hundred engineers. What should it say?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the shared credential and attribute usage from the application logs, which already record a user name on every request that goes through.
options.feedback: Application logs do carry a name, and they attribute what the application recorded rather than what the credential could do; anyone holding the shared key can bypass the application.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the shared credential and rotate it every month, so that a copy held by someone who has left stops working within the month.
options.feedback: Rotation shortens the window without closing it, audit asked for the day someone leaves, and every rotation forces a redistribution to everyone else.

options.label: C
options.text: Issue one credential per engineer, which is what makes attribution per person and same-day revocation possible at all.
options.feedback: Correct: one key per developer rather than a shared key is what makes per-developer usage attribution and individual offboarding work, and a key helper lets each person rotate without redistributing settings.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the shared credential and add a second one for contractors, so that internal and external usage can at least be told apart.
options.feedback: Two credentials give two buckets rather than people, and the same question returns the first time audit asks who issued one specific request.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that implementation guidance has to make the requirement achievable at the layer that enforces it, and here that layer is the credential. Issuing one key per developer rather than a shared key is documented as what makes per-developer usage attribution and individual offboarding work, and a key helper allows per-developer rotation without redistributing settings to the whole fleet. The audit asks two things, who made a request and how access ends on a given day, and both are properties of the credential. The distinction against reading the application logs is that they describe what the application chose to record, while the shared key remains usable by anyone who has a copy of it, including outside the application.

RULE: One credential per person is what makes attribution and same-day offboarding possible; a shared key can only ever be rotated.

TRAP: Confusing what the application logs with what the credential proves, so attribution rests on a record the key holder can bypass.

TRY IT: Pick one request from last week and try to name the person behind it using only what the gateway holds, then work out what you would have to do today if that person left.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-rollout

questions.question: A teacher at Grupo Aurora Educación reports that the automatic tutor gave a wrong explanation of a statistics exercise, and two colleagues say they have seen something similar. The platform team works to a budget per student that leaves no room for a broad rewrite, and the academic committee that signs off on changes meets once a month. Ignacio has to decide how the team answers this report. What order should they follow?

options.label: A
options.text: Change the prompt for that topic → confirm with the teacher that the new answer is right → move on → revisit the topic next term.
options.feedback: A quick fix on the reported case is tempting and it is also how a system accumulates one patch per complaint, with nothing to say whether other topics got worse.

options.label: B
options.text: Collect reports until the committee meets → group them by subject → prioritize the largest group → change the system afterwards.
options.feedback: Waiting for the committee keeps the loop tidy and slow, and the cases are most valuable as tests the moment they arrive, while the budget argues for the smallest measured change.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the three teachers to grade a sample of answers → compute an accuracy figure → decide whether it justifies a change → inform the committee.
options.feedback: Hand grading by three teachers is expensive for the signal it returns, and it answers how bad it looks rather than how often it actually happens.

options.label: D
options.text: Measure in production how often the failure happens → turn the confirmed cases into eval cases → change and re-run the set → report the measured change.
options.feedback: Correct: production monitoring shows real behavior at scale, real failures are the documented source of eval cases, and a re-run set turns a complaint into a measured change you can report back.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that evals and production monitoring are complementary rather than alternatives: evals give fast iteration, while production reveals real user behavior at scale and catches what synthetic tests miss. So the first move on a complaint is to find out how often that failure really occurs, then to convert the confirmed cases into eval cases, since tasks drawn from real failures are the documented starting point and non-engineering stakeholders are expected to contribute them. Re-running the whole set is what shows that the change helped without breaking a topic that worked. The distinction against patching the prompt is that a patch answers one teacher, whereas a re-run set answers the committee and the other hundred and eighty thousand students.

RULE: Measure how often before you change anything, turn the real failure into a test case, and report the measured difference back to whoever reported it.

TRAP: Patching the reported case, so every complaint produces a change nobody can measure and no test that would catch it coming back.

TRY IT: Take the last complaint your team received, find out how often that failure occurs in production, and check whether it exists as a test case today.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom's fault diagnosis agent carries eleven tools. On roughly a fifth of fiber incidents it runs the copper line test instead of the fiber terminal check, and the logs show calls rejected for an invalid port argument before one finally succeeds. Each wrong call costs about nine seconds against a contractual first response of sixty. The two tools are described as a test on the subscriber loop and a test on the subscriber connection point, and both take a port argument, one as a string and one as an integer. Paula has one week before the next audit. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The model is mismatched to the task, and a more capable tier would tell two similar network tests apart and use the right parameter type.
options.feedback: A stronger model does read ambiguous descriptions better, but it spends seconds you do not have against a sixty-second commitment, and the ambiguity returns with the next pair of tools.

options.label: B
options.text: The tool descriptions never say when each test applies, and the arguments are easy to get wrong, so the agent is choosing by resemblance.
options.feedback: Correct: wrong paths point at tool descriptions and invalid-parameter errors point at descriptions and examples, and both are fixed in the tool definitions rather than in the model.

options.label: C
options.text: The agent has too many tools loaded, and eleven definitions in context crowd the decision until it picks whichever one it read last.
options.feedback: Capability bloat is real and eleven tools is worth reviewing, but the agent is not choosing at random: it is choosing between two tools whose descriptions do not distinguish them.

options.label: D
options.text: The prompt lacks worked examples of fiber incidents, and three to five of them would teach the agent which test a fiber fault needs.
options.feedback: Examples help a model apply a rule it cannot infer, yet the rule is missing from the interface itself, so every prompt using these tools would need the same patch.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to read the symptom against the interface before reading it against the model. The guidance on writing tools for agents maps both symptoms directly: agents that go down completely wrong paths point at bad tool descriptions, and repeated errors for invalid parameters point at descriptions that need clearer wording and examples, or at arguments that should be made harder to get wrong. Both fixes are edits to the tool definitions, which fit in a week, add no latency and carry over to every prompt that uses those tools. The distinction against a model upgrade is the commitment in the contract: a heavier tier spends time you do not have to paper over a gap that two rewritten descriptions close.

RULE: If an engineer could not pick the right tool from its description, neither can the agent: fix the interface before you change the model.

TRAP: Reading a tool-selection error as a capability gap, when what the agent had to choose between were two descriptions that say the same thing.

TRY IT: Print the descriptions of two tools your agent confuses, hand them to a colleague with no context, and ask which one they would call for a given ticket.

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros holds a claim automatically whenever its fraud step flags it, and a held claim waits nine days on average. The regulator requires every automatic decision to be explainable to the policyholder, and the operations team cannot say how often a hold turns out to be unjustified, because nothing about the flags is tracked. Camila, who owns the product, has one sprint before the quarterly filing. What should she do first?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell the policyholder plainly why the claim was held and what to do next, and start tracking flag rates with precision and recall.
options.feedback: Correct: clear feedback to the affected person and regular measurement of what is being flagged are the documented practices for a system that blocks.

options.label: B
options.text: Have the model write a justification for each hold and show that generated text to the policyholder as the explanation of the decision.
options.feedback: A fluent narrative reads like an explanation, but nothing ties it to the signal that actually raised the flag, so it evidences neither the reason nor the rate.

options.label: C
options.text: Publish the fraud indicators the step relies on, so that any policyholder can check the reasoning behind a hold without help.
options.feedback: Transparency is about what the affected person can know about the system and its output, not about handing the detection rules to whoever wants to evade them.

options.label: D
options.text: Raise the flag threshold until the number of holds falls, so fewer policyholders are affected while the filing is prepared.
options.feedback: Moving a threshold without a measured error rate trades one unknown for another, and it leaves the policyholder exactly as uninformed as before.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that transparency concerns what the affected person can know about the system and its output, and it is separate from explaining the mechanism inside it. The documented production practice for a system that blocks or holds is to give the affected person clear feedback, to track what is being flagged, and to assess the classifier regularly with metrics such as precision and recall. Without that measurement Zafiro cannot say whether a hold is usually right, which is the first thing the regulator will ask about a nine-day wait. The distinction against having the model justify each hold is that a generated narrative reads like an explanation while carrying no evidence that it describes why the claim was flagged.

RULE: Transparency is telling the affected person what happened and what to do next; an explanation with no measured error rate behind it is a story, not evidence.

TRAP: Treating a fluent justification written after the fact as the explanation of a decision, when nothing links that text to the signal that triggered it.

TRY IT: Take fifty flags from last month, have a specialist label each one right or wrong, compute precision and recall, then read the message the policyholder received and check it says why and what to do.

options.label: B
options.text: The schema declares no required list, so every call that leaves a property out is rejected before the tool runs at all.
options.feedback: Marking properties required is sound schema hygiene, and it is not what these rejections are: the calls carry the wrong values rather than too few of them.

options.label: C
options.text: Neither the parameter names nor the one-line description says what value belongs in each field, which is the documented cause of invalid-parameter errors.
options.feedback: Correct: a parameter called user rather than user_id, under a description that explains nothing, is the documented source of invalid-parameter errors, and descriptions are named as the single biggest factor in tool performance.

options.label: D
options.text: The result answers with an internal identifier and transport fields instead of semantic ones, which is documented to cost precision on the next step.
options.feedback: Correct: the guidance is to drop low-level identifiers and return the fields the agent reasons with, because resolving opaque identifiers into meaningful language measurably improves precision and avoids repeat fetches.

options.label: E
options.text: Descriptions are not read once a definition is deferred, so rewriting this one adds tokens and changes nothing about how the tool gets called.
options.feedback: Deferral keeps a definition out of the context until it is needed; once the tool is surfaced its description is exactly what the model reads, and tool search matches against it as well.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a tool definition is an interface written for a reader who cannot ask questions, so both ends of it have to be legible: what goes in and what comes back. On the input side the documentation asks for unambiguous parameter names, offering user_id rather than user as its own example, and for a description covering what the tool does, when it applies, what each parameter means and what it does not return, at least three or four sentences; it also names errors for invalid parameters as the symptom of descriptions that are too thin. On the output side it asks for high-signal content: semantic, stable identifiers instead of opaque internal references, and only the fields the agent needs for its next step, which is why an agent handed an identifier and a transport field goes back for the document it already had. The distinction against the catalog-size answer is that this agent is failing inside the tools it chose, not while choosing among many.

RULE: Write the definition for a reader who cannot ask: name the parameters so they explain themselves, and answer with the fields the next step actually needs.

TRAP: Blaming the size of the catalog for failures that live inside one definition's parameter names and its return shape.

TRY IT: Hand your most-called tool's definition to a colleague with no context and ask them to fill its parameters, then look at its result and count the fields the agent never uses.

questions.question: Ceibo Telecom commits by contract to a first response within ninety seconds on corporate lines. The fault-diagnosis assistant drafts that response, and the quality team has shown that a second pass, in which the draft is reviewed against the diagnostic checklist and rewritten, fixes about a quarter of the weak answers. Each pass costs roughly twenty seconds, and on some cases the review keeps asking for the same change. How should the team build it?

options.label: A
options.text: A single pass with the checklist folded into the drafting prompt, since a review that can loop has no place inside a contractual window.
options.feedback: Folding the checklist in is the right instinct when refinement adds nothing measurable; here it was measured and it does, so this gives up a quarter of the weak answers unnecessarily.

options.label: B
options.text: Three drafts generated in parallel against the checklist, keeping the one the reviewer scores highest before the window closes.
options.feedback: Several attempts judged against each other buy confidence when the attempts differ, and this triples the drafting cost while leaving the window at the mercy of the slowest branch.

options.label: C
options.text: Draft and review in a loop with a hard cap on iterations and a fallback that sends the best draft so far when the cap is reached.
options.feedback: Correct: clear criteria plus measured gains from refinement is the fit for this pattern, and the documented failure mode of stalling loops is handled with an iteration limit and a fallback.

options.label: D
options.text: Draft and review in a loop that stops when the reviewer asks for no further change, with an alert raised when a case exceeds the window.
options.feedback: Letting the reviewer decide when to stop is exactly the loop that stalls when the generator cannot address the feedback, and an alert reports the breach instead of preventing it.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an evaluator and optimizer pair fits when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement provides measurable value, and both signals are present: the checklist is the criterion and a quarter of weak answers improve. Its documented operational failure is that iterative loops can stall when the generator cannot address the feedback, and the named mitigation is a maximum iteration limit with fallback strategies, which is what turns the pattern into something you can put under a ninety-second contract. The distinction against the single pass is that the gain here has been measured rather than assumed, so the reason to avoid the loop is unbounded latency, and a cap removes that reason.

RULE: Refine in a loop only when the criteria are clear and the gain is measured, and always bound it: a cap with a fallback is what makes the loop safe under a contract.

TRAP: Leaving the stopping condition to the reviewer, so a loop that cannot converge spends the whole window before anyone notices.

TRY IT: Run your review step over twenty real drafts, count how many needed a third pass, and time what a two-pass cap would have cost against your own window.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://claude.com/blog/multi-agent-coordination-patterns

questions.question: Terminal Puerto Claro runs a manifest assistant for hauliers whose booking window is measured in minutes, and it retrieves rows from the manifest database through a search tool. On every failing case the traces show that the correct rows were returned, yet the assistant names the wrong container. Each row arrives with forty fields, among them internal identifiers, mime types and thumbnail links, while the consignee appears only as a party identifier. With a carrier review in two weeks, where should Ignacio look?

options.label: A
options.text: At the number of rows the tool returns, since a wider candidate set would give the assistant more chances to find the right container.
options.feedback: Returning more rows is the fix when the right one is missing, but the traces show it was already present in every failing case.

options.label: B
options.text: At the ranking, by adding a reranking pass over the rows so that the most relevant one arrives at the top of the list.
options.feedback: Reranking repairs a correct row buried far down a list; here the row reaches the prompt and the assistant still reads it wrongly.

options.label: C
options.text: At index freshness, since confidently wrong answers of this kind usually follow a content refresh the retrieval index has not picked up.
options.feedback: A stale index is a real cause of confident errors, but its signature is language that no longer exists in the source, not a correct row read wrongly.

options.label: D
options.text: At the shape of the tool result, trimming it to high-signal fields and resolving opaque identifiers into names the model can use.
options.feedback: Correct: when retrieval delivers and the answer still fails, the documented place to look is the result format rather than the retrieval stage.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to separate a retrieval failure from a grounding failure before touching the pipeline. The traces settle which one this is: the rows the answer needs come back every time, so no change to recall, ranking or index freshness can help. The documented guidance for tool results is to return only high-signal information and to avoid low-level technical identifiers, because fields such as names are what inform the agent's next action, while resolving opaque identifiers into meaningful language measurably improves precision and reduces hallucination. Forty fields of mostly internal plumbing, with the consignee hidden behind an identifier, is exactly the result shape that defeats a retrieval stage that has already done its job.

RULE: When the right rows come back and the answer is still wrong, fix the result format, not the retrieval.

TRAP: Reading every wrong answer as a retrieval failure, when the trace already proves the evidence reached the model.

TRY IT: Print one raw tool result from your agent, cross out every field a human reviewer would not need in order to answer the question, and count the share of tokens you just removed.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

questions.question: AndesWare packaged its release-notes workflow as a custom Skill so that 400 developers stop pasting the same instructions. The platform team attaches it from the API like this: {"container": {"skills": [{"type": "custom", "skill_id": "skill_01ab", "version": "latest"}]}, "tools": [{"name": "search_prs", "description": "Finds merged pull requests"}]}. In the nightly pipeline the Skill never activates: the model answers from the conversation and the notes come back in the old shape. The pipeline runs for every squad and has to produce the same document every time. What does this configuration produce?

options.label: A
options.text: The Skill is never loaded, because Skills attached through the API require the code execution tool and this request declares only a search tool.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented API integration delivers Skills in the container parameter and requires the code execution tool, which is the runtime that reads the Skill's files.

options.label: B
options.text: The Skill loads and its whole body is added to every request, which is why the nightly run costs more and its output drifts between squads.
options.feedback: Until a Skill is triggered only its name and description sit in context, around a hundred tokens, and the body loads on activation; installed Skills are not what makes a request expensive.

options.label: C
options.text: The Skill is rejected because more than twenty Skills would be attached to one request once every squad has a version of its own.
options.feedback: Twenty Skills per request is the documented ceiling and a single Skill is nowhere near it, so the count is not what is stopping this from running.

options.label: D
options.text: The Skill loads, and pinning the version to latest is what makes the nightly document reproducible from one run to the next.
options.feedback: Latest is the opposite of a pin: it resolves to whatever the newest version is that day, which is what a pipeline that must repeat itself should avoid.

questions.explanation:
The general rule with Skills is that packaging is only half the configuration. A Skill attached through the API is delivered inside the container parameter and needs the code execution tool in the same request, because that is the runtime that loads the Skill's instructions and bundled files; without it the model simply answers from the conversation, which is what the pipeline shows. A second defect waits behind the first: a version of latest floats to the newest version, so a nightly job that must emit the same document should pin an explicit version instead. The distinction against the cost explanation is that an unused Skill costs about a hundred tokens of metadata, not the weight of its body.

RULE: A Skill attached from the API needs the code execution tool in the same request, and a pipeline that must repeat itself pins a version instead of taking latest.

TRAP: Assuming that attaching a Skill is enough to run it, when the runtime that loads it was never declared in the request.

TRY IT: Attach one Skill from the API without the code execution tool and then with it, and compare whether the Skill appears in the response and what the run costs.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/skills-guide https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview

questions.question: Red Vicuña Salud triages incoming patient messages into six categories. The emergency category is about two percent of the volume and a missed one is the failure the medical direction cares about, while the other categories tolerate an occasional error. The team has budget for a second look at the messages the first classification flags as possibly urgent, but not for the whole stream. What should they do with that subset?

options.label: A
options.text: Split the triage into independent subtasks run at the same time, with one instance reading symptoms and another reading clinical history.
options.feedback: Breaking a task into independent subtasks run in parallel is the other face of the same pattern, and it divides the work rather than raising confidence in one decision.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the same classification on the flagged subset several times and act on the agreement between the runs.
options.feedback: Correct: running the same task multiple times is what this pattern offers when several attempts are needed for higher confidence, and the flagged subset keeps the cost inside the budget.

options.label: C
options.text: Send the flagged subset to the most capable model in the family and take its single classification as the final answer.
options.feedback: A more capable model raises the average, and one answer still gives no measure of how sure the system is about the case in front of it.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a line to the triage prompt telling the model to err on the side of caution whenever an emergency is possible.
options.feedback: Wording can shift the threshold, and it moves errors from one side to the other rather than producing a second opinion on the cases that matter.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that parallelization comes in two forms, and they answer different questions: sectioning breaks a task into independent subtasks run at the same time, while voting runs the same task several times when multiple attempts are needed for higher confidence. What the medical direction wants here is confidence in one decision, so the second form is the fit, and restricting it to the messages already flagged is what keeps a repeated call affordable on two percent of the stream instead of all of it. The distinction against sectioning is that dividing the decision into symptom reading and history reading produces two partial views, not a measure of agreement on the category.

RULE: Split the task when the subtasks are independent; repeat the task when what you need is confidence in one answer.

TRAP: Confusing sectioning with voting, so a decision is divided into parts when what was missing is a measure of how sure the system is.

TRY IT: Take two hundred triaged messages, run the emergency classification three times on each, and see how often the runs disagree and what those disagreements look like.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

questions.question: A platform team is working through the Security Rule safeguards for a system that stores electronic protected health information, and one of the implementation specifications it has to apply is labeled addressable rather than required. What does that label mean?

options.label: A
options.text: It is optional, so the team may leave it out whenever it judges the residual risk to that data to be low.
options.feedback: This is the most common misreading of the word. The designation does not make a specification optional, and skipping one on a judgment call alone is not compliant.

options.label: B
options.text: It becomes mandatory only once a breach involving that particular safeguard has been reported to the regulator.
options.feedback: Nothing in the rule defers a safeguard until an incident. Risk analysis is a standing obligation that has to be performed and re-evaluated regularly.

options.label: C
options.text: It has to be implemented exactly as written, and no equivalent alternative is accepted in its place.
options.feedback: That describes a required specification. The addressable designation exists precisely to allow a documented equivalent where the written one does not fit.

options.label: D
options.text: The team implements it, or documents why it is not reasonable there and puts an equivalent alternative in place.
options.feedback: Correct: the choice is between the specification and a documented equivalent, assessed against what is reasonable and appropriate in that environment.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that an addressable specification is not an optional one. Required specifications must be implemented, while the addressable designation explicitly does not mean optional: the entity assesses whether the specification is a reasonable and appropriate safeguard in its environment and, where it does not implement it, documents that rationale and implements an equivalent alternative measure where reasonable. The choice is therefore between the control and a documented substitute, never between the control and nothing. The distinction against reading it as required is that required leaves no room for an alternative, while addressable does, provided the reasoning is written down and kept.

RULE: Addressable does not mean optional: you implement it, or you document why it does not fit and implement something equivalent instead.

TRAP: Reading addressable as discretionary, when the only discretion it grants is the choice of an equivalent safeguard that you then have to document.

TRY IT: Pick one addressable specification in your own environment and write the two lines the rule expects: why the specification as written does not fit, and what equivalent measure stands in for it.

SOURCE: https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html

questions.question: The Agencia Nacional de Ingresos runs an agent over taxpayer filings that can attach an internal note, request documentation from the taxpayer and reclassify a filing. Four officers confirm every tool call today, and the queue is four days behind on a flow of 9,000 filings a day. The agency's audit rules say that any action reaching the taxpayer or changing the record has to be attributable to a named officer who approved it. What should Sofía, the technical lead, change?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch the session to the mode where a model classifier approves or denies each call, keeping a person only for the exceptions.
options.feedback: That mode swaps the human for a model judgment, which is exactly what an audit rule demanding a named officer will not accept for those actions.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the confirmation on every call and add two more officers to the rota, since removing any gate weakens the control audit relies on.
options.feedback: More reviewers on the same reflex buys throughput, not control: a prompt on every call is the documented recipe for approval fatigue.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the confirmation only on the calls that reach the taxpayer or change the record, and let the internal notes run without a prompt.
options.feedback: Correct: the gate stays exactly where the audit rule bites, and the steps nobody outside the agency ever sees stop competing for the officers' attention.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the confirmations and log every tool call with the officer's identity, so that the audit trail stays complete afterwards.
options.feedback: Logging is required and useful, but it records what happened. It does not place anybody in the loop before an irreversible action is taken.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is to spend the human gate where it changes the outcome: a confirmation on every call degrades into a reflex, and the documented failure is approval fatigue, where a very high approval rate creates a false sense of security instead of control. Scoping the prompt to the calls that leave the agency or alter the record keeps a named officer accountable exactly where the audit rule bites, and lets the internal steps run at the volume the queue demands. The distinction against handing approval to a model classifier is that the rule asks for a named officer, and a classifier is a model judgment rather than a person. Logging after the fact records what happened; it does not decide whether it happens.

RULE: Put the human gate where the action cannot be undone: a prompt on every call becomes a reflex, and a reflex is not a control.

TRAP: Confusing a complete audit log with a human in the loop: one tells you what happened, the other decides whether it happens at all.

TRY IT: List every tool your agent can call, mark the ones that leave your organization or change a record, and count what share of last week's confirmations were for calls that were neither.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions

Four officers confirm every tool call today, and the queue is four days behind on a flow of 9,000 filings a day. The agency's audit rules say that any action reaching the taxpayer or changing the record has to be attributable to a named officer who approved it. What should Sofía, the technical lead, change?
options: Switch the session to the mode where a model classifier approves or denies each call, keeping a person only for the exceptions.
Keep the confirmation on every call and add two more officers to the rota, since removing any gate weakens the control audit relies on.
Keep the confirmation only on the calls that reach the taxpayer or change the record, and let the internal notes run without a prompt.
Remove the confirmations and log every tool call with the officer's identity, so that the audit trail stays complete afterwards.
html.explanation:
The general rule is to spend the human gate where it changes the outcome: a confirmation on every call degrades into a reflex, and the documented failure is approval fatigue, where a very high approval rate creates a false sense of security instead of control. Scoping the prompt to the calls that leave the agency or alter the record keeps a named officer accountable exactly where the audit rule bites, and lets the internal steps run at the volume the queue demands. The distinction against handing approval to a model classifier is that the rule asks for a named officer, and a classifier is a model judgment rather than a person. Logging after the fact records what happened; it does not decide whether it happens.

RULE: Put the human gate where the action cannot be undone: a prompt on every call becomes a reflex, and a reflex is not a control.

TRAP: Confusing a complete audit log with a human in the loop: one tells you what happened, the other decides whether it happens at all.

TRY IT: List every tool your agent can call, mark the ones that leave your organization or change a record, and count what share of last week's confirmations were for calls that were neither.

questions.question: Zafiro Seguros put the claims triage agent live after an eval suite scored 94% on a thousand labeled claims. In the first fortnight the cost per claim came out at three times the estimate, the ninety-fifth percentile response time missed the broker portal's budget, and a spot review found two replies quoting another policyholder's claim history. The suite still scores 94% and reproduces none of it. The regulator's audit is in six weeks. Which TWO gaps in the measurement explain what the suite could not see? (Select TWO)

options.label: A
options.text: The suite used a judge model weaker than the model under test, so its verdicts were never trustworthy at this scale.
options.feedback: Grading with a different model than the one being graded is the documented practice, and a weak judge is a real failure mode; none of these three symptoms is a grading disagreement.

options.label: B
options.text: The suite ran one trial per case, so part of the score is variance that a second and third run would have removed.
options.feedback: Repeating each case is how you separate a result from noise and is worth doing, but it would not have produced a cost figure, a latency figure or a privacy check.

options.label: C
options.text: The suite carries no business measure such as deflection rate or satisfaction, which is what a fortnight in production reveals.
options.feedback: Business-impact measures belong on the scorecard, yet by definition they are read after launch, so their absence is not what made these failures invisible beforehand.

options.label: D
options.text: The suite records only whether the answer was right, with no latency, cost per claim, turns or tool calls beside each result.
options.feedback: Correct: the documented metric set for agent evals tracks latency, token usage, cost per task, turns and tool calls alongside correctness, which is what would have priced this launch.

options.label: E
options.text: The suite has no safety or privacy criterion, such as the share of replies leaking another policyholder's data over a defined sample.
options.feedback: Correct: safety and privacy are written as measurable criteria over a stated sample, and a dimension with no metric cannot fail a release.

questions.explanation:
The general rule is that a launch decision needs a multidimensional criterion rather than one accuracy number: the documented worked example pairs an accuracy target with a toxicity share, an error-severity distribution and a response-time percentile on the same held-out set. Two of those dimensions are missing here. Nothing beside each result records latency, cost per claim, turns or tool calls, so the suite could not have predicted either the bill or the percentile; and nothing states safety or privacy as a number over a defined sample, so a reply carrying another policyholder's data was never a failing case. The distinction against the judge and trial-count answers is that both would change how precisely the 94% is measured, and neither adds a dimension the suite does not have.

RULE: Measure every dimension you would refuse to launch without: accuracy on its own cannot fail a system for being slow, expensive or unsafe.

TRAP: Reading a single high accuracy number as readiness, when the dimensions that broke the launch were never given a metric.

TRY IT: Take your current eval report and mark which of accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security it gives a number for; the blanks are the risks you are shipping unmeasured.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

questions.question: Grupo Aurora Educación generates practice exercise sets with worked solutions for 180,000 students. The academic board will not publish a set that scores below 92% on its review rubric, and the per-student budget caps the unit cost at about 2.5 times the cheapest configuration measured. A sweep over 400 sets on the model in use reads: low effort 78%, default effort 86%, highest effort 87%, at 1.0, 2.3 and 4.1 times that cheapest cost. Camila has now swept the whole curve and still misses the floor. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the effort to its highest level and publish at that quality, since it is the best score the sweep measured on the model in use.
options.feedback: The sweep already prices that move: one point of rubric score for nearly twice the cost of the default, still five points under the floor and past the cap the budget sets.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the default effort and add three to five worked examples to the prompt, which is the documented way to lift a rubric score cheaply.
options.feedback: Examples are the documented lever for format, tone and consistency, and the gap here is six points of judgment on the hardest sets, which a few examples do not close.

options.label: C
options.text: Pair the model in use with a stronger advisor it can consult on the hard sets, so most sets keep the cheap path and only the difficult ones cost more.
options.feedback: An advisor pairing can lift a weaker executor, and its documented precondition is to price the stronger model alone at low effort first, because that is the number the pairing has to beat.

options.label: D
options.text: Measure the next tier up at its low effort setting, which is the documented move once effort has been swept and the bar is still missed.
options.feedback: Correct: the decision table sends a workload whose quality is short to the next tier at low effort, rather than to the current tier at a higher one, and that measurement is also the baseline any multi-model scheme has to beat.

questions.explanation:
The general rule for model selection is to move effort before models, and then to move tier before effort a second time. The documented decision table reads exactly that way: when cost is too high and quality is fine, sweep effort down on the current model; when quality is not good enough, restore effort if it was lowered, and otherwise try the next tier up at its low setting. The sweep here has already walked the current model's whole curve, which flattens at 87, five points under the board's floor, while the last step passes the cap the budget sets, so there is nothing left to buy on this tier. Measuring the tier above at low effort is also the number any two-model arrangement would have to beat, which is why it comes before the advisor pairing rather than after it.

RULE: When effort is swept and the quality bar is still missed, the next move is the tier above at its low setting, not the tier you have at its highest.

TRAP: Reading a flat effort curve as the ceiling of what is possible and paying for the top setting, when the documented escalation is a stronger tier at low effort.

TRY IT: Plot your workload's score against cost at every effort level of the model you run today, then price the next tier up at its low setting and add that point to the same plot.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/choosing-a-model

questions.question: A pharmacy benefits platform is preparing an evaluation framework for a Claude workflow that classifies member emails, drafts a concise case summary, avoids exposing unnecessary personal information, and responds in a regulated customer-service tone. The team wants the framework to guide prompt and model iterations before launch. Which evaluation design is strongest?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a small expert-curated benchmark first; use human ratings for all dimensions; delay automation until inter-rater agreement is perfect; omit rare cases initially.
options.feedback: Human grading can be flexible and high quality, but it is slow and expensive compared with automated grading. Omitting rare cases weakens the evaluation because edge cases are explicitly part of good eval design.

options.label: B
options.text: Use an LLM grader for every criterion immediately; ask for free-form qualitative judgments; aggregate the comments into a score; expand once outputs look plausible.
options.feedback: LLM-based grading is useful for complex judgments, but it should be tested for reliability before scaling. Free-form qualitative comments are harder to assess quickly and consistently than specific outputs such as binary labels or a defined ordinal scale.

options.label: C
options.text: Select exact-match accuracy as the primary target; sample only the most frequent email templates; score every output against one golden label; review failures after launch.
options.feedback: Exact match can be useful for categorical outputs, such as intent classification, but it is too narrow for summaries, privacy preservation, tone, and latency. Sampling only frequent templates also misses edge cases and does not mirror the full real-world task distribution.

options.label: D
options.text: Define measurable success criteria across task fidelity, consistency, privacy, tone, and operational metrics; build production-like test cases with edge cases; combine exact-match, similarity, and rubric-based LLM graders.
options.feedback: This approach starts with specific and measurable success criteria across multiple dimensions, which matches how LLM applications should be evaluated. It also uses a mixed grading strategy, applying simpler automated methods where they fit and rubric-based LLM grading where judgment is needed.

questions.explanation:
Effective evaluation design starts by defining specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant success criteria, not by choosing a single grader or metric. Anthropic notes that most use cases need multidimensional evaluation, so a workflow like this should assess task fidelity, consistency, privacy preservation, tone, and operational concerns rather than treating one scalar accuracy number as sufficient. See Define success criteria.

The dataset should resemble the real task distribution and include edge cases, because evals are only useful if they expose the failures the application will face in production. Mixed methodologies are appropriate: use code-based checks such as exact match where outputs are categorical and unambiguous, use similarity metrics where semantic consistency matters, and use LLM-based graders with detailed rubrics for nuanced judgments such as tone or privacy. Anthropic's guidance also favors automating where possible and using LLM graders with empirical outputs, such as correct or incorrect or a 1 to 5 scale, after testing reliability. See Develop tests.
