questions.question: A marine insurance underwriting team is designing two Claude-powered workflows. One extracts a fixed set of fields from standardized claim emails at very high volume, where unit cost is a major constraint. The other helps senior underwriters analyze unusual loss scenarios, where reasoning quality matters more than raw speed. The architecture review board wants a model strategy that supports cost, productivity, and performance goals without overbuilding. What should the architect recommend?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the lowest-cost Claude model for both workflows and add retries when answers are weak.
options.feedback: This option is incorrect because it optimizes for unit cost while ignoring task fidelity and productivity. Retries can increase latency and cost, and they do not reliably compensate for choosing a model that cannot meet the reasoning requirements.

options.label: B
options.text: Match the model and effort level to each workflow based on measured quality, latency, and cost targets.
options.feedback: This option is correct because the two workflows have different business value drivers. Anthropic guidance treats model selection and effort as architecture tradeoffs among capability, speed, and cost, so each workload should be evaluated against its own targets.

options.label: C
options.text: Choose one Claude model for both workflows to reduce operational variation across the platform.
options.feedback: This option is incorrect because operational simplicity is only one design concern. A single-model strategy can be reasonable in some environments, but it is not the best fit when the workloads have clearly different cost, latency, and capability needs.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the most capable Claude model and maximum effort level for both workflows from the start.
options.feedback: This option is incorrect because it optimizes for capability without regard to cost or latency. It may be appropriate for the hardest reasoning workload, but it overbuilds the high-volume extraction workflow unless evaluations show that level of capability is required.

questions.explanation:
Architecture decisions for Claude systems should be tied to business value pillars such as cost, productivity, quality, and performance SLAs. Model choice is not just a technical preference; it is a tradeoff among capability, response speed, and production cost. Anthropic’s model guidance emphasizes comparing models based on workload requirements rather than defaulting to the largest or smallest model for every use case.

For a high-volume, standardized extraction workflow, the right design is often to test whether a faster, lower-cost model and an appropriate effort setting meet the required quality threshold. For complex underwriting reasoning, a more capable model or higher effort may be justified because the value of better reasoning outweighs incremental latency or cost. The key is to validate these choices with evaluations and measurements, not with assumptions.

The strongest architecture recommendation is therefore to segment workloads and choose the least expensive, lowest-latency configuration that still meets the required business outcome for each one. See Anthropic’s Models overview and Effort documentation for the relevant model-selection and effort tradeoffs.

questions.question: A city transit authority's digital services group is proposing a Claude feature that investigates rider complaints by pulling logs, summarizing evidence, and sending a result to an operations manager later. Product leaders ask why the team should not simply build the whole workflow on direct prompt calls. Which architectural recommendation best communicates the trade-off?

options.label: A
options.text: Recommend streaming Messages responses for the workflow, and use SSE events as the mechanism for multi-hour task persistence.
options.feedback: Streaming is useful for receiving incremental response events from a Messages request. It is not a persistence or orchestration model for multi-hour task execution.

options.label: B
options.text: Recommend Message Batches for the editor workflow, and use the discount as the primary reason for production routing.
options.feedback: Batch processing can reduce cost for large volumes of Messages requests when immediate responses are not required. It does not replace an agent harness for an operational workflow that investigates, manages state, and reports results over time.

options.label: C
options.text: Recommend Claude Managed Agents for the asynchronous workflow, and reserve the Messages API for cases needing a custom agent loop.
options.feedback: This correctly maps the architectural choice to the workload shape. Claude Managed Agents are documented as a pre-built configurable agent harness suited to long-running and asynchronous work, while the Messages API is better when the team needs direct prompting access and fine-grained loop control.

options.label: D
options.text: Recommend the Messages API for the asynchronous workflow, and rely on it to preserve prior turns between requests.
options.feedback: This is plausible if the team wants full control, but it misstates how the Messages API handles state. The Messages API is stateless, so the application must send the relevant conversation history on each request.

questions.explanation:
The architectural distinction to communicate is not that one surface is universally better, but that each optimizes for a different responsibility boundary. The Messages API gives direct model prompting access and fine-grained control, which is valuable when your application owns the loop, state, retries, tool orchestration, and lifecycle decisions. That flexibility also means the API is stateless, so your system must provide the conversation history and manage continuity.

Claude Managed Agents shift more of that agent harness responsibility into managed infrastructure. For a workflow that may run beyond a single synchronous interaction and report back later, that is the trade-off stakeholders need to understand: less custom control over every loop detail, but a better fit for long-running and asynchronous work. See the official comparison in Working with the Messages API.

Batch processing and streaming solve different problems. Message Batches are for high-volume asynchronous request processing and cost reduction, not for replacing an agent lifecycle. Streaming over SSE improves response delivery for a request, but it should not be presented as durable multi-hour task persistence.

questions.question: A renewable energy trading desk asks its AI platform team to use Claude to summarize daily market risk memos. Traders, compliance reviewers, and operations staff each describe the target as “usable,” but they have not agreed on what makes a summary acceptable, what examples should be tested, or which latency and cost constraints matter. The product sponsor wants engineers to begin prompt iterations so there is something to show next week. What should the architect do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Draft several prompt variants using the sponsor’s wording, then let stakeholders choose the most appealing demo output.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it starts prompt engineering before the team has defined what success means or how outputs will be tested. A demo can create momentum, but it can also optimize for subjective appeal rather than durable requirements.

options.label: B
options.text: Adopt a single user satisfaction score, then tune prompts until that score improves across early stakeholder reviews.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because most production use cases need multiple success dimensions rather than one universal metric. A satisfaction score may be useful, but it is too coarse to capture factuality, relevance, privacy, latency, and price tradeoffs.

options.label: C
options.text: Facilitate a discovery session to define measurable criteria, representative eval cases, and nonfunctional targets before prompt iteration.
options.feedback: This is correct because the team lacks agreed success criteria, evaluation data, and constraints. Structured discovery should turn vague stakeholder language into measurable targets before engineering effort focuses on prompt changes.

options.label: D
options.text: Select the most capable available model first, then defer evaluation design until traders report recurring issues.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because model selection should be informed by task requirements and evaluation results. Using a stronger model may help some criteria, but it does not replace discovery around quality, compliance, latency, and cost.

questions.explanation:
When stakeholders use broad terms like “usable,” the architect’s job is to convert that language into specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant criteria that can guide evaluation and lifecycle decisions. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes replacing vague goals with measurable task targets, often across several dimensions such as task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy preservation, context use, latency, and price. See Define success criteria.

Prompt iteration is valuable, but it should not be the first move when the team has not defined success or an empirical test method. The prompt engineering overview assumes that success criteria, ways to test against them, and an initial prompt foundation are already in place, and recommends establishing those basics first when they are missing. See Prompt engineering overview.

Discovery also prevents treating every requirement gap as a prompting problem. If latency or cost fails an evaluation, a model choice or architecture change may be a better lever than further prompt edits. Good requirement gathering therefore captures both output-quality expectations and operational constraints before the team commits to a solution path.

questions.question: A university library's digital archives group is adding Claude to answer researchers' questions over 700,000 OCR-corrected finding-aid notes and object descriptions. Researchers usually ask thematic questions, such as finding records about mutual aid networks in immigrant neighborhoods, and the team needs source attribution without sending the full archive in every request. Which integration approach best matches this data shape and query pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Attach the Web Search tool, set max_uses for each request, and let Claude search for archive topics.
options.feedback: Web Search is designed for current, changing, or open-ended web information, not for searching a private internal archive. Capping searches controls usage, but it does not make web search the right retrieval mechanism for a curated offline corpus.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Web Fetch for archive questions, retrieve matching pages during the request, and summarize fetched content.
options.feedback: Web Fetch is appropriate when the prompt identifies a specific page or document to retrieve. It is not a general semantic search layer for open-ended thematic questions across a large collection.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a semantic embedding index, retrieve relevant chunks per query, and provide them as search_result blocks.
options.feedback: This matches a large private corpus with semantic, thematic queries because embeddings support similarity-based retrieval without putting the whole archive in context. Returning the retrieved chunks as search_result blocks gives Claude structured retrieval results suitable for source attribution.

options.label: D
options.text: Place the complete archive in the prompt, enable prompt caching, and ask Claude to find relevant passages.
options.feedback: Prompt caching can reduce cost and latency for repeated prefixes, but cached tokens still count toward the context window. Sending an entire 700,000-record archive is not a scalable retrieval strategy and can degrade quality as irrelevant context grows.

questions.question: A robotics manufacturer's developer productivity team is reviewing a Claude agent that answers build-failure questions. The agent is configured with 42 tools spanning CI, package registry, deployment, incident management, and repository systems. In practice, users ask it to inspect failed jobs, read recent commits, and open follow-up issues. The team sees confused tool calls and wants to reduce capability bloat without losing the needed workflow. Which change is best?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the full catalog and add prompts warning Claude not to use unrelated tools.
options.feedback: Prompt guidance can help, but it does not remove unused capabilities or their context cost. The unrelated tools remain available for selection, so the core capability-bloat problem is still present.

options.label: B
options.text: Set tool_choice to any so Claude must call one of the configured tools.
options.feedback: This changes whether Claude must call a tool, not which tools are available. It can make capability bloat worse in practice because the model must choose from the same oversized catalog even when no tool is appropriate.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to a higher-capability model while preserving the same tool catalog.
options.feedback: A stronger model may improve reasoning, but it does not reduce the number of tools, their schemas, or their exposure. The configuration still carries unnecessary context and operational surface area.

options.label: D
options.text: Expose only the tools needed for failed-job inspection, commit lookup, and issue creation.
options.feedback: This directly reduces the number and scope of tools available to the agent while preserving the workflow users actually need. A smaller, task-specific toolset also reduces tool-definition context and makes tool selection easier.

questions.explanation:
Tool configuration is part of system architecture, not just prompt decoration. When a request includes tools, their names, descriptions, and schemas consume input tokens, and tool interactions can add tool_use and tool_result content to the conversation. The official Tool use overview explains these execution and context boundaries.

The best mitigation for capability bloat is to narrow the available capabilities to the workflow the agent is meant to perform. Here, failed-job inspection, commit lookup, and issue creation are the needed actions, while deployment and incident-management tools add avoidable selection surface. Anthropic's Implement tool use guidance also emphasizes clear tool definitions with boundaries, consolidation of related operations, and avoiding bloated tool responses.

Controls such as tool_choice do not solve overexposure. any requires Claude to call one of the provided tools, while auto lets Claude decide whether to call a tool, but neither removes an unnecessary tool from consideration. Prompts and larger models are compensating measures at best; they do not reduce context overhead or the agent's available capabilities.

questions.question: An online education platform's AI architecture group is adding Claude to two product areas: automatic tagging of millions of short lesson comments for moderation routing, and an instructor copilot that helps redesign struggling course modules. Leadership wants cost control without missing latency expectations for the tagging path or reducing quality where expert instructors depend on nuanced analysis. Which TWO recommendations should the architect include?

options.label: A
options.text: Route each workflow through a model selected for its tested capability, speed, and cost profile.
options.feedback: This is correct because model selection should reflect the business value and operating constraints of each workflow. A high-volume routing task and a nuanced redesign assistant are likely to justify different capability, latency, and cost tradeoffs once tested.

options.label: B
options.text: Standardize both workflows on the highest-capability model and maximum effort setting for operational simplicity.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it may overbuild the high-volume tagging path and increase cost or latency without a measured need. Operational simplicity is valuable, but it should not override the stated business constraints across distinct workloads.

options.label: C
options.text: Define quality, latency, and unit-cost targets, then tune model choice and effort against representative evals.
options.feedback: This is correct because success criteria need to be specific and measurable before architecture choices can be optimized. Testing model choice and effort against representative workloads helps avoid optimizing only for cost, only for speed, or only for quality.

options.label: D
options.text: Choose the lowest-cost model for both workflows and add manual review after user complaints appear.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it treats cost as the only value pillar and delays quality measurement until after users are affected. A low-cost model may be appropriate for some tasks, but it should be validated against the workflow's required quality and latency targets.

questions.explanation:
Good Claude architectures align technical choices with the business value of each workflow. The right model is not simply the most capable or the cheapest one, it is the one whose capability, speed, and cost profile fits the job being done. Anthropic's Models overview frames model choice as a practical selection decision across capability and cost, rather than a single default for every use case.

For production systems, the architect should convert business goals into measurable acceptance criteria. The guidance in Define success criteria and build evaluations emphasizes specific, measurable targets, including task fidelity, latency, and price. The effort setting can also be tuned as part of this tradeoff, but it should be evaluated against real examples because higher effort can improve difficult reasoning while increasing token use and latency.

The main anti-pattern is optimizing one pillar in isolation. Using the highest-capability model everywhere can waste budget and harm responsiveness for routine high-volume work, while using the lowest-cost model everywhere can miss quality requirements for expert-facing transformation workflows. Segmenting workloads and validating them with representative evals is the practical way to preserve productivity, cost discipline, and performance SLAs together.

questions.question: A precision agriculture analytics team is iterating on a Claude workflow that drafts irrigation recommendations for growers. A revised prompt appears to improve citation consistency in demos, but the team also cares about recommendation usefulness, tone, safety, latency, and cost. Which plan best supports deciding whether the revised prompt should replace the baseline?

options.label: A
options.text: Define measurable criteria, run both prompt versions on representative eval cases with edge cases, automate grading where reliable, and compare results against the baseline.
options.feedback: This approach starts with measurable success criteria and compares the revised prompt against the existing baseline on task-specific evals. It also reflects the recommended preference for scalable automated grading where reliable, while preserving edge cases and multiple evaluation dimensions.

options.label: B
options.text: Compare a few outputs in the Console, select the prompt with the higher 5-point quality score, and promote it without checking latency or cost.
options.feedback: The Console evaluation workflow can compare prompt outputs and use 5-point grading, so this is plausible for early iteration. It is incorrect because a few examples and one quality score do not cover a representative distribution or criteria such as latency, cost, and safety.

options.label: C
options.text: Ship the revised prompt to all growers, monitor support tickets for common complaints, and adjust the prompt after a week of production use.
options.feedback: This skips controlled comparison against the baseline and relies on noisy downstream feedback. Support tickets can be useful signals, but they are not a substitute for defined success criteria and empirical evaluation before rollout.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask a small expert panel to review only the most difficult failures, choose the preferred wording, and skip broader automated testing.
options.feedback: Expert review can help with nuanced judgments, but using only a small set of difficult failures creates a biased eval sample. The documented eval design guidance favors task-specific eval sets that mirror the real distribution and automation where feasible.

questions.explanation:
Good iteration starts by making the comparison measurable. Anthropic's guidance emphasizes that prompt engineering should follow clear success criteria, empirical tests, and a baseline prompt, rather than relying on demos or intuition alone. For a production workflow, the criteria should usually be multidimensional, so citation consistency should be evaluated alongside usefulness, tone, safety, latency, and cost.

A sound A/B style evaluation compares the revised prompt to the current baseline on a representative eval set, including realistic edge cases. Code-based grading is preferred when the output has clear objective properties, while LLM-based or human grading can be reserved for nuanced judgments after its reliability is tested. The Claude Console can help compare prompt versions and re-run an eval suite, but its documented role is iterative evaluation, not live production traffic splitting.

For more detail, see Anthropic's Prompt engineering overview, Define success criteria and build evaluations, and Claude Console Evaluation tool.

questions.question: A biomedical imaging startup's platform team is investigating intermittent Claude API failures in a production annotation service. Their logs currently show only timestamps and HTTP status codes, and engineers have been grouping 429 and 529 responses under the same incident category. Which change best improves the team's debugging and operational triage workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Capture request IDs and error types, then route 429 and 529 responses through distinct runbook paths.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude API failures include structured status and error-type information that should drive triage. Capturing the request ID also gives support and engineering teams a concrete identifier for investigating a specific API response.

options.label: B
options.text: Capture stop reasons and output tokens, then route max_tokens and pause_turn cases through incident escalation.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because stop_reason appears on successful Messages API responses rather than being the API error mechanism. Values such as max_tokens and pause_turn can explain why a successful response stopped, but they do not replace error status, error type, or request ID logging.

options.label: C
options.text: Capture full request payloads and response text, then retry every 4xx and 5xx response with identical backoff.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because not all 4xx responses are transient or appropriate to retry. Official SDKs already retry specific transient failures by default, and a useful incident workflow should preserve structured error details rather than relying on full payload capture.

options.label: D
options.text: Capture only status codes and timestamps, then route 429 and 529 responses through one rate-limit workflow.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because 429 and 529 represent different operational conditions. A 429 indicates rate limiting or acceleration-limit behavior, while a 529 indicates platform overload, so combining them hides the likely remediation path.

questions.explanation:
Operational debugging for Claude integrations should preserve the identifiers and classifications that make an incident traceable. The API returns specific HTTP status and error-type pairs, and every response includes a request-id header, while error bodies also include request_id. Capturing these values lets teams correlate a user-visible failure with API-side diagnostics and provide the right information when escalating to support.

The key triage distinction in this scenario is that 429 and 529 should not be treated as the same condition. A 429 rate_limit_error points to rate limits or acceleration limits and may include retry-after, while a 529 overloaded_error indicates platform overload. The official SDKs retry transient failures automatically twice by default using exponential backoff, but retry behavior does not remove the need to classify and log failures correctly.

stop_reason is useful for interpreting successful Messages API responses, for example whether the model ended normally, hit max_tokens, or paused. It is not the right primary signal for API error triage. For the documented error model and request ID behavior, see Anthropic API errors; for rate-limit behavior, see Anthropic API rate limits.

questions.question: A commercial aviation maintenance group is deploying a Claude agent that reviews aircraft sensor alerts, drafts technician notes, and can open maintenance work orders. Most work orders are routine, but grounding an aircraft immediately affects operations and must be reviewed by a licensed maintenance controller. Which design best preserves useful automation while reducing the risk of an unreviewed high-impact action?

options.label: A
options.text: Require Claude to explain its confidence before opening each maintenance work order.
options.feedback: A confidence explanation can help reviewers understand the reasoning, but it does not enforce a human decision before a high-impact action. The agent could still take the grounding action without approval.

options.label: B
options.text: Require a larger Claude model for all alert triage and work order creation.
options.feedback: A more capable model may improve reasoning quality, but it is not an authorization control. High-impact actions still need an explicit gate when policy or risk requires human validation.

options.label: C
options.text: Require daily audit review of aircraft-grounding actions after work orders are created.
options.feedback: Post hoc audit is useful for accountability and incident investigation, but it is a detective control. It does not prevent an unreviewed grounding decision from affecting operations.

options.label: D
options.text: Require a human approval step before executing the aircraft-grounding tool call.
options.feedback: This keeps Claude useful for analysis and drafting while placing a human checkpoint at the point where operational risk becomes high. Human approval should happen before the tool executes, not only after the action is taken.

questions.explanation:
For agentic systems, human-in-the-loop validation is most valuable at the boundary between low-risk assistance and high-impact action. Claude can gather context, summarize evidence, draft recommendations, and prepare a proposed tool call, but the architecture should require a person to approve the action before execution when the action is costly, hard to reverse, safety-relevant, or visible to others.

This is different from merely asking the model to be careful. Prompt guidance can shape behavior, but it is not an enforcement layer. In Claude Code and Agent SDK style systems, permission prompts, approval callbacks, hooks, and tool restrictions are the kinds of mechanisms used to control whether a tool call proceeds. See Anthropic's documentation on Agent SDK permissions and Claude Code permissions.

Audit logging and confidence explanations can still be useful. They support reviewability, debugging, and governance reporting, but they do not substitute for a pre-execution approval gate. A sound mental model is to let Claude automate preparation and evidence synthesis, then make the system enforce human validation exactly where authority to take the risky action would otherwise be delegated to the model.

questions.question: A legal e-discovery vendor's AI platform team runs a production service that only sends Claude inference requests for one workspace. The service currently authenticates with a static workspace API key set to Never expire in CI, and the CI system can issue workload identity tokens from the organization's IdP. Security wants to reduce credential exposure and avoid privileges outside the service's inference use. Which change best addresses the gap?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the static workspace API key and rotate it after incidents.
options.feedback: Reactive rotation does not remove the standing long-lived credential from CI. A workspace API key is scoped to a workspace, but it does not provide the same endpoint-level restriction as the inference-specific WIF scope.

options.label: B
options.text: Configure Workload Identity Federation with workspace:inference for the target workspace.
options.feedback: This replaces a long-lived static secret with short-lived Claude API access tokens exchanged from the workload's IdP identity. The workspace:inference scope limits the workload to inference endpoints in the specified workspace, matching the service's stated need.

options.label: C
options.text: Grant organization admin membership so workspace access is inherited.
options.feedback: Organization admins automatically receive Workspace Admin access across workspaces, which is broader than the service requires. This also does not address the exposure risk from keeping a long-lived CI secret.

options.label: D
options.text: Create an Admin API key and store it in the deployment pipeline.
options.feedback: Admin API keys are distinct credentials for administrative API access, not a least-privilege fit for an inference-only service. This would expand access to administrative surfaces rather than narrowing the workload to inference.

questions.explanation:
The secure design is to align both credential lifetime and authorization scope with the workload. Anthropic documents that Claude API authentication can use either a static x-api-key or Workload Identity Federation, where a workload exchanges an IdP-issued JWT for a short-lived Claude API access token, as described in Claude authentication.

For authorization, the relevant WIF scope is workspace:inference, which grants inference endpoints only in the rule's workspace. The WIF reference also makes clear that scopes are coarse, so architects should choose the narrowest documented scope rather than assuming per-resource or read-vs-write permissions exist.

Workspace scoping still matters: API keys and WIF rules are evaluated in the context of workspaces, and workspace keys can access only that workspace's resources, as covered in Workspaces. However, a static workspace key with no expiration remains a standing secret, while WIF better fits CI and service workloads that can prove identity through an IdP.

Admin credentials are the wrong direction for this scenario. The Administration API uses distinct Admin API keys or OAuth bearer tokens with org:admin scope, which are intended for administrative operations and would create unnecessary privilege for an inference-only service.

questions.question: A wealth management firm's client-advice platform sends Claude the same large advisory methodology, compliance instructions, tool definitions, and few-shot examples for every request. Each request then adds a timestamp, client-specific portfolio facts, and the advisor's question. The team wants to reuse the stable prompt content, reduce repeated input processing, and measure whether the change is working. Which TWO changes should the architect make?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the methodology guide after the advisor question so changing content appears before the reusable material.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prompt caching is prefix-based, not suffix-based. Putting changing content before stable content makes the reusable material depend on a different prefix each time.

options.label: B
options.text: Place reusable tools, system guidance, and examples before the varying suffix, and mark the last stable block with cache_control.
options.feedback: This is correct because prompt caching reuses exact prompt prefixes, and the prefix is built in the order tools, system, then messages. Marking the last stable block avoids tying the cache entry to the timestamp or client-specific content that changes on every request.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable automatic caching on the full request while leaving the timestamped user block as the last cacheable block.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because automatic caching places the breakpoint on the last cacheable block. If that block changes every request, exact prefix matching will not produce reliable hits for the stable material.

options.label: D
options.text: Report cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, and input_tokens together when tracking cache performance.
options.feedback: This is correct because cached prompts split input accounting across multiple usage fields. Using input_tokens alone would understate total input when cached content is read or newly written.

questions.explanation:
Prompt caching is designed for repeated prefixes, not for arbitrary repeated text anywhere in a request. The cacheable prefix is evaluated in the documented order tools, system, then messages, up to and including the selected cache breakpoint. For a request with a stable methodology and a varying timestamp or user-specific suffix, the stable content should come first and the breakpoint should sit on the last block that remains identical across calls.

Automatic caching is useful for growing conversations, but it can be the wrong fit when the last cacheable block changes every request. In that layout, an explicit breakpoint is usually the safer design because cache writes occur only at marked breakpoints and cache hits require exact matching of the cached prompt segment. Cache metrics also require the right mental model: input_tokens is only the uncached portion after the last breakpoint, while total input is cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens. See the official Prompt caching documentation for the caching model, usage fields, TTL behavior, and breakpoint guidance.

Each request then adds a timestamp, client-specific portfolio facts, and the advisor's question. The team wants to reuse the stable prompt content, reduce repeated input processing, and measure whether the change is working. Which TWO changes should the architect make?
options: Move the methodology guide after the advisor question so changing content appears before the reusable material.
Place reusable tools, system guidance, and examples before the varying suffix, and mark the last stable block with cache_control.
Enable automatic caching on the full request while leaving the timestamped user block as the last cacheable block.
Report cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, and input_tokens together when tracking cache performance.
html.explanation:
Prompt caching is designed for repeated prefixes, not for arbitrary repeated text anywhere in a request. The cacheable prefix is evaluated in the documented order tools, system, then messages, up to and including the selected cache breakpoint. For a request with a stable methodology and a varying timestamp or user-specific suffix, the stable content should come first and the breakpoint should sit on the last block that remains identical across calls.

Automatic caching is useful for growing conversations, but it can be the wrong fit when the last cacheable block changes every request. In that layout, an explicit breakpoint is usually the safer design because cache writes occur only at marked breakpoints and cache hits require exact matching of the cached prompt segment. Cache metrics also require the right mental model: input_tokens is only the uncached portion after the last breakpoint, while total input is cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens. See the official Prompt caching documentation for the caching model, usage fields, TTL behavior, and breakpoint guidance.

questions.question: A video game studio's engine tooling group wants to add Claude Code to a nightly CI workflow. The job should review the files changed in the branch, produce results a dashboard can parse, and finish without requiring a developer to keep a terminal session open. Which TWO implementation choices best fit this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Pipe `git diff` output into `claude -p` from the CI job.
options.feedback: This uses Claude Code's non-interactive automation path, which is designed to run a prompt and then exit. Piping changed-file information into the command keeps the workflow composable with existing CI shell steps.

options.label: B
options.text: Regenerate `CLAUDE.md` with a full file inventory before each run.
options.feedback: `CLAUDE.md` is intended for persistent project instructions, conventions, and non-obvious workflow guidance. Filling it with a changing file inventory bloats the context and makes important instructions easier to miss.

options.label: C
options.text: Open an interactive Claude Code session and capture terminal text.
options.feedback: An interactive session is useful for live development, but it is a poor fit for unattended CI automation. Scraping terminal text is also brittle compared with using a supported structured output format.

options.label: D
options.text: Select `json` or `stream-json` output for the dashboard parser.
options.feedback: Structured output is the right fit when another system needs to consume the result. Claude Code's print mode supports machine-readable output formats, so the dashboard does not need to scrape human-oriented terminal text.

questions.explanation:
For CI and shell automation, the key mental model is that Claude Code can be used as a composable command-line tool rather than only as an interactive coding surface. The documented non-interactive mode is claude -p, also available as --print, which runs a query and exits. That makes it suitable for jobs that pipe in logs, diffs, or file lists and then hand the result to another program.

When downstream software consumes the result, prefer a supported structured output format such as json or stream-json instead of scraping an interactive transcript. The Claude Code CLI reference documents print mode, piped input, and output format options, while the Claude Code best practices page shows using claude -p in loops and pipelines for scaled developer workflows.

CLAUDE.md is still valuable, but for stable guidance such as build commands, coding standards, and repository-specific conventions. The Claude Code memory documentation cautions that bloated instruction files reduce adherence, so dynamically stuffing a full repository map into memory is the wrong optimization for a CI review job.

questions.question: A payments infrastructure team's release engineering group wants a local Git hook to analyze failed test output. The hook should send the recent log text to Claude, emit a result that another script can parse, and then return control to the shell without requiring a developer to continue an interactive session. Which implementation best fits this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Pipe the test log into `claude -p` with the analysis prompt and request JSON output.
options.feedback: This uses Claude Code's non-interactive automation path, which accepts piped input and exits after producing a response. Requesting JSON output makes the result suitable for a downstream script to parse.

options.label: B
options.text: Append the failing log to `CLAUDE.md` and run a normal `claude` session afterward.
options.feedback: `CLAUDE.md` is for persistent project instructions, coding standards, and workflow guidance. Using it for transient test logs bloats startup context and does not create a clean machine-readable hook result.

options.label: C
options.text: Open an interactive `claude` session from the hook and paste the test log into it.
options.feedback: An interactive session is useful for exploratory development, but it does not match a hook that must finish unattended. It also introduces a manual step where the developer must remain in the session.

options.label: D
options.text: Run `/loop` inside a CLI session to poll the test output until it changes.
options.feedback: `/loop` is designed for repeated prompts within a CLI session, such as quick polling while a session is active. It is not the best fit for a one-shot Git hook that should consume stdin, produce structured output, and exit.

questions.explanation:
For shell automation, claude -p, also available as --print, is the appropriate Claude Code interface because it is designed to query Claude and then exit. It supports piped input, so a hook can pass recent test logs directly from standard input rather than relying on copy and paste or persistent files.

When another program needs to consume the result, choose an output format such as json rather than relying on free-form terminal text. This keeps the workflow composable in the Unix style: one command gathers logs, Claude analyzes them, and the next command parses the result.

Interactive sessions, scheduled tasks, and CLAUDE.md solve different problems. Interactive sessions are for developer-guided work, scheduled tasks are for recurring execution, and CLAUDE.md is persistent instruction context rather than a place to store ephemeral logs. questions.question: A regional water utility's reliability analytics team sends Claude Sonnet 4.5 a cached 185,000-token asset-history bundle, a long system prompt, tool definitions, recent inspection images, and a request that may need a long answer. The workflow is running into context pressure, and the team wants to preserve the required evidence rather than discard it arbitrarily. Which change best addresses the problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the workload to a 1M-context model, or curate the archive and logs before the call.
options.feedback: This addresses the actual context constraint by either increasing the available window with a model that supports it or reducing what is sent. Curation can include retrieving only relevant evidence, trimming stale history, or summarizing prior material before it enters the request.

options.label: B
options.text: Use token counting before the call, but keep the same model and request contents.
options.feedback: Token counting can help estimate whether a request fits before sending it, but it does not change the model's context window. If the same full input is still sent to Claude Sonnet 4.5, the underlying capacity pressure remains.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the model unchanged, and rely on prompt caching to remove the archive from context.
options.feedback: Prompt caching can reduce cost and latency for repeated prefixes, but cached tokens still occupy the context window. It does not make a large archive invisible to the model's context accounting.

options.label: D
options.text: Raise max_tokens enough to cover the archive, logs, tools, and expected answer.
options.feedback: Increasing max_tokens does not create more total context capacity. Because output tokens also count toward the context window, raising max_tokens can increase the chance that input plus possible output exceeds the model's window.

questions.explanation:
The context window is a single shared budget for the request and response. It includes the system prompt, every item in messages, tool definitions, documents, images, tool results, and the output Claude generates for the turn, including extended thinking. The key design tradeoff is that Claude can reason over everything in that working memory, but every extra artifact competes for the same finite capacity.

Prompt caching is often misunderstood in this situation. It can make repeated prefixes cheaper and faster to reuse, but the cached prefix still counts against the context window. Caching is therefore a cost and latency optimization, not a way to fit more tokens into a model than its context window supports.

For this workflow, the practical choices are to use a currently documented larger-context model or reduce the amount of evidence included in each request through retrieval, summarization, or other curation. Claude Sonnet 4.5 has a 200k-token context window, while current documented larger-context options provide 1M-token windows by default. See Anthropic's Context windows documentation for the accounting rules, model window sizes, and overflow behavior.

questions.question: A national public library consortium's digital services team is building a Claude-powered research assistant. Their catalog, holds, and archival search systems already expose a trusted remote MCP server over HTTPS with documented MCP tools. The team wants Claude, from the Messages API, to call only relevant tools during a request without the application maintaining a separate client connection to that server. Which integration approach best fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the Messages API MCP connector with an MCP server entry and a matching MCP toolset.
options.feedback: This matches the requirement to let Claude access external tools through a remote HTTPS MCP server without the application implementing its own MCP client. The current request shape uses an MCP server definition plus an MCP toolset in the tools array.

options.label: B
options.text: Put tool configuration inside the MCP server definition and omit the MCP toolset entry.
options.feedback: That reflects the deprecated configuration pattern rather than the current connector shape. Current usage separates server connection details from tool enablement by using an MCP toolset in the tools array.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a polling CLI wrapper that injects catalog results into every user message.
options.feedback: A CLI or API wrapper can be useful when an application should fetch data itself, but it does not meet the stated goal of letting Claude call relevant tools during the request. It also shifts orchestration and context loading back into the application.

options.label: D
options.text: Connect the server as a local STDIO MCP server directly through the Messages API request.
options.feedback: The Messages API MCP connector requires a remote MCP server exposed over supported HTTP transports. Local STDIO servers cannot be connected directly through this connector.

questions.explanation:
MCP is the appropriate integration mechanism when Claude needs standardized access to external tools, data sources, or services, especially when a trusted remote MCP server already exists. In the Messages API, the MCP connector lets Claude connect to remote MCP servers without the application implementing a separate MCP client, provided the request uses the current beta header and the current request shape.

The mental model is that mcp_servers defines how to reach the server, while a tools entry of type mcp_toolset controls which tools from that server are available. This separation is important because the current connector no longer puts tool configuration directly inside the server definition. The connector is not a general MCP client for every transport or capability, since it currently supports MCP tool calls and requires a publicly exposed HTTP server using supported transports, so local STDIO is the wrong fit here.

Use API or CLI integration when your own application should perform the external action and pass results to Claude, or when the external system is not available through a suitable MCP server. Use agent-to-agent patterns when independent agents need to coordinate workstreams, not simply when Claude needs access to an external service's tools. See the official MCP connector documentation for the supported request shape, beta header, and connector limitations.

questions.question: A specialty chemicals manufacturer's platform engineering team runs a Claude-powered quality analysis service in one production workspace. The same deployment is being expanded with a nightly automation that will list organization members, remove departed employees, and audit API key metadata across workspaces. Engineers propose reusing the service's existing workspace API key for the new automation. Which change best addresses the authorization gap?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a separate Admin API credential for the organization-management automation, and keep the workspace key for inference.
options.feedback: Organization-management operations require Admin API authorization, which is distinct from normal Claude API workspace keys. Keeping the inference key separate preserves the workspace scoping boundary while using the appropriate credential type for administrative actions.

options.label: B
options.text: Exchange an IdP token for a WIF token with workspace:developer, and reuse it for both workloads.
options.feedback: Workload Identity Federation can reduce static credential exposure, but the documented workspace scopes do not provide full organization administration. The workspace:developer scope grants non-administrative Claude API endpoints in a workspace, not the organization-level Admin API access needed here.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the existing workspace API key into the Default Workspace, and reuse it for both workloads.
options.feedback: API keys are scoped to a single workspace and can access only that workspace's resources. Moving a key to a different workspace would not turn it into an organization-level administrative credential.

options.label: D
options.text: Add the required anthropic-version header to each request, and reuse the current key for both workloads.
options.feedback: Direct Claude API calls require the anthropic-version header, but that header does not grant additional permissions. A correctly formatted request can still fail authorization when the credential is the wrong type or scope.

questions.explanation:
The key design issue is separating workspace-scoped inference access from organization administration. A normal Claude API key is scoped to a single workspace, so it is appropriate for calling Claude API endpoints for that workspace, but it is not a substitute for Admin API credentials when a workflow manages users or audits API key metadata across the organization.

The Admin API has its own credential requirements: an Admin API key beginning with sk-ant-admin..., or an OAuth bearer token with org:admin scope. Those credentials are role-sensitive and organization-only, so reusing a production inference key would be both ineffective for the required administrative operations and a poor separation-of-duties design. See Administration API and Workspaces.

WIF is valuable when a workload should avoid long-lived static API keys, but its documented scopes are still coarse and must match the workload's authorization needs. A WIF token with workspace:developer or workspace:inference is not equivalent to org:admin. The general API request headers, including anthropic-version, are required for valid API calls, but they do not change what the credential is authorized to do. See Authentication and WIF reference.

questions.question: A humanitarian logistics nonprofit's platform team is redesigning a Claude workflow that turns disaster field reports into supply plans. The task has dependent stages: extract needs, reconcile inventory, identify conflicts, and draft a plan. Failures are hard to debug because one response hides which stage went wrong, and an operations lead must approve the conflict analysis before plan drafting. Which two changes best apply decomposition techniques while preserving practical control?

options.label: A
options.text: Return each parallel tool result as soon as it completes so Claude can continue the next dependency.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because when Claude returns multiple tool use blocks in one assistant turn, the application must return one tool result for each tool use together in the next user message. It also does not fit a dependent workflow where later stages rely on reviewed earlier outputs.

options.label: B
options.text: Set effort to max and keep the workflow as one prompt so internal reasoning handles every stage.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because adaptive thinking and effort can improve reasoning, but they do not provide an approval gate or inspectable intermediate artifacts. Effort is guidance for thinking depth, not a workflow control mechanism.

options.label: C
options.text: Split the workflow into sequential API calls that expose extraction, conflict review, and final drafting outputs.
options.feedback: This is correct because explicit prompt chaining is useful when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline. A required approval point between conflict analysis and plan drafting is a strong reason to make that boundary visible.

options.label: D
options.text: Use structured prompts with named XML sections, ordered steps, and representative examples within each stage.
options.feedback: This is correct because decomposition can happen inside each prompt through clear structure, explicit ordering, and separated context. Examples help Claude understand the expected format and edge cases without relying on an ambiguous monolithic instruction.

questions.explanation:
Complex Claude workflows should be decomposed where the architecture needs observability, control, or enforceable boundaries. Anthropic documents that explicit prompt chaining is useful when teams need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline, even though Claude can handle many multistep tasks internally with adaptive thinking and orchestration. See Chain complex prompts.

In this scenario, a separate conflict-analysis checkpoint is not just a reasoning preference, it is a process requirement. Splitting the work into sequential calls lets the platform store and evaluate each artifact, pause for human approval, and then pass the approved result into the drafting step. Within each step, structured instructions, named sections such as instructions, context, and input, ordered steps, and representative examples reduce ambiguity.

Raising effort can be appropriate for harder reasoning, but it is not a substitute for explicit workflow decomposition. The adaptive thinking documentation states that effort guides thinking depth rather than acting as a hard budget or exposing a controllable pipeline, as described in Adaptive thinking.

Tool use can also decompose work, but the application remains responsible for executing client tools and returning results correctly. For parallel tool calls, Claude may emit multiple tool_use blocks, but the application must return the corresponding tool_result blocks together in the next user message, with tool results before any text. See Tool use overview and Parallel tool use.

questions.question: An urban planning consultancy is preparing an internal Claude assistant that drafts zoning variance summaries. Business sponsors ask for "a reliable launch with a sensible SLA," while reviewers disagree about whether speed, citation quality, or cost should matter most. Which TWO actions best align expectations and create a useful stakeholder feedback loop?

options.label: A
options.text: Define specific success criteria with stakeholders, including quality, privacy, latency, and price targets, before launch.
options.feedback: This is correct because expectation alignment should start with measurable criteria rather than a vague launch goal. Including multiple dimensions such as task quality, privacy, latency, and price helps stakeholders agree on what tradeoffs the SLA actually represents.

options.label: B
options.text: Review stakeholder feedback against the agreed criteria on a regular cadence, and revise targets when priorities change.
options.feedback: This is correct because a feedback loop is useful only when feedback is interpreted against shared expectations. Regular review keeps the team aligned when business priorities shift, while preserving a measurable basis for decisions.

options.label: C
options.text: Set one SLA around average response time, and defer quality and cost review until usage grows.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because latency alone is not enough for most Claude use cases. The documented guidance emphasizes multidimensional criteria, so a single speed target can mask poor task fidelity, privacy handling, or cost outcomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Launch with a broad goal such as improved reviewer satisfaction, and tune prompts after complaints accumulate.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because broad goals do not give engineering or business stakeholders a common way to judge readiness. Waiting for complaints also makes feedback reactive instead of tying it to measurable launch criteria.

questions.explanation:
Stakeholder alignment for a Claude system should begin by turning subjective expectations into specific, measurable success criteria. Anthropic's evaluation guidance notes that good criteria should be specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and that common criteria include task fidelity, consistency, relevance, tone, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency, and price. See Define success criteria.

An SLA is not just an uptime or latency statement. For an AI-assisted workflow, it often represents a negotiated set of tradeoffs across quality, speed, cost, risk tolerance, and user experience. A durable feedback loop compares stakeholder observations against those agreed criteria, rather than treating every complaint as a new priority or optimizing one metric in isolation.

The stronger actions create a shared measurement frame before launch and maintain it through periodic review. The weaker actions rely on vague satisfaction goals or a single latency metric, both of which make it harder to decide whether the system is improving, regressing, or simply optimizing the wrong outcome.

questions.question: A biomedical device manufacturer's post-market surveillance team is designing a Claude-based system for incoming clinician reports. Each report can be assigned to one of several stable categories, such as device malfunction, labeling confusion, adverse event follow-up, or general product question. Each category has different source documents and response rules, and the team wants predictable latency and cost while still grounding answers in current internal guidance. Which TWO architectural choices best fit this design?

options.label: A
options.text: Start with an augmented LLM that uses retrieval and limited tools for grounding.
options.feedback: This is appropriate because the system needs current internal guidance and controlled capabilities, not open-ended exploration. Retrieval and limited tools can ground responses while preserving a simpler architecture.

options.label: B
options.text: Create an orchestrator-workers workflow that decomposes every report into subtasks.
options.feedback: This is not the best match because the scenario does not require dynamically breaking each report into many independent subtasks. Orchestrator-workers is more appropriate when the needed subtasks vary and a central model must coordinate them.

options.label: C
options.text: Route each report to a category-specific prompt and tool set after classification.
options.feedback: This is a good fit because the inputs fall into stable categories that can use distinct handling logic. A routing workflow keeps the path predefined while still allowing category-specific context and tools.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a fully dynamic agent to decide its own process and tool sequence.
options.feedback: This is less suitable because the task has known categories and predictable processing needs. A dynamic agent can be useful for open-ended problems, but it adds latency and cost that the scenario is trying to control.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic distinguishes workflows from agents within the broader category of agentic systems. Workflows use predefined code paths to coordinate LLM calls and tools, while agents let the model dynamically direct its own process and tool use. For inputs that can be classified into stable categories, a routing workflow is usually a better architectural fit than giving the model broad autonomy.

The same guidance recommends starting with the simplest solution possible, because agentic systems can improve performance but often increase latency and cost. Here, the system needs grounded answers from internal guidance and category-specific handling, so an augmented LLM with retrieval and limited tools provides the necessary capabilities without prematurely adopting a more complex agent loop.

A fully dynamic agent would be more compelling if the reports required open-ended investigation, flexible planning, or unpredictable tool sequences. An orchestrator-workers workflow would be more compelling if each report needed variable decomposition into multiple coordinated subtasks. See Anthropic's discussion of these patterns in Building effective agents.

questions.question: An airline maintenance analytics team is adding Claude to classify repair log entries into a JSON object consumed by an automated routing service. The current prompt says, "Return valid JSON only," but occasional malformed JSON still causes downstream retries. The team needs a guardrail that makes normal responses conform to a fixed schema before the router accepts them. Which change best addresses the risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Configure JSON outputs with output_config.format using the required decision schema.
options.feedback: Structured outputs are designed for schema-constrained responses, which directly addresses malformed JSON and schema drift. The application should still inspect response metadata such as stop_reason before treating any response as a routable decision.

options.label: B
options.text: Prefill the assistant response with an opening brace before each request.
options.feedback: Assistant prefilling is a formatting technique, not a schema enforcement mechanism. It is also not supported on several current Claude models, so it is not a robust guardrail for a production router.

options.label: C
options.text: Repair malformed JSON in the router before passing decisions downstream.
options.feedback: A repair layer may reduce some parse failures, but it does not make Claude's output conform to the intended schema. It can also mask upstream format problems instead of applying a guardrail at generation time.

options.label: D
options.text: Add more few-shot examples that demonstrate the desired JSON response shape.
options.feedback: Examples can improve consistency and are useful for steering format, but they do not enforce schema compliance. A model can still produce malformed JSON or omit required fields under prompt-only formatting.

questions.explanation:
For machine-consumed decisions, the safest pattern is to make the output contract part of the model request rather than relying only on prose instructions. Anthropic documents Structured outputs as the mechanism to constrain Claude's response to a schema, using JSON outputs through output_config.format or strict tool use through strict: true. See Structured outputs for the supported mechanisms.

Prompting techniques such as examples, XML tags, or wording like "JSON only" can improve consistency, but they are not the same as guaranteed schema conformance. Anthropic's consistency guidance explicitly points to Structured Outputs when the application must always receive valid JSON that conforms to a schema, while other techniques remain best-effort steering. See Increase output consistency.

A production guardrail should also treat response metadata as part of the contract. Even with a schema, the application should branch on stop_reason and avoid routing responses that ended because of a refusal, token limit, or another non-normal completion. That keeps schema enforcement and safety-state handling separate, which is usually simpler and safer than trying to infer validity from text alone.

questions.question: A cybersecurity operations center is designing a Claude-powered assistant for high-severity alerts. Each alert may require querying different log systems, correlating identities, checking cloud configuration, opening follow-up tickets, or stopping when evidence is insufficient. The useful next step often depends on intermediate results, and the team accepts higher latency for better autonomous investigation within strict tool permissions. Which architectural pattern best fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Use routing that classifies each alert once and sends it to a category-specific prompt.
options.feedback: Routing is useful when inputs fall into distinct categories that can be classified accurately. The scenario requires adaptive investigation after intermediate results, not only selecting one predefined path at the beginning.

options.label: B
options.text: Use prompt chaining that passes every alert through the same fixed sequence of prompts.
options.feedback: Prompt chaining works best when the work can be cleanly decomposed into fixed subtasks. It is a poor fit when later steps depend heavily on unpredictable findings from earlier tool results.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a single augmented LLM call with retrieval and examples for all alert types.
options.feedback: An augmented LLM with retrieval and examples is often the simplest effective design, but a single call is limited when the next action depends on tool results. It would not naturally support iterative querying, correlation, and conditional stopping across multiple systems.

options.label: D
options.text: Use an agentic design that lets Claude choose investigation steps and tools at runtime.
options.feedback: This is correct because the path cannot be fully known in advance and depends on intermediate evidence. An agentic design is appropriate when Claude needs to dynamically direct its process and tool use, provided the tool surface and permissions are controlled.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic distinguishes workflows from agents within the broader category of agentic systems. Workflows use predefined code paths, while agents let the model dynamically decide its own process and tool use. In this scenario, the investigation path depends on what each query reveals, so a fixed prompt chain or one-time route would force a structure that does not match the problem.

The right mental model is to start with the simplest pattern that satisfies the task. A single augmented LLM, meaning an LLM enhanced with retrieval, tools, and memory, is often sufficient for straightforward knowledge tasks. Here, however, the stated need for iterative tool selection and evidence-driven next steps justifies the additional latency and cost of an agentic design.

Anthropic's guidance in Building effective agents emphasizes that agentic systems can improve task performance but introduce tradeoffs. An architect should choose agents when autonomy over process is necessary, and choose workflow patterns like prompt chaining or routing when the path can be reliably specified ahead of time.

questions.question: A university admissions office is piloting a Claude-based assistant that drafts applicant file summaries for human reviewers. The dean asks for a launch date and a service commitment, but reviewers are giving inconsistent feedback because they value completeness, tone, privacy handling, speed, and operating cost differently. What should the architect do next to align expectations?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the reviewer pool until feedback trends converge naturally.
options.feedback: More feedback can help, but it does not solve ambiguity in what the team is optimizing for. Without agreed criteria, a larger pool may simply produce more inconsistent judgments.

options.label: B
options.text: Launch broadly and use escalation tickets as the feedback loop.
options.feedback: This waits for failures after deployment instead of aligning expectations before launch. Escalations are useful operational signals, but they are a poor substitute for measurable launch criteria and a planned evaluation process.

options.label: C
options.text: Define measurable success criteria and SLA thresholds with the stakeholders.
options.feedback: This directly turns subjective feedback into shared targets that can be evaluated and discussed. It also supports multidimensional evaluation, since quality, privacy, latency, and price may all matter for the workflow.

options.label: D
options.text: Route all requests to the fastest model before collecting more feedback.
options.feedback: Optimizing speed first assumes latency is the primary stakeholder concern. The scenario shows several competing dimensions, so this could harm fidelity, tone, or privacy expectations without an agreed tradeoff.

questions.explanation:
When stakeholders disagree about what “good” means, the architect should first translate expectations into specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant success criteria. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes that useful criteria often span several dimensions, including task fidelity, consistency, relevance, tone and style, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency, and price. See Define success criteria.

For an SLA or launch commitment to be meaningful, it needs explicit thresholds tied to the real user workflow, not just a general promise that the assistant will be “high quality” or “fast enough.” In practice, that means aligning admissions leaders, reviewers, compliance stakeholders, and platform owners on what will be measured, how tradeoffs will be handled, and what evidence is required before expansion. Larger review groups, faster routing, and post-launch complaint monitoring can all have roles later, but none of them creates the shared yardstick needed for expectation alignment.

questions.question: A maritime insurer’s underwriting operations team has an internal Claude assistant for reviewing renewal submissions. It is configured with 64 tools across policy search, document lookup, CRM updates, email sending, billing adjustments, and incident-response systems. Several policy-search and document-lookup tools return similar results and have overlapping schemas. Underwriters use it to find relevant clauses, compare submitted documents, and draft a short rationale. The team wants to reduce irrelevant tool plans, lower context usage, and avoid expanding operational access. Which two configuration changes best address the issue?

options.label: A
options.text: Set `tool_choice` to `any` so Claude must call one configured tool on every request.
options.feedback: `tool_choice: any` forces Claude to use one of the provided tools, but it does not reduce the number of tools in context. With an oversized catalog, forcing a tool call can make irrelevant tool use more likely rather than less likely.

options.label: B
options.text: Consolidate overlapping retrieval tools and clarify each tool’s boundaries and limitations.
options.feedback: Consolidating related operations into fewer tools reduces context overhead while preserving needed capabilities. Clear descriptions that say when a tool should and should not be used help Claude select tools more accurately.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep every connector enabled and add a prompt asking Claude to prefer retrieval tools.
options.feedback: A prompt can guide behavior, but it does not remove unneeded capabilities or reduce tool-definition tokens. Keeping unrelated connectors available preserves the same attack surface and selection burden.

options.label: D
options.text: Expose only the retrieval and document-comparison tools needed for underwriting review.
options.feedback: This directly reduces capability bloat by removing tools that are outside the assistant’s intended workflow. Fewer available tools also reduce the tool definitions included in the prompt and narrow the model’s selection space.

questions.explanation:
Capability bloat is both a context-management problem and a control-surface problem. When tools are provided, their names, descriptions, and schemas contribute input tokens, and tool use adds further tool_use and tool_result content. Anthropic’s tool-use documentation notes that tools also affect the system prompt and that adding tools is not free in cost or context: Tool use overview.

The right design is to expose the smallest toolset that fits the underwriting workflow, then make those tools easier to choose correctly. Anthropic recommends detailed plaintext tool descriptions, including what each tool does, when it should and should not be used, caveats, and limitations. It also recommends consolidating related operations into fewer tools and returning only high-signal information, as described in Implement tool use.

tool_choice is not a substitute for tool governance. Modes such as any or a forced named tool change whether Claude must call a tool, but they do not remove irrelevant tools from the request. Similarly, asking Claude in a prompt to avoid unrelated connectors is weaker than removing those connectors from the assistant’s configuration, because the tools still consume context and remain available for selection.

questions.question: A fashion retailer's catalog platform is adding two Claude routes: a high-volume image and text enrichment pass for millions of routine product listings, and an interactive merchandising analyst assistant that needs strong reasoning while keeping response time and token spend practical. Which two model-selection actions best fit these trade-offs?

options.label: A
options.text: Route the analyst assistant to fast mode on any selected model, treating latency optimization as model independent.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because fast mode is documented narrowly, not as a universal setting across all models. It is available as a research preview for Claude Opus 4.8 and Opus 4.7 at premium pricing, so it is not a model-independent way to meet practical cost and latency goals.

options.label: B
options.text: Route the interactive analyst assistant to Claude Sonnet 5, balancing intelligence, speed, and production token cost.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude Sonnet 5 is positioned as the best combination of speed and intelligence. It fits an interactive workload that needs stronger reasoning than a routine enrichment pass while avoiding the higher cost profile of Opus or Fable.

options.label: C
options.text: Route routine catalog enrichment to Claude Fable 5, prioritizing it as the least expensive default for simple work.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude Fable 5 is not the least expensive current model in the documented pricing table. It is positioned for next-generation intelligence for long-running agents, not as the cost-minimized default for simple high-volume processing.

options.label: D
options.text: Route routine catalog enrichment to Claude Haiku 4.5, prioritizing fast, cost-effective processing for simple multimodal work.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude Haiku 4.5 is positioned as the fastest model with near-frontier intelligence and has the lowest listed input and output prices among the current models. Since all current Claude models support text and image input, using Haiku for routine multimodal enrichment does not rely on a missing capability.

questions.explanation:
Model selection in Claude is a practical optimization problem across capability, speed, cost, and workload shape. The Choosing a model guidance explicitly frames selection around these trade-offs, and the Models overview positions Claude Haiku 4.5 as the fastest model with near-frontier intelligence and Claude Sonnet 5 as the best combination of speed and intelligence.

For the routine catalog route, the key is throughput and unit economics, not maximum reasoning depth, so claude-haiku-4-5 is the better fit. For the interactive analyst assistant, claude-sonnet-5 is a balanced production choice because it preserves stronger reasoning while keeping latency and cost more practical than choosing a premium model by default.

The distractors confuse positioning with economics or treat a special feature as broadly available. The Pricing documentation shows that Fable 5 is priced above Haiku 4.5, and fast mode is a narrow premium feature for specific Opus models rather than a universal latency switch.
