questions.question: A telehealth network's platform team is preparing a Claude integration for patient-message summarization. The first release will send PHI through the Claude API at api.anthropic.com, and a later release may use Amazon Bedrock for a separate deployment. The legal team also needs GDPR transfer documentation for EU users. Which TWO actions should the architect recommend before production?

options.label: A
options.text: Move PHI prompt testing into Console or Workbench after accepting Commercial Terms and enabling ZDR.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Anthropic's documented HIPAA and ZDR coverage is not universal across all product surfaces. Console and Workbench processing are listed as excluded from the relevant HIPAA-ready API path, so they should not be used as a shortcut for PHI testing.

options.label: B
options.text: Document the Anthropic DPA and SCCs for direct API use, and assess Amazon Bedrock's controls separately.
options.feedback: This is correct because Anthropic's DPA with Standard Contractual Clauses is incorporated into the Commercial Terms for commercial products such as Claude API. The Amazon Bedrock path has a different processor boundary, so its terms and retention or compliance controls must be reviewed separately.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable ZDR for the parent account and rely on it for every organization and Amazon Bedrock deployment.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because ZDR must be enabled per organization and does not automatically extend to other organizations under the same account. It also does not make third-party platform deployments inherit Anthropic's API retention posture, since those platforms have their own processor and control model.

options.label: D
options.text: Complete HIPAA setup by signing a BAA and using a HIPAA-enabled Claude API organization for PHI traffic.
options.feedback: This is correct because Anthropic describes HIPAA-ready Claude API integrations as requiring a signed BAA and a HIPAA-enabled organization. HIPAA readiness is not the same thing as simply deleting data quickly, so ZDR alone is not the required control for PHI workloads.

questions.explanation:
For regulated workloads, the main architectural question is not just which model is used, but which product surface, organization, and processor boundary handles the data. Anthropic's API and data retention documentation distinguishes the Claude API at api.anthropic.com from third-party platform paths, and it also explains that ZDR is enabled per organization rather than automatically across an entire account.

For GDPR transfer documentation, Anthropic states that its Data Processing Addendum with Standard Contractual Clauses is incorporated into the Commercial Terms for commercial products such as Claude API. That helps document the direct API path, but it does not replace reviewing Amazon Bedrock's own terms and controls when the workload moves to that platform.

A signed BAA and HIPAA-enabled API organization are the relevant prerequisites for PHI traffic, while Console, Workbench, and other excluded surfaces should not be used to process PHI merely because commercial terms or ZDR exist elsewhere.

questions.question: An electric grid reliability team uses Claude Code to process vendor incident reports from an issue tracker through an MCP server. Some reports may contain hostile instructions, and unattended sessions can run shell commands against an infrastructure repository. The team has added a CLAUDE.md reminder telling Claude not to run destructive commands. Which change best reduces the risk of unsafe tool execution?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch the workflow to a larger model with stronger instruction following.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because model capability can reduce some mistakes but does not create an authorization control. A more capable model can still be exposed to prompt injection or ambiguous operational context.

options.label: B
options.text: Expand CLAUDE.md with stricter wording and more forbidden command examples.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because stronger natural-language instructions still depend on model adherence. They do not provide deterministic blocking when external content attempts to steer tool use.

options.label: C
options.text: Enforce deny rules or a PreToolUse hook for destructive shell commands.
options.feedback: This is correct because permission rules and PreToolUse hooks can block tool execution before the command runs. CLAUDE.md guidance can shape behavior, but it is not an enforcement boundary.

options.label: D
options.text: Log every shell command and review the transcript after each unattended run.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because logging is a detective control that helps with investigation after execution. It does not prevent a destructive command from affecting the repository or shared systems.

questions.explanation:
LLM systems that can use tools need controls at the tool execution boundary, not only behavioral reminders in prompt context. External issue text, tickets, web pages, and MCP data can carry prompt-injection attempts, so the architecture should assume the model may be exposed to instructions that conflict with operator intent.

Claude Code supports permission rules and hooks for this reason. A PreToolUse hook can inspect a requested tool call and deny it before execution, while permission allow and deny rules can constrain which tools or command patterns are available. This turns a safety preference into an enforceable control rather than a request for the model to remember a rule.

CLAUDE.md files are useful for project conventions and workflow guidance, but they are not a hard policy layer. Larger models, stricter wording, and after-the-fact logging may improve behavior or observability, but they do not provide the same protection against an unsafe command being run. For practical governance, combine concise instructions with enforced permissions, hooks, sandboxing, and review of connected MCP servers.

See Anthropic documentation on Claude Code hooks, Claude Code permissions, and connecting Claude Code to tools via MCP.

questions.question: A geospatial mapping vendor's release engineering group uses Claude Code to inspect 150 independent tile-rendering bug reports after each nightly build. The group wants a repeatable fan-out and aggregation pattern, while avoiding a lead session that accumulates every delegation decision and intermediate result. Which orchestration approach best fits this need?

options.label: A
options.text: Use agent view to start separate background sessions and manually monitor each report run.
options.feedback: Agent view is intended for dispatching and monitoring independent background sessions. It is plausible for parallel work, but it does not directly provide the scripted fan-out and aggregation pattern described in the scenario.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the Workflow tool to run the fan-out and aggregation logic from an executable workflow.
options.feedback: This is the best fit for coordinating dozens to hundreds of delegated tasks without managing each delegation turn in the main conversation. Dynamic workflows move orchestration into a script that the runtime executes, which reduces context pressure compared with turn-by-turn coordination.

options.label: C
options.text: Use subagents directly for each report and coordinate every delegation from the lead session.
options.feedback: Subagents are useful for focused delegated tasks inside a single Claude Code session, and they have their own context windows. However, coordinating a large number of workers turn by turn from the lead session is exactly the pattern dynamic workflows are intended to avoid.

options.label: D
options.text: Use agent teams so independent sessions exchange messages while reviewing the report queue.
options.feedback: Agent teams are appropriate when coordinated sessions need shared tasks and inter-agent messaging. The scenario emphasizes many independent inspections and aggregation, not a set of sessions that need to communicate with one another.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code has several distinct ways to parallelize work, and the right choice depends on the coordination pattern. For a large repeatable fan-out, dynamic workflows are designed to move orchestration into executable workflow logic rather than making a lead agent spend conversation turns delegating, collecting, and merging every unit of work.

Subagents are still valuable building blocks: they run within a single Claude Code session, have their own context window, and return results to the caller. That makes them strong for a few focused delegations, but less ideal when the main design problem is coordinating very large numbers of independent tasks without bloating the lead context. See the official Claude Code subagents documentation for how subagents are defined and scoped.

By contrast, agent view is for dispatching and monitoring independent background sessions, and agent teams are for coordinated sessions that share tasks and communicate. Those are not interchangeable with workflows. The official Claude Code agents documentation distinguishes subagents, agent view, agent teams, and dynamic workflows as separate orchestration approaches, so an architect should choose based on whether the system needs delegated workers, independent sessions, communicating sessions, or scripted large-scale orchestration.

questions.question: A payments compliance team's Claude API service answers analyst questions against the same 70,000-token internal policy manual on each request. Each request also includes a fresh timestamp, analyst ID, and short question. Costs remain high and time to first token is slow, even though many analysts ask about the same manual throughout the day. Which change best improves cost and latency without removing required context?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable streaming and keep prompt order unchanged so analysts see first tokens sooner.
options.feedback: Streaming can improve perceived responsiveness because tokens are delivered as they are generated. It does not reduce the input token cost of repeatedly processing the same large manual, and it does not fix cache misses caused by changing content in the prefix.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower max_tokens until most answers finish before the output limit.
options.feedback: Setting max_tokens can control the maximum output length, which can limit worst-case generation cost and latency. It is a hard cap, not a concision or quality guarantee, and responses that hit the cap may be cut off.

options.label: C
options.text: Move per-request fields after the reusable materials, then cache the last unchanged block.
options.feedback: This keeps the stable policy manual in an identical prefix across requests, which is what prompt caching can reuse. Placing the breakpoint on the last unchanged block avoids including timestamps or analyst-specific text in the cached prefix.

options.label: D
options.text: Run token counting before each request and route every oversized prompt to Haiku 4.5.
options.feedback: Token counting is useful for estimating input size, cost, and routing before sending a request. Routing every oversized prompt to a faster model is too broad because it does not address the repeated stable prefix, and model choice should still be validated against task quality requirements.

questions.explanation:
For repeated large inputs, the key mental model is that prompt caching reuses an identical prefix, ordered as tools, then system, then messages, up to the cache breakpoint. If a timestamp, analyst ID, or other changing field appears before or at that breakpoint, the prefix hash changes and the cache is much less likely to help. The right optimization is to put stable reusable material first, put variable request data after it, and cache at the end of the stable section, as described in Prompt caching.

Other latency levers solve different problems. Streaming can improve perceived responsiveness and keep long-output connections active, but it does not make repeated input processing cheaper, see Streaming Messages. Lowering max_tokens can bound output length, but the latency guidance notes that it is a hard output cap and can cut off text if reached, see Reduce latency. Token counting is valuable for estimating prompt size and routing decisions, but it is an observability and planning tool rather than a substitute for restructuring a reusable prompt prefix, see Token counting.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical manufacturing quality team is designing a Claude API service that reviews batch-deviation narratives, may call internal CAPA lookup and SOP retrieval tools, and incorporates reviewer feedback across later turns. The service must avoid releasing partial reports as complete and must continue correctly when processing requires more model or tool steps. Which design best supports the end-to-end flow?

options.label: A
options.text: Send only the latest reviewer prompt in messages, rely on the API to retain prior turns, and route each response by HTTP status.
options.feedback: The Messages API does not retain conversation history between requests, so prior turns and feedback must be included by the application. A successful HTTP response can still require follow-up handling based on stop_reason.

options.label: B
options.text: Send prior turns with a system role in messages, place tool outputs in assistant text, and release every HTTP 200 response.
options.feedback: The messages array supports user and assistant turns, while system prompts use the top-level system parameter. Releasing every successful response ignores cases where the model is asking for tool execution, continuation, or truncation recovery.

options.label: C
options.text: Send batch requests for every turn, set max_tokens to a small fixed value, and retry only after HTTP failures.
options.feedback: A small fixed max_tokens value can truncate useful output because max_tokens is an output cap, not a completion guarantee. Retrying only after HTTP failures ignores successful responses that still require tool execution, continuation, or truncation handling based on stop_reason.

options.label: D
options.text: Send saved user and assistant turns in messages, place standing instructions in the top-level system field, and route each response by stop_reason.
options.feedback: This design treats the Messages API as stateless and makes the application responsible for resending the relevant conversation history. Routing by stop_reason lets the service distinguish final output from tool use, continuation, refusal, and truncation conditions.

questions.explanation:
A reliable Claude architecture should treat the application as the owner of state. Each POST /v1/messages call sends the relevant prior user and assistant turns plus the new input, and durable instructions belong in the top-level system parameter rather than as a system role inside messages. The official Messages API create documentation describes this stateless request model.

The processing loop should not equate HTTP success with a finished business result. The response stop_reason is the control signal: end_turn can be handled as a final answer, tool_use means tools should be run and results returned, pause_turn means continue by sending assistant content back, and max_tokens or model_context_window_exceeded should be treated as truncation. The handling stop reasons documentation explains why production harnesses must branch on these values.

This creates a clean input, processing, output, and feedback loop: reviewer feedback, tool results, and recovery actions become part of the next request instead of being assumed to persist on the API side. max_tokens is only an output cap, not a guarantee of a complete response, so it is not a substitute for explicit lifecycle handling.

questions.question: A sports analytics startup's platform team is adding Claude to an analyst workspace. Each request includes the same long scouting rubric and tool definitions, followed by a short changing question. Executives ask whether enabling prompt caching means the team can stop planning rate limits and capacity separately. Which response best communicates the architectural trade-off?

options.label: A
options.text: Present prompt caching as a model-routing substitute that keeps quality stable even when prompts change and smaller models are selected.
options.feedback: Prompt caching does not choose models or guarantee task quality across model changes. Model routing still requires judging the task, latency, cost, and quality trade-offs separately from whether a prefix can be reused.

options.label: B
options.text: Present prompt caching as an availability safeguard that prevents streaming errors and context-window overflows during peak traffic periods.
options.feedback: Prompt caching can reduce cost and latency for repeated prefixes, but it is not an error-handling mechanism for streaming failures. It also should not be presented as a way to make arbitrary oversized requests fit safely.

options.label: C
options.text: Present prompt caching as a semantic answer cache that removes similar future requests from all rate-limit and capacity calculations once warmed.
options.feedback: Prompt caching does not cache semantically similar questions or complete answers. It caches the prompt prefix up to a cache breakpoint, and it does not remove all request activity from rate-limit accounting.

options.label: D
options.text: Present prompt caching as a prefix reuse optimization that lowers repeated-input cost and latency, while still planning RPM, OTPM, cache writes, and uncached input.
options.feedback: This correctly frames prompt caching as an optimization for stable prompt prefixes, not as a replacement for capacity planning. Cache reads can reduce repeated input processing and, for most Claude models, do not count toward ITPM, but RPM, OTPM, cache creation tokens, and uncached input still need to be managed.

questions.explanation:
Prompt caching is best communicated as a performance and cost optimization for repeated, stable prefixes, such as tool definitions, system instructions, and long shared context that appear before a changing user question. It is not a semantic cache of answers, and it does not remove the need to design for traffic patterns, output volume, and cache misses. The documented mental model is that the API caches the full prefix over tools, system, and messages up to the cache breakpoint, with automatic or explicit cache control options. See Prompt caching.

For stakeholder communication, the important trade-off is that caching can improve repeated-prefix economics without turning capacity planning into a solved problem. Anthropic rate limits are tracked across dimensions such as RPM, ITPM, and OTPM, and for most Claude models cache_read_input_tokens do not count toward ITPM while input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens do. That means a cached workload can still be constrained by requests per minute, generated output tokens, initial cache writes, or uncached request components. See Rate limits.

questions.question: A consumer robotics manufacturer's reliability group is investigating a release-blocking failure that spans firmware, cloud APIs, and a mobile app. The group wants several Claude Code workers to run as separate sessions on different parts of the incident, while a lead coordinates assignments and workers exchange findings during the run. Which orchestration approach best fits this need?

options.label: A
options.text: Use agent view to dispatch and monitor independent background Claude Code sessions.
options.feedback: Agent view is appropriate when the main need is launching and observing independent background sessions. The scenario requires coordinated assignments and worker communication, which goes beyond independent monitoring.

options.label: B
options.text: Use subagents to delegate each investigation stream inside one Claude Code session.
options.feedback: Subagents are useful for delegated workers, but they run within a single Claude Code session and return results to the caller. They are not separate user-managed sessions, so they do not match the stated session-level coordination need.

options.label: C
options.text: Use agent teams to coordinate separate Claude Code sessions with shared tasks and inter-agent messaging.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because the requirement is not just parallel work, but coordinated separate sessions that can communicate. Agent teams are documented for coordinated sessions with shared tasks and inter-agent messaging.

options.label: D
options.text: Use dynamic workflows to script orchestration for many delegated subagent tasks.
options.feedback: Dynamic workflows are designed for scripted orchestration of many subagents, especially when turn-by-turn delegation would be inefficient. The scenario asks for multiple separate sessions that coordinate with each other, not a scripted fan-out of subagent tasks.

questions.explanation:
The key architectural distinction is whether the work should happen as delegated workers inside one session, independent sessions, or coordinated sessions. In this scenario, the workers need to operate as separate Claude Code sessions while sharing assignments and findings, so agent teams align with the collaboration model.

Claude Code documents several parallelization patterns that are related but not interchangeable: subagents, agent view, agent teams, and dynamic workflows. Subagents have their own context windows, but they remain inside a single Claude Code session and report back to the caller. Agent view is better when you want to dispatch and monitor independent background sessions, while dynamic workflows are better when orchestration should be moved into a script for many delegated subagent tasks.

questions.question: A specialty food distributor's catalog platform ingests 40,000 supplier spec sheets every night. Each Claude request would include the same long taxonomy, attribute definitions, and curated examples, followed by one varying product description. Results are not needed until morning, and the team wants to reduce cost without removing the shared guidance. Which TWO design choices best fit this problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove most examples from the prompt and standardize on the smallest available model.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it cuts task guidance and changes model choice without evidence that quality will hold. Cost optimization should be measured against extraction accuracy, not achieved by blindly discarding useful context.

options.label: B
options.text: Run one Claude Code session that loops over all supplier files during an interactive session.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude Code sessions are stateful and interactive, not the best fit for a large scheduled extraction pipeline. This approach also risks context growth across unrelated records and does not use the batch pricing model.

options.label: C
options.text: Submit the extraction workload through the Message Batches API for asynchronous processing.
options.feedback: This is correct because the workload is high volume and does not require real-time responses. The Message Batches API is designed for asynchronous processing and provides discounted token pricing for batchable requests.

options.label: D
options.text: Place the shared taxonomy and examples before product-specific content and use prompt caching.
options.feedback: This is correct because the repeated guidance is a stable prompt prefix across many requests. Prompt caching reduces the cost of repeatedly sending the same reusable content, while still allowing each product description to vary after the cached prefix.

questions.explanation:
This scenario maps naturally to two architecture levers: batching and prompt caching. The workload is large, repetitive, and not time-sensitive, so the Message Batches API is a better fit than an interactive agent session because it is built for asynchronous bulk processing and discounted batch execution.

The prompt structure also matters. Prompt caching works best when stable, reusable content appears at the beginning of the prompt, with a cache breakpoint at the end of the unchanged prefix. In this case, the taxonomy, definitions, and examples are valuable shared context, so placing them before the per-product description lets the system reuse that prefix instead of paying full input cost on every request. See Prompt caching for the design pattern and usage accounting.

The rejected approaches reflect common architecture anti-patterns. A single long Claude Code session is optimized for agentic coding workflows, not bulk extraction at production scale, and it can accumulate unnecessary context. Blindly removing examples or choosing the smallest model may reduce spend, but it changes quality risk without tying the decision to evaluations or business accuracy requirements.

questions.question: A legal aid nonprofit is piloting a Claude workflow that screens intake forms, routes cases by issue type, drafts a plain-language next-step summary, and avoids revealing information from unrelated clients. The team wants an evaluation framework that will guide prompt and model changes before expanding to more clinics. Which TWO actions best support that goal?

options.label: A
options.text: Use human review for every case and postpone automation until after launch.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because human grading is flexible and high quality, but it is slow and expensive. Anthropic recommends automating when possible and favoring larger automated eval sets over relying only on smaller hand-graded sets.

options.label: B
options.text: Define measurable success criteria for each output dimension before selecting grading methods.
options.feedback: This is correct because evaluation design should begin with specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant success criteria. For this workflow, routing, summary quality, privacy, and tone are distinct dimensions that may need different measures.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a broad test set with realistic cases, edge cases, and mixed automated graders.
options.feedback: This is correct because eval datasets should mirror the real task distribution and include edge cases. Mixed grading lets the team use code-based checks for objective fields and rubric-based LLM grading for nuanced judgments.

options.label: D
options.text: Optimize against one overall accuracy score using only straightforward intake examples.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because most production use cases need multidimensional evaluation rather than a single scalar metric. Straightforward examples alone would miss edge cases such as ambiguous eligibility, unusual facts, and privacy-sensitive inputs.

questions.explanation:
Strong evaluation frameworks start with success criteria, not with a favorite grader or a single launch metric. Anthropic describes good criteria as specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and notes that real applications usually need several dimensions such as task fidelity, consistency, privacy preservation, tone, latency, and price. See Define success criteria.

After the dimensions are clear, the test framework should pair each dimension with an appropriate methodology. Objective outputs, such as case category labels or required field extraction, can often use code-based grading such as exact match, while nuanced outputs, such as plain-language quality or privacy handling, may need LLM-based grading with a detailed rubric and specific score format. The dataset should resemble real clinic intake traffic and include edge cases, because a model that only passes clean examples may fail under the conditions that matter most in production. Anthropic's guidance to mirror the real-world distribution, include edge cases, automate when possible, and mix evaluation methods is covered in Develop tests.

questions.question: A university research computing group uses Claude Code in shared lab workstations and sends telemetry to an OpenTelemetry collector. After enabling telemetry and exporting metrics, their dashboard shows token and cost trends, but it has no records for API errors, tool results, or authentication activity. They want to add operational event visibility without collecting prompt or response text. Which change best addresses the gap?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable distributed traces and use spans as the primary source for tool events.
options.feedback: Claude Code can optionally export distributed traces, but traces are not on by default and are separate from the documented logs/events export path. Enabling traces does not replace configuring the logs exporter for event records such as tool results or API errors.

options.label: B
options.text: Set OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER to otlp and keep prompt and response content logging disabled.
options.feedback: Claude Code exports operational events through the OpenTelemetry logs/events pipeline, not through the metrics pipeline. Prompt and assistant response content logging is disabled or redacted by default, so leaving those content flags off preserves event visibility without collecting that text.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL and wait for API error events to appear.
options.feedback: Changing the metrics export interval only affects how often metrics are sent, with a documented default of 60 seconds. API errors and tool results are events, so they require a logs/events exporter rather than a faster metrics interval.

options.label: D
options.text: Add prompt.id to token metrics and build event dashboards from metric series.
options.feedback: The prompt.id value is intended for correlating events such as prompts, API requests, and tool activity. It is intentionally excluded from metrics because using it as a metric attribute would create unbounded cardinality.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code telemetry separates different observability signals. Metrics are time-series values such as token usage, cost usage, sessions, commits, and active time. Events, including API requests, API errors, tool results, authentication activity, and MCP server connection events, are exported through the OpenTelemetry logs/events protocol.

That separation matters operationally because a team can have healthy metrics ingestion while still seeing no event records at all. To observe event names such as claude_code.api_error or claude_code.tool_result, telemetry must be enabled and OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER must be configured, for example to otlp. Metrics settings such as OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER and OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL do not cause logs/events to be emitted.

The privacy tradeoff is also explicit. Prompt content, assistant response text, tool details, and raw API bodies are redacted or disabled by default, so teams can collect operational events without automatically collecting the user-visible text. For correlation, use event fields such as prompt.id in the event stream rather than adding high-cardinality identifiers to metrics.

See the official Claude Code documentation on monitoring usage for the documented exporters, event names, metric names, and logging controls.

questions.question: A maritime insurance underwriting team uses Claude to extract risk factors from vessel inspection PDFs and draft underwriting notes. After an optimization release that changed the prompt and routed short reports to a lower-cost model, auditors report missing risk factors, unsupported facts, and worse performance on older scanned reports. Which two actions best isolate whether the failures come from prompting, hallucination, or model fit?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the previous and current prompt and model routes on the same eval set, then slice results by report type and failure category.
options.feedback: Using the same eval set provides a controlled comparison between the release variants. Slicing results helps reveal whether failures cluster around prompt changes, model routing, or specific input conditions.

options.label: B
options.text: Add stronger instructions to avoid unsupported facts, then monitor auditor complaints after the next release for recurring patterns.
options.feedback: A prompt change may be worth testing, but applying it before measurement makes diagnosis weaker. Auditor complaints are delayed, noisy, and unlikely to provide the coverage needed to separate hallucination, prompt, and model-fit issues.

options.label: C
options.text: Build a task-specific eval set from recent reports, including scanned and short-report edge cases, with metrics for extraction accuracy, unsupported facts, and latency.
options.feedback: This creates measurable criteria tied to the observed failure modes and operational goals. Including scanned and short-report cases keeps the eval aligned with the real task distribution rather than only easy examples.

options.label: D
options.text: Route all reports to the highest-capability model, then remove failing scanned reports from the benchmark until scores stabilize.
options.feedback: Routing everything to a stronger model may mask the model-routing problem without showing which cases require it. Removing difficult scanned reports is an evaluation anti-pattern because it excludes known edge cases from the benchmark.

questions.explanation:
When several symptoms appear after an optimization, the safest mental model is to turn the complaint stream into an evaluation design problem. Define success criteria tied to the product behavior, such as extraction fidelity, unsupported claims, and operational metrics, then test against cases that resemble production rather than the easiest examples.

Anthropic's guidance on Define success criteria and build evaluations emphasizes specific, measurable, achievable, relevant criteria and task-specific evals with edge cases. A fixed eval set lets you compare old and new prompts or model-routing decisions under controlled conditions, while slicing failures by document type and failure class helps distinguish a prompt instruction issue from a hallucination or grounding issue or a poor model fit for a subset of inputs.

Ad hoc prompt hardening and broad model upgrades can be reasonable experiments after the failure mode is measured, but they are weak first diagnostic steps. They can hide regressions, increase cost, or improve one symptom while leaving another unobserved, especially when edge cases such as scanned reports are removed rather than represented in the benchmark.

questions.question: An airport operations software team uses Claude Code across several engineering workstations and exports aggregate cost and token metrics to an OpenTelemetry backend. During an incident review, they need to reconstruct how a single user prompt led to later API requests and tool activity, but they do not want to destabilize their metric dashboards with high-cardinality labels. Which change best supports the investigation?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable raw prompt and assistant text logging and correlate activity by matching message content.
options.feedback: Raw prompt and assistant response logging is disabled or redacted by default and should not be required for operational correlation. Matching on message text is also less reliable and less privacy-preserving than using the documented event correlation identifier.

options.label: B
options.text: Add prompt.id to token metric attributes and build per-prompt panels in the metrics backend.
options.feedback: This treats a per-prompt identifier as a metric dimension, which is the pattern the documentation avoids. Metrics backends perform poorly when labels have unbounded cardinality, and prompt.id is excluded from metrics for that reason.

options.label: C
options.text: Configure log event export and correlate exported events using prompt.id while keeping metrics aggregated.
options.feedback: This uses Claude Code events for per-prompt investigation while preserving metrics for aggregate time-series analysis. The prompt.id field is intended to connect a user prompt with related API and tool events, and it is intentionally not part of metrics to avoid unbounded cardinality.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable only distributed trace export and disable log events for prompt.id event correlation.
options.feedback: Claude Code distributed tracing is optional and can link each user prompt to the API requests and tool executions it triggers. However, traces produce spans rather than the documented log and event records containing prompt.id, and disabling log export removes that event stream.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code observability separates metrics from events. Metrics such as claude_code.token.usage and claude_code.cost.usage are time-series signals meant for aggregate dashboards, while events provide richer operational records such as user prompts, API requests, API errors, tool results, and tool decisions.

For incident reconstruction, the important mental model is to use the right telemetry signal for the job. A per-prompt identifier is useful for linking related events, but it is a poor metric label because every prompt can create a new value. Claude Code therefore uses prompt.id for event correlation and intentionally excludes it from metrics to avoid unbounded metric cardinality.

Telemetry must also be explicitly enabled, and log events require configuring OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER. Prompt and assistant response text logging are separate opt-ins, so a team can export operational events without collecting raw prompt or response content. See the official Claude Code monitoring documentation at Monitoring usage.

questions.question: A genomic diagnostics lab’s report automation team is designing a Claude workflow that drafts clinician-facing variant interpretation notes. The prompt includes fixed lab policy, variable patient phenotype text, retrieved literature snippets, and a few examples of preferred wording. The team prototypes in Claude Console before deploying with the Messages API, and it wants consistent narrative sections while avoiding accidental elevation of untrusted retrieved text. Which TWO prompt design choices best fit documented Claude guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Convert every retrieved literature update into a mid-conversation system message so later turns treat it as higher authority.
options.feedback: Retrieved literature is untrusted content and should not be elevated into system content. Mid-conversation system messages are a specific feature with model and platform constraints, not a general mechanism for RAG content.

options.label: B
options.text: Build a Console template with {{patient_context}} and {{literature_snippets}} variables, using XML tags and structured examples.
options.feedback: Templates separate fixed prompt text from variable inputs, which fits patient-specific and retrieval-based content. XML tags and relevant examples help Claude distinguish instructions, inputs, and examples for more consistent narrative output.

options.label: C
options.text: Place fixed lab policy and output rules in the top-level system field, and keep patient input in request content and retrieved tool output in tool_result blocks.
options.feedback: This keeps operator instructions in the proper place for instructions that apply from the start of the request. It also separates user-specific content and retrieved third-party material from higher-authority system content.

options.label: D
options.text: Put lab policy, patient context, and retrieved snippets into a system message as the first item in messages.
options.feedback: Initial system instructions should use the top-level system field, not a system message as the first entry in the messages array. This also mixes trusted operator instructions with untrusted or user-specific content.

questions.explanation:
For instructions that define the assistant’s role, policy boundaries, and output expectations from the start, use the Messages API’s top-level system field. The working-with-messages guidance explains that initial system instructions belong there rather than as the first item in messages: Working with messages.

The key guardrail is authority separation. System content is treated as operator instruction, so raw retrieved documents, web pages, tool outputs, and other third-party content should not be promoted to system messages. Patient or user-specific input can be supplied as request content, while retrieved third-party literature should be clearly delimited as untrusted context and kept in tool_result blocks when it is produced by tools. Anthropic’s mid-conversation system message documentation also warns that this feature is not a general replacement for the top-level system prompt and has specific placement, model, and platform rules: Mid-conversation system messages.

For the Console prototype, templates are a good fit because they separate fixed instructions from variable content using {{double_bracket}} variables, such as patient context or retrieved snippets. For consistent narrative sections, XML structure and few-shot examples help Claude parse which text is instruction, which text is context, and which text is an example, without requiring a rigid schema. See Prompting tools and System prompts for the template, XML, and example-based guidance.

questions.question: A national museum consortium's platform team uses Claude Code for automated repository maintenance. Sessions often run Bash commands that execute instrumented integration tests. Leadership wants one observability program that tracks Claude Code adoption, tool decisions, and the applications' own telemetry in an OTLP collector. The team plans to define OTEL_* variables only in Claude Code settings. Which strategy best avoids blind spots at scale?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable Claude Code telemetry and provide the applications' OTEL configuration in their own execution environment.
options.feedback: This separates Claude Code telemetry from telemetry emitted by programs Claude Code launches. Claude Code can export its own metrics, events, and optional traces, but it does not pass OTEL_* variables into spawned subprocesses such as Bash commands.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the Prometheus metrics exporter for all Claude Code metrics, events, and application spans.
options.feedback: Prometheus is supported for Claude Code metrics, not for all telemetry signals. Claude Code events use the OTel logs/events protocol, and application spans must be emitted by the applications themselves.

options.label: C
options.text: Configure Claude Code OTLP exporters and rely on spawned Bash commands to inherit the same OTEL variables.
options.feedback: This would leave the applications' telemetry unconfigured when those applications are launched from Claude Code. Claude Code explicitly does not pass OTEL_* variables into spawned subprocesses, so inheritance is the wrong assumption.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable raw API body logging and use those event payloads as the primary source for application traces.
options.feedback: Raw API body logging is a privacy-sensitive logging feature, not a substitute for application traces. It can include the entire conversation history and is off by default, so it should not be used as a broad observability workaround.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code observability is OpenTelemetry-based, but it is scoped to Claude Code itself. To collect Claude Code signals, the team must enable telemetry, for example with CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, and configure the appropriate exporters for metrics, events, and optional traces. The monitoring documentation describes these signals and exporter options in Claude Code monitoring usage.

The key integration boundary is subprocess execution. Claude Code does not pass OTEL_* variables into spawned Bash commands, hooks, MCP servers, or language servers. That design prevents Claude Code's own telemetry configuration from accidentally becoming the telemetry configuration for every tool it launches, but it means instrumented applications need their own environment or runtime configuration when they run under Claude Code.

At scale, teams should treat Claude Code telemetry and application telemetry as related but distinct sources. Claude Code metrics and tool decision events help explain adoption and permission behavior, while application spans and logs must come from the application runtime. Privacy-gated prompt, response, tool content, and raw API body logging can support targeted debugging, but they are not a safe or complete substitute for properly configured application observability.

That design prevents Claude Code's own telemetry configuration from accidentally becoming the telemetry configuration for every tool it launches, but it means instrumented applications need their own environment or runtime configuration when they run under Claude Code.

At scale, teams should treat Claude Code telemetry and application telemetry as related but distinct sources. Claude Code metrics and tool decision events help explain adoption and permission behavior, while application spans and logs must come from the application runtime. Privacy-gated prompt, response, tool content, and raw API body logging can support targeted debugging, but they are not a safe or complete substitute for properly configured application observability.

questions.question: A regional electric utility's customer communications team is piloting a Claude workflow that drafts outage updates for call center agents. Operations leaders want a service commitment for the next storm season, while legal, finance, and customer experience reviewers are giving conflicting feedback about acceptable answer quality, privacy handling, response time, and operating cost. What should the architect do next to align expectations before committing to the service target?

options.label: A
options.text: Select the most capable model and defer cost targets until reviewers approve the drafts.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it treats quality as the only meaningful dimension. Price and latency are documented success criteria, so deferring cost targets can create misaligned expectations and an unsustainable service commitment.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask each reviewer to approve outputs informally and use majority opinion as the launch gate.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because informal approvals do not create specific, measurable, or repeatable criteria. Majority opinion can hide important constraints, such as privacy preservation or latency requirements, that should be explicit.

options.label: C
options.text: Define measurable success criteria across quality, privacy, latency, and cost with the stakeholders.
options.feedback: This is correct because expectation alignment should start by converting stakeholder preferences into measurable criteria. It also reflects that most Claude use cases require evaluation across multiple dimensions, not a single vague quality goal.

options.label: D
options.text: Commit to the requested response-time target and gather reviewer feedback after launch.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it sets the service target before resolving what stakeholders mean by success. Post-launch feedback is useful, but it does not replace pre-launch alignment on measurable acceptance criteria.

questions.explanation:
For stakeholder communication, the architect's job is to turn broad preferences into an operating contract the team can evaluate and maintain. Anthropic's evaluation guidance emphasizes that good success criteria should be specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and it calls out dimensions such as task fidelity, consistency, relevance, tone, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency, and price. See Define success criteria.

An SLA or service target should not be negotiated from a vague promise like "high quality" or "fast enough." In practice, the team should agree on a scorecard that reflects the actual tradeoffs stakeholders care about, then use that scorecard to decide what launch readiness and ongoing service commitments mean. This prevents one group, such as operations or finance, from accidentally optimizing away another group's requirement, such as privacy or customer tone.

The incorrect approaches all skip part of that alignment loop. Launching first, relying on informal majority approval, or choosing the largest model before defining cost and latency expectations can produce short-term momentum, but they leave the team without a shared basis for evaluating feedback or defending the SLA.

questions.question: A commercial real estate due diligence team uses Claude to review lease excerpts and determine whether a rent escalation clause meets an internal checklist. The current prompt already returns the requested fields, but it often misses interactions between exceptions, caps, and renewal terms. The team has disabled extended thinking for latency, and the application can extract XML-tagged sections before displaying the answer to users. Which prompt change is the best next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the checklist into the top-level system parameter, then keep the user prompt short.
options.feedback: This uses a valid API structure for system-level instructions, and it may help keep the checklist consistently available. However, it does not directly address the missed multi-step interactions because the output process remains a single-step judgment.

options.label: B
options.text: Add one ideal example for a common lease clause, then ask Claude to generalize from it.
options.feedback: Examples can improve consistency, but a single common-case example is unlikely to cover the edge-case interactions described. Anthropic recommends relevant, diverse examples, typically several examples, when using few-shot prompting.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to reason through the checklist in a <thinking> section, then put the final fields in an <answer> section.
options.feedback: This directly targets multi-step reasoning errors while preserving a clean final output for the application. Since extended thinking is disabled, structured manual reasoning is an appropriate fallback, and XML sections let the app separate reasoning from the answer.

options.label: D
options.text: Add an instruction to be extremely careful, then keep the current single-step output format.
options.feedback: This may slightly steer behavior, but it does not give Claude a structured way to work through interacting checklist conditions. Vague accuracy instructions are weaker than explicit steps or structured reasoning when completeness and order matters.

questions.explanation:
The failure pattern is not primarily about output formatting, because the current prompt already returns the requested fields. It is about applying a checklist across interacting conditions, so the prompt should make Claude reason through those conditions before producing the final answer. When built-in thinking is not being used, Anthropic documents manual reasoning prompts with structured tags such as <thinking> and <answer> as a fallback technique, while XML tags help Claude distinguish instructions, context, intermediate work, and final output. See Prompting best practices.

Few-shot prompting would be a strong candidate if the main problem were inconsistent tone, structure, or classification boundaries, but the option using only one common-case example does not address exceptions and rare interactions well. A better few-shot approach would use several relevant and diverse examples, wrapped clearly in XML, but the scenario points more directly to missing multi-step reasoning. Moving the checklist into the top-level system parameter is valid for persistent context and role instructions, as shown in the Messages API create reference, but valid placement alone does not create a reasoning procedure for interacting lease terms.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical clinical-operations automation team is writing an architecture decision record for a protocol-deviation review assistant. The workflow launches background investigations that can continue after an analyst closes the browser, and the team wants to avoid owning orchestration infrastructure for agent progress and continuation. Which implementation guidance best fits the architecture decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the Messages API and document that prior turns persist automatically across requests.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the Messages API is stateless. An application using it must send the relevant conversation history on each request rather than relying on Claude to retain prior turns.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the Messages API and document a first message with role system for global instructions.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because global instructions that apply from the start should be placed in the top-level system field. Treating a system message as the first entry in messages is not the recommended construction and is not valid under the documented placement rules.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude Managed Agents and document the integration around the managed agent harness.
options.feedback: This is correct because the scenario calls for work that can continue asynchronously and does not require a custom application-owned agent loop. Claude Managed Agents provide a pre-built, configurable harness in managed infrastructure, which fits that lifecycle and ownership model.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Claude Managed Agents and document a custom application-owned loop for each agent step.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it mixes the managed-agent choice with the implementation burden that the managed harness is intended to avoid. If the application needs fine-grained control over a custom loop, the Messages API is the architecture designed for that style.

questions.explanation:
The key architectural distinction is ownership of the agent loop. The Messages API documentation describes the Messages API as direct model-prompting access for custom agent loops and fine-grained control, while Claude Managed Agents provide a pre-built, configurable harness in managed infrastructure for long-running and asynchronous work.

In this scenario, the team wants background work that can outlive an interactive browser session and does not need bespoke orchestration. That points to documenting a managed-agent integration rather than making the product team own every turn, tool decision, and continuation mechanism.

If the team did choose the Messages API, the implementation guide would need to be explicit that requests are stateless and must include the needed conversation history each time. It should also place instructions that apply from the beginning in the top-level system field, rather than treating a first messages entry with role: "system" as the normal pattern.

questions.question: A municipal emergency management office is piloting a Claude Code based agent that monitors weather feeds, summarizes incident reports, drafts public advisories, and can call an MCP tool that sends alerts to residents. Staff want monitoring and drafting to run without interruption, but any resident-facing alert must be approved by the duty officer. Which design best applies human-in-the-loop validation?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a larger model for alert decisions and remove approval prompts.
options.feedback: A more capable model may improve reasoning quality, but it does not replace authorization for high-impact actions. Removing prompts increases the risk that a public-facing action occurs without human validation.

options.label: B
options.text: Allow the alert-sending tool and instruct Claude to ask before using it.
options.feedback: Prompt guidance can reduce accidental actions, but it is not an enforcement mechanism. If the tool is otherwise allowed, the system still depends on model behavior rather than a permission boundary.

options.label: C
options.text: Log every alert-sending call and review the audit trail after each shift.
options.feedback: Audit logging is useful for investigation and accountability, but it happens after the action has already occurred. It does not prevent an unapproved public alert from being sent.

options.label: D
options.text: Require approval for the alert-sending tool while auto-approving monitoring and drafting actions.
options.feedback: This preserves automation for low-risk work while putting a human approval gate on the high-impact external action. Human-in-the-loop validation is most effective when it is attached to the specific tool or permission boundary where irreversible or visible action occurs.

questions.explanation:
Human-in-the-loop controls should be placed at the action boundary, not merely in the model's behavioral instructions. In this scenario, monitoring feeds and drafting advisories are useful autonomous tasks, while sending an alert is visible to the public and difficult to unwind. The right pattern is to let low-risk steps proceed while requiring explicit approval before the tool that sends the alert can execute.

Claude Code and the Agent SDK provide permission mechanisms that can enforce this kind of boundary. For example, permission rules and callbacks can route specific tool calls to approval, and MCP tools can be marked as requiring user interaction when the approval prompt is part of the intended workflow. See Anthropic's documentation on Configure permissions and Require approval for a specific tool.

Prompting Claude to be careful is still valuable, but it is a behavioral control rather than a hard gate. Logging is a detective control, and model choice is a quality control. Neither provides the same governance protection as requiring a human to approve the specific tool call that creates external impact.

questions.question: A live events ticketing platform's developer productivity team is standardizing Claude Code usage for two recurring needs. Engineers want a reusable code-review worker that runs inside the current session, keeps review details out of the main context, and can only inspect files. The same team also runs occasional repository-wide migrations that coordinate many delegated tasks and should not store every orchestration step in the lead conversation. Which two design choices best fit these needs?

options.label: A
options.text: Define a focused custom subagent with read-only tools and a clear task description.
options.feedback: This fits a reusable worker that runs within a single Claude Code session and uses its own context window. Specifying only read-oriented tools applies least privilege instead of relying on inherited permissions.

options.label: B
options.text: Omit the tools field in the subagent file to make the worker read-only.
options.feedback: For custom subagents, the tools field is optional, but omitting it causes the subagent to inherit all available tools. That is the opposite of enforcing a read-only tool surface.

options.label: C
options.text: Use dynamic workflows for high-volume migration orchestration across many delegated tasks.
options.feedback: Dynamic workflows are intended for scripted orchestration when runs coordinate many subagents. This keeps the orchestration in a script executed by the runtime rather than accumulating every coordination step in the conversation context.

options.label: D
options.text: Launch agent teams for the code-review worker so it can run inside one session.
options.feedback: Agent teams are for coordinated sessions with shared tasks and inter-agent messaging. A reusable worker inside the current session is a subagent pattern, not a separate team of communicating sessions.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code has several parallelization patterns, and the architecture choice should match the coordination boundary. Subagents are delegated workers inside a single Claude Code session; they have their own context window and return results to the caller. That makes them a good fit for focused review, analysis, or debugging roles where the main session should receive a summarized result rather than every intermediate detail.

Custom subagents are defined as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter, where name and description are required and tools is optional. Because omitting tools allows inheritance of all tools, a read-only reviewer should explicitly list only inspection tools. The Claude Code subagents documentation describes these semantics, including tool inheritance and the role of subagents within one session.

For large fan-out work, dynamic workflows address a different tradeoff: they move orchestration into a script run by the runtime, which is better when coordinating many delegated tasks would otherwise bloat the lead conversation. Agent teams and background sessions are useful for independent or communicating sessions, but they are not the right abstraction for a single reusable in-session worker. The Claude Code agents overview distinguishes subagents, agent view, agent teams, and dynamic workflows so architects do not treat every multi-agent feature as interchangeable.

questions.question: A specialty pharmacy's automation team uses a Claude Code workflow connected to an internal MCP server. The workflow can check insurance status, draft pharmacist notes, request refill clarifications, and call a tool that releases controlled-substance shipments. Pharmacists want routine research and drafting to proceed unattended, but shipment release must involve an on-duty pharmacist each time. Which design best applies human-in-the-loop validation?

options.label: A
options.text: Add destructive metadata to the release tool and let auto mode decide whether each call proceeds.
options.feedback: Tool annotations such as destructive hints are metadata, not enforcement. Auto mode can reduce routine prompts, but it is not a substitute for a deterministic per-call approval requirement on a regulated action.

options.label: B
options.text: Require approval for the release tool and route each request through the pharmacist approval flow.
options.feedback: This preserves automation for low-risk work while putting a human approval gate directly in front of the high-impact action. In Claude Code and the Agent SDK, permission prompts and approval callbacks are the appropriate control point for deciding whether a tool call may proceed.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable bypass permissions for pharmacy tools and instruct Claude to ask before release calls.
options.feedback: A prompt instruction is advisory and can be missed or overridden by later context, so it is not a reliable enforcement layer. Bypassing permissions makes the tool surface more permissive, which is the opposite of a robust human-in-the-loop control.

options.label: D
options.text: Log every release tool call after execution and notify the pharmacist queue for review.
options.feedback: Logging and notification are detective controls that help with auditing after the fact. They do not prevent an unapproved shipment release from occurring, so they do not satisfy the need for human validation before execution.

questions.explanation:
Human-in-the-loop validation is most effective when the approval gate is placed at the point where an irreversible or regulated action would execute. In this scenario, routine information gathering and drafting can continue with fewer interruptions, while the controlled-substance release tool should require explicit approval before the tool call runs.

Claude Code permission controls are designed around this boundary: hooks, deny and ask rules, permission modes, allow rules, and runtime approval callbacks determine whether a requested tool call proceeds. MCP servers can set _meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"]: true in the tools/list response, with Claude Code v2.1.199 or later, to prompt on every call even in acceptEdits, auto, and bypassPermissions modes. See Handle approvals and user input, Configure permissions, and Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP.

The key governance distinction is preventive control versus detective control. Prompt-only guidance, annotations, auto mode, and after-the-fact logging may reduce or reveal risk, but they do not provide the same assurance as a mandatory approval path before the high-impact tool executes.

questions.question: A railway maintenance analytics team is adding Claude to a work-order triage service. Its asset-management vendor provides a trusted remote MCP server over HTTPS using Streamable HTTP. A separate track-sensor diagnostic utility is only available as a local STDIO MCP server on an engineer's laptop. The service will call Claude through the Messages API on the Claude API platform and wants to minimize custom integration code. Which TWO integration choices best match these constraints?

options.label: A
options.text: Register the local diagnostic server in mcp_servers with its command and reference it from a matching MCPToolset entry.
options.feedback: This is incorrect for the Messages API MCP connector because its MCP server definitions use remote URL-based servers, not local command-based STDIO servers. Local STDIO can be useful in other MCP client environments, but it is not directly supported by this connector.

options.label: B
options.text: Configure both servers with the deprecated MCP beta header and place tool_configuration inside each server definition.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the older MCP connector beta version is deprecated. The current pattern moves tool configuration into the tools array as MCPToolset objects rather than putting tool_configuration inside the MCP server definition.

options.label: C
options.text: Connect the vendor server with the Messages API MCP connector using the current beta header and an MCPToolset entry.
options.feedback: This is correct because the Messages API MCP connector is designed to connect Claude directly to remote MCP servers without requiring a separate MCP client. The current request shape uses an MCP server definition plus a tool entry of type mcp_toolset, and the current beta header is required.

options.label: D
options.text: Handle the local diagnostic server outside the direct Messages API MCP connector unless it is exposed through a supported remote transport.
options.feedback: This is correct because the Messages API MCP connector cannot connect directly to local STDIO MCP servers. The team would need to use another integration approach, such as a client-side MCP connection or a supported remote HTTP or SSE MCP server, before Claude can use it through this path.

questions.explanation:
The key integration distinction is whether Claude is connecting through the Messages API MCP connector or through some other client-side integration path. The connector is appropriate when you have a trusted remote MCP server that is reachable over the supported HTTP-based transports, and you want Claude to access that server's tools without your application implementing an MCP client. The current API shape uses mcp_servers together with a tools entry of type mcp_toolset, and requires the current mcp-client-2025-11-20 beta header.

The local STDIO server is the important edge case. STDIO MCP servers are common in local development and Claude Code style environments, but the Messages API connector currently supports only remote MCP tool calls over supported HTTP transports. An additional Claude agent does not change that transport limitation, and the deprecated request shape should not be used for new designs. See the official MCP connector documentation for the connector role, limitations, and current request format.

questions.question: An online learning platform's assessment automation team has a Claude assistant for instructors. It is configured with 58 tools across LMS submissions, rubric lookup, gradebook writes, student messaging, billing, proctoring, and incident systems. Instructors use it only to retrieve submissions, find rubric criteria, and draft feedback. The team notices irrelevant tool plans and increasing token usage from tool definitions. Which configuration change best addresses the capability bloat?

options.label: A
options.text: Expose a smaller, namespaced tool set aligned to submissions, rubrics, and feedback drafting.
options.feedback: This directly reduces capability bloat by removing tools outside the instructor workflow and keeping the remaining tools focused. Namespacing and tighter boundaries also help Claude choose among the remaining tools more reliably.

options.label: B
options.text: Wrap each integration as a client tool and execute every call in the application.
options.feedback: Changing execution responsibility does not remove unnecessary capabilities from Claude's available tool set. Client tools also require the application to execute calls and return tool results, which adds integration work without solving the catalog size problem.

options.label: C
options.text: Set tool_choice to any and leave the existing LMS, billing, and messaging tools enabled.
options.feedback: This forces Claude to call one of the provided tools, but it does not reduce the number of tools in context. It can make irrelevant tool use more likely when a request should be answered without a tool call.

options.label: D
options.text: Add broader descriptions to every tool while keeping all integrations available to the agent.

questions.explanation:
Tool configuration is an architectural control surface. The tools parameter is not free: tool names, descriptions, and schemas contribute input tokens, and client tool calls add tool_use and tool_result blocks to the conversation. The official tool use overview describes these execution and context effects in Tool use overview.

The strongest response is to reduce the exposed capability set to the workflows the assistant actually needs, then make those remaining tools easy to select. Anthropic's guidance for implementing tools recommends clear plaintext descriptions that describe when a tool should and should not be used, meaningful namespacing, consolidation of related operations, and high-signal tool results, as described in Implement tool use.

tool_choice is not a substitute for pruning. Modes such as any or forcing a named tool control whether and which provided tool is called, but they do not reduce context usage or remove unnecessary operational access. Similarly, converting integrations into client tools changes who executes the operation, not whether Claude must reason over a bloated tool catalog.

questions.question: An aerospace parts distributor's legal operations team is building a long-running Claude agent that uses the Anthropic memory tool to remember matter-handling preferences between requests. The app will execute memory tool commands in a client-side handler on a shared server. Which two controls should the architect require to reduce documented safety risks before enabling this in production?

options.label: A
options.text: Rely on Claude's normal refusal behavior and skip application-side filtering for memory writes.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because refusal behavior is not a complete enforcement boundary for persisted storage. The memory tool documentation recommends stronger application-side validation for sensitive information.

options.label: B
options.text: Permit memory commands to use existing absolute matter paths and enforce access through prompts.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prompts are behavioral guidance, not a hard filesystem boundary. Memory handlers should constrain tool paths to the intended memory area rather than allowing arbitrary absolute paths.

options.label: C
options.text: Validate every memory path after canonical resolution and reject any request that escapes /memories.
options.feedback: This is correct because the application, not Claude, executes memory file operations. Canonical path validation helps prevent traversal attempts from reaching files outside the intended memory directory.

options.label: D
options.text: Redact sensitive values before memory writes and cap stored file sizes and view results.
options.feedback: This is correct because memory can persist information across turns and sessions, so sensitive data and uncontrolled growth are governance risks. Application-side filtering and size limits provide safeguards beyond model behavior.

questions.explanation:
The memory tool gives Claude a way to request persistent reads and writes, but the host application is responsible for executing those commands safely. Anthropic's documentation states that your handler must reject paths outside /memories, including traversal patterns such as ../, and should use canonical path checks to confirm that resolved paths remain inside the intended directory.

Persistence also changes the risk profile: information written to memory may survive beyond the current request, so relying only on model behavior is not enough for legal, regulated, or confidential workflows. Redaction before writes, storage caps, and limits on how much content view can return reduce the chance of retaining sensitive material or flooding future context with excessive data.

Prompt instructions can help shape Claude's behavior, but they do not replace enforcement in the tool runner. For this kind of agent, the mental model is that Claude proposes file operations and your application decides what is actually allowed. See Anthropic's Memory tool documentation for the path traversal, sensitive information, and size-control guidance.

questions.question: A food safety certification nonprofit uses Claude to answer auditors' questions from inspection standards. The workflow was originally tuned on short FAQ questions, but it is now being used for nuanced exception cases without a formal test set. Reviewers report invented clause references, inconsistent answers to paraphrased questions, and poor performance on ambiguous facility scenarios. Which action should the architecture team take first?

options.label: A
options.text: Run a task-specific eval suite covering real cases, edge cases, and measurable grading criteria.
options.feedback: This gives the team evidence about which behaviors are failing and under what inputs. Representative evals with edge cases can separate issues like unsupported facts, inconsistency, and poor handling of ambiguous scenarios before the team chooses a fix.

options.label: B
options.text: Route all questions to a more capable model, then compare reviewer escalations after several weeks.
options.feedback: Changing the model can mask or reduce some failures, but it does not diagnose whether the root problem is prompt design, evaluation coverage, or task mismatch. Waiting on escalations also delays feedback and does not provide controlled comparisons across representative cases.

options.label: C
options.text: Rewrite the system prompt with stronger grounding instructions, then redeploy and monitor complaint volume.
options.feedback: A prompt rewrite may eventually be part of the fix, but doing it first is an ad hoc change without a baseline. Complaint volume is also a noisy lagging signal and may not reveal which task slices regressed.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask experts to hand-grade a small failure sample, then tune until reviewer consensus improves.
options.feedback: Expert grading can be useful for nuanced judgments, but a small failure-only sample does not reflect the real task distribution. It is also slower and less scalable than automated or rubric-based grading where those methods are feasible.

questions.explanation:
When an LLM system shows mixed symptoms such as unsupported references, inconsistent answers, and weak edge-case handling, the first diagnostic move is to establish measurable evaluations rather than immediately changing the prompt or model. Anthropic's guidance emphasizes defining specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant success criteria, then building evals that reflect the real task distribution, including edge cases. See Define success criteria and build evaluations.

A useful eval suite for this scenario would separate dimensions such as factual support, consistency across paraphrases, and performance on ambiguous exception cases. Once those results are segmented, the team can make a better engineering decision, such as revising the prompt, changing model routing, adding grounding, or adjusting the workflow. The distractors all jump to possible remedies before collecting reliable evidence, which can hide the actual failure mode and make later optimization harder.
