questions.question: A precision agriculture startup's field-operations platform team is writing an implementation guide for a crop-advisory assistant. The existing service must keep ownership of routing, transcript storage, grower-specific policy checks, and prompt assembly before each Claude call. Which guidance should the implementation guide provide?

options.label: A
options.text: Document a Messages API integration that starts the messages array with role system and appends user turns after it.
options.feedback: This puts system instructions in the wrong place for instructions that should apply from the start. The recommended pattern is the top-level system field, and a system message cannot be the first entry in the messages array.

options.label: B
options.text: Document a Claude Managed Agents integration that delegates routing and continuation to Anthropic managed infrastructure.
options.feedback: Claude Managed Agents are positioned for a pre-built configurable agent harness, especially long-running or asynchronous work. In this scenario, the existing service must retain fine-grained control of routing, checks, storage, and prompt assembly, so this is not the best architectural fit.

options.label: C
options.text: Document a Messages API integration that sends only the newest user turn and relies on the API to retain prior context.
options.feedback: This treats the Messages API as if it stored conversational state between requests. The API is stateless, so an implementation that omits prior context would lose information unless the application includes it again.

options.label: D
options.text: Document a Messages API integration that rebuilds each request from stored history and places persistent instructions in the top-level system field.
options.feedback: This guidance matches a custom agent loop where the application owns routing, storage, controls, and prompt assembly. The Messages API is stateless, so the implementation guide should make clear that each request includes the needed conversation history and that start-of-conversation instructions belong in the top-level system field.

questions.explanation:
The important architecture distinction is control boundary. The Messages API gives direct model-prompting access for custom agent loops, which fits systems where your application owns routing, transcript persistence, policy checks, and prompt assembly. The documentation explains that Messages API requests are stateless, so the application must send the full conversational history needed for each request rather than assuming Claude remembers earlier turns. See Working with messages.

Implementation guidance should also be precise about instruction placement. Persistent instructions that should apply from the start should use the top-level system field. Although some models support system-role messages after a user turn subject to placement rules, documenting a first messages entry with role: "system" is not a safe pattern because a system message cannot be the first entry in messages. Claude Managed Agents can be the right choice when a team wants a managed harness for long-running or asynchronous work, but they are not the best fit when the stated design goal is to keep orchestration and request construction in the existing application.

questions.question: A digital pathology lab's developer platform team is troubleshooting bursts of 429 rate_limit_error from a Messages API service that drafts case summaries with a Claude Sonnet model. Their internal dashboard estimates output token usage by summing each request's max_tokens value, so it reports OTPM exhaustion even when many responses stop after a few hundred tokens. Which change best improves the team's operational diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Include cached-read tokens in ITPM totals and prioritize reducing prompt cache hit volume.
options.feedback: This is incorrect for a Sonnet-based service because cached-read tokens generally do not count against ITPM for most Claude models. Reducing cache hits would likely increase cost and latency pressure without addressing the stated output-token diagnosis problem.

options.label: B
options.text: Record actual output tokens from responses and alert on observed output volume by model class.
options.feedback: This is correct because OTPM is evaluated from actual output tokens generated, not the max_tokens value requested. Measuring observed output volume by model class gives the team a rate-limit signal that matches how the Messages API limits are applied.

options.label: C
options.text: Classify stop_reason: max_tokens responses as rate limit errors and retry them immediately.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because stop_reason appears in successful Messages API responses and is not itself an HTTP error mechanism. Retrying immediately can worsen rate-limit pressure, especially when the actual issue is a 429 rate_limit_error that should be handled using rate-limit-aware behavior.

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce every request's max_tokens value and continue using that field as the OTPM signal.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because max_tokens does not count toward OTPM, so using it as the metric keeps the dashboard misleading. Lowering max_tokens may cap long generations, but it does not fix the team's incorrect operational measurement.

questions.explanation:
The important distinction is that rate-limit accounting uses specific dimensions, not a single generic token estimate. The Messages API tracks limits such as RPM, ITPM, and OTPM by model class, and the documentation states that max_tokens does not count toward OTPM because OTPM is evaluated from the actual output tokens generated. See Rate limits.

For operational debugging, the team should instrument the usage that the platform actually enforces. If a dashboard sums max_tokens, it can report false OTPM saturation even when responses are short, which sends engineers toward the wrong remediation. Recording actual output tokens from responses and grouping them by model class gives a more faithful signal for alerting, capacity planning, and incident triage.

A 429 response should still be treated as a rate-limit condition, distinct from other failures, and retry behavior should respect rate-limit semantics. The API errors documentation describes 429 rate_limit_error separately from server and overload errors, and notes that official SDKs retry transient failures with exponential backoff while honoring retry-after when present. See Errors.

questions.question: An archival film restoration studio's metadata platform migrated a provenance assistant from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Claude Sonnet 4.5 to match another pipeline's model configuration. Each request includes a 650,000-token cached catalog prefix plus a short analyst question, and the API now rejects the call before Claude begins generating. The analysts need the full catalog in context for this workflow. Which change best addresses the failure?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a lower max_tokens value for requests that include the full catalog.
options.feedback: Reducing the response allowance helps only when the combined input and possible output are the issue. Here the input itself already exceeds the model's context window, so the API rejects the prompt before generation.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the model-context-window-exceeded-2025-08-26 beta header for full catalog requests.
options.feedback: This beta header opts earlier models into newer behavior for some requests where input tokens plus max_tokens exceed the window. It does not expand the context window or make an input-only overflow fit.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a 1M-token model for requests that include the full catalog.
options.feedback: This addresses the actual constraint because the full request needs a context window large enough to hold the catalog and the rest of the request. Claude Sonnet 4.5 has a 200k-token context window, while models such as Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 5 have 1M-token windows.

options.label: D
options.text: Use prompt caching for requests that include the full catalog.
options.feedback: Prompt caching can reduce cost and latency for repeated prefixes, but it does not reduce how many tokens occupy the context window. A cached 650,000-token prefix still exceeds a 200k-token model's capacity.

questions.explanation:
The important distinction is between cost optimization and context capacity. Prompt caching can make a repeated prefix cheaper and faster to process, but cached tokens still count toward the model's context window. If the input alone exceeds the selected model's window, the API returns a 400 invalid_request_error with a prompt too long condition rather than starting generation.

Model selection is therefore part of context engineering. Claude Sonnet 4.5 has a 200k-token context window, while Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and several current Opus, Fable, and Mythos models have 1M-token windows by default. For a workflow that truly requires a 650,000-token catalog in the prompt, the practical fix is to use a model whose context window can accommodate it, then still budget for system prompts, tool definitions, messages, documents, images, and output. See the official Context windows documentation for the accounting model, model-specific window sizes, and overflow behavior.

questions.question: A marine insurance syndicate's claims automation team runs Claude Opus 4.8 on the Claude API. The workflow starts with company claim-handling policy, then an operator may introduce a revised review rubric after several turns. Claimant documents and adjuster notes arrive as retrieved content, and the team wants later turns to follow the revised rubric without treating the claimant materials as operator instructions. Which prompt architecture best fits documented guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the starting policy, revised rubric, and claimant materials into one user message, ask Claude to identify priorities, and refresh the same block on each turn.
options.feedback: This avoids invalid message placement, but it weakens the authority model by mixing operator policy with retrieved evidence. Asking Claude to infer priorities is less reliable than separating instructions from context explicitly.

options.label: B
options.text: Put the revised rubric into retrieved content alongside claimant materials, keep only a short system field, and rely on examples to make the rubric higher priority.
options.feedback: Few-shot examples can steer format and style, but they do not replace proper instruction hierarchy. A revised operator rubric should not be mixed with untrusted retrieved material when the goal is to preserve authority boundaries.

options.label: C
options.text: Put the starting policy in the first messages entry as a system role, add claimant materials as later system messages, and use XML tags to separate policy from evidence.
options.feedback: Initial system instructions belong in the top-level system field, and a system message cannot be the first entry in messages. Putting claimant materials into system content also elevates untrusted content to operator-instruction status.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the starting policy in the top-level system field, add the operator's revised rubric as a valid mid-conversation system message, and keep claimant materials in tool_result content with clear XML tags.
options.feedback: This preserves the authority boundary between operator instructions and untrusted retrieved content. It also uses the mid-conversation system message feature only for an operator-authored update on a supported model and platform.

questions.explanation:
Claude prompt architecture should separate operator instructions from context supplied by users, tools, retrieval systems, or external documents. Initial instructions that apply from the start normally belong in the top-level system field, while retrieved or otherwise untrusted third-party content should stay in tool_result blocks rather than being promoted into system content. See Working with messages and Mid-conversation system messages.

Because the scenario uses Claude Opus 4.8 on the Claude API, a later operator-authored rubric can be introduced with the documented mid-conversation system message feature, provided its placement rules are satisfied. XML tags are useful for making policy, evidence, examples, and inputs easier for Claude to parse, but they are not a security boundary and do not make untrusted text safe to place in a system message. Anthropic's prompting guidance recommends structured tags for clarity, as described in System prompts.

questions.question: A clinical trial analytics group runs Claude through Amazon Bedrock to answer protocol questions. Each request includes the same 70,000-token trial protocol and review rubric, followed by a short, participant-specific question that changes every call. The team wants to reduce repeated processing of the stable material without changing answer content. Which implementation best fits this deployment?

options.label: A
options.text: Mark the participant-specific question with a cache point and rely on prefix lookback matching.
options.feedback: Cache writes occur only at marked cache points, and cache hits require exact matching of the cached segment. Marking a block that changes every request prevents effective reuse of the stable protocol prefix.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the protocol after the user question and compare only Bedrock's input token count.
options.feedback: Prompt caching works on prefixes, so reusable content should be positioned before the changing request-specific content. When caching is used, the base input token count alone is not the full accounting picture because Bedrock reports cache read and cache write input usage separately.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable top-level automatic caching and let the system choose the final cacheable block.
options.feedback: Automatic caching is convenient on supported platforms, but it is not supported on Bedrock. It would also tend to target the latest cacheable block, which is risky when the suffix changes on every request.

options.label: D
options.text: Place an explicit cache point on the last stable protocol block and monitor Bedrock cache read/write usage.
options.feedback: This uses explicit prompt caching on the reusable prefix, which is the appropriate caching approach for this deployment. Monitoring Bedrock's cache read and cache write input token usage verifies whether the stable prefix is being written and reused.

questions.explanation:
Prompt caching reuses previously processed request prefixes, not arbitrary repeated text anywhere in the prompt. The prefix order is tools, then system, then messages, up to and including the cache point or breakpoint, so the reusable protocol and rubric should appear before the participant-specific question.

For this scenario, an explicit cache point on the last stable block is the best fit because the deployment is on Amazon Bedrock, where top-level automatic caching is not supported. Exact matching matters: if the cache point is placed on a changing user question, timestamp, or other request-specific suffix, the cache entry will not match on later calls.

Cache performance should be checked through Bedrock's cache read and cache write input token usage, rather than Anthropic direct API field names such as cache_read_input_tokens or cache_creation_input_tokens. The accounting principle is the same: cached reads, cache writes, and uncached input are separate categories, so looking only at the base input token count can misrepresent the request's total input footprint. See Anthropic's Prompt caching documentation for the supported caching modes, breakpoint behavior, platform caveats, and usage accounting.

See Anthropic's Prompt caching documentation for the supported caching modes, breakpoint behavior, platform caveats, and usage accounting.

questions.question: A municipal water utility's platform reliability team runs a daily shell script that collects slow-query summaries from several services. They want Claude Code to classify likely root causes, pass the collected text directly from the script, and emit machine-readable progress records into an existing log processor while the job runs. Which TWO implementation choices best meet these goals?

options.label: A
options.text: Start an interactive `claude` session and paste the collected summaries when the prompt appears.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because an interactive session depends on a human-facing conversation flow. It does not fit a daily shell automation path that should pass data directly and return control to the script.

options.label: B
options.text: Pipe the collected summaries into `claude -p` with the classification prompt supplied by the script.
options.feedback: This is correct because `claude -p`, also available as `--print`, is the documented non-interactive automation mode that queries and then exits. It supports piped input, so the shell script can pass collected text directly instead of requiring an ongoing interactive session.

options.label: C
options.text: Set `--output-format text` and have the log processor infer structure from the response prose.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because `text` is intended for human-readable output, not reliable structured processing. A downstream log processor should consume a structured format rather than infer fields from prose.

options.label: D
options.text: Set `--output-format stream-json` so the log processor receives structured events as the job runs.
options.feedback: This is correct because `stream-json` is a documented output format for `claude -p`. It fits a workflow that needs machine-readable records during execution rather than only a final human-readable answer.

questions.explanation:
For shell automation, the key distinction is between an interactive Claude Code session and print mode, invoked with claude -p or --print. Print mode is designed to run a query and exit, which makes it appropriate for scripts, scheduled jobs, and pipelines that should not leave a developer in an open chat session.

Claude Code also follows a Unix-style workflow: data can be piped into the command, and the prompt can describe what Claude should do with that input. When another program must consume the result, choose an output format intentionally. stream-json is the better fit when the caller wants machine-readable events during execution, while json is useful for a structured final result and text is best for humans.

The anti-pattern is to make automation depend on conversational behavior or prose parsing. Pasting into an interactive session creates a manual step, and parsing human-readable text is brittle because wording can change even when the answer is semantically correct. See the official Claude Code CLI reference for the documented --print, input, and output format behavior.

questions.question: An energy trading desk's market commentary service generates long intraday narratives from live market data. Traders report a blank interface while the response is generated, and a recent attempt to lower `max_tokens` caused some narratives to end mid-sentence with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`. The team must keep the same model and preserve complete narratives, and batch processing is not involved. Which change best improves user-perceived latency without relying on truncation?

options.label: A
options.text: Set `stream: true` and update the client from server-sent event deltas.
options.feedback: This is correct because streaming lets the application receive and render partial output as Claude generates it. It improves perceived responsiveness without reducing the output cap or changing the model.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower `max_tokens` further and instruct the model to finish before the cap.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because `max_tokens` is a hard output cap, not a guarantee that the model will produce a well-formed shorter answer. If the response reaches the cap, it can be cut off and reported with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`.

options.label: C
options.text: Call the token counting endpoint first and block requests above a threshold.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because token counting helps estimate input size for cost, routing, and prompt budgeting before message creation. It does not make an accepted long response start rendering sooner.

options.label: D
options.text: Place `cache_control` on the changing feed block and reuse it across requests.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prompt caching works on identical prompt prefixes up to a cache breakpoint. Placing the breakpoint on changing per-request content creates different prefixes, which prevents reliable cache hits.

questions.explanation:
For an interactive application where the main complaint is waiting for the first visible text, streaming is the most direct optimization that preserves the same model and full answer. The Messages API can stream responses with stream: true using server-sent events, so the client can render content block deltas as they arrive rather than waiting for the complete message. See Anthropic's Streaming documentation and the latency guidance in Reduce latency.

max_tokens should not be treated as a concision or quality control. It is a hard cap on output, so lowering it can reduce worst-case output length but may also produce incomplete text, with stop_reason: "max_tokens". Token counting is valuable when estimating prompt size, cost, or routing decisions, but the Token counting endpoint returns an input-token estimate before message creation rather than reducing the time before generated text appears.

Prompt caching is powerful when requests share a stable prefix, such as large system instructions, tool definitions, or reusable context. It caches the ordered prefix of tools, system, then messages up to the breakpoint, so changing content at or before that point changes the prefix and can miss the cache. The Prompt caching documentation is clear that cache breakpoints should be placed on stable reusable prefixes, not on fresh feed data that changes every request.

questions.question: A philanthropic foundation's grant operations team is building a Claude-based reviewer for scholarship applications. Every application follows the same review path: extract applicant facts, compare them with retrieved eligibility rules, draft reviewer notes, then run a final rubric check before a human sees the result. The team wants predictable cost and clear intermediate outputs for audit review. Which architectural pattern best fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Give Claude broad tool access and let it choose each next review step dynamically.
options.feedback: This describes an agentic approach, which is useful when the next action cannot be predicted in advance and depends on open-ended intermediate results. In this scenario, the review path is fixed, so dynamic control adds complexity without a matching benefit.

options.label: B
options.text: Implement a predefined sequence of LLM and retrieval steps with checks between stages.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because the task has a stable sequence of cleanly separable subtasks. A predefined workflow gives the team inspectable intermediate artifacts and avoids paying the latency and cost of unnecessary autonomous exploration.

options.label: C
options.text: Use one augmented LLM call with retrieved policies and examples for the full review.
options.feedback: An augmented LLM can be sufficient for many applications, especially when retrieval and examples provide enough context. Here, the need for audit-friendly intermediate outputs and a fixed multi-stage process makes a structured workflow a better architectural fit.

options.label: D
options.text: Route each application to a specialized prompt based on its scholarship category.
options.feedback: Routing is useful when inputs fall into distinct categories that can be classified accurately and handled by different paths. The scenario emphasizes one common review sequence for every application, not category-specific processing.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic distinguishes workflows from agents within the broader category of agentic systems. Workflows orchestrate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths, while agents let the model dynamically direct its own process and tool use. See Building effective agents.

This scenario is a strong fit for a workflow because the process is known ahead of time and decomposes into fixed stages: extraction, eligibility comparison, note drafting, and rubric checking. That maps naturally to prompt chaining, where each step can receive a constrained input, produce an inspectable output, and pass a controlled result to the next step.

An autonomous agent is better reserved for cases where the useful next action is not known in advance, such as open-ended investigation or tool selection that depends heavily on intermediate findings. A single augmented LLM call with retrieval, tools, or memory is the foundational building block, and often the simplest sufficient solution, but it provides less structure for staged validation when auditability is a primary design requirement.

questions.question: A consumer electronics repair network is building a Claude-based assistant over thousands of troubleshooting guides, firmware release notes, and service bulletins. Technicians ask narrow fault-code questions, the full corpus cannot fit in a request, and answers must point back to the retrieved evidence. Which design best supports retrieval quality and source attribution?

options.label: A
options.text: Chunk documents by coherent sections, embed chunks as documents, embed questions as queries, and pass retrieved search_result blocks with citations enabled.
options.feedback: This design separates indexing from generation and uses retrieval-oriented embeddings in the intended roles. Enabling citations on search_result blocks lets Claude cite the evidence supplied by the RAG system.

options.label: B
options.text: Skip vector indexing, send manuals as citation-enabled document blocks, rely on citation chunking, and ask Claude to select the matching passages.
options.feedback: Document citation chunking helps Claude cite content already provided in the request, but it is not a vector index or retrieval system. The stem says the corpus cannot fit in a request, so retrieval must happen before Claude receives the context.

options.label: C
options.text: Chunk guides only at file boundaries, embed each guide as a document, retrieve whole files, and pass full manuals with citations enabled.
options.feedback: Whole-document vectors can blur together many unrelated troubleshooting topics, which is a poor fit for narrow fault-code questions. It also increases the amount of irrelevant context sent to Claude and makes attribution less precise.

options.label: D
options.text: Cache the manual corpus as a stable prompt prefix, reuse cache reads for each question, and treat cached context as the retrieval layer.
options.feedback: Prompt caching reduces cost and latency for repeated prompt prefixes, but it does not build an index or select relevant passages. Cached tokens still occupy the context window, so caching does not solve a corpus-scale retrieval problem.

questions.explanation:
A practical RAG architecture usually has a separate ingestion and retrieval layer: split source material into chunks that preserve meaningful local context, embed those chunks for search, retrieve the most relevant results for the user question, then send only those results to Claude. Anthropic's embeddings guidance points developers to embedding providers such as Voyage AI rather than an Anthropic embedding model, and its quickstart uses input_type="document" for corpus items and input_type="query" for user questions. See Embeddings.

For attribution, search_result content blocks are designed for results returned by your own search or RAG system. They let you provide retrieved passages, source information, titles, and citation support when citations: {"enabled": true} is included. They do not perform indexing or retrieval by themselves. See Search results.

It is important not to confuse Claude's citation processing with retrieval indexing. The citations documentation explains how provided documents are chunked for citation purposes, for example sentence-level chunking for plain text and PDFs, but that mechanism applies after content is already in the request. See Citations.

Prompt caching is also a different optimization. It can reduce repeated-context cost and latency, but it caches prompt prefixes rather than creating a searchable corpus or selecting passages for a new question. See Prompt caching.

questions.question: An airline maintenance training group is developing a Claude workflow that reads mechanic write-ups, identifies the likely system area, drafts a troubleshooting checklist, preserves confidential employee details, and uses a concise instructor tone. The team needs an offline evaluation framework to compare prompt and model revisions before instructors use it. Which approach is strongest?

options.label: A
options.text: Send all responses to one general LLM judge; ask whether each answer is acceptable; tune the prompt against the judge's free-form comments.
options.feedback: LLM-based grading is useful for complex judgments, but it should use detailed rubrics and specific outputs such as binary labels or scales. Free-form acceptability comments are harder to measure reliably and should not be scaled without validation.

options.label: B
options.text: Build a large set of routine manual examples; measure exact-match accuracy for the system area; defer checklist quality, privacy, and tone to post-launch review.
options.feedback: Exact-match grading is appropriate for clear categorical tasks, but this workflow has several important dimensions beyond classification. A routine-only dataset also misses edge cases and does not mirror the full task distribution.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a small expert-curated set of ideal answers; have senior mechanics manually rank each prompt version; select the revision with the highest average preference score.
options.feedback: Human review can be high quality, especially for domain-specific judgment, but relying on a small manual set is slow and difficult to scale. A single average preference score can also hide failures on privacy, tone, or edge cases.

options.label: D
options.text: Define measurable criteria for classification, checklist relevance, privacy, tone, and latency; assemble representative and edge-case cases; use code checks and rubric-tested LLM judges.
options.feedback: This is correct because it starts from measurable, multidimensional success criteria rather than a single grader choice. It also combines representative test data, edge cases, automated checks for structured outcomes, and tested LLM grading for nuanced judgments.

questions.explanation:
Strong evaluation design for Claude applications begins with success criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, not with the selection of a favorite grading mechanism. The official guidance also emphasizes that many applications need multidimensional evaluation, because a workflow can be accurate on one dimension while failing on privacy, tone, latency, or contextual relevance. See Define success criteria for the documented framing.

The best framework mirrors the real task distribution, includes edge cases, and automates grading where possible. In practice, that means using code-based checks such as exact match for structured labels, while using rubric-tested LLM-based grading for subjective dimensions such as checklist usefulness or tone. Anthropic's evaluation guidance favors scalable automated test coverage over relying only on small, expensive human-graded sets, while still recognizing that human review can be useful for calibration. See Develop tests for documented eval design principles and mixed grading methods.

questions.question: A tax advisory firm's knowledge engineering team is designing a Claude assistant over 40,000 internal research memos and anonymized precedent notes. Advisors usually ask broad conceptual questions, such as how similar deal structures were treated in prior work, and partners require source attribution while keeping each request focused. Which retrieval design best fits this data shape and query pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Index the memos with embeddings, retrieve relevant chunks per query, and send them as citation-enabled search_result blocks.
options.feedback: This matches a large internal corpus with semantic, concept-oriented questions. Embeddings support semantic retrieval, and search_result blocks are the documented way to pass custom RAG results when built-in source attribution is needed.

options.label: B
options.text: Place the full memo library in a cached prompt prefix, then ask Claude to identify and cite the relevant sections.
options.feedback: Prompt caching can reduce cost and latency for repeated prefixes, but cached tokens still occupy the context window. Sending the full corpus also works against the goal of keeping the request focused, and more context can degrade recall and accuracy.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Web Search for each advisor question, then rely on the returned citations to identify matching internal examples.
options.feedback: Web Search is suited to current, changing, or open-ended web information, not a private internal memo repository. Its citations are tied to web search results, so it does not retrieve anonymized internal precedent notes unless those are exposed through an appropriate retrieval system.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Web Fetch against the internal search portal, then let Claude discover the most relevant memos from that page.
options.feedback: Web Fetch is for retrieving a specific page or document, not for performing open-ended discovery across a large corpus. It does not replace a semantic retrieval layer that selects relevant internal chunks before Claude answers.

questions.explanation:
For a large private knowledge base with broad conceptual queries, the core design is to retrieve a focused subset before calling Claude. Embeddings are the documented path for semantic similarity tasks, and the embeddings guidance shows using different input types for corpus documents and user queries so retrieval is shaped to the role of each text. See Embeddings.

When the retrieved material comes from a custom RAG pipeline and the answer needs source attribution, use search_result content blocks rather than pasting informal snippets. Search-result citations are block-granular, so splitting retrieved chunks into smaller text blocks can improve attribution precision. See Search results.

Loading everything into the prompt is the common anti-pattern here. Claude's context window includes system prompts, messages, tool results, documents, tool definitions, and generated output, and prompt caching does not remove cached tokens from that window. The context-window guidance also notes that more context is not automatically better, because accuracy and recall can degrade as token count grows. See Context windows.

Web tools solve different retrieval problems. Web Search is for current or open-ended web information, while Web Fetch retrieves a specific page or document, so neither is the right primary mechanism for semantic retrieval over a private internal corpus. See Web search tool.

questions.question: A biotech patent search team runs an interactive Claude assistant that summarizes prior-art references for researchers. Offline tests show the current prompt is accurate enough for launch, but beta users report that answers feel slow during exploratory searches. The team wants configuration decisions that improve responsiveness while preserving the accuracy demonstrated by the tests. Which TWO actions best fit this goal?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch all requests to the fastest available model and rely on spot checks.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because model choice is an accuracy and latency trade-off, not a one-way optimization. A broad switch without regression testing risks losing the quality established by the offline evaluations.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower max_tokens aggressively until the latency target is consistently reached.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because max_tokens is only a hard cap on generated output. Using it aggressively can cut off responses mid-sentence or mid-word, which may reduce latency at the cost of answer completeness and quality.

options.label: C
options.text: Stream responses and track time to first token alongside end-to-end latency.
options.feedback: This is correct because streaming can improve perceived responsiveness by showing output as it is generated. Measuring time to first token captures that user-visible improvement better than relying only on full-response latency.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove unnecessary input context and shorten expected answers while rerunning accuracy tests.
options.feedback: This is correct because input tokens and output tokens are primary drivers of latency. Rerunning accuracy tests keeps the optimization tied to the validated behavior rather than assuming shorter prompts or outputs remain equally accurate.

questions.explanation:
Latency work should start from a prompt that already performs the task well, then apply targeted optimizations and verify that quality still holds. Anthropic's latency guidance emphasizes three practical levers: choose an appropriate model for the speed and quality requirement, minimize input and expected output tokens, and use streaming when user experience depends on responsiveness.

Time to first token is especially important for streamed interfaces because it measures how quickly users see the first visible output, while end-to-end latency measures when the full response completes. Reducing token volume can lower latency, but it must be done carefully because removing context or shortening answers can change accuracy. max_tokens is a blunt control because it caps output length and can truncate a response, so it should not be the main quality-preserving latency strategy. See Anthropic's latency reduction guidance for the underlying trade-offs.

questions.question: A university admissions operations team is preparing a Claude workflow that routes applicant emails and drafts staff replies. The pilot is useful, but reviewers disagree about privacy handling, tone, escalation thresholds, throughput, and how to detect regressions after launch. Which plan best supports the workflow across discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, and iteration?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the workflow into claude.ai with double-brace variables, ask staff to score a few live replies manually, and treat low complaint volume as readiness evidence.
options.feedback: Console prompt templates use double-brace variables, but claude.ai chat does not support prompt templates or variables. A few manual live scores and low complaint volume are also weak substitutes for pre-launch evals that reflect the real task distribution and edge cases.

options.label: B
options.text: Define measurable acceptance criteria, create a representative variable-driven eval set with edge cases, compare prompt versions before handoff, and monitor stop_reason plus eval trends after launch.
options.feedback: This plan starts by aligning stakeholders on measurable success criteria across the concerns raised in the scenario. It then connects design, handoff, monitoring, and iteration through representative evals, prompt comparisons, and production inspection of successful response stop reasons.

options.label: C
options.text: Run the prompt improver, approve the longer template after a small leadership review, document the final prompt, and monitor only HTTP failures after launch.
options.feedback: The prompt improver can be useful, but treating it as the primary lifecycle control skips empirical evaluation against stakeholder criteria. Monitoring only HTTP failures misses successful responses that still require attention, such as responses stopped by limits, tool use, refusal, or context window behavior.

options.label: D
options.text: Freeze the pilot prompt, collect anecdotal counselor feedback during the rollout, add examples when complaints appear, and reconsider model choice during the next budget cycle.
options.feedback: This plan lacks a measurable baseline and makes iteration reactive rather than evidence-driven. Anecdotal feedback can inform improvements, but it does not replace representative test cases, grading, and version comparisons.

questions.explanation:
Lifecycle management for a production Claude workflow should begin with explicit success criteria, not with prompt tweaks. Anthropic describes good criteria as specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and notes that most real workflows need multiple dimensions such as task fidelity, tone, privacy preservation, latency, and price. See Define success criteria.

Those criteria need to become an eval process that mirrors the real task distribution and includes edge cases. The Console Evaluation Tool supports iterative work through prompt variables, test cases, side-by-side comparisons, grading, versioning, and rerunning an eval suite after prompt changes, as described in Evaluation Tool.

For monitoring, an architect should not treat only HTTP failures as production signals. Successful Messages API responses include stop_reason, and Anthropic distinguishes those stop reasons from failed requests. Inspecting stop_reason helps teams notice lifecycle issues that are valid API responses but still operationally important, as documented in Handling stop reasons.

A sustainable handoff gives stakeholders an agreed definition of quality, gives implementers a repeatable way to compare changes, and gives operators concrete production signals for iteration.

questions.question: A global executive search firm's compliance engineering team has a contractual requirement that candidate interview transcripts sent to Claude be handled under its Zero Data Retention arrangement. The team proposes using the Message Batches API for overnight scoring because immediate responses are not needed and the workload is high volume. Which recommendation best addresses the key governance risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable one-hour prompt caching so repeated scoring instructions avoid repeated transcript storage.
options.feedback: Prompt caching optimizes repeated prompt prefixes for cost and latency, but it is not a substitute for choosing a ZDR-eligible feature. The candidate transcripts would still be included in batch requests and subject to the batch retention model.

options.label: B
options.text: Submit the transcripts in batches and delete each batch immediately after results are retrieved.
options.feedback: Deleting completed batches can reduce how long results remain available, but it does not make the feature ZDR eligible. The data must still be stored server-side during asynchronous processing and result retrieval.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a ZDR-eligible synchronous Messages workflow unless batch retention is contractually permitted.
options.feedback: This is correct because Message Batches are not eligible for Zero Data Retention and store request and response data according to the feature's retention policy. If the contractual requirement is ZDR, the architecture should avoid routing those transcripts through a non-ZDR feature unless the legal and compliance terms explicitly allow that retention.

options.label: D
options.text: Use unique custom_id values and rely on Workspace isolation for transcript separation.
options.feedback: Unique custom_id values are important for matching unordered batch results to inputs, and Workspace isolation limits who can access batches within the platform. Neither control changes the feature's data retention status or satisfies a ZDR-only requirement.

questions.explanation:
The critical failure mode is treating an operational optimization as if it preserves the same privacy posture. Message Batches are designed for asynchronous, high-throughput processing and discounted pricing, but the feature is explicitly not eligible for Zero Data Retention. Anthropic documents that batch request and response data is stored for the feature's standard retention period, with results available for a limited time after creation, so the data handling model is different from a ZDR-eligible synchronous request path.

For sensitive workloads, governance decisions should start from the data handling requirement, then choose the execution pattern. Batch features are appropriate when delayed processing and temporary server-side storage are acceptable, for example large-scale evaluations or bulk analysis without strict ZDR constraints. If transcripts must remain under a ZDR arrangement, the safer design is to use a ZDR-eligible Messages workflow or obtain explicit contractual approval for the batch retention behavior before processing production data.

Operational controls such as deleting results, using meaningful custom_id values, or relying on Workspace isolation can still be useful, but they do not convert a non-ZDR feature into a ZDR feature. See Anthropic's Batch processing documentation and API and data retention guidance for the relevant retention and eligibility details.

questions.question: A mobile game studio's trust and safety platform processes millions of player reports each month. Each request contains a short chat excerpt, a small set of labels, and sometimes a screenshot; output is a brief classification with a confidence note. Human moderators handle the rare ambiguous cases, and the team's main goals are low latency and low token cost rather than maximum autonomous reasoning. Which model-selection action best fits these trade-offs?

options.label: A
options.text: Route routine cases to Claude Haiku 4.5, and escalate only ambiguous disputes to a stronger model.
options.feedback: Claude Haiku 4.5 is positioned as the fastest model with near-frontier intelligence and has the lowest listed base price among the current models. The workload is short, high volume, and includes only occasional images, which all current Claude models support, so a Haiku-first route fits the stated latency and cost priorities.

options.label: B
options.text: Route all cases to Claude Fable 5, and rely on its agent orientation for throughput.
options.feedback: Claude Fable 5 is positioned for next-generation intelligence in long-running agents. This scenario does not require long-running autonomous work, and Fable 5 has higher listed base pricing than Haiku 4.5 for a task dominated by volume and latency.

options.label: C
options.text: Route all cases to Claude Sonnet 5, and use prompt caching as the primary cost control.
options.feedback: Claude Sonnet 5 is positioned as the best combination of speed and intelligence, which makes it attractive for balanced production workloads. It is still more expensive than Haiku 4.5, and prompt caching reduces repeated prefix costs rather than making every routine classification the lowest-cost model route.

options.label: D
options.text: Route all cases to Claude Opus 4.8, and lower effort to reduce routine-review latency.
options.feedback: Claude Opus 4.8 is positioned for complex agentic coding and enterprise work where advanced capability outweighs cost. The effort parameter is a valid optimization lever on Opus 4.8, but choosing Opus as the default for brief, routine, high-volume classification mismatches the workload.

questions.explanation:
Model selection should start from the workload shape: how hard the reasoning is, how much context and output are needed, how latency-sensitive the route is, and how token costs scale at production volume. Anthropic's Choosing a model guidance frames this as a trade-off among capabilities, speed, cost, and effort.

For short, high-volume classification with occasional screenshots and human escalation for edge cases, Claude Haiku 4.5 is the best default because it is documented as the fastest model with near-frontier intelligence. The Models overview also shows that current Claude models support text and image input, so the presence of screenshots is not a reason by itself to move to a larger model.

The larger models remain useful routing targets when the task changes. Claude Sonnet 5 is the balanced choice when stronger intelligence is worth higher cost, Claude Opus 4.8 is aimed at complex agentic coding and enterprise work, and Claude Fable 5 is positioned for long-running agents. Pricing reinforces the default route here: the official pricing documentation lists Haiku 4.5 at a lower base input and output price than the other current models, which matters when millions of requests are expected.

questions.question: A regional insurer's claims documentation team is building a Claude-based assistant for adjusters. Most requests ask for an explanation of policy wording, require citing current internal manuals, and follow the same answer style. The team has no need for Claude to take actions in external systems, and leadership prioritizes low latency and predictable cost. Which architectural pattern best fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Implement an orchestrator-workers workflow that splits every question into parallel analysis tasks.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the requests are not described as complex tasks requiring multiple coordinated subtasks. Orchestrator-workers patterns are better suited when decomposition and delegation add value.

options.label: B
options.text: Implement an autonomous agent that chooses investigation steps and tools during each request.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the scenario does not require dynamic tool selection or open-ended process control. An agent would add latency and cost without a clear need for autonomous decision making.

options.label: C
options.text: Implement a routing workflow that classifies each question before invoking category prompts.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the stem does not indicate distinct categories with different handling paths. Routing is useful when categories can be accurately classified and need specialized downstream logic.

options.label: D
options.text: Implement a single augmented LLM call that retrieves policy passages and uses examples.
options.feedback: This is correct because the task mainly needs grounded answering, stable style, and current reference material rather than autonomous planning. Retrieval and in-context examples are part of the augmented LLM pattern, which is the simplest appropriate building block here.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic distinguishes workflows, which follow predefined code paths, from agents, where the model dynamically directs its process and tool use. The guidance is to start with the simplest solution that meets the need, because more agentic designs can improve performance on some tasks but often increase latency and cost.

In this case, the assistant primarily needs grounded answers over internal manuals and consistent formatting. A single augmented LLM call with retrieval and in-context examples provides the needed grounding and style control without introducing unnecessary orchestration. See Anthropic's discussion of augmented LLMs, workflows, and agents in Building effective agents.

Routing would be more appropriate if the system had stable, separable request categories that required different prompts or sources. An autonomous agent is better for open-ended tasks where the right next step depends on intermediate results, while orchestrator-workers fits tasks that benefit from decomposing work across multiple subtasks.

questions.question: A maritime logistics platform's engineering enablement team is rolling out Claude Code to 900 developers. After a pilot, their observability backend is close to its time-series cardinality limit, and security policy prohibits storing prompts or responses. Product engineering managers still need adoption trends and visibility into tool approval patterns across teams. Which monitoring strategy best fits these constraints?

options.label: A
options.text: Set OTEL variables only for spawned Bash commands, collect application traces, and infer Claude Code adoption indirectly.
options.feedback: Claude Code does not pass OTEL_* variables into spawned subprocesses such as Bash tool commands, hooks, MCP servers, or language servers. Application telemetry can be useful, but it does not replace Claude Code's own metrics and events for adoption and permission-pattern monitoring.

options.label: B
options.text: Enable Claude Code telemetry, export metrics and events, reduce high-cardinality metric attributes, and leave content logging disabled.
options.feedback: Claude Code telemetry must be explicitly enabled before configured exporters produce observability data. Metrics support adoption and usage trends, events can capture tool decisions, and documented metric attribute controls help manage cardinality while sensitive prompt and response logging remains off by default.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable prompt and response logging, include session identifiers on all metrics, and aggregate usage through raw event payloads.
options.feedback: Prompt and response logging are privacy-gated because they may expose sensitive content, so enabling them conflicts with the stated security policy. Including session identifiers broadly can also increase metric cardinality, which worsens the backend capacity issue.

options.label: D
options.text: Use cost metrics as billing records, disable tool decision events, and reconcile team usage only through invoice exports.
options.feedback: Claude Code cost metrics are documented as approximations for trend and attribution analysis, not billing truth. Disabling tool decision events also removes the signal managers need for understanding accepted and rejected tool actions.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code observability is built on OpenTelemetry, but exporter configuration alone is not enough: CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 is required before Claude Code emits metrics, events, or optional traces. The documented metrics support usage views such as sessions, tokens, cost approximations, code edits, commits, and active time, while events such as claude_code.tool_decision provide permission decision context without requiring prompt or response capture.

At scale, the main tradeoff is not just collecting more data, it is curating the signal so the observability system remains usable. Attributes such as session identifiers, account identifiers, email, and custom resource attributes can create high cardinality, so the documented include controls should be used deliberately rather than enabled indiscriminately.

Content logging is a separate privacy choice. User prompts, assistant responses, tool details, tool content, and raw API bodies are controlled by explicit environment variables and are off by default, which makes leaving them disabled the right fit when policy forbids storing conversation content. For implementation details and the list of supported metrics, exporters, privacy gates, and cardinality controls, see Claude Code monitoring usage.

questions.question: A municipal water utility's asset management team must convert 120,000 legacy inspection narratives into maintenance records. The input for each item is independent OCR text, results are due over the weekend, and the asset database rejects records that do not match its required fields. Which TWO design choices best translate this problem into a Claude-based solution?

options.label: A
options.text: Run one long conversation that accumulates every narrative and every generated record in active context.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because accumulating all items in a single conversation wastes the context window and increases the chance of context degradation. Independent records should be processed as separate requests or batches rather than preserved as one growing history.

options.label: B
options.text: Submit the extraction workload through the Message Batches API and handle results after asynchronous processing completes.
options.feedback: This is correct because the records are independent and do not need interactive, immediate responses. The Batch API is designed for asynchronous high-volume processing and can reduce token cost for non-time-sensitive workloads.

options.label: C
options.text: Prefill the assistant response with the opening JSON object and parse the remaining text with regex repairs.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prefilling is not the right control mechanism for current Claude models, and last-turn prefills are unsupported on Claude 4.6 and later. Regex repair also pushes schema correctness into brittle post-processing instead of constraining and validating the model output.

options.label: D
options.text: Use structured outputs with a schema matching the asset database fields and route incomplete responses for review.
options.feedback: This is correct because the downstream system requires records in a fixed shape. Structured outputs constrain Claude toward a schema, while incomplete outputs such as token-limit stops still need explicit handling.

questions.explanation:
This workload has two important architectural signals: the items are independent, and the business does not need real-time responses. That makes asynchronous batch processing a strong fit, because the system can submit many separate Claude requests and collect results later instead of maintaining a large interactive session. Anthropic's Message Batches API is intended for large volumes of requests that can be processed asynchronously.

The fixed database contract points to structured outputs, not free-form prose with best-effort parsing. Structured outputs use a schema to guide the response shape, but architects should still handle cases where the model cannot produce a valid object, such as refusals or responses cut off by max_tokens. See Anthropic's Structured outputs documentation for the mental model and failure modes.

A single ever-growing conversation is a context-management anti-pattern for this use case. The context window is a scarce working memory, and unrelated prior records do not help extract the next independent record. The better design is to keep each extraction request focused, validate outputs against the required schema, and reserve human review for exceptions rather than for every formatting failure.

questions.question: An environmental law clinic's engineering team is building a Claude assistant over local ordinances, permit PDFs, and prior hearing transcripts. The corpus is too large to send in full, and attorneys need answers that can be traced to retrieved passages. Which TWO design choices best support a reliable RAG pipeline?

options.label: A
options.text: Mark the recurring policy prompt with `cache_control`, then use cached prefixes as the retrieval index for later queries.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prompt caching reduces cost and latency for repeated prompt prefixes. It does not create, update, or query a persistent retrieval index.

options.label: B
options.text: Split materials into semantically coherent chunks, embed chunks with `input_type="document"`, and embed user questions with `input_type="query"`.
options.feedback: This is correct because the retriever needs chunk-level representations that match the granularity of likely answers. Anthropic's embeddings guidance shows corpus items embedded as documents and user questions embedded as queries before nearest-neighbor search.

options.label: C
options.text: Index complete source documents as single vectors, then rely on Claude document citations to find granular evidence.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because document-level vectors make retrieval coarse and can bury the relevant passage inside a large file. Claude citations apply to content already provided to the model, not to the design of the vector index.

options.label: D
options.text: Return retrieved chunks as `search_result` content blocks with source and title metadata when passing evidence into Claude.
options.feedback: This is correct because `search_result` blocks are the documented way to provide results from your own search or RAG system to Claude. They preserve source information for the model and can support citations, but they do not perform retrieval themselves.

questions.explanation:
A strong RAG design separates retrieval from generation. The retrieval layer should index semantically coherent chunks so nearest-neighbor search can select evidence at a useful level of detail, then embed corpus chunks and user queries with the retrieval-specific input types documented in Anthropic's Embeddings guide.

After retrieval, pass the selected evidence into Claude in a form that preserves attribution. Anthropic documents search_result content blocks for results from your own RAG system, including fields such as source, title, and content, with optional citations enabled, as described in Search results. That mechanism helps Claude answer from retrieved evidence, but it is not an indexing or search engine.

Automatic citation chunking for provided documents is a separate model-facing behavior, not a substitute for vector-index chunking. Similarly, cache_control can reduce repeated prompt-prefix cost and latency, as covered in Prompt caching, but cached prompt prefixes should not be treated as a retrieval database.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical market-research team is separating its Claude integration into two Anthropic organizations under the same billing account: a production organization that processes EU interview transcripts through the Claude API at api.anthropic.com, and a sandbox organization used for representative test data. Legal asks how to satisfy GDPR transfer documentation, while security assumes retention settings carry across both organizations. Which recommendation best addresses the compliance risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Verify ZDR separately for each in-scope organization and use the incorporated DPA with SCCs for Claude API processing.
options.feedback: This addresses both parts of the scenario without assuming account-wide inheritance. Anthropic states that ZDR must be enabled per organization, and its DPA with SCCs is incorporated into the Commercial Terms for commercial products such as Claude API.

options.label: B
options.text: Move sandbox processing to Microsoft Foundry and apply Anthropic API retention controls to that deployment.
options.feedback: This confuses the processor boundary for third-party platforms. For Microsoft Foundry, the cloud provider is the data processor, so the team must consult that platform’s retention and compliance controls rather than applying Anthropic API retention assumptions.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Console or Workbench for sandbox tests and treat them as covered by the same ZDR commitment.
options.feedback: This relies on a surface that is not covered by ZDR according to Anthropic’s retention documentation. Even if production API requests are eligible, Console and Workbench processing should not be assumed to have the same retention behavior.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable ZDR once at the billing account level and archive the Commercial Terms as the only transfer record.
options.feedback: This incorrectly treats ZDR as an account-level setting that applies to every organization. The documentation states that ZDR does not automatically extend to other organizations under the same account.

questions.explanation:
Compliance architecture depends on identifying the exact surface, organization, and processor relationship used for each workload. For Claude API at api.anthropic.com, Anthropic’s API retention documentation describes the scope where Anthropic is the data processor and explains that Zero Data Retention must be enabled per organization, not merely per account. See API and data retention.

For GDPR transfer documentation, Anthropic states that its Data Processing Addendum with Standard Contractual Clauses is automatically incorporated into the Commercial Terms for commercial products such as Claude API. questions.question: An online education platform's learner-support team A/B tests a revised Claude prompt for replies to confused students. The variant improves answer correctness on a 200-case sample but worsens rubric-scored empathy, increases median latency, and raises token cost. The team has not defined launch thresholds for these metrics. What should the architect recommend next?

options.label: A
options.text: Launch the variant because correctness improved, then use production complaints to decide whether empathy needs another iteration.
options.feedback: This overweights one metric and delays evaluation of known regressions until after broad exposure. Production complaints are noisy and incomplete, especially for quality dimensions like empathy, latency, and cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep editing the prompt on the 200 sampled cases until all reviewer scores improve, then replace the baseline.
options.feedback: This risks overfitting to a small set rather than testing against a representative task distribution. It also lacks explicit launch thresholds, so the team still has no objective standard for deciding whether to ship.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the variant to the smallest available model to reduce latency and cost, then skip the prompt comparison.
options.feedback: Changing models can be a valid way to address latency or cost, but choosing the smallest model without checking task fit is not a reliable optimization plan. Skipping comparison removes the evidence needed to know whether quality regressions were fixed or worsened.

options.label: D
options.text: Define launch thresholds across the relevant metrics, adjust the candidate against those gaps, and rerun a representative eval before rollout.
options.feedback: This treats the result as multidimensional rather than optimizing for correctness alone. Defining thresholds and rerunning a representative eval creates a disciplined iteration loop before replacing the baseline.

questions.explanation:
Good iteration starts by turning an observed result into a measurement problem. A prompt variant that improves one dimension while regressing others is not an automatic win, because LLM application success is usually multidimensional: correctness, tone, privacy, latency, and price may all matter for the user experience and business constraints.

Anthropic's guidance on defining success emphasizes specific, measurable criteria and eval sets that mirror the real task distribution, including edge cases. See Define success criteria and build evaluations. Once those criteria exist, A/B comparisons become useful because each candidate can be judged against the same thresholds rather than against a vague preference.

The prompt engineering loop should also avoid assuming every regression is solved by more prompt wording changes. Anthropic notes that prompt engineering should come after success criteria and empirical tests, and that latency or cost may sometimes be better addressed through model selection rather than prompt changes alone, as described in Prompt engineering overview.

The practical pattern is: define the metrics, compare baseline and candidate on representative cases, make targeted changes based on measured failures, and rerun the whole suite. Shipping based on a single improved metric, tuning only against a narrow sample, or skipping the comparison step all weaken the evidence needed for a safe rollout.

questions.question: An airline operations control center uses Claude to draft disruption-response plans. Each request includes the same tool definitions, safety policy, and 30 routing examples, followed by a live flight snapshot with a timestamp and the dispatcher’s current question. The team enabled prompt caching but observes repeated cache writes and few cache reads, while the final snapshot must still be included on every call. Which change best improves prompt reuse?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep automatic caching and move the timestamp into the first line of the shared system prompt.
options.feedback: Moving per-request data into the shared system prompt makes an earlier part of the cache hierarchy change on every call. That reduces reuse because prompt caching matches prefixes exactly across tools, system content, and messages.

options.label: B
options.text: Switch the cache entry to a 1-hour TTL while leaving the breakpoint on the changing snapshot.
options.feedback: A longer TTL extends how long an entry can be reused, but it does not make non-identical content match. If the cached segment includes a timestamped snapshot that changes on every call, the cache will still miss.

options.label: C
options.text: Place an explicit cache breakpoint on the last stable instruction or example block before the flight snapshot.
options.feedback: This caches the reusable prefix while leaving the changing snapshot and question outside the cached segment. Cache hits require exact matching, so the breakpoint should sit at the end of content that remains identical across the requests meant to share the cache.

options.label: D
options.text: Place cache_control on the final dispatcher message so the complete request is cached each time.
options.feedback: Marking the final changing message creates cache entries for content that will not match the next request. Cache writes occur at marked breakpoints, but later reads can only reuse a previously written prefix when that prefix is identical.

questions.explanation:
Prompt caching reuses a request prefix, not arbitrary repeated fragments inside a changing prompt. The cached prefix is formed in the documented order tools, then system, then messages, up to and including the cache breakpoint. For a prompt with a stable policy and examples followed by a live, request-specific suffix, the breakpoint belongs on the last stable block before the suffix.

Automatic caching is useful for many growing conversations because it moves the cache point to the last cacheable block. In a pattern where the last block changes every request, that convenience can work against you, because cache hits require exact matching of the previously written segment. Explicit breakpoints give the architect control over which portion is reusable, while still allowing the dynamic snapshot and dispatcher question to be sent normally as uncached input.

A 1-hour TTL changes cache lifetime and pricing, but it does not relax matching rules. Likewise, moving timestamps into shared instructions or caching the final dynamic message turns the reusable prefix into a per-request prompt, which defeats the purpose of caching. See Anthropic’s Prompt caching documentation for the cache hierarchy, automatic versus explicit breakpoints, TTL behavior, and usage fields.

questions.question: A renewable energy trading desk's risk analytics team is designing a Claude workflow. Analysts submit scenario questions, Claude may request internal position or price tools, and analysts can provide corrections that should affect later turns. The service must publish a report only after the model has actually finished rather than after a merely successful API call. Which architecture best supports the full input, processing, output, and feedback loop?

options.label: A
options.text: Store analyst corrections separately, send summarized context only, publish the first nonempty assistant text, and run requested tools asynchronously for later review.
options.feedback: Keeping corrections outside the prompt means later turns may not reflect the feedback that analysts expect the model to use. Publishing the first text block can incorrectly treat tool requests, pauses, or truncated output as complete work.

options.label: B
options.text: Store a conversation ID, send only the latest analyst turn with a top-level system prompt, publish on HTTP 200, and append tool output to audit logs afterward.
options.feedback: The Messages API does not retain conversation state by conversation ID, so the application must send the relevant prior turns itself. HTTP 200 only means the request succeeded, and it does not prove the model has reached a final answer.

options.label: C
options.text: Store the transcript, send prior user and assistant turns with a top-level system prompt, branch on stop_reason, and feed tool results or continuations back before publishing.
options.feedback: This design matches the stateless Messages API model by reconstructing the needed conversation history on each request. It also treats the response stop reason as the workflow state, so tool use, continuation, and truncation cases are handled before any report is released.

options.label: D
options.text: Store prior turns and tool results, set max_tokens to the desired report length, publish when that limit is reached, and ask analysts to reopen incomplete cases.
options.feedback: The max_tokens value is an upper bound on generated tokens, not a target length or completion signal. A response that stops because of max_tokens should be treated as a truncation condition, not as a reason to publish.

questions.explanation:
An end-to-end Claude architecture should treat the Messages API as a stateless processing step: each request includes the relevant prior user and assistant turns, while system instructions belong in the top-level system parameter. The model response is not just text, it is also a state transition for the application.

The reliable pattern is to inspect stop_reason after a successful response. A tool_use stop means the application should execute the requested tool and send the result back in the next turn, pause_turn means the application should continue by returning the assistant content, and max_tokens or model_context_window_exceeded should be treated as truncation rather than completion. This is why publishing solely on HTTP success, nonempty text, or a token cap creates gaps in the feedback loop.

For the input side, see the official Create a Message documentation. For the processing and output state machine, see Handling stop reasons.

questions.question: A specialty retailer's merchandising analytics team is piloting a Claude workflow that turns supplier emails into buying-decision briefs. Executives want a launch SLA described as "fast and dependable," while buyers, legal reviewers, and finance leaders disagree about what matters most: nuanced summaries, privacy handling, turnaround time, or per-brief cost. What should the architect do before committing to the launch SLA?

options.label: A
options.text: Adopt the strictest stakeholder preference as the release gate, then defer cost and latency targets.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because optimizing for one stakeholder's strictest preference can make the service impractical or misaligned with other needs. Most production use cases require multidimensional evaluation rather than a single uncompromising gate.

options.label: B
options.text: Route the workflow to a larger model, then use reduced escalation volume as the launch criterion.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because changing model choice does not resolve the expectation gap by itself. Escalation volume may be useful as one metric, but it does not directly capture all required dimensions such as privacy, cost, latency, or summary quality.

options.label: C
options.text: Translate stakeholder priorities into measurable success criteria, then validate the workflow against a representative evaluation set before setting targets.
options.feedback: This is correct because vague expectations need to become measurable criteria before they can support an SLA. A representative evaluation set creates a shared feedback loop for comparing quality, privacy, latency, and cost tradeoffs on realistic work.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish a provisional response-time SLA, then collect reviewer comments during launch to refine quality expectations.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it commits to a service target before stakeholders agree on what success means. Feedback after launch can improve the system, but it is a weak substitute for defining acceptance criteria upfront.

questions.explanation:
For stakeholder alignment, convert ambiguous goals like "fast and dependable" into specific, measurable success criteria before committing to an SLA. Anthropic evaluation guidance emphasizes criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and notes that practical systems often need multiple dimensions such as task fidelity, consistency, relevance, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency, and price. See Define success.

The engineering tradeoff is that an SLA is only meaningful when everyone agrees what is being promised and how it will be measured. A representative evaluation set gives stakeholders a concrete feedback loop for reviewing realistic examples, negotiating thresholds, and understanding cost and latency consequences before launch. Publishing targets first, choosing one stakeholder's preference, or switching models may be useful later, but none of those actions establishes a shared basis for service commitments.
