questions.question: A national tax-preparation platform's architecture team is designing a Claude Messages API service that ingests a client question, prior preparer comments, and retrieved tax documents, may call internal calculation and citation tools, and sends a draft memo for preparer review. Corrections from preparers must influence later turns, and incomplete generations must not be filed as final memos. Which architecture best supports the full input, processing, output, and feedback loop?

options.label: A
options.text: Submit each request as a fresh prompt, send the top-level system prompt only on the first call, publish on HTTP 200, and collect preparer comments outside the model loop.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prior turns and reviewer feedback would not influence later calls if they are kept outside the prompt state. Sending global instructions only on the first call is also insufficient for a stateless API design, and a successful HTTP response can still require tool handling, continuation, or truncation recovery.

options.label: B
options.text: Use max_tokens as the desired memo length, retry until output reaches that size, treat tool_use as a final response, and summarize corrections in application logs.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because max_tokens is only an upper bound on generated tokens, not a target length. A tool_use stop reason means the application should run the requested tool and return results, not publish the response as complete.

options.label: C
options.text: Persist the canonical turn history, send it with a top-level system prompt, route each response by stop_reason, and append tool outputs or preparer corrections before the next call.
options.feedback: This is correct because the Messages API is stateless, so the application must supply the relevant conversation history on each request. Branching on stop_reason lets the service distinguish final answers from tool calls, pauses, refusals, and truncation conditions before deciding what to do next.

options.label: D
options.text: Populate cache with max_tokens: 0 in batch jobs, omit earlier assistant turns, handle only HTTP errors, and request a new memo after each correction.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because max_tokens: 0 is not supported inside Message Batches. Omitting earlier turns and handling only HTTP failures breaks the feedback loop and misses successful responses that still ended with non-final stop reasons.

questions.explanation:
An end-to-end Claude architecture needs an application-owned state loop: collect inputs, assemble the relevant prior turns, call the model, inspect the response state, perform any required external work, and feed the result or human correction back into a later request. The Messages API is stateless, so multi-turn behavior comes from resending the structured messages history rather than relying on server-side conversation memory.

For the initial or global system instructions in this design, the top-level system parameter is the appropriate place to put policy and operating guidance. The service should also treat max_tokens as an output cap, since the model may stop earlier and truncation must be handled explicitly rather than inferred from output length.

Reliable orchestration depends on handling stop reasons. A tool_use stop reason should route to tool execution and returned tool results, pause_turn should continue by sending assistant content back, and max_tokens or model_context_window_exceeded should be treated as truncation conditions. HTTP success only means the API returned a response, not that the business artifact is ready to file.

questions.question: A digital publishing platform's developer experience team is standardizing Claude Code for two recurring workflows. One workflow is a reusable accessibility-review worker that should run from the current coding session, keep detailed inspection context separate, and only read project files. The other workflow is a set of unrelated prototype branches that engineers want to launch and monitor as separate workstreams, with no need for the workers to communicate. Which two design choices best fit these needs?

options.label: A
options.text: Use agent view to dispatch and monitor the prototype branches as independent background sessions.
options.feedback: Agent view is the appropriate documented approach for launching and monitoring independent background sessions. It matches unrelated workstreams that do not need shared tasks or inter-agent messaging.

options.label: B
options.text: Define a project custom subagent for accessibility review and restrict it to Read, Grep, and Glob.
options.feedback: This fits a delegated worker that runs within the current Claude Code session while using its own context window. Restricting the tool list prevents the subagent from inheriting broader capabilities that are not needed for read-only review.

options.label: C
options.text: Define the accessibility subagent without a tools field so it is limited to read-only inspection.
options.feedback: Omitting the tools field does not make a custom subagent read-only. The documented behavior is that a subagent inherits all tools when the tools field is omitted.

options.label: D
options.text: Use subagents for the prototype branches so each branch becomes a separate user-managed session.
options.feedback: Subagents are not separate user-managed sessions. They run inside a single Claude Code session, use their own context window, and return results to the caller.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code has several parallelization patterns, and the architecture choice depends on the shape of coordination you need. Subagents are best for focused delegated workers inside one session, especially when you want isolated context and a constrained tool surface. A custom subagent is defined as a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter, and the tools field should be set explicitly when least privilege matters, because omitting it causes the subagent to inherit all tools. See the official Claude Code subagents documentation.

For independent workstreams that engineers want to dispatch and watch separately, agent view fits better than subagents because it is documented for independent background sessions. If those sessions needed shared tasks and inter-agent messaging, agent teams would be the more appropriate pattern; if the problem involved scripted orchestration of many subagents, dynamic workflows would be relevant instead. The high-level distinction among these approaches is summarized in the official Claude Code agents documentation.

questions.question: An online food delivery marketplace's developer productivity team enables Claude Code telemetry and sends both metrics and events to an OpenTelemetry collector. During a rollout test, API request events show up in the backend within a few seconds, but cost and token dashboards still look empty when engineers check them 15 seconds after each prompt. The collector shows no export errors. Which action best matches the documented telemetry behavior?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable distributed traces so cost and token measurements are emitted through traces.
options.feedback: Distributed traces are optional and not enabled by default, but cost and token data are documented as metrics. Enabling traces is not the direct fix for dashboards that are reading metric time series too soon.

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce OTEL_LOGS_EXPORT_INTERVAL so API request events and token metrics flush together.
options.feedback: OTEL_LOGS_EXPORT_INTERVAL controls logs and events, not metrics. Changing it may affect how quickly events appear, but it does not change the cadence for cost or token metric export.

options.label: C
options.text: Add prompt.id to metric labels so each request appears immediately in dashboards.
options.feedback: The prompt.id field is intended for correlating events, not for metric labels. Claude Code intentionally excludes it from metrics because using per-prompt identifiers would create unbounded cardinality.

options.label: D
options.text: Tune OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL or wait for the metrics export cycle before judging ingestion.
options.feedback: Claude Code exports metrics and events through separate OpenTelemetry paths, and their default intervals differ. Metrics default to a 60 second export interval, so checking after 15 seconds can make healthy metric ingestion look broken.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code observability is OpenTelemetry-based, but metrics and events are exported through different protocols and can arrive on different schedules. The documented defaults are important for operational interpretation: metrics use OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL with a default of 60000 ms, while logs and events use OTEL_LOGS_EXPORT_INTERVAL with a default of 5000 ms. Seeing events quickly while cost and token metrics lag is therefore not enough evidence that metric export is broken.

For dashboards and smoke tests, engineers should either wait long enough for the metric cycle or deliberately lower OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL when faster feedback is needed. Logs settings do not flush metrics, traces are a separate optional signal, and high-cardinality identifiers such as prompt.id belong in event correlation rather than metric dimensions. See the official Claude Code monitoring usage documentation for the supported exporters, default intervals, metric names, event names, and cardinality guidance.

questions.question: A precision agriculture startup separates customer datasets into several Claude workspaces. A regional operations lead only needs to manage API usage and keys for the Latin America workspace, but a review shows the lead has been assigned the organization admin role, which gives Workspace Admin access to all workspaces, including unrelated European and enterprise workspaces. Which change best addresses the authorization gap?

options.label: A
options.text: Move unrelated customer datasets into the Default Workspace and restrict new keys to named workspaces.
options.feedback: Moving data into the Default Workspace does not solve the lead's overbroad administrative role. It can also make boundaries less clear because the Default Workspace has special behavior and is not a substitute for assigning least-privilege workspace roles.

options.label: B
options.text: Rotate the lead's existing API keys and recreate them with a 7-day expiration for each workspace.
options.feedback: Key expiration reduces the lifetime of a credential, but it does not correct an overbroad human role assignment. The lead would still have administrative access beyond the Latin America workspace while the role remains unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the organization-level admin assignment with an explicit workspace-level role for the Latin America workspace.
options.feedback: This directly narrows the principal's authorization boundary to the workspace where access is needed. Workspace roles are the appropriate control when the requirement is limited to one workspace rather than organization-wide administration.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the current role and review Compliance Activity Feed events for cross-workspace changes.
options.feedback: Audit review can help detect activity after it occurs, but it does not remove the ability to administer unrelated workspaces. Least privilege requires limiting the granted role rather than relying only on monitoring.

questions.explanation:
The central design issue is the difference between organization-level authority and workspace-level authority. Anthropic documents workspaces as the main scoping boundary for Claude API resources, and API keys are scoped to a single workspace, but human roles can still create broader access if assigned at the organization level.

In this scenario, the operational requirement is limited to one workspace, so the safer integration design is to remove the organization-wide administrative assignment and grant only the workspace role needed for that workspace. This follows least privilege by reducing what the user can do before any credential is minted or any API call is attempted.

Credential rotation and expiration are useful controls for reducing exposure from leaked or stale keys, but they do not fix an excessive role assignment. Similarly, audit logs such as the Compliance Activity Feed are valuable for investigation and monitoring, but they are detective controls rather than authorization boundaries.

For the relevant access model, see Anthropic's Workspaces documentation. For related credential behavior, see Claude authentication.

questions.question: A university library's digital collections team is designing two Claude workloads: overnight enrichment of millions of archival records and a live curator workspace where staff expect an answer while editing a record. Finance asks whether the team can standardize on the Message Batches API because it is cheaper. Which two points should the architect include when explaining the trade-off?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the Message Batches API for offline enrichment when asynchronous completion is acceptable.
options.feedback: The Message Batches API is documented for large volumes of Messages requests when immediate responses are not required. The overnight enrichment workload fits that trade-off because lower cost is valuable and no user is waiting on each individual response.

options.label: B
options.text: Treat batch jobs as conversation state so later requests can omit prior history.
options.feedback: Batch processing does not change the stateless nature of Messages requests. For multi-turn behavior, the application is still responsible for supplying the relevant conversation history on each request.

options.label: C
options.text: Route the live curator workspace through batches because discounted requests return interactively.
options.feedback: The batch discount does not make batch processing an interactive response path. Batch processing is asynchronous, so it is not appropriate for a staff member waiting for an answer while editing a record.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the live curator workspace on synchronous Messages requests for immediate responses.
options.feedback: A live editing workspace has an interactive response requirement. The Messages API provides direct model prompting access, which is the better fit when the application needs a response during the user workflow.

questions.explanation:
This decision is a good example of communicating an architectural trade-off rather than presenting the cheapest option as universally best. The Message Batches API is designed for high-volume asynchronous processing, and Anthropic documents it as useful when immediate responses are not required, with a 50% cost reduction for batch workloads. That makes it a strong fit for offline archival enrichment, where completion can be managed as a background job.

The live curator workspace has a different success criterion: the user expects an answer while working. For that path, direct synchronous use of the Messages API better matches the user experience, even if it costs more than batch processing. The Messages API is also stateless, so neither synchronous calls nor batch jobs remove the need for the application to manage and resend the relevant conversation context.

See Anthropic's documentation on Batch processing and Working with messages for the relevant design constraints.

questions.question: A medical device manufacturer's validation engineering group is integrating Claude into an internal Messages API service that drafts test protocols for multiple device families. Their prototype includes every SOP, test template, failure-mode catalog, and example protocol in each request, although each request usually covers one device family and one test type. The team wants to reduce context usage while keeping specialized guidance available when relevant. Which change best fits this goal?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the manuals into deeply nested Skill reference folders so only lower-level files are opened during specialized tasks.
options.feedback: Splitting content is useful, but deeply nested references are not the recommended pattern. The best-practice guidance is to keep reference files shallow, since deeply nested references can lead Claude to preview partial files rather than read complete content.

options.label: B
options.text: Package each validation domain as an Agent Skill with concise metadata and shallow reference files, and enable the required API Skills configuration.
options.feedback: This uses Agent Skills for progressive disclosure, so Claude sees the discovery metadata first and loads detailed instructions or references only when a Skill is relevant. For API use, Skills also require the documented beta headers, code execution tool, and container skill configuration.

options.label: C
options.text: Append all validation manuals to the system prompt and ask Claude to ignore sections unrelated to the current product family.
options.feedback: This preserves the monolithic context pattern that is causing the problem. It increases token usage and exposes Claude to irrelevant material on every request instead of letting relevant guidance be discovered when needed.

options.label: D
options.text: Copy the full validation library into each Skill description so Claude can choose from complete details during startup.
options.feedback: A Skill description is part of the always-loaded discovery surface, not a place for large procedural content. The description must be concise and explain what the Skill does and when Claude should use it, while detailed guidance belongs in the Skill body or referenced files.

questions.explanation:
Progressive disclosure is the key integration pattern for this scenario. Agent Skills are designed so that only Skill metadata is loaded at startup, the SKILL.md instructions are read when the Skill is triggered, and additional resources are read only when referenced. That lets an application keep specialized validation knowledge available without stuffing every SOP and example into every request.

The correct approach also respects the documented shape of Skills. The always-loaded discovery surface should be a clear name and description, while larger details should be split out, with SKILL.md kept reasonably small and reference files kept shallow. See the official Agent Skills overview and Agent Skills best practices.

For a Claude API integration, Skills are not just prompt files. The service must use the documented Skills and code execution beta configuration, including the code execution tool and container.skills structure described in the Skills guide. The monolithic system-prompt option fails because it keeps irrelevant material in the working context, the oversized description option misuses the discovery metadata, and the deeply nested reference option conflicts with the recommended authoring pattern.

questions.question: A specialty pharmacy's patient engagement team is replacing a prototype that sends every request to the same high-capability Claude configuration. One path classifies short refill replies into a fixed set of intents and has strict latency and unit-cost targets. Another path helps pharmacists draft prior-authorization appeal narratives from clinical notes, where quality directly affects staff productivity and patient access. Which recommendation best aligns the architecture to the business value pillars?

options.label: A
options.text: Route both paths to Claude Haiku 4.5, and escalate drafts only after pharmacists reject them.
options.feedback: This may reduce initial cost, but it underweights the productivity and quality requirements of the appeal assistant. A reactive escalation path can add rework and delay, which conflicts with the business goal of helping pharmacists produce strong drafts efficiently.

options.label: B
options.text: Route the refill classifier to a higher-capability model, and move appeal drafting to Claude Haiku 4.5 for throughput.
options.feedback: This reverses the workload fit. The fixed-intent classifier is the better candidate for a faster, lower-cost model, while appeal drafting needs stronger reasoning over clinical context.

options.label: C
options.text: Route both paths to Claude Opus at maximum effort, and use caching to offset the refill classifier cost.
options.feedback: This over-provisions the simple classifier and makes latency and cost harder to control. Prompt caching can help repeated stable prefixes, but it does not make an unnecessarily expensive model choice the best architecture for short dynamic requests.

options.label: D
options.text: Route the refill classifier to Claude Haiku 4.5, and use a higher-capability model for the appeal assistant.
options.feedback: This matches model capability to the business value of each path. Simple, high-volume classification should optimize for speed and cost, while a clinical drafting assistant can justify more capability because quality and pharmacist productivity matter more.

questions.explanation:
Architecture decisions for Claude workloads should start from the value pillar each path is trying to optimize. A high-volume, fixed-intent classifier primarily stresses efficiency, cost, and latency, so it should be served by a faster, lower-cost model if evaluation results confirm acceptable accuracy. A pharmacist drafting assistant has a different value profile: it is lower volume, quality-sensitive, and tied to productivity and patient access, so a higher-capability model is easier to justify.

The model-selection mental model is not “use the best model everywhere.” It is to match capability, response speed, and cost to each workload, then validate that choice with task-specific evaluations. Anthropic’s model guidance describes choosing among models based on capability, speed, and cost in the Models overview. For models that support it, the effort setting provides another lever for trading reasoning depth against latency and token consumption, as described in Effort.

The distractors fail because they optimize one pillar while ignoring another. Using the most capable configuration everywhere can waste budget and miss performance SLAs, while using the cheapest configuration everywhere can move cost into human rework. The strongest architecture right-sizes each path, then uses evals and production measurements to confirm that cost, latency, and quality targets are all being met.

questions.question: A maritime freight insurer's claims automation team is preparing a Claude workflow that drafts loss summaries for adjusters. Executives want a public support target before renewal season, while adjusters, compliance reviewers, and finance leaders are giving inconsistent feedback about what makes the workflow acceptable. What should the architect do next to align expectations?

options.label: A
options.text: Publish the requested service commitment now, then revise the target after production feedback accumulates.
options.feedback: This reverses the expected order by committing before stakeholders agree on what acceptable performance means. Production feedback is useful, but it should not be the first mechanism for defining launch expectations.

options.label: B
options.text: Collect open-ended reviewer comments for several weeks, then let the implementation team choose the launch standard.
options.feedback: Open-ended comments can reveal concerns, but they do not by themselves establish measurable criteria. Letting the implementation team choose the standard also bypasses the stakeholder alignment needed for a credible service commitment.

options.label: C
options.text: Translate stakeholder priorities into specific evaluation criteria, including quality, privacy, latency, and price, before setting the service commitment.
options.feedback: This creates a shared definition of success before the team commits to an SLA or support target. It also captures the multidimensional nature of Claude application quality, where accuracy, privacy, latency, and cost may all matter.

options.label: D
options.text: Route all claims through the most capable model, then ask reviewers whether the summaries feel acceptable.
options.feedback: Using a stronger model may improve some outputs, but it does not define the success criteria or resolve tradeoffs such as latency and price. Asking whether outputs feel acceptable keeps the feedback loop subjective and hard to govern.

questions.explanation:
For stakeholder alignment, the architect should turn broad expectations into specific, measurable success criteria before making an SLA or service commitment. Anthropic's evaluation guidance emphasizes criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and it lists dimensions such as task fidelity, consistency, relevance, tone, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency, and price. See Define your success criteria.

The practical mental model is that an SLA is not only an uptime or response-time promise. For an AI workflow, stakeholders often care about several dimensions at once: whether the output is useful, whether sensitive data is handled properly, how quickly the system responds, and what it costs to operate. A good feedback loop makes those dimensions explicit so reviewers can judge the same target instead of using incompatible personal standards.

The other approaches all preserve ambiguity. Publishing the commitment first creates rework and stakeholder risk, model escalation treats quality as the only dimension, and open-ended comments without measurable criteria make launch readiness hard to evaluate consistently.

questions.question: A renewable energy exchange's governance engineering team is adding an automated audit collector. It must read Claude authentication and administrative events for corporate investigations, but it must not call inference endpoints, manage users, or access chat and file contents. The prototype currently tries to use the same standard workspace API key as the trading assistant service. Which change best closes the security gap?

options.label: A
options.text: Create an Admin API key and use it for the audit collector.
options.feedback: An Admin API key can access the Compliance Activity Feed, but it is not the narrowest credential for this requirement. Admin API credentials are also associated with administrative API capabilities, which the collector does not need.

options.label: B
options.text: Provision a Compliance Access Key scoped only to Activity Feed access.
options.feedback: This uses the credential type intended for Compliance API access and limits the collector to the audit source it needs. It avoids reusing an inference key and does not grant broader user management or content access.

options.label: C
options.text: Reuse the workspace API key and deny inference calls in application code.
options.feedback: A regular Claude API key is not a Compliance API key and cannot call the Compliance API. Application checks also do not change the server-side authorization granted by the credential.

options.label: D
options.text: Issue an Analytics API key and restrict the collector to event queries.
options.feedback: An Analytics API key is not a Compliance API key. It is the wrong credential type for reading the Compliance Activity Feed.

questions.explanation:
The key design issue is separating credential type from the application task. A standard Claude API key is scoped to a workspace for Claude API resources, but it is not authorized for the Compliance API, so reusing the trading assistant's key fails both functionally and as a least-privilege design.

For an audit collector that only needs authentication and administrative event records, the appropriate integration is a Compliance Access Key scoped to the Activity Feed. Anthropic documents that Compliance Access Keys can be scoped for Activity Feed access, while regular Claude API keys cannot call the Compliance API and Analytics API keys are not Compliance API keys. See Compliance API access and Compliance Activity Feed.

An Admin API key is a plausible but broader choice. The docs note that an Admin API key can access the Compliance API Activity Feed only, but Admin API credentials are distinct administrative credentials, and the scenario explicitly excludes user management and other administrative actions. The safer architecture is to give the collector only the specific audit-feed capability it needs.

questions.question: An aerospace supplier's contract analytics team is building an internal Claude service for engineers reviewing long procurement packages. A typical request includes 600k to 800k tokens of contract text and exhibits, followed by cross-document questions that need strong reasoning but not a long-running autonomous agent. The team wants a practical balance of intelligence, latency, and token cost for interactive use. Which model-selection action best fits these trade-offs?

options.label: A
options.text: Route the workload to Claude Haiku 4.5 as the default model.
options.feedback: Claude Haiku 4.5 is the fastest and lowest-cost current model, which makes it attractive for short, high-volume tasks. It has a 200k-token context window, so it does not fit 600k to 800k token requests without additional context reduction.

options.label: B
options.text: Route the workload to Claude Fable 5 as the default model.
options.feedback: Claude Fable 5 has a 1M-token context window and is positioned for next-generation intelligence in long-running agents. For this interactive review workload, it is less cost-effective than choosing a balanced model unless the team specifically needs Fable's agentic strengths.

options.label: C
options.text: Route the workload to Claude Opus 4.8 as the default model.
options.feedback: Claude Opus 4.8 supports the long context requirement and is strong for complex agentic coding and enterprise work. Making it the default overuses a higher-cost option when the stated goal is a balanced interactive service rather than maximum capability for the most complex tasks.

options.label: D
options.text: Route the workload to Claude Sonnet 5 as the default model.
options.feedback: Claude Sonnet 5 fits the 1M-token context requirement and is positioned as the best combination of speed and intelligence. It is a practical default when the workload needs strong reasoning over long inputs but does not justify the highest-cost model for every request.

questions.explanation:
Model selection is a trade-off among capability, speed, cost, and the amount of context or output the workload requires. The documented model comparison positions Claude Sonnet 5 as the best combination of speed and intelligence, while Fable 5 is oriented toward long-running agents, Opus 4.8 toward complex agentic coding and enterprise work, and Haiku 4.5 toward the fastest near-frontier use cases. See the official models overview and choosing a model guidance.

The key constraint in this scenario is that requests can reach 600k to 800k tokens, so the model must support a 1M-token context window. That rules out using Claude Haiku 4.5 as the default for the full request, even though it is fast and inexpensive, because its documented context window is 200k tokens. Among the 1M-token candidates, Claude Sonnet 5 is the best fit for an interactive analytics service that needs strong reasoning while keeping latency and cost practical.

Choosing the most capable or most agent-oriented model for every request is a common architecture anti-pattern because it spends premium tokens without tying that spend to a demonstrated need. A robust production design can still reserve Claude Opus 4.8 or Claude Fable 5 for escalations, but the default route should match the typical workload rather than the worst imaginable case.

questions.question: An online exam proctoring vendor uses Claude to review appeal packets and produce a moderation recommendation for human reviewers. The gateway accepts any HTTP 200 response, extracts fields from the text, and forwards the recommendation. In load testing with unusually long packets, some forwarded recommendations are visibly cut off or indicate the model did not provide a usable decision. Which change best implements a guardrail for this integration?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase `max_tokens` for appeal packets, and forward any response that can be parsed into the expected fields.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a larger token budget may reduce truncation frequency but does not create a safety boundary. A response can parse successfully while still being incomplete, refused, or stopped for a reason that requires special handling.

options.label: B
options.text: Check `stop_reason` on every successful response, and quarantine incomplete or refusal outcomes before forwarding decisions.
options.feedback: This is correct because successful Messages API responses can still indicate outcomes that are not usable as normal decisions. A guardrail should branch on the documented stop signal, then retry, rephrase, reset context, or escalate rather than forwarding partial or refused content.

options.label: C
options.text: Add stricter formatting instructions to the prompt, and forward responses that do not raise HTTP errors.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prompt instructions are not a reliable substitute for inspecting response status fields. HTTP success only means the API returned a response, not that the model produced a usable moderation decision.

options.label: D
options.text: Inspect `stop_details` for every response, and quarantine only responses with a populated policy category.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because `stop_details` can be null, including for refusal-related cases, and it is null for non-refusal stop reasons. The primary control point is the response's `stop_reason`, with `stop_details` used only as optional additional context where present.

questions.explanation:
For production guardrails, treat the Messages API response as a structured control object, not just as text plus an HTTP status. Anthropic documents that every successful response includes stop_reason, with values such as end_turn, max_tokens, refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded. These are not HTTP errors, but they can determine whether the output is safe to use downstream.

In a moderation or compliance pipeline, HTTP 200 is not an approval signal. The application should explicitly decide which stop reasons count as usable completion for that workflow, and route truncation, context-window exhaustion, tool pauses, or refusals into retry, rephrasing, context reset, or human review paths. Relying on parsed text or prompt instructions alone is brittle because the model may produce partial content or a successful refusal response.

For details, see Anthropic's Handling stop reasons guide and the Refusals and fallback documentation.

questions.question: A quantitative trading firm's developer infrastructure team configures Claude Code telemetry through a managed settings file with telemetry enabled and both metrics and logs exported to an OpenTelemetry collector. Claude Code cost metrics, token metrics, API request events, and tool decision events appear in the backend, but custom telemetry emitted by hooks and MCP servers is absent. The team wants consistent observability while preventing individual developers from overriding the Claude Code telemetry settings. What should they do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep Claude Code telemetry in managed settings and configure hooks and MCP servers with their own OTEL environment.
options.feedback: This preserves centrally enforced Claude Code telemetry while addressing the separate subprocess issue. Claude Code does not pass OTEL_* variables to spawned subprocesses such as hooks and MCP servers, so those processes need their own telemetry configuration.

options.label: B
options.text: Switch metrics to the Prometheus exporter and disable the logs exporter during collector testing.
options.feedback: Changing the metrics exporter does not make subprocess telemetry appear. Disabling the logs exporter would also remove Claude Code events, which are part of the visibility the team already has.

options.label: C
options.text: Move Claude Code OTEL variables from managed settings into each developer's shell startup configuration.
options.feedback: This weakens central control because user shell configuration can vary and can be changed by individual developers. It also does not reliably solve subprocess telemetry for every hook or MCP server runtime.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable prompt and assistant response logging so Claude Code forwards more detailed log payloads.
options.feedback: Prompt and assistant response logging controls whether redacted content is included in Claude Code event payloads. It does not cause OTEL_* variables to be inherited by hooks or MCP servers.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code observability is OpenTelemetry-based, with metrics exported through the OTel metrics protocol and operational events exported through the OTel logs/events protocol. Telemetry must be explicitly enabled with CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, and metrics and logs use separate exporter settings such as OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER and OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER.

Managed settings are the right place to enforce organization-wide Claude Code telemetry because environment variables defined there have high precedence and cannot be overridden by users. However, Claude Code intentionally does not pass OTEL_* variables to subprocesses it spawns, including Bash tools, hooks, MCP servers, and language servers. That means Claude Code telemetry can be healthy while separately instrumented subprocesses remain invisible unless those subprocesses receive their own OTel configuration. See Claude Code monitoring usage for the telemetry model, exporter settings, managed settings behavior, and subprocess environment boundary.

questions.question: A global streaming platform's localization engineering team uses Claude to produce subtitles from transcripts, glossary rules, regional style guides, and reviewer notes. The current workflow is a single large prompt, and failures are difficult to compare because the team has not defined pass criteria. Subtitle editors also need to inspect terminology and style issues before a final subtitle file is generated, but they do not need to see every internal reasoning step. Which two changes best apply decomposition techniques for this redesign?

options.label: A
options.text: Define measurable localization criteria and held-out test cases before choosing prompt, model, or chaining changes.
options.feedback: This is correct because effective decomposition should be driven by measurable success criteria, not by adding structure for its own sake. Without evals, the team cannot tell whether a chained workflow, a structured prompt, or a model change actually improves the localization task.

options.label: B
options.text: Enable omitted thinking output and treat the shorter visible response as proof of cheaper reasoning.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because omitted thinking does not mean the reasoning was free or absent. The billed output token count can include thinking tokens even when the visible thinking content is not returned.

options.label: C
options.text: Convert every reasoning substep into a separate API call because multi-step tasks should always be chained.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because explicit chaining is not the default recommendation for all complex reasoning. Claude can handle many multi-step tasks internally with adaptive thinking and orchestration, and excessive chaining adds latency, cost, and operational complexity.

options.label: D
options.text: Split the workflow into draft, terminology review, and refinement calls with the review output available to editors.
options.feedback: This is correct because explicit prompt chaining is useful when the system needs to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline. The terminology and style review is a meaningful checkpoint before final generation, so separating it supports practical control.

questions.explanation:
Good decomposition starts with observable success criteria. Before changing the architecture, the team should define what correct localization means, for example terminology accuracy, subtitle timing constraints, regional style adherence, and reviewer acceptance, then test candidate designs against held-out cases. Anthropic's prompt engineering guidance emphasizes that prompt engineering begins from empirical evaluation, and that not every failure is best fixed by prompting alone: Prompt engineering overview.

Explicit prompt chaining is most valuable when the product needs a reviewable intermediate artifact or a fixed pipeline. Here, editors need to inspect terminology and style issues before final subtitle generation, so a draft → review → refine pattern is appropriate. Anthropic documents this as a practical chaining use case, while noting that adaptive thinking and orchestration can handle much multi-step reasoning without forcing every step into a separate API call: Chain prompts.

The anti-pattern is decomposing mechanically. Splitting every reasoning step into separate calls can make the system slower and harder to operate without improving quality. Similarly, display: "omitted" for thinking affects what is visible, not whether thinking tokens contribute to latency and billing, as described in Extended thinking.

questions.question: A regional transit authority's developer experience team is piloting Claude Code monitoring for 600 engineers. Their rollout template sets `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=prometheus` and `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp`; dashboards show no Claude Code telemetry. Compliance prohibits retaining prompts, responses, tool contents, or raw API bodies, while security still wants fleet-wide visibility into tool accept and reject decisions. Which two actions should the team take?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch log events to Prometheus and scrape decisions through the same path as metrics.
options.feedback: Prometheus is a supported exporter for Claude Code metrics, not for logs and events. Tool decision events should use a supported logs exporter such as OTLP, rather than trying to scrape them as Prometheus metrics.

options.label: B
options.text: Collect tool decision events and leave prompt, response, tool content, and raw API body logging disabled.
options.feedback: The `claude_code.tool_decision` event is designed to capture tool accept and reject decisions, including fields such as the tool name and decision source. The sensitive content logging controls are off by default, so leaving them disabled satisfies the stated privacy constraint while still collecting decision events.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable Claude Code telemetry explicitly and keep metrics and logs on signal-specific supported exporters.
options.feedback: Claude Code telemetry is not enabled just because exporter variables are configured. The deployment must set `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1`, and the existing metric and log exporter choices align with the documented supported signals.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable raw API body logging and review permission decisions with full conversation context.
options.feedback: Raw API body logging is privacy-sensitive and can include the entire conversation history. It is not required to observe tool decisions, and enabling it would conflict with the requirement not to retain prompts, responses, tool contents, or raw API bodies.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code observability uses OpenTelemetry, but it has two separate layers to configure: telemetry must be enabled with CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, and each signal must use an exporter that supports that signal. In this scenario, prometheus is appropriate for metrics, while otlp is appropriate for logs and events.

The security requirement is best met through the documented claude_code.tool_decision event, which records tool permission decisions without requiring prompt or response capture. Content logging controls such as OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT, and OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES are privacy-gated and off by default, so an observability design should avoid turning them on unless there is a clear, approved need.

At scale, the mental model is to separate operational telemetry from sensitive conversation content. Metrics and decision events can support adoption, usage, and security monitoring, while raw bodies and content logs create a much larger privacy and retention burden. See Anthropic's Claude Code monitoring usage documentation for the supported exporters, telemetry enablement setting, and privacy-sensitive logging controls.

questions.question: A national food bank network's grant operations team is piloting Claude to summarize partner applications for review committees. Program directors want summaries that capture eligibility issues, finance reviewers want budget risks surfaced, legal wants sensitive household details handled carefully, and operations wants decisions prepared before weekly meetings. The sponsor asks the architect to “just start improving the prompt” so the pilot can move quickly. Which next step best supports structured discovery and requirement gathering?

options.label: A
options.text: Facilitate a discovery workshop that translates each stakeholder’s expectations into measurable criteria, representative test cases, and latency, cost, privacy constraints.
options.feedback: This is correct because structured discovery should turn vague stakeholder preferences into specific, measurable, relevant targets before prompt iteration begins. It also recognizes that the workflow has multiple evaluation dimensions, not just summary quality.

options.label: B
options.text: Define one aggregate quality score for all reviewers, then tune prompts until that score improves across test samples.
options.feedback: A single aggregate score can hide failures that matter to a particular stakeholder group, such as privacy preservation or budget-risk coverage. Most real use cases require multidimensional evaluation across several criteria.

options.label: C
options.text: Select a faster model for the workflow first, then revisit output quality after cost and latency targets are met.
options.feedback: Model selection can be an appropriate way to improve latency or cost, but those targets still need to be gathered and balanced against other requirements. Prioritizing one dimension first risks optimizing the wrong tradeoff.

options.label: D
options.text: Draft several prompt variants from the sponsor’s examples, then ask each stakeholder group to select the most acceptable output.
options.feedback: This starts prompt engineering before the team has defined what success means or how outputs will be evaluated. Stakeholder preference review can be useful later, but it is too subjective as the first requirements step.

questions.explanation:
Structured discovery should happen before intensive prompt iteration. Anthropic’s prompt engineering guidance assumes you already have a clear definition of success, empirical ways to test against it, and a first-draft prompt, and recommends establishing those basics first when they are missing. See Prompt engineering overview.

The right mental model is to convert stakeholder language like usable, safe, or ready for review into measurable success criteria and representative evaluation cases. The criteria should cover the dimensions that matter for the lifecycle of the system, such as task fidelity, relevance, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency, and price. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes replacing vague goals with specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant targets, and notes that many use cases need multidimensional evaluation rather than one universal metric. See Define success criteria.

Prompt variants, model changes, and scoring schemes are implementation or evaluation tactics, not substitutes for discovery. They become useful once the team has agreed on what must be tested and which tradeoffs are acceptable. In practice, good lifecycle management means aligning stakeholders first, then using prompts, model routing, evaluations, and cost controls to satisfy the agreed criteria.

questions.question: A disaster relief coordination center is piloting a Claude workflow that classifies shelter requests, drafts dispatcher notes, and reviews public web snippets that may contain adversarial instructions. The team needs launch gates before comparing prompt versions. Which evaluation plan best fits the use case?

options.label: A
options.text: Set one overall reviewer preference score, then investigate accuracy, latency, cost, and safety only when reviewers report unacceptable regressions.
options.feedback: A single reviewer preference score is too vague and collapses distinct risks into one subjective measure. Human review can be useful, but relying on it as the only launch gate is slower, less scalable, and less diagnostic than multidimensional criteria.

options.label: B
options.text: Set launch criteria from request counts, HTTP error rates, average response length, and the number of blocked prompts found in server logs.
options.feedback: Request counts and response length are weak substitutes for token and tool-usage accounting when estimating cost. HTTP error rates also miss successful responses where Claude refuses, since refusals should be detected through the response stop reason.

options.label: C
options.text: Set the first gate to minimize TTFT with a smaller model, then measure answer quality and safety after latency targets are consistently met.
options.feedback: Latency is important, but optimizing it before measuring whether the workflow works can produce a fast system that fails the task. Anthropic guidance recommends establishing quality first, then applying latency-reduction strategies with measured tradeoffs.

options.label: D
options.text: Set separate thresholds for task accuracy, baseline latency and TTFT, token and tool-usage cost, refusal and toxicity rates, and direct and indirect injection outcomes.
options.feedback: This defines measurable success criteria across quality, responsiveness, operating cost, safety, and security. It treats prompt injection as both a direct and indirect threat, and it uses latency and cost dimensions that match how Claude applications are actually measured.

questions.explanation:
Good evaluation design starts with specific, measurable success criteria, not a single broad goal such as “works well.” Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes that most applications need several dimensions, such as task fidelity, safety, latency, and price, because improving one dimension can degrade another. See Define success criteria and build evaluations.

For this scenario, classification quality can be measured with accuracy, F1, or another task-appropriate score, while responsiveness should include latency measures such as baseline latency and time to first token for streaming experiences. Cost should be based on token and tool usage rather than request count alone, since Claude pricing distinguishes input, output, cache-related tokens, and some server-side tool usage. See Reduce latency and Pricing.

Safety and security also need explicit metrics. Refusals are normal successful Messages API responses and should be tracked using stop_reason == "refusal", not inferred only from HTTP errors. Because the workflow processes public web content, the evaluation should include indirect prompt-injection cases as well as direct adversarial user prompts, as described in Handling stop reasons and Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections.

questions.question: A pediatric telehealth provider's clinical operations team is piloting Claude to convert post-visit clinician notes into family-facing care summaries. Clinicians want medical accuracy, patient advocates want plain language, legal wants privacy-sensitive details handled appropriately, and operations wants summaries delivered quickly at predictable cost. The sponsor asks the architect to begin prompt revisions so the team can review examples in the next steering meeting. What should the architect do next?

options.text: Ask the sponsor for one overall acceptance score and optimize future iterations against that score.

questions.question: A commercial architecture firm's permitting team wants Claude to help reviewers evaluate renovation submissions. Each case includes several plan sheets, site photos, and short excerpts from the applicable local code. Reviewers ask follow-up questions during the review, and the firm has noticed that small labels and dimensions in drawings are often important. Which TWO design choices best translate this business need into a Claude-based solution?

options.label: A
options.text: Scope each review session to the active case materials and relevant code excerpts.
options.feedback: This keeps the model grounded in the current permit packet and avoids filling the context with unrelated cases. It also aligns with context management principles, where only useful, task-relevant material should occupy the working context.

options.label: B
options.text: Run all reviews in one long-lived conversation so prior permit history remains present.
options.feedback: A continuously growing conversation can introduce irrelevant context and degrade reliability as the context window fills. Prior examples or policies should be curated deliberately, not retained as an ever-expanding transcript.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a vision-capable Claude model and provide a crop or zoom tool for detailed drawing regions.
options.feedback: This matches the multimodal nature of the work, where images and small visual details are part of the core task. A crop or zoom capability can improve performance when Claude needs to inspect dense or small regions of an image.

options.label: D
options.text: Downsample every plan sheet into a thumbnail before sending it to Claude.
options.feedback: Reducing image size can lower latency and token cost, but thumbnails risk making labels and dimensions illegible. For this scenario, visual fidelity matters, so compression and resizing should be tested rather than applied blindly.

questions.explanation:
This scenario is best served by treating the permit packet as a multimodal, case-scoped review problem. Claude can accept image inputs, and Anthropic's vision guidance notes that image clarity, text legibility, and resizing decisions affect performance. When small labels or dimensions matter, adding a crop or zoom capability gives Claude a practical way to focus on relevant regions instead of relying on a single full-page view.

The other architectural concern is context hygiene. Claude's context window is working memory, not a permanent enterprise knowledge base, and adding unrelated historical permit records can create noise, cost, and recall degradation. A better design loads the active case materials and relevant code excerpts, then uses curated reusable guidance or retrieval patterns when broader institutional knowledge is actually needed.

Blindly downsampling every plan may save tokens, but it trades away the very details the business process depends on. Keeping all reviews in one conversation is a common agentic anti-pattern because it lets irrelevant state accumulate; use fresh or scoped sessions, summaries, or explicit artifacts instead. See Anthropic's Vision guidance and Context windows documentation for the underlying design considerations.

questions.question: A maritime insurance analytics team uses Claude to draft risk summaries for underwriters. The current prompt is accurate in offline evaluations but includes a long style guide and asks for a five-paragraph narrative, even though underwriters only need a short decision memo. A trial with a concise prompt and two-paragraph output format preserves the required factual accuracy. Which configuration change best improves latency while maintaining the evaluated behavior?

options.label: A
options.text: Set a much lower max_tokens value on the existing prompt.
options.feedback: Reducing max_tokens can reduce worst-case output length, but it is a blunt control. The cap can cut off the response mid-sentence or mid-word, so it does not reliably preserve the validated memo behavior.

options.label: B
options.text: Add more examples to improve consistency before deployment.
options.feedback: Additional examples can help some prompts, but they also increase input tokens. In this scenario, accuracy is already acceptable with the concise configuration, so adding context works against the stated latency goal.

options.label: C
options.text: Adopt the concise evaluated prompt and request the shorter output format.
options.feedback: This directly reduces both input tokens and expected output tokens, which are documented latency levers. Because the concise version has already been evaluated for factual accuracy, it improves latency without relying on an unvalidated behavior change.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to the most capable model for all summaries.
options.feedback: A more capable model may improve quality for some tasks, but it is not the most direct latency optimization. Model choice is a speed and quality trade-off, so changing models should be justified by task fit and validated rather than assumed to reduce latency.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's latency guidance emphasizes that teams should first build a prompt that works well, then apply latency optimizations to that working baseline. The strongest change here is to reduce unnecessary input tokens and expected output tokens using a prompt and response shape that has already passed evaluation.

max_tokens is useful as a hard output cap, but it is not a precise way to make an answer concise. A low cap can truncate the answer mid-sentence or mid-word, which can damage the product behavior even if latency improves. Similarly, changing to a more capable model or adding examples may be reasonable for quality problems, but neither is the best fit when the task already has an evaluated concise configuration.

The practical mental model is that latency work should preserve the validated task behavior while removing avoidable work from the request. For interactive products, teams should also distinguish baseline latency from time to first token when streaming affects perceived responsiveness. See Anthropic's guidance on reducing latency.

questions.question: A renewable energy startup's firmware team wants a Make target that summarizes compiler warnings across embedded projects. The Make target should accept warning text from existing shell commands, return control to Make after one response, and produce output that a follow-up script can parse. Which implementation best fits this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Pipe the warning stream into `claude -p` and request `--output-format json` for the result.
options.feedback: This uses Claude Code's automation-oriented print mode, which is designed to query and then exit. Piped input fits a shell and Make workflow, and JSON output gives the follow-up script a structured result to parse.

options.label: B
options.text: Open an interactive `claude` session and paste the warning stream into the prompt.
options.feedback: An interactive session is useful for exploratory development, but it does not naturally return control to Make after a single automated response. Manual pasting also breaks the goal of consuming output from existing shell commands.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a Desktop scheduled task that reads the warnings and updates a local report.
options.feedback: A desktop scheduled task can be useful for work triggered outside the current shell flow, including recurring or manually run tasks. It is not the best fit for a Make target that consumes the current warning stream and returns a parseable result during that invocation.

options.label: D
options.text: Write the warnings into `CLAUDE.md` and run Claude Code from the project root.
options.feedback: `CLAUDE.md` is for persistent project instructions such as coding standards, workflows, and architecture notes. It is not the right place for transient compiler output generated by a Make target.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code can be used as a composable command-line tool, not only as an interactive coding session. For shell automation, claude -p or --print is the mode intended to query Claude and then exit, which fits Make targets, scripts, and other one-shot developer workflows.

The practical design pattern is to keep transient data in the pipeline and keep persistent guidance in configuration. Warning logs, diffs, or command output should be piped into the command that invokes Claude, while durable project conventions belong in files such as CLAUDE.md. When downstream tooling needs to consume the answer, selecting an output format such as json is more appropriate than relying on a human-oriented interactive transcript.

Interactive sessions, scheduled desktop tasks, and project memory features can all improve developer productivity in other contexts, but they optimize for different jobs. The best fit here is the Unix-style automation path: existing commands produce text, Claude analyzes it once, and another script consumes the structured result. See the official Claude Code CLI reference and Claude Code memory documentation for the relevant command and persistent instruction behavior.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical trial operations team uses structured outputs to normalize adverse-event narratives into JSON. The team is HIPAA-covered, and an engineer proposes generating a per-study JSON schema whose property names and enum values include patient identifiers so downstream systems can route records without a separate lookup table. What should the architect recommend?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the identifiers from enum values into schema descriptions for the same fields.
options.feedback: Putting protected information in descriptions still places it in the JSON schema definition. The safer pattern is to keep schema metadata generic and perform patient-specific mapping in the application layer.

options.label: B
options.text: Use generic schema fields and enums, and map patient-specific routing values outside the schema.
options.feedback: This keeps protected health information out of the JSON schema definition while still allowing the response content to carry the case data under the applicable safeguards. Structured outputs compile and cache schemas separately from prompts and responses, so identifiers should be handled in message content or application logic instead.

options.label: C
options.text: Rely on structured outputs because schema-constrained decoding prevents disclosure outside the JSON object.
options.feedback: Schema compliance does not make the schema itself an appropriate place to store protected identifiers. Structured outputs constrain Claude's direct output format, but the schema definition has its own caching and retention behavior.

options.label: D
options.text: Disable prompt caching so the generated schema is not reused between requests.
options.feedback: Structured outputs use compiled grammar artifacts for schemas, which is distinct from ordinary prompt caching. Disabling prompt caching would not address the documented concern that schema definitions are cached separately for optimization.

questions.explanation:
Structured outputs are useful when an application needs reliable JSON shape, but they introduce a governance boundary that architects must understand. The schema is not just ordinary prompt text: Anthropic compiles JSON schemas into grammars and may cache those schema artifacts for optimization, while prompts and responses follow the feature's normal data handling rules.

For HIPAA-sensitive workflows, the safe design is to keep protected health information out of schema property names, enum values, const values, and regular expression patterns. Use generic fields such as participant_id or routing_key, then resolve those values in your own system with a lookup table or policy engine. This preserves the operational benefit of schema-constrained output without embedding sensitive data in reusable schema metadata.

The common failure mode is treating structured output schemas as if they were ephemeral request content. They are better modeled as configuration artifacts: they shape decoding, may affect latency through grammar compilation, and should contain stable, non-sensitive structure rather than case-specific identifiers. See Anthropic's guidance on Structured outputs and the broader API and data retention documentation.

questions.question: A luxury furniture manufacturer's supply-chain software team runs Claude through Amazon Bedrock because of existing procurement and audit controls. A logistics vendor exposes a trusted HTTPS remote MCP server with inventory and freight-pricing tools, and the team wants Claude to use those capabilities in launch workflows. Which integration choice best respects the documented constraints?

options.label: A
options.text: Operate an application-side MCP client and pass retrieved vendor results into the Bedrock-hosted Claude workflow.
options.feedback: This respects the requirement to remain on Amazon Bedrock while still integrating with the vendor's MCP server. The Messages API MCP connector is not available on Amazon Bedrock, so the application must handle the integration outside that connector.

options.label: B
options.text: Move tool allowlisting into the MCP server definition and use the deprecated beta connector version.
options.feedback: The deprecated connector version placed tool configuration inside the MCP server definition, but the current pattern uses an MCPToolset in the tools array. Using the deprecated request shape would not address the Amazon Bedrock availability constraint.

options.label: C
options.text: Configure the Messages API MCP connector and reference the vendor server through a current MCPToolset entry.
options.feedback: This uses the current MCP connector request pattern, but it does not fit the stated platform constraint. The MCP connector is documented for the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, and Microsoft Foundry Hosted on Anthropic, not Amazon Bedrock.

options.label: D
options.text: Expose the vendor server as a local STDIO process and connect it directly through the MCP connector.
options.feedback: Local STDIO servers cannot be connected directly through the Messages API MCP connector. The connector requires a publicly exposed MCP server over supported HTTP transports, and the platform constraint still remains.

questions.explanation:
MCP is the right protocol family when Claude needs standardized access to external tools, data sources, and services, but the specific connector matters. The Messages API MCP connector is designed to connect Claude directly to remote MCP servers without the application implementing a separate MCP client, but that convenience is limited to supported platforms and supported MCP capabilities.

In this scenario, the decisive constraint is the runtime platform: the documented MCP connector is not available on Amazon Bedrock. Because the team must stay on Bedrock, the practical architecture is to keep the MCP or vendor integration in the application layer, then provide the resulting context or workflow outputs to Claude through the Bedrock-hosted flow. See the official MCP connector documentation for the supported platforms, current beta version, and request structure.

The distractors each miss a different boundary: a current mcp_toolset request is valid only where the connector is supported, local STDIO servers are not directly supported by the Messages API connector, and tool_configuration inside the server definition belongs to the deprecated connector version. The broader integration lesson is to select not just the protocol, but the supported execution surface: MCP may be the vendor's interface, while API or application-side orchestration may still be required when the managed connector is unavailable.

questions.question: A university writing center's engineering team is piloting a Claude workflow that scores practice essays against a rubric, explains missing evidence, avoids exposing student identifiers, and uses an encouraging tutor tone. The team needs an offline framework to compare prompt and model revisions before tutors use it. Which TWO actions best support that goal?

options.label: A
options.text: Use one LLM grader to assign an overall quality label to every response, then tune prompts against that aggregate score.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a single overall label is too coarse for a workflow with multiple success criteria. It also risks relying on an LLM grader without detailed rubrics or reliability testing for each judgment type.

options.label: B
options.text: Create representative test cases with common submissions and edge cases, using code checks and rubric-based LLM graders where appropriate.
options.feedback: This is correct because effective eval datasets should mirror the real-world task distribution and include edge cases. Mixed grading methods let objective checks handle simple criteria while LLM-based grading can cover nuanced judgments after its reliability is tested.

options.label: C
options.text: Hand-pick a small set of expert-reviewed examples, grade every dimension manually, and delay automated grading until after launch.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because human grading can be high quality but is slow and expensive. For scalable iteration, the guidance favors automation when possible and more automated test cases over a small number of fully manual cases.

options.label: D
options.text: Define measurable success criteria for rubric fidelity, explanation quality, tutor tone, privacy handling, latency, and price.
options.feedback: This is correct because evaluation design should start with specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant success criteria. The workflow has several distinct goals, so separating the criteria prevents one dimension from hiding regressions in another.

questions.explanation:
Strong evaluation frameworks begin with success criteria, not with a preferred grader. For an LLM workflow that must score essays, explain gaps, preserve privacy, maintain tone, and meet operational constraints, the team should define measurable criteria for each dimension rather than collapse everything into one generic quality target. See Anthropic's guidance on Define success criteria.

The dataset should then reflect the production distribution, including routine inputs and edge cases such as ambiguous essays, missing evidence, unusual writing styles, or attempts to include identifying information. The grading strategy should be mixed: use code-based checks where outputs are categorical or easily validated, and use detailed rubric-driven LLM grading for nuanced dimensions such as tone or explanation quality. Anthropic's Develop tests documentation emphasizes mirroring real tasks, including edge cases, automating when possible, and testing LLM-based graders for reliability before scaling.

The tempting shortcuts fail for different reasons. A single aggregate score hides which capability changed after a prompt or model revision, while an all-human process usually becomes too slow to support rapid iteration. A practical test framework combines breadth, clear measurement, and grading methods matched to the property being evaluated.

questions.question: A museum digitization lab is adding Claude to a headless automation workflow that audits image metadata before publication. The only integration available for the collection system is a local command-line utility installed on the runner, and security policy does not allow exposing that utility as a public HTTPS service. The workflow needs Claude to inspect results from that utility during the task. Which integration approach best fits these constraints?

options.label: A
options.text: Invoke the installed utility through the agent runtime with narrowly scoped command permissions.
options.feedback: This uses the integration mechanism that matches the available interface, a local command in the runner environment. Narrow command permissions keep the agent useful while limiting what it can execute.

options.label: B
options.text: Create a reviewer subagent and rely on delegation to access the collection system.
options.feedback: Subagents are useful for context isolation, parallel work, and specialized instructions. They do not by themselves create a connection protocol to an external system without an allowed tool or integration.

options.label: C
options.text: Register the utility as a Messages API MCP server with an mcp_toolset entry.
options.feedback: The current MCP connector request shape uses an MCP toolset entry to enable tools from a server. That still requires a supported remote MCP server endpoint, which the scenario does not provide.

options.label: D
options.text: Connect the utility through the Messages API MCP connector as a local STDIO server.
options.feedback: The Messages API MCP connector is for remote MCP servers exposed over supported HTTP transports. It does not directly connect to local STDIO servers.

questions.explanation:
Choose the integration mechanism that matches the system boundary you actually have. Here, the external capability exists as a local command-line utility in the runner, so the practical design is to let the agent call that utility with restricted command permissions and to validate what commands are allowed.

The MCP connector in the Messages API is designed for connecting Claude to remote MCP servers without building a separate MCP client. The official MCP connector documentation states that the connector currently supports MCP tool calls and requires a publicly exposed HTTP server using Streamable HTTP or SSE, with local STDIO servers not directly supported.

Agent-to-agent mechanisms, such as subagents, solve a different problem: they split work into isolated contexts with specialized instructions and tool restrictions. A subagent can be a good reviewer or investigator, but it still needs a real tool path, such as Bash, a custom tool, or an MCP server, to interact with an external system.

For a Messages API MCP integration, the current request shape uses mcp_servers plus a tools entry of type mcp_toolset. That shape is appropriate only when the lab can provide a trusted remote HTTPS MCP endpoint, so it does not fit these constraints.

questions.question: A regional airline's operations engineering team wants Claude to update incident runbooks after outages. Each request may require inspecting logs and repository files, applying documentation changes, running validation commands, and continuing for one to two hours after the engineer submits the task. Engineers want scoped tool permissions and do not need to supervise every intermediate step. Which design best translates this business need into a Claude-based solution?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the workflow as a Claude Managed Agents session with scoped tools and runnable checks.
options.feedback: This fits a long-running asynchronous workflow where Claude needs an agent harness, tool access, and verification steps. Scoped tools and checks let the architecture constrain what the agent can do while giving it a pass or fail signal to iterate on.

options.label: B
options.text: Submit each incident through the Batch API with tool execution disabled for lower cost.
options.feedback: The Batch API is designed for asynchronous processing of many independent model requests, not for an agent that must inspect files, run commands, and iterate on changes. Disabling tool execution also removes the mechanism needed to validate runbook updates against the repository.

options.label: C
options.text: Send one synchronous Messages API request containing all logs, files, and runbook instructions.
options.feedback: A single synchronous request is a poor fit for one to two hours of tool-driven work and iteration. The Messages API is appropriate when you want direct model access and fine-grained control, but the application would need to build the long-running agent loop itself.

options.label: D
options.text: Use prompt caching for the runbook template and require engineers to monitor each step.
options.feedback: Prompt caching can reduce cost and latency when stable prompt prefixes repeat, but it does not provide an agent runtime or solve the need for unattended work. Requiring engineers to monitor each step conflicts with the stated need for minimal supervision.

questions.explanation:
The business problem points to an agentic, long-running, asynchronous workflow rather than a single completion. Claude must inspect project artifacts, use tools, modify documentation, run validation, and continue working after submission, so the design should provide an execution harness with scoped permissions and a verification loop.

Claude Managed Agents are positioned for long-running tasks and asynchronous work, while the Messages API is direct model access for teams that want to build their own orchestration. See Anthropic's overview of the two integration paths in Intro to Claude and the product documentation for Claude Managed Agents.

The synchronous Messages API option is not inherently wrong for custom agents, but it shifts responsibility for session state, tool orchestration, retries, and long-running execution to the application team. The Batch API option is attractive for offline bulk processing, but it is not the right abstraction for an iterative tool-using runbook update session. Prompt caching may be useful inside a larger design if runbook templates or instructions repeat, but caching changes token economics, not the architecture needed to perform unattended multi-step work.
