questions.question: A university admissions office's document review team adds prompt caching to a Claude workflow that always sends the same review rubric and 25 labeled examples before each applicant-specific essay. Their dashboard reads only `usage.input_tokens`, so after caching it shows near-zero input volume on requests with large `cache_read_input_tokens`. The team wants an accurate view of total prompt volume and cache effectiveness. Which change should the architect make?

options.label: A
options.text: Pause prompt caching during monitoring windows, then use the existing input-token totals.
options.feedback: Disabling caching would make measurement simpler, but it removes the optimization the team deployed. It also fails to teach the dashboard how cached token usage is actually reported in production.

options.label: B
options.text: Sum all three prompt-caching usage fields, then chart cache reads and writes separately.
options.feedback: This uses the documented token accounting model for cached prompts. When prompt caching is active, input volume is split across cache reads, cache writes, and uncached input, so tracking all three fields gives both total prompt volume and cache behavior.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch between cache-read and uncached-token fields based on whether caching was attempted.
options.feedback: This would undercount requests that create cache entries or include uncached suffixes after the cache breakpoint. It also mixes different meanings, since cache reads, cache writes, and ordinary input represent different parts of the request.

options.label: D
options.text: Place the cache breakpoint on the applicant essay, then compare repeated rubric totals.
options.feedback: Moving the cache breakpoint to a changing applicant essay is a common caching anti-pattern. Cache hits require exact matching of the cached prefix, so placing `cache_control` on request-specific content tends to reduce reuse rather than improve measurement.

questions.explanation:
With prompt caching, the usage.input_tokens field is not the full size of the request. It represents only the uncached portion after the last cache breakpoint, while cached reads and cache writes are reported separately as cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens.

The right mental model is that caching changes how repeated prompt prefixes are processed and priced, not whether those tokens are part of the request. To calculate total input volume, add cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens. To understand optimization effectiveness, also keep the fields separate so you can see whether requests are reading from cache, creating new cache entries, or missing the cache.

This distinction matters because cache reads and writes have different pricing multipliers, and cache reads are not free input. The official Prompt caching documentation describes the usage fields, cache prefix behavior, and the need to place cache breakpoints on stable content rather than request-specific suffixes.

questions.question: An online marketplace's seller-trust team is deploying a Claude Code workflow that can review buyer complaints, draft seller outreach, adjust listing visibility, and call an MCP tool that permanently disables seller storefronts. Analysts want complaint review and drafting to run without interruption, but storefront disabling must involve an authorized trust-and-safety reviewer each time. Which design best applies human-in-the-loop validation?

options.label: A
options.text: Add prompt guidance telling Claude to ask before disabling storefronts while keeping the tool auto-approved.
options.feedback: Prompt guidance can shape behavior, but it is not an enforcement boundary. For irreversible or business-critical actions, relying on the model to remember to ask is weaker than making the tool call require approval.

options.label: B
options.text: Mark the storefront-disabling MCP tool as requiring user interaction and route approvals to authorized reviewers.
options.feedback: This places the human approval requirement on the high-impact tool itself rather than relying only on model behavior. The MCP user-interaction annotation is designed for tools where approval is required on every call, including cases where permissive modes might otherwise reduce prompts.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the workflow to a more capable model and lower randomness for storefront-risk decisions.
options.feedback: A more capable or less variable model may improve judgment, but it does not enforce authorization. Human approval for a high-impact action should be implemented in the tool or permission layer, not inferred from model quality.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable broad unattended tool access and review all disabled storefronts in a daily compliance report.
options.feedback: After-the-fact review is a detective control, not human-in-the-loop validation before the action occurs. It may help auditing, but it does not prevent an unapproved storefront disablement.

questions.explanation:
Human-in-the-loop validation is most effective when it is attached to the action that needs approval, especially for actions that are hard to reverse or materially affect users. In Claude Code MCP integrations, a server can mark a tool with _meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"] so Claude Code prompts for explicit approval on every call, and does not let ordinary allow rules skip that prompt. See Require approval for a specific tool.

This pattern preserves useful autonomy for low-risk work, such as reading complaints and drafting outreach, while placing a hard checkpoint before the sensitive operation. Prompt instructions and model selection are useful supporting controls, but they are not authorization mechanisms. Similarly, logging and daily review can support governance after the fact, but they do not provide the pre-action validation needed for irreversible or high-impact tool calls.

questions.question: A regional theater chain's customer-experience platform is adding a live Claude chat transcript view. Stakeholders want to simplify the integration by treating the initial HTTP response as the only success or failure signal and estimating usage after the stream finishes. Which recommendation best communicates the architectural trade-off?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a standard HTTP client that trusts the initial status, estimates token usage locally, and retries stalled streams.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the initial HTTP status does not fully describe a streaming request's outcome. Mid-stream errors can arrive as SSE error events after an HTTP 200, and documented usage is available in stream metadata rather than requiring local estimation.

options.label: B
options.text: Parse text deltas for the UI only, ignore message_delta metadata, and treat missing message_stop events as truncation.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because parsing only display text leaves important lifecycle and usage information unhandled. A missing terminal event may indicate an interrupted stream or error condition, but truncation should not be inferred without the documented response metadata.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace streaming with synchronous calls for chats, infer token usage from text length, and monitor only request errors.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it avoids the live transcript requirement rather than communicating the real streaming trade-off. It also substitutes text-length inference for documented usage reporting and misses the need to observe stream-level events.

options.label: D
options.text: Build an SSE-aware client that tracks stream events, reads cumulative usage deltas, and handles in-stream error events.
options.feedback: This is correct because streaming responses are delivered as server-sent events, not as a single response body. The integration needs to process the event sequence, use the cumulative usage values reported in message_delta events, and handle SSE error events that can occur after an HTTP 200.

questions.explanation:
For a streaming architecture, the important trade-off is that the client gains lower perceived latency and incremental display, but it must implement the server-sent events protocol correctly rather than treating the response like a normal blocking HTTP call. Anthropic documents a stream lifecycle that includes message_start, content block events, one or more message_delta events, and message_stop; the usage values in message_delta are cumulative.

The stakeholder-friendly framing is not that streaming is less reliable, but that it moves part of correctness into the client harness. A robust client should parse stream events, update the UI from content deltas, read usage from the documented metadata, and handle SSE error events that may arrive after the initial request has already received HTTP 200. See Anthropic's Messages streaming API documentation for the event flow and error behavior.

questions.question: A professional sports league's integrity operations team is writing an implementation guide for a Claude assistant that helps investigators review match-fixing tips inside an existing case portal. The portal owns authentication, transcript storage, routing to internal systems, and escalation workflows. During review, engineers disagree about whether Claude will remember earlier portal turns automatically and where persistent investigation policy should be placed. Which guidance should the implementation guide provide?

options.label: A
options.text: Build each Messages API request with the needed conversation history, put persistent policy in the top-level system field, and include synthetic assistant turns only when useful.
options.feedback: This is correct because the Messages API is stateless, so the application must send the conversation history needed for each request. Persistent instructions that should apply from the start belong in the top-level system field, and synthetic assistant messages are allowed when the application needs to represent prior state.

options.label: B
options.text: Send only the newest portal message after the first request, put persistent policy as the first system role message, and rely on retained server context.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the Messages API does not retain conversational state across requests for the application. It is also unsafe guidance because a system message cannot be the first entry in the messages array under the documented placement rules.

options.label: C
options.text: Store only investigator-visible summaries in the portal, put persistent policy after retrieved evidence, and tune sampling settings to preserve prior turns.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because sampling settings do not preserve prior conversation turns or substitute for sending the needed context. Placing durable policy after variable evidence also makes the guidance harder to reason about than using the documented top-level system field.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the portal workflow to Claude Managed Agents, put persistent policy in ordinary user messages, and delegate transcript persistence to the agent harness.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the scenario describes an embedded workflow where the existing portal owns routing, authentication, transcript storage, and escalation. Claude Managed Agents are positioned for managed, long-running, asynchronous agent work, not as a required replacement for a custom loop that needs fine-grained control.

questions.explanation:
The key architectural distinction is whether your application needs direct model access with fine-grained control or a managed agent harness for long-running, asynchronous work. In this scenario, the existing portal already owns routing, identity, transcripts, and escalation, so an implementation guide for the Messages API should make the application's responsibilities explicit rather than implying hidden server-side session memory.

The Messages API is stateless: each request should include the prior turns, synthetic state summaries, documents, or other context that Claude must consider for that response. The guide should also tell developers to put instructions that must apply from the start in the top-level system field, rather than treating a first messages entry with role: "system" as the standard pattern. See Anthropic's Messages API documentation for the documented request model, system instruction placement, and the distinction between Messages API control and Claude Managed Agents.

The guide should also tell developers to put instructions that must apply from the start in the top-level system field, rather than treating a first messages entry with role: "system" as the standard pattern. questions.question: An aerospace maintenance consortium's reliability engineering team is building a Claude service that ingests an engineer's defect report, prior review comments, and retrieved maintenance manual excerpts. Claude may request internal part-history or fault-tree tools, engineers can flag a draft as inaccurate, and the platform must not file incomplete drafts as final reports. Which architecture best supports the full input, processing, output, and feedback loop?

options.label: A
options.text: Send prior turns in messages, keep global instructions in top-level system, branch on stop_reason, run requested tools, continue pauses, and append engineer feedback as later turns.
options.feedback: This design matches the stateless Messages API model by sending the relevant conversation history on each request and using the top-level system parameter for global instructions that apply from the start. It also treats stop_reason as part of the processing loop, so tool requests, pauses, and truncation conditions are handled before a report is considered final.

options.label: B
options.text: Send each defect report as a new single-turn request, store reviewer feedback only in audit logs, publish every HTTP 200 response, and rerun manually after complaints.
options.feedback: This design loses the feedback loop because later requests do not include prior review comments as conversation history. It also confuses transport success with task completion, since a successful response can still have a stop_reason that requires more processing.

options.label: C
options.text: Put startup global instructions as the first system message in messages, raise max_tokens for every request, publish the first response, and summarize corrections outside the conversation.
options.feedback: Global instructions that apply from the start should be placed in the top-level system parameter rather than modeled as the first conversation turn. Raising max_tokens only increases the output cap and does not guarantee that the model has completed the task.

options.label: D
options.text: Batch all draft requests with max_tokens set to 0, wait for generated reports from the batch, ignore tool_use stops, and reconcile engineer corrections offline.
options.feedback: max_tokens set to 0 is for populating prompt cache without generating a response and is not supported inside Message Batches. Ignoring tool_use stops breaks the tool execution loop, so requested internal data would never be returned to Claude.

questions.explanation:
A reliable Claude architecture should treat a request as one step in an application-level loop, not as a fire-and-forget text generation call. The Messages API create endpoint is stateless: the application sends the relevant prior user and assistant turns in messages, while global instructions that apply from the start belong in the top-level system parameter.

The response must be routed by stop_reason, as described in Handling stop reasons. For example, tool_use means the application should execute the requested tool and send back tool results, pause_turn means the application should continue by sending the assistant content back, and truncation-related reasons such as max_tokens or model_context_window_exceeded should not be filed as final output.

max_tokens is a cap on generated output, not a completion guarantee, so simply raising it does not replace stop-reason handling. Engineer corrections become useful only when they are represented in later turns or otherwise included in future request context, which closes the feedback loop from output review back into the next input.

questions.question: A cultural heritage archive's metadata engineering team uses Claude Opus 4.8 through the Claude API to draft catalog records. The workflow starts with archive-wide cataloging rules, may receive a trusted curator's revised rule after several turns, ingests OCR text and dealer-catalog excerpts from third-party sources, and is maintained as a reusable prompt in Claude Console. Which TWO prompt design choices best fit documented guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove XML sections and examples from the template, and use a prefilled final assistant turn to enforce the output shape.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because XML structure and examples are documented ways to help Claude parse mixed instructions, context, examples, and inputs. Prefilling the final assistant turn is not a reliable current-model guardrail, and it is no longer supported on several current models.

options.label: B
options.text: Put the opening cataloging policy as the first messages entry, and elevate retrieved excerpts into later system messages when relevant.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a system message cannot be the first entry in the messages array for initial instructions. It also incorrectly promotes untrusted retrieved content into system content, which gives data the authority of operator instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Place fixed cataloging policy in the top-level system field, and keep collection-specific text in Claude Console variables such as {{record_text}}.
options.feedback: This is correct because initial instructions that apply from the start normally belong in the top-level system field. Claude Console prompt templates are designed to separate fixed prompt content from variable content using double-bracket variables.

options.label: D
options.text: Add trusted curator updates as valid mid-conversation system messages, and keep retrieved OCR and catalog excerpts outside system content.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude Opus 4.8 on the Claude API supports mid-conversation system messages for trusted instruction updates when placement rules are followed. Retrieved third-party content should not be placed in system messages because system content is treated as operator instructions.

questions.explanation:
The useful mental model is that system content carries operator authority, while OCR, retrieved documents, web pages, and other third-party text are data the model should analyze. Initial operating rules should therefore go in the top-level system field, while variable record text belongs in template variables or ordinary message and tool-result content. See the Messages API guidance on working with messages and the Claude Console guidance on prompting tools.

Mid-conversation system messages are a narrow mechanism for trusted instruction updates, not a general-purpose place to paste new context. They are supported for Claude Opus 4.8 on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, and Microsoft Foundry, and they have placement and precedence rules. The relevant guidance is documented in mid-conversation system messages.

XML tags and few-shot examples are not mandatory syntax, but they are strong prompt-design tools when a prompt mixes rules, inputs, examples, and desired output style. They improve parseability and steer format and tone, while strict schema guarantees require product features such as Structured Outputs rather than only prompt wording. The general prompting guidance is covered in system prompts and prompt engineering.

questions.question: A supply-chain analytics vendor uses Claude for Teams and wants Claude Code defaults to apply organization-wide for users on both corporate-managed laptops and unmanaged contractor machines. The platform team does not want to depend on device MDM or per-repository setup, though individual repositories may still define their own lower-level settings. Which approach best fits these requirements?

options.label: A
options.text: Configure server-managed settings from Admin Settings and ensure clients can reach api.anthropic.com.
options.feedback: This is correct because server-managed settings are configured centrally for Claude for Teams or Claude for Enterprise rather than being deployed through device management. They require access to api.anthropic.com, and they provide an organization-level control path that does not depend on repository files.

options.label: B
options.text: Deploy managed-settings.json through endpoint management to each developer machine.
options.feedback: Endpoint-managed settings can enforce organization policies on managed devices, but this option depends on device-level deployment. It does not fit the stated need to avoid relying on MDM or other endpoint management for unmanaged contractor machines.

options.label: C
options.text: Commit shared settings to .claude/settings.json in every repository used by the team.
options.feedback: Project settings are useful for team-shared repository configuration, but they depend on each repository containing the file. They also do not meet an organization-wide requirement that applies independently of per-repository setup.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask each engineer to add the required defaults to ~/.claude/settings.json.
options.feedback: User settings are local to an individual account and are the lowest-priority settings scope. This relies on each engineer configuring their machine correctly and does not provide centralized organization-wide control.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code settings are layered across Managed, command-line, Local, Project, and User scopes, with managed settings taking the highest precedence for general settings. Project files such as .claude/settings.json are appropriate when a repository needs shared defaults reviewed through source control, while ~/.claude/settings.json is for an individual user's defaults.

For a Claude for Teams or Claude for Enterprise organization that needs central policy without endpoint deployment, server-managed settings are the right fit. They are configured by an organization Owner or Primary Owner in Admin Settings, and clients must be able to reach api.anthropic.com to receive them. This is distinct from endpoint-managed settings delivered by MDM, OS policy, registry, or managed files. See Server-managed settings and Claude Code settings.

questions.question: A biotech lab's computational biology team has a pre-merge script that gathers notebook diffs, dependency changes, and lint findings into one text stream. They want the script to send that stream to Claude Code, produce output their review bot can parse, and finish without a human continuing a session. Which TWO implementation choices best fit this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Start a normal Claude Code session from the script and parse the live interactive transcript.
options.feedback: An interactive session is useful for developer collaboration, but it does not naturally satisfy a one-shot automation requirement. Parsing an interactive transcript is more fragile than using the documented non-interactive mode and output formats.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the aggregated findings to `CLAUDE.md` before launch and remove them after review.
options.feedback: `CLAUDE.md` is intended for persistent project instructions such as coding standards, workflows, and architectural guidance. Using it as a per-run data transport would bloat session context and is the wrong mechanism for streaming script output.

options.label: C
options.text: Pipe the aggregated findings into Claude Code and request `json` or `stream-json` output.
options.feedback: Claude Code automation supports piped input, which fits a script that already produces a text stream. Selecting a machine-readable output format lets the review bot parse the result more reliably than free-form terminal text.

options.label: D
options.text: Run Claude Code with `--print` from the script so the command performs one query and exits.
options.feedback: `--print` is the non-interactive automation mode for Claude Code. It is designed for scripted workflows that query Claude and then return control to the calling process.

questions.explanation:
For shell automation, the practical mental model is that Claude Code can behave like a Unix-style command: feed it data, ask a question, get output, and let the caller continue. The documented non-interactive path is claude -p or --print, which is described as querying via the SDK and then exiting. That matches scripts, bots, and pipeline steps much better than opening a conversational terminal session.

The input and output choices matter just as much as the invocation mode. Piping the pre-merge findings into Claude Code avoids copying intermediate files into long-lived instruction context, while --output-format json or --output-format stream-json gives downstream automation a format designed for parsing. By contrast, CLAUDE.md should carry durable guidance that applies broadly across sessions, not transient review payloads that change on every run.

See the official Claude Code CLI reference for the automation flags and formats, and How Claude remembers your project for the intended role of CLAUDE.md.

questions.question: A public transit authority's developer platform team rolls out prompt caching for Claude Code workflows and wants an aggregate dashboard showing whether cached token reads are increasing and whether total spend per model is falling. Security policy prohibits collecting prompt text, assistant response text, tool details, or raw API bodies. Telemetry is already enabled and metrics are exported to an OpenTelemetry collector. Which instrumentation change best supports this dashboard?

options.label: A
options.text: Build dashboards by adding `prompt.id` as a metric attribute, plus grouping token and cost series per prompt.
options.feedback: `prompt.id` is intended for correlating events such as user prompts, API requests, and tool activity. It is intentionally excluded from metrics because using it as a metric attribute would create unbounded cardinality.

options.label: B
options.text: Build dashboards from `claude_code.token.usage` grouped by `type` and model, plus `claude_code.cost.usage` grouped by model.
options.feedback: This uses Claude Code's documented metrics for token and cost tracking. The token metric distinguishes `cacheRead` and `cacheCreation` from other token types, and the cost and token metrics include model attribution without requiring prompt or response content.

options.label: C
options.text: Build dashboards by enabling prompt text logging and parsing repeated prefixes, plus grouping inferred spend by model.
options.feedback: Prompt text logging is redacted or disabled by default and would violate the stated security policy. It is also an indirect and less reliable way to measure cache reads when Claude Code already exports token usage metrics for that purpose.

options.label: D
options.text: Build dashboards from `claude_code.api_request` log events only, plus setting the metrics exporter to `none`.
options.feedback: API request events can include useful per-request cost and token details when logs are exported. They are less appropriate for this metrics-based dashboard than the documented time-series metrics, and disabling metrics would remove the already available aggregate metric stream.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code observability separates metrics from events. Metrics are exported as OpenTelemetry time series and are the right fit for aggregate dashboards such as spend, token usage, and cache effectiveness, while events are exported through the logs/events protocol for operational records and correlation.

For this scenario, the important metric is claude_code.token.usage, which uses the type attribute to distinguish input, output, cacheRead, and cacheCreation. Pairing it with claude_code.cost.usage and grouping by model lets the team monitor whether prompt caching is producing more cache reads and whether spend is changing by model.

Content logging is the wrong tradeoff here because prompt and assistant content are redacted or disabled by default, and enabling them would collect data the security policy forbids. Similarly, prompt.id belongs in event correlation, not in metrics, because high-cardinality identifiers can destabilize time-series systems.

See the Claude Code documentation on monitoring usage for the documented telemetry exporters, metric names, token type attributes, and the distinction between metric aggregation and event correlation.

questions.question: A multiplayer game studio's developer platform team is standardizing Claude Code across several repositories. They need a reusable reviewer that runs from the current coding session, keeps its detailed inspection context separate, and can inspect source files without editing files or executing shell commands. They also need to prevent engineers' personal subagent definitions from accidentally changing which reviewer Claude invokes. Which two design choices should the team make?

options.label: A
options.text: Control the effective subagent by its name frontmatter and use higher-precedence definitions for enforced standards.
options.feedback: Claude Code identifies subagents by the name in their frontmatter, not by the Markdown filename. If the team needs an enforced standard, managed settings have the highest documented priority over project and user definitions.

options.label: B
options.text: Omit the tools field and describe read-only behavior in the subagent prompt for simpler permission management.
options.feedback: Omitting the tools field does not make the subagent read-only. The documented behavior is that a subagent inherits all tools when tools are not specified, which is the opposite of least privilege.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a project custom subagent with name and description frontmatter, and list only read-oriented tools.
options.feedback: This uses a subagent for a delegated worker inside the current Claude Code session while keeping the worker focused. Explicitly listing tools prevents the subagent from inheriting broader permissions that could allow edits or command execution.

options.label: D
options.text: Place a same-filename subagent in each user directory and rely on filenames to determine invocation priority.
options.feedback: Filenames are not the documented identity mechanism for subagents. Project and user subagents are scanned recursively, but identity comes from the name frontmatter field, and user definitions do not outrank project or managed definitions.

questions.explanation:
Subagents are the right abstraction when you want a delegated worker inside one Claude Code session, with its own context window and a returned result, rather than a separate user-managed session. The official subagent documentation describes custom subagents as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter where name and description are required, and tools is optional. See Claude Code subagents.

For permission design, the important tradeoff is between convenience and least privilege. If tools is omitted, the subagent inherits all tools, so a reviewer that must only inspect files should explicitly receive only the tools it needs. This keeps the worker focused and reduces the chance that it edits files or runs commands when the workflow only calls for review.

Definition resolution is another architecture concern in multi-agent setups. Claude Code uses the subagent name frontmatter as identity, and documented precedence puts managed settings above the --agents CLI flag, then project definitions, then user definitions, then plugin definitions. The broader agents page distinguishes subagents from other orchestration approaches such as background sessions, agent teams, and dynamic workflows, which helps avoid treating every multi-agent feature as interchangeable. See Claude Code agents.

questions.question: An independent tax advisory firm's automation team uses Claude to draft reviewer notes for client filings. Some jobs are short W-2 anomaly checks, while others include tool definitions and scanned PDF attachments. The current service estimates size from raw character counts, sends all jobs to the same high-capability model, and users wait for the full response before seeing any text. Which two changes should the team prioritize to improve cost-performance and perceived latency without cutting off required output?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable streaming for interactive note drafting, then render server-sent event deltas as text becomes available in the UI.
options.feedback: This is correct because streaming improves perceived responsiveness by letting the application display output as it arrives. It does not reduce the total tokens generated, but it directly addresses the blank waiting state for interactive users.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a token-counting preflight using the same structured inputs, then route small routine jobs to Claude Haiku 4.5 when evals support it.
options.feedback: This is correct because token counting is designed for preflight cost, routing, and prompt-size decisions, and it accepts structured inputs like system prompts, tools, images, and PDFs. Routing routine jobs to a faster model can improve latency and cost, provided the team validates quality on its own evaluations.

options.label: C
options.text: Set a low max_tokens value for all note drafts, then rely on the cap to make responses concise and complete.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because max_tokens is a hard output cap, not a guarantee of concise or complete writing. If the model reaches the cap, the response can be cut off and the API reports stop_reason as max_tokens.

options.label: D
options.text: Place cache_control on the final per-client message, then expect matching substrings inside later requests to reuse cached tokens.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prompt caching works on ordered prompt prefixes, not arbitrary repeated substrings. If the breakpoint includes per-client content that changes, later requests are unlikely to reuse the same cached prefix.

questions.explanation:
For mixed workloads, a strong cost-performance design separates preflight estimation, model routing, and interactive delivery. The token counting endpoint is appropriate before sending requests because it accepts the same structured message inputs used for generation, including tools, images, and PDFs, and returns an estimated input token count. See Anthropic's Token counting documentation.

Once the team has reliable estimates, it can route straightforward, low-risk jobs to a faster model such as Claude Haiku 4.5 when evaluations show the quality tradeoff is acceptable. This follows the latency guidance to choose faster models for speed-critical applications and reduce unnecessary token work where possible, described in Reduce latency.

Streaming is a separate optimization for perceived latency. With stream: true, the application receives server-sent events and can render text deltas as they arrive, so users are not staring at an empty interface while a long answer is generated. The event behavior is documented in Streaming.

The rejected approaches confuse mechanisms with outcomes. A small max_tokens limit can stop generation mid-response rather than making answers reliably concise, and prompt caching only reuses stable prefixes ordered as tools, system, then messages. It does not search for matching substrings inside changing client-specific requests, as explained in Prompt caching.

A small max_tokens limit can stop generation mid-response rather than making answers reliably concise, and prompt caching only reuses stable prefixes ordered as tools, system, then messages. It does not search for matching substrings inside changing client-specific requests, as explained in Prompt caching.

questions.question: A renewable energy trading desk uses Claude to summarize grid incident reports and recommend dispatch actions. After a release, analysts see unsupported claims, missed operational constraints, and weaker answers when short reports are routed to a faster model. Engineers disagree whether to revise the prompt, change routing, or add more review steps. What should the architecture team do first to diagnose the failures?

options.label: A
options.text: Route every incident report to the most capable model, then monitor analyst complaints for two weeks.
options.feedback: This could mask a model-mismatch problem, but it does not diagnose whether prompt behavior, data characteristics, or routing caused the regression. Complaint monitoring is slower and less controlled than an evaluation set with defined success criteria.

options.label: B
options.text: Build a task-specific eval set with measurable criteria, then compare prompt and model variants on representative cases.
options.feedback: This is the best first diagnostic step because it turns vague symptoms into measurable failure modes. A representative eval set can separate prompt-following issues, unsupported factual claims, and model-fit regressions before the team chooses a fix.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask senior analysts to hand-review recent bad outputs, then patch the prompt for each observed error.
options.feedback: Human review can provide useful labels and examples, but relying on a small set of hand-reviewed failures is hard to scale. Patching each observed error risks overfitting to anecdotes instead of measuring performance across the real task distribution.

options.label: D
options.text: Rewrite the system prompt to prohibit unsupported claims, then deploy the revised prompt to all traffic.
options.feedback: This may address one symptom, but it is an ad hoc prompt tweak without evidence that the prompt is the main cause. It also does not test whether the faster model is unsuitable for some cases or whether edge cases are underrepresented.

questions.explanation:
When a Claude application shows mixed symptoms such as missed instructions, unsupported facts, and weaker results on one route, the first move should be to make the problem measurable. Anthropic guidance emphasizes defining success criteria and building evaluations before prompt engineering, because otherwise teams tend to chase anecdotes rather than isolate causes.

A good diagnostic eval should reflect the application’s real task distribution, including edge cases such as short incident reports, ambiguous constraints, and reports likely to trigger unsupported claims. The team can then compare the previous release, the new prompt, and the model-routing choices against the same test cases, using criteria such as factual support, constraint coverage, action quality, latency, and cost.

Prompt rewrites, model upgrades, and human review are all plausible interventions, but they answer different questions and can hide the actual failure mode. The practical tradeoff is that evals require upfront work, yet they create a reusable measurement harness that lets the team distinguish prompt failure, hallucination, and model mismatch before optimizing. See Anthropic’s guidance on Define success criteria and build evaluations.

questions.question: An academic journal's editorial technology team is designing a Claude-based manuscript triage system. Each submission must receive the same fixed set of independent checks, such as scope fit, ethics statement completeness, statistical reporting quality, image disclosure completeness, and conflict-of-interest language. The team wants to reduce wall-clock review time while preserving separate check results for an editor-facing summary. Which architectural pattern best fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Implement a single augmented LLM call with retrieval and examples that performs the entire review in one response.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a single augmented LLM call may be sufficient for simpler applications, but it does not directly address the need to reduce wall-clock time across independent checks. It also makes the individual review dimensions less cleanly isolated than separate workflow steps.

options.label: B
options.text: Implement a routing workflow that classifies each submission into one review path and skips unrelated checks.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because every submission needs the same set of checks rather than selection among distinct categories. Routing is better when inputs can be classified accurately into different paths that should receive different handling.

options.label: C
options.text: Implement a parallelization workflow that runs the fixed checks as separate calls and aggregates the results.
options.feedback: This is correct because the work consists of fixed, independent checks whose results can be combined after execution. A workflow is appropriate because the code path is predefined, while running the checks separately can reduce wall-clock latency compared with a purely sequential design.

options.label: D
options.text: Implement an open-ended agent that decides which checks to run and which tools to use for each submission.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the required checks are known in advance and do not require Claude to dynamically direct the process. An agentic approach would add cost and latency tradeoffs without a clear benefit for this fixed review structure.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic distinguishes workflows from agents within the broader category of agentic systems. Workflows use predefined code paths to orchestrate LLMs and tools, while agents let the model dynamically decide its process and tool use. In this scenario, the review dimensions are known ahead of time and do not depend on each other, so the system does not need open-ended autonomy.

A parallelization workflow fits because the architecture can fan out the fixed checks, then aggregate their outputs into an editor-facing result. This preserves predictable structure while improving wall-clock latency when the checks can run independently. By contrast, a routing workflow would choose among different paths, and a single augmented LLM call with retrieval and examples would be simpler but would not directly exploit the independence of the checks.

The broader design principle is to start with the simplest architecture that meets the requirement, then add agentic autonomy only when the task benefits from dynamic planning. Anthropic's guidance in Building effective agents emphasizes this tradeoff because agentic systems can improve task performance but often increase latency and cost.

questions.question: A maritime insurance claims platform's incident-response team is troubleshooting a synchronous summarization service that calls the Messages API after placing scanned policy packets inline in the request body. Failures are consistently returned as 413 request_too_large when individual JSON payloads exceed 60 MB. Which operational change best addresses the failures?

options.label: A
options.text: Retry 413 responses with exponential backoff until the platform accepts the original payload.
options.feedback: A 413 response is not a transient rate-limit or server-overload condition. Retrying the same oversized payload adds operational noise and will not help unless the request body is changed.

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce or split inline content so each Messages API request remains within the endpoint request-size limit.
options.feedback: A 413 request_too_large response indicates that the request body exceeds the size limit for the endpoint being called. For the Messages API, the documented request-size limit is 32 MB, so the operational fix is to make each request smaller before sending it.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the same synchronous workload to the Batch API so larger request bodies are always accepted.
options.feedback: The Batch API has a different request-size limit, but it is a different endpoint and workflow from synchronous Messages API calls. It also has its own finite limit, so it is incorrect to treat it as accepting larger bodies unconditionally.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase max_tokens so Claude can process larger scanned packets before producing the summary.
options.feedback: The max_tokens setting controls the maximum generated output tokens, not the size of the HTTP request body. Increasing it does not make an oversized input payload acceptable to the Messages API.

questions.explanation:
For operational debugging, treat the HTTP status and error type as a signal about the failing layer. A 413 request_too_large points to request payload size, not model output length, rate limiting, or platform overload. The documented request-size limits are endpoint-specific: the Messages API and Token Counting API are limited to 32 MB, the Batch API to 256 MB, and the Files API to 500 MB. See the official Anthropic API errors documentation for the status and error-type mapping and the endpoint size limits.

The practical mental model is that the server must accept and parse the request before Claude can reason over its contents. If the body is too large, tuning generation parameters such as max_tokens does not address the problem. Retrying is useful for transient categories such as rate limits or 5xx failures when appropriate, but a deterministic oversized request should be reduced, split, or redesigned to use a suitable ingestion path.

When investigating production failures, teams should also preserve request identifiers from responses so support and engineering teams can correlate incidents. Rate-limit behavior is a separate category: 429 rate_limit_error uses rate-limit semantics such as retry-after, while 413 request_too_large requires changing the payload shape. The Anthropic rate limits documentation covers those rate-limit mechanics separately.

questions.question: A regional bank's credit operations team uses Claude to draft explanations for loan application decisions from policy documents and applicant records. A release changed both the prompt and model routing, and simple applications now go to a lower-cost model. Compliance reviewers now see unsupported denial reasons, inconsistent treatment of borderline income cases, and poorer explanations for applications with multiple applicants. Which action best diagnoses whether the regression is caused by prompt behavior, hallucination, or model fit?

options.label: A
options.text: Rewrite the prompt with stronger grounding instructions, then manually inspect a few recent reviewer complaints.
options.feedback: A prompt rewrite may eventually be useful, but it changes the system before the team has isolated the failure mode. A few manual examples are too narrow to distinguish prompt regressions from model routing issues or task-distribution gaps.

options.label: B
options.text: Route all applications to the highest-capability model, then monitor whether reviewers report fewer failures.
options.feedback: Using a stronger model may reduce some errors, but it does not diagnose whether the original problem was prompt behavior, hallucination, or routing. Reviewer reports alone are also a noisy and delayed signal compared with controlled evaluation.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a task-specific eval set with representative edge cases, then compare prompt and model variants using defined graders.
options.feedback: This directly separates likely causes by measuring the old and new prompt, routing policy, and model choices on the same representative cases. Including edge cases such as borderline income and multiple applicants helps determine whether failures are broad prompt issues, unsupported factual claims, or model-fit problems.

options.label: D
options.text: Require human approval for every generated explanation, then defer optimization until production feedback stabilizes.
options.feedback: Human approval is a risk-control measure, not a diagnostic method for identifying the technical source of regression. It may be appropriate for compliance workflows, but it does not provide a structured comparison of prompts, models, and edge cases.

questions.explanation:
When multiple changes ship together, the fastest path to a credible diagnosis is to hold the cases constant and vary the system components deliberately. Anthropic's evaluation guidance emphasizes starting with specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant success criteria, then building task-specific evals that reflect the real distribution and edge cases. In this scenario, unsupported denial reasons can be measured with groundedness or citation-style rubrics, inconsistent borderline decisions can be measured with paired or paraphrased cases, and model mismatch can be tested by running the same cases through each routing candidate.

The important engineering tradeoff is that ad hoc prompt edits and model upgrades can mask symptoms while leaving the cause unknown. A controlled eval set lets the team compare the previous release, the revised prompt, and each model route under the same grading rules, using code-based grading where possible and LLM-based grading only with tested rubrics for more nuanced judgments. This matches the documented evaluation workflow in Define success criteria and build evaluations, which recommends task-specific evals, automation where possible, and enough volume to cover edge cases rather than relying on a small set of manual anecdotes.

questions.question: A professional sports league's media operations group is designing Claude support for two workloads. One workload classifies millions of short broadcast clips into a fixed taxonomy for downstream search, with a tight per-clip budget and near-real-time indexing SLA. The other workload helps producers develop new story packages from interviews, statistics, and archival notes, where creative quality and staff leverage matter more than unit cost. Which TWO recommendations should the architect include?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the lowest-cost model configuration for both media workloads.
options.feedback: This may reduce classification costs, but it risks under-serving the producer workflow. Optimizing only for unit cost ignores the productivity and transformation value that can justify a more capable model.

options.label: B
options.text: Use a more capable model configuration for the producer ideation path.
options.feedback: This aligns model capability with the workload where quality, synthesis, and productivity gains create the most business value. Higher capability can be justified when the task is lower volume and the outcome depends on nuanced reasoning or creative transformation.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the highest-capability model configuration for both media workloads.
options.feedback: This may improve quality on the producer workflow, but it over-serves the fixed classification path. It weakens the cost and latency posture for a high-volume workload where simpler model choices may satisfy the SLA.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a lower-cost, faster model configuration for the clip classification path.
options.feedback: This aligns the high-volume classification workload with cost and latency goals. Model selection should account for capability, speed, and production cost rather than defaulting every path to the most capable option.

questions.explanation:
Architecture choices should map each Claude workload to the business value it is expected to deliver. A high-volume, fixed-taxonomy classification path is primarily constrained by cost, efficiency, and performance SLAs, so a faster, lower-cost model configuration is the natural starting point if evaluations show it meets quality requirements.

By contrast, the producer ideation workflow is less about raw throughput and more about productivity and transformation. When Claude must synthesize interviews, statistics, and archival material into useful creative directions, a more capable configuration can be worth the higher token cost because the business value comes from better expert leverage and higher-quality output.

The key design pattern is workload segmentation, not one-size-fits-all model selection. Anthropic's model guidance frames model choice as a tradeoff across capability, speed, and cost, and Anthropic's effort guidance describes effort as a lever for balancing intelligence, latency, and token consumption. See Models overview and Effort.

questions.question: An aerospace avionics software group is rolling out Claude Code observability to 2,000 engineers. Security leaders want fleet-wide dashboards for tool approvals and rejections, and audit reviewers want to investigate whether policy changes affected those decisions over time. Which monitoring strategy best supports this at scale?

options.label: A
options.text: Export Claude Code tool decision events and correlate them with a versioned permission configuration history.
options.feedback: This captures the documented permission decision events while preserving the configuration context needed for audits. Claude Code reports decision metadata such as tool name and source, but a config source does not identify the specific rule or policy that matched.

options.label: B
options.text: Parse config-sourced tool decision events to identify the exact allow or deny rule that matched.
options.feedback: This relies on detail that Claude Code does not expose in the event. A config source indicates the decision came from configuration, but it does not reveal the specific allow or deny rule, enterprise policy, flag, or permission mode.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude Code cost metrics to infer tool approval patterns across users and repositories.
options.feedback: Cost metrics are intended for trend and attribution analysis, not permission decision analysis. They also are approximations and should not be treated as the source of truth for detailed operational auditing.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable raw API body logging and reconstruct permission decisions from full conversation transcripts.
options.feedback: Raw API body logging is privacy-sensitive and off by default, and it can include the entire conversation history. It is not the right primary mechanism for scalable permission monitoring when Claude Code already emits tool decision events.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code observability is built on OpenTelemetry, and permission decisions are represented as events rather than as billing or usage aggregates. The documented claude_code.tool_decision event records accept or reject decisions, the tool identifier, the tool name, and a source such as config, hook, or a user approval category. See Anthropic's Claude Code monitoring usage documentation for the supported signals and event semantics.

The important architectural point is that telemetry should be treated as an observation stream, not as a complete policy database. When the source is config, Claude Code does not expose which exact permission rule, enterprise policy, command-line flag, or permission mode produced the decision. For auditability at scale, store and version the permission configuration separately, then correlate event timestamps, users, repositories, and deployed configuration versions during review.

Enabling broader content logging is not a substitute for structured observability. Prompt, response, tool detail, tool content, and raw API body logging are progressively more sensitive and disabled by default, with raw body logging able to include full conversation history. A mature monitoring design uses the narrowest signal that answers the operational question, then adds privacy-sensitive content only when policy and investigation needs justify it.

questions.question: An international humanitarian nonprofit's grants operations group is piloting a Claude workflow that drafts donor compliance summaries. Program officers, legal reviewers, and finance leaders disagree about acceptable fidelity, privacy handling, tone, response time, and per-summary cost. The grants director wants a launch commitment before the next funding cycle. Which TWO actions best align expectations and keep the feedback loop useful before launch?

options.label: A
options.text: Commit to a single availability target and defer quality concerns to post-launch escalation tickets.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it narrows the commitment to one operational dimension while the stated disagreement spans quality, privacy, tone, latency, and cost. Escalations can help after launch, but they do not establish shared expectations before stakeholders depend on the workflow.

options.label: B
options.text: Run stakeholder reviews against the agreed criteria on pilot cases and adjust launch targets from the results.
options.feedback: This is correct because a feedback loop is useful only if reviewers evaluate the same outputs against shared standards. Using pilot results to refine targets helps make the eventual service commitment evidence-based rather than aspirational.

options.label: C
options.text: Define specific, measurable acceptance criteria across fidelity, privacy handling, tone, latency, and per-summary cost.
options.feedback: This is correct because stakeholder feedback needs to be translated into criteria that can be tested and discussed consistently. A multidimensional set of criteria also prevents one stakeholder's preference, such as speed or cost, from silently overriding quality or privacy needs.

options.label: D
options.text: Route all requests to the most capable model and treat higher capability as resolving stakeholder disagreements.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because model choice alone does not define what acceptable performance means for the organization. A more capable model might improve some outcomes, but it does not replace measurable criteria or a stakeholder review process.

questions.explanation:
Expectation alignment for a Claude deployment should begin by turning vague goals into measurable success criteria. Anthropic's evaluation guidance emphasizes criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and it explicitly includes dimensions such as task fidelity, consistency, relevance, tone, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency, and price. See Define success criteria.

In practice, an SLA or launch commitment should be downstream of this agreement. If stakeholders disagree about what matters, the architect should create a shared rubric, review representative pilot outputs against it, and use the results to set realistic targets. A single availability or latency target is not enough when the workflow's acceptability also depends on fidelity, privacy, tone, and cost. Similarly, choosing a larger model may be part of an optimization decision later, but it does not by itself create an aligned feedback loop or a defensible service commitment.

questions.question: A specialty chemicals manufacturer's regulatory affairs team is redesigning a Claude workflow that reviews 80-page safety dossiers and drafts a narrative compliance memo. The workflow is maintained in Claude Console before API deployment. Each run includes fixed corporate review rules, variable product data, retrieved standards excerpts, and a reviewer’s question. The team wants better consistency and long-document performance, but does not require guaranteed JSON schema compliance. Which prompt design change best fits documented guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a Console prompt template that keeps fixed review rules in the top-level system field, wraps variable materials in XML tags, and places the reviewer’s question after the long dossier.
options.feedback: This keeps startup instructions in the appropriate top-level system field and uses Claude Console variables for run-specific content. XML structure helps Claude distinguish instructions, context, and inputs, while placing the query after long documents aligns with long-context prompting guidance.

options.label: B
options.text: Put the fixed review rules as the first system entry in messages, paste retrieved standards into later system messages, and place the reviewer’s question before the dossier.
options.feedback: Initial system instructions normally belong in the top-level system field, and a system message cannot be the first entry in messages. Retrieved or third-party content should not be elevated into system content because system content is treated as operator instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Add stricter wording that Claude must follow the memo layout, put all source documents after the reviewer’s question, and omit examples to reduce prompt length.
options.feedback: Clear instructions help, but this misses stronger documented practices for long-context and format consistency. For long documents, Anthropic recommends placing the long inputs near the top and the query near the end, and few-shot examples are a reliable way to steer structure.

options.label: D
options.text: Build the reusable workflow in claude.ai with double-bracket variables, remove XML wrappers around the inputs, and rely only on examples to control the memo structure.
options.feedback: Claude Console supports prompt templates and variables, but the documentation states that claude.ai currently does not support prompt templates or variables. Examples are useful for steering format and tone, but removing structure around mixed inputs makes the prompt easier to misinterpret.

questions.explanation:
The best design separates fixed operator instructions from variable run content. Initial rules that apply from the start should go in the top-level system field, while product data, retrieved excerpts, and the reviewer’s question can be represented as template variables in Claude Console using {{double_brackets}}. See the Messages guidance on system prompts in Working with messages and the Console template guidance in Prompting tools.

For a long dossier workflow, prompt layout is part of the architecture. Anthropic recommends putting long documents or inputs near the top of the prompt and the query near the end, especially for complex multi-document inputs, and using descriptive XML tags so Claude can distinguish instructions, context, examples, and user inputs. The prompt engineering documentation also recommends relevant, diverse, structured examples when you want consistent format, tone, or structure. See System prompts for the XML, examples, and long-context guidance.

questions.question: A medical device manufacturer's postmarket surveillance team is building a Claude workflow to summarize support cases that may contain PHI. The production integration will call the Claude API from an Anthropic organization that has a signed BAA and is HIPAA-enabled. QA wants to reproduce production failures by pasting the same cases into Console/Workbench, while security argues the project cannot launch unless Zero Data Retention is also enabled. Which recommendation best aligns the architecture with the documented compliance boundaries?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep PHI workloads on the HIPAA-enabled Claude API path, use de-identified cases in Console/Workbench, and treat ZDR as separate from HIPAA readiness.
options.feedback: This keeps regulated data in the API environment covered by the HIPAA-ready setup and avoids using Console/Workbench for PHI processing. HIPAA readiness for the Claude API depends on the BAA and HIPAA-enabled organization, while ZDR is a separate retention feature rather than a prerequisite for PHI workloads.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the workflow to Amazon Bedrock, apply Anthropic's API retention settings, and use Console/Workbench only for failed cases.
options.feedback: For Amazon Bedrock, the cloud provider is the data processor, so Anthropic's API retention controls for api.anthropic.com do not govern that use. Using Console/Workbench for failed cases would still introduce a separate excluded surface for sensitive production data.

options.label: C
options.text: Accept the Commercial Terms for SCC coverage, process PHI in a non-HIPAA sandbox, and enable ZDR after launch if needed.
options.feedback: The DPA and SCCs address data processing and international transfer terms, not HIPAA readiness for PHI workloads. A non-HIPAA sandbox would not become appropriate for PHI merely because ZDR might be enabled later.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable ZDR for the production organization, test PHI cases in Console/Workbench, and rely on the BAA for production API traffic.
options.feedback: ZDR is enabled per organization, but enabling it for the production organization does not make excluded surfaces appropriate for PHI processing. Console/Workbench processing is not covered by the same eligible API feature boundary for PHI handling, so pasting real PHI there would not align with the documented exclusions.

questions.explanation:
For PHI workloads, the key architectural boundary is where the data is processed. Anthropic documents HIPAA-ready Claude API integrations for organizations with a signed BAA and a HIPAA-enabled organization, and it distinguishes that from Zero Data Retention, which is a retention configuration rather than a HIPAA prerequisite. QA should therefore reproduce issues with de-identified or synthetic cases in surfaces such as Console/Workbench instead of moving real PHI outside the eligible API path.

ZDR is valuable when an organization needs eligible prompts and responses not stored at rest after the API response is returned, but it is not universal. It must be enabled per organization and does not automatically apply across other organizations under the same account. The documented retention boundary also changes when Claude is accessed through third-party platforms, because for Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry, the cloud provider is the data processor and its controls must be reviewed.

GDPR and transfer documentation are a different compliance concern. Anthropic states that its DPA with SCCs is automatically incorporated into the Commercial Terms for commercial products such as Claude API, but accepting those terms does not substitute for HIPAA scoping or for keeping PHI out of excluded product surfaces. See Anthropic's API and data retention documentation and the DPA guidance at How do I view and sign your Data Processing Addendum (DPA)?.

questions.question: A city transit agency's digital services team is building a Claude feature that answers rider questions using current route schedules, fare rules, and service alerts. The supported questions follow a narrow answer format, require no actions in external systems, and early evaluation shows that a single model call with retrieved policy snippets meets the team's accuracy target. Leadership is considering a more autonomous design because it sounds more flexible. Which architectural choice best fits the stated constraints?

options.label: A
options.text: Use an orchestrator-workers workflow for every rider question.
options.feedback: An orchestrator-workers workflow is a workflow pattern for coordinating multiple worker tasks under an orchestrator. Nothing in the scenario indicates that each question needs decomposition across several specialized workers.

options.label: B
options.text: Use a prompt chaining workflow with multiple required LLM stages.
options.feedback: Prompt chaining fits tasks that decompose cleanly into fixed subtasks where each stage feeds the next. The described feature already meets quality targets with one grounded call, so adding stages would be avoidable complexity.

options.label: C
options.text: Use an agent that dynamically chooses tools and investigation steps.
options.feedback: An agent is useful when the model must decide its own process and tool use based on intermediate results. The scenario does not require autonomous action selection, and the added flexibility would likely add unnecessary latency and cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Use an augmented LLM with retrieval and representative in-context examples.
options.feedback: This is the simplest architecture that satisfies the stated need. It uses the model with relevant context and examples without adding orchestration that would increase latency and cost.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic distinguishes workflows, where LLMs and tools follow predefined code paths, from agents, where the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use. The practical design principle is to start with the simplest solution that satisfies the task, because more agentic systems can improve performance on some problems but usually trade off latency and cost.

Here, the task is narrow, grounded question answering with a stable response shape and no external actions. An augmented LLM, meaning an LLM enhanced with retrieval, tools, or memory, is the right foundational pattern when retrieved context and examples are enough. Prompt chaining, orchestrator-workers, and fully autonomous agents are better reserved for cases where the task genuinely needs fixed multi-stage decomposition, coordinated subtasks, or dynamic decision-making.

For the underlying architectural distinction and the recommendation to prefer simple designs before adding agentic complexity, see Anthropic's engineering guidance on Building effective agents.
